As the verse in the first chapter, the "Introduction," states:
A single segment of radiance—when the eyebrows are raised, it is instantly brilliant.
It is only because one does not see for oneself that one is pitied by others. Maitreya feigns halting his horse; Mañjuśrī falsely applies the whip.
If you wish to take this up yourself, do not depart from the very edge of the eye.

"Preface" (*xu*) means "source" (*you*) and "beginning" (*shi*). It refers to the causal origins from which the teaching is set forth and the gradual commencement from which the ritual practice arises.

Furthermore, "preface" (*xu*) means "thread" (*xu*). Just as a silkworm cocoon yields all its silk once the thread is found, so too does a sutra reveal its entire purport once the preface is attained.
Therefore, although this chapter serves as the prologue to the entire scripture, it in fact encompasses the whole work.
Because it marks the beginning and end [of this teaching], it is simply titled the "Introductory Chapter. Within it, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* is expounded;

the Buddha enters the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings, whereupon the heavens rain down four kinds of flowers, the earth quakes in six ways, and a single ray of light from between his eyebrows manifests the signs of the ten realms.

Thereupon, Maitreya raises his doubts and Mañjuśrī provides the definitive answers. From the origin to the conclusion, this constitutes the fundamental intention for the appearance of all Buddhas in the world.

He has disclosed everything completely, leaving no further residue. As for the remaining three cycles of teaching—namely, those on Expedient Means, Parables, and Causes and Conditions, up to the manifestation of the jeweled stupa, the gathering of the emanated bodies, the emergence of the bodhisattvas, and the discourse on the Lifespan—these are all included therein.
There is nothing that does not simply clarify the matters manifested within the light; there is no other path. "Pin" (品) means category.
By classifying meanings and types, the title of the chapter is established. It is placed at the beginning of the entire scripture and is designated as the "First."
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats.

"Thus" (*evam*) is a term that points to the Dharma. "Such a Dharma as this, I have heard from the Buddha" indicates that there is a transmission of the realized Dharma and that it was not spoken by oneself.
From "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) onwards, the time, place, and audience of the teaching are set forth.
In the Sanskrit language, *Rājagṛha* is called "King’s House City. The name of the country is *Magadha*, which means "Not [Ignorant]."
It is called "Harmful" because there is no execution or killing. It is also called Magadha; this translates as "Heavenly Net," which is the name of the king.
The country is named after its king. This king was the father of King Pāṇḍupāda. Since remote kalpas, this king has ruled over a thousand kingdoms.
While the king was touring the mountains, he encountered a female lion. The people fled in all directions, yet she mated with the king. Later, when her months were full...
He came and gave birth to a son within the palace. The king, knowing him to be his own son, spread the word: "I have no children; this is a gift from Heaven. He was raised as the crown prince.
His feet were mottled with spots, so the people of the time called him Pāṇḍupāda (Spotted-foot). Later, he succeeded to the royal throne.

He took extreme delight in eating meat and constantly commanded his cooks that there should never be a shortage. Once, by chance, meat was lacking, so he took a recently deceased young child from the west of the city to serve as a meal.
The king remarked that it was "exceedingly delicious" and commanded, "This meat must be prepared every day.

The cooks then captured one person daily for his meal, causing the entire kingdom to be filled with grief and terror. Consequently, a thousand minor kings raised armies, deposed the king, and installed [a new ruler].
In Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, there was a king of the rākṣasas who ruled as sovereign over the mountain. He had made a vow with the mountain deity to sacrifice a thousand kings to the mountain.
He had already captured nine hundred and ninety-nine, lacking only King Viśvaprakāśa. Later, while on watch, he seized him.
The king wept bitterly, lamenting that although he had lived by the truth since birth, he had now violated his word. The spotted-footed one released him.
Puming returned to his kingdom, performed great acts of charity, and installed his crown prince. He then came back to face his death; his countenance was joyful and his mind at peace.

When Panzu questioned him, he replied, "I have been able to hear the Holy Dharma. Panzu then ordered him to preach it. [Puming] extensively praised the mind of compassion and reviled the act of killing, subsequently reciting verses on impermanence.
Upon hearing these, Panzu immediately realized the first stage (bhūmi). Each of the thousand kings then took [a portion of the remains].
A drop of blood. Three strands of hair. A vow to the mountain deity. Spotted-foot (Pāṇḍu) and the thousand kings together established the city of Rājagṛha.

They made it their capital among the five mountains, and it remained a great kingdom. Each of the thousand minor kings entrusted his own kingdom to his son and took turns governing the affairs of the great kingdom;
therefore, it is called "King’s Abode" (Rājagṛha). It is also said that when Spotted-foot attained the Way, he granted amnesty to the thousand kings. The thousand kings...
Because he was pardoned in that place, it is called "King’s Pardon" (Rājakārāma); however, the compilers of the sūtras borrowed this name as a synonym for "dwelling.

Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain is translated here as "Spiritual Vulture Peak," so named because its peaks have the shape of vultures. On this mountain there are five vihāras: first, the Cave of the Lord of Devas;
second, the Seven-Leaf Cave; third, the Cave of the Nāga Spirit; fourth, the Lesser Solitary [Cave]; [and fifth, the Great Solitary Cave].

The Mountain of Power (*Balaparvata*). The fifth is Gṛdhrakūṭa. Regarding the "great assembly of bhikṣus": their capacity and measure are noble and supreme, surpassing all non-Buddhists, and they are revered by the Lord of Devas;
therefore, they are called "great. As for "bhikṣu," in the language of Qin (Chinese) it means "pure livelihood" (*viśuddhājīva*).

[The term] "begging for food" (*piṇḍapāta*), "destroying afflictions" (*kleśabheda*), "being able to maintain the precepts" (*śīladhara*), and "frightening Māra" (*māravidrāvaṇa*)—these four meanings are contained within the single Indian name. Therefore, [the original term] is retained.
Regarding the title "Assembly" (衆): the Sanskrit term is *saṃgha*, which translates here as "harmonious assembly. A single person is not called a harmonious assembly;
only those numbering three or more are termed a harmonious assembly. As for the term "Arhat," it also contains three meanings:

because "my births have been exhausted and I shall not undergo further existence," they are called "non-arising" (*anutpāda*); because the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted, [they are called "worthy of offerings"].

He is named "Slayer of the Thieves" (Arhat) because he possesses the virtues of wisdom and abandonment, and is worthy of being a field of merit for humans and devas; thus he is named "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).
Containing these three meanings, he also retains his original title.

"All outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted; there are no further afflictions (*kleśa*). Having attained one's own benefit, all fetters of existence (*bhavasaṃyojana*) are ended, and the mind has attained mastery.

This is a praise of his virtues. Regarding "all outflows," there are three outflows: namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

All cravings within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are called the outflow of desire; cravings in the two higher realms are called the outflow of existence; and ignorance throughout the three realms is called the outflow of ignorance.
"Outflows" (*āsrava*) refer to the two delusions of views and thought. "Various fetters of existence" refers to the fetter of desire, the fetter of existence, and the fetter of ignorance.

They are called "outflows" when speaking in terms of the fruit, because they cause one to leak and fall into birth and death; they are called "fetters" when speaking in terms of the cause, because they bind and continue the process of rebirth.
What is now meant by "severing afflictions and exhausting outflows and fetters" is that the cause is extinguished and the fruit is lost.
Furthermore, those who have attained their own benefit alone emerge from the three realms and do not wish to deliver sentient beings; thus, they deviate from the myriad virtues.
Those whose minds have attained mastery indulge in the bliss of nirvana and do not seek the Buddha-way; thus, the fruit lacks perfection and permanence.
These are what the Gate of the Patriarchs calls "a crane standing amidst withered pines," "a drop of water freezing on a droplet," or "one sitting atop a hundred-foot pole."

Their names were Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana, Aniruddha, Kapphiṇa, Gavāmpati, Revata, Pilindavatsa, and Bakula.
Mahākauṣṭhila, Nanda, Sundarananda, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Ānanda, Rāhula— such great arhats, renowned among the masses, and others like them.
This is his personal name; Kātyāyana is his clan name, which translates as "Fire-Vessel. His ancestors served fire, and it was from this that their lineage derived its name.
"Ajñāta" translates as "First Understanding," because he was the very first among those on Jambudvīpa to attain the Way.
In the past, during a time of famine, the Buddha transformed himself into a large red-eyed fish; he held his breath without gasping, manifesting the appearance of death. [The wood...]
There were five craftsmen who had previously used axes to hack away at his flesh. At that time, the Buddha made a vow, saying: "In a future age, I shall deliver these individuals first;
my primary wish is to grant them the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*). For this reason, he was named Ājñāta. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Within my Buddha-dharma, as for those who are broad-minded, compassionate, and widely learned, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya is foremost among those who were the first to receive the flavor of the Dharma."
Mahākāśyapa—here translated as "Great Kauruṣya"—was a descendant of those who practiced the Way in ancient times. A divine tortoise appeared bearing the charts of the immortals;
because his lineage was named after this virtue, he was also called "Drinking Light" (Kāśyapa), for the radiance of his body outshone all other things.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (or *Dharma-piṭaka*), after the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a goldsmith who, because the golden color of a stūpa image had become tarnished and damaged, at that time...
There was a poor woman who obtained a gold bead by begging. She requested a goldsmith to adorn it for her;

the goldsmith was delighted, and when the work of polishing and embellishing was complete, he made a vow to become her husband without marriage. For ninety-one kalpas, throughout human and celestial realms, their bodies were constantly golden in color.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among those who practice the dhūta austerities within my Buddha-dharma, Mahākāśyapa is foremost.
Uruvilvā is translated as "Pumpkin Grove" (*bimbara-vana*); he resided there because he lived in reliance upon that grove.

Nadi is translated as "River," and Gayā is translated as "City. These three brothers all served the sacrificial fire. During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, they together firmly set up the sacrificial pillar.
On account of this, they became brothers. The elder brother was the preceptor of King Bimbisāra and had five hundred disciples; each of the two younger brothers had two hundred and fifty.
They practiced the teachings of their elder brother. The Buddha performed ten kinds of miraculous transformations to convert them:

namely, that he was not harmed by a venomous dragon, was not burned by the dragon’s fire, was not drowned in the Ganges River, and took fruit from three directions while taking rice from here [the human realm], as well as from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

He took the ambrosia; knowing [the king] was dissatisfied, he vanished; knowing [the king] was mindful [of him], he appeared. The fire was extinguished yet flared up again; the axe was raised but would not descend.
He manifested many such auspicious responses (*prātihārya*). Although the king witnessed these various transformations, his perverse attachments remained unaltered.

He spoke again, saying: "Though Gautama possesses supernatural powers, they do not equal the truth of my Way. The Buddha then said to him: "You are not an Arhat, nor have you attained the Way. Suddenly, [his delusions] were cleared away.
They attained enlightenment, and both master and disciples were subdued. His two younger brothers also followed him in returning to the Buddha, and they became one thousand bhikṣus.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among the bhikṣus, Uruvilvā is foremost in being able to protect the fourfold assembly and provide them with the four requisites so that they lack for nothing.
Nadi is foremost in having a tranquil mind, subduing all fetters, and practicing with diligence."
First: The bhikṣu Gayā was foremost in contemplating all dharmas and realizing that they are entirely without attachment;

he was most excellent in skillfully teaching and transforming others. ○ Śāriputra is translated as "Body-Son" (Shenzi). This is because his mother possessed a beautiful body, and he was born from her body.
A sutra states: In the past, a maternal uncle and nephew were both weavers. Knowing of the king’s treasure storehouse, they dug into the earth to steal it.
He obtained a great quantity of precious treasures. The treasurer informed the king, who said, "Do not let it be known. The thief soon arrived; the king waited in ambush and seized him.
The nephew then ordered his uncle to enter [the city] again. Having been captured, the nephew feared he would be recognized by others, so he immediately decapitated his uncle.
The king ordered that the corpse be placed at a crossroads and summoned the nephew’s kinsmen. Later, because a crowd of merchants had gathered there in a noisy commotion...
The nephew covered it with firewood; the king continued to watch for an opportunity to seize it. Again, taking advantage of children playing and dancing, he threw fire upon it to burn it.
Furthermore, he provided wine for the watchers to drink until they were deeply intoxicated; he then placed the bones inside a wine bottle and departed.
The king, vexed by his craftiness, sent out a woman to entice him. He strictly guarded the water’s edge and instructed his daughter, saying: "When anyone comes—"
He was summoned. That floating tree-trunk was in the water; the guards thought it was a person, but upon looking at it, they saw it was a trunk.

For several days they remained unprepared, and because of this, he managed to come and have intercourse with the woman. The woman seized his garment, but he immediately handed her the hand of a corpse and departed.
The woman cried out loudly and looked at it; it was indeed the hand of a corpse. Consequently, she became pregnant and gave birth to a son who was handsome. The King ordered—
The wet nurse carried him out; those who heard his crying seized him. One day, they went beneath a bread-baking oven, and the baker gave him a cake while he cried.
The king ordered him to be carried out again, so the wet nurse was made drunk with strong wine and departed, carrying the child with her.
He departed for another country. The people of that country admired his plans and wished to give him the daughter of their chief minister in marriage, but he did not consent.
Consequently, they gave him the name "The Child. He was then betrothed to the daughter of the king of his own country, and the king granted his permission.

The king, however, suspected him of being the former thief and sent five hundred horsemen, all equipped with saddles, horses, and clothing identical to his own, to go and welcome the bride. At that time, the king of his own country recognized him as...
The former thief was praised for his craftiness and deceit, and the king gave him his daughter in marriage.
At that time, the nephew was Śāriputra, and the uncle was Devadatta. The two nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, protected the city of Rājagṛha;
they sent down rain in due season, so that there were no years of famine in the land. Consequently, the king and the people established a great assembly every year, arranging three high seats.
The Master of Treatises was seated as the Crown Prince. At that time, Śāriputra was eight years old; he went to the assembly hall and asked people about the three seats.
When they answered him fully, he immediately bypassed the crowd and ascended the debate dais. All the Confucian scholars were ashamed and refused to engage in debate with him.
Everyone said, "To defeat this boy would not be sufficient to bring us renown; if we fail him, the humiliation would be great.

They all dispatched their attendants to convey their greetings and inquire after him. His answers surpassed their questions and expressed his own excellence, completely demolishing all their banners such that none dared to face him.
By the time he was sixteen years old, he had thoroughly mastered the secular classics and was proficient in every field of learning.
Among the sixteen great nations, his erudition and debate were peerless; he was the foremost in the five regions of India. Later, while traveling on the road, he encountered Aśvajit.
His deportment was dignified and orderly. He then inquired about the Teacher’s Dharma, to which [the monk] replied: "All phenomena arise from conditions; they likewise cease because of conditions.
This is what my teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, constantly proclaims. Upon hearing this verse, he immediately attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
He went to where the Buddha was, and within seven days, he thoroughly mastered the profound ocean of the Buddha-Dharma. On the fifteenth day, he attained Arhatship.

Han-guo (Anuruddha) was the preceptor of Rāhula. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Within my Buddha-dharma, Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom that is inexhaustible and in decisively resolving matters without doubt.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana is translated as "radish" (*laifukgen*) and also as "pea" (*hudou*).
These two items were the favorites of ancient seers, and thus they named their clan after them. In the past, he once assisted a Pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha shaved his head, washed, dyed, and sewed his *kāṣāya*, and made a vow to attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Formerly, a group of five hundred non-Buddhist teachers and disciples used incantations to move a mountain; after a month had passed, the mountain had already begun to tremble.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "If this mountain moves, much harm will be done. He then sat cross-legged in the air above the summit of the mountain. The mountain—
It remained unmoved. The non-Buddhists said to one another, "The mountain of our doctrine has moved; we calculated that it would surely shift by now.
Why does it not move? This must be the work of the śramaṇa. Realizing their own power was weak, they turned their hearts toward the Buddha’s Way.
The two nāgas Nanda and Upananda dwell in the ocean at the edge of Mount Sumeru. Whenever the Buddha flies through the air to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven palace, the two nāgas become enraged.
[The Nāgas] felt resentment, saying: "How is it that this shaven-headed man has passed over us?

Later, when the Buddha wished to ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the two nāgas exhaled black clouds and dark mists, obscuring the three luminaries. All the bhikṣus desired to subdue them, but the Buddha did not permit it.
Maudgalyāyana said, "I am able to subdue this dragon. The dragon coiled its body seven times around Mount Sumeru;
its tail lashed at the ocean waters, and its head rested upon the mountain peak. Maudgalyāyana manifested his body to double its size, coiling fourteen times around the mountain;
his tail extended beyond the outer seas, and his head rested upon the Brahma palace. The dragon’s anger intensified, and it rained down vajra-sand. Maudgalyāyana transformed the sand into jewels.

The flowers were light, soft, and lovely; yet the dragon’s anger did not cease. Maudgalyāyana transformed his body into a minute form and entered the dragon’s body, passing from its eye and exiting through its ear, then entering through its ear and exiting through its nose. He gnawed and bit at its body, causing it to suffer intense pain.
Only then did the dragon submit. Maudgalyāyana withdrew both his massive and minute forms, assumed the appearance of a śramaṇa, and led these two dragons to the Buddha.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among my disciples, as for those who possess supernatural powers and can fly light as a feather to the ten directions, Maudgalyāyana is the foremost.

Mahākātyāyana is translated here as "Textual Ornament" (*Wénshì*). The *Dīrgha Āgama* records that there was a non-Buddhist who held the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), asserting that there is no future world. [Kātyāyana] replied: "Are the sun and moon of today for this world alone? or... [text fragment].
Regarding the other world: if there were no other world, there would be no tomorrow. Furthermore, it is said: "I see people die and not return;
how can one say they undergo suffering? Therefore, we know there is no other world. Answer: Suppose a criminal is detained; could he ever return [to his former life]? Furthermore, it is said:
"If one is born in the heavens, why does one not return? Therefore, we know there is no other world. Answer: It is like a person...
Suppose one has fallen into a latrine and managed to escape; would you be willing to enter it again? Furthermore, one day in heaven corresponds to a hundred years here on earth.

If one is born there for three or five days, one will have no leisure to turn the mind toward the Way. Even if one were to return, by then your body would have already been transformed; how could you know of it?
It is also said that when sinners are boiled in cauldrons, the lids are sealed tight so that even if one waits, one cannot see their spirits emerge. Therefore...
[The opponent] says, "I know there is no other world. [The Master] replies, "When you sleep during the day, do those standing beside you see your spirit depart?
He further says, "I have flayed the skin of the dead, cut their flesh into pieces, and crushed their bones, yet I could not find the spirit. Therefore, I know there is no other world."
Answer: It is like a child splitting firewood; if one were to split it into inch-long pieces and seek fire therein, could fire ever be found?
Furthermore, he said: "I weighed a dead man and he was even heavier. If the spirit had departed, he should have been lighter. If no spirit departs, then there should be no other world."
Answer: It is like iron that becomes light when combined with fire, but becomes heavy once it loses the fire. When a person possesses the spirit (*śen*), they are light;
when a person dies and loses the spirit, they become heavy. Furthermore, I have seen people at the point of death who, turning back, sought their spirit but could not find it.

"Therefore, one knows that there is no other world. [The opponent] replies: "It is like a person who, seeking the sound of a conch shell, turns it upside down; would he ever obtain the sound? He further says:
"Though you refute me in various ways, my attachment to the self has persisted for so long that I cannot abandon it. [The proponent] replies: "It is like a person gathering hemp.
At first, seeing the hemp plant, he takes the hemp; next, he discards the hemp and takes the bark; next, he discards the bark and takes the fibers; next..."
One discards the thread to take the cloth; next, one discards the cloth to take the silk; next, one discards the silk to take the silver; next, one discards the silver to take the gold.
Discarding the inferior to take the superior—how could this not be possible? Furthermore, it is said: "It is not only I who speak thus;
all people speak likewise. Why do you claim that I am wrong? The answer is: It is like two merchants who encounter a ghost. The ghost appears as a human being...
Xing said, "The road ahead has plenty of rice and sufficient fodder; why load these? One merchant immediately discarded them.
Upon reaching the road ahead, both man and ox were hungry and were devoured by ghosts. Another merchant said, "If we obtain fresh grass and rice..."
Therefore, the old grain and straw may be discarded; neither humans nor oxen will be eaten by ghosts. Such false claims made by people are like the deceptive words of a ghost:
"If you do not accept my words, it is as if you refuse to discard the old grain and straw. Now that you have obtained the new, why do you not discard the old?
Furthermore, they say, "I cannot give them up; if you urge me to do so, I will become angry. The answer is: You are like a pig farmer on the road.
He encountered some excrement; he took it up with his head and carried it back. On the road, he encountered rain, and the liquid dripped down, soiling his head.
A bystander told him to discard it, but he instead grew angry at the one who had advised him. In this manner, through successive refutations, the non-Buddhists were finally subdued.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "In skillfully discerning meanings and expounding the Dharma, Kātyāyana is foremost. ○ Aniruddha: This is translated as "Free from Poverty."
In the past, during an era of famine, he offered millet porridge to a pratyekabuddha. For ninety-one kalpas, his karmic retribution was fully satisfied;
thus he was named Akiṃcana (The One Without Poverty). The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:

During a time of famine in the final dharma-period of Puṣya Buddha, there was a pratyekabuddha named Liṭa who went begging but returned with an empty bowl, having obtained nothing. A poor man saw this and was moved by compassion, saying:
He asked, "Can you eat this coarse grain? The man replied, "I can. He then offered him what he had been eating.

After he had finished eating, [the ascetic] performed the eighteen transformations and departed. Later, when the man went out to gather more grain, a rabbit hopped onto his back and transformed into a dead man.

He attained liberation without a companion. Waiting for darkness, he returned home and laid the rabbit on the ground; it immediately became a man made of gold. As he pulled out a finger, another grew in its place;
as he took a foot, yet another emerged. He used them without end. When wicked men and evil kings came wishing to seize them, they saw only corpses;
yet what he beheld was entirely pure gold and treasure. Therefore, he was called "The One Without Poverty" (Aparājita). It is also said that in the past, he was a *kṣatriya*...
A thief entered a Buddhist temple to steal property; as the Buddha’s lamp was about to go out, Aniruddha prodded it with an arrow.
Seeing the Buddha, his hair stood on end, and he thought to himself: "If others would even renounce their possessions, how could I steal? He then abandoned his intent and departed.

By this cause and condition, he attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) that sees through all things. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "In my Dharma, those who possess the divine eye that penetrates all sights [are as follows...]"
Aniruddha was foremost [among those with divine vision]. He was the second son of King Droṇodana. ○ Kapphiṇa is translated as "Lunar Mansion" (Hángxiù).
His parents prayed to the mansion-star (Kṛttikā) before he was born. He was skilled in calculating the stars and planets and clearly understood celestial diagrams;
he derived his name from his proficiency in these matters. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "In my Buddha-dharma, the one most skilled in calculating the stars, planets, sun, and moon is Kapphiṇa."
1. Furthermore, when he first went forth, wishing to go to where the Buddha was, he encountered rain at night and took up lodging in a potter’s workshop, using grass as his seat.
Another bhikṣu also followed him later seeking lodging; [the elder] immediately pushed the grass over to give it to him.
He sat down on the spot. Later, during the middle watch of the night, another bhikṣu asked him, "Where do you wish to go? He replied, "I am seeking the Buddha.
The other bhikṣu then preached the Dharma for him, and he suddenly attained the Way. This latter bhikṣu was none other than the Buddha himself;

because he had shared a room and stayed together with that [other bhikṣu], he was able to behold the Dharmakāya, and thus he was named Fangsu (Room-Constellation). This is based on the place where he attained the Way.
He received this name. ○ Kauṇḍinya (Kiao-fan-po-ti). This translates as "ox-chewer" or "ox-track. In the past, for five hundred lifetimes, he was a bull king.
After the oxen had finished eating, he would constantly engage in empty chewing. Because the residual karmic retribution was not yet exhausted, he continued to chew and gulp incessantly.
Therefore, he is named Gomukha (the Ox-Chewer). People merely observe his outward form and do not recognize his virtue. If one mocks an Arhat with contempt, one incurs great sin.
Because he avoided such human offenses, he constantly dwells in the heavens; for the devas know of his virtue and do not mock his appearance. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Those who delight in the heavens and do not delight in the human realm are the foremost among the 'ox-track' bhikṣus."
1. Revata (also called Revata). This is translated as "Provisional Union. The *Śāstra* states:

While staying overnight in an empty pavilion, he saw two ghosts contending over a corpse. He was asked to adjudicate the matter; yet whether he followed logic or yielded to injustice, neither would have escaped harm.
He therefore answered according to the facts. The great ghost tore off his hands and feet, while the small ghost took the corpse to replace them, and then ate him.
He wiped his mouth with his hand and departed. Because of this affliction, he could not discern whose body it was; he consequently began to doubt from where this body had come.
"If it is my own body," he thought, "I see with my own eyes that it has been pulled out. If it is another's body, it follows me wherever I go or stay.
Due to these doubts, whenever he encountered someone, he would ask, "Do you see my body? The monks said, "This person is easy to deliver."
He then said, "This body was originally the discarded remains of another; it does not belong to oneself. Thereupon, he attained the Way.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among those who sit in meditation and enter *dhyāna*, such that their minds are not distracted or confused, the bhikṣu Revata is foremost.
Piliṅgaputra (Bilengqieposuo) is translated as "Residual Habit. Having been a Brahmin for five hundred lifetimes, although he had attained the Way...
Although she had attained the fruit [of arhatship], her residual habits remained prominent. As she crossed the Ganges River, she said to the river deity, "Hey, you little slave!

Stop the current! The river deity parted the waters for her. The deity went to report this to the Buddha, who instructed her to offer an apology. She immediately joined her palms and said, "Little slave, do not be angry.
The assembly laughed and said, "She apologizes and yet insults him further. The Buddha said, "Her fundamental habit is such; in truth, she has no pride."
Regarding the mind: The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that among those who sit in austerity beneath trees, avoiding neither wind nor rain, Vatsa is foremost.
○ Bakula (translated as "Good Appearance" because his physical features were upright and handsome) was once a poor man during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from a headache; the Venerable One, having previously been a pauper, offered him a harītakī fruit.
His illness was cured. Because of his gift of fruit, for ninety-one kalpas he enjoyed happiness and prosperity among gods and humans, never once suffering from illness.
In his final birth, he was born into a brahmin family; his mother died early, and his father took a second wife.
Being young, Kula saw his stepmother making cakes and followed her to ask for some. The stepmother, filled with hatred and resentment, immediately drove Kula away.
He was thrown onto a griddle; though the griddle was red-hot, it could not burn or harm him. Later, when his mother boiled meat, Kuṇāla again asked for some.
His mother became even more enraged; she then threw him into a cauldron, yet he could not be cooked. Later, when his mother went toward the river, Kuṇāla followed her.

She immediately threw him into the water, where a large fish swallowed him. When the fish was caught and brought to the market, he encountered his father, who bought it and returned home. At that time—
When the belly of the fish was opened, Kulla was still alive. He calmly told his father, "Please do not harm your son.
When the father saw his son, he emerged joyfully. Having grown up, he left the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship.

At one hundred and sixty years of age, he delighted in tranquility, always dwelling in seclusion and taking no pleasure in the midst of crowds; even regarding the stūpa of his relics, he preferred solitude and quietude.
King Aśoka paid homage to the various stūpas of the arhats. Next, he arrived at one particular stūpa and spoke this verse:
"Though one may personally refine away ignorance, there is little benefit to the world. As he offered twenty cowrie shells, the cowrie shells flew out from the stūpa and settled upon the King's feet.
[The King remarked: "Those who are secluded, possessing few desires—their stūpas are likewise so. The *Ekottarika-āgama* says: "Even if one’s lifespan were extremely long, it would ultimately not..."
Bakkula was foremost among those who died young and always delighted in dwelling in seclusion, never remaining amidst the crowds.

○ Mahākauṣṭhila—translated here as "Great Thigh"—was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra. From the past, he had always been victorious in debate over his sister; however, once she became pregnant, he could no longer defeat her in debate.

Knowing that she carried a man of wisdom within her, even the entrusting of his own eloquence to her resulted in his defeat; how much more so would this be the case once she had left the household life? Thus, he abandoned [the world].
He went to South India and studied eighteen sūtras. At that time, the multitude laughed at him, saying, "It has been difficult for you to master them over several lifetimes;
how could you hope to do so in a single life? He sighed deeply and said, "At home I was surpassed by my sister; having left the home life, I am now held in contempt by others.
Vowing to study without ceasing, he had no leisure even to trim his nails. People of the time called him the Brahmacārin Long-Nails (Dīrghanakha). Having finished his studies, he returned home.

He asked where his nephew was. Someone replied, "He has become a disciple of the Buddha. At this, he conceived great arrogance, thinking, "My nephew was renowned throughout the Five Indies at the age of eight;
what kind of arts or magic does that śramaṇa possess to have enticed my sister's son? He then went straight to the Buddha's dwelling.
Vimalakīrti debated the meaning of the Dharma with the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One asked, "What do you take as your fundamental tenet?
Vimalakīrti replied, "I take the non-acceptance of all things as my tenet. The World-Honored One asked, "Do you accept this view? At this, Vimalakīrti shook his sleeves and departed.

While on the road, he suddenly realized his error and sighed, saying, "My position has failed me in two respects. If I accept this view, I fall into a gross error; if I do not accept it, I am likewise defeated."
He saw that he was not accepted. The location of his expulsion was minute; no humans, devas, or followers of the Two Vehicles knew where he had fallen.
Only the World-Honored One and the great Bodhisattvas knew where he had fallen. Thereupon, together with five hundred followers, he left the household life at once and realized arhatship.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "He attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), being able to answer whenever challenged."
Kauṣṭhila is foremost. ○ Nanda is also called Gopāla-Nanda; this translates as "Good Joy.
He was one of the hundred thousand Śākyas whom King Śuddhodana compelled to leave the household life. ○ Sundarananda.
This was translated as "Yanxi" (艶喜). He was the Buddha’s own younger brother, born on the ninth day of the fourth month.

He was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha, yet his countenance and bearing were so preeminent that he stood out from all others; if he were among a crowd, those who did not know him would say, "The Buddha has come.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "In Magadha there was a naked ascetic (*nirgrantha*) of great intelligence, whom the people of the country called 'The Wise One' (*Jñānin*)."
When he finished debating with Śāriputra, his tongue was rendered speechless; he then conceived a wholesome mind and desired to leave the household life within the Buddha’s Dharma.
Seeing that Nanda’s appearance was exceptionally magnificent, he sighed and said, "Even this short and small bhikṣu possesses wisdom beyond measure;

how much more so would one of noble stature? Nanda was immediately ordained and left the household life. His wife was Sundarī, who was exceedingly beautiful; she did not [leave him] even for a meal or a breath.
They departed. The Buddha and Ānanda entered the city to beg for alms. Next, they arrived at the gate of Nanda’s residence and stood there.
Nanda came forward to pay his respects to the World-Honored One. At that moment, Sundarī thought to herself, "If I let him go, the World-Honored One will certainly ordain him.
She then pulled at his robe, not allowing him to leave. Nanda said, "Let me go for a moment so that I may pay my respects."
Once the Blessed One had departed, I immediately turned back. Sundarī said, "We must make a pact before you may go as you please.
She moistened her forehead with cosmetic paste and told him, "This mark has not yet dried; you should return at once.
If you are late, the penalty shall be five hundred gold coins. Nanda replied, "So be it," and went directly to the gate where he prostrated at his feet and took [the mark].
Nanda came with an alms bowl filled to the brim with excellent food and carried it to the entrance of the gate. The World-Honored One then departed together with Ānanda;
the World-Honored One manifested a sign so that Nanda would not take the bowl. Nanda held the bowl and followed silently as the World-Honored One reached the monastery.
Nanda held out his bowl to present it to the World-Honored One. When the meal was finished, the Buddha asked him, "Nanda, will you eat my leftovers?
He replied, "I will eat them. After the Buddha had given the food to Nanda, he asked, "Are you able to go forth [into the homeless life]?
He replied, "I shall go forth. The Buddha then said to Ānanda, "Shave Nanda's hair and beard. Thus it was answered.
He replied, "As the World-Honored One has instructed. He immediately sought out a barber to shave his head.
Nanda then clenched his fist and said to the barber, "I shall soon become a Wheel-Turning King. If you shave my hair, I will cut off your wrist! The barber was greatly terrified;
he packed away his tools and was about to take his leave. Ānanda informed the Buddha, and the Buddha—
He then went himself and asked, "Nanda, have you gone forth? He replied, "I have gone forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One personally took a vessel of water and poured it over his head; an attendant then shaved him.

Nanda then thought to himself, "I have now respectfully followed the World-Honored One and gone forth this morning; by evening, I shall return home. When evening arrived, he set out on the road to return.
On the road, the World-Honored One manifested a great chasm so that [Nanda] could not proceed. He remained in grief and distress throughout the night.
At dawn, the Buddha, together with five hundred bhikṣus, accepted an invitation; Nanda sought to remain behind to guard the monastery, intending to flee.
The Buddha ordered him to close the door of his room and sweep the floor. He opened the doors to the north and south and swept away the filth here and there.

Fearing that the Buddha would return, he immediately fled. On the road, he encountered the Buddha; he hid himself beneath a tree. The Buddha caused the branches of that tree to lift high upward, so that his body was revealed.
Seeing this, the Buddha called him back and asked, "For what reason do you wish to leave? He replied, "Yesterday I parted from my wife and have been waiting for her."
He returned the food, thinking only of his wife eating it. The Buddha then led him to tour the heavens, followed by a tour of the hells, after which they rested.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: *Pūrṇa* is translated as "Full"; *Maitrāyaṇī* is translated as "Compassionate.
In the Western Regions, men are called *na* and women are called *nī*. This name was derived from the two conditions of his father and mother.

He was thoroughly versed in all inner and outer scriptures without exception. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "In skillfully expounding at length and discerning the principles of meaning, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is foremost.
When he wished to return to his native land to benefit sentient beings, the Buddha said, "That country is corrupt and evil;

how will you transform them? He replied, "I shall cultivate patience. If people revile me, I shall consider myself fortunate that they do not strike me with their fists. [If they strike with] fists...
When he was beaten, he was fortunate not to have been struck with a wooden staff; when struck with a wooden staff, he was fortunate not to have been struck with a blade;

and when struck with a blade, he was fortunate to have escaped the poisonous vessel of the five turbidities. Because his patience was thus fulfilled, he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (Full Compassion).
Subhūti is translated here as "Born of Emptiness. At the time of his birth, the storehouses were all empty. A diviner said: "He possesses the mark of understanding emptiness."

Auspicious. Thus he was named Kūṭadanta (Empty-born). The practices he cultivated took emptiness as their foundation; he constantly entered the concentration of emptiness and dwelt in the samādhi of non-contention.
He was skilled in expounding the Dharma of emptiness, and whatever he proclaimed, he analyzed in terms of emptiness.

When the Buddha descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, people from all over the land flocked together, vying with one another to prostrate in worship. Yet the Venerable One sat upright in his stone chamber, contemplating all dharmas.
"Emptiness. Form is not the Buddha; even consciousness is not the Buddha. The eye is not the Buddha; even the mind is not the Buddha.

At this, he suddenly awakened to the Way and attained the vision of the Dharmakāya; thus he was named Kūṇapa (Empty-born). Among all the disciples, he was foremost in understanding emptiness. ○ Ānanda.
This is translated as "joyful" (*prāmodya*). It is also translated as "untainted. The *Madhyama Āgama* states:

"If the fourfold assembly hears what Ānanda says, whether much or little, there are none who do not rejoice. When he wishes to ask a question, he first clears his throat, and the great assembly all rejoices.
If the fourfold assembly observes his silence, or his walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, or his gestures, instructions, and every movement or shift of position, they likewise [rejoice]."
Ānanda was filled with joy. At the age of twenty-five, he requested to serve the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Ānanda, you surpass those who served me in the past.
Those who served me in the past understood only after my teaching was finished; now, before I have even spoken a word, Ānanda already understands.
Ānanda served the Buddha for twenty-five years. Of the eight thousand *khaṇḍas* (sections) he heard, he recited them all without omission, never asking about a single phrase twice.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda sat upon the lion throne. The great assembly of Kāśyapa praised him, saying: "His face is like the pure full moon; his eyes are like blue lotuses.
The great ocean waters of the Buddha-dharma have flowed into the heart of Ānanda. The *Ekottarika-āgama* states: "He knows the proper time and understands all things.
Wherever he goes, there is no doubt. What he remembers he never forgets. He is widely learned and profoundly insightful, fully capable of upholding [the teachings]."
...Ānanda was foremost. ○ Rāhula: this is translated as "Obstructing. In the past, he blocked a mouse hole;
by reason of this cause and condition, he was named Obstructing. Formerly, when the Prince sought to leave the household life, the King, his father, did not permit it.

As the Prince was persistent and would not cease, the King said, "If you have a son, I will allow you to leave the household life. The Prince then pointed to his wife’s womb and said, "After [this period]..."
"Six years. You shall give birth to a son. After the Prince had left the household, Yaśodharā became pregnant; she carried the child in her womb for six years before finally giving birth.
All the Śākyas were incensed, asking, "By what cause has this occurred? They sought to punish and kill her, and an evil reputation spread throughout the road.
Yaśodharā then set fire to a pit and made a great vow: "If I have done no wrong, may both mother and child perish together."
"If these are truly my remains, let the heavens bear witness. As she embraced her son and threw them into a pit, the pit transformed into a pond, and lotus flowers supported their bodies.
Only then did the king and the people of the country lay their doubts to rest. Later, when the Buddha returned to the kingdom, Yaśodharā had Rāhula offer the Buddha a *modaka* (joy-pill).
Because Rāhula was still a child, he ultimately brought it up to the Buddha; through this, Yaśodharā’s slander was finally quelled.
The Grandfather King was filled with joy; though he had lost his son, he had gained this grandson. As a Wheel-Turning Monarch (*cakravartin*), what cause for regret could I have?
I had hoped that as he grew up, the divine treasures would arrive, yet the Buddha sought to have him leave the household life. The Father King did not grant permission.
When Yaśodharā was about to ascend the high tower, Maudgalyāyana flew through the air to fetch her. The Buddha ordained her as a renunciant and entrusted her to Śāriputra as his disciple.

While serving as a śrāmaṇera, she delighted in speaking falsehoods; whenever kings, ministers, or lay devotees came wishing to see the Buddha, she would tell them all that he was not there, thereby preventing countless people from seeing the Buddha due to her lying.
For this reason, the Buddha frequently rebuked him. When the Buddha returned from his travels, he had Rāhula wash his feet.

The Buddha picked up the foot-basin with his foot, turned it over three times and righted it three times, and then placed it face down on the ground, ordering Rāhula to pour water into it. Rāhula turned the basin over and poured the water, but it would not stay.
The Buddha said, "You are now speaking falsely, just like this overturned basin; you likewise cannot retain the water of the Buddha's Dharma."

It is established. Now I shall speak the truth; do not speak falsely. Among my disciples, those who are foremost in secret conduct and well-known to all—those whom everyone recognizes in their hearts and perceives with their own eyes—I declare that these are all leaders of the great assembly.
Furthermore, there were two thousand persons, both those in training and those beyond training;
the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī together with her retinue of six thousand; and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, mother of Rāhula, also accompanied by her retinue.

This describes the assembly of those in training (*śaikṣa*). Those for whom reality is fully realized and delusions are exhausted, such that there is nothing further to be accomplished, are called those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);

these are the Arhats. Those who investigate reality and sever delusions, desiring to reach the state where reality is fully realized and delusions are exhausted, are called those both in training and beyond training (*śaikṣāśaikṣa*).
Mahāprajāpatī is translated here as "Great Path of Compassion" (*Dà Àidào*); she is also called Gautamī.
Māhī; this translates as "Leader of the Nun Community," and she was the Buddha’s maternal aunt. Yaśodharā;
this translates as "Flower-Color" and also as "Fame"; she was the mother of Rāhula.
There were eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

They had all attained *dhāraṇī* and the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*). They turned the irreversible wheel of Dharma, made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of buddhas, and planted the roots of all virtues in the presence of those buddhas; they were constantly praised by all the buddhas.
He sighed with admiration: "He has cultivated his person through loving-kindness; he has skillfully entered the Buddha’s wisdom; he has attained great insight and reached the other shore;
his fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds; and he is able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings."
This is a praise of the Bodhisattva’s virtues. "Bodhisattva" is a half-syllable of a Sanskrit term; its full form is *bodhisattva*, which translates as "Awakened Being.
They are also called "Beings of Great Resolve," because they possess great compassion, have attained great wisdom, cultivate great causes, and realize the great fruit.
The Sanskrit term *anuttara* translates as "Unsurpassed. *Samyak-saṃbodhi*...
"Ti" (提) means "Samyaksambuddha" (正等正覺). Those who have all attained non-retrogression from Bodhi are those who shoulder the great causal conditions of the Tathāgata’s work;

they know with certainty that their attainment of Buddhahood is unmistakable. This is not like the followers of the Hīnayāna, who claim for themselves that they have already attained Nirvāṇa and no longer seek the Way.
They have all attained *dhāraṇī* and the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*). [Vimalakīrti] said: "Brahma..."
The *dhāraṇī* of speech; this is translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*). Eloquence in joyful exposition is the second of the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

A Bodhisattva of the ninth stage eliminates one hindrance and two delusions, thereby attaining the four unhindered knowledges. The one hindrance is the obstacle of being unwilling to act for the benefit of others. The two delusions are:
first, regarding the immeasurable teachings spoken and the immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables; [and second, regarding the inability to understand their distinctions].
Regarding the subsequent delusions concerning mastery over the dhāraṇīs of wisdom and eloquence:
first, there is the delusion regarding mastery over the dhāraṇīs of the immeasurable teachings spoken [by the Buddha], which refers to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
This constitutes mastery over the retention of what is expressed, because within a single meaning, all meanings are manifested. Regarding the immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables...

Mastery over *dhāraṇī* regarding phenomena refers to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*). It is mastery over the retention of the expressive designations, because within a single name one manifests all names.
Mastery over *dhāraṇī* regarding subsequent wisdom and eloquence refers to the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
It is mastery over the retention of the successive explanations and etymological definitions of speech and sound.
Because all sounds are manifested within a single sound, one possesses mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna-vaśitā*).
This refers to the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), whereby one skillfully teaches by thoroughly understanding the capacities and circumstances of others.

By severing these two delusions, the Bodhisattva attains mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*), which is not like that of the Hīnayāna, where one merely attains mastery over the mind. One turns the irreversible wheel of Dharma; having attained...

This Way is for abiding within oneself; by employing this Way, one benefits others. It is not like the Lesser Vehicle, which does not delight in preaching the Dharma but merely maintains its own secluded tranquility.
Those who make offerings to all Buddhas and cultivate all roots of virtue do so because they make offerings to all Tathāgatas and there are no roots of virtue that they do not nurture.
This is unlike the Lesser Vehicle, whose bodies are weary and lax, and who think only of—

It is emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. That which is constantly praised by all Buddhas refers to the Bodhisattva whose wisdom and virtue are vast and profound, and who sports with supernatural powers; therefore, the Buddhas exclaim in admiration.

This is unlike the followers of the Lesser Vehicle, whom the Tathāgatas commonly dismiss as "withered sprouts and rotten seeds. It refers to the Bodhisattva who cultivates the body through compassion and skillfully enters the Buddha-wisdom.

One regards the three realms as one's home and views the four modes of birth as one's children; by borrowing the means of delivering sentient beings to enter the Buddha-wisdom, it is called "skillfully entering.
This is not like the Hinayana, which views the three realms as a prison and regards the four modes of birth as enemies and bandits.
"Thoroughly penetrating great wisdom and reaching the other shore": "penetrating" (tong) refers to the process of investigating and putting [the truth] into practice;
"reaching" (da) refers to profound cultivation and self-realization. "Great wisdom" is precisely the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-jñāna*).

Because the Bodhisattva contemplates emptiness through *prajñā* while benefiting sentient beings through *upāya*, they are able to ascend majestically to the shore of the Way, unlike the followers of the Lesser Vehicle who realize only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
"His wisdom remains even amidst the middle stream. Regarding "his fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds":
fame is the guest of reality. Since the Bodhisattva's actual practice is vast, his fame is likewise universal.

This is unlike those of the Lesser Vehicle who seek only their own benefit, whose fame remains confined within a single country. "He is able to deliver immeasurable sentient beings" refers to his power of aspiration.

It is inexhaustible; the saving of sentient beings is endless. This is not like the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which, having attained its own benefit, does not find joy in the accomplishment of sentient beings.
The School of the Patriarchs calls this "embers emitting flames from cold ashes" or "flowers blooming on withered wood"—it is to take another step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole.
Their names were: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva,
Nityodyukta Bodhisattva, Anikṣiptadhura Bodhisattva, Ratnapāṇi Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva,
Sūradatta Bodhisattva, Ratnacandra Bodhisattva, Candraprabha Bodhisattva, Pūrṇacandra Bodhisattva, Mahābala Bodhisattva, and Anantabala Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattvas, including the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Trailokyavikrama, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnakūṭa,
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāstṛ, together with eighty thousand such Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas.
In the Sanskrit language, Mañjuśrī is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode). The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* states:

"Although he speaks of all dharmas, he does not give rise to the notion of 'dharmas,' nor does he give rise to the notion of 'non-dharmas'; therefore, he is called Wondrous Virtue. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "He clearly perceives the Buddha-nature."
They are like Samantabhadra and others. Regarding Avalokiteśvara, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Sentient beings who see him will surely attain bodhi;
those who call his name shall be freed from all sufferings. Thus, the Buddha Ratnagarbha said:
"You observe all sentient beings and give rise to great compassion; henceforth, you shall be named Avalokiteśvara. Regarding Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: [as follows].
Wherever I set foot, the trichiliocosm and the palaces of Māra tremble; therefore, I am named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Regarding "unresting," the *Siddhārthabuddhi-paripṛcchā* states: "If a period of Ganges-sand eons were made into a single day and night..."
Thirty days constitute one month; twelve months constitute one year. Only after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas does one encounter a single Buddha.
In this manner, at the abodes of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they practice all forms of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and cultivate and accumulate merit.
Thereafter, they receive predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) with minds that never cease and without weariness; therefore, it is called "Unceasing" (*Akṣaya*).

[The character for] "rest" [is omitted]. Regarding "Treasure-Palmed" (Ratnapāṇi): the *Pǔchāojīng* (*Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra*) states that he has donned the armor of supreme virtue, such that until he attains Buddhahood, none can obstruct or destroy it, nor cause him to abandon the Mahāyāna.
Even in his dreams, he does not set his mind upon the two vehicles (the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha paths), but always uses his wisdom-mind to preach and expound for others.
Because he has no greed or attachment toward precious treasures, he is named Treasure-Palmed. Regarding "Medicine King" (Bhaiṣajyarāja), [it is from] the *Beihuājīng* (*Karunāpuṇḍarīkasūtra*).

He said: "I vow that when the one thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa attain enlightenment, I shall make offerings to them all; when these Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa, I shall erect stupas for them all;
during the sufferings at the end of the kalpa, I shall protect and deliver all beings; and amidst the calamities of war and pestilence, I shall become a King of Physicians."
Thereafter, he attained Buddhahood. The Buddha Ratnagarbha said: "I shall now name you Mahāviśuddhibhaiṣajyarāja. In the future, you shall become a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata.

Regarding "Ratnacandra," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi-sūtra* states: "If bodhisattvas constantly cultivate the pure conduct of a youth (*kumāra-brahmacarya*), such that they do not even mentally conceive of the five desires, let alone experience them with the body, they are therefore called 'Jewel' (Ratna)."
Candra (Moon). Bhadrapāla is translated here as "Good Protector" (Śubharakṣita). The *Suyāmasūtra* states: "If sentient beings hear his name, they will certainly attain samādhi.
Maitreya is translated here as "Kindly One" (Maitrīputra). The *Suyāmasūtra* states: "If sentient beings see him, they immediately attain the samādhi of loving-kindness.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīkasūtra* states that he made a vow to protect sentient beings amidst the kalpas of swords and fire.

Regarding the "Guide" (śāstṛ): The *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā* states, "If a bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward sentient beings who have fallen into wrong paths and causes them to enter the right path, without seeking any reward for their kindness, he is therefore called a Guide."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra was present together with his retinue of twenty thousand devaputras.
There were also the devaputra Candraprabha, the devaputra Samantagandha, and the devaputra Ratnaprabha. The Four Great Kings were present together with their retinues of ten thousand devaputras.
The devaputra Īśvara and the devaputra Maheśvara were present together with their retinues of thirty thousand devaputras. Sā...
The Lord of the Sahā World, the Brahmā King Śikhin Mahābrahmā, and others such as Prabhāsa Mahābrahmā,
together with their retinue of twelve thousand devaputras.
This describes the eight classes of beings. When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, those of diverse species all comply with it;

thus the eight classes of dragons and devas arrive without consultation and draw near without appointment. It is like the North Star, which remains unmoving while the myriad stars all pay homage to it.
Regarding the "Heavenly Beings" (tianren): in Sanskrit they are called Śakra-devānām-indra, which translates as "The Able Lord. He nurtures and protects all that is wholesome.
Because he is able to act as the Lord of Devas, this deity dwells upon the summit of Mount Sumeru and governs the four continents in their entirety.
As for the Moon Devaputra, he is the Son of the Moon Deity. "Moon" (candra) means "to wane"; it is so called because it possesses deficiency.

Its lower surface is composed of *vaiḍūrya* gem and crystal; it is so named because it can both cool and illuminate. He is called "Deva" because of his sovereignty, and "Son" because of his loving-kindness.
It is said: The Devaputra Ratnaprabha is the Devaputra Sūrya (the Sun). "Sun" means reality (*satya*), because it is always full and substantial.
Its lower surface is likewise composed of *koṭika* jewels and fire-pearls, for they are capable of heating and illuminating.
The Devaputra Samantagandha is the Devaputra Nakṣatra (the Stars). As for the Four Great Kings: the one in the east is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra; this is translated as...
Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Holder of the Nation) means that he protects and sustains the land for the sake of bringing peace and benefit to sentient beings.
He dwells on the Golden Mountain and leads two classes of spirits: first, the Gandharvas—translated here as "Seekers of Fragrance"—who are the musicians of Śakra;
second, the Piśācas—translated here as "Eaters of Vital Essence"—so called because they consume the vital essence of sentient beings and the five grains. He protects Pūrvavideha in the east.
Next is Virūḍhaka of the south; this is translated as "Increase," for he is able to cause both himself and others to increase their roots of goodness.
He dwells on Mount Vaiḍūrya and leads two classes of spirits: first, the Kumbhāṇḍas, which means "Terrifying";
second, the Pretas, which means "Ghosts of Malevolent Spirits. He protects Jambudvīpa in the south. Next is Virūpākṣa of the west; this is translated as...
Virūpākṣa (Broad-Eyed) dwells on the White Silver Mountain and leads two classes of spirits: first, the *nāgas*; second, the *piśācas*, which means "fever-demons" in Chinese.
He protects the western continent, Aparagodānīya. In the north is Vaiśravaṇa, which means "Much-Hearing," so called because his fame for merit and virtue spreads in all four directions.
He dwells on the Crystal Mountain and leads two groups of beings: first, the *yakṣas*, which means "demon" in Chinese...
The *Jigui* (Disease-demon) is so called because it flies through the air with great speed. The two *Rākṣasas*—here translated as "The Fearful"—protect the northern continent of Uttarakuru;
as each presides over two divisions, they prevent ghosts and spirits from disturbing the world, and are thus named the Four Heavenly Kings who Protect the World (*Lokapāla*).

The Moon King (*Candradeva*) and others are internal ministers of Śakra, serving as his high officials such as the Chancellor (*Keng*) and the Prime Minister (*Xiang*). These are the Four Great Heavenly Kings.

These are the external ministers of Śakra, like generals. The "Sovereign" (Īśvara) refers to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), the highest heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The "Great Sovereign" (*Maheśvara*) refers to Maheśvara, who dwells at the summit of the Great Trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*) within the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*);
because he is most sovereign there, he rides a white ox, holds a white fly-whisk, and can know the Great Trichiliocosm in a single thought-moment.
Because of the raindrops, it is called *Sahā*. This is translated as "Endurance" (*Kanshin*), because its sentient beings endure the three poisons and various afflictions;

it is also so called because it is a place where the five destinies dwell together. As for "Brahmā," this is translated as "Free from Desire," meaning that one has newly departed from the defilement of desire and attained the fundamental meditative concentration (*mauladhyāna*).
*Śikhin* is translated as "Crest" (*Chingji*), meaning there is a fleshy protuberance on the crown of the head.
His topknot is shaped like a conch shell; thus he is also called Śikhin (Conch-Topknot) and Jvalaśiras (Flame-Peak), for the calamity of fire reaches up to this peak.
He is also named Drumaśikhi, because in that country fire is called *druma*. The Mahābrahmā of Radiant Light is none other than the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
since the beings of this heaven lack discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), and are devoid of speech, they use light as their mode of communication.
Therefore, the word "etc. includes the third and fourth dhyānas. The formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) are not mentioned because they lack physical form.
There are eight dragon kings (*nāgarāja*): the Dragon King Nanda, the Dragon King Upananda, the Dragon King Sāgara, and the Dragon King Vāsuki...
The Naga King Śubha, the Naga King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Naga King Anavatapta, the Naga King Mānasvin,
the Naga King Utpala, and others, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.
Nanda means "Joy. Bhaṭṭa means "Virtuous. These brothers constantly protected the kingdom of Magadha;

because the rains fell in their proper seasons and the common people were all joyful, [the land was prosperous]. Sāgara is translated here as "Ocean," for it is the most excellent among the great oceans.
Aśvatarī-putra is translated as "Many Heads. Takṣaka is translated as "Many Tongues," because he delights in speech.
Therefore, it is also said that [it] can cause harm; this refers to the fact that when one exhales while in a state of anger, both humans and animals may die.
Anavatapta is translated here as "Without Heat. It is named after its lake. All the nāgas of Jambudvīpa suffer from three afflictions:
first, hot winds and hot sands that scorch their skin, flesh, bones, and marrow, causing them great suffering; second, the sudden rising of violent winds that blow...
In their palaces, they lose their precious ornaments and garments; the dragon bodies manifest themselves, causing them suffering and distress.
Thirdly, when the dragons are enjoying themselves, the King of the Garuḍas enters the palace, seizing and devouring the newborn dragon offspring, which produces fear and affliction.
This lake is free from these three calamities, and is thus named Anavatapta (Without Heat-Affliction). Mānasa—this is translated as "Great."
The asura Śarabha pushed back the ocean to submerge the city of Sudarśana; this dragon coiled its body to block the seawater.
*Utpala* is translated here as "blue lotus"; it is named after the pond because this flower emerges from that pond.
Although the dragon king also consumed food of a hundred flavors, at the very last mouthful, he was transformed into a frog.

There were four kinnara kings: the Kinnara King Dharma, the Kinnara King Sudharma, the Kinnara King Mahādharma, and the Kinnara King Dharmadhara. Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
*Kiṃnara*. This is translated as "Doubtful Deity. They resemble humans, with a single horn upon their heads and extremely handsome faces;

those who see them give rise to doubt. They are categorized within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*). These are the deities who perform the Dharma music for the Heavenly Emperor. They dwell on mountains of the seven treasures and possess extraordinary physical marks;
they ascend to perform music when the Buddha preaches the Dharma. While the various devas play stringed instruments and sing, the *Pañca* drums the lute.

And as they were reciting this Dharma-gate, there were four gandharva kings: the Gandharva King Delight-in-Mountains, the Gandharva King Delight-in-Sound, the Gandharva King Beautiful, and the Gandharva King Beautiful-Sound. Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.

*Gandharva*. This is translated as "Seeker of Fragrance" (*xunxiang*), because they take fragrance as their food; it is also called "Fragrant Aggregate" (*xiangyin*), because fragrance issues from their bodies.
These are the deities who perform secular music for the Heavenly Emperor. "Music" refers to performances such as *dhvaja-varta* (tumbling acrobatics).
"Musical sounds" refer to drums, cymbals, strings, and song. "Exquisite" refers to the superior category among *dhvaja-varta* performances. "Exquisite sounds" refers to musical sounds.

As for those of superior rank among the middle class, there are four asura kings: the asura king Bāli, the asura king Kharaskandha, the asura king Vemacitra, and the asura king Rāhu; each is accompanied by several hundreds [of followers].

Accompanied by a thousand retinues, the asuras—here translated as "those without wine"—go to the four continents to gather flowers and brew wine from the ocean. However, through the karmic power of fish and dragons, it is transformed into salt water.
Because they vow to cut off [the production of] wine out of anger and envy, they are called "those without wine. They are also called "non-gods" (asura), for they frequently practice deceit.
They are seductive. Because they lack the conduct of the heavens, those who cultivate merit today while harboring a mind of competitiveness and flattery are mostly reborn as such beings.
Thus it is said: "Terrifying with their jagged peaks; startling with their towering heights; all emerging with three heads and further endowed with eight arms."
"Crossing mountains and treading upon the sea; grasping the sun and upholding the clouds; seeking food in the heavens and brewing wine in the ocean"—this refers to them.
*Vāli* means "bound," because he is tied around the neck with five evil objects from which he cannot escape, and because he is constantly bound by Śakra.
*Kharaskandha* is translated as "Broad Shoulders. As for "encircling the waters of the sea," it refers to Vemacitra.
*Tara* means *vima*, which here signifies "thread. *Citra* means "various. Because she can use a single thread to magically produce various things, she is so called.
Furthermore, it is said that she is the "Pure Mind," because she caused the waters of the ocean to emit sound. She requested the Gandharva maiden Śacī;
through the karmic power of Śakra, her father was made to dwell in the Hall of Seven Leaves (*Saptaparṇa*). Thus...
He took her as his wife. Later, she slandered her father, leading to a military conflict. He waded through the waters of the ocean with his feet and attacked Sūrya (the Sun) with his hands.
Śakra, by the power of Prajñā, was unable to cause him harm. Rāhu; this is translated as "Obstructing Holder," because he obstructs and holds the sun and moon.
It is also called "Causing Affliction," because he is able to conceal the sun and moon with his hands, thereby causing distress to the gods. His body...
It is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and one thousand yojanas in width at its mouth.
Its body is adorned with precious jewels because it delights in gazing upon celestial maidens and divine groves. It constantly engages in battle with Śakra;

if the people of the four continents fail to filially support their parents and make offerings to śramaṇas, the gods will manifest their power and rain down swords from the sky above. If they do not act thus, [the gods will not do so].
The devas entered their palaces and did not come forth; moreover, the sun emitted light that blinded their eyes so they could not see.

They raised their palms to block the sun, and the people of the world all said it was a solar eclipse. Or they made loud noises, and the people of the world all said it was the roar of celestial beasts.
That which is consumed by the asuras is identical to that of the devas, except for the very last mouthful, which transforms into blue mud.

There were four garuḍa kings: the Garuḍa King Mahātejas, the Garuḍa King Mahākāya, the Garuḍa King Mahāpūrṇa, and the Garuḍa King Manojña. Each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
*Kalaviṅka* (Garuḍa). This is translated as "Golden Wing" (*Jinshi*), because its wings are adorned with various precious colors.
It dwells atop the great trees of the Four Heavenly Kings; the distance between its two wings is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*.
If one were to face an enemy, it would be called "Great Gullet" (*Dashi*), for *shu* refers to the throat. This is because it constantly holds dragons within its gullet. As for "greatly full":
They take dragons as their food, for they always satisfy their desires. These birds possess supernatural powers:

the male transforms into a celestial king (*devaputra*), and the female transforms into a celestial maiden (*apsaras*). Their dwelling place contains a palace of jewels, and their food consists of a hundred flavors.

Yet, because their karmic retribution requires them to eat dragons, the one who possesses the wish-fulfilling gem on its neck is this *garuḍa*, which devours one [dragon] every day from the eastern mountain.
There were five hundred small dragon kings; it was the same in the other three directions, revolving in succession. Their lifespan was eight thousand years.
At the end of their lives, they lost their power and desired to devour the young dragons. The dragon mothers cried out in distress, unable to prevent them from eating, and thus became enraged.
They emerged from Mount Vajra, piercing through the ocean and the earth-wheel, but they could not pass through the wind-wheel. The wind repelled them, and they returned through the original hole.
He surged upward and reached Vajra Mountain. This occurred seven times in succession. Returning to the mountain peak, he passed away;
his flesh split open and fire erupted, threatening to consume the Jewel Mountain. Nanda rained down rain to extinguish it. His flesh rotted and his heart surged forth;
a wind-wheel also fell upon the mountain seven times, becoming a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). The dragon obtained it and became its king.
King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, together with several hundreds of thousands of attendants, each bowed at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Vaidehī means "Contemplation" (Sanskrit: *Vaidehī*); she was the consort of King Bimbisāra. Ajātaśatru means "Unborn" (Sanskrit: *Ajātaśatru*).
Jīvaka was the king of Rājagṛha. A major sutra states: "Because the Buddha-nature does not arise, the enemy of afflictions arises;
because the enemy of afflictions arises, one does not see the Buddha-nature. If afflictions do not arise, one immediately sees the Buddha-nature."
The *Puchao jing* (Sutra on Universal Transcendence) states: "Ajātaśatru, having repented before Mañjuśrī, attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).

At the end of his life, he entered the Tāla Hell; upon entering, he immediately emerged and was reborn in an upward-directed buddha-field, where he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When Maitreya appears in the world, he will return to this realm under the name Bodhisattva Acala, and later shall become a buddha named Pure Realm (*Vimaladhātu*)."
"Come. Sit to one side" means that they each withdrew to sit with their faces turned toward the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who made offerings to him, revered, honored, and praised him, as he [taught] for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
He preached the Mahāyāna sūtra titled "The Immeasurable Meanings," the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas.

As for those who made offerings, they gave him what he desired; as for those who showed respect, they exhausted all their ritual propriety; as for those who honored him, they exerted the utmost sincerity;

and as for those who praised him, they reached the limit of extolling his excellence. The fourfold assembly exhausted their sincerity and displayed the height of their reverence, yet the World-Honored One had no [need for] it.
In response, he wished to bestow upon the great assembly the sublime Dharma obtained within the Bodhimaṇḍa;

however, fearing they might not be able to bear its weight, he first preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* to awaken their latent capacities. These two characters, "immeasurable" (*wúliàng*), [serve this purpose].

There are two meanings. First, because there is no limit or measure, it is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*). This belongs to the gate of the true nature (*dharmatā*), for it is the dharma of equality.
Second, because the gates of the Dharma are manifold, it is called "immeasurable. This belongs to the gate of skillful means (*upāya*);
that is to say, by means of limitless dharmas, one provisionally opens various immeasurable gates of the Dharma for saving sentient beings. Although the World-Honored One has four... [text ends]

For over ten years, he refined the fourfold assembly. However, these four assemblies remained within the confines of the measurable dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-pramāṇa*), adhering to the principle of a single liberation and unable to abandon their finite minds to enter the infinite meaning.
Therefore, the World-Honored One first preached this sutra to shake them. Thus the sutra says: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha, together with eighty thousand bodhisattvas..."
They addressed the Buddha together, saying, "By what dharma-gate should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice if they wish to swiftly accomplish bodhi?
The Buddha said, "There is a dharma-gate named 'Immeasurable Meanings. A bodhisattva who wishes to study this dharma-gate..."
One should observe that all phenomena have been quiescent in their essential nature and characteristics from the very beginning, like empty space, without any duality of dharmas.
