Furthermore, one should penetrate deeply into all phenomena: such is the characteristic of dharmas—that they arise as such dharmas;
such is the characteristic of dharmas—that they even cease as such dharmas. The characteristic of dharmas is thus (quiescent in their essential nature and characteristics, like empty space).

In emptiness, there are no two distinct dharmas; the four marks are all suchness (*tathatā*). This refers to the subsequent passage: "Such are its marks, such is its nature," and so on, up to "such is its beginning, end, and ultimate reality. This is precisely the profound and immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas.

The measure of the immeasurable is the realm of the Tathāgata’s own self-manifesting cognition; it is what is called the "mind-measure of no-mind. It is what is called the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm, which is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharmakāya.

Having thus observed the beginning and end of these four characteristics and fully understood them all, one next observes that all phenomena do not abide for even a single thought-moment, arising and ceasing anew at every instant.
Furthermore, one observes their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing within that very moment. Having observed in this way:
He enters into the faculties, dispositions, and inclinations of sentient beings. Because their dispositions and inclinations are immeasurable, his preaching of the Dharma is immeasurable.
Because his preaching of the Dharma is immeasurable, its meanings are also immeasurable. These immeasurable meanings arise from a single dharma. As for that single dharma:
This is precisely signlessness (*animitta*). Such signlessness is signless and non-sign; non-sign is signless. This is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
If one can thus cultivate this single dharma-gate of infinite meanings, one will certainly and swiftly attain the realization of Bodhi.

This is the observation of sentient beings. Because their dispositions and desires differ, one employs a single dharma to unfold immeasurable meanings; these immeasurable meanings are precisely what is meant by "the many. This is how, according to the dispositions and desires of sentient beings, the single vehicle path (*ekayāna-mārga*) is differentiated and taught as three.

In reality, it is fundamentally a dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor. This is its gate of wisdom, which is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. The preceding section was the gate of observing the true nature (*lakṣaṇa-dvāra*); this section is the gate of observing arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*).

To distinguish various immeasurable dharma-gates by means of the gate of the immeasurable is nothing other than desiring that they abandon conceptual thought and return to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The *Mahāvyūha-sūtra* states:
"Since the World-Honored One first attained the Way more than forty years ago, he has constantly expounded for the sake of sentient beings the meaning of the four marks:
the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, impermanence and non-self, and neither large nor small, neither arising nor ceasing—the single mark."
It is signless; the nature and characteristics of phenomena are originally empty and quiescent.

If there are those who hear this, they shall all attain the stage of Heat, the stage of Summits, the stage of Patience, and the stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma; as well as the fruit of the Stream-enterer and so forth, up to the path of the Pratyekabuddha.
They shall resolve their minds on Bodhi, ascend from the first bhūmi and the second bhūmi, up to the tenth bhūmi. This is the meaning of all the dharmas explained in the past.
How does this differ from what has been taught now, such that it is called the profound, unsurpassed Mahāyāna?
In the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, it is said that if a bodhisattva practices, they will certainly attain bodhi. The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Great Adornment:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! Since I sat upright beneath the Bodhi tree at my place of enlightenment for six years, I attained bodhi."
"Ānanda, when one observes all dharmas with the Buddha-eye, they are ineffable. Why is this? Because the dispositions and desires of sentient beings differ;
because their dispositions and desires differ, he has preached the Dharma in various ways through the power of skillful means for more than forty years, yet has not yet revealed the ultimate reality.
For this reason, there are differences in how sentient beings attain the Way, and they do not quickly achieve [enlightenment]."
Bodhi (which can be seen as the bestowal of the prediction of buddhahood, for this is the original intent). Good son, it is like water that can wash away filth;
whether from wells, ponds, rivers, streams, or canals, it is able to wash away all manner of impurities. Such is the water of the Dharma.
It is also like this. It can wash away the defilements of the afflictions of sentient beings.
Good son, the nature of water is one, yet rivers, streams, wells, ponds, brooks, channels, and the great ocean are each distinct from one another. The nature of dharmas is also like this:
it washes away worldly toil and is equal without distinction. Yet the three fruits and four fruits, and the two paths, are not the same. Good son...
My son, although water is of one nature, a well is not a pond; a pond is not a river or a stream; and a brook or a canal is not the ocean.
It is just so with the various dharmas taught by the Tathāgata. The teachings given at the beginning, middle, and end are all capable of washing away afflictions;

yet the beginning is not the middle, and the middle is not the end. Although the words and phrases of these teachings at the beginning, middle, and end are not identical, their meanings are each distinct. Well done!
"Good man, I rose from beneath the King of Trees for the sake of the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, and turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths;
I also taught that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and quiescent, subject to change and instability, arising and ceasing in every moment.
Thereafter, for the sake of the bhikṣus and the assembly of bodhisattvas, I proclaimed the twelve links of dependent origination and the six pāramitās, and likewise taught all..."
The Dharma is originally empty and quiescent; it undergoes constant change without abiding, arising and ceasing from moment to moment.

Now, once again, I preach this Mahāyāna *Anantaparyāya Sūtra* here, and it is likewise explained in this way. Therefore, what was first taught, what was taught in the middle, and what is now being taught—though the words and phrases are the same, their meanings are each different.
Because the meanings differ, the understandings of sentient beings differ; because their understandings differ, they attain the Way.

The attainment of the fruit is likewise different. Good son, from the time I first attained the Way and began to preach the Dharma until this very day, I have preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* without a single word of contradiction.

I am able to respond universally to all sentient beings with a single voice, and I am able to respond universally to all bodies with a single body. Good son, this is the profound and inconceivable nature of all Buddhas.
Discourse on the Realm: This is not something known by the followers of the Two Vehicles, nor can it be reached by Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes;

only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully comprehend it. What is taught from beginning to middle to end is that all things are fundamentally empty and quiescent, undergoing constant change without abiding, arising and ceasing in every thought-moment.

This is what is called the non-dual speech of the Tathāgata; this is what is called being good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. Because sentient beings each follow their own inclinations and natures, and because they engage in conceptualization and discrimination, their understandings and entries differ from one another. Therefore, it is said: "This Dharma is not something to be grasped through conceptualization or discrimination."

It can be understood; only the Buddhas are able to know it. This sutra and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* mutually elucidate one another; therefore, this passage is cited here. If the wise contemplate this, they will have already grasped more than half of the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. (I do not tire of these detailed texts.)
The "Dharma for teaching Bodhisattvas" is, by contrast, revealed not to be the Dharma for teaching the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
The phrase "protected and remembered by the Buddha" likewise reveals that it is not something protected and remembered by those of the Small Vehicle.

It is, for example, like the wish-fulfilling jewel, which is protected and remembered by the Māgadha Dragon King, but is not cherished or delighted in by frogs or earthworms. This sutra is like the Lotus Sutra.
Being of the same root and following the same thread, it is also called "the Dharma for instructing Bodhisattvas" and "that which is protected by the Buddha's mindfulness.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, he sat cross-legged and entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings; his body and mind remained unmoving.

In the Sanskrit language, it is called *samādhi*; this translates as "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*) or "equipoise" (*samāhita*). It is so named because one holds the mind with equanimity, directing it toward a single object.
Having preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, he immediately entered the "Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings. Thus, it is evident that for the World-Honored One, his speech reaches his body;
what he speaks is precisely what he practices, and what he practices is precisely what he speaks. Therefore, as soon as he had spoken this sūtra...
Furthermore, he now directly presents this *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* face-to-face, like a wall of copper and iron, suddenly before everyone’s eyes.
He intends to have the great assembly take responsibility for what existed prior to the empty kalpa and realize it before the Buddha appeared in the world.
But tell me, who among you is a fellow student? Is it Bodhidharma or Luzu?

At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly. The entire Buddha-world shook in six ways.
When the World-Honored One entered meditative concentration, the heavens were startled and the earth shook; thus the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers, and the earth quaked in six ways.

*Mandāra* is translated here as "soft" (*rōnan*); *Mañjūṣaka* is translated as "pleasing" (*shiki*). As for the scattering of the four flowers, it signifies the overturning and breaking of the four great elements.
The six quakes refer to: moving, rising, surging, shaking, roaring, and crashing. To sway and flutter restlessly is called [the sixth].
To "move" (dòng) means to rise from below toward a higher level; to "arise" (qǐ) means to suddenly leap upward; to "leap" (yǒng) means to spring up abruptly;

to "shake" (zhèn) means to have a low, rumbling sound; to "roar" (hǒu) means to emit a powerful, resonant sound; and to "strike" (jī) means to produce a crashing, clashing resonance. "Shaking" refers to sound, while "moving" refers to form.

Sound encompasses both roaring and striking, while movement encompasses both arising and leaping. As for the earth shaking in six ways, it is because it overturns and destroys the root-knots (mūla-grantha).
At that time, within the assembly— monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as various minor kings and universal monarchs—
all these great multitudes attained what they had never experienced before. With joy, they joined their palms and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
Subhūti, while he was sitting in meditation among the cliffs, the devas rained down flowers and praised the Venerable One for his excellent exposition of the Prajñāpāramitā.
When the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings, heaven and earth were shaken;

yet the entire assembly of such a great multitude did not know where it had fallen, nor was there a single person who could comprehend the World-Honored One’s Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings, nor was there a single person...
They praised the World-Honored One’s skillful exposition of the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*.
Each one stared with wide-open eyes, single-mindedly contemplating the Buddha, yet they did not know who it was they were contemplating or what the Buddha was. As an ancient worthy said:
"All of you are sitting in the midst of the great ocean; your heads are already submerged, yet you stretch out your hands and ask others for water to drink. This is precisely that.

At that time, the Buddha emitted a ray of light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, which illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception.
From below, it reached down to the Avīci Hell; from above, it extended up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Within this world, one could see clearly all the sentient beings of the six realms of existence in those lands, as well as the present Buddhas currently residing in those lands, and hear what those Buddhas were teaching.
They preach the Dharma of the sutras, and they see those bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who have attained the Way through various practices;
furthermore, they see the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with their various causes and conditions and various inclinations and understandings.

They practice the bodhisattva path through various manifestations and appearances; they further see various buddhas entering parinirvāṇa, and they further see, after those buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, the construction of stupas made of the seven precious gems from their relics.

World-Honored One, seeing that the eyes of the great assembly were dull and their heads were bewildered, and having no other recourse, I could only briefly manifest spiritual powers by emitting light from between my eyebrows to annotate the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* and the "Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings," so as to cause the great assembly to seek a clear understanding at the tips of my brows and the corners of my eyes.
This is what is meant by: "Out of pity for a three-year-old child, one does not spare even two stalks [of hair]."

This is merely a matter of eyebrows. Nevertheless, even so, if one is a person with blood beneath the skin, they will certainly refuse to make their livelihood within the shadows and glimmers of others.

Have you not seen how Chan Master Wenxi first went to Mount Wutai seeking an audience with Mañjuśrī, only to be thoroughly deceived by Mañjuśrī right before his eyes? Later, he visited Yangshan and attained a point of entry.

He was subsequently appointed as the *dianzuo* (steward). Mañjuśrī would constantly appear atop the rice porridge cauldron. The Master took a bamboo stirring paddle and struck him, saying: "Mañjuśrī is Mañjuśrī; Wenxi is Wenxi.

He composed a verse of praise for this encounter: Mañjuśrī is Mañjuśrī; Wenxi is Wenxi. The Buddha’s golden body is not a thing to be seen. If you wish to see the Buddha’s true form, Look at the ladle stirring the porridge.
The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip; the sweet melon is sweet from stem to blossom. Having practiced the path for three great kalpas, you are nevertheless disparaged by this old monk.
Thus an ancient worthy said: "A celestial immortal appears amidst the clouds of color, holding a red silk fan to shield his face."
"Fix your gaze upon the immortal; do not look at the fan in the immortal's hand. Question: "It is said that the Buddha emits light from between his eyebrows.

Is there a specific teaching regarding this? Answer: "If one speaks of the standard convention of emitting light, then the emission of light from the eyebrows serves as a bestowal of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).
However, if one discusses its underlying meaning, there is a distinct explanation. The eyes, ears, nose, and tongue each possess their own unique capacity. As for the eyebrows..."
The hair is situated above; therefore, the mouth asked the nose, "Eating and drinking are my domain, and speech is my domain. What ability do you possess that you dwell above me?
The nose replied, "Among the five sacred peaks, the Central Peak occupies the position of honor; it is for this reason that I dwell above."
The nose then questioned the eyes: "By what merit do you occupy the position above me? The eyes replied: "We are like the sun and the moon; we truly possess the power of illumination.
For this reason, we reside above. The eyes then asked the eyebrows: "What function do you perform that your station is ranked above ours? The eyebrows replied:
"I am truly without merit; I feel ashamed to occupy this high position. If I were below you, and my eyes were above yours, what face would I show you?
Thus, Bao Yue said in his ascent to the hall: "The ancients said that when the Way is in the eye, it is called 'seeing';

when it is in the ear, it is called 'hearing. But tell me, when it is in the eyebrows, what do you call it? After a long silence, he said: "In sorrow, we share their grief; in joy, we share their delight."
Shared joy. All people know the utility of the useful, yet they do not know the great utility of the useless.
When masters of the school take this as an example for matters that transcend the ordinary, is it perhaps like the radiance emitted from between the eyebrows? Question:
For what reason is the light emitted so as to illuminate eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction? Answer: If one speaks in terms of principle, although the Lesser Vehicle...

It is said that immovability truly exists within movement. Although one may be liberated from the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), one has not yet departed from the aggregates (*skandha*) and realms (*dhātu*).

The Tathāgata, wishing to cause beings to transcend the aggregates and realms and realize the wisdom of immovability (*akampya-jñāna*), therefore causes his radiance to shine universally upon the eastern direction.
An ancient master said: "The wisdom of immovability is fully perfected; it only lacks one's own personal acceptance. Speaking in terms of phenomena, this applies to the land of Zhendan (China).
It is a great vessel for the Mahāyāna. Therefore, the Buddha’s light shone everywhere. Reaching the time of Emperor Ming of the Han, the Semblance Dharma first entered [China].
Reaching the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang, Bodhidharma came again to manifest this matter. Since then, the lamps have been passed down in succession, their flames infinite.
That this light shines universally across heaven and earth is entirely due to the power of this single radiance. If the Buddha’s light did not...
If one is illuminated [by this light], one has no affinity with this land; therefore, in the single country of Zhendan (China), the Buddha-dharma is thus.
It is likewise in all the other eighteen thousand lands of the eastern direction. Thus, one should know that the emission of light is truly not for a minor cause.
Regarding those who see that land from within this world, the two characters "this" and "that" must be understood clearly; one must know this.
The eighteen thousand lands are all the natural radiance of the original ground; they flow forth from this very source. Thus, as the ancient masters said:
"The entire earth is one's own radiance; throughout the entire earth, there is not a single person who does not dwell within one's own radiance.
When the World-Honored One entered the immeasurable samādhi, the immeasurable became one. A single light illumines the ten thousand.
Eight thousand lands constitute one immeasurable world. Eighteen thousand lands are pervaded without exception; this refers to their horizontal pervasiveness.

Reaching upward to the heavens and downward to the earth, this refers to their vertical extent. Among those manifested within the light, the sentient beings of the six realms are the six classes of ordinary beings.
The present Buddhas are the Buddha Vehicle. Those who have practiced and attained the Way are the Śrāvakas.
Those who ride the Pratyekabuddha vehicle are the Pratyekabuddhayāna; those who practice the Bodhisattva path are the Bodhisattvayāna. These are the four noble ones.
In sum, they are the patterns of the ten realms, all currently within the light of equality.

Through various causes and conditions, various faiths and understandings, and various appearances, practicing the Bodhisattva path is a single, unified matter—just as when a person believes and then acts accordingly.

Generosity is the path of the bodhisattva. Thus, whether it be kingdoms, cities, wives, or children, or even one’s own head, eyes, marrow, and brain, one gives them all away with joy, without the slightest stinginess. Therefore, generosity is the causal condition for entering the Way.
When there is such a heart of joy within, there will necessarily be such a sign of joy without. Furthermore, it is like a person who has faith that upholding the precepts is...
Regarding the Bodhisattva path, maintaining the precepts is the causal condition for entering that path.
Therefore, one’s mind remains unmoved by any forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles. Internally, there is such an unshakable mind; externally, there is such an unshakable appearance.
If the mind dwells in patience, there is an external appearance of gentleness, humility, and propriety. If the mind practices diligence, there is an external appearance of attentive regard.
The aspect of heroic vigor: within there is the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), while without there is the appearance of being like damp ash or withered wood;
within one practices wisdom (*prajñā*), while without there is the appearance of being rolling and lively. This is what is meant by "that which exists within manifests externally.
Thus, matters such as the beginning and end of birth and Buddhahood, or the cultivation and realization of the Three Vehicles, are all inseparable from a single pore of the Tathāgata.

Within this radiance, that which the Buddhas of the three periods have discoursed upon for immeasurable kalpas without exhausting it is likewise nothing other than the phenomena manifested within the light of this single pore. Thus, such radiance is inseparable from the daily activities of sentient beings;
yet, in their daily activities, they remain muddled and unaware of it. The World-Honored One has provided us with this model.
I wish for people to consult the map to seek out the noble steed.

Thus we know that the Tathāgata’s emission of light is like pointing to a well to show one who is thirsty where the water is located. Nevertheless, it is somewhat like a mute person making hand gestures.
Yet it is not as good as the Patriarch speaking directly from his own mouth. Long ago, when Chan Master Guling returned from his travels, his preceptor sent him to perform menial service.
One day, while bathing, the preceptor ordered the master to scrub away the grime;
he then patted the master’s back and said, "A fine Buddha hall, yet the Buddha is not holy. The preceptor turned his head to look at him, and the master said, "Though the Buddha is not holy..."
Furthermore, one is able to emit light. As the ancient masters have said: "All of you possess a priceless jewel within yourselves.

From the gateway of the eyes, it emits light that illuminates the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; from the gateway of the ears, it emits light that perceives and distinguishes good and evil sounds.
Thus, these six gateways constantly emit radiance day and night; this is also called the Samādhi of Emitting Light. So it was taught.
It has been spoken; the commentary has also been provided. Thus, there is no need for others to labor over conjecture or inquiry.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought: "Now the World-Honored One manifests these signs of spiritual transformation.
For what cause and condition does such an auspicious omen exist? Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered into samādhi; this is inconceivable and manifests rare wonders."
"There is a matter that must be asked of someone; who is there capable of answering?
He further thought, "This Mañjuśrī, son of the Dharma King, has already drawn near to and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past;
he must surely perceive this rare and extraordinary sign. I shall now question him. At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās [all gathered].
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and others all had this thought: "This is a manifestation of the Buddha’s light and supernormal powers;

whom should we now ask about it? At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to resolve his own doubts, also observed the minds of the fourfold assembly—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as the devas, nāgas, spirits, and others gathered there.
He asked Mañjuśrī, "By what causes and conditions has this auspicious sign of supernatural power appeared,
emitting a great radiance that illuminates eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, such that the adornments of those Buddha-fields are all clearly seen?"
This is Maitreya raising his doubts and requesting instruction. Those with a beginner's mind have dull consciousness and have not yet understood how to seek [the truth].
Out of compassion, the Bodhisattva raises these doubts and makes this inquiry. As the preceding text states, "One cultivates the body through compassion and attains great wisdom";

therefore, it was necessary for Maitreya to pose the questions and Mañjuśrī to lead the responses. "To form a thought" means to privately reflect and deliberate. "Spiritual transformations" (ṛddhi-vikurvaṇā) refers to...
This refers to the radiance. It is manifested through the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata.
As for the question, "By what causes and conditions does this auspicious sign appear?", it is precisely to bring forth a state of doubt.

Ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle encounter such emission of light every day, yet because they lack this state of doubt, they let it pass by; therefore, they do not attain great wisdom and do not obtain its enjoyment.

Because Maitreya gave rise to doubt, it was actually intended to cause people to give rise to doubt. Now that the Buddha has descended, one should contemplate seeking someone to consult for a definitive resolution.
The thought is: "The Buddha is not currently in meditative absorption, so it is certainly appropriate to ask him; yet the Buddha is now in absorption, so whom should I ask?
Furthermore, this radiance cannot be fathomed by ordinary consciousness, nor can it be expressed through words."
To describe it through words and forms, one must have personally witnessed it with one's own eyes to know it with certainty.
If one relies on intellectual deliberation or conjecture, all such verbal descriptions are merely the "livelihood of ghosts"—like scratching an itch through a boot;
they can never truly reveal it. Within this assembly now, I do not know who has personally seen it with their own eyes. Reflecting upon this myself, I thought: Mañjuśrī...
Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; he has already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and must surely have seen this Immeasurable Light.
I shall question him, for he will certainly know its whereabouts. As the saying goes: "To know the path down the mountain, one must ask those who have come down.
At that time, the bhikṣu descended, and the four classes of beings were freed from doubt—namely, that [the Buddha] was indeed within this very mountain.

"The clouds are so deep that one knows not where they reach. At that time, Maitreya descends; this is precisely the presentation of a doubt and a request for resolution, meaning that what one does not understand oneself brings calamity upon others.
As for the distinction between "spiritual transformations" (*shenbian*) mentioned above and "supernatural powers" (*shentong*) mentioned here:

the term "transformation" (*bian*) refers to wondrous functions that cannot be fathomed; the term "penetration" (*tong*) refers to being unimpeded wherever one touches. This is what is meant by "when one reaches an impasse..."
Transformation. Through transformation comes penetration. In the realm of the numinous, Buddhas and sentient beings are equal. However, sentient beings do not realize this in their daily activities;

therefore, they cannot exhaust its depths. Because they fail to exhaust its depths, every step is obstructed. Since they cannot achieve transformation and penetration, what the Buddha calls "transformation" and "penetration," sentient beings call "hindrances" and "obstructions."
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, asked in verse:
"Mañjuśrī, for what reason does the Guide emit from the white tuft between his eyebrows a great light that shines everywhere, raining down māndārava flowers?"
Mañjuṣaka flowers and sandalwood-scented breezes gladdened the hearts of the multitude. By these causes and conditions, the ground was entirely adorned and purified;
this world shook in six ways, and at that time the fourfold assembly was filled with joy, their bodies and minds feeling a sense of sublime ease.
"An unprecedented occurrence.

This verse first describes what was seen, and subsequently asks the reason for it; this describes the emission of light, the raining of flowers, and the shaking of the earth, as the great assembly rejoices.
The single phrase "delighting the hearts of the multitude" powerfully depicts the scene at that moment. It says:
The floral vapors and fragrant breezes intermingled and brushed against one another, causing people’s hearts to rejoice and their spirits to be at ease;
even the very ground was adorned and purified.
The radiance from between his eyebrows illuminated eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, all of which became like the color of gold, reaching down as far as the Avīci Hell.
Extending upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
This describes how the light traversed horizontally and reached its limit vertically.

Within all worlds, the six classes of sentient beings follow their destinies through birth and death; according to the conditions of their wholesome and unwholesome karma, they receive retributions that are either auspicious or inauspicious.
"All this is seen therein.
This passage describes the beginning and end of the six classes of ordinary beings. "The destination of birth and death" refers to where the mind tends.
"The conditions of good and evil karma" refers to the performance of deeds. "The excellence or inferiority of the retribution received" refers to the experiencing of the results.
Furthermore, I behold the Buddhas, the holy lords and lions, expounding the sutras that are subtle and supreme. Their voices are pure, emitting gentle sounds;
they instruct countless billions of bodhisattvas with profound and wondrous Brahma-voices, which cause all to delight in hearing them.
In each world, they preach the True Dharma through various causes and conditions and immeasurable parables, illuminating the Buddha-dharma and awakening sentient beings.
If there are those who encounter suffering and weary of old age, illness, death, and rebirth, they preach Nirvana for them, so that they may reach the end of all suffering.
If there are those with merit who have made offerings to the Buddha and aspire to the supreme Dharma, I speak of the Pratyekabuddha path for them.
If there are sons of the Buddha who cultivate various practices and seek unsurpassed wisdom, I speak of the pure path for them. Mañjuśrī, I abide here.
What has been seen and heard is thus; it includes thousands of millions of matters, and though they are numerous, I shall now briefly explain them.
This narrates the beginning and end of all Buddhas. As the sovereign among sages, he is called the "Sage Lord" (Śāstṛ). He preaches the Dharma with fearlessness.

Therefore, it is called "Lion. As the principle enters deeper and becomes more subtle, it is called "minute" (*sūkṣma*). As the expression emerges further and becomes more refined, it is called "wondrous" (*praṇīta*).
That which is proclaimed through word and meaning is entirely of a single characteristic and a single flavor; therefore, it is called "foremost" (*anuttara*). "Direct sound" refers to renown;
"sound with winding turns" refers to resonance (*svara*). Sound that is pure and clear is so because that which is spoken is immaculate.
Because it is the Dharma of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), the voice that can speak it is also pure, like the clashing of metal and the striking of jade.
"Gentle sound" refers to speech that is mild, supple, and compliant;
because that which is spoken is the gentle Dharma, the sound that speaks it is likewise gentle. This is because [other sounds] are impure, harsh, and painful.
These words teach the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and those of the Lesser Vehicle among gods and humans; yet, with pure and gentle speech, they teach the Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, the Brahma-voice uttered by the Tathāgata is profound, far-reaching, and subtle, such that it causes those who hear it to rejoice and leap for joy, forgetting all fatigue. Thus, these Lords of Sages, throughout the eighteen thousand worlds...
What is taught is entirely not the partial or inferior teachings; it is all the Great Vehicle’s impartial and correct Dharma.
Furthermore, fearing that [beings] might be unable to comprehend it due to its profundity, remoteness, and subtlety, he again uses various causes, conditions, and parables to guide them in detail.

One must strive to cause the Buddha-dharma to shine brightly, like raising the sun and moon to hang over the myriad worlds, so that all sentient beings may open their understanding and attain awakening, ultimately returning to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Therefore, for those who take joy in renouncing birth and death and seek nirvana, one preaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, causing them to exhaust suffering and attain happiness. For those who cultivate pure merit and seek [liberation],...
Regarding the "Supreme Dharma" (*abhyudgata-dharma*): it refers to teaching the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas, enabling them to sever their conditions and attain a superior nature.

It is called the "Supreme Dharma" because it surpasses the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). For those who cultivate the myriad practices and seek the Buddha-wisdom, he teaches the pure path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), enabling them to enter the sublime through awakening.
From the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī," it says: "As for what I see regarding the birth and Buddhahood [of beings], from beginning to end..."
They are numerous and inexhaustible; I have now merely provided a brief outline of their general character.
I see that in that land, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges seek the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions; some practice giving.
Gold, silver, coral, pearls, maṇi-jewels, tridacna, agate, diamonds, and all manner of rare treasures;

male and female servants, carriages, and precious decorated litters—joyfully giving these away, they dedicate the merit toward the Buddha-way, vowing to obtain this vehicle, the foremost in the three realms.
Praised by all the Buddhas, there are some bodhisattvas who give away precious chariots drawn by four horses, adorned with railings and flowered canopies;
furthermore, one sees bodhisattvas who give their own flesh, hands, feet, wives, and children, seeking the unsurpassed path; and again, one sees bodhisattvas...
With head, eyes, body, and life, they joyfully delight in giving, seeking the wisdom of the Buddha.

Mañjuśrī, I have seen various kings go to the presence of the Buddhas to inquire about the unsurpassed path; they then abandon their pleasant lands, palaces, ministers, and concubines, and shave off their hair and beards.
"And yet they wear the Dharma robes.
This passage describes the beginning and end of practicing the Path as those who have attained the Way through the Three Vehicles.

The two lines, "By various causes and conditions, they seek the Buddha-way," constitute the general description. The section beginning with "Some practice giving" and so forth constitutes the specific description; first, it describes those in the household life.
The Bodhisattva takes giving as the causal condition for entering the Way. "Gold, silver, and so forth" refers to the seven treasures.
"Slaves" refers to those who perform service. "Vehicles" refers to the means for coming and going.
"Jeweled litters and carriages" means that he joyfully gives away carriages and litters adorned with various jewels. Having already given them, and...
Furthermore, one cultivates the Bodhisattva’s dharma of dedication and vows, relinquishing the vehicle of jewels to attain the Buddha-vehicle, so as to be praised by all Buddhas.
One does not wish for a golden carriage or a jeweled palanquin, which would merely be objects of envy for worldly people.
As for the "jeweled chariot drawn by four horses," one relinquishes the chariot and simultaneously relinquishes the horses. As the *Shi* says, "The fine horses, four of them. Therefore it is said:
The "four horses," the railings, and the flowered canopies are the ornaments of a chariot. "Xuan" (軒) means high;
it refers to the "xuan" in the term *xuánzhì* (to tilt forward or backward), signifying that [the vehicle] is high, broad, and magnificently adorned. All of the above are external embellishments.

Furthermore, there are those who seek the Buddha-way by sacrificing their own bodies, such as giving away their flesh, hands, and feet—examples including cutting off flesh to feed a hawk or casting oneself down to feed a tiger. Moreover, there are...

To seek the Buddha-dharma by relinquishing one's head, eyes, body, and limbs—such as the youth of the Snowy Mountains who gave up his entire body for the sake of half a verse—is what constitutes internal giving (*adhyātma-dāna*).
Furthermore, it refers to seeing various kings approach the Buddha to inquire about the Way and hear the Dharma.
Those who renounce their lands and leave the household life are exemplified by such individuals as Wondrous Adornment (*Suvarṇaprabhāsa*).
As in these various cases, there are those who renounce worldly treasures to seek the treasure of the Dharma; who renounce worldly vehicles to seek the Buddha-vehicle;
who renounce the illusory body to seek the Dharma-body; and who renounce pleasant lands to seek the Pure Land. All of these take giving as the causal condition for entering the Way.
Some see a bodhisattva acting as a bhikṣu, dwelling alone in quietude and delighting in reciting the sūtras.

Others see a bodhisattva who is courageous and diligent, entering deep mountains to contemplate the Buddha-way. Still others see one who has abandoned desire, constantly remaining in empty and secluded places.

They deeply cultivate meditative concentration and attain the five supernormal powers. Furthermore, they see bodhisattvas sitting in tranquil meditation with palms joined, praising the Kings of Dharma with ten million verses.
They also see bodhisattvas whose wisdom is profound and whose resolve is firm, who are able to question the Buddhas and, having heard their teachings, receive and uphold them all.
Furthermore, I see sons of the Buddha, fully endowed with meditative concentration and wisdom, who expound the Dharma for the multitude using immeasurable parables;
they delight in preaching the Dharma, transforming other bodhisattvas, shattering the hosts of Māra, and beating the drum of the Dharma. I also see bodhisattvas sitting in tranquil silence.

He did not take joy in being honored by devas and nāgas. Furthermore, he saw the Bodhisattva dwelling in the forest emitting light, rescuing those in the hells from suffering and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
He also saw the sons of the Buddha who never slept, walking in meditation within the groves, diligently seeking the Buddha-way.

Furthermore, I see those who possess the precepts, whose dignified demeanor is flawless and pure as a precious gem, seeking the path to Buddhahood. I also see sons of the Buddha who abide in the power of patience;
even when arrogant people revile them with foul language or strike them with blows, they are able to endure it all in their quest for the path to Buddhahood.

Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas who have abandoned all frivolous laughter and foolish companions, associating with the wise, single-mindedly eliminating distraction, and withdrawing their thoughts to dwell in mountain forests for hundreds of millions of years in order to seek the Buddha-way; or one sees Bodhisattvas [partaking of] fine delicacies and food and drink.

He offered a hundred kinds of medicinal decoctions to the Buddha and the Sangha; he gave exquisite robes and superior garments worth ten million, or even priceless robes, to the Buddha and the Sangha;
and for thousands of millions of billions of beings, he offered sandalwood jewel pavilions and various wonderful bedding to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Pure gardens with flourishing flowers and fruits, flowing springs and bathing pools—such as these he offered to the Buddha and the Sangha.
With various such sublime offerings, he gave with joy and without weariness, seeking the unsurpassed path. Or there were bodhisattvas who preached the Dharma of tranquility.
Through various instructions for countless sentient beings, some see the Bodhisattva contemplating the nature of all phenomena as being without dual characteristics, just like empty space;
others see the Son of the Buddha with a mind free from attachment, seeking the unsurpassed path through this wondrous wisdom.
This describes the causes and conditions for a renunciant bodhisattva entering the Way. Regarding "dwelling alone in a quiet and secluded place":
this refers to those who avoid the clamor and bustle of human society and prefer remote, tranquil, and solitary locations.

As for "using the recitation of sutras as a cause and condition for entering the Way," there was once the Duke Wenzhong of Ouyang, while serving in Luoyang, who went on a day excursion to Mount Song. He left behind his attendants and servants.

Leaving his mind unrestrained, he went forth and arrived at a mountain temple. Upon entering the gate, cultivated bamboos filled the courtyard; the frost was clear and birds were singing, the scenery vivid and bright.
Wenzhong rested upon the steps of the hall, where an old monk sat nearby reading a sutra with composure.

When Wenzhong spoke to him, the monk did not look back or respond much. Wenzhong marveled at this, asking, "How long has it been since you, O Daoist, have resided on this mountain? He replied, "It has been very long."

He asked again, "What sutra do you recite? He replied, "The Lotus Sutra. Wenzhong said, "Among the eminent monks of antiquity, when they faced the moment of life and death, they all departed with laughter and ease.
By what path did they achieve this? He replied, "It was simply through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*).
Wenzhong asked further, "Why is it that nowadays there is such silence and nothingness? The old monk smiled and said, "People of antiquity cultivated..."
"Mindfulness resides in concentration and wisdom; how could one be distracted at the moment of death? People today dwell in distraction at every thought;
how could they attain concentration at the moment of death? When Wenzhong heard this, he was so greatly startled that he did not even realize his knees were pressed against the ground.
"Vigor and diligence" means to advance straight ahead without fear—this is called vigor; to be courageous and ever more keen—this is called diligence. With a single mind, one does not...
To concentrate amidst distraction is called "refinement" (*jing*). To refine without indolence is called "progress" (*jin*).

In ancient times, those who lived alone in the mountains would contemplate the "critical phrase" (*huatou*) and give rise to the "doubting mind" (*yiqing*), contemplating with single-minded focus and harboring no second thought. This is what is meant by the saying:
"With a single staff, one goes freely wherever one pleases, straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand crags. Here, vigor (*vīrya*) is employed as the means for entering the Way.

Regarding the causes and conditions: furthermore, as seen in the passage "leaving desire," there are those who, while remaining as householders, are able to leave behind the defilements of desire in the lower realms and dwell in secluded places to cultivate the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), such as the four *dhyānas* or the eight liberations.

Those who attain the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)—namely, the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and mastery over the physical environment—do so by relying on the cultivation of the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) as the means for entering the Path.
Regarding the "causes and conditions": furthermore, one sees the Bodhisattva descend and enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), praising [the Buddha] with verses.
This is what is called "speaking in silence" and "silence in speaking. By means of *dhyāna*, he supports sublime wisdom; by means of pen and ink, he supports his true nature.

This act of borrowing the composition of verses to praise the Buddha serves as the cause and condition for entering the Path. For those whose wisdom is profound and whose resolve is firm, the worldly wise are unable to comprehend them.
It is said that his wisdom was profound; external inducements could not enter him. It is said that his resolve was firm:

throughout the six periods of the day and night, he took only the upholding of the Buddha-dharma as his task, with no other affairs whatsoever. "Able to question" means able to inquire with thorough scrutiny. "Upholding" means able to practice with earnest devotion.
Whenever there was doubt, he would inevitably ask; once asked, he would immediately act. To obtain one phrase and practice one phrase—this is what is called "knowing."
This refers to those who practice both [concentration and wisdom] in tandem. Regarding the phrase "borrowing the upholding [of the Dharma] as the causal condition for entering the Path":
following the section on the "perfection of concentration and wisdom," this clarifies that Bodhisattvas from the ninth stage upward, while in the midst of death, give rise to life;

they fuse concentration and wisdom together, and through the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), they employ immeasurable metaphors to preach and explain for the sake of the multitudes. Nevertheless, although these Bodhisattvas delight in preaching the Dharma...

This is not a mere idle or meaningless statement. For in this degenerate age, false teachers are as numerous as hemp and millet; they all praise lust, anger, and ignorance, while disparaging precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Unless one possesses the dual integration of concentration and wisdom, is endowed with eloquence, and has attained the eye of the true Dharma, [one cannot discern such things].

To let the Lion’s Roar be made would mean that the True Dharma of the Tathāgata becomes entirely the speech of Māra. Therefore, when a Bodhisattva delights in preaching the Dharma, it is certainly not for his own sake;
he desires solely to transform those of a similar kind, to crush the citadels of Māra, and to bring about universal peace with ease.
He does not allow demonic influences to cause delusion or confusion; having no other choice, he strikes the Dharma drum—how truly this is a heart that seeks to save the world!

This person, who borrows the preaching of the Dharma as a causal condition for entering the Way, sits in profound stillness beneath the tree, breaking through the rush-mat seat and piercing through the iron wall until white mold flows from his lips. When even the hundred birds have no place to seek him out, he then—
Even when the Buddha came to praise him, he did not deign to cast a glance; how much less could the veneration of devas and nāgas have moved his mind?
This refers to those such as Dharma, Laozu, and Lanzan. These are examples of those who used meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as the causal condition for entering the Way:
they emitted light while dwelling in the forest and rescued beings from the sufferings of hell, leading them to enter the Buddha-way. As it is said:
When the Bodhisattva of the Avataṃsaka emits light such that sentient beings in the eight difficult conditions who touch this light suddenly transcend the stages of the ten bhūmis,
this is an instance of a bodhisattva utilizing the emission of light to rescue those in suffering, serving as a causal condition for entering the Path.

Regarding the phrase "never having slept" and so forth: when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) becomes dull and heavy, it is called *tṛṣ* (drowsiness); when the five sensory faculties (*pañca-indriya*) are shrouded in darkness, it is called *nidrā* (sleep).
This refers to the practice of being diligent and tireless—day and night, three times each—seeking a definitive resolution. As the ancient masters said: "Stay alert; do not let others deceive you.
This is an instance of borrowing the practices of the sutras as a causal condition for entering the Way, as seen in the [text] titled *Jie jing xing*. Furthermore, one observes that...
Regarding "precepts and so forth": "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. Its purity is not matched by secluded mountain streams, and its whiteness cannot be compared to flying snow.
As the *Śīla-sūtra* says: "Precepts are like the sun and moon, and also like jeweled necklaces.
This refers to cases such as the swan and the pearl or the grass and the tether—these are instances where upholding the precepts is borrowed as a causal condition for entering the Path.
Those who abide in the power of patience can endure being reviled and beaten, even to the point of having their limbs severed joint by joint, just like the *kṣānti-ṛṣi* Sadāparibhūta and others.
Regarding those who rely on patience as the causal condition for entering the Way, [the text states] from "free from all frivolous laughter" downwards:
the Buddha does not smile for seven reasons; he does not smile out of desire, nor out of anger.
It was not out of delusion, nor negligence, nor private gain, nor for the sake of honor and nobility, nor for wealth and abundance;
he smiled only when bestowing the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) upon those of the Three Vehicles.

Even among worldly people, there is nothing they grant so recklessly as a frown or a smile—how much more so for a Son of the Buddha, who must certainly remain far removed from such things. Master An of the Song Dynasty’s Guangxiao Temple resided at Qingtai Temple.

While in meditative concentration, he saw two monks leaning against a railing and conversing. Initially, there were celestial deities who protected them; they listened for a long time and then dispersed.
Shortly thereafter, malevolent spirits spat upon them and reviled them, even sweeping away their footprints.

When he inquired about the reason for this, he learned that the two monks had first discussed the Buddha-dharma, then recounted their long separation, and finally spoken of their means of sustenance. From that point on, An never again mentioned such matters throughout his life.

Mundane affairs—let us set aside worldly matters for a moment. Since ghosts and spirits have already swept away their traces, how much more so those who gather in noisy crowds, engaging in rootless gossip, jesting, mocking, and deriding?
Because they cause harm, the foolish should be avoided; because they provide benefit, the wise should be approached.
Those who withdraw their thoughts to the mountain forests cannot be startled by crashing thunder, nor shaken by violent winds.
He is able to move. One thought-moment is ten thousand years; he is one for whom ten thousand years are but a single thought-moment.

This refers to those who borrow the practice of collecting the mind as a causal condition for entering the Way, such as Huichi and others. [They regard] food, drink, medicine, clothing, and bedding [as mere requisites].
"Even to gardens and bathing pools" refers to taking offerings made during the four seasons as the causal conditions for entering the Way.
"Expounding the Dharma of quiescent extinction through various instructions" means that the methods for teaching people do not consist of only a single path.
For example, like the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who universally predicted the Buddha-nature of the fourfold assembly; or like Deshan and Linji, who used the staff and the shout as the Buddha.

As for these matters—even such acts as rolling a ball, dancing with a ritual tablet, blowing on a tuft of cloth, or raising a whisk—all are instances where the Way is present before one's eyes, leaving no room for words;
hence the term "various. This refers to those who borrow the single-pointed holding of the upward direction as the causal condition for entering the Way.

As for "contemplating the nature of all dharmas": contemplating their characteristics reveals them to be fundamentally false, while contemplating their nature reveals it to be fundamentally true; thus, nature and characteristics are non-dual.
It is like empty space. This taking of the contemplation of the mind as the causal condition for entering the Path means that the mind has no attachments:

it does not seek by attachment to the Buddha, it does not seek by attachment to the Dharma, and it does not seek by attachment to the Sangha. It does not follow conditions externally, nor does it dwell in concentration internally;
the mind has no expectations. This is called seeking the Unsurpassed Way. This takes sublime wisdom as the causal condition for entering the Path.
As for the conditions, Mañjuśrī, there are also bodhisattvas who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to the relics.

Furthermore, they see sons of the Buddha constructing innumerable stūpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which adorn the realms; these jeweled stūpas are sublime and measure five thousand yojanas in height.

It was exactly two thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Each stupa and temple featured a thousand banners and pennants, with jeweled canopies draped like lattices and precious bells chiming in harmony.
Gods, dragons, spirits, humans, and non-humans constantly made offerings of incense, flowers, and musical performances.
Mañjuśrī, for the sake of making offerings to the śarīras, the sons of the Buddha adorned the stūpas and temples;
the realm became naturally extraordinary and wondrously beautiful, like the king of celestial trees with its flowers in full bloom.

This verse refers to the construction of stupas and temples after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa to enshrine his relics. "Each with a thousand banners and streamers" describes the ornamental adornments of the stupas.
"Jewels interlaced below" indicates that outside the banners and streamers there are canopies, and outside the canopies there are further ringing bells.

"For the sake of making offerings" means that the stupas and temples were adorned specifically for the purpose of honoring the relics; it is because of these stupas and temples [that such merit is obtained].
Because it is thus adorned, the realm itself is also naturally distinguished, magnificent, and exquisite.
The adornment of stupas and temples within the realm is like the adornment of flowers upon the celestial king of trees (Kalpavṛkṣa). As for this celestial king of trees:
This is the Pārijātaka tree of Śakra, Devendra. In the Sanskrit language, it is called Pāriyātra.

The tree is one hundred yojanas high, its branches and foliage cover fifty yojanas, and its fragrance is perceived for fifty yojanas. During the summer months, the sons of the gods rest and take their ease beneath the tree.

The Buddha emitted a single ray of light, and I, along with the assembled multitude, beheld this realm in all its various and exquisite splendor. Such is the supernatural power and rare wisdom of the Buddhas;
they emit a single pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands. We have witnessed this and attained what we have never experienced before.
"O Mañjuśrī, Son of the Buddha, we pray that you resolve the doubts of the assembly. The fourfold congregation looks up to you with joyful reverence, as do I.

For what reason has the World-Honored One emitted this radiance? O Son of the Buddha, please answer at this time; resolve our doubts and bring us joy. What benefit does this emission of light provide?"
The Buddha sits at the site of enlightenment. Is he about to preach the sublime Dharma he has attained? Or will he bestow a prophecy?

He reveals the various Buddha-lands, adorned and purified with myriad jewels, and causes us to behold the Buddhas. This is no small matter. Mañjuśrī, you should know that the fourfold assembly, the nāgas, and the spirits are all gazing intently at you, wondering what you will say.
This refers to what was seen within the light of this knot, which was requested for clarification. It says: "The Buddha emitted light from his brow;
I and the great assembly, receiving this radiance, saw eighteen thousand worlds, variously wondrous and sublime. We also know that this light..."
This arises from the spiritual power and the power of wisdom of all Buddhas;
it is rare in the world, and thus they are able to emit a single pure light that illuminates immeasurable lands. Yet we have never seen this before, and now we are able to behold it.
How could we not feel fortunate? Yet, we do not know the causes and conditions for this, and thus all harbor doubts.
Since you, O Benevolent One, have long attended upon the Buddha and are his son, you must have personally witnessed it and surely know the causes and conditions behind it.
We pray that you will resolve these doubts for us; furthermore, the fourfold assembly looks up to you with joyful anticipation, gazing intently at you.
We two—meaning myself as well—do not know the reason for the World-Honored One’s emission of light; at this time, we have likewise fallen into a web of doubt.
We gaze upon you, O Benevolent One; Son of the Buddha, you must now provide a decisive response to resolve the doubts of the assembly and to resolve my own doubt, so that joy may arise.
Furthermore, harboring my own conjectures and uncertainties, I offer this indirect inquiry: I do not know.
By what Dharma does the Tathāgata wish to benefit people that he now manifests this radiance?

Perhaps it is the Great Matter realized by the World-Honored One beneath the Bodhi tree when he beheld the morning star—a wondrous Dharma that, until now for forty years, has been kept secret and not spoken, never yet bestowed upon others. Could it be that today’s emission of light is for this very purpose?
Regarding the sublime Dharma obtained within the Bodhimaṇḍa that you have kept secret and not spoken: do you now wish to speak it to others?
Or do you wish to bestow upon others that which has never before been granted to anyone, so that they may receive and uphold it without loss?
Otherwise, why would you manifest eighteen thousand worlds within your light and cause us to behold all the Buddhas?
Indeed. Therefore, we know that the emission of light today is certainly not due to some minor cause.
Nevertheless, as for my own conjecture, the principle may well be so; yet, because I have not witnessed it with my own eyes, I still harbor some doubts.

Thus, the fourfold assembly, the nāgas, and the spirits all refrain from looking toward me and instead gaze upon you, O Venerable One. I pray that you will explain and resolve this for their sake. Ultimately...
"For what purpose has this light been emitted?
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and the other great beings, sons of good family:
"As I contemplate it, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, now intends to proclaim the Great Dharma, to rain down the Great Dharma-rain, and to blow [the Great Dharma-conch]."
“Blowing the Dharma conch, beating the great Dharma drum, and expounding the great Dharma principles”—this is the response led by Mañjuśrī.
Maitreya said: “The wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha while seated at the site of enlightenment—is it for the purpose of preaching this, or is it for bestowing a prophecy?
He then fully recounted the entire matter of the World-Honored One’s emission of light. Now...
Mañjuśrī spoke again: "As I contemplate it, you should preach the Great Dharma," and so forth.
He then once more annotated the light, employing what is known as "direct pointing and indirect guidance," "striking from the left and right," and "the testimony heard through a wall.
As for those who rain down the Great Dharma rain: forty years ago, the three types of grass and two types of trees were irrigated according to the seasons; now, he intends to...
The rain of the Dharma, which is equal and of a single flavor, moistens and nourishes all beings. Thus, the subsequent passage states:
"The single-flavored rain produced by those clouds falls equally at one time, its moisture universally suffusing [all].
As for "blowing the great Dharma conch," forty years ago he used various parables, causes, and conditions to guide, encourage, and exhort; now, he wishes to use a single...
With his voice, he universally addresses the great assembly. Thus, the subsequent passage says: "I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, and so forth;
with a single voice, I proclaim this meaning. As for "beating the great Dharma drum":

forty years ago, he beat the drum of skillful means to urge on sentient beings attached to desires so that they might attain the fruits of the Two Vehicles. Now, he wishes to beat the drum of lethal poison to urge them on.
To lead those who are indolent and followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) to the place of the Jewel, the subsequent passage states: "I now declare for you the most ultimate reality;
none of the assembly of Śrāvakas have attained final Nirvāṇa. This refers to the Great Dharma teachings which were kept secret and not disclosed during the forty years prior;
now, before an assembly of hundreds of thousands of humans and devas, he intends to reveal them completely, as if placing them upon a full platter. Therefore...

The following passage states: "The twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become buddhas; if there are those who hear this Dharma, not one among them shall fail to attain buddhahood. This is precisely what that means.
"Good sons, in the past I have seen this omen among the Buddhas of the past: after emitting such light, they immediately preached the Great Dharma.
Therefore, you should know that the present Buddha’s manifestation of light is likewise so;
desiring to cause all sentient beings to hear and know the Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe, he has manifested this omen."
This is to cite the past as evidence for the present. Those who have witnessed this auspicious omen say that it is not a matter of mere conjecture, nor is it hearsay;
rather, I personally saw it with my own eyes in the presence of past Buddhas.
After such light was emitted, they immediately preached the Great Dharma; therefore, I infer that it must likewise be so now. Regarding what occurred forty years ago...
It is said that because there are five natures based on the nature of these three vehicles, people easily believe it.

However, if one says that the three vehicles are the one vehicle, or that the five natures are a single nature, this is difficult for people to believe. Ordinarily, it is only said that the Buddha alone has attained perfect enlightenment;
today, to say that even the Arhats of the Hīnayāna shall all become Buddhas is difficult for people to believe. Ordinarily...

It has only been said that one attains Buddhahood after practicing for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; therefore, the teaching that "the mind of this very day is itself Buddha" is difficult for people to believe.

Now, before this assembly of devas and humans, I wish to expound this difficult-to-believe Dharma, desiring to cause the great multitude to know the principle that "this very mind is itself Buddha," wherein there is neither two nor three. It is for this reason that I manifest these auspicious signs.
"O sons of good family, in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata."

The Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, proclaims the True Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end;
its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is exquisite, it is pure and unadulterated, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure, holy life.
For those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he teaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to deliver them from birth, old age, and sickness.
He attains death, which is ultimate nirvana. For those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, he teaches the Dharma corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination.
For all bodhisattvas, he teaches the six pāramitās, enabling them to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and achieve the knowledge of all modes.
This passage introduces the Lamp of Primordial Radiance (*ādityajyotir-dīpa*), which first expounds the Three Vehicles and subsequently the ritual of the One Vehicle.

"Sun, Moon, and Lamp" is a specific epithet for his radiance; because this Buddha’s light continues unceasingly day and night—like the sun, the moon, and a lamp—the name "Sun-Moon-Lamp-Radiance" symbolizes his virtue, namely, his mastery of the way that penetrates both day and night.
It is this very one who possesses such knowledge. "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One) is a general title; it refers to one who has come from the path of reality to achieve perfect enlightenment.

"Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings) means that having perfected the Way and completed all virtues, he is worthy of receiving offerings. "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly All-Knowing One) means that not even a single speck of dust remains unestablished, while all myriad virtues are fully present.
"Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna" (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct) means that both merit and wisdom are adorned, and the realization of conduct is brought to its ultimate limit.

Therefore, the Sugata is so called because he possesses mastery over the flow [of existence] and is honored everywhere. The Knower of the World is so called because there is nothing among the affairs of the three worlds that he does not know.
The Unsurpassed Being is so called because he transcends the myriad phenomena to stand alone at the forefront, surpassing all sages to emerge preeminent.
The Tamer of Men is so called because he restrains all non-Buddhists and subdues the hosts of Māra and his enemies. The Deva...

The Teacher of Humanity is so called because he serves as a model for the people and provides a standard of emulation for Śakra and Brahmā. The Buddha is so called because his own awakening and his awakening of others have brought the perfection of enlightened practice.

The World-Honored One is so called because he fully encompasses the ten titles and stands uniquely supreme among those who transcend the world. Regarding the preaching of the True Dharma (*saddharma*):
it was previously referred to as the "Wondrous Dharma" and also as the "Great Dharma"; here it is called the "True Dharma. Although the names differ, they all [refer to the same reality].
It is a single dharma; it is, in fact, all dharmas. Therefore, it is called "Great. It is free from all marks; therefore, it is called "Right.

It is neither identical with nor separate from [all dharmas]; it is both identical and non-identical. Therefore, it is called "Wondrous. It is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end. These three instances of the word "good" [constitute its excellence].
This is not the goodness of good and evil; it is the goodness of ultimate goodness. It points to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Although the teachings differ across the three periods, they all without exception return to the ground of ultimate goodness. It is like eating honey: both the center and the edges are sweet.
Yet, because its meaning is profound and far-reaching and its expression is skillful, people simply fail to understand it. This is why it is profound and far-reaching, and skillful.
"Exquisite" means that immeasurable meanings all converge into a single meaning, and immeasurable sounds are all but a single sound, because they are pure, unitary, and unmixed.

From the beginning, middle, and end, they are entirely complete. Being primordially devoid of substantiality, it is the characteristic of the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*)—pure, clear, and free from blemish.
Thus, the "Chapter on Brahma-Conduct" asks: "Is the body the Brahma-conduct? and so forth, up to: "Is the precepts the Brahma-conduct?"
Thus one practices. Observing in this way, one grasps nothing regarding the body, clings to nothing in cultivation, and dwells nowhere in phenomena.
The three periods of time are empty and still; there is no agent of action and no recipient of retribution. This world does not shift.
That world is unchanging and immutable. In this regard, what dharma is called "holy life" (*brahmacarya*)? From where does the holy life come?
To whom does it belong? What is its essential nature? By whom is it performed? When one investigates in this manner, the holy life is found to be unattainable.
If bodhisattvas can accord with such contemplative practice, they will not [cling] to any phenomena.
Two understandings arise: all Buddha-dharmas swiftly manifest before one; at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one attains perfect enlightenment.

This is what is meant by "cultivation and realization are not non-existent, yet defilements cannot reach them"—this is called the pure and white Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*), and it is also called the Samādhi of One Practice.
Thus Baizhang said: "From the beginning, this has been that very thing; there is no need to know it or understand it."
"It is he, yet it is not he. Yunyan said: "To manifest patterns and colors is precisely what constitutes defilement. He further explained:

"That which is called 'the beginning' refers to the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; 'the middle' refers to the Dharma of Dependent Origination; and 'the end' refers to the Dharma of the Six Perfections.
These three vehicles of the Dharma are all words employed for a single occasion to respond to the capacities of sentient beings. In reality, [the Buddha] intended to..."
They all attained Bodhi and perfected the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is why [the teaching] is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
Next, there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa. Next, there was another Buddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa.
These twenty thousand Buddhas all shared the same name: Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp). They also shared the same clan name: Bharadvāja.
Maitreya, you should know that from the first Buddha to the last, they were all of the same name, Candrasūryapradīpa, and were fully endowed with the ten titles.
The Dharma they preached was excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end.

This refers to twenty thousand Lamp-Light Buddhas who attained Buddhahood in succession, whose names and surnames were identical, and even the protocols for their preaching of the Dharma were the same.

That is to say, as one lamp is extinguished, another continues; because the lamps succeed one another without end, they are "that which has spatial form," yet that which is not form has never possessed north or south.
They are "that which has temporal duration," yet that which is not duration has never... [possessed] qi.
There have been days and nights; thus, one born in Qi dreams only of the state of Qi.
Later, having gone to Song, then to Qi, then to Liang, the mind has no fixed location. That which is dreamed during the night may extend beyond the night; the mind has no temporal limit.
That a single light shines eastward across eighteen thousand worlds is what is meant by the mind having no fixed location. This transcends...
Infinite, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa.
Twenty thousand Buddhas all shared the same surname and attained Buddhahood in succession; this is what is meant by "the mind has no time.
Therefore it is said: "The ocean of infinite lands is not separated from the tip of a single hair; events from kalpas as numerous as atoms exist only in the present."
As for that last Buddha, before he had left the household life, there were eight princes: the first was named Meaningful Intent;
the second, Good Intent; the third, Immeasurable Intent; the fourth, Jewel Intent; the fifth, Increasing Intent; the sixth, Doubt-Dispelling Intent;
the seventh, Resonant Intent; and the eighth, Dharma Intent. These eight princes possessed majestic power and sovereignty, each ruling over four continents.

When the princes heard that their father had left the household life and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they all renounced their royal positions and likewise followed him into the homeless life.
They resolved upon the Mahāyāna, constantly cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and all became Dharma-preachers.
They had already planted the roots of all goodness under ten million Buddhas.
This refers to the final period of Dharma-teaching under the lamp-lighter (Dīpaṃkara), the ritual of which was likewise the same. Speaking in terms of the actual events:
when Dīpaṃkara was a householder, he fathered eight sons, each of whom managed a portion of the family estate. When the father left the home life, the eight sons followed him into homelessness.
Father and sons were of one mind; where there is such a father, there must be such sons. This is what is called the "gait of the elephant king."
The elephant cub follows. To speak in terms of principle: before he left the household life, there were eight princes, each ruling over four continents.
Before Dīpaṃkara had yet resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he was entangled by the eight consciousnesses and obstructed by the four elements.

That is to say, first one is deluded as to the mind, becoming decisively confused that it resides within the physical body of the four elements. When one is deluded, one is deluded together with others at that time.

Furthermore, when Dīpaṃkara renounced the household life, his eight sons followed him in doing so; at the very moment they first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they attained perfect awakening.

The eight consciousnesses likewise follow in generating the Mahāyāna intention. This is what is meant by "if there is awakening, there is awakening together"—the mechanism of the simultaneous pecking and hatching.
As for the reason why the eight princes remained at home yet were all named "Mati" (Intention), it is because the eight consciousnesses are all termed "manas" (intention). It is just like this.

It is said: "The eye-intention, the ear-intention, and so forth. The visual consciousness perceiving forms is called the "intention with meaning" (yòuyì). The auditory consciousness, being sharp and acute, is called the "good intention" (shànyì).

The olfactory consciousness smelling fragrances is called the "immeasurable intention" (wúliàngyì). The gustatory consciousness skillfully expounding the jewel of the Dharma is called the "jewel intention" (bǎoyì).

The tactile consciousness perceiving touch is called the "increasing intention" (zēngyì). The mental consciousness cognizing phenomena is called the "doubt-removing intention" (chúyíyì). These seven consciousnesses take the eight [consciousnesses] as their objects.
The resonance that follows sound is called the "meaning of resonance. The eighth [consciousness], which contains and stores all phenomena, is called the "meaning of phenomena" (*dharmārtha*).
If, at the time of leaving the household life, these eight sons are all named the "Great Vehicle Meaning," it is because they have achieved a single, perfectly interfused precious awakening;
because those who constantly practice pure conduct gradually purify their deluded consciousness; and because those who all become Dharma masters together turn the wheel of the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Teaching of Innumerable Meanings*, a Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas and one which is protected by the Buddhas.
Having finished preaching this sūtra, he sat cross-legged in the midst of the great assembly and entered the *Samādhi of the Station of Innumerable Meanings*, remaining with body and mind unmoving.
At that moment, it rained *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers from the heavens.
Rohita flowers, mañjuṣaka flowers, and mahāmañjuṣaka flowers were scattered over the Buddha and the great assembly.
The entire world-system shook in six ways. At that time, within the assembly, there were bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās].

The upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as the various minor kings and universal monarchs—this great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
With joy, they joined their palms and gazed upon the Buddha with single-minded devotion. At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a ray from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
The light of the marks shone upon eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction, pervading them all without exception, just as these various Buddha-lands are seen now.
This clarifies that the auspicious omens of the past were identical to those of today.
Maitreya, you should know that at that time there were twenty billion bodhisattvas in the assembly who desired to hear the Dharma.

When these bodhisattvas saw this light universally illuminating the Buddha-field, they experienced what they had never known before and wished to understand the causes and conditions for which this light was manifested.
These words that raise such doubts are the same as those of today.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Wonderful Light who had eight hundred disciples. It was during the era of the Buddha Sun Moon Lamp Brightness.
Emerging from samādhi, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma*, a teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas.
