For sixty minor kalpas, he did not rise from his seat. Those in the assembly who were listening likewise remained seated in one place;
for sixty minor kalpas, their bodies and minds remained unmoving as they listened to what the Buddha spoke, perceiving it as if it were the duration of a single meal. At that time—
Among the assembly, not a single person—whether in body or mind—gave rise to weariness or fatigue.
This was because they saw that it was inevitable that after Dīpaṃkara-ratnarcis emitted his light, he would preach the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of Prabhāsa.
To speak in terms of the facts: Dīpaṃkara preached the Lotus Sūtra on account of Prabhāsa. Not...
Regarding the eight sons: it refers to meeting a swordsman on the road who then presents his blade. Therefore, the subsequent passage states:

"As I have taught the Dharma, only you are able to realize and know it. Speaking in terms of principle, the lamp’s brightness is the essence of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*), while the wondrous light is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
If one wishes for original enlightenment to achieve Buddhahood, it must necessarily arise through the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*); it does not occur otherwise.
Because it pertains to emotional consciousness. Regarding "the teaching of the Dharma for Bodhisattvas": this sutra does not fall into the hands of those belonging to other vehicles;

it can only be transmitted and received by those who are of extraordinary capacity. Regarding "that which is protected and remembered by the Buddha": those of the Lesser Vehicle consider themselves to have no share in it.
Furthermore, because he does not guard or dwell upon them, sixty minor kalpas are like the duration of a single meal.

To speak in terms of events: the Bodhisattva’s diligence is such that his mind has no dual thoughts; as when he is roused by indignation, he forgets to eat and neglects sleep, so that sixty minor kalpas are like the duration of a single meal.
To speak in terms of principle: the ten periods of past and present do not depart from the present moment of thought (*cittakṣaṇa*). Thought...
If there were no movement, how could there be time and kalpas? It is precisely because his body and mind were unmoving that he experienced no weariness.
After the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had preached this sutra for sixty minor kalpas, he [addressed] the Brahmās, Māras, and Śramaṇas.
In the midst of the assembly of brahmins, devas, and asuras, he proclaimed these words:
"This very day, at midnight, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa without remainder. At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa.
The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa immediately bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment, declaring to the bhikṣus: "This bodhisattva Guṇakośa shall next become a buddha, and his name shall be..."
Having purified his body, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, after bestowing this prophecy upon the Buddha,
entered the parinirvāṇa of Buddhas during the middle watch of the night.
This means that after the Lamp-Light (Dīpaṃkara) had finished preaching the sutra, he immediately announced his parinirvāṇa; after announcing his parinirvāṇa, he bestowed a prophecy (vyākaraṇa);
and after bestowing the prophecy, he entered parinirvāṇa. He first announced his parinirvāṇa to admonish those who are indolent; next, he bestowed the prophecy.

He handed over his family estate; thus the Dharma had a place to which it could be entrusted. As for "subsequently entering extinction," this refers to bringing his life to an end once the family estate has been entrusted.
Question: Why did Dīpaṃkara bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon Guṇakara, yet not bestow it upon the prince who was the heir to the succession?
Answer: If we speak in terms of historical events, Yao passed the throne to Shun, and Shun passed it to Yu; only those possessing virtue occupied these positions.
Although the Prince by Right of Birth (neishao wangzi) has planted the roots of virtue, he has not yet reached the treasury of virtue.

Therefore, the throne was abdicated to the Treasury of Virtue (de zang) to demonstrate the ultimate public spirit of the world and to honor the position of the Dharma King. If we speak in terms of principle, even the Prince by Right of Birth would still be unwilling [to accept it].
He occupies the position of rectitude; how much more so when it comes to receiving the transmission of the throne? Question:

Since the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached the Lotus Sūtra because of Prabhāsa, why did he not bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon Prabhāsa? Answer: That Candrasūryapradīpa succeeded one after another in attaining Buddhahood was due to Prabhāsa.
That Candrasūryapradīpa preached the Lotus Sūtra was likewise due to Prabhāsa. If Prabhāsa were to receive...
If the Dhyāna-prince were to fall into the extremes of beginning and end, his light would not be called "wondrous.

Since he has fallen into the extremes of beginning and end, he certainly could not continue the lamp-light to achieve both a beginning and an end; nor would the lamp-light have been used by him to preach the Lotus Sūtra.
Therefore, one who can continue the lamp-light to achieve both a beginning and an end must surely rely upon the wondrous light that is neither beginning nor end.
This is why the Lamp of Wisdom preached the Lotus Sūtra; it was also necessarily due to the wondrous light that is without interruption.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for a full eighty minor kalpas, expounding it for the sake of others.
The eight sons of the Buddha Sun-Moon-Lamp were all disciples of Wonderful Light; through Wonderful Light’s instruction and transformation, he caused them—

They were firm in their resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. After these princes had made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, they all attained the Way of the Buddha. The last one to attain Buddhahood was named Dīpaṃkara.
This clarifies that Wondrous Light (Prabhāketu) continued the light of Lamp-Light (Dīpaṃkara) and served as his teacher in the past.
Had there not been Wondrous Light, the Buddhas of the past would not have attained Buddhahood; thus, all sentient beings realize the essence of lamp-light.
Yet, because they do not take Wondrous Light as their teacher, though they are perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) throughout the day, they have never truly experienced perfect enlightenment.
Question: Why did the Eight Princes not take their father as their teacher, but instead took Wonderful Light (Prabhāketu) as their teacher?
If we speak in terms of worldly affairs, the ancients would exchange their own sons for the purpose of instruction; thus, Rāhula took Śāriputra as his teacher, honoring the position of the master.
If we speak in terms of principle, the Eight Princes took Dīpaṃkara as their father, who is their fundamental essence. As for Wonderful Light...
The Light is the Teacher; it is one’s fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Although the practitioner initially attains this fundamental [wisdom], its power is not yet sufficient.

One must necessarily rely upon the fundamental wisdom through the labor of forty-two stages of refinement. Only when the dust has been eliminated and the defilements exhausted does one advance to the Sublime.
That the eight consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom—is this not the power of the Sublime Light? As the saying goes: "The father gives birth..."
The Sun, Moon, and Lamp-Brightness (Sūryacandrapradīpa) exist therein; the Master completes it through the Wondrous Light (Prabhāsa).
Thus we know that the Wondrous Light is neither cause nor fruit, yet it can function as both cause and fruit. The *Avataṃsaka* calls it the Wisdom of Universal Radiance;
the *Laṅkāvatāra* calls it the Noble Wisdom of Self-Awakening. When Śākyamuni’s single ray of light shines eastward, he reveals this Wondrous Light. He speaks of no...
The *Pramāṇasūtra* states that when preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it was this Subhāṣita (Wondrous Light) who was spoken of.

As the Buddhas Candrasūryapradīpa (Sun-Moon-Lamp Radiance) succeeded one another in attaining Buddhahood, they transmitted this Subhāṣita. This Subhāṣita is that which a practitioner should focus their intent upon;

it must not be hastily understood as mere words or conventional language. Thus, the single lamp of Candrasūryapradīpa is divided into two lamps—the single lamp [of the Buddha] and [the lamp of the disciple].
He bestowed this lamp upon Guṇasaṃbhava as the Dharma King; the Single Lamp bestowed it upon Suprabha as the Dharma Master.
Suprabha then transmitted this lamp to the past Dīpaṃkara; Dīpaṃkara, in turn, bestowed it upon the present Śākyamuni;
and Śākyamuni further transmitted it to the future Maitreya. Thus, all Buddhas of the three periods of time rely upon the Sun, Moon, and Lamp-Light.
Lamp-King, with Sublime Light as his lamp-master, has continued this lineage of lamps unbroken until the present day; all of this is due to the power of Lamp-King and Lamp-Master.
These two—the Dharma-King and the Dharma-Master—constitute the transmission of the Tathāgata’s spiritual lineage.

The fundamental intent behind the appearance of all Buddhas in the world lies precisely here. If one clarifies this point, the subsequent text will be resolved as easily as slicing through meat with a sharp blade.

Regarding the term "Dharma King": one is called a Dharma King because there is no path not realized, no virtue not perfected, no merit not completed, no practice not fulfilled, and no station not reached to its ultimate limit.

A Dharma Master is one who studies the Way of the Dharma King, cultivates the virtues of the Dharma King, practices the conduct of the Dharma King, turns the wheel of the Dharma King’s sutras, observes the precepts of the Dharma King, and enters [the state of the Dharma King].

The meditative concentration of the Dharma King; the wisdom of the Dharma King. Having thus passed through immeasurable kalpas until one’s merit is perfected and practice is fulfilled, one who subsequently succeeds to the rank of the Dharma King is called a Dharma Master.

Therefore, the position of Dharma Master is the foundation for entering the rank of the Dharma King. It is said: "If this is so, then one should first confer the rank of Śrāvaka Dharma Master, and next..."
To bestow the rank of Dharma King would be the proper sequence. Why, then, is the rank of Dharma King bestowed upon him directly? It is said:
By bestowing the rank of Dharma King first, one intends for him to perform the duties of a Dharma Master; it is not yet the time for him to succeed to the throne of the Dharma King.
Regarding those who do not enter [the path] by means of a Dharma Master, the subsequent passage records the prophecy granted to Śāriputra:

"In a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas have passed, you shall make offerings to several hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, uphold the True Dharma, and fulfill the path practiced by Bodhisattvas (this is the station of the Dharma Master). You shall then attain..."
He shall become a Buddha named Huaguang (Flower Radiance; this refers to the rank of Dharma King). He bestows a prediction upon Kāśyapa, saying:
"In a future age, you shall behold three hundred trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and you shall serve, provide offerings to, revere, respect, and praise them."
To widely proclaim the immeasurable path and Dharma of all Buddhas (this is the rank of Dharma Master); to attain Buddhahood in one's final body (this is the rank of Dharma King).
Thus, one knows that the rank of Dharma King must be entered through the Dharma Master.
Therefore, the subsequent passage in which five hundred arhats and eight thousand bhikṣus vow to uphold this sutra in other lands constitutes their initial vow.
This is the practice of the Dharma Master’s duties. Question: "The positions of Sovereign and Master are worldly conventions. Since the Buddha-dharma is equal, why employ them? Answer:
"If there were no sovereign within the supramundane dharma, the Buddha-dharma would have no master. [Without one,] the eight classes of beings—devas, nāgas, and so forth—"
There would be no one to turn to for refuge. If the supramundane Dharma had no teacher, then the lineage of the Tathāgata’s Way would be severed and not continued.
Therefore, one who weighs and balances the principles of the Way is called a Dharma King (*dharmarāja*), while one who transmits and makes the Dharma flow is titled a Dharma Master (*dharmabhāṇaka*).
This is just as Confucius, possessing virtue but lacking the throne, was called the "Sage Teacher" (*shengshi*); whereas Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu possessed both virtue and the throne.

"Lung" (隆) refers to the title of a Sage-King (*cakravartin*). Question: The Gate of the Patriarchs (*zongmen*) teaches only that one should directly take up responsibility, realizing Buddhahood within one's own mind;
this is the end of it. What further Buddha is there to be accomplished? What further sentient beings are there to save?
Yet you now wish to practice the deeds of a Dharma Master for immeasurable kalpas and thus succeed to the rank of the Dharma King. Therefore, Sengzhi Da said: "The Buddhas of the three periods..."

"Buddha! The old woman east of the city did not rejoice upon seeing the Buddha. If this is so, then the patriarchal position far surpasses the position of the Buddha.

If one does not understand the words of the Patriarch, then taking up these four characters "directly" (*zhixia*) means that one has already taken upon one's own shoulders, as a single burden, the great causal matter of attaining Buddhahood and saving sentient beings.
It is just like Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou, who took the world as their own responsibility; this is because their faculties were great and their roots of faith were deep.
Because ignorance is slight and afflictions are thin, upon hearing the Great Dharma once, one directly accepts it;

thus, one is immediately able to give rise to compassion and exercise pity, entering the marketplace to extend a helping hand, receiving beings and benefiting living things, performing the work of a Dharma Master regardless of the duration of kalpas.
Walking with faith, one proceeds until merit is perfected and practice is fulfilled, only then entering wondrous enlightenment—what is called "the channel being completed when the water arrives."
If one were to say that the Patriarchs, having attained awakening, simply ceased all activity and had nothing further to do, how would this differ from the Lesser Vehicle?

Such a view slanders the Patriarchs. Observe those within the assembly—Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, Maitreya, Bhaiṣajyarāja, and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata—and all the great Bodhisattvas who, from kalpa to kalpa and birth to birth, practice the Bodhisattva path without yet resting; how could the Patriarchs have done otherwise?
Shutting one’s door and folding one’s hands, one might say, "I do not seek the Buddha; I do not deliver sentient beings.
Yet, masters such as Yunmen and Huangbo spoke these words precisely because they wanted people to apply effort at the very root of their own feet and not rely on others;
thus, they used such stern and rigorous language to inspire later generations. This is by no means...
This is the compassionate heart of an elder; how could one then say that the Buddha is insufficient to be accomplished? The meaning is this:
since even approaching the Buddha—the guide of the three realms—is not permitted, how much more so should one avoid approaching the various poisons of ignorance and afflictions?
This is what the ancient masters meant when they said: "Not approaching in the most secret places is what is called true approach. Regarding this...
As it is also said in the following passage: "To not associate with anything at all—this is called the first station of association.
People today lack even a ten-thousandth part of the capacity of the Patriarchs;

moreover, they have never even ventured into the gate of the Patriarchs' teaching, yet they force others to take up the burden. They do not realize that what they can carry is nothing but a heap of ignorant relics.
These bricks of affliction—when have they ever dreamed of the Patriarchs? Yet they dare to speak with great arrogance, saying:
"There is no birth to be delivered from; there is no Buddha to be realized. Formerly, the monk Haoyue asked Changsha: "Among the good spiritual friends throughout the world..."
"Have you also realized the nirvana of the three virtues? The monk said, "Virtuous One, you ask about the nirvana of fruition;

what about the nirvana of the causal stage? [The Master] said, "The nirvana of fruition. The monk said, "Even the good spiritual friends of the world have not yet realized it. [The Master] asked, "Why is that?"

“[I have] not yet realized it. The Monk said, “Your merit is not yet equal to that of the various sages. [The Master] asked, “If your merit is not yet equal to that of the various sages, how can you be called a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend)?
The Monk said, “One who clearly perceives the Buddha-nature may also be called a *kalyāṇamitra*.
[The Master] asked, “What is nirvāṇa within the causal state? The Master said, “Virtuous One, it is you. To savor carefully these few words of Changsha, they are for settling the mind.

It is a whole medicine capable of curing the maladies of madness that have persisted for a thousand ages. Thus, in the "Expedient Means" (Upāya-paṛiccheda) chapter, one sees the Tathāgata’s intention in appearing in the world;

This is the model for entering the rank of the Dharma King; therefore, I have disclosed it to others, speaking tirelessly and without ceasing.
Among his eight hundred disciples was one named Seeking Fame (Yaśaskāma), who was greedily attached to gain and offerings.

Maitreya, you should know this: who else could that Bodhisattva Wonderful Light have been at that time? It was none other than myself.
And as for the Bodhisattva Seeking Fame, he was none other than you.

This clarifies that Wondrous Light (Prabhāsa) was the teacher of the future Maitreya. Because his learning was broad but not profound, he is said to have "sought fame. Because he did not find the correct gateway, he lacked mastery.
Because he practiced for a day and neglected it for ten days, he forgot much of what he had learned.

Although he did not penetrate the sutras, he nonetheless cultivated various miscellaneous virtues; thus it is said that he "planted all manner of roots of goodness. When Maitreya descended, he pointed out and exposed [the truth], saying: "In the past..."
The wondrous light of the Sun is none other than Mañjuśrī of today; the one who sought fame in the past is none other than Maitreya of today.
You were present at that same assembly at that time—how could you not know this, yet instead come to question me?
Maitreya said, "Mañjuśrī, you should know. Mañjuśrī replied, "Maitreya, you should know. Thus these two elders deferred to one another.
This is because of their gravity. A question is asked: Both the Eight Princes and Qiuming took Miaoguang as their teacher;
yet why is there such a vast difference, like that between heaven and earth, regarding the speed with which they attained Buddhahood? It is because their application of mind was different.

When the Eight Princes first followed him into the monastic life, they immediately gave rise to the Mahayana aspiration and realized the principle that "the mind is itself Buddha," so they did not run outward.
However, because one exerts effort and practices with diligence from beneath one's own heels, progress is swift.
A bodhisattva who seeks fame, on the other hand, makes his livelihood out of words and letters; his mind is constantly indolent, so he forgets what he has just read.
This is what is meant by "discriminating names and characteristics without knowing when to rest," and thus it is slow. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If one attains the perfect faculties..."
The faculties are not yet perfected; days and kalpas increase exponentially. How true it is! A practitioner should take this as a mirror.

Now, seeing these auspicious signs, they are no different from those of old. Therefore, I reflect that today the Tathāgata shall preach a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wonderful Law*, the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas' mindfulness.

This is the concluding text where Mañjuśrī provides the answer. He states that the reason he must know [the Buddha] will preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is because the light he perceives today is no different from what he saw in the past; it is the light of the former [teaching].

The auspicious signs of today regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* should be understood in the same way. By using the past as a witness for the present, we know that the Wondrous Dharma will certainly be preached. At that time, Mañjuśrī, wishing to restate this meaning within the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"I recall a past life, immeasurable and incalculable eons ago, when there was a Buddha, the Honored One among Men, named Candrasūryapradīpa."
The World-Honored One expounded the Dharma, delivering immeasurable sentient beings and countless billions of bodhisattvas, causing them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom.
This verse shows that at the very beginning, in the Lamp-Light [Buddha-field], he preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, enabling them to attain the Wisdom of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Before the Buddha had left the household life, his eight princes, seeing the Great Sage renounce the world, also followed him to practice the holy life.
At that time, the Buddha preached the Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Immeasurable Meanings*, extensively analyzing it for the great assembly.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, he sat cross-legged upon the Dharma-seat in a samādhi called the "Abode of Immeasurable Meanings.
Heavenly *māndārava* flowers rained down, and celestial drums resounded spontaneously. The devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits made offerings to the Honored One among Men.
"All the Buddha-fields immediately trembled greatly.

This verse shows that at the end of the Lamp-Light [Buddha's] life, he left the household life, preached the sutras, entered meditative concentration, rained down flowers, and shook the earth— all identical to what occurs today.

The Buddha emitted a light from between his eyebrows, manifesting various rare and wondrous events. This light shone upon eighteen thousand buddha-fields in the eastern direction, revealing to all sentient beings the places where they undergo the retribution of their karma through birth and death. There were some who beheld those buddha-fields adorned with a multitude of precious jewels.
The color of lapis lazuli and crystal arises from the light of the Buddha’s radiance.

Therein one sees the hosts of devas and humans, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras, each making offerings to that Buddha. Furthermore, one sees all the Tathāgatas spontaneously attaining the path of Buddhahood.
The color of his body is like a mountain of gold; he is upright, majestic, and most subtle and wondrous.

Like a statue of pure gold appearing within clear lapis lazuli, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, expounds the profound meaning of the Dharma. In each and every Buddha-land, the multitude of śrāvakas is incalculable.
"By the light of the Buddha’s radiance, all those great assemblies were seen.
This verse refers to seeing the final lamp-light emitting rays and manifesting auspicious signs, which is identical to today. "Manifesting to all," and so forth.
Seeing that within the light the beginning and end of the six classes of ordinary beings appear as one and the same—this arises from the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
The character "see" (見) should be read as "should" (應); this is most intimate and profound.

To say that one can today see the Buddha-land and see the devas and humans is not due to another, but entirely due to the reflection of one's own single point of wondrous light; it is by this very light that they are seen.
"Clarification" (Ming) is precisely the root of attaining Buddhahood; therefore, when it resides within the Buddha-body, it is called "Buddha-light.

This point clarifies that even the offerings made by the eight classes of beings to the Buddha are likewise due to this light. Furthermore, as seen below, the vision of the Tathāgata’s attainment of the Way is identical to this.
Regarding those who naturally attain the Buddha-way: they simply emit this light and naturally become Buddhas, without depending on cultivation or refinement.
Within the Buddha’s light, one sees his golden body, majestic and subtle, just like a statue of pure gold appearing within clear lapis lazuli.
Below the World-Honored One, one likewise sees the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, all because of the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
As for those who saw that great assembly: when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, eighteen thousand lands and countless listeners all gathered together;
each was able to see one another because of this radiance, as their eyes gazed into one another's eyes.
This point refutes the śrāvakas. When they see forms and hear sounds, it is also by means of this light. An ancient said:
"You see it, and I also see it; why then do you not understand?"
There are some bhikṣus dwelling amidst mountain forests who diligently uphold the pure precepts as if guarding a bright pearl.
Furthermore, they see bodhisattvas practicing generosity, patience, and so forth, their number like the sands of the Ganges; this is due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
Furthermore, I see various bodhisattvas who have deeply entered various meditative concentrations; their bodies and minds are tranquil and unmoving as they seek the unsurpassed path.
Moreover, I see various bodhisattvas who know the mark of the quiescence of all phenomena; each within their own land, they preach the Dharma to seek the Buddha-way.
This verse describes the path practiced by bhikṣus and bodhisattvas; its beginning and end are likewise the same. This is due to the illumination of the Buddha’s light.
It punctuates and clarifies that the bodhisattva’s practice of the six pāramitās also proceeds by means of this light.
An ancient master said: "It is like a single field of land upon which anyone may plow and sow; there is not a single person who does not receive the power of this grace."
At that time, the fourfold assembly, seeing the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa manifest such great supernormal powers, their hearts were filled with joy,
and they each asked one another: "What are the causes and conditions for this?"
This verse means that the assembly’s arising of doubt is likewise the same. "Each asks one another" refers to each person deliberating within themselves, speaking to themselves.
The Honored One, revered by devas and humans, has just arisen from samādhi. He praises the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light: "You are the eye of the world; all turn to you for refuge and faith.
You are able to uphold the treasury of the Dharma. Just as I have taught the Dharma, only you can verify and know it."
After the World-Honored One had offered this praise, causing Wonderful Light to rejoice, he preached this Lotus Sutra for a full sixty intermediate kalpas without rising from his seat.
This supreme and wondrous Dharma that was spoken was entirely received and upheld by the Dharma Master Wonderful Light.
This verse follows the emission of light, at which time the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was preached; this demonstrates what is certain for the present.
This sutra is taught for those who have set forth upon the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*). It must be that Miaoguang (Wonderful Light) is capable of hearing the wondrous Dharma;
therefore, a student who wishes to hear the wondrous Dharma must first have their own Wonderful Light brought forth and developed, after which every word and utterance proceeds from it.
It flows forth from within my own breast; only then do its radiance and flames illuminate heaven and earth.

To praise Wondrous Light with the eyes of the world is like saying that it is not because of the eyes one cannot see forms, or that it is not because of Wondrous Light one cannot uphold the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
Because of the Dharma I have preached, only you, Wondrous Light, are able to realize and know it; therefore, by means of the True Dharma, I—

The Eye-treasury and the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* are entrusted to you. Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One first praise Wonderful Light (*Prabhāketu*) to cause him to rejoice, and only thereafter preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for him? Answer: This is the Buddha’s work in accordance with human sentiment.
Bringing all this forth at once—who could fail to feel joy and be able to take up and bear the Great Matter?
Therefore, even if one possesses wondrous light, if it does not cause that great joy to pervade the entire body, one cannot shoulder the Great Dharma.
Only when great joy pervades the entire body is one capable of undertaking this Great Matter. Thus, at the end of Śākyamuni’s...
Later, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, when the World-Honored One held up a flower to show the multitude, only Kāśyapa broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa; I now entrust them to you."
Having spoken this Lotus Sūtra and brought joy to the assembly, the Buddha immediately on that day addressed the multitude of devas and humans:
"The meaning of the true reality of all phenomena has already been explained for you; tonight at midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa."
"You must practice with single-minded diligence and abandon all negligence. Buddhas are exceedingly difficult to encounter; they appear but once in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
The sons of the World-Honored One, hearing that the Buddha has entered nirvana, each harbors grief and distress: 'How swift was the Buddha's passing!'"
The Holy Lord, King of Dharma, comforts immeasurable multitudes. When I enter parinirvāṇa, you may suddenly feel grief and fear;
yet this Bodhisattva Guṇagañja has already attained thorough penetration into the outflow-free reality of suchness. He shall next become a Buddha.
He was named Śuddhakāya. He also delivered immeasurable multitudes. That night, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
As when the fuel is exhausted and the fire is extinguished, his relics were distributed, and immeasurable stūpas were erected. The number of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs was like the sands of the Ganges.
"Redouble your diligence to seek the unsurpassed path.
This verse announces his passing and records his entry into extinction. Having first announced his passing, he caused Miaoguang to rejoice.
Furthermore, he caused the great assembly to rejoice; the Dharma-treasury had found its destination, and his mental and physical endeavors were complete. He then addressed the assembly, saying:
"The original intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world was to cause the great assembly to realize the meaning of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Now that I have finished expounding the true mark of all phenomena for you, you all have joyfully received and borne this. The original aspiration for my appearance in the world is now fulfilled."
"Kṣemaka, at midnight I shall enter parinirvāṇa. He further exhorted them, saying: "Although I have explained the path of liberation, I am merely a guide for you all.
Though you receive this with joy and gratitude, you must still exert yourselves and practice with diligence;
do not be negligent. Furthermore, Buddhas are difficult to encounter, like a blind turtle finding a floating log."
If the Buddha remains in the world, there is still something upon which to rely; if the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, there will be nothing upon which to rely.
You all should conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter, and you should believe the Tathāgata’s words of truth and reality;

do not give rise to indolence. [The passage] from "The World-Honored One descended" below is the verse of the prophecy. As for "the sons," they are the eight sons of Dīpaṃkara. When the noble sons heard the proclamation of his passing into extinction...
He harbored sorrow. The Dharma King, seeing him harbor sorrow, comforted him; this too is a Buddha-activity and a matter of human feeling.

From this point downward, the Buddha [speaks] in verse regarding his entry into parinirvāṇa. "As when the fuel is exhausted, the fire is extinguished" means that because the fuel is exhausted, the fire is seen to be extinguished;

yet in reality, the transmission of the fire continues, and one does not know its exhaustion. "One should redouble one's diligence" means that having received the Buddha’s entrustment, one increases one's efforts.
This Dharma Master Wondrous Light upheld the treasury of the Buddha’s teachings. During eighty intermediate kalpas, he widely proclaimed the Lotus Sūtra.
These eight princes were all converted and inspired by Wondrous Light; they have become firm in the unsurpassed path and shall behold countless Buddhas.
Having made offerings to all Buddhas, they followed and practiced the Great Way, succeeding one another in attaining Buddhahood and receiving successive predictions of enlightenment.
Finally, there was a God among Gods named Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the guide of all sages, who delivered and liberated immeasurable multitudes.
This verse indicates that Wondrous Light was the teacher of the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara. Regarding their successive attainment of Buddhahood:
Dīpaṃkara continues the illumination; light follows upon light without end.
At that time, this Dharma Master Wonderful Light had a disciple whose mind was constantly filled with indolence and who was greedily attached to fame and profit.
Seeking fame and profit without satiety, he frequented the homes of the noble and well-born; he abandoned what he had studied and recited, falling into forgetfulness so that his mastery was lost.

For these reasons, he was named Seeking Fame. He also performed various wholesome deeds, encountered countless Buddhas, made offerings to those Buddhas, followed and practiced the Great Way, and perfected the six *pāramitās*. Now he beholds the Lion of the Śākyas.
In the future, he shall become a Buddha named Maitreya, who will extensively deliver sentient beings in numbers beyond measure.
After that Buddha has passed into extinction, you, who were then indolent, shall be he. The Dharma Master Wonderful Light is none other than my own self now.

This verse concerns Wondrous Light (Prabhāsa), who will serve as the teacher for Maitreya in the future. "Frequently visiting the homes of the noble" means that worldly ties have not been severed and one pursues external things.
"Abandoning what has been practiced and recited" means that the mindfulness of the Way is slight while worldly sentiments are thick.
"Neglecting and forgetting so as to lack proficiency" means that the mind is not single-minded and one does not seek the Way deeply. Having attained... [the text ends].
Regarding those who see innumerable Buddhas: this refers to the eight princes whose resolve and mindfulness were firm. Having attained [the path], they saw the Buddhas;
seeking renown, they practiced various wholesome deeds and likewise saw the Buddhas. Although their cultivation of merit and wisdom differed, they all equally reached the point of seeing the Buddhas.
Having already seen the Buddha, one must certainly desire to make offerings to all Buddhas and practice the Way in accordance with them;
only then will one attain the dual adornment of merit and wisdom, perfecting one's power and completing one's conduct to become a Sambhogakāya Buddha. You were the one who was formerly indolent.
Those spoken of as those who redoubled their diligence after the extinction of Dīpaṃkara are none other than the Eight Princes. As for those who were indolent after his extinction:
"You yourself are that very person. Whether it be Maitreya and the eight princes receiving their predictions together in a single assembly,
or this being so remote that Śākyamuni personally received his prediction during the time of Dīpaṃkara while Maitreya received his prediction within Śākyamuni’s own assembly—
this vast distance exists because Śākyamuni constantly practiced with diligence.
"Maitreya is constantly indolent; therefore, practitioners should take the eight princes of Śākyamuni as their model and not emulate Maitreya.
I saw that the original auspicious light of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was like this; by this I know that the present Buddha intends to preach the Lotus Sūtra."

The present signs are as they were in the original auspicious omens; these are the skillful means of all Buddhas. Now the Buddha emits a radiance to assist in bringing forth the meaning of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
All you people should now know: join your palms and wait with a single mind. The Buddha shall rain down the rain of Dharma to satisfy those who seek the Way.
For all those seeking the three vehicles who harbor doubts or regrets, the Buddha shall eliminate and sever them, so that they are exhausted without remainder.

The first six lines of the verse praise what has been witnessed to clarify that he will certainly preach the Lotus Sūtra. The two characters "original light" (ben-guang) must be understood with great weight;
it means that sentient beings originally possess this radiance, and for this reason, he will certainly preach this sūtra today.
Thus we know that Maitreya’s raising of doubts was the Lamp of Compassion; Mañjuśrī’s leading the response was the Lamp of Wisdom;
Śrīgarbha’s receiving the prediction was the Lamp Illumining the World; and the succession of the eight princes to Buddhahood was the Inexhaustible Lamp.

Since the original lamp was fundamentally the Sun-Moon-Lamp-Clarity Buddha, it is said that the omen of the original light was such as this. That the present signs are like the original omens is precisely [the fulfillment of that].

This means that the light of the present Buddha is no different from the light of the Buddhas of antiquity. From "The present Buddha" downward, it clarifies that emitting light is a skillful means (*upāya*).
The two characters "assisting and eliciting" (*chū-fa*) do not merely exhaustively express the intent behind Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s emission of light;
rather, they fully articulate the intent of all Buddhas and the patriarchs of successive generations.

When Śākyamuni has not yet appeared in the world, regardless of whether one is an ordinary being or a sage, as long as one belongs to the realm of sentient beings, beneath each and every heel there is a venerable Ancient Buddha of Lamp-Light who radiates light day and night without ceasing; this is called the "original light" and the "original auspicious sign.
If this original light were absent within the realm of the hells, molten copper would be poured into the mouths [of the denizens], and boiling hot fires would rage.
In the mind, who is it that ascends the mountain of blades and traverses the forest of swords, enduring such agony?
In the realm of hungry ghosts, if there were no original light, who would be crying out for food with flaming mouths and needle-like throats?
In the realm of animals, if there were no original light, who would be those with fur and horns, leaping, galloping, and neighing? In the realm of asuras, if there were no original light...

With three heads and six arms—who would be the one to engage in wrathful combat? Within the heavenly realms, if this fundamental light did not exist, who would experience sensual pleasures or cultivate meditative concentration?
If the Buddhas lacked this fundamental light, who would attain perfect enlightenment and deliver sentient beings?
If the Bodhisattvas lacked this fundamental light, who would practice the six perfections? If the Śrāvakas lacked this fundamental light, who would realize cessation?

Who is it that performs spiritual transformations? The Pratyekabuddhas do not possess this original radiance. Who is it that seeks the supreme Dharma? Among gods and humans, there is no such original radiance.
Hearing a call, one immediately responds; seeing an object, one knows it at once. Raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye, turning, moving, bowing, or looking up—who is it that does these things?
Therefore, know that this radiance is inherently possessed and is manifested upon every single thing and every single phenomenon.
When holding a needle, it manifests upon the needle’s point; when raising a brush, it is revealed at the tip of the brush; when reading a sutra, it appears upon the sutra;
when carrying firewood or drawing water, it manifests within the firewood and water. Although it manifests everywhere, there is nowhere that does not receive this power of grace.
Yet you remain buried in the pit of the five aggregates and cast away in the armor of "nothingness," failing to give rise to doubt.
The mind does not know how to investigate; though it possesses vast and majestic spiritual power, it fails to employ it.
Thus, when putting on clothes or eating, one simply regards them as merely putting on clothes or eating. When engaging in informal discourse (*chàhuà*), one treats it as merely informal discourse.

Consequently, while every aspect is manifest, one misses the mark at every turn. Therefore, the World-Honored One exerted himself to emit this radiance, creating a model for the sake of [the practitioners].
People should recognize that within their own heels there is a trace of the primordial radiance of the ancient Buddha.
It is just like a single spark buried in ashes, unable to flare up. Today, the World-Honored One carries wood and grass to assist it in generating light and emitting flames;
therefore, it is called "assisting and developing. Not only does emitting light constitute assisting and developing, but so too does preaching.
The *sūtras* bestow predictions; there is nothing that does not assist in its awakening. It is not only Śākyamuni who assists in its awakening;
even the patriarchs of successive generations have all assisted in its awakening. Formerly, while Deshan was standing in attendance upon Longtan, Longtan said, "It is late and the night is quiet;
why do you not go down the mountain? The Master replied with a respectful farewell and departed. He then returned and said, "It is dark outside. Longtan lit a paper lamp for him.
Dongshan Shanzhao was crossing a river with his teacher, Longtan Chongxin. As the teacher reached out to steady him, Dongshan blew out the paper lantern, extinguishing its light.
At this, Shanzhao attained great enlightenment and prostrated himself. Longtan asked, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate yourself?
Shanzhao replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of all the old monks under heaven. At that time, Dongshan had blown out the paper lamp given to him by Longtan.
But tell me, what did he realize? It is not only the patriarchs of successive generations who assist in its awakening;
even frogs, earthworms, walls, and tiles serve to trigger your realization.
Thus, one knows that Xiangyan’s realization was not in the bamboo, Lingyun’s realization was not in the flower, and Jushi’s realization was not in the finger. Attendant...
The point of awakening does not lie in the whisker of cloth. Now, regarding the phrase "like the original auspicious sign":
the word "like" precisely means that the light of Śākyamuni today and the light of the ancient Buddhas are not far apart from one another.
A monk asked Yanguan, "What is the Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha? The Master said, "Bring me the pure water pitcher. The monk brought it.
When the water pitcher arrived, the Master said, "Place it back in its original position. The monk returned it to its former place and came back again to question him.

The Master said, "The ancient Buddhas have long since passed away; this is precisely that meaning. This passage serves as the introductory foundation for the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Upāya-paryāya).
It speaks of those seeking the three vehicles who harbor doubts and regrets in their hearts and cannot find peace, waiting—
The Buddha arose from samādhi and said, "I shall now shave it off for you all at once, and grant you peace of mind.
