Chapter Two: The Expedient Means (Upāya).
The verse says:
After withdrawing his radiance, what was he doing before the eight classes of beings? He sought to exchange the wish-fulfilling jewel for the money used to soothe a child's crying.
If even a single sentient being remains caught in the net of doubt, who can escape the miasma of their afflictions?
The void suddenly falls to the earth, and everywhere the blue heavens are revealed;
this chapter emits light. This is the expedient means of wordlessness. This chapter borrows verbal expression to clarify the expedient means of wordlessness.
Therefore, by using an expedient to explain an expedient, it is simply called an "expedient. This Dharma is not...
It may be shown through words and phrases as being characterized by quiescence, yet it cannot be described by language.
This Dharma is not something that can be understood through conceptualization or discrimination; it cannot be fathomed by the conscious mind.
Since it cannot be described by language nor fathomed by the conscious mind, names are established according to its intended meaning.
He established this title and gave a forced interpretation, saying: "The Buddha-vehicle is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; how could it be anything other than the ultimate?
Therefore, it is said that for those who have not yet opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and have not entered the One Buddha-vehicle, this One Buddha-vehicle is the truth."

This is not an expedient means. If, even when addressed as one, [the Buddha] does not establish it, and even the single word "Buddha" is not welcomed, then to speak of this as the One Buddha Vehicle is an expedient means; it is not the ultimate reality.

Thus we know that the division of the one into three in the past was certainly an expedient means, while the unification of the three into one today is the use of an expedient means to eliminate expedient means.
This, too, is a skillful means—namely, using a wedge to extract a wedge, or using words to dispel words. It is true that the One Buddha Vehicle is a skillful means;
even the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are skillful means. Therefore, one should know that the wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable, and cannot be grasped with a limited mind.
If one were to grasp today’s One Buddha Vehicle as being ultimately real, how would this differ from [grasping at] other views?

If one adheres to the three vehicles of former times, then it would follow that not only this single chapter is designated as a "skillful means" (*upāya*), but rather all twenty-eight chapters of this entire sutra are skillful means.

Furthermore, it would follow that not only this sutra is a skillful means, but all the *sūtras* of the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of scripture spoken over the forty-nine years [of his teaching] are likewise skillful means. Moreover...

It is not only all the sūtras that constitute skillful means (*upāya*); even the emission of light, the shaking of the earth, and the raining down of clouds of flowers and incense are none other than skillful means—they are all the "traps" (*śuān*) for reaching the truth (*tì*).
Formerly, Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty asked Chan Master Hongbian, "What is called 'skillful means'?
He replied, "Skillful means is the gateway of provisional ingenuity that conceals reality and covers up appearances. It is applied...
To receive those of middling and inferior capacity, employing skillful means to guide and instruct them is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Even if one were to speak for those of superior faculties, asserting that expedient means should be abandoned and only the Unsurpassed Way taught, this too is but discourse on expedient means.

This extends even to the Patriarchs, who forgot their achievements and ceased their labors; they likewise did not transcend the traces of expedient means. Thus it is said: "If you can realize before the sound, it is clearly a hawk."
Passing through Silla, he took charge beyond the words; this was already like being an unpleasant lacquer bucket.
Waiting for you to open your mouth and move your tongue—what could that possibly accomplish? Therefore, the subsequent text says: "I shall analyze and explain it for you.
The two characters "for you" (*wei ru*) are precisely words spoken according to the other's intent, as there was no other choice. Changsha addressed the assembly, saying: "If I..."
I have consistently upheld and proclaimed the religious teachings. Although the grass before the Dharma Hall is a fathom deep, having no other choice, I shall speak to you all:
the entire world of the ten directions is but a single eye of the śramaṇa; the entire world of the ten directions...
This śramaṇa’s entire body is the light of the ten directions; the entirety of the worlds of the ten directions is within his own light;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single person who is not himself.
I have always told you people: the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all sentient beings of the dharma-realm are the light of the Mahāprajñā.
Before this light has yet been emitted, where could you people possibly have gained full understanding?
Before the light was emitted, there were neither Buddhas nor sentient beings; how then could mountains, rivers, and lands have come into existence? That being so, what...
This is the true meaning. Wait for Mount An to nod its head, and I shall speak it to you.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi and addressed Śāriputra: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable;
the gateway to this wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter, beyond the comprehension of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

The following section is a general praise of ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*) and expedient wisdom (*upāya*), which corresponds to what the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* calls the "penetration of the principle" (*siddhānta-naya*) and the "penetration of the teaching" (*deśanā-naya*).
In the past, Fan Zeng was fond of Xiang Yu. When Zeng urged Xiang Yu to kill the Marquis of Pei (Liu Bang), he took advantage of the banquet held at Hongmen;
amidst the assembly, he repeatedly raised the jade pendant he wore, showing it to Xiang Yu three times. Xiang Yu remained silent and did not respond. The World-Honored One knew this...

The followers of the Two Vehicles adhere to the principle of a single liberation; therefore, the Buddha first preached the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* to shake them, which was a "ring" shown by means of speech.

Furthermore, knowing that they were abiding in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the World-Honored One next demonstrated the "Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings" to them, which was a "ring" shown by means of the body.
Moreover, knowing that they were dwelling within the realm of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the World-Honored One...
He emitted white light from his ūrṇā-kośa to awaken them; this was a demonstration of the meaning through the mind. Yet, what could be done about the non-response of those of the Two Vehicles?
An ancient worthy said: "The entire earth is this great gate of liberation; taking it by the hand and pulling them toward it, they refuse to enter—what can be done?
Therefore, the World-Honored One, unable to restrain his impatience, emerged from samādhi and, entrusting himself to all Buddhas, went forth to sell [the Dharma].
He manifests his own supernatural powers; therefore it is said that the wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable.
But how is it known to be so profound and immeasurable? Ordinarily, you are praised as the foremost in wisdom.
According to what you perceive with your own eyes, the body of the Tathāgata is sixteen feet tall, and within it there are eyes, ears, nose, and tongue.
There are hands, feet, shoulders, and the crown of the head; there are arms, calves, foreheads, and brows; there are spleens, flanks, chests, and bellies;

there are thighs, hips, cheekbones, and cheeks; there are teeth, gums, and palates; there are the hundred skeletal members and joints; there are the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor characteristics;
and there are countless pores—as described above—each of which is capable of performing immeasurable and boundless [deeds].

As for the Buddha’s deeds, let us set them aside for now. However, today I have briefly emitted a ray of light from the single pore between my eyebrows, which shines throughout eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction, penetrating from the highest heavens to the lowest depths, boundless and shoreless.
Even if you were to deliberate and measure it, you could not know its lower limit; how much less could you know that within each and every one of my countless pores?
Each possesses such radiance that it universally illumines the Dharma-realm and performs great Buddha-works.

Furthermore, how could one know that within each of the six-foot body’s eyes, ears, hands, feet, limbs, joints, bones, and flesh, there are likewise infinite rays of light, each performing great Buddha-works?
Moreover, how could one know that I possess immeasurable and boundless Tathāgatas who pervade the entire Dharma-realm?

He conceals his body; each individual body possesses immeasurable marks (*lakṣaṇa*), each mark possesses immeasurable secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), and each secondary characteristic possesses immeasurable colors.

Even the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, feet, shoulders, crown of the head, and so forth, are all immeasurable, and they entirely fill the ocean of worlds of the Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*) throughout ten billion worlds within a single thought-moment.
At the same time, they perform immeasurable and boundless Buddha-works. How could you possibly know this?
Furthermore, since you cannot even perceive the light emitted from a single pore within my sixteen-foot body, you certainly do not know the ocean of the Buddhas' most profound wisdom;
the expanse of their limitless knowledge is unfathomable. It is like a mere puddle in a cow's hoofprint...
Even the space within a mustard seed’s pore cannot be known; how much less could one know the profoundly deep great ocean or the immeasurable void?

Therefore, when Sudhana enters a single pore-land of Samantabhadra, he traverses worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields with each step. He proceeds in this manner until—
Even throughout the limits of the future, one cannot know the sequence of the oceans of lands within a single pore—their adornments, their formation, and even their destruction;
nor can one know the sequence of the oceans of Buddhas, from their arising to their passing away; nor, likewise, can one know the limits of the realm of sentient beings.
What is called the wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep, exceedingly profound, immeasurable, and boundless, just as has been described above.
This is the realm of the Tathāgata’s own realization, his own awakening, and his own enjoyment; it is only natural that you do not know it.
Since the various Buddhas attained enlightenment, for forty years they have opened the gate of wisdom.
To those among humans and devas with the appropriate faculties, they taught the ten wholesome dharmas; to those with the faculties of śrāvakas, they taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths;

and to those with the faculties of pratyekabuddhas, they taught the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. You all have already heard these repeatedly and practiced them thoroughly; now, each of you...
Among them, some have realized the fruit of a śrāvaka, and some have realized the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
You yourselves also claim to understand the Dharma of the Tathāgata, to have attained the path of the Tathāgata, and to have entered the gate of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;

yet in reality, you have never understood the Dharma of the Tathāgata, attained the path of the Tathāgata, or entered the gate of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. This is because you have merely been dwelling [in that state].
The grass hut is still outside the gate; therefore, it is the gate of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are likewise unable to know. Why is this?
Because the Buddha has personally attended upon countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas and has fully practiced the teachings of all those Buddhas.
The immeasurable dharmas of the path, characterized by courageous and diligent exertion, have brought forth a universal reputation and the accomplishment of profound and unprecedented dharmas.
This explains the reason why the true wisdom of all Buddhas is so profoundly deep and immeasurable.
When I say that my own wisdom is profoundly deep and immeasurable, such that you do not know it, is this not for no reason? It is because of my past...

Throughout his causal stages—through kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth—he has never been separated from the Buddha. He has taken the Buddha as his teacher and constantly followed the Buddha’s example in his studies.
Furthermore, the teachers he served were not merely one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas; he has previously attended upon hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of countless Buddhas.
If one serves a teacher but does not learn from them, it is as if they were not a teacher at all. One must learn from them...

If one follows the Way but does not practice it, it is as if one has not studied it at all. Thus, one takes a single Buddha as one's teacher, studies the entirety of that one Buddha’s Dharma, and practices the entirety of that one Buddha’s Dharma.

One serves hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of countless Buddhas, studies the entirety of those hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of countless Buddhas’ Dharmas, and practices the entirety of those hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of countless Buddhas’ Dharmas.

Dharma. Because I have studied thus with diligence and practiced thus with earnestness—studying ever more courageously and practicing ever more vigorously—not even a hair’s breadth of weariness or laxity has arisen in my mind throughout immeasurable kalpas.

Consequently, the fame of my courageous and vigorous exertion pervades the oceans of lands as numerous as atoms. Thus, I am able to accomplish that which all Buddhas have realized: the profound and...
One should measure this unprecedented phenomenon: that its roots are deep and its fruits are luxuriant, such that the name and the reality correspond.
How can you be like those who, within the Buddha-dharma, give rise to weariness and indolence, failing to produce even a single thought of joyful aspiration?
How can you be like those who sit in non-action without moving, intoxicated by nirvana and never awakening? As Zhuangzi said:
If the accumulation of wind is not thick, it will lack the power to support great wings.
Therefore, for those [wings] that span ninety thousand li, the wind must be beneath them. How profound this is!
What has been taught according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand in its underlying intent.

Śāriputra, since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings through various causes and conditions and various parables, employing countless skillful means to guide sentient beings and cause them to leave behind all attachments.
This explains why the provisional wisdom of all Buddhas is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. As for why my gate of wisdom is said to be difficult to understand and difficult to enter:
it is because, while in the stage of a causal practitioner, I studied to exhaust the path of Bodhi of all Buddhas;
I studied to exhaust the path of saving sentient beings of all Buddhas; and I practiced to exhaust the path of Bodhi of all Buddhas. I practiced to exhaust the [path of] all Buddhas...

This is the path for delivering sentient beings. Therefore, I shall take the depths of what I have studied and practiced over the three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of the past, and the depths of my own self-realization and self-awakening, and according to what is appropriate for each sentient being, I shall guide them by entering through their respective gateways.
If they are infants, I guide them according to the way of infants to make them rejoice;
if they are men, I advance them by means of the way of men to cause them to give rise to joy.
Yet they do not truly understand the intent behind what I have said. Why is this? Because since my attaining Buddhahood, I have realized the Dharma of equality and seen...
All sentient beings within the triple world are entangled by the threads of false conceptualization;

they are tethered at every turn and attached to everything everywhere. Therefore, I accord with their faculties and inclinations, employing various causes and conditions to release them from their adhesions, or providing various parables to untie their bonds, or extensively expounding upon the [Dharma].
He employs immeasurable and countless expedient Dharma-gates to guide sentient beings; there is not one that does not serve merely to extract nails and pull out wedges for them.
In truth, not a single dharma is ever given to anyone. Now, you all produce understanding based merely on the words.
To grasp a single good point and clasp it tightly to one's heart; to hold onto a single method and be smugly self-satisfied;
or to study the words of a single master and feel privately delighted—these are all like seeking a *huailiu* (a fine steed) upon a tethering stake for a donkey.
How could such people ever understand what I have taught?
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata has already fully perfected the *pāramitā* of skillful means, knowledge, and vision.
This pair of inquiries seeks the reason for the Tathāgata’s employment of the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate truth.

It states that the World-Honored One has exhausted his study of the Buddha-way and exhausted his practice of the Buddha-way, thereby accomplishing all unprecedented dharmas. Such was the original intention of the Tathāgata.
One seeks the path of the Buddha for the benefit of all sentient beings, not for one's own solitary excellence.
Why, then, do you not directly bestow upon them that which has been attained from the Buddhas?

Instead, why do you conceal the immeasurable and profound wisdom of the Buddhas and, like a single drop from the ocean of the Buddhas, teach in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings? What is the reason for this? There is none.

Is it not that you are being stingy and fail to give? Is it not that you have forgotten your original vow? Is it not that you are making arbitrary discriminations? Therefore, he explains himself as follows:
"Although the Tathāgata has fully studied and fully practiced all the dharmas of the Buddhas' path, he does not bestow them directly upon others;
rather, he preaches the Dharma according to their capacities for a specific reason. Thus, the Tathāgata does not neglect the small, nor does he [neglect] the great."

None are omitted; all are able to accord with reality without discrimination, because the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the two pāramitās of knowledge-vision (*jñāna-darśana*) and skillful means (*upāya*). Thus, to those whose capacities are such that they may be granted the Buddha’s knowledge-vision, he grants the Buddha’s knowledge-vision;
to those whose capacities are not fit to receive the Buddha’s knowledge-vision, he [grants] the Dharma...
It is appropriate to entice those who are inclined toward that [superior path]. If one possesses the reality but lacks skillful means (*upāya*), they will sink into the middle or lower realms.

If one employs skillful means while abandoning reality, the great root of capacity will be distorted and suppressed. Because these two—skillful means and reality—are practiced in tandem, one is able to bring all things to completion, whether great or small, without leaving anyone behind.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound, immeasurable and unimpeded.
His powers and fearlessnesses, his dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis penetrate deeply to the infinite. He has accomplished all unprecedented dharmas.
The preceding passage spoke of the perfection of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana-pāramitā*).

However, it was not known what kind of phenomena these were that the Buddha knows and sees—phenomena which all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to know or see. Thereupon, he himself provides an explanation:
That which the Tathāgata knows is vast; that which he perceives is profound and far-reaching. It is certainly not something that can be fully fathomed by your shallow knowledge and inferior views.

Indeed, within the ocean of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), whether the Tathāgata picks up a single flower or plucks a blade of grass, or coughs and snaps his fingers, or emits light and causes the earth to tremble—none of these are anything other than the inconceivable true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
For this reason, the four immeasurable minds, the four analytical knowledges, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses,
the gates of dhyāna-concentration, the gates of liberation, and the gates of samādhi attained by the Tathāgata each penetrate deeply without limit.
This constitutes the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas of drawing near to the Buddhas and accomplishing all [qualities] in the presence of those Buddhas.
It is an unprecedented phenomenon: namely, that one attains supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena.
Thus, not knowing a single phenomenon is called the Buddha’s knowledge; not seeing a single phenomenon is called the Buddha’s vision. There is not even a hair's breadth left unexhausted.

This immediately falls into the cognitive views of sentient beings. Thus, an ancient worthy said: "To not see a single dharma while maintaining the view of non-existence is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun.
To be unaware of a single dharma while guarding a knowledge of emptiness is like a flash of lightning arising in the great void."
The Buddha knows and the Buddha sees thus; how could this be something that your shallow knowledge and limited vision can discern?
Therefore, when Chan Master Huilang first met Mazu, Mazu asked, "What do you seek in coming here? He replied, "I seek the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Mazu said, "The Buddha has no knowledge or vision; knowledge and vision are but demons. Regarding the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), they are: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), [compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity].

[These are] compassion (*karuṇā*), joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Because those of the Hīnayāna do not deliver sentient beings, they do not know [these]. The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are as follows:

the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), which is the wisdom that expounds immeasurable teachings from a single teaching; the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), which is the wisdom that expounds immeasurable meanings from a single meaning; the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), which is the wisdom that expounds immeasurable sounds from a single sound;

and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), which is the wisdom of preaching the Dharma according to the capacities [of listeners]. Because those of the Hīnayāna do not delight in preaching the Dharma, they do not know [these].

The Ten Powers (*daśabala*) are as follows: 1. The power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*): [this refers to] knowing those who can be delivered and those who cannot. 2. The power of knowing the ripening of karma throughout the three times (*karmavipāka-jñānabala*):

[this means] knowing whether there are obstructions or no obstructions. 3. The power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriyaparāpara-jñānabala*): [this means] knowing that the faculties such as faith are of weak, medium, or superior degrees. 4. The power of knowing various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*): [this refers to] the various elements of the three vehicles, the five natures (*pañcagotra*), and so forth;

"element" (*dhātu*) here means nature. 5. The power of knowing various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*): [this refers to] inclinations such as craving for wealth, or delighting in fame and reputation, etc.; it is also called the power of desire (*chanda-bala*). 6. The power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*).

The power of knowledge regarding the various conducts of sentient beings—whether they follow the path of transcendence or the path of non-transcendence—and their respective capacities to reach the fruit;

the power of knowledge regarding dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and their defilement or purification (such as being with-outflow or without-outflow); the power of knowledge regarding recollection of past abodes (knowing former names, clans, suffering, pleasure, and so forth);

the power of knowledge regarding the divine eye (perceiving death here and birth there, falling into good or evil destinies, and distinctions such as large or small, beautiful or ugly); and the power of knowledge regarding the eradication of all latent tendencies (which is the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows). These are not sought by those of the Hīnayāna.
The Buddha-way. Because he does not study the ten powers (*daśabala*), he does not know [them].

○ Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*): first, the fearlessness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vaiśāradya*). (Some raise this objection: "If the Buddha is omniscient, why did he ask when monks arrived from other regions whether they were dwelling in peace? The Buddha is secure and fearless regarding this objection, answering: 'I am an omniscient person.

However, this is merely to accommodate the worldly sentiments between teacher and disciple in the future. Second, the fearlessness of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*). (Objection: If the Buddha says of himself...)

Regarding the fearlessness of having exhausted the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*): Why did the Buddha, who had already exhausted all outflows, speak with loving words to Rāhula while rebuking Devadatta? The Buddha remained secure and undaunted by this challenge, declaring, "I have indeed exhausted all outflows; I spoke thus merely to discipline them according to their individual faculties.

Regarding the fearlessness of proclaiming the obstacles to the path (*antarāyikadharmavyākaraṇa-vaiśāradya*): [The challenge] asks, "If the Buddha says that sensual desires (*kāma*) can obstruct the path, why do those who have attained the fruits of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) still possess attachment to wives and children?

The Buddha was without timidity of heart regarding this challenge, answering, "I say that sensual desires can obstruct the path; however, they obstruct only the non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and arhats, not those in the first two fruits. Regarding the fearlessness of proclaiming the exhaustion of suffering (*sarvāsravakṣayajñāna-vaiśāradya*): [The challenge] asks, "If the Buddha says that all..."

If the Noble Path can bring an end to suffering, why does the Arhat experience the pain of wounds, ulcers, and snakebites? Why is it that the Buddha remains secure and fearless amidst such hardships? The answer is: I have taught that the Noble Path truly brings about the ultimate limit of the exhaustion of suffering; however, this refers only to the future, not the present.

First, it is the abandonment of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*); second, it is the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*); third, it is the departure from obstacles; and fourth, it is the path of departure. The followers of the Lesser Vehicle do not exhaust all obstacles and possess timidity;
therefore, they do not understand this. As for liberation, it is inconceivable liberation and unobstructed liberation.
The liberation of pure observation; the liberation of universal illumination; the liberation of the Tathāgatagarbha; the liberation of accordance with the unimpeded wheel;
the liberation of penetrating the three periods of time; the liberation of the treasury of the dharma-realm; and the liberation of the wheel of light.
There is liberation from all remaining realms. Taking these ten as the foremost, he has fully accomplished immeasurable hundreds of thousands of gates of liberation.
The followers of the Lesser Vehicle attain only three liberations; therefore, they do not know this. Regarding *samādhi*:
the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, the Samādhi of the Square Net, the Samādhi of the Ocean Seal, the Samādhi of Knowing the Treasury of Adornments of the Past, and Wisdom...
The Samādhi of the Treasury of Radiance; the Samādhi of Thoroughly Knowing the Buddha-Adornments of All Worlds;
the Samādhi of the Great Body of Diverse Sentient Beings; the Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma Realm;

and the Samādhi of the Unobstructed Wheel—taking these as the foremost, he has fully accomplished immeasurable hundreds of thousands of samādhis. [In contrast,] those of the Lesser Vehicle are addicted to the tranquility of meditative concentration.
Therefore, they do not know it.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to analyze all things in various ways and skillfully expound all dharmas; his words and phrases are gentle and supple, delighting the hearts of the multitude.
The preceding passage spoke of the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means), yet it was not known what kind of skillful means this was. It is therefore further explained:
The Buddha knows and the Buddha sees that which is free from the marks of mental objects; it cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination.
It is free from the marks of verbal expression; it cannot be elucidated by teeth, paper, or ink. Thus, were it to fall once into thought or once into the medium of words, it would be lost.
There is nothing that is not a skillful means for guiding others. It is like the sun and moon, both luminous, each illuminating its own domain;

the twenty-eight lunar mansions, each presiding over its own sphere; the hundred medicines, all growing together, each curing its specific ailment; and the fox-fur cloak, which provides against the cold.
Fine linen and coarse cloth are both used to ward off the heat; boats and carriages take different paths, yet both serve the traveler.
Thus, the Tathāgata employs skillful means that are easy to enter and speech that is gentle and compliant, skillfully expounding all the sūtras for the sake of all sentient beings.
Without exception, these are humble manifestations of guidance and instruction, perfectly suited to the minds of the multitude, causing them to give rise to joy and attainment.

"I have brought you close to me and caused you to enter the Buddha-way; yet, none of these are the true Dharma, for the Tathāgata does not speak a Dharma that falls within the realm of words and letters. Thus, the Tathāgata has not bestowed a single dharma upon anyone.
Why, then, do you all cling to a single meaning of liberation and remain stuck as if rooted to the spot?"
Śāriputra, to speak in brief: the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.

This concludes the preceding section and introduces the following one. If one were to wish to exhaustively describe all that the Tathāgata has realized, even if one spent immeasurable kalpas doing so, one could not finish;
how then could it be known merely by saying "the four immeasurables" and so forth? Therefore, universally...
The Venerable One said: "The atoms within a buddha-field and the thoughts of the mind may be counted; the waters of the great ocean may be drunk up; space may be measured and the wind may be bound.
Yet no one can fully describe the merits of the Buddha. If one were to summarize the essentials, it could be encompassed by this single phrase:
'The Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas. It is as if one were to contemplate this."
"There is no falsehood" summarizes the great meaning of the three hundred chapters [of the *Shi Jing*]. The above section entirely clarifies the four phrases concerning the wisdom of all Buddhas;
the following section extensively explains that the wisdom of all Buddhas is exceedingly profound and immeasurable, such that it cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Stop, Śāriputra. There is no need to say more. Why is this? The Buddha has accomplished a foremost, most rare, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.
Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaustively realize the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas). As for what these phenomena are:
Such are their characteristics; such is their nature; such is their substance; such is their power; such is their activity; such is their cause; such is their condition;
such is their fruit; such is their retribution; such is the ultimate equality of their beginning and end.

The single word "cessation" (*śamatha*) is the essential teaching that the Tathāgata has spoken from his full mouth; yet he remains vague and does not speak it further—this is precisely the point intended to stir up Śāriputra.

It is like a common proverb: once something is finished, there is no need to bring it up again. Furthermore, [the Buddha] himself explains the reason for wanting to speak and yet not speaking, saying:
"That which I have spoken is the foremost, most rare, and most difficult to understand of all that the Buddha has accomplished."
This Dharma I now preach to you—how is it any different from explaining the affairs of the Hall of Central Secretariat to a firewood-carrier from a village of three households?
He would know nothing of their ultimate significance. One must speak of household matters to those who belong to that household;
only then can they be understood. This is what is meant by "only the sage knows the sage. Therefore, only the Buddha...
He shares the same purpose and aspiration as the Buddha. What he has attained, I have also attained; what I have realized, he has also realized.

Their minds illuminate one another, and their eyes gaze upon one another; thus they are able to investigate the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and furthermore, they are able to exhaustively fathom that true nature.
What is this true nature? It is called "suchness" (*tathatā*). (By "nature," one means the characteristic of form. Such as...

Such is its nature (nature refers to the Buddha-nature); such is its essence (essence refers to the Dharma-body); such is its power (power refers to the power of vows); such is its activity (activity refers to its functioning).

Such are the causes (cause refers to one's own cultivation); such are the conditions (condition refers to that which assists and triggers); such are the fruits (attainment is called fruit); such are the retributions (the response to the fruit is called retribution);
such are the beginning and end (beginning refers to initial birth; end refers to entry into extinction). These are ultimately equal (equality means sameness).
By virtue of these ten aspects, all are dharmas of a single characteristic and a single flavor, fundamentally without dual characteristics. Buddhas and sentient beings are ultimately equal.
Fundamentally, there is no high or low. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is called 'awakening' refers to the essence of mind being free from thought.
This state of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space; it is the single characteristic of the dharma-realm, which is the Tathāgata’s impartial dharmakāya.
Only upon attaining this dharmakāya is one said to have opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Therefore, at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), the Tathāgata, regarding the One..."
All phenomena accomplish the fruit of supreme perfect enlightenment. Wisdom enters the three periods of time, being entirely equal in their nature.
Their bodies fill all worlds; their voices universally accord with the lands of the ten directions, entering them equally in all realms.
Their bodies constantly sit pervasively at all sites of enlightenment (the *vipāka*); these are the great deeds of the Buddhas throughout the three periods of time.
Like the ocean (the cause), he constantly manifests birth in all Buddha-lands (the condition).

His boundless forms and marks are perfectly full of radiance, universally illuminating the Dharma-realm without distinction (the characteristic). From every single tip of a hair, he is able to contain all worlds without obstruction (the function).
He individually manifests immeasurable powers of supernatural penetration to teach, transform, and subdue [beings].
All sentient beings (the power) pervade the worlds of the ten directions without coming or going (the beginning and the end;
this is precisely the "ten bodies acting in concert" from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra). This is simply one such manifestation. It is not so for you:
the Dharma-body is formless, yet you take the thirty-two marks of your retribution-body as real, failing to realize that the formless Tathāgata pervades the Flower Store World-system (*Huazangjie*).
Therefore, the Great Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata does not take marks as his essence; rather, it is this markless, quiescent dharma.

The Tathāgata has no intrinsic nature (svabhāva). You all falsely cling to the idea that the Tathāgata truly possesses an intrinsic nature, believing that only the Buddha alone possesses the tathāgatagarbha and is able to achieve perfect enlightenment, while others cannot. Yet you do not realize that there is no [such nature].
The Buddha-nature of the intrinsic nature fills all of space. As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
"When the Tathāgata attains perfect enlightenment, he universally perceives all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment, and even universally perceives all sentient beings entering nirvāṇa."
What is called "absence of nature" (niḥsvabhāva) is precisely the nature of the absence of nature, which is the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
The Tathāgata has no [fixed] body, yet you all falsely cling to the six-foot form as his body, failing to realize that the body of the Tathāgata pervades all places.
As the Great Sūtra says: "Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should perceive the body of the Tathāgata in immeasurable locations. It is not...
One should perceive the body of the Tathāgata within a single dharma, a single thing, a single body, a single land, and a single sentient being.

One should perceive the body of the Tathāgata pervading all places, just as space reaches all locations—whether material or immaterial—neither arriving nor not arriving. The body of the Tathāgata is likewise: it pervades all dharmas and all...
He attends to all lands, all bodies, and all sentient beings. Why is this? Because the body of the Tathāgata is no-body;
yet for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests that body. That which is called the Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space;
it appears in form according to objects, just like the moon reflected in water. Now you know only that the Tathāgata has descended.
Māra relies on external things as his power, yet he does not know that the Tathāgata’s power of vows pervades the entire realm of sand-grains.
As the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra says: "The vow-power of Vairocana Buddha pervades the realm of sand-grains; within all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel.
You all know only that the Tathāgata performs the work of a Buddha by manifesting before sentient beings to deliver them.

You consider this to be a deliberate act, yet you do not know that it is the inconceivable activity of the Tathāgata, which delivers sentient beings and accomplishes Buddha-work in every atom and in every land.
As the Great Sūtra says: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, appearing universally before all living beings.
This is precisely what is meant. You merely know that the Tathāgata’s six years of ascetic practice were the cause, but...

Throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past, you have served and made offerings to countless Buddhas in the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*) while cultivating the bodhisattva practices;
there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed that was not a great cause for you to sacrifice your body and life as a bodhisattva.
You merely know [the teachings] given at places such as Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) in Rājagṛha.
The Dharma benefits sentient beings by acting as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for them.

Yet you do not know that during the Adorned Eon (*vyūha-kalpa*) in the World of Supreme Sound (*Jinsheng*), at the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and at the time of King Awesome Voice (*Bhīṣmagarjitasvara*), [the Buddha] served as a prince, a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), and a bhikṣu, already acting as a dominant condition for immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings. You all know only of the Bodhi...

You take the attainment of perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree as the ultimate fruit, yet you do not know that throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, one attains perfect enlightenment beneath every single Bodhi tree.

You know only that the Tathāgata’s land of reward is within this Sahā world, yet you do not know that the land of reward resides within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*). You know only that the Tathāgata enters...

They take the descent into the womb, the dwelling in the womb, the emergence from the womb, the renunciation and practice, the attainment of the Way, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the entry into nirvana as the beginning and end;
yet they do not know that the lifespan of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible, never having been born and never having ceased.
Not only this, but they further conceive inferior thoughts toward the various Buddhas, saying: "The Tathāgata [possesses] the thirty-two..."
"His marks—I do not possess them. The nature of the Tathāgata—I am not endowed with it. The body of the Tathāgata—I fall short of it.
The power of the Tathāgata’s vows—I cannot equal it. The activities of the Tathāgata—I am incapable of them.
The causes for seeking Buddhahood that the Tathāgata pursues—are not my concern. The conditions for delivering sentient beings that the Tathāgata employs—are not what I require."
"The fruit of the Tathāgata is not something I dare to hope for; the retribution of the Tathāgata is not something I dare to admire;
the matters of the Tathāgata’s beginning and end, his root and branch, I do not dare to expect even a ten-thousandth part of.

Yet, one does not realize that one's own self is fundamentally equal to the ultimate state of the Tathāgata. Not only this, but one further gives rise to a sense of self in relation to sentient beings."

The perception of one's own feet: having emerged from the three realms and transcended the four modes of birth, one regards oneself as having attained the mark of purity, while regarding the sentient beings of the three realms as possessing the mark of impurity;
having attained the nature of a noble one (*ārya*), one regards sentient beings as being of the nature of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
He considers himself to have attained the inconceivable body of transformation, yet he views sentient beings as bodies of karmic fruition.

He considers himself to have attained the five powers, yet he views sentient beings as the power of karma. He considers himself to have attained divine efficacy, yet he views sentient beings as the functioning of karma.
He considers himself to have attained the cause of purity, yet he views sentient beings as karma itself.
Regarding causes, they consider themselves to have attained pure conditions, yet they view sentient beings as having defiled conditions;
they consider themselves to have attained pure fruits and pure retributions, yet they view sentient beings as having karmic fruits and karmic retributions;
they consider themselves from beginning to end to be people who have transcended the three realms, yet they view sentient beings as seeds for the burning house. They fail to realize this at all.
One knows that oneself is ultimately equal to all sentient beings; yet, because one conceives a notion of inferiority toward the Tathāgata, one is unwilling to seek the Buddha-way upward;
and because one conceives a notion of self-sufficiency toward sentient beings, [one does not exert oneself].
"You do not delight in delivering sentient beings through the lower [vehicles]. The Dharma is fundamentally equal, yet you yourself have made it divergent.

The Dharma is fundamentally signless, yet you yourself have obstructed it. The Dharma is fundamentally without attachment, yet you yourself have grasped at it. Such a wondrous Dharma can be known only by a Buddha."
Only the Buddha can see it; you shall never be able to know it, nor shall you ever be able to see it. These words show that the Buddha’s wisdom is exceedingly profound;
such is the extent to which the followers of the Two Vehicles neither know nor see it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Hero of the World is immeasurable; Neither the devas nor the people of the world, Nor any class of sentient beings, Is able to know the Buddha."
The Buddha’s powers and fearlessnesses, his liberations and various samādhis, as well as all other qualities of a Buddha—none can fathom them.
The first four lines of this verse state that neither humans nor devas, nor those of the two vehicles, know the Buddha.

Having relinquished the royal throne, cast aside sensual pleasures, severed the two types of death, extinguished the five stages of dwelling, become the teacher of the three realms, and acted as the father of the four modes of birth, he is therefore called the Hero of the World (Lokavīra). How could it be otherwise?
"To be undisturbed by wealth and honor, unshaken by poverty and lowliness, and unbowed by power and majesty—this is all there is to it.
Therefore it is said: 'Leaving the household life is the business of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish.

Yet, even though this is so, there is not a single person who can truly know the Buddha. The Buddha is like space: fundamentally without form or measure, and fundamentally cannot be seen through form nor heard through sound."

Because they seek [only for themselves]. The Buddha’s power descends; it is said that these individuals not only do not know the Buddha, but moreover do not know the Dharma, because this Dharma cannot be measured by means of conceptualization or discrimination.
Originally following countless Buddhas, I have fully practiced all paths. This most profound and subtle Dharma is difficult to see and difficult to comprehend.
Having practiced these various paths for immeasurable billions of kalpas, I attained the fruit at the site of enlightenment; I have known and seen it all.
Such is this great fruit of retribution, with its various natures, characteristics, and meanings; only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions are able to know and perceive these matters.
This Dharma cannot be demonstrated; its words and signs are quiescent. Among all other classes of sentient beings, there are none who can understand it.
Setting aside the assembly of Bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm, it is next said that "only a Buddha knows" and "only a Bodhisattva knows.

Furthermore, during my own causal stage, when I was in the presence of immeasurable pure Buddhas, I personally performed sweeping and cleaning, responded to their instructions, and practiced every movement—bending, turning, bowing, and rising—as well as all practices from the Six Perfections to the myriad deeds; there was nothing I did not cultivate.
One studies, practicing and upholding everything without exception; yet even so, one is still unable to see or fully comprehend this most profound and subtle Dharma.

Only after countless eons have passed, when merit is perfected and practice is fulfilled, and one sits beneath the Bodhi tree to attain supreme perfect enlightenment, does one finally behold this most profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma. Thus, one knows that such is its nature.
The marks and their retributive fruits are the ultimate, equal Dharma. Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom them;
among others, not a single person can know this. Why is this? This Dharma is originally quiescent and extinguished;

it cannot be pointed out by means of physical forms, nor can it be discussed through words and phrases. One must realize it for oneself and awaken to it personally before one can truly perceive its marks.
It is so. Those in the fourfold assembly present here all seek it within words and forms, searching for it upon the branches of their emotions and the faculties of their minds;
therefore, not a single person among them is able to attain understanding. Only those of extraordinary capacity, upon hearing this Dharma once, [attain it].
Accept it directly. It is like taking a burden of one hundred and twenty catties and carrying it on one shoulder, proceeding straight ahead, unable to be caged or called back.
Like a fragrant elephant crossing a river, he cuts through the current and passes over.
Such people as these are called Bodhisattvas of great resolve with firm power of faith. Formerly, at Mount Wutai, Master Zhi...
Chan Master Tong was under the guidance of Master Guizong. One night, he suddenly cried out repeatedly, "I have attained great enlightenment!
The next day, when the assembly had gathered, Guizong said, "Come forward, you who attained great enlightenment last night. The Master stepped forth.
Guizong asked, "What principle did you perceive that you say you have attained great enlightenment? The Master replied, "A nun is originally made by a woman. [End of] Mingzhou.
Chan Master Damei Fachang first visited Daji and asked, "What is the Buddha? Daji replied, "This very mind is the Buddha.
The Master attained great enlightenment immediately. Later, a monk asked him, "What did you gain from seeing Master Mazu?"
He then settled on this mountain. The Master said, "The Great Master told me, 'This very mind is Buddha,' so I have been dwelling right here.
The monk asked, "Lately, the Great Master’s teaching of the Dharma has become different. The Master asked, "In what way? The monk replied, "He also says, 'Neither mind nor Buddha.
The Master said, "This old fellow has been causing confusion for quite some time now; let him be."
"It is neither mind nor Buddha. I simply maintain that 'mind is itself Buddha. When the monk reported this to Mazu, Mazu said, "The plum has ripened.
Such individuals possess firm and solid power of faith; they are the very embodiment of one who cannot be turned back even by a thousand calls.
The assembly of disciples of the Buddhas, who have made offerings to all Buddhas, whose outflows are entirely exhausted, and who dwell in their final bodies—
even such persons as these cannot withstand its power.
This generally clarifies that those of the Hīnayāna cannot shoulder the Great Dharma. Those who have exhausted all outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) are people like cold ashes or withered wood;
their power and capacity are shallow and meager, making them unfit for such a heavy responsibility. One must instead be like withered wood blooming with flowers.

Only when cold ashes flare up with flame can one truly attain it. Long ago, there was a laywoman who supported a hermit for twenty years, constantly sending a young woman to provide him with meals and attend to his needs.
One day, she ordered the woman to embrace the hermit and asked, "At this very moment, what is it like?
The hermit replied, "A withered tree leans against a cold cliff; throughout the three months of winter, there is no warmth. The woman...
He reported this to the Elder (Pāpīyān). The Elder said, "For twenty years I have provided offerings only to receive such a worldly man.
He then expelled him and burned down his hut.
Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
Even if those as numerous as Śāriputra, as well as all other disciples, were to fill the ten directions and all the lands throughout the ten directions,
and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they still could not know it.
This refers to those whose natures and faculties are sharp and quick-witted;

even before a word is spoken, they comprehend it through their mind-consciousness, and for this reason, they are likewise unable to shoulder the Great Dharma. For example, when Zen Master Xiangyan Zhixian was at Baizhang’s place:
By nature, he was of sharp intelligence, yet he could not attain realization through Zen meditation. Upon the passing away of his master, he went to study under Guishan.
Guishan asked him, "When your parents were not yet born, try and say a single word. The Master was at a loss and sighed to himself, "A painted cake cannot satisfy hunger.
He repeatedly requested that Guishan explain it to him, to which Guishan replied, "If I were to explain it to you, in the future..."
He scolded me and sent me away, saying, "What I am speaking is my own business; it has nothing to do with you.

The Master then took his lifelong writings and burned them, saying, "In this life, I shall not study the Buddha-dharma. I will instead become a simple monk who prepares porridge and rice, so as to spare my mental energy from such toil.
He then wept as he took his leave of Guishan and traveled directly to Nanyang, where he visited the remains of National Teacher Huizhong.

Daowu’s traces thus came to an end there. One day later, while clearing away grass and trees, he happened to throw a tile or a stone that struck a bamboo tree, producing a sound. Suddenly, he attained awakening. He then bathed, burned incense, and prostrated from afar toward Mount Wei, saying: "The Master’s great compassion exceeds that of my own parents. Had you explained this to me at that time, how could I have reached this point today? Thereupon, he composed a verse: The Great Master’s compassionate heart was vast; He would have revealed it for me then and there. If I had heard it at that moment, I would not have waited until now. I am like a person born deaf, Who has suddenly regained their hearing. From this day forward, I shall never again doubt the Buddhas or the patriarchs. How could I have known that the Way Was so near and yet so far? I have been wandering in birth and death for eighty years, Yet I did not realize it was right here. he refined his practice through austere asceticism, and his conduct was peerless. Daowei held him in deep esteem.
One day, Daowei asked him, "Disciple (Ajari), while you have been here with this old monk, you have never asked a single turning word. The Master replied, "Where would you have me direct my mouth?"
Guishan said, "Why do you not say, 'What is the Buddha? The Master then made a gesture with his hand to cover Guishan’s mouth.
Guishan sighed and said, "You have truly attained the marrow. Furthermore, while Nanquan was serving rice to the assembly of monks, Mazu asked, "What is inside this bucket?
The Master said, "Old man, shut your mouth! Why do you speak such words? Mazu then desisted.
Only when one possesses these eyes can one begin to understand how to read the sutras.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals.
It is like the udumbara flower, which appears but once in a long while. Śāriputra, you all should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false."

"False. This is an exhortation to believe. Only then did the fourfold assembly cease to harbor doubts; therefore, he emitted light to arouse their doubt, and further praised his virtues to arouse their doubt.
This doubt was indispensable. Once they were in a state of doubt, he was about to preach the Great Dharma. This—
Doubt must not exist; therefore, the rarity of the udumbara flower is used to strengthen one's faith.
This is why the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to the occasion. How great indeed is the significance of the term "occasion" (kāla)! Zhongni said:

"To speak when it is appropriate, yet fail to speak to someone, is to lose the person. To speak to someone when it is inappropriate, yet proceed to speak, is to lose the words. Thus he spoke of the "occasion."
Subsequently, he spoke of the word "time. This is that which all sages revere; therefore, when the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma, he must necessarily act according to the time.
If there are those who are like dregs or mere branches and leaves within the assembly, yet one speaks with them [as if they were capable], this is a failure of speech.

It is not the right time. If there are those in the assembly who hear [the teaching] and believe it with reverence, or who hear it and respond with joy and praise, yet one does not speak with them, this is a failure regarding the person; it is not the right time.

If the fourfold assembly has been consistently kept in a state of non-action and has never previously harbored doubt or attachment toward this matter, yet one suddenly speaks to them, this is a failure regarding the words.

It is also untimely. If, upon hearing this matter for the first time, one is immediately struck with alarm and doubt, yet refuses to let it go and resolutely desires to investigate and clarify it—like one who thirsts for nectar or a bee yearning for fine honey—and yet you do not speak to them [of it].
This is to lose a person; it is an untimely matter. First, within this assembly there are currently no followers who are like branches or leaves, which makes it a time when teaching is appropriate.
Second, there are those here who possess reverence and faith, which also makes it a time when teaching is appropriate. Forty years ago...
Generally, no one has harbored doubts regarding this matter; yet now, the entire assembly here is in doubt. This is the third reason it is the opportune time to speak.
Furthermore, in the ordinary course of things, every word, every smile, every movement, and every stillness of the World-Honored One is never uttered or displayed in vain;
there must always be its proper occasion. How much more so for this great causal nexus—a teaching that is ultimately equal, yet difficult to understand and difficult to believe?
Is there anything that should not be spoken at the improper time? Yet, such a time is difficult to encounter.
Forty years ago, no one ever harbored doubts regarding this matter; only now have doubts begun to arise.
Forty years ago, I wished to speak of it, but there was no opportunity to do so; therefore, I remained patient and did not reveal it. Now, however, there is an occasion to speak.

This is the opportune moment. Since there is both the opportune moment for discourse and the matter one wishes to explain—like an arrow already upon the bowstring that cannot but be released—it is said:
"Such a wondrous Dharma is preached by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at the proper time.
To say "such a wondrous Dharma" refers precisely to such characteristics, such nature, and so forth, up to the ultimate consummation of the beginning and the end.
This is the Dharma of equality. Throughout forty years, I have never revealed it; only today do I finally disclose it.
It is just like the udumbara flower, which appears but once in an age. In the Sanskrit language, it is called *udumbara*; here it is translated as "Auspicious Omen."
Only when a Buddha or a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) is about to appear in the world do auspicious signs manifest;
this is like the meaning of the saying that when the Yellow River clears, a sage is born. It is said that such a time is so difficult to encounter—how could one possibly neglect it?
Therefore, he further cautioned them, saying: "For forty years prior, I kept this secret and did not speak of it, waiting until this very moment."
As soon as I speak to you, I say: "You all must believe what the Buddha has taught; it was certainly not uttered in vain or frivolously.
I fear that the great assembly might treat this with ease or regard it as a trivial matter; therefore, I have exhorted you with such earnestness.
This is precisely the heart of a compassionate grandmother, striving to the utmost for the sake of others. If it were Deshan or Linji, however, they would have had no need for so much [verbosity].

Frivolous and trivial! With a blow from the staff and a shout, one is divided into many bodies right where one stands. As for the Buddha-dharma and the Patriarchal-dharma, you must truly fix your eyes upon them.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; their underlying intent is difficult to understand. Why is this? By means of my...
By means of numerous skillful methods, various causes and conditions, parables, and verbal expressions, he expounds upon all dharmas;
yet these dharmas cannot be understood through conceptualization or discrimination.
The following clarifies the gateway of his wisdom. It is difficult to understand and difficult to enter; even all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know it.
Therefore, it is said that what was taught according to suitability has an intent that is difficult to comprehend. [The Buddha] said:
"In the past, I saw that you were attached to birth and death and lacked the will to seek liberation. For this reason, in the Deer Park, I turned the Wheel of the Four Truths."
The Wheel of Dharma explains that within the three realms there is the suffering of birth and death, and explains that beyond the three realms there is the bliss of nirvana.
This is done as a skillful means to entice you; do not remain attached to the birth and death of the three realms. It is like exchanging a melon filled with honey for a bitter gourd.
This does not mean that the three realms are truly a prison, nor that sentient beings are truly enemies, nor is it...
This means that there is truly a nirvana to be realized. Yet you all cling to this nirvana and are unwilling to deliver sentient beings;
instead, you remain submerged and stifled within a jar of pickles. My intention is difficult to understand in such a way.

Because I see that you all are attached to nirvana and do not seek the Buddha’s wisdom, I therefore employ methods of suppression and encouragement, praise and censure, within the assembly of the Vaipulya sutras.
This means that even those who have committed the five heinous crimes and those who are companions of worldly afflictions can all resolve their minds for enlightenment and can all become Buddhas.

However, as for those of the Two Vehicles, they are like withered sprouts or rotten seeds; they will never resolve their minds for Bodhi, and there is no possibility of them ever attaining Buddhahood.
This, too, was an expedient means used to exhort you, intended to cause you to relinquish [the pursuit of] nirvana and advance toward the Buddha-way.
It does not mean that you truly cannot resolve to attain bodhicitta, nor that you truly cannot achieve the fruit of Buddhahood.
Yet you sit idly awaiting nirvana, content to remain inferior and severing yourselves from your share of the Tathāgata’s precious treasury;
you do not give rise to even a single thought of delight in the playful supernatural powers of the Bodhisattva-dharma.
Such is the difficulty of understanding my underlying intention. Furthermore, I see that you do not rejoice in the preaching of the Dharma, nor...

Because you are willing to deliver sentient beings, I have, within this assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, commanded you to preach the Dharma and provide instruction for all bodhisattvas, and to take charge of the various requisites; thus, I have entrusted this treasury to you.
Yet you yourselves harbor no desire to take even a single meal [for yourselves]. Such is the difficulty of understanding my underlying intention. Nevertheless, the root of your illness—
In what respect? It is because they do not understand that what is spoken according to circumstances arises from an interpretation based on the literal words.
How could they know that the various Dharma-gates taught by the Buddhas fundamentally have no path of the intellect and do not fall within the realm of discursive thought?

They are merely things brought forth at the hand of faith, used to untie the bonds according to the situation, acting as yellow leaves used to stop a child's crying; they can never be grasped by the conscious mind.
To deliberate and measure—this means that you, with your conceptualizing minds, attempt to fathom the Tathāgata;

yet you do not realize that as long as one remains within thought, one is separated by thousands and tens of thousands of miles. Therefore, you ultimately fail to understand what the Tathāgata has taught.
Indeed, even regarding what the Tathāgata has taught, only the Buddhas themselves can reach its ultimate consummation; you likewise cannot know it.
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great cause and condition.
Śāriputra, what is meant by saying that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great cause and condition?
It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so as to bring them to purity; for this reason, they appear in the world.

He appears in the world because he wishes to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; he appears in the world because he wishes to cause sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
he appears in the world because he wishes to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Śāriputra, it is for this single great causal purpose that all Buddhas appear in the world.
The World-Honored One further questioned: "For what reason is it that those of the Two Vehicles do not know this, while only the Buddhas are able to know it?
It is because all Buddhas share the same mind and the same vow, having together realized this one great cause and condition (*mahāntam dharmam*), and together acting for this one great cause."
Because it is for the sake of transcending the world. That which is called the "one great causal condition" (*ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya*) is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This Buddha’s knowledge and vision is that which is known and seen by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, at the time they realize the fruit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

It is the equality of essence and characteristics, substance and function, causes and conditions, and karmic retributions—from the beginning to the ultimate end. It is the Dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor. This is...
That all Buddhas attain enlightenment by taking this as the cause, and that all Buddhas deliver sentient beings by taking this as the condition—
since the Buddhas rely upon this Dharma both as cause and condition, it is a most momentous event in the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world.

Since the Buddhas have already realized this Dharma and desire for each and every person to realize it together with them, the Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma for the sake of the two vehicles, nor does he appear in the world for minor causes and conditions.
He speaks only of the Mahāyāna Dharma of ultimate equality, and he appears in the world solely for this one great matter and cause. Therefore, he has appeared.
The "Chapter on the Manifestation" states: "The Tathāgata appears through immeasurable matters and immeasurable conditions;
these immeasurable matters and immeasurable conditions constitute the one great causal condition (*ekamahā-kāraṇa-pratyaya*).

Desiring to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to attain purity, he appears in the world. This sentence, however, reveals the original intent for his appearance in the world.
He spoke with full candor, saying: "All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata;
however, because they are defiled by deluded thoughts and attachments, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision cannot be manifested, nor can they be purified.
The appearance of a Buddha in the world is nothing more than the desire to cause sentient beings to manifest the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby enabling them to attain purity."
What is described in the following passage—the elder’s hidden treasure, the jewel within the garment, and the great white ox-cart—refers precisely to these things.
The treasure must be opened by oneself; therefore, it is said, "I wish to cause sentient beings to open it. To "open" means to push and clear away [the covering] with one's own hands.
The jewel in the garment must be known by oneself; therefore, it is said, "I wish to cause sentient beings to awaken to it. To "awaken" means...
It is said that what has been long forgotten need not be recorded. The white ox-cart must be ridden by oneself;
therefore it is said, "I wish to cause sentient beings to enter. To "enter" means that one has arrived there with the whole body.

Thus, the Tathāgata does nothing more than point out the treasure-store to sentient beings, point out the pearl in their clothing, and point out the great white ox-cart to sentient beings. Therefore...
It is said: "It is intended to show sentient beings. To "show" means to point out clearly.
Thus, the three characters for "opening," "awakening," and "entering" all pertain to sentient beings, whereas the single character for "showing" pertains solely to the Buddha.

If one considers the general purport of this sutra, these four characters—opening, showing, awakening, and entering—encompass the beginning and end of the entire scripture. Regarding the two characters for "opening" and "showing":...
The character "Awakening" (wù) belongs to the Buddha; the two characters "entering" (rù) belong to humans.

From the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṛivarta*) through to the "Dharma-preacher" chapter (*Dharmabhāṇaka-paṛivarta*), this sutra clarifies these two terms, "opening" and "awakening. "Opening" refers to what is called opening the gate of expedient means.

For instance, the teaching in the "Expedient Means" chapter is certainly an expedient means; yet because Śāriputra attained awakening, it is said: "Only today do I know that this is truly [the Buddha’s teaching]."

O Son of the Buddha, the "Chapter on Similes" is also a skillful means; yet because the four great disciples attained awakening through it, they said, "Today we are truly śrāvakas, truly arhats. The "Chapter on Causes and Conditions" is likewise a skillful means.

The five hundred disciples, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), all attained awakening; thus it is said: "I now know for the first time that [the Buddha] is truly a Bodhisattva," and so forth.
This constitutes the opening of the three cycles of expedient means (*upāya-mukha*) to cause the fourfold assembly to attain awakening.

From the "Jeweled Stūpa" chapter (*Ratnakoṭi-parivarta*) onwards, the two characters "entry" (*ru*) and "manifestation" (*shi*) are explicitly shown. "Manifestation" (*shi*) refers to what is called the manifestation of the true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
Just as in the past, when Prabhūtaratna manifested his stupa and body, and Śākyamuni transformed the land so that the emanations from the ten directions gathered in one place,
even up to the manifestation of the tongue-mark and the emission of light from the brow-hair— all of these were direct demonstrations of what the Buddha knows and sees to show to people.
As for the bodhisattvas who make vows to uphold this sutra, they should all fully carry out its practice just as the World-Honored One has commanded.
This is the person who enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is the Tathāgata manifesting the true aspect to cause people to enter it.
The remaining six chapters, beginning with "Bhaiṣajyarāja," are merely models for those who uphold this sutra to serve as a guide for entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Therefore, one first realizes that within oneself there exists this single volume of the Great Sutra.
Only after one has received, upheld, and maintained [the teaching] so that its circulation remains uninterrupted can one subsequently enter it.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* takes faith, understanding, practice, and realization as the essentials of the entire sutra, while this sutra takes opening, showing, awakening, and entering as its central theme.
Formerly, Master Fada of Hongzhou asked the Sixth Patriarch about the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The Patriarch said: "You..."
"Reciting this sutra—what is its essential principle? The Master said, "I am a dull-witted student; how could I know its fundamental purport?
The Patriarch said, "Recite it once, and I shall explain it for you. The Master then recited it aloud. Upon reaching the "Chapter on Expedient Means," the Patriarch said, "Stop.
This sutra fundamentally takes the appearance of the World-Honored One through causes and conditions as its principle, even though it employs many kinds of parables."
There is nothing that transcends this. Why? Because the causal conditions are themselves the one great matter, and the one great matter is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

You must be careful not to misinterpret the meaning of the sutra. If you see others saying that "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" belong solely to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and that we have no share in it—if you interpret it thus, you are entirely slandering the sutra and defaming the Buddha. Since he...

This is the Buddha. Having already fully realized and seen [the truth], what need is there to open it further? You should believe that this knowledge and vision of the Buddha is none other than your own mind;

it has no separate essence. It is simply because all sentient beings obscure their own wondrous clarity, greedily clinging to sensory objects, and with external conditions disturbing the internal, they willingly undergo such toil. Thus, you must labor for him to arise from samādhi and undergo various hardships.
I advise you to rest and not seek outside; [the Buddha-nature] is no different from the Buddha, which is why it is said that one "opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If you merely exhaust yourself with fixated thoughts as your daily practice, how is this different from an ox that loves its own tail?
This section could serve as a commentary on an entire sutra.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas. Whatever they do is always for a single purpose:
solely to use the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to instruct and awaken sentient beings.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings using only the Single Buddha Vehicle; there is no other vehicle, whether a second or a third.”
Furthermore, the Dharma-gates through which the Buddhas deliver sentient beings are vast and immeasurable; they do not consist solely of language and written words.

Therefore, in the Dharma of the Bodhisattva, even lifting a foot, pressing a finger, raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye, clearing one's throat, or snapping the fingers—all these are nothing other than preaching the Bodhisattva Dharma to others, nothing other than illuminating this Great Matter, and nothing other than this very matter.
To point the way for others is nothing more than requiring them to awaken to this matter. Thus, the Tathāgata does not merely expound the Bodhisattva Dharma to sentient beings with his speech;
he also expounds the Bodhisattva Dharma to sentient beings through his entire body and every part of his being.
Therefore, one should know that the Tathāgata has never spoken of a Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), nor has he ever spoken of Three Vehicles (Triyāna).
The Dharma, from beginning to end, reveals to people only the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) so that they may awaken and enter it.

Yet, when one arrives at the gate of the Patriarchs, shaking bells and rattling staffs, rolling balls without ritual tablets, the braying of donkeys and the barking of dogs, blowing on a goat’s hair, raising a whisk, wielding the staff or the shout, manifesting anger or joy—all these are none other than for this one purpose. This is it.
Heaven attains it and becomes clear; Earth attains it and becomes tranquil; the sun and moon attain it and become bright; ghosts and spirits attain it and become numinous.
This is what is meant by "when one is penetrated, all things are complete. As the ancient masters said:
"Vividly clear at the tips of the hundred grasses—vividly clear is the meaning of the Patriarchs. This is precisely that.
Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise.

Śāriputra, the Buddhas of the past, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, diverse causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, have expounded the various dharmas for the sake of sentient beings;
yet these dharmas are all for the purpose of the Single Buddha Vehicle. These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from those Buddhas...
In the end, they all attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). Śāriputra, in the future, there will also be Buddhas who appear in the world;
they too, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression, shall expound the various dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
These dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. When these sentient beings hear the Dharma from the Buddha, they shall... [investigate it to the ultimate].

In the end, they all attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Śāriputra, in the present, throughout the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-fields in the ten directions, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bring great benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings.

These Buddhas also, by means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful means (*upāya*), through various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

All dharmas—these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. These sentient beings, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, will ultimately all attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Śāriputra, these Buddhas teach and transform only bodhisattvas, because they desire to reveal to sentient beings the knowledge and vision of a Buddha;
because they desire to awaken sentient beings to the knowledge and vision of a Buddha; because they desire to cause sentient beings...
Because they have entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
below, he extensively cites the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time to testify that this Dharma is not spoken by the Tathāgata alone within this Sahā world,
