but is also taught by my own emanations and projections throughout the ten directions.
In every world-system, they likewise speak in this manner. Furthermore, it is not only I and my emanated Buddhas who speak thus;
all Buddhas of the three periods of time also speak in the same way. Thus, this single volume of the Great Sūtra exhausts the three periods of time and pervades the ten directions;
it reaches upward to the heavens and extends downward to the earth, expounding the Dharma in every atom of dust.
It is spoken in every land, spoken by every person, spoken by every thing, spoken at every moment, and spoken in every thought-instant; it has never ceased.

Yet people themselves do not recognize it. Thus, where the mouth opens and the tongue moves, they immediately interpret it as speech; where eyebrows are raised and eyes blink, they again interpret it as a logical principle.
This extends even to the brightness of the sun, the darkening of clouds, the stirring of the wind, the rising of dust, the soaring of kites, and the leaping of fish.

Leaping. The cock crows and the dog barks. Flowered medicinal railings. The cypress tree. Everywhere. Furthermore, if one interprets these as objective phenomena, one fails the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma and fails to attain the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Śāriputra, I am now likewise so. Knowing that all sentient beings have various desires and deep-seated attachments, I preach the Dharma for them through various causes, conditions, parables, and expressions, employing the power of skillful means according to their inherent natures.
Śāriputra, all this is for the sake of enabling them to attain the Single Buddha Vehicle and the knowledge of all modes. Śāriputra.
In the worlds of the ten directions, there is not even the vehicle of the two [vehicles], let alone the three.
Because the Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions all speak thus, I too shall emulate the ritual of those Buddhas and likewise speak in this way.
Question: Since the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods have already established this matter...
"It is true. World-Honored One, why did You not directly reveal this Dharma to people forty years ago?
For what reason did You keep it secret and not speak of it, instead teaching various skillful means, causes and conditions, and parables? The answer is: "Because of their capacities.
Since the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ and their inclinations vary, there are those whose faculties and natures are well-suited for the Mahāyāna."
There are those who prefer the Lesser Vehicle; those who prefer the vehicle of humans and devas; those who prefer wealth; those who prefer beauty;
those who prefer fame; those who prefer sound; those who prefer fine flavors; those who prefer ostentation; those who prefer frugality; those who prefer conflict; those who prefer valor;
those who prefer riding on fat horses and wearing light garments; and those who prefer tranquility and silent stillness.
Those who delight in curiosity, those who delight in the arts, those who delight in lofty purity, those who delight in fastidious integrity—
even with their various and differing inclinations— I know them all. Therefore, according to the particular biases and attachments of their natures,
I open various doors and teach various dharmas, guiding them through the fields of knowledge they already understand, gradually leading them all [to liberation].

Entering the Buddha-vehicle and attaining all-knowledge is like leading the hundred rivers to return to the sea, or melting jars, plates, hairpins, and bracelets into a single metal, or churning butter, curd, and clarified butter into a single flavor. Why is this?

Because throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, there is no duality of dharmas. As an ancient worthy said: "To encounter a fellow traveler on the Way is already a fault; [to do so for] a lifetime..."

Śāriputra, when the task of studying has been completed, you should know that the Buddhas appear in the five turbidities of this evil world—namely, the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
Thus, Śāriputra, during the chaos of the turbid eon, the defilements of sentient beings are heavy; they are stingy and greedy.
Envy. Because they have accomplished various unwholesome roots, the Buddhas, through the power of skillful means, distinguish and teach three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.

Question: If the Tathāgata necessarily intends to speak of three from the standpoint of there being no three, then the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise [speak of three] where there are no three.
Why are three [aspects] taught in this context? The answer is: because it accords with the time.
Since the Tathāgata was born into this defiled and evil age, he could not fail to accord with the capacities of those beings. As for the term "kalpa-turbidity" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*): *kalpa* means "time.

When the world declines and the Way is lost, the realm is in turmoil like fish and birds that find no peace; the common people are exhausted in their search, yet they seek nothing of the ancient past.
A world of purity can no longer be found; this is what is called the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of the age). Ice and charcoal clash within the heart;

greed and hatred emerge alternately; empty flowers obscure the eyes; and deceit and guile arise everywhere. Throughout the entire world, one cannot find a single person who is free from artifice and ignorance, who maintains purity and embraces simplicity;
this is what is called the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (the defilement of afflictions). They do not even spare their own lives.

In this so-called world, people conceal their hearts in wealth and property; they do not submerge themselves in form and sound, yet they remain tethered by their sensory perceptions and consciousness.
To seek those who, having satisfied their bellies, sport in joy, or who strike the earth with clods of clay while singing—such persons can no longer be found.

This is what is called the turbidity of sentient beings. The pure customs have been eroded; morality and virtue have become diluted. The apertures of the emotions open wider day by day, and the primordial unity of *hundun* dissolves daily.

They die, each privately possessing a single art and each guarding a single skill; they pursue their preferences and apply themselves to their crafts, vying for the extraordinary and contending for splendor.

Yet, among them, one who can open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is impossible to find. This is what is called the turbidity of views. As their cravings deepen, their celestial faculties grow shallower;
they possess little of the spirit of wind and clouds, but much of the sentiment of children. Within the sea of birth and death, they emerge with their heads...
With their heads submerged, those who seek to attain the natural wisdom of life cannot be found. This is what is called the turbidity of destiny (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
The Tathāgata appeared in the world precisely at such a time; observing them with his Buddha-eye, he truly feels deep compassion for them.

How much more so for those whose bodies are completely shattered and whose faces are covered in dust—those who, regarding what pertains to themselves, would not even pluck out a single hair [for others]. In...
As for others, they indulge in greed without satiety; this is truly the foundation of the three miserable realms and the root of all evils.
Being utterly dull and ignorant, they are difficult to discipline and difficult to subdue.

If one does not administer remedies according to their dispositions and natures, but instead bestows the One Vehicle directly upon them, it would already be a great blessing if one did not even have to apply the cane. How could one possibly force them [to practice]?
How true it is! Therefore, the Buddhas have compassionately bestowed skillful means, dividing the single vehicle into three to establish a clever progression of stages.
They set up the "City of Transformation" to entice beings forward. Thus, the *Nèidélùn* (Treatise on Internal Virtue) says:
"A single water cannot harmonize a soup; a single tree cannot construct a house; a single garment does not suit all bodies; a single medicine cannot cure diverse ailments; a single color..."
Without these, there would be no embroidery for the patterns of culture; a single note could not harmonize with the lute and zither; a single word could not encourage the multitude toward goodness;
and a single precept could not prevent manifold transgressions. How can one then find it strange that the gradual and sudden approaches differ, and that the Dharma-gate is not made uniform?
Thus, as for the gateways of skillful means, how could they be otherwise?

Śāriputra, if any of my disciples who claim to be arhats or pratyekabuddhas have not heard of nor known of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, and the matter of teaching and transforming bodhisattvas, they are not disciples of the Buddha; they are not arhats;
they are not pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, Śāriputra, those bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who claim to have already attained arhatship—
“Han, this is his final body; he has attained ultimate nirvana and no longer aspires to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
You should know that such people are all those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Why is this?
If there were a bhikṣu who had truly attained arhatship and yet did not believe in this Dharma, it would be impossible—unless it were after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.”
"There is no Buddha present before you.
This is spoken with words of urgency to stir them, in order to strengthen their faith. The Great Sutra says: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit;
faith enables one to enter the Buddha-dharma with joy; faith can increase the merit of wisdom; faith can lead one inevitably to [enlightenment]."
Regarding the stage of the Tathāgata, it is said: "If a person lacks faith, one does not know what can be achieved. It is further said:

"If one's faith in the Way is not sincere, how can one be said to exist [in the Way], and how can one be said not to exist? The single word "faith" is the gateway through which all sages enter the Way.
Therefore, before the teaching was spoken, he first used the three types of cessation to resolve their doubts; after the teaching was spoken, he furthermore...
By using perilous words, he stirs their faith; from this, one may know that he arouses their doubts precisely in order to strengthen their faith.
That he guides them gradually and skillfully can be seen here in a single glimpse. Therefore it is said:

"If my disciples, claiming for themselves that they have attained the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, consider this to be final liberation and believe there is nothing further to do, they have never heard the Tathāgata [teach] for the sake of the One Vehicle."
He has appeared in the world for a great cause and condition. Furthermore, he has never heard that the Tathāgata teaches and transforms only bodhisattvas;
consequently, he would not be a disciple of the Buddha, nor would he be an arhat, and he could not be included among the ranks of the disciples.
Furthermore, there is a class of people who, having attained a minor fruit, identify it as the final body of a Tathāgata;
they regard the nirvāṇa they have realized as the ultimate nirvāṇa of a Tathāgata, believing that no further Buddha-fruit can be attained and no further nirvāṇa can be realized.
Even if they hear that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition, they no longer aspire to seek it, thinking: "I myself..."

There is such a person who will certainly never turn their mind [toward the Dharma]. Such individuals not only fail to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, but have not even attained the fruit of Arhatship;
they cannot be called Arhats, but are termed persons of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Regarding "overweening pride," the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra* states: "If there is a bhikṣu who thinks to himself, 'I have severed greed'..."
To think, "I have severed greed and hatred; I have severed delusion," is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To think that the dharma of greed is one thing, the dharma of hatred another, the dharma of delusion another, and the dharmas of the Buddhas another, is called overweening pride.

To claim there is something to be acquired, something to be realized, or something to be understood, is called overweening pride. [One should rather] see all dharmas as empty and see them as signless.
To perceive the wishless, to perceive non-arising, and to perceive the unconditioned is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
To perceive the impermanence of phenomena while still perceiving that phenomena exist is called overweening pride. This is what is meant by the overweening pride of the Śrāvaka vehicle.

It is due to this single impulse that there subsequently appear so many disciples in the following text who are entrusted with the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood. Therefore, [the text] proceeds below.
He further questioned him, saying: "It is appropriate that these people do not believe in the Buddha Vehicle and thus fail to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Yet, they have now realized Arhatship for themselves; why then do you refuse to call them Arhats and instead label them 'persons of overweening pride' (adhimānika)?
Therefore, he explained it himself again, saying: 'How could there be a bhikṣu who has truly attained Arhatship and yet refuses to believe in the teaching of the Bodhisattva?'"
This is simply not possible. Because such individuals refuse to believe in the Bodhisattva Dharma, they cannot be called Arhats;

it would even be appropriate to call them people of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). However, with the exception of the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present, there may be Arhats who do not believe in the Buddha Vehicle—those who are "honored in places where there is no Buddha."
This is it. Why is this so? After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the meaning of such sūtras as these will be difficult to find.
If they should encounter other Buddhas, they will then attain definitive understanding within this Dharma. Śāriputra, you all—
You should with single-minded resolve believe and understand, and receive and uphold the words of the Buddha. The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, speak no falsehood;
there is no other vehicle, but only the Single Buddha Vehicle.
This is further an exhortation using gentle words to inspire faith. Furthermore, he asks: "Though there is no Buddha present before us now, even the Pratyekabuddhas were disciples of the Buddha;
why then do you not believe in the existence of the Buddha-vehicle? Therefore, he explains again:
"This single Buddha-vehicle is what the Buddha himself preached while present in the world; yet people of that time still did not believe, even though they had heard it."

If those who depart from their seats at the mere mention of the wind [of doubt] do so, how much more so for one who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, has not heard the Buddha’s teaching firsthand yet desires to insist upon its necessary truth?

Even after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, though one has not personally heard the Buddha’s words, it is rare indeed to find one who is willing to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain the meaning of this sutra.
At such a time, even if one cannot immediately take full responsibility for it, one must have at least a single moment of faith.

Ever faithful. Nevertheless, by relying on the power of this practice of upholding, reading, and reciting—which serves as the force of habitual cultivation that prevents forgetting—one establishes a remote cause.
Should one encounter another time when a Buddha appears in the world, upon hearing this Dharma from that Buddha, the capacity of the listener and the teaching will coincide;
with a thousandfold understanding and a hundredfold certainty, one will definitively attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). It is due to this single exhortation that the following passage occurs.

There are six kinds of Dharma masters who circulate this teaching; therefore, know that those who, being present before it, believe in this sutra, shall attain Buddhahood upon establishing their ground in this very life.

If one does not believe in this sutra while present before it and is unwilling to take responsibility for it, yet is willing to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain its meaning, becoming one of these six kinds of Dharma masters, they too shall attain Bodhi in a future world.
"Venerable ones, these are all the words of the Tathāgata’s sincere truth. You should have deep faith in them; do not give rise to further doubt.

What are called the words of sincere truth? They consist of nothing more than the eight characters: 'There is no other vehicle; there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle. Therefore, the Sixth Patriarch said:
'All of you, your own minds are the Buddha. Do not harbor further uncertainty. Outside, there is not a single thing that can [be grasped]...'"

All that is established is the fundamental mind, which gives rise to the myriad kinds of phenomena. If one wishes to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one must attain the samādhi of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇasamādhi*) and the samādhi of a single practice (*ekavyūhasamādhi*). If, in all places, one does not dwell upon appearances;

if, amidst those appearances, one does not give rise to hatred or love, nor engage in grasping or rejecting; and if one does not harbor thoughts of benefit, ruin, or similar matters—one will abide in tranquil serenity.
Quiescence—empty, harmonious, and detached—is called the Samādhi of One Aspect (*ekalakṣaṇa-samādhi*).

If, in all walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, one maintains a purely direct mind that does not move from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this truly constitutes the Pure Land; it is called the Samādhi of One Practice (*ekavyūha-samādhi*).
If a person possesses these two samādhis, it is like the earth having seeds: it can contain and nurture them, bringing their fruit to fruition. This is the Samādhi of One Aspect.
The same applies to those who follow the single practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Monks and nuns who harbor overweening pride, Upāsakas with arrogance, and upāsikās lacking faith."
Such were the fourfold assembly, numbering five thousand. They did not perceive their own faults; they possessed deficiencies in their precepts and cherished their blemishes.
These were those of small wisdom who had already departed—the dregs and chaff from among the assembly—gone because of the Buddha’s majestic power.
Such people have meager merit and are unable to receive this Dharma. This assembly is without branches and leaves; it consists only of those who are pure and substantial.
Śāriputra, listen well.

This verse sets forth the ten types of mental afflictions that cause one to withdraw from the assembly. (1) To claim what has not been attained as attained, and to claim what has not been realized as realized;
(2) to harbor arrogance born of self-conceit and fail to practice humility; (3) to settle for being inferior oneself and lack faith in the profound Dharma;
(4) to rely solely on one's own strengths while remaining ignorant of one's own shortcomings; and (5) to have an incomplete holy life, like a leaking cup.
Five, they are not fit vessels. Six, they conceal their flaws and hide their blemishes, feigning and adorning their outward appearance.

Seven, their wisdom and capacity are narrow and small; they are incapable of great responsibilities. Eight, they delight in swallowing dregs and husks, rather than rejoicing in the refined and essential. Nine, they lack inner merit and virtue.
It is difficult to receive the Great Dharma; this is the ninth [difficulty]. To pluck leaves and seek branches without exhausting the root is the tenth.
Because of such people, they only know how to make a living within the ghost cave, yet they are unwilling to investigate thoroughly beneath their own feet.
Therefore, they did not wish to hear it and departed. Now, since there are no such persons among those gathered here, all are those who truly investigate the Buddha-dharma.
This being the very time for me to preach the Dharma, you too should collect your minds and listen.
Thus, he exhorted them, saying: "Śāriputra, listen well. By saying "listen well," he meant that one should not [judge] by what was heard in the past.

It entangles one's mind. One should bring every phrase back to oneself; do not further attempt to understand it through clever intellect or scholarly insight, nor through the medium of written words and spoken language.
The Dharma attained by all Buddhas, through the power of immeasurable skillful means, is taught for the sake of sentient beings.

Whatever thoughts arise in the minds of sentient beings, the various paths they travel, their diverse desires and natures, and the good and evil karma of their past lives—the Buddha knows all these completely.
By means of various conditions, parables, and the power of skillful speech, he causes all to rejoice;
he speaks sūtras, gāthās, and itivṛttakas, jātakas, and adbhutadharmas, as well as nidānas, avadānas, and geyas.

In the *Upadeśa-sūtras*, for those of dull faculties who delight in inferior teachings and are greedily attached to birth and death, who do not practice the profound and wondrous path under the countless Buddhas, and who are distressed and distracted by manifold sufferings—for their sake, I preach *nirvāṇa*. I have established this skillful means.
I cause them to enter the wisdom of the Buddha. I have never before said to you, "You shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
The reason I have not said so is that the time for such a teaching had not yet arrived. Now is precisely that time; I shall definitively proclaim the Mahāyāna. These ninefold teachings of mine—
"Teaching in accordance with sentient beings, taking entry into the Mahāyāna as the foundation—for this reason I preach this sutra.

This verse describes the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate. The three lines regarding "the Dharma attained by all Buddhas" collectively summarize the Tathāgata’s realization of the Dharma of equality, and his opening of immeasurable Dharma-gates to teach sentient beings. [The phrase] "the Dharma attained... [is thus explained].

These refer to the aforementioned "unprecedented phenomena," "difficult-to-understand phenomena," "profound and subtle phenomena," "phenomena attained at the site of enlightenment," "inconceivable phenomena," "ultimate phenomena," "the True Dharma," and "the Wondrous Dharma.
Although these names differ, they are all, in total, the phenomena realized and awakened to by the Tathāgata himself. That is to say, the Tathāgata has realized this equality.
The "immeasurable dharmas" refers to the teaching of immeasurable and various dharma-gates for sentient beings by means of immeasurable and various skillful expedients.
The phrase "sentient beings" below correctly reveals that because the inclinations and desires of sentient beings differ, the teachings given to them also differ.
"Recollection" (nian) means contemplation; "various" (zhongzhong) signifies multiplicity. This is the path practiced.
"Those" refers to the ten wholesome paths of action, the four noble truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, the six perfections, and even material gain, profit, and fame.

"Various" (*śakya*) means an indefinite number. To delight in these is "desire" (*chanda*); to habitually cultivate them is "nature" (*prakṛti*); and that which is performed through desire and nature is "karma.

That the Buddha knows all this completely means that because the Buddha has attained the ten powers (*daśabala*), he possesses the power of knowing the various inclinations and understandings (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*).

He knows the paths traversed by sentient beings. By the power of knowledge regarding the superiority or inferiority of faculties, he knows the inclinations and dispositions practiced by sentient beings, such as the five faculties beginning with faith, which exist in soft, medium, or superior degrees.

By the power of knowledge regarding various realms, he knows the thoughts in the deep minds of sentient beings, namely the three vehicles, the five natures, and so forth. By the power of knowledge regarding the karmic retribution of the divine eye, he knows the [destinies] of sentient beings...
One creates karma such as good and evil, which brings about results such as the desirable and the undesirable;
only the Buddha knows this, and thus, through the power of skillful means (*upāya*), he administers medicine according to the illness, causing all who take it to give rise to joy.

*Sūtra* in the Sanskrit language is here translated as "Kie-king" (契經), meaning a teaching that accords with principle (*dharma*) and accords with the capacity of the listener (*sattva*). *Gāthā* is here translated as "repeated verse" (*geya*), or...
This is taught for those of dull faculties, or for those who have not yet heard [the Dharma]. "Past events" (*itivṛttaka*) refers to the deeds performed throughout immeasurable eons.
"Birth stories" (*jātaka*) refers to the accounts of taking birth throughout immeasurable eons. These are taught for those confused about their past lives.
For those of great faculties, the "unprecedented phenomena" (*adbhutadharma*) are taught; that is, the primordial absence of things, which is ultimately level.
These are the categories of teachings. For those of inferior faculties, he teaches through causes and conditions (*nidāna*). For those of middling faculties, he teaches through parables (*avadāna*).
For those who clearly understand both phenomena and principle, he teaches *geya*, which refers to independent verses (*udāna*).

For those who do not clearly understand either phenomena or principle, he teaches *upadeśa*, which is translated here as "discursive treatises" (*yìlùn jīng*). Furthermore, for a certain class of dull-witted humans and devas, he does not...
They delight in the Mahāyāna, yet cherish only the teachings of the Hīnayāna; they are addicted to causes and attached to results, refusing to relinquish them.

They bob up and down in the river of birth and death; though they encounter the Buddhas, they do not practice the supreme Dharma. Having not yet transcended the eight sufferings, it is difficult for them to avoid the five signs of decay.
Out of necessity, the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths is turned three times, so that they may be liberated from the suffering of birth and death and realize Nirvāṇa.
[They] delight in [this]. However, this too is but a temporary, skillful means; it is not a definitive teaching, nor is it the ultimate Dharma.
In reality, [I] secretly bestow [the truth] and subtly entice [them], causing them to enter the wisdom of the Buddha, yet I have never clearly proclaimed it.
You all shall, in the future, all attain Buddhahood. The reason why I do not speak [of it now] is due to your faculties.
Because their faculties were not yet pure and the time for such teaching had not arrived, [I did not speak].
Now that your faculties are pure and the time for my teaching has arrived, it is fitting that I remove the barriers and directly bestow the Mahāyāna Dharma of universal emptiness.
You should know that the ninefold teachings previously expounded were all spoken according to the inclinations of others; they are not the fundamental [teaching].
I harbor [this intention]: it is solely because I wish to lead all sentient beings into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that I preach the Lotus Sutra today;
this is the purpose behind my intent.
There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, who are gentle and of sharp faculties, and who, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, have practiced the profound and wondrous Way.

For these sons of the Buddhas, I have preached this Mahāyāna sūtra. I prophesy that such people shall attain the path to Buddhahood in a future life, because they mindfully recollect the Buddha with a profound heart and practice and maintain the pure precepts. Upon hearing that they shall attain Buddhahood, great joy pervades their entire bodies.

The Buddha, knowing their mental dispositions and conduct, therefore preaches the Mahāyāna for them. Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, upon hearing the Dharma I preach—even if only a single verse—they shall all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
This clarifies that the Great Dharma is preached for those of great capacity. Regarding the term "Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*):

it refers to one who is able to succeed to the family legacy of the Tathāgata. Regarding "purity of mind": it means not taking the myriad dharmas as companions or opposing them with the various sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
It is not like being greedily attached to the five desires, or like a foolish fly stuck in saliva, unwilling to let go. Regarding "gentleness" (*mṛdu*): it refers to being harmonized...
They are compliant and gentle, easily transformed and guided; they are not like those who are stubborn, coarse, and wild, like mad elephants difficult to subdue.

Those of sharp faculties depart at the mere flick of the whip; they are not like those who delight in inferior teachings, like lame donkeys or sluggish horses that refuse to move forward despite being spurred.
They have heard of the profound and wondrous path practiced by immeasurable Buddhas.
Upon hearing [the teaching], they immediately respond. They are not like those who encounter a Buddha yet do not seek the supreme Dharma, missing the opportunity right before their faces.
Such a capacity is truly a great root; such a person is worthy of being called a child of the Buddha and is capable of receiving the Great Dharma.

For them, I not only preach the Mahāyāna teachings, but I also bestow upon them the prediction of Buddhahood (vyākaraṇa). Why is this? Because of their profound mind, they practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Therefore, because they uphold the precepts; because those with profound resolve delight in cultivating all wholesome dharmas; because those who mindfulness of the Buddha aspire to seek unsurpassed bodhi;
and because those who uphold the precepts are fully endowed with pure and stainless brahmacarya—such are the capacities [of these practitioners].
Upon hearing the prophecy once, great joy pervaded his entire body, and he took it upon himself with both shoulders.
Because his resolve was so profound, his mindfulness of the Buddha so earnest, and his root of precepts so pure, the Buddha knew his mind and understood his conduct;
therefore, He taught him the Mahāyāna. Yet this Mahāyāna is the Dharma of equality; it makes no distinction between those of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties. Mind—
Even with a defiled mind, one may attain purity; it suffices for a single phrase to permeate the spirit, and all shall become Buddhas. It is just like a wondrous medicinal gāthā:
if one merely lets it touch the lips, there is no illness that cannot be cured. Do not harbor even a hair’s breadth of doubt within your breast and refuse to take it.
Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except for the Buddha’s skillful means.
He employs only provisional names to guide sentient beings, for the purpose of expounding the wisdom of the Buddhas.

Below this, the reasons why one must necessarily teach the Mahāyāna are explained in detail. There are five points. First: because when sought thoroughly throughout the ten directions, no other vehicle exists.
It is said that in the lands of all Buddhas, from the limits of heaven to the depths of the earth, there is only a single Dharma and no second thing;
it is only that the Buddhas, through the power of skillful means, forcibly establish various provisional names. One does not know these... [text ends]
These various provisional designations are all intended to guide sentient beings and cause them to enter the Buddha-wisdom; for this reason, the One Vehicle must be taught.
When Buddhas appear in the world, this alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. Ultimately, they never [rely] upon the Lesser Vehicle.
To deliver and save sentient beings.
Second, because the Way of all Buddhas is the same, it is said that the original intention for all Buddhas to appear in the world is solely this one matter;
there is no second matter. How could I dare to violate the ritual protocols of all Buddhas by presenting what is not the true Dharma to others?
Therefore, he never uses the methods of the Lesser Vehicle to save sentient beings; he invariably teaches the One Vehicle.
The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle, and according to the Dharma he has realized—adorned with the powers of concentration and wisdom—he thereby delivers sentient beings.

I have personally realized the unsurpassed path, the equal Dharma of the Mahāyāna. If I were to transform even a single person by means of the Hīnayāna, I would fall into stinginess and greed; such a thing is impossible for me.
Third, because they abide in the One Vehicle themselves. This means that all Buddhas abide entirely within the impartial dharma of the Mahāyāna;
only by using what they have personally realized to deliver all sentient beings can they be said to be truly impartial. If they were to realize the Great Dharma for themselves alone...
To transform others by means of inferior teachings is itself stinginess; it is to fall into greed and attachment, which leads to partiality and inequality.
It does not matter whether one transforms many people with inferior teachings—one falls into the state of stinginess even by transforming a single person with such teachings.
How could such a thing be permissible? Therefore, one must necessarily preach the One [Vehicle].
"Vehicle. To give a small portion is what is meant by stinginess; to guard against giving much is what is meant by greed.
If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not deceive them, nor does he harbor thoughts of greed or envy; he has severed all evils within the dharmas.
Therefore, the Buddha alone among those in the ten directions is free from fear. Adorned with the marks upon my body, my radiance illuminates the world;
honored by immeasurable multitudes, I proclaim for them the seal of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā-mudrā*).

Fourth, because of taking refuge in the Buddha with faith. If a person does not long for other vehicles but only aspires to the Great Dharma, they take refuge in the Buddha with faith, believing that the Tathāgata does not deceive out of malice because people cannot see him, nor does he speak falsely out of ignorance because they do not know him.
Furthermore, they believe that he has never been stingy with the Dharma and withheld it from others, nor has he ever envied others.

He will grant me the Dharma. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has exhausted the five stages of dwelling and is honored wherever he may be, he is able to respond immediately to every invocation without the slightest hesitation or fear. How could he possibly fail to speak for my sake?

It is only because I do not believe in the Buddha-vehicle that I fear it would be of no benefit were he to speak; therefore, he does not speak for my sake. Thus blaming myself, I redoubled my efforts.
With deep faith, at that time he immediately manifested a body adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, just as today.

He emitted light from the white tuft between his brows, universally illuminating the world, and for their sake he preached the Dharma-seal of the true nature (*dharmatā*). For this reason, he must preach the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
As for the term "seal" (*mudrā*), it refers to the true nature of the One Vehicle; it is like the seals and insignia of a royal court. Yet, by means of this single seal, one seals all things.
Śāriputra, you should know this by the nature of the Dharma: I originally made a vow, desiring to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself.
As I vowed in the past, that wish is now fulfilled; I have transformed all sentient beings and caused them all to enter the Buddha-way.

Fifth: Because of the original vow of the Tathāgata, he says: "Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have established a great vow, that when I attain Buddhahood, I shall deliver all sentient beings so that they all become Buddhas. Know that I am without distinction.
Now, desiring to fulfill this original vow, I must therefore preach the One Vehicle."
If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way; yet those without wisdom are confused and deluded, refusing to accept my teaching.
I know these beings have never cultivated the roots of goodness; they are firmly attached to the five desires, and because of their ignorant craving, they give rise to affliction.
Due to the causes and conditions of various desires, they fall into the three evil realms and transmigrate within the six destinies, undergoing all manner of bitter poisons.
Assuming the subtle form of an embryo, they constantly grow and develop from lifetime to lifetime. Those of meager virtue and little merit are oppressed by manifold sufferings.
They enter the dense forest of false views—such as "existence" or "non-existence"—and relying upon these various views, they fully possess the sixty-two [views].
Deeply attached to illusory dharmas, they stubbornly cling to them and will not relinquish them. Arrogant and self-conceited, their minds are crooked and insincere.
For thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, they have not heard the name of the Buddha, nor have they heard the True Dharma;
such people are difficult to deliver. Therefore, Śāriputra, I employ skillful means to teach them the various paths for exhausting suffering and show them nirvana.
Although I speak of nirvana, it is not true extinction. All phenomena, from their very origin, have always been characterized by quiescence.
Once the sons of the Buddha have practiced the Way, they shall become Buddhas in future ages. Possessing the power of skillful means, I reveal the teachings of the three vehicles.
All the World-Honored Ones preach the single vehicle path. Now, this great assembly should all eliminate their doubts and delusions;
the words of the Buddhas do not differ, for there is only the one vehicle and no second.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata reveals the provisional teachings (*upāya*). Question: If this is so, why does he further speak of two [vehicles] and three?
Answer: Because the capacities (*indriya*) of sentient beings differ. If this Dharma is taught to those of great wisdom, they will joyfully receive and uphold it.
If this Dharma is taught to those of inferior faculties and little wisdom, the Dharma will not accord with their faculties; this is called confusion and disorder.

This is a perversion. It is not merely a matter of lack of faith; rather, they give rise to confusion. I know that these sentient beings have not planted roots of goodness and are firmly attached to the five desires.
This is all due to the two kinds of ignorance (*avidyā*)—which initiate karma and moisten rebirth—further giving rise to various afflictions such as anger.
Because their minds are deluded by these afflictions, they become addicted to the five desires and create all manner of karma. Thus, it is through delusion and karma...
Therefore, they fall into the three miserable realms (tridurgati) and undergo various retributions; this is the defilement of sentient beings (sattva-kaṣāya).
Because of transmigration, although they possess vast majestic power, they are unable to employ it; instead, they enter the womb of their parents and receive this minute physical form.
From lifetime to lifetime, as birth succeeds birth, craving and attachment increase, delusions and karma grow, and merit and virtue daily diminish. Regarding fire...
Within this house, they are constantly being scorched and boiled by a great fire, unable to escape on their own; this is what is meant by "impurity.

Having then conceived the aspiration to leave the burning house, they fail to encounter an enlightened teacher and instead cultivate deviant paths, relying upon the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

Furthermore, sixty-two views arise; this is the turbidity of views (*dṛṣ�ṭi-kaṣāya*). Due to attachment to these various views, they regard the *saṃbhogakāya* as their self, clinging to it with firm affection and refusing to let go.
Relying on this "self," they give rise to arrogance, becoming haughty and boastful, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the unsurpassed path.
Not realizing that all these are but empty, delusional, and floating minds, none of which are real—this is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*).
Their speech is not straightforward, and hidden malice arises; for thousands of millions of eons they shall not hear the Buddha-dharma.
Such people are extremely difficult to deliver—this is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kāṣāya*). Because they have fallen into this world of five turbidities, they remain entangled.

Because it is never interrupted, I have provisionally opened up various skillful means to teach the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as the path to the exhaustion of suffering, and further shown the bliss of nirvana to entice beings out of suffering.
Yet, although I speak of the bliss of nirvana, this is merely to dispel the suffering of birth and death; it is not the actual reality of the Tathāgata’s sphere of activity or its intrinsic nature.
This is *nirvāṇa*. Because the Tathāgata’s self-nature *nirvāṇa* has been quiescent from the very beginning and is fundamentally extinguished, it does not undergo further extinction.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, if you are willing to believe in this *nirvāṇa*, take it upon one shoulder and practice this path with diligence;
in a future life you will surely attain Buddhahood, without having to wait for three births or sixty kalpas. I—
Although various Dharma gates have been established to instruct sentient beings, these are all skillful means.

To speak according to the ultimate reality, the Buddhas of the three periods of time teach only the One Vehicle, for there is no second dharma. Now, let this great assembly not harbor even a single thought of doubt;
you must certainly receive this with an open mind, for all Buddhas, with one voice and in unison, teach only this.
"The One Vehicle, because there is no second vehicle. When Yangshan was a śrāmaṇera, his voice was loud as he recited the sutras.
Master Luyuan scolded him, saying, "This śrāmaṇera’s recitation of the sutras sounds just like crying. Yangshan asked, "What about Huiji?
And what about you, Master? The Master then looked at him. Yangshan said, "If it is 'what,' how does it differ from crying? The Master then desisted.
This refers to the single, non-dual vehicle.
Throughout countless kalpas in the past, there have been immeasurable Buddhas who attained parinirvāṇa—hundreds, thousands, tens of millions, and billions in kind, their number beyond measure.
In this way, these World-Honored Ones, through various causes, conditions, and parables, and by the power of countless skillful means, have expounded the characteristics of all dharmas.
All these World-Honored Ones alike preach the Single Vehicle Dharma (Ekayāna), transforming immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.

Furthermore, the Great Holy Lords, knowing the deep-seated desires of all beings in the world—whether devas or humans—employ further diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
If there are classes of sentient beings who encounter the Buddhas of the past, [they are led to this teaching].

If they hear the Dharma and practice giving, or maintain precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom—cultivating the Buddha-wisdom in these various ways—all such persons have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, if there are people with virtuous and gentle hearts...
All such sentient beings have already attained the path of Buddhahood.

After the various Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, those who make offerings to their relics shall erect billions of kinds of stupas made of gold, silver, and crystal; of mother-of-pearl and agate; and of ruby, lapis lazuli, and pearl.
Pure, vast, and magnificently adorned, they embellish all the stupas. Some erect stone temples made of sandalwood, aloeswood, *mṛdvīkā* wood, and other timbers;
or those made of brick, tile, clay, and earth. Even if one constructs a temple for the Buddha by piling up earth in the midst of a wilderness, [the merit is immeasurable].
Even those who, in play as children, gathered sand to make stūpas for the Buddha—all such persons have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
If anyone, for the sake of the Buddha, establishes various images, carving them with all their characteristic marks, they too have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Some are made of the seven precious gems; others of brass, red or white copper, tin, lead, or pewter; and some of iron, wood, or clay.
Or those who, using glue, lacquer, and cloth, have fashioned and adorned images of the Buddha—such people as these have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Or those who have painted images of the Buddha, with features adorned by the hundred blessings, whether doing so themselves or employing others—they have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
Even those who, in childhood play, have drawn images of the Buddha with grass, wood, or a brush, or even with their fingernails—
all such persons gradually accumulate merit, become fully endowed with the heart of great compassion, and have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.

They merely transform bodhisattvas and deliver immeasurable multitudes. If a person, at a stupa or temple, before a precious image or a painted image, makes offerings with flowers, incense, banners, and canopies with a reverent heart;
or if they cause others to perform music, beating drums and blowing horns and conchs—
Xiao flutes, pipes, qins, konghous, pipa lutes, gongs, and bronze cymbals—such various exquisite sounds as these, all are held up as offerings.
Or with a joyful heart, they may sing praises of the Buddha’s virtues; even a single small sound has already led them to attain the Way of the Buddha.
If a person, even with a distracted mind, offers as little as a single flower to a painted image, they will gradually come to see countless Buddhas.
If there are those who prostrate, or even merely join their palms, or raise a single hand, or even slightly lower their heads, making offerings to this image,
they will gradually behold immeasurable Buddhas, personally attain the unsurpassed Way, and extensively deliver countless multitudes.

They enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder, like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted. Even if a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and utters "Namo Buddha" but once, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
Regarding those Buddhas of the past, whether they were still in the world or had passed away—
"If there are those who hear this Dharma, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
This clarifies that the Buddhas of the past also taught the Dharma through skillful means (*upāya*), which is singular and without duality.

Furthermore, it states below that it is not only the teaching of the Three Vehicles that constitutes these skillful means; rather, they are aids for eliciting [realization]. Moreover, it is not merely by means of...
Light serves as a skillful means (*upāya*) for assistance and inspiration. There are many other kinds of extraordinary skillful means that provide such assistance and inspiration;

for example, erecting stupas and temples, crafting images of the Buddha, or offering a single flower, raising a single hand, joining the palms, or bowing the head—all these are nothing other than aids for manifesting the one great matter in the daily lives of sentient beings, which is entirely identical to the radiance emitted by the Tathāgata.
They are equal and without distinction; that is to say, whatever actions are performed, they always serve a single purpose. Master Pang said: "In daily activities there is no difference;
it is only that I alone find harmony. Whether it be supernatural powers or subtle functions, I employ them alike in carrying water and hauling firewood."
This is precisely the meaning. Because sentient beings regard this as ordinary, the World-Honored One praised it as marvelous.
He intended for people to know that this extraordinary matter resides right within the midst of daily life;

therefore, he manifested it by assisting its arousal at the place where light was emitted, and further assisted in its revelation within the context of daily activities. "If there are those below... first clarifies the cultivation of the six perfections.

"The myriad practices" means that all have already attained the Buddha-way. The two characters "already attained" (*yicheng*) state that one's own possession of Buddha-nature is the cause (*yin*), while the six perfections and myriad practices are the conditions (*yuan*). This is just like fire within wood or gold within ore;
the act of drilling the wood or smelting the ore constitutes the conditions. From the words "All Buddhas" [onward], the text next clarifies cultivation.
Those who practice the ten wholesome paths, the Four Noble Truths, and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination all attain the Buddha-way.

From the various Buddhas down to those who offer the three types of relics with the three kinds of wisdom, erecting stupas of the seven treasures or constructing temples of sandalwood—even those who pile up earth to make a temple or gather sand to form a stupa.
"Those who all attain the Buddha-way," though differing in refinement or coarseness, are equal because their lands are wondrous.
When the World-Honored One was walking with the assembly, he pointed to the ground with his finger and said, "At this spot, a Brahma-temple (stūpa) should be built.

Śakra took a single blade of grass, planted it in the ground, and said, "The construction of the Brahma-temple is complete. This is precisely that principle. If one were to descend [to explain it], [it would be as follows]: Four Ming.

Those who fashion images of the Buddha shall all attain the Way of Buddhahood. [Section on Painting: Those who paint images of the Buddha with colors and pigments shall all attain the Way of Buddhahood.

[Section on Reverence: If there are those who reverently offer worship to images of the Buddha—some offering incense, flowers, banners, and canopies with a reverent heart, and some offering various sublime sounds with a reverent heart—they shall all attain the Way of Buddhahood.
Regarding those who practice cultivation: there are those who offer worship with joyful songs and hymns praising the Buddha’s virtues;
those who offer worship to painted images with a distracted mind; those who offer worship by joining their palms and bowing their heads with a distracted mind;
and those who offer worship by uttering "Namo Buddha" once with a distracted mind. Such minor causes all lead to the realization of the Buddha-way, even though the devotion may be casual.
They are not the same, because they pertain to the Equal and Wondrous Minds (*samatā-samyak-citta*).

That which is called "melting jars, basins, hairpins, and bracelets into a single gold," or "churning butter, curd, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into a single flavor"—is this the power of Dīpaṃkara, or rather the power of Prabhāsa?
To call it "extraordinary" is indeed appropriate. Long ago, when Devadatta was at the point of death, he uttered "Namo... but had not yet reached the character for "Buddha" before—
He fell into hell. The Buddha prophesied that upon his emergence from hell, he would become a pratyekabuddha named Namu.
Furthermore, there was one who worshipped celestial deities in a foreign land; he fashioned a golden head for the image, but when bandits came to seize it, he uttered "Namu Buddha."
The image then appeared to have a golden head. The next day, when the assembly gathered, the heavenly image had lost its head.
The crowd said, "Although we fashioned this image, no deity came to inhabit it. If a deity had inhabited it, how could it have lost its head?
A deity then descended and said, "When the thief came to take the head, he chanted 'Namo Buddha. This startled all the deities, and thus I gained the opportunity. That is why it was lost."
[The thief] offered his head. The crowd said, "Is heaven not equal to the Buddha? Since it is not equal to the Buddha, why do you not honor and serve him?
Even a bandit who merely cries out "Namo Buddha" obtains the head of heaven; how much more so for a worthy person who cries out "Namo Buddha"—would they not attain unsurpassed Bodhi?
The future World-Honored Ones shall be immeasurable in number; all these Tathāgatas likewise teach the Dharma through skillful means.
All Tathāgatas, by means of infinite expedients, deliver and liberate all sentient beings, causing them to enter the untainted wisdom of the Buddha.
If there are those who hear this Dharma, not one among them shall fail to become a Buddha. This is the fundamental vow of all Buddhas:

"The Buddha-path that I have practiced, I desire that all sentient beings may likewise attain. Though the Buddhas of future ages may speak in hundreds of thousands of billions of ways, [this remains their core resolve].
The countless dharma-gates are in reality but a single vehicle. The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, know that all phenomena are eternally without intrinsic nature.
Since the lineage of the Buddhas arises from conditions, they therefore preach the One Vehicle. This Dharma abides in its own place; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.
Having realized this at the site of enlightenment, the Teacher spoke through skillful means.
This clarifies that future Buddhas likewise teach the Dharma through skillful means; it is singular and without duality.

Therefore, once it touches the faculty of hearing, there is nothing that does not lead to Buddhahood. From the phrase "the original vows of all Buddhas" below, he speaks of the fundamental vows of all Buddhas; thus, he says "one."
Regarding the "Vehicles": the Buddhas, beneath their two feet, teach the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) for the purpose of giving rise to the great root.
As for the phrase "two feet," it refers to the fulfillment of merit and the fulfillment of wisdom. Regarding the statement "knowing that phenomena are eternally without nature":

"knowing" means awakening; "phenomena" refers to the mind of sentient beings; "eternal" means true eternity and immutability; and "without nature" means being devoid of both self-nature and other-nature.
If this Dharma were not eternal, it would result in annihilationism; how then could there be five natures?
If the natures were fixed as five, then Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all sentient beings would certainly never be able to become Buddhas.

Because one knows that this Dharma is eternal yet lacks a fixed nature, each person’s nature is formed according to their own habitual perfuming—what is called "the unchanging following conditions" (avikāra-anuvartana). Following...
It is unchanging. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The nature of that which has no nature is precisely Buddha-nature.
Although this Buddha-nature is possessed by all sentient beings, it can only be awakened through the long-term perfuming of the Mahāyāna teachings.
This is why the World-Honored One necessarily taught the One Vehicle. Thus, the Sixth Patriarch said: "Your Buddha-nature is like a seed;
my preaching of the Dharma is like seasonal rain. Encountering this nourishing moisture, all shall sprout and grow."
Those who receive my intent will certainly attain Bodhi; those who rely on my practice will surely realize the wondrous fruit.
This teaching below opens up the provisional means. It says that this Dharma is the "true person of no station," fundamentally having no rank or position.

Yet, within the ranks of all dharmas—the four types of sages and the six classes of ordinary beings—all are positions where this Dharma dwells. Thus, one knows that in every instance and every dharma, [it is present].

There is nothing that is not the single mark of equality and quiescence. However, it is only when one sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and opens the Buddha-wisdom that one truly knows this Dharma.
Having attained equal and perfect enlightenment and known this Dharma, one employs the power of skillful means (*upāya*) to open various gates and preach various teachings.
Therefore, know that whether one speaks of the Great or the Small [Vehicle], there is nothing that is not this One Dharma.

Worshipped by devas and humans, the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions—numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges—have appeared in the world for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings.
They, too, preach this very Dharma, knowing the supreme tranquility through the power of skillful means.

Although they manifest various paths, their ultimate aim is the Buddha-vehicle. They know the various conducts of sentient beings, the inclinations of their deep minds, the karmic actions practiced in the past, their desires, natures, and powers of diligence, as well as the sharpness or dullness of their faculties; by means of these various causes and conditions, [they teach].
Parables and verbal expressions are taught through appropriate skillful means.
This clarifies that the Buddhas of the present likewise first realize the dharma of quiescence and subsequently teach the three vehicles by means of skillful means.
In reality, all are of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). "Knowing what sentient beings practice" refers to the various paths they traverse.
"What is contemplated by their profound mind" refers to what is thought by the minds of sentient beings.
"Karma practiced in the past" refers to the wholesome and unwholesome karma of previous lives. "Desires, dispositions, diligence, and so forth" refers to the manifold varieties of desire.
This is my nature.
Now I am likewise; for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, I proclaim the Buddha-way through various gateways of the Dharma.
By the power of my wisdom, I know the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings, and through skillful means I teach all dharmas so that they may all attain joy.
This Śākyamuni himself also claims that what was previously taught as the three vehicles is in fact the one vehicle. To be unoppressed by manifold sufferings is called "peace" (an).
For chaotic thoughts not to arise is called "concealment" (yin). To elaborate the text and expound the meaning is called "proclamation" (xuan).
To emit light and enter meditative absorption is called "manifestation" (shi).
Śāriputra, you should know that with my Buddha-eye I observe the sentient beings of the six realms.

Deprived of merit and wisdom, they enter the perilous path of birth and death, where suffering continues without interruption. Their bodies are attached to the five desires, like a yak that loves its tail.
Shrouded by craving and attachment, they are blind and see nothing; they do not seek the Buddha of Great Power nor the Dharma that severs suffering.
Deeply immersed in various false views, they seek to abandon suffering through further suffering. For the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
This clarifies the reason for revealing the provisional. To lack merit is called "poverty"; to lack wisdom is called "distress. The perilous path of birth and death refers to the three evil realms.
The uninterrupted succession of suffering is the fruit of suffering; the five desires are the cause of suffering.
It is said that the reason I teach the Three Vehicles is because, at the time I first attained the Way, I revealed the Buddha-... [text truncated]
With knowledge and vision, he then used his Buddha-eye to penetrate and observe the ten directions.

He saw the sentient beings of the six realms who do not cultivate the wisdom of the Buddha, revolving through birth and death without interruption. When he investigated the cause of this, he found it all stems from being attached to the five desires.
It is like a yak that loves its own tail, only to be ultimately harmed by others. Since sentient beings are thus possessed by craving and attachment...
They obscure themselves, becoming addicted to the five desires; they see only their pleasure and fail to see their suffering, like those who are blind and sightless.
Having become attached to the subtle form within the womb, they further crawl along the perilous path of birth and death.
Consequently, they cast aside their own one Honored One—the majestic, dignified Buddha of great power—and disregard him, refusing even to seek his cessation.

Regarding the method for suffering: though one may willingly accept death, if spiritual awareness is thereby revealed and one desires to transcend the three realms, yet fails to encounter a wise teacher or hear the True Dharma, one will instead fall into the net of false views.

To further cultivate false precepts and false concentrations as causes for transcending the world and seeking escape from the three realms is like digging the earth to find heaven, or seeking ice within fire—how utterly futile it is!
It is well. Out of compassion for these deluded sentient beings, the Tathāgata has given rise to great pity and shall deliver them all.
When I first sat at the site of enlightenment, I contemplated the tree and also walked in meditation; during those twenty-one days, I reflected upon such matters.
"The wisdom I have attained is subtle, wondrous, and supreme. Yet the faculties of sentient beings are dull; they are attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance.
How can such as these be delivered? At that time, the Brahma Kings and the various Śakras, Lords of Devas, [spoke thus].

The Four World-Protecting Kings, Maheśvara, and the rest of the celestial hosts, with their hundreds of thousands of millions of followers, joined their palms in reverence and paid homage, entreating me to turn the wheel of Dharma. I then reflected within myself: "If I were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle..."
Sentient beings are submerged in suffering; they cannot believe in this Dharma. Because they destroy the Dharma and lack faith, they fall into the three evil realms.
I thought: "I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana. Then I recalled the skillful means employed by the Buddhas of the past.
"The path I have now attained should likewise be taught as the Three Vehicles.

This passage below recounts the seven days of contemplation; it represents the Lord’s inner reflections throughout forty years, revealing his thoughts with complete sincerity to show that both the teaching of the Three and the teaching of the One are entirely in accordance with the ancient Buddha-dharma.
This was not composed by me. I say that when I beheld these sentient beings suffering and arose with the intent to rescue them, there were still many difficulties involved.

Thus, when I first sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained perfect enlightenment, I gazed at the tree as it grew, desiring that the great Bodhi tree might provide shade and coolness for all sentient beings. However, it was necessarily...
"Three reflections" means to act only after mature reflection and careful examination. "What I have attained," etc., describes the first seven contemplations.
It says that the wisdom I have attained is profoundly deep and immeasurable; it is unprecedented and most excellent.
Furthermore, observing sentient beings, their five faculties—faith and the rest—are shallow, meager, and inferior; they are already entangled by the five desires and further [afflicted by...]
Obscured by ignorance, such is my Dharma and such is the capacity of beings; how then can they attain liberation?

Because within samādhi I gave rise to this single thought—the mind to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings—Brahmā, Śakra, and all the devas simultaneously flocked together to request that I turn the wheel of the Dharma. Thus, dragons arose and clouds gathered; tigers roared and the wind blew.

[He] was born. I then descended. This refers to the contemplation during the second seven-day period. If I were to immediately turn the supreme wheel of Dharma while sentient beings were drowning in the great ocean of suffering, the Dharma would not accord with their capacities, and their capacities would not grasp the Dharma.
Not only would it fail to inspire faith in them, but it would instead cause them to give rise to slander and destroy the True Dharma. If they were to slander the Dharma...
They will inevitably fall into the three miserable realms. Thus, preaching the Dharma would be of no benefit to living beings and, on the contrary, would be harmful to them.

Therefore, it would be better for me not to preach the Dharma at all and instead enter Nirvana quickly. "Reflecting upon... and so forth refers to his contemplation during the three periods of seven days.
When the Buddhas of the past realized the fruit of the Way, they immediately opened various gates of expedient means (*upāya*) to transform and deliver sentient beings.
"Sentient beings, as I now preach the Dharma, I shall likewise take the past Buddhas as my model.
While he was reflecting thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared and comforted him with Brahma-sounds: "Excellent, Śākyamuni!"
The foremost Teacher has attained this unsurpassed Dharma; following all Buddhas, he employs the power of skillful means.
We, too, have all attained this most wondrous and supreme Dharma, and for the sake of all classes of sentient beings, we distinguish and expound the three vehicles.
Those with little wisdom delight in inferior teachings and do not believe they can become Buddhas themselves; for this reason, through skillful means, I distinguish and explain various fruits.
Although I speak of the three vehicles, it is solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas.
This describes the consolation and encouragement offered by all the Buddhas. He states that he contemplated for three weeks, desiring to employ skillful means to accord with the minds of the Buddhas;
therefore, the Buddhas manifested their bodies to comfort and instruct him, praising him by saying:
"Since Śākyamuni has attained the Tathāgata’s path of equality and serves as the supreme guide for both the mundane and supramundane realms, yet you still do not consent..."
To act with self-will and self-assertion, yet to be able to follow the skillful means practiced by all Buddhas—is this not excellent?
Thus, we Buddhas have all attained the most wondrous, supreme, and equal Dharma;

nevertheless, because the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ and their inclinations are each distinct, we also speak of three vehicles through differentiation within non-differentiation. Why is this? Because...
Their wisdom is narrow and inferior; they take pleasure only in the dharmas favored by the poor, do not believe that they themselves are Buddhas, and are unwilling to accept this responsibility.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, through the power of skillful means, taught the path of the three vehicles as a place for a temporary rest along the way.
In reality, however, it was solely for the purpose of instructing bodhisattvas, and was not a genuine transformation through the path of the Lesser Vehicle.
Śāriputra, you should know: Having heard the profound, pure, subtle, and wondrous voice of the Holy Lion, I cried out, "Namo to all Buddhas," and further formed this thought:
"I have appeared in this turbid and evil world; as all the Buddhas have taught, I too shall practice in accordance with their instructions."
Having reflected upon this matter, he proceeded at once to Vārāṇasī. The mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be expressed in words;
yet, by the power of skillful means, he preached it for the sake of the five bhikṣus. This is called the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and from it there arose the sound of nirvāṇa.

And as for the Arhats, the distinct names of the Dharma and the Saṅgha—since time immemorial, I have constantly taught and demonstrated the dharma of Nirvāṇa, wherein the suffering of birth and death is forever extinguished; this is what I have always said.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the three [vehicles] in the past was an emulation of the ritual protocols of the ancient Buddhas.
First, upon hearing words of consolation, one utters "Namo Buddha," which is an expression of reverent devotion. Having already offered such reverence, one further reflects:
"Since I have now emerged from within this world of five turbidities, I shall follow the opening of the gate of skillful means as taught by the Buddha. Now...
Having resolved to follow and act in accordance with the Tathāgata, and having completed these reflections, he proceeded to the Deer Park.
There, he turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths three times; yet the path and dharma of the One Vehicle that I have realized is, from the very beginning, quiescent and extinguished.
There could not have been any sound; how, then, could there have been such designations as "Dharma" and "Saṃgha"?

It was through my skillful establishment of expedient means, perfectly coinciding with the appropriate capacities [of beings], that when I preached the Four Truths for the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, this Dharma of quiescent extinction first attained transformation and circulation, and thus the name "Turning the Wheel of the Dharma" came into being. That is to say:
Taking the Dharma realized as *nirvāṇa*, taking the person who realizes it as an *arhat*,
and taking the one who turns the wheel of Dharma as a Buddha— thereupon, this single-flavored Dharma was split into three.
This is called the "Three Jewels of Distinct Characteristics. He further praised it, saying:
"This Dharma of Nirvana is that which I have extolled and revealed throughout kalpas of long antiquity.
If you all attain this Dharma, birth and death will be forever exhausted, and you shall not undergo further existence. Because there is such benefit, for forty years I have constantly spoken thus."

Śāriputra, you should know: I see sons of the Buddha who are resolutely seeking the path of the Buddha—immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis—all of whom, with hearts of reverence, have come to where the Buddha is.
They have all previously heard from various Buddhas the Dharma taught through skillful means.
I then had this thought: "The reason the Tathāgata has appeared is to preach the Buddha-wisdom; now is precisely the time for it.
This was the Tathāgata himself declaring that he would today preach the One Vehicle, which is also an emulation of the ritual protocols of the Buddhas of antiquity.
I have also seen those of great capacity who take no pleasure in inferior teachings; whose power of faith is firm and stable, and who aspire to seek unsurpassed bodhi.
With hearts of reverence, these sons of the Buddha come to my presence. Throughout past kalpas, these [have practiced...]
I have heard that the Buddhas preach the Dharma of skillful means; when their faculties are matured and they turn their minds toward aspiring for the Great Vehicle, I then reflect:
"The Tathāgata has truly appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition (ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya), not for the minor causes and conditions of the two vehicles.
He wishes to preach the Buddha-wisdom, and now is precisely the time for it; how could he fail to preach it? This is what is meant by: "If..."
When people place their faith and take refuge in the Buddha, I preach for them the Seal of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*).
Because I am fully endowed with the two *pāramitās* of skillful means (*upāya*) and knowledge-and-vision (*jñānadarśana*), I adapt my teaching to both the great and the small, leaving none behind.
Śāriputra, you should know that those of dull faculties and small wisdom, who are attached to signs and full of pride, cannot believe in this Dharma.
Now, joyful and fearless among all bodhisattvas, I set aside expedient means with straightforwardness and teach only the unsurpassed Way.
When the Bodhisattvas heard this Dharma, the net of their doubts was entirely removed. The twelve hundred Arhats shall all likewise become Buddhas.
Just as the Buddhas of the three periods of time have employed the ritual for preaching the Dharma, so do I now likewise preach the Dharma of non-discrimination.
The following section concludes the preceding discussion regarding the intent behind teaching both the Great and the Small Vehicles. It says:
"You should know that at this time, while I was precisely expounding the Buddha-wisdom, there were still those dull-rooted arhats who were unwilling to turn their minds;

they clung to one corner [of their limited understanding] without returning, and hearing the Great Dharma, they were struck with alarm and doubt. They remained fixed in *nirvāṇa* without relinquishing it, dwelling upon the 'dharma-self'."
They give rise to arrogance. Such people as these are unable to produce faith in the profound Dharma; indeed, there are those who even brush aside their robes and depart.
Now, however, there are those who abandon their old habits to admire the Mahāyāna, coming to my presence with a heart of reverence.
To seek the sublime Dharma—how could it be easily obtained? Therefore, I rejoice that he was not born of fear or timidity, but willingly accepted the responsibility;
he is a vessel for Bodhisattvas. I have immediately cleared away the branches and byways for him, pointing directly to the great highway of Chang’an.
Thus, upon hearing this Dharma, the Bodhisattva immediately gave rise to reverent faith, and the net of doubt was entirely removed. If...
Even the Arhats, upon hearing this Dharma, gave rise to reverent faith and likewise received their predictions of enlightenment.

Thus, for small matters I have spoken three times, and for great matters I have spoken once; from beginning to end, everything follows the eternal regulations of the ancient Buddhas and is not my own invention.
Therefore, when I today preach the Dharma of non-discrimination, I am likewise emulating the ritual of the ancient Buddhas.

Listen well! The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is rare; it is difficult to encounter them even after a vast interval. Though they may appear in the world, it is further difficult for them to preach this Dharma.
To hear this Dharma throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas is likewise difficult; and those who are able to listen to this Dharma—such people are also rare indeed.
Just as the udumbara flower, which all beings love and delight in, appears only once in a great while— a rare wonder for devas and humans— so too,
when one hears the Dharma with joy and praise, even uttering but a single word, it constitutes an offering to all the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Such a person is most rare, surpassing even the udumbara flower. You should have no doubts: I am the King of all Dharmas.
I announce to the great assembly: I teach and transform all bodhisattvas solely through the path of the One Vehicle; I have no disciples who are śrāvakas.
The prose section stimulates their faith with words of peril, while the verses further strengthen that faith through four challenges.
First, it speaks of the difficulty of a Buddha’s appearance in the world, as the subsequent text states: "For one hundred and eighty kalpas, time passed in vain without a Buddha";
and again, "Beyond hundreds of thousands of kalpas, such a sign has never been seen"; and furthermore, "In the immeasurable kalpas of the past, [it was] empty..."
"Since the passing [of the Buddha], there has been no such thing as this. Regarding the phrase "Even if," it next states that the teaching of the Dharma is difficult.
For forty years, he was able to endure this matter for the sake of inferior ordinary people who grasp at signs;

he never revealed it until their faculties were matured and their resolve became pure, and they came to understand and believe him in their hearts. Is this not indeed difficult? Regarding the phrase "Immeasurable," it is the third [point].

It is said that hearing the Dharma is difficult. Even those who possess the remaining achievements of the Era of Awesome Sound (Vikurvaṇa-rāja) and carry the lingering traces of the Victorious One’s wisdom are still unable to even raise a single eyebrow to take up this matter;
is this not indeed difficult? As for the ability to listen below [the level of such sages], four points show that hearing the Dharma is difficult:

it is not only difficult for one to attain sudden enlightenment upon a single hearing, but it is also difficult for the Dharma to arise within the faculty of hearing even after it has passed through the ear.
To slander [the Dharma] and yet not give rise to resentment or jealousy is also difficult. As when Namo Aśokottama loudly proclaimed [his name], tiles and stones were rained down upon him;

even at the assembly on Vulture Peak, there were those who withdrew from their seats—is this not indeed difficult? Thus we know that while the *bāgē* (folk songs) may be harmonized by the multitude, the *xuěqǔ* (melodies of snow/snow-white purity) respond but rarely.

Let us set aside for a moment the difficulty of a Buddha appearing in the world, or the difficulty of preaching the Dharma; as for those who hear the Dharma and attain awakening and entry—[this is even more rare].
It is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower. That one merely hears it and does not give rise to slander, resentment, or envy is itself the appearance of an udumbara;
how could it be easy? Let alone those who hear the Dharma and attain realization through it—they exceed even the udumbara in rarity.
To hear this Dharma and, instead of giving rise to resentment or jealousy, to feel joy;
to refrain from slander and instead offer praise—such a person is rare, rarer even than the udumbara flower. This is equivalent to making offerings to all Buddhas, without any difference.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas flow forth from this sutra. Thus it is the fourth rarity.
Such is the benefit, such is the case. Now that you have heard this Dharma today, how could you fail to conceive the thought that it is difficult to encounter?
Why then do you harbor further doubts and delusions? Therefore, I urge you: "You must have no doubts. Moreover, I am the King of Dharma;
