I possess mastery over the Dharma and shall never deceive or mislead future generations. Thus, I now—
Within the realms of humans and devas, the Sun emitted a great sound, universally proclaiming to the great assembly:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time appear in the world solely to teach and transform bodhisattvas through the Dharma of the single vehicle of equality; there is no other vehicle."
"You all should have deep faith and be free from doubt.
You, Śāriputra, as well as the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, should know that this wondrous Dharma is the secret essence of all Buddhas."
In this world of the five turbidities, sentient beings such as these—who take pleasure only in attachment to various desires—will ultimately not achieve the Buddha-way.
In future ages, wicked people, hearing the Buddha preach the One Vehicle, will be deluded and fail to believe or accept it; they will destroy the Dharma and fall into evil paths.
For those who possess a sense of shame and remorse and are pure, and who aspire to seek the Buddha-way, one should extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle for such as these.
Śāriputra, you should know that the Dharma of all Buddhas is thus: by means of thousands of millions of skillful expedients, they preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.

Those who have not practiced this learning cannot understand it clearly. Now that you all already know these matters of the skillful means employed by the Buddhas, the Teachers of the World, you shall no longer have any doubts;
your hearts will give rise to great joy, and you will know for yourselves that you shall become Buddhas.

The following section concerns the entrustment and circulation [of the teaching]. As for the "secret essentials": if one merely directs the mind toward them, there is immediate efficacy; how then could these not be secret? To speak of them openly is precisely to reveal them;
how then could these not be essential? They are just like the crest-jewel of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), a vital instrument of the state that he is unwilling to bestow lightly upon others.
Why is this? Because the people of this degenerate age are addicted to various desires and seek only worldly gain.
Regarding the causes and effects of the heavens, because they do not seek the path of the Buddha, these matters are kept secret and not spoken of.
Formerly, when the First Patriarch Bodhidharma first met King Wu of Liang, the King asked, "I have printed scriptures and fashioned images; what merit does this bring?
He replied, "In truth, there is no merit. The King asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? He replied, "Vast and empty—there is no sage."
The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me? He replied, "I do not know. The Emperor was not in accord with him, so he subsequently went to Shaolin and sat facing a wall for nine years;
this serves as a model. Therefore, he exhorted them, saying: "This wondrous Dharma, even the Buddhas of the three periods of time did not dare to lightly divulge.
You all should likewise preserve and protect it; do not propagate it recklessly. It should be...
[The Buddha] descended. This clearly explains that [the teaching] must not be transmitted to those who are not suitable vessels.

As for "evil persons," it does not mean only those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) or the ten evil deeds; rather, anyone who hears this sutra and fails to believe it, instead giving rise to slander, is no different from one who has committed the five heinous crimes or the ten evil deeds. Such individuals sever the lineage of the Buddhas and fall into the Avīci Hell.

Prison. Therefore, when encountering such persons, it is absolutely forbidden to speak [of the Dharma]. Regarding "those with shame" (*hrī*) and below: this further clarifies that one should bestow [the teaching] upon anyone encountered. As for "shame" (*hrī*):
it means thinking, "I possess the majestic and dignified marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*); how could I willingly engage in such inferior matters? As for "remorse" (*apatrāpya*):
when seeing others receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of becoming a Buddha, one reflects to oneself, "Since they are a Great Man, I..."
Why should it not be so? Those who possess a sense of shame and remorse are simply ordinary people who reproach and blame themselves; Śāriputra is an example of this.
The absence of marks of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*) is called "clarity" (*śuci*), and the absence of marks of non-phenomena (*adharma-nimitta*) is called "purity" (*viśuddhi*).
Since they possess shame and remorse and yet do not cling to marks, they aspire to seek the Buddha-way and take no pleasure in other vehicles. Such persons are single-minded and resolute.
First: Only those who are true vessels for the Mahāyāna dharma are fit to receive and transmit it. You should extensively praise this sutra for their sake, causing them to give rise to joy.
Śāriputra, the following summarizes the path and dharma attained by all Buddhas: it does not exceed the realization of this single dharma; there is nothing more extraordinary.
Therefore it is said, "The dharma of all Buddhas is thus. This refers to what is called "contemplating with truth."
This is the Dharma of the Dharma King; such is the nature of the Dharma King’s Dharma.

Not only is that which all Buddhas realize one and the same, but even the Buddhas’ saving of sentient beings does nothing more than take this single Dharma to support the left and brace the right, merely following along to untie people's bonds.
There is no "real dharma" given to others; this is what Linji meant by "the Buddha-dharma is not many things. This...
Regarding these Dharma-gates, those who have not yet studied them certainly do not know this.

Now that I have laid it all out before you upon the platter, with nothing further withheld, you should know that the Buddhas, as guides for the world, do nothing more than bestow this single Dharma according to the needs of individuals; there is nothing else, nor is there anything extraordinary. You [should] furthermore...
Do not give rise to doubt; you should give rise to great joy. Accept it directly and know with certainty that your attainment of Buddhahood is unmistakable.
Thus the Sixth Patriarch said: "Make a Buddha of your own mind; do not harbor further hesitation. Li Duye said: "One who studies the Way must be an iron man;
taking the hand by the heart, he makes the decision at once. He takes directly toward unsurpassed Bodhi, regarding all right and wrong as nothing."
Do not concern yourself with it.

Chapter Three: The Parable (The Simile of the Burning House).
The verse says:
This decaying house is already terrifying; How much more so with its many clusters of suffering! The wind of delusion blows through the night, And the fires of karma blaze crimson across the heavens.
Within the smoke of the kalpa-stone, all is exhausted; Amidst the flames of Mount Meru, all is empty.
Who would have known that the realm of golden hue originally lay to the east of the broken wall?
The "Exemplifier" (aupamya) relies on objects to draw analogies; it takes the meaning of using one thing as an illustration for another, such as comparing a handheld fan to the moon.
The azure dog resembles a cloud; the circular canopy resembles heaven; the square chariot resembles the earth. These are merely taken for their resemblance and are not actual entities.
Long ago, there was one who had never seen a qilin. He asked someone who had once seen a qilin, "What is a qilin like?
The one who had seen it replied, "A qilin is like a qilin. The questioner said, "If I had ever seen a qilin, I would not have asked you."

To say, "The qilin is like a qilin," how could this possibly be understood? The observer then says, "The qilin has the body of a deer, the tail of an ox, the hooves of a deer, the back of a horse, and yet it has horns.
Upon hearing this, the questioner suddenly understands. This is because the description was revealed through analogy for one who had never before seen a qilin;
therefore, it is called a "parable" (dṛṣṭānta). This chapter, based on the fact that the twelve hundred people did not understand, explains the three teachings.
Because this is the primary causal condition, an analogy is established to clarify its meaning. The single gate is used as a metaphor for the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*);

the three carts represent the Three Vehicles; and the great white ox-cart represents the Buddha Vehicle. Why is this so? For the very root of birth and death within the triple world arises entirely from this subtle *karmic consciousness*.
Ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle cannot fathom it; if it were taught all at once, they would be unable to believe it with deep conviction.

Therefore, they are caused to cultivate the teachings of the Three Vehicles, severing the six consciousnesses and the three poisons, so as to emerge from the triple world, realize nirvana, and attain mastery over the mind.

Yet, they have never yet transformed the karmic consciousness (ālayavijñāna) to obtain the four wisdoms, eliminate the cognitive obstructions (dharmāvaraṇa), and realize the emptiness of phenomena (dharmaśūnyatā).
Therefore, this chapter uses the parable of the various disciples to clarify the Three Vehicles of the past,

which cause one to empty the six consciousnesses and emerge from birth and death; it clarifies the One Vehicle of the present, which seeks to transform the karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) into Bodhi.
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy and, rising immediately with palms joined, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now, having heard this Dharma-sound from the World-Honored One, my heart leaps with joy; I have attained what I have never experienced before."
First, regarding the description of those who experience exultant joy upon awakening: this clarifies the Great Matter.

Their joy pervades their entire bodies such that they are unaware of their own hand-clapping and foot-stamping. One night at Zihu, a monk shouted before the Sangha Hall, "Thief! The assembly was all startled.
A monk inside the hall came out, seized him, and said, "Venerable Karmadāna, the thief is right here; catch him!"
"I have attained it. The monk said, "It is not I. The Master said, "It is indeed so; it is simply that you are unwilling to take responsibility for it. Furthermore, an ancient worthy said:
"For thirty years I have used my mind to conjecture, several times casting this heart into the ashes. Now, in my decline, I meet one who knows me: Li Bai was originally a scholar!

Those who leap for joy with exultation are precisely... (Note: The final phrase "歡喜踊躍者" (Those who leap for joy) appears to be an incomplete fragment or a lead-in to a further description of those who attain realization.)
This is Śāriputra encountering one who knows him; he directly accepts and realizes it at that very moment.
Why is this so? Because in the past, I heard such a Dharma from the Buddha and saw various bodhisattvas receiving the prediction of their future buddhahood.
Yet we were not included in this matter; we feel profound personal sorrow at having lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.
World-Honored One, whenever I dwell alone in mountain forests or beneath trees, whether sitting or walking, I constantly think:
"We have entered the same Dharma-nature together; why has the Tathāgata delivered us by means of the Hīnayāna teachings? This is our own fault, not [the Buddha's]."

World-Honored One, why is this? Had we waited for you to explain the underlying cause by which one achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, we would certainly have attained liberation through the Mahāyāna.

However, not understanding your skillful means and the teachings given according to what was appropriate, we accepted the Buddha-dharma upon first hearing it; we immediately believed and received it, reflecting upon it and attaining realization.

Next, he recounts his past failure: "When the World-Honored One was in the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras, preaching the Mahāyāna sūtras for the sake of the bodhisattvas and bestowing predictions upon them, we, though previously present at that Dharma assembly and having heard the Buddha’s teachings, were not included among those granted predictions.
We were deeply distressed and did not know the reason why; thus, we lost the Tathāgata’s knowledge [of us]."
[The text] says: "Behold! The World-Honored One descended [from his seat], expressing a sense of sorrow and saying: 'In my ordinary conduct of the four postures, I have privately lamented this:
how is it that we, together with all these bodhisattvas, are gathered in one assembly; that we equally contemplate the emptiness of nature and equally enter the dharma-nature;
and that we are likewise disciples of the Tathāgata, originally without any distinction? Why then does the Tathāgata single out..."
"The Dharma of the equality of the Mahāyāna is that by which Bodhisattvas receive their predictions; yet you deliver us by means of the Dharma of the Hīnayāna.
Is this not a case where the Tathāgata’s mind is partial, falling into the fault of inequality?

Therefore, whenever such a thought arises, we are immediately filled with distress. Now we hear the World-Honored One say: 'I have personally realized the unsurpassed path of the Mahāyāna's equality...'"
...the Dharma of equality. Had you taught us by means of the Lesser Vehicle, I would have fallen into stinginess and greed; such a thing would have been unacceptable.
Thus we know that the World-Honored One is not at fault for any inequality; the fault lies with ourselves. For this reason, [the Buddha] reveals his own fault, saying:
"If we had, from the beginning, been willing to wait for the World-Honored One to clearly explain the causes of the Three Vehicles..."
That which was provisionally established for the sake of accomplishing unsurpassed bodhi—at that time, we certainly did not contemplate attaining the realization of a lesser fruit.

The Tathāgata will surely deliver us by means of the Mahāyāna. This is because when the World-Honored One initially refused to reveal to us the underlying cause—that it is the matter of accomplishing bodhi—our [aspirations] were at their greatest.

Furthermore, at first we did not understand that the Tathāgata was speaking through skillful means. As soon as we heard the Buddha’s words, we accepted them with faith, taking them to be literal truth.
We contemplated them day and night, attaining the realization of the lesser fruits, yet we did not seek the path of Buddhahood.
For this reason, the Tathāgata did not preach the Mahāyāna Dharma for us, nor did he grant us the prediction of our future buddhahood. This...
Then the fault lies with oneself. One generates interpretations based on words; yet the Tathāgata truly has no fault of inequality. It is as they say:
"Only after waking does one realize that alcohol deludes a person."
"World-Honored One, from the past until now, throughout the day and night, I have constantly reproached myself.

But today, having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented Dharma never heard before, all my doubts and regrets have been severed; my body and mind are at ease, and I have attained swift peace and security.
Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha—born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma, and having obtained a share of the Buddha-Dharma."
I, Sanqing, have now attained this. Because we have habitually refused to content ourselves with being followers of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), we have reproached ourselves bitterly day and night;
therefore, upon hearing for the first time today that Arhats can become Buddhas, it is as if something unheard of in the past has now been heard.
That which I had not previously attained, I have now attained; that which I formerly doubted and regretted, today I am at ease and secure.
Furthermore, I previously thought of myself as no true son of the Buddha, unable to inherit the family legacy of the Tathāgata.
Today I know that I am indeed a true son of the Buddha, capable of inheriting the family legacy of the Tathāgata. Previously, I thought only that...

Having previously been one who had attained nirvana yet lacked the portion of the Buddha-dharma, today I finally know that my entire body dwells within the mouth of the Buddha and my whole being resides within the transformation of the Dharma; I possess the portion of the Tathāgata’s precious treasury.
How could I not rejoice and leap for joy? Thus we know that because there was the reprimand of the past, there is now this leaping for joy of the present.
Because there was remorse for the past, there is now joy; because there was doubt and regret for the past, there is now tranquility and security.
If one had not reproached oneself in the past, had not felt remorse, and had not experienced doubt and regret, how could there be this present state of exultant joy and tranquil security?
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having heard this sound of the Dharma, I have attained what I never had before. My heart is filled with great joy, and the net of my doubts has been entirely removed."
Since long ago I have been protected by the Buddha’s teaching and have not lost the Mahāyāna. The Buddha’s voice is most rare and marvelous; it can eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings.
I have already attained the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), and hearing [the Dharma] has likewise removed my grief and distress.
The first four lines constitute a general verse summarizing the section on "rejoicing and leaping for joy. The passage beginning with "In the past...
elucidates the line "the net of doubt has been entirely removed. It states that my former doubts were precisely doubts concerning my own loss of the Mahāyāna.

Now, hearing these words that there is only one, without a second or a third, I finally realize that from the past, when the Buddha conferred upon me the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, I had in truth never lost the Mahāyāna. It was merely that I myself was unwilling to accept it.
Today, having willingly accepted it, I know that the Dharma spoken today is not alone [in being the Mahāyāna].
"How rare! Indeed, the Dharma taught by the Buddha in the past was also most rare. Why is this?
When I had not yet emerged from the three realms and was still among sentient beings, hearing this Dharma removed my worldly grief and affliction.
Having attained the exhaustion of outflows and become an Arhat, I have emerged as one who has transcended the three realms; yet, for forty years, I have..."

We were excluded from the ranks of those granted predictions [of enlightenment] and did not receive the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharma transformation; therefore, we constantly reflected upon this and were always filled with anxiety and distress.
Today, suddenly hearing the words that Arhats shall become Buddhas, we realize that we have not failed to attain the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, our distress over not receiving a prediction of Buddhahood is now dispelled. As it is said:
With a rain of a single flavor, he nourishes the flowers of humanity; such is the reason why this Buddha’s voice is so exceedingly rare.
Whether dwelling in mountain valleys or beneath forest trees, whether sitting or walking in meditation, I have constantly contemplated this matter.
Alas, I reproach myself deeply: how have I deceived myself? We too are sons of the Buddha; we have equally entered the dharma of outflowlessness.
Yet we are unable, in the future, to expound the unsurpassed path—the golden body with its thirty-two marks, the ten powers, and the various liberations.
Within this same single Dharma, I have not attained these things: the eighty minor marks of excellence, the eighteen unique qualities, and such merits as these;
I have lost them all. Yet when I walk alone in meditation, I see the Buddha amidst the great assembly.
His fame fills the ten directions, and he brings vast benefit to sentient beings. Reflecting that I have lost this advantage, I feel as though I have deceived myself.
Day and night, I constantly contemplate this matter, wishing to ask the World-Honored One whether I have indeed lost it or not.
I have often seen the World-Honored One praise all bodhisattvas; for this reason, day and night, I have deliberated upon such matters.

The following verses lament past losses. When it says, "In my former days, my grief and affliction were not dispelled," it means that because I was unwilling to accept the Lesser Vehicle, I sat by and lost the Bodhisattva-dharma taught by the Tathāgata. I reflect on this constantly, feeling deep personal pain.
Self-reproach: How is it that we deceive ourselves in this way? We and the Bodhisattvas both take the Buddha as our teacher;
we are all sons of the Tathāgata; we have equally entered into the Dharma-nature and equally attained the untainted (anāsrava).
Why is it that the Bodhisattva alone is able to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings in future ages, while I alone am unable? Is this not self-deception? This is painful.
He reproaches himself for being inferior to the Bodhisattvas. From "The golden-colored [body]" downward, he bitterly reproaches himself for having lost the Tathāgata’s merit of self-benefit.
From "I alone" downward, he again bitterly reproaches himself for having lost the Tathāgata’s merit of benefiting sentient beings.
"I am one who deceives myself" means that while the Tathāgata has realized the Dharma of equality, he would never willingly deceive or delude me with a Dharma of inequality.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not deceive them; he teaches for them the Seal of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā).
Thus, one should know that it is I who have deceived and deluded myself; it is simply that the Tathāgata has not spoken for me.

Furthermore, this buddha-nature is perfectly identical to the great void; it is neither deficient nor redundant. How could it be that the Tathāgata alone possesses buddha-nature and attains equal and perfect enlightenment?
I am awake, yet alas, I alone am without it. Therefore, day and night, whenever I reflect upon this, my hair stands on end.
I wish to take this matter and consult the World-Honored One: "Is it truly that I have lost this benefit?
Or is it that, though it exists, I have abandoned myself and cast it away? This is why I reflect day and night, filled with doubt and regret.
Furthermore, I have seen the Tathāgata within the great assembly praise the Bodhisattvas as dragon-elephants while disparaging those of the Lesser Vehicle as lame donkeys.
Upon hearing these words, our hearts were deeply unsettled; day and night we deliberated, thinking:
"We and the Bodhisattvas are truly of equal standing. Why does the Tathāgata single out the Bodhisattvas for praise while deprecating us?"
This is why I have reproached myself with such pain day and night and am filled with sorrow.
Now I hear the Buddha’s voice, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate; it is untainted and inconceivable, leading all beings to the site of enlightenment.
I formerly adhered to false views and served as a teacher to various brahmins. The World-Honored One, knowing my mind, uprooted my errors and preached nirvāṇa.
I completely eliminated all false views and attained realization of the Dharma of emptiness. At that time, I thought to myself: "I have reached extinction."

Only now do I realize that this was not true extinction. When I attain Buddhahood and am endowed with the thirty-two marks, revered by devas, humans, yakṣas, nāgas, and spirits—only then can it be said that I have forever reached extinction without remainder.
The Buddha, amidst the great assembly, declared, "I shall become a Buddha. Hearing such a sound of the Dharma, all my doubts and regrets were entirely removed;
this verse now expresses that attainment. Now I hear the World-Honored One say that throughout the forty years since he began teaching, he has expounded various kinds of dharmas.
All of these are skillful means. Whether praising or disparaging, they always have but one purpose:

there is nothing that does not use the inconceivable, untainted Dharma of the Mahāyāna to instruct people, desiring only to cause them to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to sit at the site of enlightenment to achieve perfect awakening.
In reality, there is no such thing as praising or disparaging the Mahāyāna, the Hīnayāna, or the vehicles of humans and devas.
...so it was. Formerly, Baiyun Yuan visited Yangqi. Yangqi asked, "Who is your preceptor? The Master replied, "The Venerable Yuru of Chaling.
Yangqi said, "I have heard that he fell while crossing a bridge and composed a verse about it that was quite extraordinary.
Do you remember it? The Master recited: "I possess a bright pearl, Long confined by the dust of worldly toil. This morning, the dust..."
Jinguangsheng arose, illuminating ten thousand peaks and mountains with his radiance. Qiji rose with a smile, leaving the Master staring in astonishment.
He could not sleep all night. At dawn, he questioned him; it happened to be the end of the year. Qiji said, "Did you see those people performing the exorcism ritual yesterday?"
Jian said, "I see. The Master said, "You fall short of him by a single tally. Jian was startled and asked, "What is the meaning of this?
Qi said, "He loves being laughed at; you fear being laughed at. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.

When Ciming visited Fenyang, Fenyang silently regarded him with esteem, yet every time he saw him, he would scold and revile him, or disparage him. Whatever he taught to others from other quarters was all merely conventional worldly talk.
The Vulgar One complained one night, saying, "I have been at this Dharma assembly for two summers now, yet I have received no instruction.
I have only increased my worldly afflictions. Thinking of how time slips away and that I have not clarified the matter of my own life, I have lost the benefit of leaving the household life.
Before he had finished speaking, Yang stared at him intently and scolded, "This evil teacher dares to deceive and exploit me! In a rage, he raised his staff and drove him out.
The Master intended to offer a rebuttal, but Yang covered his mouth. Thereupon, he attained great enlightenment and said: "Thus I know that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary sentiment;
what is called laughing, joking, scolding, or praising—all is nothing other than the Buddha-work.

'Neither two nor three'—my original intent was to preach the Dharma as appropriate to the occasion, meaning that the World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma is fundamentally neither two nor three."

The reason why [the Buddha] speaks of the Great or the Small according to what is appropriate, and either praises or disparages, is because we formerly served non-Buddhist teachers and studied the teachings of false views;
the World-Honored One, knowing our inner thoughts and affairs, directed himself toward our inclinations to uproot our false foundations.
Therefore, the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle’s nirvāṇa was taught to entice them; this is like using one wedge to extract another.

Having realized nirvāṇa, they were content with what they had attained as sufficient, considering themselves people who had transcended the three realms and having no further tasks to perform. They sat and guarded their sublime and wondrous states, no longer striving toward Bodhi.

Consequently, within the assemblies of the Vaipulya sūtras, they were praised and commended [for their initial progress] while being censured and rebuked [for their complacency], thereby stimulating them to advance.
We have been striving in our practice, yet we did not know this. Today the World-Honored One has clearly declared:
"Although I speak of nirvāṇa, even that is not true extinction. Only now do we realize that it is not the ultimate liberation.

If one attains Buddhahood, such that the five stages of dwelling are completely exhausted and the two deaths are forever extinguished, only then is it the true, remainderless nirvāṇa—the reality of intrinsic emptiness.
Regarding the "state" (viṣaya): one must realize that the attainment of the minor fruits in the past was entirely self-deception; it was not the fault of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, today, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s prediction of my own Buddhahood, all doubt and regret have been completely eliminated.
This is why I am filled with joy and leap for gladness. As the *Introduction Chapter* states: "If there are those seeking the three vehicles who harbor any doubt or regret, the Buddha..."

These should be severed and eliminated until they are exhausted without remainder. As the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta* states: "Regarding the matters of appropriate skillful means, there shall be no further doubts.
Here it says: "Having heard such a sound of the Dharma, all doubts and regrets have been removed. These passages correspond to one another.
When I first heard what the Buddha taught, my heart was filled with great alarm and doubt: "Could it be that a Māra has manifested as a Buddha to disturb and confuse my mind?
But through the Buddha’s various causes and conditions, his skillful speech and parables, my mind became as calm as the ocean; having heard this, the net of my doubts was severed.
The Buddha has said that in the past, immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa, while dwelling in skillful means, all likewise taught this Dharma.
The Buddhas of the present and the future, their number being beyond measure, likewise employ various skillful means to expound such a Dharma.
"O World-Honored One, from your birth, your renunciation, your attainment of the Way, and your turning of the wheel of Dharma—all have been taught through skillful means.
The World-Honored One teaches the true Path; Pāpīyas does not possess such things. For this reason, I know with certainty that it is not Māra who has become a Buddha."

Because I had fallen into the net of doubt, I thought this was the work of Māra. But hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice—profound, far-reaching, and most subtle—as he expounded the pure Dharma, my heart was filled with great joy;
my doubts and regrets were forever exhausted, and I came to dwell securely within true wisdom.
"I shall certainly become a Buddha, revered by devas and humans, turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and teaching and transforming all bodhisattvas.

This is a retrospective account of their astonishment and doubt. They said, "In our forty years [of following the Buddha], we have never heard the voice of a śrāvaka being granted the prediction of Buddhahood.
Now, suddenly hearing these words, we are both startled and doubtful, bewildered and unsettled, suspecting that the Buddha—"
"Māra! The Buddha, through his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), has guided and supported us; our minds are vast and as stable as the great ocean.
Having heard his words and further examined his mind, we know that this was not the work of Māra. We now have deep faith in these words, and the net of doubt is completely torn asunder.
[The passage] "The Buddha said" below correctly reveals the Tathāgata’s skillful means, stating that throughout the three periods of time...

All Buddhas teach the Dharma through skillful means; there is not a single instance that is not for a specific purpose. Thus, one should know that all that the Tathāgata speaks is true speech and is certainly not the teaching of Māra.
It was only because I myself had fallen into the net of doubt that I suspected the Buddha might be Māra.
Now, having heard such gentle, compliant, and harmonious sounds from the Tathāgata—whose meaning is profound and whose words are subtle and exquisite—I realize that...
As for this eloquent exposition: all is of one mark and one flavor, the pure and white holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Therefore, the roots of my doubt are forever exhausted, and I give rise to great joy. No longer do I cling to the provisional vehicle of former days;
today I abide securely within true wisdom. Nor do I linger in the minor fruits of former days; today I know with certainty that I shall become a Buddha and turn the Great [Dharma Wheel].
The Wheel of Dharma transforms and teaches Bodhisattvas; this is the domain for which Śāriputra has taken responsibility.

Xiangyan said, "If [the Buddha] had explained it to me at that time, how could there have been the events of today? From this, one knows that throughout the forty years of the World-Honored One’s teaching...
This is not to refute the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle; it is precisely for the sake of those of today. Huanglong Nan said:

"It is because there are many people nowadays who listen to the Dharma with ease. One wishes to treat them like farmers who dry their fields from time to time to make them parched and thirsty, so that when they are finally irrigated, the fine grain may flourish.
This is also his meaning. This is the Buddhas and Patriarchs forging and refining the sages.
This is the wondrous secret instruction.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "I now declare this among the great assembly of devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas:
in the past, for the sake of the unsurpassed path, I have constantly instructed and transformed you in the presence of twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas."
"You, too, have followed me and received instruction throughout the long night. It was because I guided you through skillful means that you were born into my Dharma.
Śāriputra, in the past I taught you to aspire to the Buddha-way, yet now you have completely forgotten it and instead claim that you have already attained parinirvāṇa.
Now, wishing to cause you to remember your original vow and the path you were practicing, I [have spoken] for the sake of all śrāvakas..."
I have heard this Mahāyāna sūtra called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas.

Śāriputra, in a future age, after immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable kalpas have passed, you shall make offerings to many thousands of myriads of koṭis of buddhas, uphold the true dharma, and fulfill the path practiced by bodhisattvas; you shall then attain [buddhahood].
The Buddha, titled Flower Radiance Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.
This is the Tathāgata’s confirmation and bestowal of a prophecy. One must wait for faith before being granted a prophecy;

one speaks only after faith is established, for if one lacks faith, they will perceive it as an affliction. Because Śāriputra had attained awakening through causes and conditions, the Buddha further recounted his past-life causes and conditions to enlighten him, saying: "For the sake of this great causal matter, in the past..."
In the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas, I have constantly guided you through skillful means (*upāya-dvāra*).
You, too, have followed me through the long night of saṃsāra to receive instruction. Due to these past conditions, life after life, we have always been together in one place.
Yet, throughout my past kalpas, I have never actually taught you by means of the Hīnayāna; from the very beginning, I have instructed you to set your will upon [the Mahāyāna].
You aspire to the Buddha-vehicle. How can you now forget your original vow, considering a small attainment as sufficient and claiming to have attained nirvana?
Although you have forgotten your original vow, my own words have issued from my own mouth;
they remain vivid in my mind and have never been forgotten. Now, wishing to help awaken your past original vows, I therefore—

Cherishing the lips and skin [to preach], he proclaims this sutra. That the Bodhisattva’s causes and the Tathāgata’s fruits of the Path are entirely contained herein is why it is called "The Dharma for Teaching Bodhisattvas" and that which is protected and remembered by the Buddha.

Observing this, one knows that throughout immeasurable kalpas, whether moving or still, in every thought-moment and every instant, there was nothing the World-Honored One did other than to instruct people in their aspiration for the Buddha-way. How could this be...?

This concludes one lifetime. "Śāriputra, below" refers to the bestowal of a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). It means that after you have heard this great sutra, you shall immediately take this sutra as the cause;

in future ages, throughout immeasurable kalpas, you will serve immeasurable Buddhas, study immeasurable paths, and cultivate immeasurable practices, until the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled, reaching the point where the water arrives and the channel is completed, thereby attaining supreme, perfect enlightenment.
Awakening is named Flower Radiance (*Huaguang*). This is precisely the entry from the rank of Dharma Master into the rank of Dharma King. It is as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
"Taking non-arising and non-ceasing as the cause, one subsequently perfectly achieves the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition."
As for the name "Flower Radiance" (Huāguāng), it is because he enters the awakening of radiant light by means of the flowers of wisdom.
The land is named "Free from Defilement" (Lí Gòu); its terrain is level and even, pure and magnificently adorned, peaceful, secure, and prosperous, with a vast multitude of devas and humans.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli. There are eight intersecting roads, demarcated on their sides by cords of gold.

Alongside these are rows of trees made of the seven treasures, which are always laden with flowers and fruit. The Tathāgata Padmaprabha likewise teaches and transforms sentient beings through the three vehicles.
Śāriputra, when that Buddha appears, although it is not an age of evil, he nevertheless preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles due to his original vows.
The land is named Vimala (Free from Defilement), which is like the "Great Tang," "Great Song," or "Great Brilliance" [of our own era]; this is the land of recompense where the Sambhogakāya resides.
That the land is level and even means it is without elevations or depressions, and without inclinations or slopes; it is pure and magnificently adorned.
It is adorned with various jewels and free from the defilements of the five turbidities. It is secure and peaceful, being free from the suffering of the three calamities and the eight difficulties.
It is prosperous and joyful, being free from the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. It is filled with gods and humans, being free from the three evil realms.
Its ground is made of lapis lazuli, being free from pits, hollows, mounds, or hills. It possesses eight intersecting roads.
"Without" means there is no enclosure, obstruction, or curvature. "With golden cords" means there are no fences or boundaries.
"Constantly possessing jewel trees, jewel flowers, and jewel fruits" means there are no trees that can wither, no flowers that can fade, and no fruits that can ripen [and perish].
Śariputra raised a difficult objection, saying: "The Tathāgata appeared in an age of five turbidities; therefore, by way of comparison..."

He then preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles to guide and assist all sentient beings. Since the Land of Reward of Flower-Light is not a world of turbidity but is originally a pure land, and since there are no followers of the Two Vehicles there—being exclusively composed of Bodhisattvas—why does he also teach and transform sentient beings by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles?
Answer: Although the land of Flower-Light is not an evil age, it is due to his original vow that he preaches the Three Vehicles.
Dharma. Although he has now attained the fruit [of Buddhahood], he does not abandon his former resolve;
therefore, that eon is named Mahāratnavyūha (Great Jewel Adornment). Why is it called Mahāratnavyūha?
Because in that land, bodhisattvas are regarded as the great jewels. Those bodhisattvas there are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable, beyond all calculation and analogy.
It is beyond the reach of metaphors; there is no one capable of knowing it except through the power of a Buddha’s wisdom. When they wish to walk, precious lotuses receive their feet.

These bodhisattvas have not newly resolved their minds; they have long planted the roots of virtue and have purified their brahma-conduct under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas.
They are constantly praised by all Buddhas and always cultivate the Buddha-wisdom. They are fully endowed with...
Possessing great supernormal powers, they are well-versed in the gateways of all dharmas; they are upright and without guile, and their resolve is firm and steadfast.
Such bodhisattvas fill that land. Śāriputra, the lifespan of the Buddha Puṣpārāma is twelve small kalpas, excluding the time when he was a prince and had not yet attained buddhahood.
The people of that land have a lifespan of eight small kalpas. After the Tathāgata Puṣpārāma has passed ten...
After two intermediate kalpas, he bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Sthiramati the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

He addressed the bhikṣus: "This Bodhisattva Sthiramati shall next become a Buddha, named Puṣpadantapadavikrāmin, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha. His buddha-field shall also be like this, Śāriputra."

"No. After the parinirvāṇa of that Flower-Light Buddha, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas."
"Kalpa" means time. "Great Jewel Adornment" (Mahāratnavyūha) is the era name, similar to [the reigns of] Hongwu, Jiajing, and Wanli.
Regarding the Bodhisattvas as the "Great Jewel Adornment": in this land, the adornment of national boundaries is not considered the Great Jewel;
rather, because this land consists entirely of Bodhisattvas who adorn the realm, and there are no followers of the Two Vehicles, it is thus [designated].
The Bodhisattva is a great treasure. This is like the meaning of Jiu Fan (Zhongzi) regarding benevolence and kinship as treasures, or the state of Chu regarding goodness as its treasure.
"Those various [beings] below" reveals the great number of Bodhisattvas. "These various [trees] below" reveals the vastness of the Bodhisattvas' cultivation of virtue.
"In the absence of [time] below" shows the long duration of the Bodhisattvas' service to the Buddhas. "Constantly acting as [a servant] below" shows the Bodhi... [text fragment ends].
"Sā" signifies great renown; "Chángxiū" (常修) means constantly practicing the lower [stages]; "Jiàn" (見) reveals the depth of the Bodhisattva’s entry into the Way;

"Shànzhī" (善知) manifests the universality of the Bodhisattva’s deliverance of sentient beings. "Upright and sincere, without artifice" refers to being like unrefined gold or raw jade, devoid of any contrived embellishment.
Therefore it is called "substance. Like a bowstring or an arrow, it is without deviation or crookedness; therefore it is called "straight.
It is the realization of reality and the awakening to truth, without the slightest pretense; therefore it is called "without falsehood. The four marks do not shift, and the eight winds do not move;
therefore it is called "firm in resolve and mindfulness. Such Bodhisattvas fill that land. This eon is thus named "Great Treasure."
"Adorned" refers to his physical marks. "Śāri" below refers to his lifespan. "Bestowing the prediction of firm fulfillment" refers to the transmission of the robe and bowl.

The Buddha’s name, "Flower-Foot Peaceful Practice," signifies that he has perfected the myriad practices and proceeds with them in tranquility. The land's name, "Free from Defilement," signifies that the Way of all Buddhas is the same.
"True Dharma" signifies that faith, understanding, practice, and realization are all fully complete. "Semblance..."
As for the Dharma, there may be deficiencies in its faith, understanding, practice, or realization.

The text of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) does nothing more than directly bestow upon [the recipient] the adornments of their future Buddha-land and eon, the number of their retinue, and the length of the Buddha’s lifespan;
there is no other discourse. It is just like a family: when a father is on the verge of death, he leaves a single testamentary document concerning his fields and—
The family assets and household utensils shall each be itemized and clearly accounted for; furthermore, write one more seal upon the pillar and hand it to my son, and that will be the end of it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
In a future age, Śāriputra shall become a Buddha, a Honored One of Universal Wisdom, named Puṣpārāma (Flower Light). He shall deliver immeasurable multitudes and make offerings to countless Buddhas.
Fully accomplishing the practices of a bodhisattva and the merits such as the ten powers, he shall realize the unsurpassed path.
After the passage of immeasurable kalpas, there was a kalpa named Mahāratnavyūha and a world named Vimala. It was pure and free from all defilement;

its ground was made of lapis lazuli, its paths were demarcated by golden cords, and it was filled with trees of various colors made of the seven treasures, which were always laden with flowers, fruits, and seeds.
The bodhisattvas in that land are always firm in their resolve and mindfulness; they have fully perfected the supernatural powers and the *pāramitās*.
Having well studied the bodhisattva path under countless Buddhas, such great beings as these were transformed by the Buddha Flower-Light.
When the Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and renounced worldly glory; in his very last body, he left the household life and attained the Way of Buddhahood.
The Buddha Padmaprabha dwelt in the world for a lifespan of twelve small kalpas, and the people of that land had a lifespan of eight small kalpas.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for thirty-two minor kalpas, extensively delivering all sentient beings.

Once the True Dharma has completely vanished, the Semblance Dharma shall endure for thirty-two [minor kalpas], and his relics shall be widely disseminated, receiving universal offerings from devas and humans.

All that was performed by the Buddha Padmaprabha was exactly like this. That Most Honored One among two-legged beings, supreme and without peer—that is your very self; you ought to rejoice in yourself.
The first two verses praise the bestowal of the prophecy. "Beyond [the kalpa]... and so forth praises the adornment of the land, the eon, and the retinue.
"The Buddha... and so forth refers to the Buddha Puṣyarṇa; it is also like Śākyamuni’s renunciation of the golden wheel to leave the household life and attain the Way.
One should omit the phrase "becoming a prince" from the prose commentary. "Puṣyarṇa... and so forth praises the Buddha’s lifespan, the True Dharma, and the Semblance Dharma. The preceding...
The Cloud [of Wisdom] gave rise to great joy, knowing for himself that he would become a Buddha. This Cloud—that is you yourself;
you should rejoice and reflect upon this accordingly.
At that time, the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others...

The great assembly of gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, seeing Śāriputra receive the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before the Buddha, were filled with great joy and leaped for immeasurable delight.
Each of them removed the upper garment they were wearing to offer it as an act of worship to the Buddha. Śakra-devānām-indra...

The Brahma King and others, together with countless sons of gods, likewise made offerings to the Buddha with celestial fine garments, celestial *māndārava* flowers, *mahāmāndārava* flowers, and so forth.
The celestial garments they scattered remained suspended in the void, revolving of their own accord.
A hundred thousand myriad kinds of celestial music simultaneously resounded throughout the void, and rain fell.
A multitude of celestial flowers rained down, and they spoke these words: "In the past, the Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī;
now he has once again turned the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma."

Regarding Śāriputra receiving his prediction and the fourfold assembly, devas, and nāgas leaping for joy with exultation: it is like seeing one flower and knowing that spring has arrived throughout the world;
by predicting the destiny of one person, it is known that every person possesses their own lot. The verse says: Those dwelling in nests know the wind; those dwelling in burrows know the rain.
Śāriputra receives his prediction; the devas and nāgas rejoice. The fourfold assembly and all the devas are all liberated.
Regarding the offering of celestial robes to the Buddha: knowing them to be the robes that cover the Tathāgata, one thus relinquishes what is cherished.
This is what the ancestral house refers to as "casting off the foul-smelling robe of the hawk and donning the gown of Qingzhou. Regarding the scattering of flowers as an offering to the Buddha:

it is to repay the intent behind the preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Regarding the playing of celestial music: it is to repay the sound of the bestowal of predictions of enlightenment. By means of these three kinds [of offerings].
All these things are what the devas cherish; thus, to offer what one cherishes to the Buddha is the height of reverence.
Because the Buddha bestows upon others the Dharma he himself employs for his own realization, each offers to the Buddha the very objects they themselves employ.
As for the celestial garments revolving in mid-air, this is the manifestation of inanimate things leaping for joy. A verse says: "A single whole body sits upon a white ox, riding..."
The sheep leaps across the deer and seeks it outside; the celestial robe still turns in the void.
Why is it that the human mind does not turn its head? Under these words, all the devas praise the Buddha’s turning of the wheel.

When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of the Dharma once more. The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying: "Mañjuśrī, for forty-nine [years]..."
"I have dwelt in the world for twelve years and have never spoken a single word. You requested that I turn the Wheel of Dharma once more;
have I ever turned the Wheel of Dharma before? Now tell me: is the perspective of the devas the same as Mañjuśrī’s, or is it different? Examine this carefully."
At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past, at Vārāṇasī, you turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths, analyzing and explaining all phenomena—the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates."
Now, once again, you turn the most wondrous, unsurpassed Great Wheel of Dharma. This Dharma is exceedingly profound and subtle; few are those capable of believing it.
Since ancient times, we have frequently heard the World-Honored One’s teachings, yet we have never before heard such a profound and sublime supreme Dharma.

The World-Honored One has preached this Dharma, and we all rejoice in it. Now that the one of great wisdom, Śāriputra, has received the prediction of his exalted attainment, we too shall likewise surely become Buddhas, most honored and unsurpassed throughout all worlds.

The Buddha-way is inconceivable; he teaches according to what is appropriate through skillful means. Whatever meritorious deeds I have, whether in this life or in past lives, as well as the merit from seeing the Buddha—all these I dedicate entirely to the Buddha-way.

Regarding the "extinction of the five sentient beings": this refers to the sentient beings of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), all of whom possess suffering and its accumulation (*duḥkha-samudaya*) and are subject to arising and extinction.
Therefore, it speaks of the four truths of the arising and extinction of all phenomena. The "unsurpassed great wheel of Dharma" is the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.
"Rejoicing" means that upon seeing others rejoice, one likewise gives rise to joy. The passage beginning with "Great Wisdom" clarifies the intent of rejoicing:

namely, "Since he is a great man, so am I. The two lines concerning the Buddha-way likewise signify the realization that the One Vehicle path is taught as three vehicles according to what is appropriate.
The passage beginning with "That which I have [attained]" refers to the dedication toward the Buddha-way. By means of this dedication...
They turn toward the Buddha-way; this is why these celestial robes revolve through the void. An ancient worthy said, "It is not the wind or the banner that moves;
it is the mind of the noble one that moves. This also says, "It is not the celestial robes that revolve; it is the minds of the eight classes of beings that revolve."

At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I now have no further doubt or regret, for I have personally received before the Buddha the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
As for these twelve hundred who have attained mastery over their minds, they formerly dwelt on the stage of learners;
the Buddha constantly taught and transformed them, saying: 'My Dharma can bring one to leave behind birth, old age, sickness, and death, reaching ultimate [liberation].'"

"Nirvāṇa! Those who are still in training and those who have completed their training each believed they had attained nirvāṇa by means of their own detachment from the view of self, the views of existence and non-existence, and so forth.
Yet now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, having heard what we have never heard before, we all fall into doubt and confusion. How excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret."

This is Śāriputra’s presentation of his doubts and formal request for instruction. He states that having already grasped the principle of "the mind itself is Buddha," and further hearing the account of his past-life causes and conditions, his lingering doubts were suddenly extinguished. He now shoulders this burden with both shoulders;

it is neither because the Tathāgata commanded him to acknowledge it, nor is it because he has forced himself to accept it. Therefore, it is said: "I have personally attained [this realization] before the Buddha."
This is the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*). The following passage expresses their doubts.

Their intention was that these twelve hundred people of similar class, who had heard the Tathāgata’s Dharma forty years ago and all realized *nirvāṇa*, each thought for themselves that they had already attained extinction (*parinirvāṇa*).
Having already attained the ultimate goal, they now hear the bestowal of the prophecy. Not only do they fail to believe it, but they instead fall into a city of doubt.
The reason they fall into this city of doubt is that they think to themselves: "If there is indeed such a matter as the bestowal of a prophecy, why was it not spoken forty years ago?
Why must one wait until today? This is because they do not understand the reason why it was not spoken forty years ago.
Therefore, today, although he has heard the words that an Arhat can become a Buddha, he still falls into doubt and hesitation, refusing to accept it.
I pray that you will analyze and clarify the causes and conditions for why this was not spoken forty years ago;
only then shall he be able to leave behind his doubts and give rise to faith. From this passage, we see that Śāriputra habitually harbored self-doubt and regret, moved by—

Because they were wounded by self-reproach and self-censure, they gave rise to faith upon hearing [the teaching] once. As for the twelve hundred [monks], they were habitually situated within a state of indifference;
thus, they gave rise to doubt upon hearing [the teaching] once. These four great disciples do not equal even a single tally of Śāriputra.
Furthermore, doubt is the very mechanism for awakening; without doubt, there is no awakening. Thus, one knows that the state of doubt on this day—
Furthermore, this is the awakening potential for those who will come in the future.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "Did I not previously say that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, by means of various causes and conditions..."
Are all these parables, expressions, and skillful means for teaching the Dharma intended for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
All that has been spoken is for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas. However, Śāriputra, I shall now further employ a parable.
To further clarify this meaning: "Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through analogies.
This is what the Tathāgata permitted to be said. As for his saying, "You have requested that I again explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly":
Did I not tell you before? The Tathāgata appears in the world for the sake of the one great cause;
all that he does is always for this one purpose, and everything he speaks is solely to transform bodhisattvas.
The explanation has been detailed in this way; why then should one wish to further discourse on its causes and conditions?
Since he does not understand, I shall now again clarify it by means of a simple and easily comprehended analogy.
If one can attain understanding through this metaphor, one may still be called a wise person; otherwise, one will remain ultimately ignorant.
Śāriputra, suppose there were in a kingdom, a city, or a village a great elder who was advanced in years, possessed of immeasurable wealth, and owning many fields, houses, and servants;
his household was vast, yet it had only a single gate, and within it resided a great multitude of people.
One hundred, two hundred, or even five hundred people dwell therein. The halls and pavilions are dilapidated;
the walls have crumbled, the bases of the pillars are rotten, and the beams and rafters are tilted and precarious. Suddenly, a fire breaks out all at once on every side, burning down the house.
Within this residence are the elder’s sons—perhaps ten, twenty, or as many as thirty—who are staying inside.
From here below, the great meanings from the "Expedient Means" chapter are collectively presented through parables to further elucidate them.
A kingdom, city, or village represents the three realms (*tridhātu*). The great elder represents the transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*). This elder possesses ten virtues:
first, his lineage is noble, like the descendants of the Three August Ones or the progeny of the Five Emperors; second, his rank is honorable, serving as a minister... [text continues].

1. He assisted as the Grand Coordinator (A-heng), blending salt and plum to harmonize governance. 2. Third, he was wealthy, possessing vast riches like copper hills and gold mines. 4. Fourth, he was majestic and formidable, like the severity of frost and the chill of snow.
5. Fifth, his wisdom was profound; his breast was like an armory. 6. Sixth, he was aged and venerable; his appearance was like pine and cypress trees. 7. Seventh, his conduct was pure;

his integrity was as flawless as jade and璧 (bi) discs. 8. Eighth, he was complete in ritual; his deportment was orderly and dignified. 9. Ninth, he was revered by those above; great men looked up to him.
Virtue. "The ten types of inferior people taking refuge" refers to the common masses taking refuge in his heart.

Possessing these ten virtues, he is called an *upāsaka* (elder), which is analogous to possessing the ten titles and being called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*). That his years have declined and advanced is analogous to the imminent arrival of *nirvāṇa*.
That his wealth is immeasurable is analogous to immeasurable wisdom. This sentence is the general statement; what follows is the specific explanation. "Fields and houses" is analogous to...

Great compassion is [the master]. The servants and attendants are a metaphor for skillful means (*upāya*). That the house is vast and extensive is a metaphor for taking the triple world (*tridhātu*) as one's home.
That there is but a single gate is a metaphor for how, within the triple world, the universal consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*) serves as the sole gateway.
An ancient worthy said: "The karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no fundamental basis to rely upon. This is precisely what is meant.

As for the five hundred people dwelling therein, it is a metaphor for sentient beings of the five destinies, all of whom reside within the cave of karmic consciousness. The four lines concerning the hall and pavilion are as follows:
This reveals that the three realms are the transformation lands of the Buddha, which possess the characteristics of decay and destruction.

They are not like the Reward Land of the Tathāgata, where the ground is made of diamond (*vajra*), and the palaces, halls, pavilions, beams, rafters, and walls are all accomplished from the wondrous jewels of *maṇi*.
Wind cannot enter them; rain does not moisten them; fire cannot burn them; and water cannot [submerge them].

They are drowning. As for the fire burning the house and its contents, this is a metaphor for how all within the triple world are being tormented by the intersecting fires of the five signs of decay and the eight sufferings.
That the children are also inside the house is a metaphor for those who possess the capacities of the three vehicles and have a slight degree of awakening;
they too remain within the cavern of karmic consciousness. Although these children have a slight awakening and desire to escape the triple world, [they are unable to do so].
Failing to encounter an enlightened teacher, they have strayed onto deviant paths; because they seek to abandon suffering through further suffering, they are unable to escape.

This is not like the sentient beings of the five realms of existence, who are muddled and dim-witted, entirely lacking in discernment. When you speak of ten people, yet others speak of a hundred, it is because those who possess awakening are few, while those who remain in ignorance are many.
When the elder saw this great fire rising from all four sides, he was immediately seized with great alarm and fear, and thought to himself:
"Although I am able to escape safely through this gate that is being consumed by flames, my children within this burning house are attached to their play and delights;
they do not perceive or understand, nor are they alarmed or terrified, even as the fire approaches their bodies and its agonizing pain cuts into them."
They feel no weariness or distress, nor do they have the intention to seek escape.

Next, the text clarifies that the elder gives rise to compassion. That the elder is startled and terrified upon seeing the fire is because he is shocked out of pity for his children and fearful out of concern for their lives;
this is the sorrow of identifying with them as one body. This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s eye observing the beings of the six realms.
"Arising" means giving rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). "And then acts as follows" is a metaphor for the initial seven contemplations. It says:
"Because my five abidings (*pañca-vihāra*) are thoroughly exhausted, I am at peace; because the two deaths are forever extinguished, I am hidden.

By transforming consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*), I have emerged from the gates of the triple world (*tridhātu*). Yet, alas for these children, who regard the triple world as a place of lingering attachment; thus they delight in and cling to it."
They are unaware of awakening; taking the three realms as a playground for amusement, they frolic about without alarm or fear.

Although various sufferings oppress their bodies—even to the point where the marrow withers, the vital essence is exhausted, the head rots, and the forehead is scorched—they do not harbor a single thought of weary detachment, nor do they exhibit even a trace of terror. Therefore, they never seek to escape.

This is the meaning [of the previous passage]. This is an analogy for the preceding text: "The faculties of these sentient beings are dull; they are attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance," and so forth.
Śāriputra, this elder thought to himself: "I have strength in my body and hands; I should carry them out from the house using my arms, or using a lap-cloth, or using a small table."
This metaphor illustrates the two weeks of contemplation. "My hands and body possess strength" is a metaphor for the power of spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi*) and the power of wisdom (*prajñā*).
"The lap-sack and the desk" are metaphors for the power of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*) and fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
These are all objects for the Tathāgata’s own enjoyment. The intent is that, with the strength of his hands and body, he might place his children in the lap-sack and carry them out.

Furthermore, it is as if one were to place various sons upon a table or desk and lift them out; this is analogous to how, had the preceding passages merely praised the One Vehicle, they would not have been able to inspire faith in such texts as this Dharma.
He further reflected: "This house has but a single door, and it is moreover narrow and small. My children are young and lack discernment;
they are attached to their playthings and might fall down and be consumed by the fire. I shall speak to them of the terrors of this place;
this house is already burning, and they should quickly depart at once so that they do not suffer injury from the flames. Having thought thus, he...
Having reflected thus, he informed his sons of everything exactly as he had contemplated: "Sons, come out quickly!
Although the father compassionately enticed and exhorted them with kind words, the sons were attached to their play and refused to believe or accept him.

They felt neither alarm nor fear, having no intention at all to leave, nor did they know what constituted the fire, what the house was, or what it meant to be lost; they merely [looked] to the east...
They ran about playing, looking only toward their father. At that time, the elder had this thought:
"This house has already been consumed by a great fire; if I and my sons do not exit at once, we will surely be burned to death.
I must now employ a skillful means to enable my sons to escape this calamity. The father knew that each of his sons had previously cherished different preferences.
There are various rare and wondrous objects of play; you will surely take pleasure in them and become attached to them.
Therefore, he says to them: "The playthings you delight in are rare and difficult to obtain. If you do not take them now, you will surely feel sorrow and regret later.
Such various carts—drawn by goats, deer, and oxen—are now outside the gate for you to enjoy yourselves with. You should quickly depart from this burning house."
"Come. Whatever you desire, I shall grant it all to you.

This is a metaphor for the application of skillful means through seven days and three nights of reflection. To reflect again is called "more" (geng); to reflect a third time is called "furthermore" (fu geng).
Regarding the statement that within the triple world, birth and death arise solely with the *karmic consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*) as the master:
this consciousness is profoundly deep and subtle. You children are still immature and lack understanding;

if I were to explain it to you immediately, you would lack the capacity for comprehension and might become confused and fail to grasp it. Yet, if I do not explain it, I fear you will remain immersed in and attached to worldly desires. Therefore—
They are unable to abandon these places of pleasure and sport; yet if they should stumble even once, they will ultimately be consumed by fire.
Such sentient beings are stubborn and difficult to transform; they must be disciplined through harsh words and terrifying matters, saying:
"This is hell; this is the realm of hungry ghosts; this is the animal realm; these are the states of hardship; this is folly."
This human life: this is killing, this is the retribution for killing; this is sexual misconduct, this is the retribution for sexual misconduct;
this is delusion, this is the retribution for delusion—and so on, up to these three calamities and these eight difficulties.
All of these have the six consciousnesses and the three poisons as their cause, which evoke the fruit of this body’s birth, aging, sickness, and death. Furthermore, this very house—
"Now it is already burning. If you do not seek deliverance early, you will surely fall, until your very flesh is consumed by putrefaction.
Having reflected thus, he informed his sons in detail of what he had contemplated.
This is to entice him to come out quickly; this parable explains the origin of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*). Although the father is of low status, the son does not accept his instruction.
This means that even though he is addressed with words that are firm, harsh, and urgent, and with matters that inspire terror, because his attachment is so deep, [he does not comply].

Having become thoroughly accustomed to wandering about, they consider it their own pleasure and refuse to believe or accept [the truth]. They feel no fear whatsoever and have no intention of escaping;
furthermore, they do not know what constitutes the cause of suffering, what constitutes the fruit of suffering, or what is meant by "falling away."
He merely wandered about to the east and played to the west, staring at his father with wide eyes, remaining placidly indifferent.
Seeing how deep was his delusion and how extreme his confusion, [the father] then used a parable below to explain cessation and the path.
Since those words of urgent exhortation could not penetrate him, and matters of fear could not move him, he further employed objects that were pleasing...
He used places of play to entice them. Therefore, the elder again thought to himself: "This house has already been consumed by fire and is now close to my very body.
If I do not come out at this moment, both I and my children will be burned by the flames.
Furthermore, in this degenerate age, one cannot use formal speech; a fool cannot be addressed with upright words. Thus, I must think of a skillful means to lure them out."
An objection is raised: "The World-Honored One has already emerged safely through the gate of the burning house;
why then do you say that I and my children will surely be consumed by fire? The answer is: "The Tathāgata manifests his body within the three realms to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
When they emerge, he emerges; when they enter, he enters. If his children are ill, the parents are also ill; this is what is meant by 'being of one essence' (sahaja-kāya)."
Great Compassion shares in the sorrows of others. The father knows what lies below; he contemplates how to replace instruments of suffering with instruments of joy.
He knows the distinctions in their past habitual tendencies and natures, and he also knows the things they currently delight in; therefore, he offers them what they cherish.
This is what is meant by "no one knows a son as well as his father. Furthermore, it is said "below" to serve as a metaphor for the Three Vehicles.
"Come down! is said to encourage them to realize [the truth]. "Such as these" indicates the location of the chariots;
"now outside the gate" means that these three chariots are outside the burning house, not within it.
"Whereby you may sport" demonstrates the function of the chariots, meaning that by mounting them, one may exercise the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) at will.
"I am sovereign. You all, go down quickly; I permit you to come out.
As for the sheep, deer, and ox carts that accord with your desires, I shall give them to you immediately."
At that time, the sons, hearing of the rare treasures and playthings described by their father, had their desires satisfied;
their hearts were each filled with vigor and resolve (śūra), and they pushed and shoved one another, racing together in competition to escape from the burning house.
"These children have emerged from the burning house. "Their wishes being fulfilled" means that their capacities and the teaching have met.
"Each with a heart of courageous vigor" refers to striving forward. "Pushing and shoving one another" means mutually refining and sharpening each other through study.

Pushing against one another with their hands is called "pushing. Parting one another with their hands is called "shoving. Their racing together represents the collective practice of the Eightfold Noble Path.
Their vying to escape the burning house represents the collective realization of the fruit of Arhatship (the stage of no-more-learning). Question: This house has only a single door;
this is a metaphor for the cycle of the three realms, which possesses only karmic consciousness. Now that those of the Lesser Vehicle have already exited—

If one can purify and eliminate the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*) within the three realms, why does another passage state that those of the two vehicles do not know the *karmic consciousness*?
Answer: The root source of birth and death within the three realms is, in reality, the eighth *karmic consciousness*, which acts as the sovereign lord.
The seventh [consciousness] follows what is produced and to what it is bound. Although the eighth is named "karmic," [it is so called because it is the basis for the accumulation of karma].

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not create karma itself; it is actually the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that creates karma, thereby inducing the eighth consciousness to undergo birth and death.

Because the faculties of those of the Hīnayāna are inferior and they desire to exit the triple world quickly, and because this [eighth] consciousness contains such vast latent deposits (*ālayavijñāna*) that they cannot be purified all at once, [the Buddha] pointed to the mental consciousness that creates karma as [the ātman].
This is the cause of birth and death. By exhausting the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness), one attains the *nirodhasamāpatti* (attainment of cessation).

Once the *manovijñāna* is exhausted, one is able to transform a portion of the *karmavijñāna* (karma-consciousness) and thereby exit the triple world. Thus, the eighth [consciousness] is no longer drawn into the cycle of birth and death;
it would also be appropriate to call this "exiting the gate of the karma-consciousness. However, this can only be known by the Tathāgata; the followers of the two vehicles truly do not know it.
This refers to causing that path to be perfected and its virtues complete, while remaining unaware of it oneself. Question:

Since the followers of the Two Vehicles have already transformed their *ālayavijñāna* (karmic consciousness) and have thus emerged from the triple world (*tridhātu*), for what reason are they further instructed to advance in the cultivation of Buddha-wisdom to transform consciousness into gnosis (*jñāna*)? Answer:
Did we not say previously that the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) contains and stores seeds most extensively, involving both the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena?

While those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) have merely emptied themselves of the grasping at a self and have already abandoned the *ālayavijñāna*, they have not yet emptied the grasping at phenomena; thus, they still remain within the state of maturation (*vipāka*).

Therefore, one should know that it is not only sentient beings within the realms who reside within the *karmic consciousness*; even the practitioners of the Two Vehicles outside the realms, up to and including Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), are likewise therein.
Furthermore, they have not yet been able to completely eliminate karmic consciousness; they still remain within it.
Therefore, one first causes them to exit the karmic consciousness within the realm, and subsequently causes them to give rise to karmic consciousness outside the realm.
At that time, the elder saw that his sons had all emerged safely;
they were sitting in an open space at the crossroads, free from all obstructions, their minds composed and joyful, leaping for joy.
This householder is filled with joy. His safe emergence signifies that he is no longer oppressed by birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

His standing at the crossroads signifies his realization of the principle of the Four Noble Truths. His sitting in the open space signifies his abiding in the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*).
His freedom from further obstructions signifies the exhaustion of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). His mind being serene signifies that he has attained mastery over the mind. He leaps up...
Those who leap for joy are those who delight in the pleasures of others.
At that time, the sons each said to their father, "Father, we pray you grant us now the playthings you previously promised:
the goat-carts, the deer-carts, and the ox-carts. Śāriputra, at that time the elder gave each of his sons one large [cart].
A chariot. This chariot was high and wide, adorned with various jewels. It was surrounded by railings, with bells suspended on all four sides.
Furthermore, above it, a canopy was spread, likewise embellished with rare and diverse precious gems. Precious cords were interlaced across it, and various flower garlands hung down.
A soft, elegant seat was layered upon it, and a crimson pillow was placed there. It was drawn by white oxen, their coats pure and clean, their forms...
His body was handsome and well-proportioned; he possessed great physical strength, walked with a steady and upright gait, and moved as swiftly as the wind.
Furthermore, he was attended by many servants who guarded him. Why was this? Because this great elder possessed immeasurable wealth, and his various treasuries were all overflowing.
He thought to himself: "My riches are limitless; it would not be right to give them inferior, small carts."
"O sons, these young children here are all my own children; my love for them is without partiality.
I possess such great chariots made of the seven treasures, in number beyond measure. You should regard them with an equal mind and give each one of them;
it is not right to make distinctions. Why is this? Because even if I were to provide these goods to the entire kingdom, they would still not be exhausted—how much less so for my sons!"
At that time, the sons each mounted a great carriage; they had obtained what they had never experienced before, which was not what they had originally expected.
This refers to the sons requesting carriages. It is as the Sixth Patriarch said: "Having sat upon the white ox-cart, they go outside the gate again to seek the three carts.
The passage beginning with "Śāriputra" and below refers to the equal bestowal of the great carriages. What was previously stated—“vowing to seek Buddhahood”—[is fulfilled here].
