The Way is that which is upright and straightforward, wherein skillful means are relinquished. That the vehicle is high and broad is a metaphor for the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), which vertically exhausts the past and horizontally pervades all space.
That it is adorned with various jewels is a metaphor for its abundance of myriad virtues. That it has railings all around...
The *dhāraṇī* provides protection and defense. The bells suspended on the four sides represent the preaching of the Dharma through the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
The canopy with its curtains and awnings represents the universal covering of compassion. The adornment with various jewels represents the myriad virtues adorning this compassion.

The crisscrossing of precious cords represents the firm stabilization of this compassion by means of the great vows. The hanging of various flower tassels represents the four [bases of] supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*).
"Collecting" means to gladden and exhort sentient beings. "Laying out a double-layered, elegant mat" means to comfort all beings with a mind of equanimity.
"Placing a crimson pillow" means to settle and bring ease to the multitude of living beings through the Dharma of the precepts. "Yoked with white oxen" refers to...
This is one who possesses great power and great wisdom; it is for this reason that he drives this chariot.

That his complexion is full and pure, and his physical form is beautiful, means that the roots of virtue have been planted and his body is moistened; that there is much within is manifested outwardly.
That he possesses great strength and vigor means he is capable of undertaking great matters. That his gait is level and upright means his movements are...
It is in accord with the proper measure; it enters upon the level path. "Its speed is like the wind" means that its wisdom and skill are agile and swift.
"Furthermore, it has many attendants" means that its skillful means (*upāya*) are complete. Nanquan said: "Master Wang has raised a water buffalo since childhood.
If I intend to pasture it at the Eastern Creek, I cannot avoid consuming the King’s water and grass. If I intend to go to the West..."
"Herding cattle by the stream, one cannot avoid consuming the water and grass belonging to the king; it would be better to accept things as they are, bit by bit, for in the end, nothing is seen.
Dà'ān said, "For thirty years I stayed at Míushān, eating Míushān’s rice and defecating Míushān’s excrement, yet I did not study Míushān’s Chan.
I simply watched a single water buffalo. If it strayed onto the path or entered the grass, I would immediately—"
Turn his nostrils back around. As soon as he offends the crops, he is whipped.
Having been tamed for a long time, this poor fellow now accepts human speech. Now he has transformed into a white ox in the open field;
it is always right before one’s face, standing wide-eyed all day long, and even if you try to drive it away, it will not go. Tell me, where is it right now? Nanyue.
It is said: "It is like a cart yoked to an ox. If the cart does not move, one may strike the cart; one may likewise strike the ox.
Śākyamuni handed down a great white ox, and the Patriarch further left behind a water buffalo.
These are at the disposal of all people to plow fields and sow seeds; you must by no means trespass upon the crops. Therefore, [the text] provides the following inquiry and explanation.
The meaning of "bestowing a great carriage" is that his wealth is boundless; this is a metaphor for being fully endowed with the riches of the Dharma.

"All treasuries overflowing" is a metaphor for the *śrāvaka*, *pratyekabuddha*, *bodhisattva*, and *tathāgata* stores (garbhas), or alternatively, for the ten stores such as faith, precepts, and so forth.
It is said that within the various treasuries, the Tathāgata’s immeasurable wealth of Dharma is fully present. Furthermore, [the Buddha] says:
"My wealth and possessions are infinite; I ought not to give these small carts to my sons. Now, all these young children are my sons; I must not show partiality.
If I were to give each son a sheep-cart, a deer-cart, or an ox-cart, then my love would be biased."
Because of partiality and favoritism, I bestow upon each of you great carts equally with a mind of impartiality.
As for the reason why [I do so], it further explains the intent behind this equal distribution: I possess this immeasurable treasury of Dharma, and it is precisely these things that I give.
"It provides for the entire kingdom and bestows gifts upon all; even so, there is no lack of anything.
How much less could it be that my own biological sons should not be granted equal shares? Nevertheless, what is lacking in the portions of these sons that you wish to grant them equally?
One must not speak of such dreams before a fool. At that time, the sons received the chariots and were filled with joy.
This is beyond expectation. "Not what was originally expected" means that originally there was no intention to hope for anything, yet one has obtained the supreme Great Treasure of the Dharma King;
how could this not be a matter beyond expectation? Therefore, it is said: "I have attained what I never had before."
“Śāriputra, what do you think? Would that elder be guilty of any falsehood in giving precious great chariots to his sons?
Śāriputra replied, ‘No, World-Honored One. That elder merely enabled his sons to escape the disaster of fire and preserve their lives;
it is not a falsehood. Why is this? If they have preserved their bodies and lives, that in itself constitutes [the fulfillment of his purpose].’”
If he has already obtained these delightful objects of play, how much more so when he employs skillful means to rescue them from that burning house?
World-Honored One, even if this elder were to give not even the smallest single chariot, he would still not be guilty of falsehood. Why is this?
Because the elder first formed this intention: "I shall use skillful means to enable my children to escape. For this reason, there is no falsehood.
It would be a delusion. How much more so when the elder, knowing his own wealth to be immeasurable, desires to benefit his sons by giving them all equal great chariots?
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said."
This demonstrates that the investigation is not in vain. Therefore, he called Śāriputra and asked him: "The sons requested carts, yet the elder did not give them small carts;
instead, he bestowed great carts equally upon all. How do you understand this matter? Could there be any falsehood in it? He replied, "No.
The intention was that if even the failure to give small carts is not false, how much less so [the giving of great carts]?
Is there any falsehood in bestowing such great chariots equally? Why is this so?

It is because that elder, seeing his children within the burning house, delighting in play and lacking the intent to seek escape, employed skillful means to cause them to leave the burning house, so as not to allow their Dharma-body or the life-force of their wisdom to suffer any injury; this is precisely [the case].
As for the actual matter: why must one necessarily provide toys and articles of amusement before something can be considered a reality?

Why is this so? Because there is nothing that people cherish more than their own bodies and lives. Since your sons have preserved their bodies and lives and have not suffered the harm of the fire, they have already obtained the articles of amusement;
it is not necessary to further grant them the three carts. How much more so, O Tathāgata, since you originally perceive [the truth]...
Is it not that he, out of necessity, lured those who were addicted to the burning house to exit its gates?
Furthermore, let us set aside for a moment the fact that not providing the deer carts and ox carts was not false;
even not providing the smallest goat carts would not have been false. Why? Because it was the elder’s original intention not to give small carts to the people, but merely—
Using skillful means to entice them, he causes his children to emerge from the gate of the burning house.

For this reason, although he does not give them small carts, it is not a falsehood; how much less so for the Tathāgata? Knowing for himself that his wealth is immeasurable, his original intention was to benefit his children.
Without waiting for their request, he is willing to gladly bestow upon them great carts and the like.
"Son, could there be anything false in this? The Buddha spoke as follows, confirming that his words were consistent with principle:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is also like this. He is the father of all the world.
Regarding all fears, decays, afflictions, anxieties, and the obscuration of ignorance, he has forever exhausted them without remainder and has fully accomplished immeasurable knowledge."

He possesses the powers and fearlessnesses, great supernormal powers, and the power of wisdom; he is fully endowed with the perfection of skillful means and wisdom, as well as great kindness and great compassion.

He is ever free from weariness or fatigue, constantly seeking what is good to benefit all beings, and thus enters the triple world—the dilapidated and decaying house on fire—to deliver sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, and from ignorance.
Shrouded in darkness by the fires of the three poisons, they are taught and transformed so that they may attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

From this point downward, the Dharma is applied to the analogy. That the Tathāgata is the father of the triple world corresponds to the elder mentioned above who possesses a great household enterprise.
The Tathāgata emerges from the triple world yet enters the triple world; this is why he is the father of the triple world.

The Father of the Four Modes of Birth. Regarding the passage "among all those below," this clearly demonstrates that the Tathāgata originally attained realization from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and was not born as a celestial being.
As for the phrase "fearing decline and affliction, etc.," it means that by transforming immeasurable fears, he accomplished immeasurable powers of fearlessness;
by transforming immeasurable declines and afflictions, he accomplished immeasurable great supernormal powers (*mahā-ṛddhi*); and by transforming... [the rest of the sentence continues].
Transforming immeasurable anxieties and afflictions, they achieve immeasurable power of knowledge and vision. Transforming immeasurable ignorance, they achieve immeasurable power of great wisdom.
Transforming immeasurable obscuring afflictions, they achieve immeasurable power of skillful means and wisdom.
Transforming the intent to kill, they ascend to share the same power of compassion as all Buddhas. Transforming malice...

With a mind that shares in the power of sorrow and longing common to the six realms below, one transforms indolence into the power of diligence and becomes endowed with various kinds of vast supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*).
Thus, one is able to constantly seek out wholesome deeds to benefit all beings.
Therefore, manifesting within the three realms to deliver sentient beings is like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water. This is called the "basis of all sufferings."

The suffering of birth refers to the fact that as soon as one touches the ground, the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) is not severed. That which causes transformation and decay is called the suffering of old age;
it refers to the withering of physical form and the pallor of complexion. That which oppresses the field of the body is called the suffering of illness;
it refers to groaning upon a bed and sighing within the chambers. That which extinguishes all the faculties is called the suffering of death; it refers to the falling away of the light of the eyes.
The earth is the dispersion of the four great elements. To seek and not find is sorrow; to find and then lose again is grief.
To encounter adverse conditions is suffering; for suffering to continue without end is affliction.
Because it is free from fear, it can deliver sentient beings from the fear of birth and death. Because it is free from decay, affliction, sorrow, and distress, it can deliver sentient beings.

...from the sorrows, griefs, sufferings, and afflictions. Because he alone is free from the obscuration of the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*), he is able to deliver sentient beings from the fire of the three poisons and the darkness of their delusion.

Because he alone has accomplished the powers of knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana-bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), he is able to teach and transform sentient beings, enabling them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. In short, it can be said that the Tathāgata’s self-awakening is perfect and thus able to...
He also awakens others.
He sees all sentient beings being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction;

they undergo various sufferings for the sake of the five desires and material gain, and because of their greedy attachment and pursuit, they experience manifold sufferings in the present and [will do so] hereafter.

They undergo the sufferings of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts. Even if born in the heavens or among humans, they experience the suffering of poverty and hardship, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of encountering the hated.

Immersed in such various sufferings as these, sentient beings frolic with joy, neither perceiving nor understanding them; they feel no alarm or dread, nor do they give rise to revulsion, nor do they seek liberation.
"O Śāriputra, [beings] are liberated. Within this burning house of the three realms, they run hither and thither; though they encounter great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity.
Śāriputra, when the Buddha sees this, he reflects: 'I am the father of sentient beings;
I ought to uproot their suffering and distress, and grant them the immeasurable and boundless bliss of the Buddha's wisdom, so that they may sport therein. Śāriputra, the Tathāgata..."

Again, he thought: "If I were to rely solely on my power of spiritual transformations and my power of wisdom, abandoning skillful means, and were to praise for all sentient beings the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, his powers, and his fearlessnesses, sentient beings would not be able to attain deliverance through these."
Why is this? These sentient beings have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction;
they are being burned by the burning house of the triple world. How, then, could they understand the wisdom of the Buddha?
The phrase "the elder brings forth compassion" means that those who see him do so by observing with the Buddha-eye. All eight sufferings are associated with fire.
Four sufferings are as previously explained; the remaining four are further elucidated here. "Association with the unloved" is called the suffering of encountering the hated.
The separation from what is beloved is called the suffering of parting from the loved. The failure to achieve one’s hopes is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

The accumulation of all these preceding sufferings is called the suffering of the intense burning of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-paridāha*). When combined with the four preceding sufferings, these are known as the eight sufferings of human existence.
Alternatively, if birth, aging, and so forth are consolidated into a single suffering, they are termed the five sufferings; these likewise consist of the objects of the five desires and wealth.

To experience various kinds of suffering for the sake of gain is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. Furthermore, as explained below, this is the suffering of the five aggregates being in a state of intense burning (*pañca-skandha-paridāha*).

That is to say, being greedily attached to the five desires and material profit, one pursues them with the certainty that they must be obtained; thus, one does not avoid hardships and perils even if it means entering the palaces of dragons or the dens of tigers.
Having already experienced suffering in the present life, one further falls into the three miserable realms (*trāya*); yet, one may also be reborn among gods or humans.
There still remain those who suffer from poverty and hardship. Regarding the phrase "poverty and hardship": to lack wealth is called "poverty"; to lack kinsmen is called "distress" (窮);
to lack ease and comfort is called "hardship" (困). It should be understood that the two phrases concerning separation from what is loved correspond to two types of suffering.
"To be submerged therein" means to have one's entire body immersed in suffering. Not only are they unaware of this suffering, but they even find joy in it.
They delight in play; because they are only filled with joy, they are unaware and unconscious; because they are only engaged in play, they are neither startled nor terrified.
Because they are unaware and unconscious, they do not weary of suffering or its origin; because they are neither startled nor terrified, they do not seek liberation.
Within this burning house of the three realms, they run hither and thither, drowning and perishing without knowing how to return home.
They remain immersed in suffering for the rest of their lives yet do not regard it as a calamity; this is why the Tathāgata gives rise to compassion.
From the passage beginning "Śāriputra," down to the end, [the text] describes the contemplation performed during the three weeks. It says: "Since they are my children, I am their father."

"I should now, by means of my power of spiritual transformation and my power of wisdom, cause them to suddenly uproot the suffering of karmic consciousness and suddenly bestow upon them the bliss of the Buddha-wisdom, enabling them to sport within the field of great nirvāṇa; only then will my original vow be fulfilled.

Thus he spoke, subsequently establishing expedient means. "If I were to employ only my power of spiritual transformation to extensively praise the Buddha-vehicle without practicing these expedients..."

It is appropriate not to require them first to sever the three poisons of the six consciousnesses, transcend the triple world, and realize nirvana, but rather to desire that they suddenly perform the deeds of a bodhisattva, abruptly abandon the karmic consciousness, and immediately enter the Buddha-wisdom; for there is a fear that their capacity may be small while the Dharma is great.
If the Dharma does not meet with the individual's capacity, they cannot attain deliverance. Why is this?

Because they have not yet emerged from the triple world, they are still being scorched by the five desires, the three poisons, and the fires of the eight sufferings; they will have no leisure even to extinguish these, so one must speak to them accordingly.
How could one possibly understand the profound and immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas?
It is just as if one were speaking of the wealth and nobility of an emperor to someone in the midst of fetters; what benefit would that bring?
Therefore, it is necessary to employ skillful means (upāya) to deliver them.
Śāriputra, it is just as that elder, although he possessed strength in his body and arms, did not employ it;
rather, through earnest skillful means, he diligently rescued his children from the peril of the burning house, and only then bestowed upon each of them a precious and substantial great carriage.
This presents the essential meaning within the analogy. It connects the preceding text and initiates the subsequent text.
The passage beginning with "Just as that householder" connects the preceding text; the passage beginning with "But with earnestness" initiates the subsequent text.
The Tathāgata is also like this. Although he possesses power and fearlessness, he does not employ them;

rather, by means of wisdom and skillful means, he rescues sentient beings from the burning house of the triple world. He preaches the three vehicles—the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the buddha—and says to them:
"Do not take pleasure in dwelling within the burning house of the triple world; do not crave its coarse and wretched things."
These are forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. If you give rise to craving through attachment to them, you will be consumed by them.
You must quickly escape the triple world; you shall then attain one of the three vehicles: the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, or the Buddha-vehicle.
I now guarantee this for you; it shall never be in vain. You should simply cultivate diligence with vigor. It is through such skillful means that the Tathāgata entices and advances the multitude.
Śāriputra spoke again, saying: "You should all know that these three vehicles of the Dharma are all praised by the Noble Ones;

they are sovereign and unconditioned, requiring no further seeking or reliance. By mounting these three vehicles, one enjoys oneself through the untainted faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and so forth, thereby attaining immeasurable peace and happiness."
"The Tathāgata" and below: though his body possesses great power, he does not employ it;
rather, "he merely uses" [it] through diligent skillful means to strive in rescuing his children from their distress.

"Do not take pleasure in dwelling within the burning house of the triple world" is an exhortation for them to leave suffering. As the *Book of Shang* says: "Like a fire spreading across the plains, it cannot be faced."
How much more so for those who are immersed within it? Do not covet that which is coarse, inferior, and base; these are the objects perceived by the six consciousnesses.

This is an exhortation to sever the accumulation [of suffering]. Eyebrows like silkworm moths and teeth as white as jade are axes that hew down one's nature; the lutes, flutes, pipes, and strings [are likewise destructive].

These are thieves that plunder the mind; the fragrance of flowers, incense, and wine are the go-betweens for committing evil deeds; sweet, crisp, and fatty foods are medicines that rot the intestines;
and silken clouds and mist-like gauze are the mechanisms that enslave the body. Therefore, I urge you not to be greedy. Greed is the function of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If one becomes greedily attached, craving arises; where there is craving, one is consumed by it. Thus, craving and attachment—[do not...]

Birth has occurred; the moisture of birth has already ceased. Thus, Udraka Rāmaputra, by means of mundane wisdom, suppressed the afflictions of the lower realms, attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). At that time, the ruler of the land held him in high esteem and welcomed him into the inner palace.
A woman prostrated herself at his feet. When Udraka Rāmaputra touched the woman’s hand, desire arose within him, and he consequently lost his five supernormal powers. Therefore...
"Know that wandering through the three realms is entirely driven by craving and attachment. To pass through this barrier is to emerge from the dust as an Arhat. Descend quickly;
if you exhort him to cultivate the Way, he will surely realize the fruit. "I shall now descend," [the Master said], "and again entice him with gentle words, saying:
'I shall now act as your guarantor for this matter; I shall take full responsibility and will certainly not deceive you. Although...

Nevertheless, it is thus: you must still exert yourself in cultivation and progress; do not give rise to weariness or indolence, only then will you receive the Tathāgata’s gradual and skillful guidance as described above.
Furthermore, he encourages them by extensively praising the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) that assist the path, namely:

the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*), the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), the five powers (*pañca balāni*), and the seven factors of awakening (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*).

The Eightfold Noble Path, up to the nine meditative absorptions and the three doors of liberation—these dharmas of the path are all the crucibles for forging the noble ones and the essential gateways for transcending birth and death.

Therefore, the Buddhas praise them with the utmost words, declaring that these dharmas of the path are things that are sovereign, unbound, and free from dependence or seeking. As for what is meant by "sovereign," if one knows...
Regarding suffering: if one is free from it, there is no longer the painful fruit of the oppression of birth and death, but rather the bliss of mastery over body and mind.

Regarding lack of bondage: if one cuts off the origin [of suffering], there is no longer the causal basis for the bondage of the three realms, but rather the bliss of being unrestrained and unconfined.
Regarding lack of dependence: if one realizes cessation, then "my births are ended; I shall not undergo further existence."

One does not frolic in the burning house; one who has no seeking, if they cultivate the Way, will be a traveler passing through the three realms with nothing to hope for, free from greed and attachment to the world.

By mounting these three vehicles and practicing this Dharma, they realize the bliss of nirvana, no longer suffering from the scorching of the eight sufferings of the three realms, and are no longer constrained by coarse and base forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. Thus...
They shall attain immeasurable peace, security, and happiness.

Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who possess an internal nature of wisdom, who hear the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and with faith accept it, practicing with diligent vigor and desiring to quickly escape the triple world and seek nirvāṇa for themselves—this is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle. It is like those aforementioned...

Sons, it is like those who, seeking the goat-drawn carts, emerged from the burning house. If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, receive it with faith, and with diligent and earnest application seek spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), delighting in solitary tranquility and deeply understanding the causes and conditions of all phenomena—this is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
It is like those sons who, seeking the deer-drawn carts, emerged from the burning house. If there are sentient beings...

Born, they hear the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and with faith and acceptance, they diligently cultivate and exert themselves to seek all-knowledge, the Buddha-knowledge, self-arisen knowledge, teacherless knowledge, and the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, as well as the powers and fearlessnesses.

Out of compassion for immeasurable sentient beings, they bring them peace and happiness, benefit devas and humans, and deliver all across. These are called Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas; because they seek this vehicle, it is so named.

They are mahāsattvas. Just as those sons, seeking ox-carts, emerged from the burning house—this statement that the sons cultivate the Path and realize extinction corresponds to their emergence from the burning house. Those who possess the nature of wisdom within...
There are seeds from former lives. Those who hear the Dharma and receive it with faith are those for whom these seeds are activated by conditions.

Those who apply themselves with earnest diligence, desiring to exit the triple world, are practicing the Way. Those who seek nirvana for themselves are realizing cessation. To desire to seek it swiftly is the sickness of the Lesser Vehicle;
because of this haste, one does not reach the goal, and because of this self-seeking, one’s realization is not great. Consequently, one deviates from the myriad practices.
That the fruits lack perfection and permanence is entirely due to the fault of seeking them for oneself with haste. This is termed "inferior," which is a concluding designation.
Those with dull faculties are called followers of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which is also termed the Inferior Vehicle; this is like the metaphor of the lower carriage.

Those who seek spontaneous wisdom (svayambhū-jñāna) allow themselves to awaken naturally, without seeking a teacher. Those who delight in solitary tranquility remain as single practitioners, guarding themselves alone.
"He does not seek friends; this is a Pratyekabuddha. One who deeply understands the causes and conditions of all phenomena observes the twelve links of dependent origination;
this is a Pratyekabuddha. The faculties of a Pratyekabuddha are sharper than those of a Śrāvaka, yet inferior to those of a Bodhisattva."
These are called the wisdoms of the two vehicles, and they are also called the Middle Vehicle. All-Knowing Wisdom (*sarvajñatā-jñāna*) is the Wondrous Observational Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
Buddha-Wisdom (*buddha-jñāna*) is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Natural Wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) is the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*).

Unlearned Wisdom (*anācāryaka-jñāna*) is the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Alternatively, these may be categorized as the wisdoms of Bodhisattvas, Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas. By means of...
The Bodhisattva practices the ten thousand deeds in unison and studies all four wisdoms; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna and also the Supreme Vehicle (Agrayāna).

Śāriputra, it is just as that elder, seeing his children safely emerge from the burning house and reach a place of fearlessness, reflects upon his own immeasurable wealth and bestows great chariots equally upon all his sons. The Tathāgata is likewise.

He is the father of all sentient beings. When he sees immeasurable billions of sentient beings emerge from the suffering of the triple world and the perilous paths of fear through the gateway of the Buddha's teaching, attaining the bliss of nirvana, the Tathāgata then reflects thus:
I possess immeasurable and boundless powers of wisdom, fearlessness, and so forth—the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas. All these sentient beings are my children;
I bestow the Mahāyāna equally upon them, not allowing anyone to attain extinction alone, but bringing them all to extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.
For those sentient beings who have escaped the triple world, I grant the meditative concentrations of all Buddhas.
Liberation and so forth—these articles of enjoyment are all of one characteristic and one kind; they are praised by the noble ones and are capable of producing the foremost pure and wondrous bliss.
This clarifies that after emerging from the burning house, they are equally granted the great chariots. One must first cause them to reach the place of fearlessness;

only then are the great chariots equally bestowed. This is because one proceeds only after filling each stage of the pools; the teaching does not allow for skipping over stages. The Tathāgata likewise acts in this manner.
It is like that elder who saw his children safely emerge from the burning house and reach a place of fearlessness.
At that time, the Tathāgata likewise provides—by implication—the great chariots, corresponding to his own reflection on his immeasurable wealth and so forth.
This also contains the meaning of the preceding passage: "My wealth and goods are infinite; my treasuries are overflowing. Now, these young children have no partiality in their love."

O Assembly, you should maintain an impartial mind and grant each of them equal status. Grant them all that which is equal to the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*) of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, bestow upon them the profound, boundless, and immeasurable liberations and meditative concentrations into which the Buddhas have deeply entered.
This is to replace the liberation and the concentration of extinction of the Hīnayāna. Regarding "instruments of entertainment," "instruments" refers to tools or equipment;
it is only when these instruments exist that such pleasure exists. In the past, sentient beings used coarse and inferior forms and fragrances as their instruments.
In their daily lives, they were attached to amusements and took pleasure in them.

Therefore, the World-Honored One offered them the nine meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and three liberations (*vimokṣa*), which are characterized by mastery and freedom from bondage, and which provide immeasurable peace and happiness, in exchange for those pleasures.
Thereafter, they became attached to these meditative attainments and were unwilling to relinquish them. The Tathāgata then [presented] the single characteristic and single dharma of all Buddhas...
The requisites for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and liberation (*vimokṣa*) can produce the supreme, pure, and wondrous bliss; one exchanges [the former] for these.

By exchanging these requisites for those requisites, it is like bartering gold for gold. Therefore, the requisites for the enjoyment of meditative concentration and liberation in the three vehicles are praised by the noble ones.
The requisites for the enjoyment of meditative concentration and liberation of the Buddhas are likewise called "noble."
This is what is praised. Otherwise, how could they ever be willing to renounce their instruments of entertainment? Regarding the statement that it is "pure, wondrous, and supreme":

the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is impure because it still possesses the cycle of death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*); the Tathāgata, however, is pure because he has eternally extinguished both forms of death.
The Lesser Vehicle is not supreme because it realizes only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); the Tathāgata, however, has realized both forms of emptiness (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*).

Therefore, it is wondrous. The Lesser Vehicle is not the foremost because it only liberates one from the afflictions of views and thoughts; the Tathāgata, having exhausted the five stages of dwelling, is the foremost.
Śāriputra, it is like that elder who first used the three carts to entice his children, and only afterwards gave them the Great [Vehicle].
The chariot is adorned with precious jewels and is the foremost in security. Yet that elder is free from the fault of falsehood.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he is without falsehood. Initially, he teaches the three vehicles to guide sentient beings, and subsequently, he delivers them solely by means of the Great Vehicle.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable power of wisdom and fearlessness.
The treasury of all dharmas is able to bestow the Mahāyāna Dharma upon all sentient beings; yet they are simply unable to receive it in its entirety.
Śāriputra, for this reason, you should know that by the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas, the One Buddha Vehicle is explained as three.

This combined analysis demonstrates that [the teaching] is not false. As it says below, "As with the metaphor," this refers to the Tathāgata; "as with the Dharma," this is the application to the principle.
"Why is this? and so forth, provides the interrogation and explanation. First, the three vehicles were taught, and subsequently, the Buddha-vehicle was bestowed equally; thus, it is not a falsehood.
The underlying intent is that the Tathāgata’s original purpose was always to bestow the Mahāyāna Dharma, and he never intended to bestow the Hīnayāna Dharma.
However, because their faculties were inferior, they could not fully receive [the teaching]; therefore, it was bestowed according to their capacity.
"Śāriputra, below," concludes the response to the question. You previously asked: "I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the fourfold assembly;
why did you speak of two vehicles and three vehicles for forty years, yet now speak of the One Vehicle? Thus, the conclusion of the answer states: "There is no other reason than this. By means of...
For forty years, their faculties were narrow and inferior, and they were unable to receive [the teaching].
For this reason, during those forty years, I have split the single Buddha-vehicle into three.
The Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Suppose there is an elder who has a large house; the house is long-standing and ancient, and moreover dilapidated, with its halls and chambers high and perilous."

The bases of the pillars are crushed and decayed; the beams and rafters are slanting and leaning; the foundations and steps have collapsed; the walls are crumbling and split apart; the plaster has fallen away.

The thatched roof was collapsing in disarray; the rafters and eaves were askew and falling away; the surrounding walls were crooked and bent; and filth and impurities filled every corner. There were five hundred people there.
They dwell therein. The verses provide a thorough and detailed depiction of the previously mentioned abridged locations; it is truly a portrait of the three realms.
For instance, the phrase "a wealthy man has a large house" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata taking the three realms as his home; therefore, it is called a "large house."
This refers to the existence of the elder. That his house is ancient and moreover dilapidated is a metaphor for how, since beginningless delusion, this realm has existed;
and this world, having endured for vast eons, is already decayed and worn out, yet many such corrupt and evil things remain settled within it.
The eight phrases following "the hall and house" explain the antiquity of the house.
Therefore it is so. "High and precarious" means towering and dangerous. "Crushed and rotten" means shattered and decayed.
"Tilting and leaning" means falling over and slanting. "Collapsed and ruined" means crumbled and destroyed.
"Ruined and split" means the exterior is collapsed while the interior is cracked. "Dilapidated and fallen" means it has crumbled and peeled away.
"Misaligned and detached" means it is uneven and loosely disintegrated. Because this transformed land takes the nature of consciousness as its hall and dwelling, it is precarious and high;
because it takes chaotic thoughts as its pillars and foundations, they are decayed and rotten; because it takes ignorance as its beams and rafters, they are tilted and leaning.
It slants because it takes craving as its foundation, and thus collapses. It crumbles because it takes pride as its walls, and thus falls down.
It decays because it takes defilement as its plaster, and thus peels away. It falls into disorder because it takes the two obstacles as its thatching, and thus tumbles down.

It becomes misaligned because it takes worldly toil as its rafters and eaves, and thus comes apart. This clearly demonstrates that the transformation land (nirmāṇakṣetra) is subject to decay, unlike the recompense land (vipākakṣetra).
It is because it is indestructible. As for that Land of Reward: it takes the Dharma-nature as its hall and residence; how could it ever be in peril?
It takes meditative concentration as its pillars and foundations; how could they ever decay or collapse? It takes the power of vows as its beams and rafters; how could they ever lean or fall?
With merit and virtue as its foundation, how could it ever collapse? With the precepts as its walls, how could they ever crumble?
With various fragrances as its plaster, how could they ever fall away? With compassion as its thatched roof, how could it ever be dislodged?
With the myriad practices as its rafters and eaves, how could they ever be out of alignment? Having thus explained the surrounding enclosure, it is now set forth once more.
It is inferior. "Surrounded by enclosures" means it is hemmed in on all sides by barriers; it is not like the Reward Land, which has no walls or fences in the ten directions.
"Winding and crooked" means it is coiled, spiraling, and tortuous; it is not like the Reward Land, which is level and easy to traverse.
"Pervaded by impurities" means that there is nowhere where unclean things do not exist; it is not like the Reward Land, which is pure.
Furthermore, the fact that five hundred people dwell therein specifically reveals that sentient beings of the five destinies reside together within it;
it is not like the Reward Land, which consists solely of a multitude of bodhisattvas.
Owls, hawks, eagles, and vultures; crows, magpies, doves, and pigeons; vipers, snakes, adders, and scorpions; centipedes, millipedes, and many-legged insects.
The weasels (*yòu*), the *lì* foxes, and the *xī* mice—these various species of evil insects—scramble and run about crosswise.
This section below depicts those who are human in face but bestial in heart; they are categorized within the gate of "birds.

Below the mention of the owls (*chī*), screech-owls (*xiāo*), eagles (*diāo*), and vultures (*jiù*), the sentient beings of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) are specifically clarified as all being driven by the three poisons (*tri-viṣa*), as described in the following text.
Regarding the term "yun": the *chī* is the *chīxiū*, also called the *xiūliú* or the "strange owl" (*guàichī*). Its cry brings rain;
it cannot see during the day, but at night it flies about devouring mosquitoes and gadflies. This is what is meant in the *Zhuangzi*:
"The *chīxiū* can pick out a flea by night, yet by day it cannot see Mount Tai. This is a strange bird. When human beings act contrary to the norm and become as eccentric and bizarre as this—
As for this "xiāo": it is the earth-owl (*tǔxiāo*). It gathers clods of earth to serve as its offspring; once the young have matured, both parents are devoured by them.
It is a bird of unfiliality, and among humans there are those who are similarly unfilial. The *diāo* resembles a hawk but is larger and black in color;
it is commonly called the "black *diāo*" (*zàodiāo*) and is also known as a vulture (*jiù*). Its nature is cruel and predatory; it soars over the water, fanning the fish out from the surging waves.
It seizes and devours them; it is also called the Boiling River (*fúhé*). When the Táo River reaches its banks, fish enter it;
when the Boiling River reaches its banks, fish surge up. The *diāokè* is a bird. There are those among humans who are as predatory as this bird.

As for the crow and the magpie: the crow transmits foam, while the magpie transmits twigs. The *Shī* says, "Nothing is blacker than the crow; the magpie is so strong and persistent. These lines all satirize licentiousness and excess.
The pigeon borrows others' nests for its dwelling; it is a clumsy bird. There are those among humanity whose nature is as clumsy as this.
The dove is easily reconciled with others; it is a licentious bird. There are those among humanity whose licentiousness is like this. The *luán* is a large snake.
It is also called the *fùshé* (venomous snake). "Fù" means to retaliate; when touched, it retaliates. When this venomous snake is enraged, its poison is concentrated at its head and tail.
If it stings the hand, it severs the hand; if it stings the foot, it severs the foot. This snake possesses the most extreme of poisons.

Furthermore, it is said that the *fùshé* has a needle-like protrusion on the reverse side of its nose. Among all snakes, this one alone gives birth from a womb, immediately splitting open [its belly] as it is born.
The mother’s womb: the *zhèn* bird eats it. Such is the nature of those who harbor poison within themselves. The *xié*: this refers to the entire scorpion;
it brandishes its venom to sting people. The *wúgōng*, also known as the *jíqiě*: when it sees a large snake, it climbs upon it and eats its brain.
As the *Zhuāngzǐ* says: "The *jíqiě* delights in the *dài*. There are those among humans who eat human marrow and brains yet feel no fear, just like these creatures.
Regarding these: the *yòuyán* is the centipede (*wúgōng*). Those with red necks are called centipedes; those whose necks are not red are named *yòuyán*.
The hundred-legged creature is also called the *mǎxián* and the *shāngjù*. This refers to what the *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"The *shāngjù* gallops across the river. It also states: "The hundred-legged insect dies without becoming rigid, because those supporting it are many."
There are those who assist the tyrant Jie in his cruelty just like this. The *shougong* (lizard) is the same as the *xili* (chameleon);

it is also called the *yanting*. If fed with vermilion, its body becomes entirely red. If one pounds it ten thousand times and applies it to a woman’s body, it will not fade for the rest of her life, appearing like a red mole.
It falls away only when she marries; in common parlance, it is called the *xietao*. It is adept at climbing fences and walls. When people climb...
There are those who act in such a manner. The *yòu-shǔ* (weasel) is swift at catching mice; it is commonly called the yellow weasel (*huáng shǔ láng*) and is also known as the *shùng*.
As the *Zhuāngzǐ* says: "It lowers its body and crouches to wait for its prey; leaping and bounding from east to west, it does not avoid heights or depths.
There are those among men who leap and bound about, showing no fear, just like this creature. The *lí* (wildcat) is skilled at divination; it walks...
Thus, by pausing to deliberate and measure, one’s shots will surely be successful.

There are those among men who, in a hundred attempts, hit the mark every time—just as the *xiǔshǔ* (the mole-rat), the smallest of all rats, was described by Zhuangzi as being "carried on carts and horses. It is also called the "sweet-mouthed rat" (*gānkǒu shǔ*).
Although it inflicts injury upon people, they do not perceive the pain; likewise, when people harm others in secret, the victims remain unaware.
There are those who are like this. Regarding the two phrases concerning various evils: it means that these various insects run to and fro across the world without any restraint.
In places foul with excrement and urine, where impurities overflow, dung beetles (*śalabha*), crickets (*śalabha*), and other such insects gather upon them; as do foxes, wolves, and jackals.
They chew and trample upon it; they gnaw and bite at corpses until the bones and flesh are scattered in disarray. Consequently, swarms of dogs come vying with one another to seize and devour them.
Emaciated by hunger, they were terrified and panicked, searching for food everywhere. They fought and quarreled, snarling and barking; their dwelling was filled with terror.
Such are their transformative states.
The dung beetle is also called the *kěqiāng*. The *Chōngbō zhuàn* (Account of the Rushing Waves) says: "The dung beetle has no nose, yet it perceives fragrance;
it frequents the depths of foul latrines, rolling balls of dung with its wheels. One pushes from the front while the other pulls from behind, like a pair of servants."
It turns its wheel; thus it is said that the wisdom of the dung beetle lies in its rolling of balls.
These four lines describe worldly people who are greedily attached to the realm of desire and indulge in it without relinquishing it, perceiving filth as fragrant, pure, and exquisite.
Viewed through the eye of the Dharma, how is this any different from dung beetles gathering upon stinking soil? Human indulgence in desire is just like this.

As for this person: when [the Master] was able to break through [his delusions] with a single word—asking him to carry a leather bag filled with excrement—even if celestial maidens were before him, they could not move him.
As for the fox and the wolf: the fox is a beast of seductive charm; it worships the Big Dipper and possesses spiritual power, being skilled in transformations.
As a creature, it is licentious and seductive; human beings who are seductive are like this. The wolf is like a dog.
The dog—blue-colored—is among the most violent of creatures; human violence can be just like this. "Ācāmati" (ā-cam) means to chew its flesh;
"daṃśati" (damś) means to chew its bones as well. To chew roughly is called *tṛ* (to masticate); to chew finely is called *caṣ* (to gnaw).

To tread lightly is called *kram* (to step upon); to tread heavily is called *krakṣ* (to trample). All of these describe the manner of seizing [the prey] and biting it with the mouth. These four lines depict the world.

When people are addicted to worldly flavors—treating them like rare fish, pickled meats, or choice cuts of meat from a precious banquet—the Dharma-eye views this as no different from foxes, wolves, and jackals gnawing on a corpse. From there below, packs of dogs scramble for the remains.
That which has been left in disarray by the foxes, wolves, and jackals is further seized by packs of dogs, who gather it up in heaps.
They eat them all at once in one place; yet because they are so emaciated by hunger, it does not fill their bellies.
Thus, they wander in terror from place to place seeking food—what is called begging for the remains of what is insufficient—and looking back, they move on to other places.
"Fighting, grappling, and pulling" describes the manner of struggling and seizing with force. "Gaping, snarling, and barking" describes the manner of opening the mouth wide and making sounds.
These six lines describe how there are those who are greedily attached to their pursuits and do not know contentment.
The phrase "in that dwelling" refers collectively to all the terrifying events and transformative states within the triple world.
Everywhere there were *chī* (idiots), *mèi* (sprites), *wǎngliǎng* (goblins), *yakṣas*, and malevolent ghosts who devoured human flesh;

as well as various venomous insects and evil birds and beasts that gave birth by laying eggs or through viviparity, each guarding its own offspring, when the *yakṣas* vied with one another to come and snatch them away to eat.
Once they have eaten their fill, their evil intentions flare up even more intensely; the sounds of fighting and quarreling are most terrifying.
The kumbhāṇḍa demons crouch upon earthen mounds, sometimes rising one or two feet off the ground, wandering back and forth and sporting wantonly in their unrestrained revelry.
He seizes the dog by its two hind legs and throws it down until it loses its voice; he places his foot upon its neck and takes pleasure in terrifying the dog.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose bodies are tall and large, naked, black, and emaciated, who constantly dwell therein, emitting great evil sounds and crying out for food.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts whose throats are like needles. There are also various ghosts with heads like those of oxen; some eat human flesh, while others devour dogs.
Their hair is disheveled and matted; they are cruel and violent, driven by hunger and thirst, crying out as they run about.
Yakṣas, hungry ghosts, and various evil birds and beasts, driven by the urgency of hunger, will peer through windows and lattices from all four directions.
Such perils as these are immeasurable and terrifying.
The following passage describes those whose faces are human but whose hearts are demonic; they are categorized under the "Gate of Ghosts" (*kṣetrapāla*).
Previously, animals were used to portray those who are dull-witted and ignorant; here, evil spirits are employed to depict the crafty and deceitful.
This exhaustively portrays the most terrifying aspects of the world, intending to cause people to feel alarm and to develop revulsion for worldly existence. *Chime* (goblins).
The "zhě" (possessing) refers to ghosts that bewitch people; there are those who deceive others and obscure themselves like such beings.
The "wǎngliǎng" (wandering spirits) refers to ghosts that seem to exist yet are not truly there; there are those who fabricate things out of thin air and ride upon emptiness like such beings.
The "yèchā" (yakṣa)—translated here as "swift-moving ghost"—refers to those with clever guile and transformative powers like such beings. It is said that such beings exist everywhere.

Those who employ ruses and deception, relying on demonic schemes to commit atrocities—plotting against others' family fortunes and gnawing at their flesh and sinews without ever knowing satisfaction—are they any different from the malevolent ghosts of this world? [End of section on] Venomous Insects.
It is like a bird that nourishes its offspring with fat, yet has them snatched away by others;
or one that hatches, incubates, and gives birth—protecting its young with its claws is "incubation" (*fu*), and nourishing them with milk is "lactation" (*ru*).

There are certain wicked people who only cherish and protect their own household, disregarding that others also have households; they hide and guard their own children, disregarding that others also have children.

There are those who deceive orphaned children and widows to strip away their descendants and seize their family estates, intending to pass them on to their own future generations with plans lasting for a thousand or ten thousand years.

Yet, when they eventually encounter a powerful yakṣa, that yakṣa seizes both their descendants and their estates, swallowing them all in a single gulp. As for those people whom [the original owners] previously seized—
Now, it has been swallowed up by humans once again. This is what is meant by "what comes forth from you shall return to you.
Since this yakṣa has already fulfilled his ambition, his greed will only grow more intense; he will surely seek to annex the whole world and swallow it all.
Only then would it be satisfying. Thus, there was nowhere it did not fly. The sound of its fighting and quarreling was so exceedingly terrifying as to be like this.
*Kumbhāṇḍa* means "jar-shaped ghost" (*ghaṭākṛti-piśāca*). To sit with the legs drawn up is called "squatting" (*kuṭṭana*); to sit with the legs outstretched is called "crouching" (*niṣaṇṇa*).
A "mound of earth" (*pāṃśu-stūpa*) refers to a raised embankment. There are times when it leaves the ground by one or two feet; this means its position is high.
Furthermore, he was of high station. Occupying such a lofty position, his authority and power were all the more formidable.
As he traveled back and forth, wherever he turned, there was nothing that did not yield to his capricious whims. He encountered a man who would not pluck out even a single hair from his own body;
yet the official confronted him with blades and axes and subjected him to the lash and torture, leaving the man no recourse for action and no words for protest. Having bound him—
He tramples upon their necks, causing others to feel terror while he himself derives pleasure; such is the nature of those who are so fearsome.
Furthermore, there are various *preta*s—namely, hungry ghosts—who, though large in stature, are truly loathsome in appearance.
Having no clothing to adorn their bodies and no coarse food to fill their bellies, they do nothing but cry out along the streets in search of sustenance.
They eat nothing but food. Their appearance of cold and wretchedness is such as this.
As for those whose throats are like needles—those whose hearts desire to swallow but whose throats cannot swallow—it is the state of a weary, sickly man.
Those whose heads are like ox-heads are ghosts who are also beasts. Since they are both ghosts and beasts, humans and beasts devour them together. Although these are remnants...

These beings harm others; their forms are fierce and their minds are treacherous. All this arises from being oppressed by hunger and thirst, which causes them to cry out and run about without ceasing for even a moment.

When they look toward the windows and skylights in all four directions out of urgent hunger, it means that at such a time—when they are pressed by the fire of empty hunger—they immediately turn their thoughts to seeking an escape route.
However, because the surrounding barriers are winding and obstructive, although they wish to...
Though they emerge, they cannot truly emerge; they do nothing but peer through the windows and lattices. These two phrases conclude what was previously called "sudden decay," which is as follows:
the sentient beings of the desire realm all engage in strife and contention for the sake of wealth and food.
Therefore, much has been described. If strife and contention are eliminated, one immediately attains the Samādhi of Non-contention.
This dilapidated old house belongs to a single person; that person has recently gone out, and not long after, within the house...
Suddenly a fire broke out, its flames blazing simultaneously on all four sides. Beams, rafters, and pillars burst apart with a thunderous crack;
they shattered and fell, and the walls collapsed. Various spirits and deities raised their voices in loud cries, while eagles, vultures, and other birds [flew about].
The kumbhāṇḍas and others were filled with panic and terror, unable to escape on their own.

Malevolent beasts and venomous insects hid in their burrows and holes, while the piśāca spirits also dwelt therein; due to their meager merit, they were oppressed by the fire and began to slaughter one another.
Those who drink blood and eat flesh, such as jackals and their ilk, have all already perished; various great and ferocious beasts compete to devour them.
Foul-smelling smoke billows and swirls, filling the four directions. Centipedes, millipedes, venomous snakes, and their like are scorched by the fire.
They struggle to rush out of their burrows, only for the kumbhāṇḍa spirits to seize and devour them. Furthermore, various hungry ghosts have flames blazing upon their heads;
tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they run about in frantic distress, obstructed on all sides. Such is that dwelling—extremely terrifying, filled with poisonous harm and fires.
The various difficulties are not of one kind.

"That person is inferior" means: for example, while the Tathāgata is in the world teaching and transforming sentient beings, causing them to subdue their afflictions (*kleśa*), the Tathāgata may depart for another region and be temporarily absent;
at that time, the fire of the sentient beings' afflictions breaks out. "On all four sides" is a metaphor.
Within the three realms, at the same time and in the same place, the fires of destruction break out simultaneously;
the sound of their bursting and crashing pierces the heavens and shakes the earth, such that all rafters, beams, purlins, and pillars are reduced to ashes, and all walls become mere sand and gravel.
Even those who habitually rely on reputation and exploit their influence to deceive themselves and others—whose maneuvers are like ghosts and whose plots are like gods—[shall likewise be consumed].
When the fire breaks out, there is nothing that can be done; one can do no more than cry out loudly, wallowing in self-pity and regret.
These beings are as fierce and predatory as vultures and eagles, as terrifying as *kumbhāṇḍas*, and they constantly indulge in wanton and frivolous play.
Fearing neither the divine powers nor the consequences of harming others and destroying things, when this moment arrives, one becomes utterly distraught and terrified;
wishing to escape, yet unable to do so, one bites one's own navel, but it is already too late. The "ferocious beast" below is a metaphor for mutual destruction among those of the same kind.
Those who are most foolish are like ferocious beasts and venomous snakes; those who are most deluded are like piśāca demons. This is their constant state.
At the crossroads, they gallop and scurry about, indulging in wanton play. Yet when this moment arrives, they all hide away in holes and crevices, wishing to escape this calamity;
they do not realize that their evil deeds have reached their full measure and the retribution has arrived. It is not within mountains or seas that one can find refuge and escape, much less in a hole.
Even if one were to hide away, it would be of no avail, for throughout one's life, one has never accumulated [merit].
Though one has cultivated virtue and performed meritorious deeds, one cannot escape or avoid it. When the fire comes to press upon the body, there is no way out;
one is utterly bewildered with nowhere to flee. Those who were formerly one’s wife, children, kinsmen, and companions—sharing food and drink together—even at this moment, each disregards the other.
They drink blood and eat flesh, mutually harming one another. Even those as cunning as jackals are all consumed by the flames.

They die before the flames. Furthermore, there is another class of beings who are most foolish and extremely wicked—the various great beasts of prey—who, despite having such precedents, feel no fear at all; they still vie with one another to devour corpses.
Such are those who do not awaken even unto death. Great fires break out simultaneously from all four sides; therefore, it is foul-smelling.
Smoke fills the four directions. The centipedes below represent beings of different species devouring one another.
Within the holes and crevices, they hide and flee, yet even among their own kind they slaughter one another; some attempt to escape, only to be devoured by malevolent spirits.
This clearly demonstrates that the fire of impermanence has broken out within the triple world; once it has arisen, one can neither hide to avoid it nor flee to escape it.

They will willingly await their incineration and surrender themselves to death. How tragic! Furthermore, there is another class of people who do not partake of the flavor of the Dharma in their ordinary lives;

yet when the fire reaches their heads and their entire bodies are tormented by heat, they are just like crabs falling into boiling water—手足 (hands and feet) flailing in confusion, doing nothing but wandering about in panic and distress. These four lines regarding the house summarize the poisonous beasts.
The fire disaster; all manner of terrors converge within a single gate.
This parable of the burning house is the World-Honored One’s own account of how, in the past, he used stern and piercing words to transform humans and devas through the Dharma.
Yet, among the humans and devas of the desire realm, many are addicted to the five desires, their minds like those of ghosts or beasts; therefore, he employs this analogy.
The terrifying state of strife and contention serves to awaken them, so that they may give rise to a mind of weary detachment and refrain from craving and attachment.

Although the two upper realms differ from the desire realm in their relative excellence or deficiency, the root of strife has not been severed and the signs of the five decays have not been eliminated;
because their afflictions are not yet exhausted, they remain entirely within the fires of affliction, burning day and night.
Indeed. Question: Is there a scriptural basis for the analogies provided above? Answer: Yes.

For instance, this very sutra uses the great white ox-cart as a metaphor for the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), and the sheep, deer, and ox-carts as metaphors for the three vehicles (*triyāna*). In other passages, the lion is compared to the Buddha;
the dragon-elephant (*nāga-hastin*) to the bodhisattva; and the lame donkey to the two vehicles (*dvayāna*). Since these objects are thus used as metaphors for the noble ones, [the analogy holds].
People should take these things as metaphors for fools. For example, just as the *I Ching* uses dragons and tigers to represent the Yang, it uses fish and pigs to represent the Yin;
and just as the *Shijing* uses the zhouyu to represent the benevolent and kind gentleman, it uses the chis and eagles to represent the treacherous and wicked person.
One asks: "Is it permissible for the ancient sages to have assigned greed, anger, and so forth to each [of these animals] individually? One replies: "It is permissible."
He asked: "Why do you not rely upon them? He replied: "It is simply that such a pairing is extremely well-established.
For instance, if one were to pair crows and magpies with lust, would it mean that crows and magpies are then free from anger and delusion? Therefore, I blend the three poisons together."
Thus one knows that all things which cause [affliction] are nothing other than the three poisons. It was asked:

"Since the Tathāgata’s transformed lands have the five destinies dwelling together in a mixture, then the five hundred men should correspond to the human destiny; the sons should correspond to the heavenly destiny;
the birds and beasts to the animal destiny; and the various ghosts to the ghost destiny. As for the hell destiny, it may lead humans and devas out of the three evil paths."
[Question: Is this so? [Answer: If they were correlated in such a manner, they would all be actual facts rather than metaphors.

Since they are called "metaphors," we know that the Tathāgata borrowed those examples to clarify his meaning. Thus, the five hundred people are used as an analogy for sentient beings in the five destinies.
Furthermore, taking the sons as an analogy for those possessing the faculties and natures of the three vehicles, they are all within the burning house, greedily attached to the five desires.
Thus, dung beetles and various insects are used to depict the state of craving for form; foxes, wolves, and jackals are used to depict the state of craving for flavors;
yakṣas are used to depict the manner of being wealthy yet lacking benevolence; and kumbhāṇḍas are used to depict the state of being noble yet greedy and cruel.

[This is] the state [of affairs]. Because within this realm one undergoes various sufferings due to the five desires and the pursuit of wealth and profit, the World-Honored One has exerted every effort to depict them, so as to cause people to be vigilant and not allow greed and attachment to arise, but rather to engender weariness [with the world].
How is one who craves form any different from a dung beetle gathering filth? How is one who craves flavors any different from a fox or wolf gnawing on a corpse? Wealth—
Those who lack benevolence are no different from yakṣas vying to seize [their prey]. Those who are noble yet greedy and cruel are no different from kumbhāṇḍas terrified by dogs.

Even though many such conditions are separately described, they do nothing more than entice and draw forth [beings] from the suffering of the three realms, so that they may gradually enter the Buddha Vehicle.

At that time, the owner of the house was standing outside the gate. He heard someone say, "Your children, having previously come into this house while playing, are young and ignorant, and they remain attached to their play with delight. Having heard this, the elder entered the burning house in alarm.
"It is now appropriate to provide relief so that no one suffers from the fire's harm;

this is the Elder’s manifestation of compassion. As for those standing outside the gate, they are a metaphor for the Tathāgata, who, though responding to and transforming others in other directions, [remains present].
Constantly taking this realm as its object, it does not occupy the seat of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā), but remains perpetually outside the gate to listen for news from this direction.
When it hears someone speak, this is a metaphor for the Buddhas of other directions reporting news.
A scriptural passage cited in the text states that the Buddhas of the ten directions said to Śākyamuni: "Your kinsmen who share a karmic connection with you remain within the three realms."
"The roots of goodness are about to perish; you must go and save them," and so forth. Regarding the word "previously" (*xian*) in the phrase "previously indulging in play":

this term has the same meaning as the "previously" in the later passage concerning those who "previously came seeking a son. It means that in the past, during their causal stage, these sons were unwilling to practice with diligence and instead gave themselves over to negligence and play;
consequently, they fell into the three realms. Furthermore, being young and ignorant, they did not know [the truth].
This realm is a place of peril and hardship; it is not a place where one may set foot securely. Yet, on the contrary, they take delight in it and remain attached, refusing to abandon it.
Therefore, upon hearing news of this, the Elder enters the burning house in alarm, desiring to rescue them through skillful means.
Question: Previously it was said that he observes with the Buddha-eye; why is it now said that he hears someone speak? Answer: Because...

Having heard the words of others, he then observes with the Buddha-eye and instructs his children, describing their many afflictions and hardships: the evil spirits and venomous insects, the spreading conflagration, and the succession of manifold sufferings.
The continuity [of suffering] is uninterrupted. There are venomous snakes, vipers, and various *yakṣas* and *kumbhāṇḍa* spirits;

jackals, foxes, dogs, eagles, vultures, owls, hawks, and creatures with a hundred feet—all of whom are tormented by hunger and thirst. This place of extreme dread is a realm of such unbearable suffering.
How much more so with this great fire! The sons, being ignorant, though they have heard their father’s instruction, still delight in it and continue their play without ceasing.
At that time, the elder thought to himself: "The sons are like this; they increase my grief and distress. Now, this house..."
There is not a single thing here to enjoy, yet these sons of mine are so deeply immersed in their play that they do not accept my instructions and will surely be harmed by the fire.
Even as he contemplated this and devised various skillful means, he addressed his sons, saying:

"I have all kinds of precious playthings and exquisite, wonderful chariots—chariots drawn by goats, chariots drawn by deer, and chariots drawn by great oxen—which are now outside the gate. Come out, you children!"
"I have created these chariots for you all, so that you may play and enjoy yourselves as you please.
Upon hearing this description of the various chariots, the sons immediately vied with one another, rushing out and reaching an open space, thereby freed from all suffering and distress.
The elder saw his sons emerge from the burning house and stand at the crossroads, seated upon lion thrones. He spoke to himself in celebration:
"I am now happy! These sons of mine were so difficult to raise; they were foolish, ignorant, and small of mind, yet they entered this perilous dwelling."
There are many venomous insects and fearsome malevolent spirits; fierce flames of great fire arise on all four sides.
Yet these children, greedy for pleasure and fond of play, have been rescued by me and enabled to escape this calamity. Therefore, O people, I am now joyful.
At that time, the sons, knowing their father was sitting at ease, all went to where he was and said to him:
"We pray that you grant us the three kinds of precious chariots as previously promised. Their father replied: "Come forth, my sons; I shall give you the three chariots according to your desires."

Now is precisely the right time; we pray that you will grant us this. The elder is immensely wealthy, possessing many storehouses filled with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, and coral.
With these various precious materials, he has constructed great chariots, adorned and decorated with ornamental railings all around.
Bells hang from all four sides; golden cords are falsely interlaced with nets of pearls spread above it.
Golden flowers and various necklaces dangle everywhere, adorned with a variety of colorful fabrics that surround it on all sides. Soft silks and cotton down serve as its cushions and rugs.
A most exquisite, fine cotton cloth, worth ten billion [gold pieces], brilliant white and pure, was spread over it; there were also great white oxen.
Stout and full of strength, with handsome forms, they drove precious chariots and were attended by numerous retinues who guarded them.
With these exquisite chariots, he bestowed equal gifts upon all his sons; at that time, the sons were filled with joy and leaped for gladness as they mounted these precious chariots.
Wandering through the four quarters, sporting and enjoying themselves with unimpeded freedom—this is a metaphorical explanation of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
It refers to what is called the teaching on matters of fear; that the fire of calamity spreads and extends.

The "calamity-fire" refers to the fire of the kalpa-ending conflagration. It is said that these eight sufferings are like a creeping vine that spreads and continues without end, for the fires of calamity do not cease.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the sons": although the father feels compassion and attempts to entice and exhort them with kind words, the sons have no intention at all to escape;
their ignorance is extreme, as if they had not heard him at all, failing to receive his instructions. This is [the meaning].
"At that time" [and below] extensively praises the cessation and the path. "With precious playthings" refers to exchanging coarse and wretched instruments of suffering for them.
"The sons" [and below] refers to vying with one another to push and shove as they struggle to exit the burning house.
"The elder" [and below] refers to the elder seeing his sons escape the burning house, rejoicing and congratulating himself. "At that time" [and below] refers to the sons requesting the vehicles.
Furthermore, "the elder" and those below refer to the granting of the great chariots. These chariots are constructed from various jewels;
they are not like the high and perilous halls and houses. They are adorned and magnificently decorated; they are not like the dilapidated and long-worn old dwellings.
Their surrounding railings are not like the winding enclosures. The bells suspended on all four sides do not produce the sound of bursting on all four sides.
It is cracked and split. As for the golden cords interlacing one another, it is not as if the beams and rafters were leaning and tilting.
As for the pearl nets spread and suspended above them, it is not as if the thatching were falling down in disorder.

As for the various golden flowers and necklaces hanging down everywhere, it is not as if the eaves and cornices were misaligned or detached. As for the various colored ornaments surrounding it on all sides, it is not...
If the walls and partitions were crumbling, they would not be like a foundation or staircase collapsing;

if soft silk and cotton were used for mats and bedding, it would not be like plaster falling away. If exquisite, fine woolen cloth covered them above, it would not be like mud and earth sloughing off.
There are great white oxen yoked to precious chariots; this is not like pillars with rotten roots that have collapsed.
There are many attendants who guard them; this is not like five hundred people dwelling within [the house].
Because the burning house is used to represent its ugliness, the precious chariots are used to represent their beauty. Regarding the passage beginning with "The sons": it means...

I have obtained a carriage for my use, traveling in the four directions without hindrance wherever I go. This is not like those days of desperate hunger, when I looked furtively toward the windows in all four directions.
I tell you, Śāriputra: I am likewise so; I am the most honored among the multitude of sages, the father of the world, and [the protector] of all sentient beings.
"All these are my children. They are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and lack the heart of wisdom. There is no peace within the three realms;
they are like a burning house, filled with manifold sufferings and truly terrifying. There are constant afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, death, and sorrow—such fires as these."
Blazing without ceasing—such is the burning house of the triple world from which the Tathāgata has already departed. He dwells in tranquil seclusion, peacefully settled in the forests and wilds.
Now, this triple world is all mine; the sentient beings within it are all my children. And yet, in this place...

They face many hardships and calamities; I alone am able to provide protection and refuge. Although I instruct and admonish them, they do not believe or accept my words because their attachment to the defilements of desire is so deep.
By these skillful means, I preach the Three Vehicles to cause all sentient beings to [attain liberation].
Knowing the suffering of the three realms, he reveals and expounds upon the supramundane path.

These sons of mine—whether their minds are resolved, whether they are endowed with the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, whether they have attained the stage of a pratyekabuddha, or are non-retrogressive bodhisattvas—you, Śāriputra, [should know them all].
"For the sake of sentient beings, I have used this parable to speak of the Single Buddha Vehicle.
If you all can believe and accept these words, you shall all attain the path to Buddhahood. This vehicle is subtle and wondrous, the foremost in purity throughout all worlds."
It is unsurpassed, approved by the Buddha, and worthy of praise, offerings, and prostrations by all sentient beings.
Having attained such a vehicle, one possesses immeasurable billions of powers, liberations, meditative concentrations, wisdoms, and other dharmas of a Buddha.

He causes his sons to constantly enjoy their play day and night for kalpas, so that together with the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, they may ride upon this precious vehicle straight to the site of enlightenment.
For this reason, if one searches thoroughly throughout the ten directions, no other vehicle exists.

Setting aside the Buddha’s skillful means, this is the corresponding analogy: the elder corresponds to the father; all sentient beings correspond to the sons; the burning house corresponds to the three realms; and birth, old age, sickness, and death correspond to the fire. As for the various perils, they do not correspond to each individual section [of the house].
The father corresponds to the elder; all sentient beings correspond to the sons; the three realms correspond to the burning house; and birth, old age, sickness, and death correspond to the fire.
Furthermore, those who are deeply attached to worldly pleasures refer to sentient beings within the three realms who have not yet exhausted their craving and greed,
who are addicted to the pleasures of the five desires of the mundane world, and who lack even a hair’s breadth of the wisdom-mind that transcends the world.
How could they know that the three realms are unstable, like a house on fire, and that they are filled with manifold sufferings and hardships that are utterly terrifying?
Ah! Once there was a man who had committed an offense against the king. Terrified, the man fled, and the king ordered a drunken elephant to pursue him.
In his desperate fear, the man threw himself into a deep well. Halfway down the well, he found a piece of withered grass and grasped it with his hand.
Below him, an evil dragon spat venom toward him; on his sides, five poisonous snakes likewise sought to harm him.
Two mice gnawed at the grass, which was on the verge of being severed. A great elephant stood above him, also intending to seize him. That man was thus in a state of peril and suffering.
