It is a place of extreme terror. Above is a tree, from which drops of honey occasionally fall into its mouth;

because of the attachment to that taste, it forgets its fear. The mountain well represents birth and death (*saṃsāra*). The intoxicated elephant represents impermanence (*anityatā*). The venomous dragon represents the evil realms (*durgati*).
The five poisonous snakes represent the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The decaying grass represents the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). The two rats, black and white, represent day and night.

"Month" refers to the honey-drops of the five sensual pleasures (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*). "Obtaining the honey-drops while forgetting one's fear" is a metaphor for sentient beings obtaining the honey-drops of the five sensual pleasures and thus not fearing the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). "The Tathāgata," and so forth, corresponds to the elder’s arousal of compassion.
Because the Tathāgata is outside the triple world (*traidhātuka*), he perceives that which is within the triple world as fire. If he were within the triple world...

Thus, they were greedily attached to their play and did not see the fire. "Now, this 'below'" [refers to the passage] where it is seen that although the Tathāgata is outside the triple world, he does not truly forget the sentient beings within the triple world.
"Although again, 'below'" [refers to the passage] which speaks in combination of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
That is to say, he instructs and admonishes his sons, describing various calamities and hardships; yet, although they hear what their father says, they still remain joyfully attached. Regarding this:

The two subsequent lines refer to the root of the afflictions of sentient beings within the three realms; therefore, they are specifically singled out. "By means of this" and following are intended to praise the Path and Cessation.
The supramundane path refers to the auxiliary dharmas of the path. "These various" and following are intended to describe the emergence from the burning house.
The "three knowledges" (*vidyā*) are the divine eye, knowledge of others' minds, and recollection of past lives. The "six supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) include the addition of the divine ear.
These are the supernormal powers and the exhaustion of outflows. You should descend from your carriage; it is fitting that you be granted a great chariot as an equal gift.
I have previously explained to you that all things I do are always for a single purpose. Now, once again, I shall employ this parable to illustrate the Buddha Vehicle.
One may attain faith and understanding merely through these parables and may thus be called a person of wisdom; do not harbor further doubt.
From the phrase "this vehicle" onwards, there is a broad praise of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Regarding the phrase "and other Buddha-dharmas," it means that within this vehicle, the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas are all fully present, just as the great white ox-cart carries everything without exception. [The text continues: "I have attained..."
Such is this vehicle that carries all sentient beings, sporting day and night.
Thus, for forty years prior, I have never failed to carry you all by means of the Buddha-vehicle. Now, I shall take this Great Vehicle and transfer it to you.
"You all shall mount this precious vehicle and proceed directly to the Tathāgata’s place of enlightenment.
For this reason, if one seeks with truth throughout the ten directions, there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle; there is no other vehicle.
As for the existence of other vehicles, these are all due to the power of the skillful means of the Buddhas, who differentiate and teach the three vehicles based upon the Single Buddha Vehicle."
I say to Śāriputra: "All of you are my children, and I am your father. For countless eons, you have been scorched by manifold sufferings;
I have rescued and delivered you all, causing you to emerge from the triple world. Although I previously spoke of your parinirvāṇa,"
It merely brings an end to birth and death, yet in reality, it does not cease. What must now be accomplished is solely the wisdom of the Buddhas.

If there are bodhisattvas among this assembly who can listen with a single-minded focus to the true Dharma of all Buddhas—though the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ skillful means—then [they shall attain it].
The sentient beings to be transformed are all bodhisattvas. For those of small wisdom who are deeply attached to craving and desire, the Truth of Suffering is taught for their sake;
these beings rejoice, attaining what they have never experienced before. The Buddha’s teaching of the Truth of Suffering is true and without deviation.

If there are sentient beings who do not know the root of suffering, who are deeply attached to the causes of suffering, and unable to relinquish them even for a moment—for their sake, I employ skillful means to teach the Way:
"The cause of all sufferings has greed as its root. If greed is extinguished, there will be nothing upon which they can rely."
The complete extinction of all suffering is called the Third Truth, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). For the sake of this Truth of Cessation, one practices the Path;

being freed from the bonds of all suffering is called attaining liberation (*vimukti*). From what does such a person attain liberation? It is simply by departing from the false and illusory that it is called liberation.
In truth, they have not yet attained all liberations. The Buddha says that such persons have not truly entered parinirvāṇa, because these people have not yet attained the unsurpassed Way.
It is not my intention to cause them to reach parinirvāṇa; for I am the Dharma King, sovereign over the Dharma.
I appear in the world for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings.
From this point forward, I shall provide detailed and earnest exhortations to awaken faith in you. I say:
"You are all my own children born of me; I am your father. Therefore, I do not limit my salvation and deliverance of you to but a single lifetime or a single kalpa.

For many kalpas you have been within the triple world, scorched by manifold sufferings. I, too, for many kalpas within the triple world have rescued and delivered you, causing you to emerge from all suffering.
Thus, it is not only during the forty years prior that I have preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles for you;
throughout all these successive kalpas, I have never failed to preach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles for your sake.
Therefore, when forty years ago I praised you as having already attained *nirvāṇa*, it was only because you had emerged from the suffering and affliction of birth and death within the three realms;
thus I said you had attained *nirvāṇa*. In reality, you had not yet attained the ultimate quiescence of the Tathāgata.
Now that you have awakened to the wisdom of all Buddhas, you may laugh, smile, or be angry.
Whether scolding, clearing one's throat, or spitting, whatever actions are performed are none of them without the employment of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Nevertheless, although this is so, fundamentally it has never differed from the past. One must know that the teachings given earlier and later have never been two;
they are merely changes of names and forms according to the individuals. If there were among the assembly those with the capacity of a bodhisattva who did not harbor [such views...]
Those of other vehicles desire with all their heart to hear the true Dharma of the Buddhas, yet the Buddhas instead designate this very Dharma as "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Although they employ expedient means to guide sentient beings, those beings who are thus transformed all become Bodhisattvas. Why is this?
It is because they delight in the true Dharma of the Buddhas. If, however, a person possesses little wisdom and is deeply attached to craving and desire, [the Buddhas] leave them...
Attached to the three realms, for such people as these, this Dharma is further called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Yet how could they know that the Truth of Suffering is fundamentally no different from the true Dharma of all Buddhas?

If there are sentient beings who, though weary of the fruit of suffering, do not know the cause of that fruit of suffering; who are deeply attached to the causes of suffering, yet do not know the root of those causes of suffering.
For these people, this dharma is further called the root of greed. If there is one who has already extinguished greed, then all various sufferings have no basis for remaining.
The World-Honored One further calls this dharma the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
For those who, desiring to realize this Truth of Cessation, cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), [he further...]
This Dharma is called the Truth of the Path. By practicing this path, one realizes cessation and distances oneself from the causes of all suffering within the three realms.
Furthermore, such a person is called an Arhat who has attained liberation. Thus, although there are many names, they are none other than this single Dharma;
it is merely changing the name of the soup, while the medicine itself remains unchanged. Therefore, regarding suffering—

Although the truths of origination, cessation, and the path differ from one another, there has never been a case where the truths themselves are not identical. This person raises an objection based on a lower level of understanding, asking:
"Since this person has not yet realized the Buddha’s wisdom of equality, why is he called one who has attained liberation? The answer is as follows:

Although they have not yet realized the equal wisdom of a Buddha, they nonetheless exhaust the six consciousnesses, sever the three poisons, eliminate the obstacle of self, and realize the emptiness of sentient beings.
They transcend the three realms and surpass the four modes of birth, roaming at ease in the realm of non-action and dwelling freely in the place of profound stillness.
Unrestrained and unbound, with seeing extinguished and hearing cut off, they may also be said to have attained liberation.
Question: If that is so, for what reason did the Tathāgata further state that śrāvakas do not attain parinirvāṇa? Answer:

Because they have never been empty of the maturation of karma (*vipāka*), because their dharma-obstructions are exhausted, because they have realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and because they have attained the four types of knowledge (*jñāna*). That is to say, when one examines its name, it is indeed so.
Upon investigating its reality, it is not so. Therefore, I say that such a person has not yet truly attained parinirvāṇa.
Only when one attains supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena and realizes the Unsurpassed Way does one first receive the name of the Tathāgata’s true parinirvāṇa.
As a Dharma King who has attained mastery over the Dharma, I am able to give this single Dharma various names, or speak of it as...

"Attaining liberation, not attaining liberation; or speaking of attaining nirvana, not attaining nirvana, and so forth—all these are nothing other than the desire to cause those who have not yet found peace to find peace, and to cause those who have not yet attained liberation to attain liberation.
This is why all Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of this one great causal event."
"Śāriputra, I have proclaimed this Dharma-seal for the sake of benefiting the world. Wherever you travel, do not proclaim it recklessly.
If there are those who hear it, rejoice in it, and receive it upon their heads with reverence, you should know that such persons are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive)."

If there are those who believe in and accept this Dharma of the sutra, such persons have already seen past Buddhas, paid them respectful homage and made offerings to them, and have also heard this Dharma.
If anyone is able to believe what you have spoken, they shall be as if seeing me and also seeing you.
As well as the community of bhikṣus and all the bodhisattvas—this Lotus Sūtra is taught for those of profound wisdom;
those of shallow understanding, upon hearing it, will be confused and fail to comprehend it. All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are beyond the reach of its power within this sūtra.
"Śāriputra, you are still able to enter this sutra through faith; how much more so the other śrāvakas?
Those other śrāvakas follow this sutra because they trust the Buddha’s words; it is not within the scope of their own wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra, they are characterized by pride and indolence."

Do not preach this sutra to those who harbor views of a self. To ordinary people of shallow understanding who are deeply attached to the five desires, do not preach it either, for they will hear it and fail to comprehend it.
If there are those who do not believe and instead slander this sutra, they sever all seeds of the Buddha in the world.
Or again, one may frown and harbor doubts. You should now listen as I describe the retribution for such a person's sin.
Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, there are those who slander such sutras as these four, seeing others who read, recite, copy, or uphold them.
Contemptuous, hateful, and envious, they harbor resentment. Listen now further to the retribution for this person's offense:
at the end of their life, they enter the Avīci Hell and remain there for a full kalpa; when that kalpa ends, they are reborn again, continuing in this manner through countless kalpas.
Emerging from the hells, they shall fall among the animals—such as dogs or jackals—whose forms are emaciated and wretched, dark-complexioned, and afflicted with leprosy and scabs.
They are harassed by others and further despised and loathed by people. Constantly oppressed by hunger and thirst, their flesh and bones wither away;

while alive they suffer bitter agony, and at death they are pelted with tiles and stones. Because they have severed the lineage of the Buddha, they undergo this retribution of sin. If they become camels, they are burdened with loads.
Or they may be born among donkeys, their bodies constantly burdened with heavy loads and subjected to the lash of whips and clubs; they think only of water and grass, knowing nothing else.
Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses as these. Some become jackals that enter villages, their bodies covered in scabs and sores.
Furthermore, he was missing one eye; he was beaten and pelted by various children, undergoing all manner of painful suffering, and at times even met his death.
Having died there, they further receive the body of a python; its form is vast and long, measuring five hundred yojanas.
It is deaf and dull-witted, lacking feet, crawling along on its belly. It is bitten and eaten by various small insects, suffering day and night without any respite.

Because they slander this sutra, they incur such transgressions as these. Even if they should obtain human form, their faculties will be dull and obscured; they will be short, stunted, hunchbacked, or crippled.

Blind, deaf, and hunchbacked; whatever they say, people do not believe or accept. Their breath is constantly foul. Possessed by malevolent spirits (*chī-mèi*), they are poor and lowly, driven about by others.
Suffering from many ailments, emaciated and wasted, they have no one to rely upon. Though they seek to draw close to others, [they are rejected].

People pay no heed to him. If he does acquire something, he soon forgets and loses it again. If he practices medicine, treating illnesses according to prescriptions, he instead increases others' ailments or even causes death.
If he himself falls ill, there is no one to provide relief; even if he takes excellent medicine, [it is of no avail].
Furthermore, it will grow even more severe. If others commit acts of rebellion, plunder, robbery, or theft, such persons will suffer calamities as a result of these sins.
Such sinners shall never behold the Buddha, the King of all Sages, who teaches the Dharma to transform and guide beings. Such sinners—
They will constantly be born in difficult circumstances—mad, deaf, and mentally deranged—never hearing the Dharma for as many incalculable eons as there are sands in the Ganges.
They will be born deaf and mute from birth, with their faculties incomplete, and they will dwell in the hells as if wandering through pleasure gardens, remaining in other evil realms.
Like their own dwellings, camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs shall be their haunts. Because they slander this sutra, they incur such offenses;
even if they should obtain human form, they will be deaf, blind, mute, and dumb, adorned with poverty and all manner of misfortunes, suffering from dropsy and wasting diseases.
With scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, and abscesses—such diseases as these—as their clothing; with bodies that are perpetually foul-smelling, filthy, and impure;
deeply attached to the view of self; increasing their anger; and with lust so rampant they do not distinguish between humans and beasts—this is because they slander this sutra.
Such is the nature of their transgression. I tell you, Śāriputra, that if one were to describe the offenses of those who slander this sutra, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
For these reasons, I say to you: do not preach this sutra among those who lack wisdom.
The following section concerns the entrustment for the propagation [of the teaching]. Therefore, he calls him by name once more and entrusts him, saying:
"This Dharma-seal of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of mine was spoken for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings in the world;
you must widely propagate this sutra. However, at the time of its transmission, you must be vigilant and not proclaim it recklessly. If it is not propagated..."
Having found such a person, one instead incurs slander and falls into a great pit; this is yet another matter that remains unresolved within their mind.

Therefore, he again imparts to them the method of teaching the Dharma according to individual capacity. "If there is one who... refers to those with the faculty of faith who are capable of receiving the teaching.
If they hear it but once, they immediately experience great joy throughout their entire bodies, receiving and upholding it upon the crown of their heads. This...
Those of such superior and most excellent faculties who attain the stage of non-retrogression in this very life should certainly be granted [this teaching].
Alternatively, those who upon hearing it do not fail to experience great joy pervading their entire bodies; or those who believe it upon first hearing;
or those who accept it upon first believing and never again fall back—such persons also possess sharp faculties and have, in the past, been before the Buddhas.
To those who have long planted the roots of virtue, this [teaching] should also be bestowed.

Furthermore, it is not easy for one who cannot believe or accept it to yet trust what you say without giving rise to slander; such a person has personally witnessed the assembly on Vulture Peak and should also be granted this teaching.
Therefore, on this day, I preach this sutra solely for those of great capacity, and not for others.

Those of shallow understanding: if those of shallow understanding hear this, they will not only fail to understand but will instead become confused; they will not only fail to believe but will instead fall into delusion.
This is why all those of the two vehicles, though they exhaust their thoughts and measure it with their intellects, are unable to know it.
Even among the assembly of śrāvakas, you are called foremost in wisdom, yet you still entered this sutra through faith alone; how much more so for others?

How could one enter [the Way] without hearing and believing? As for the other śrāvakas, they merely accept the Buddha’s words and follow this sutra, thinking, "This is the domain of what the Buddha knows and sees;
it has nothing to do with me. They do not believe that they themselves also possess this portion [of the Dharma], and thus fail to directly take responsibility for it.
Therefore, it should be known that these types of people are beyond the reach of their own power. It is not so.
Those who are fit to receive [the teaching] are as follows; those who are arrogant are conceited and haughty, refusing to humble their minds.

Those who are indolent have hearts addicted to ease and do not apply themselves with diligent effort. Those who hold to the view of self are attached to their own opinions, and thus the ultimate words do not enter them.

These types all possess incurable maladies and are unfit to receive [the teaching]. As for "ordinary persons" (pṛthagjana), this refers to those who have not yet entered the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding such a person: the five desires are wealth, beauty, fame, food, and sleep. To one who pursues foul odors, if one were to offer agallochum and sandalwood, it would not be what they desire;

therefore, it is unfit to give. As for those of inferior capacity, the reason I do not bestow [this teaching] upon them is that I fear they might not believe it and instead give rise to slander, thereby falling into the three miserable realms. It is not out of stinginess that I do not speak of it. Thus says the Buddha.
"Seed" means that this sutra is the mother of all Buddhas, for all Buddhas flow forth from this sutra.
"Frowning" means knitting the brows and contracting the forehead. "Harboring doubt and suspicion" means being half-believing and half-disbelieving.
"Slandering" means uttering irrational words to defame this sutra. "Contemptuously despising and hating with jealousy."
To treat someone with disregard is called "lightness. To look down upon them is called "contempt. To feel weary of and loathe them is called "hatred. To harbor envy and jealousy is called "malice.
To have a heart full of resentment is called "binding enmity. Such a person, being base, will receive the retribution of disbelief and slander.
*Avīci*—which means "without interval"—is the place where those who commit the sin of slandering the Dharma all enter, alongside those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).
The same applies here. This is the retribution for the hell realm. From beneath the earth, one receives the retribution of the animal realm.
The dog clings with stinginess to things; the jackal is delusively attached to things. Because of this clinging with stinginess and delusive attachment, they fall into these categories.

They are emaciated and gaunt because they lack the flavor of the Dharma to nourish their spirits; they are mottled and black because they lack pure and white brahmacarya; they lack majestic splendor and adornment.
Scabies and leprosy refer to being touched, harassed, and mocked. In the past one touched and harassed others; now one is again touched and harassed by others.

In the past one treated others with malice and contempt; now one is likewise treated with malice and contempt by others. To be distressed by hunger and thirst means not consuming the food of *dharmaprīti* (joy in the Dharma) and not drinking the nectar of *amṛta*.
All of these are retributions for severing the lineage of the Buddha. Question: Carrying heavy burdens...
"This is the repayment of past debts. Why do you slander this sutra? You shall likewise receive this retribution. He replied, "This sutra is the great white ox-cart;
it can carry and transport all the wealth of meritorious dharmas to bestow them upon the fourfold assembly. Yet you, on the contrary, have given rise to slander and defamation."
This is the ultimate among those who owe a debt; is it not fitting that they receive this retribution?

As for those who merely think of water and grass and know nothing else, it is because they have severed all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*); thus, apart from chewing grass and drinking water, they know nothing at all.
Those who become jackals (*śṛgāla*) do not delight in the roar of the lion, for they take pleasure in false teachings; furthermore, they lack even a single...
"Blind" means that he destroyed the Tathāgata’s true eye. "Beating and throwing [the child]" means that he treated him with contempt, hatred, and jealousy.
"Reborn as a python" is because of his harbored resentment. "His form being large and long" is because he slandered the Great Sūtra.
"Deaf, idiotic, and footless"—"idiotic" refers to delusion; it means he was attached to folly and lacked faith, and thus failed to cultivate merit and wisdom. "Wan... [The text here is incomplete].

As for "rolling about on one's belly," it is because of being sycophantic, crooked, and insincere. As for "being bitten and eaten by small insects," it is because they slandered the sutras and reviled the Buddha;
everyone gnashed their teeth in resentment, wishing to bury them in their skins and eat their flesh. Thus they receive the retribution of an animal.
"Darkness" means lack of clarity. "Dullness" means lack of sharpness. "Stunted" means short and small. "Ugly" means unsightly.
"Lame and crippled" refers to those whose feet cannot walk. "Hunchbacked" refers to those with curved backs. In sum, their appearance does not strike others as remarkable.
When they have something to say, people do not believe or accept it; their speech does not satisfy the assembly. Their breath is constantly foul; they lack—*text missing*.
It is the fragrance of the blue lotus. Those possessed by *chi-mei* (goblins) are not protected by devas or *nāgas*.
One who possesses myriad virtues and commands the multitudes is a Dharma King; yet, because one treats such a person with contempt, one becomes poor, lowly, and base, driven about by others.
Because one destroys the true body of the Vajra, one suffers from many ailments. Because one hates the unsurpassed *amṛta* (clarified butter), one suffers from consumption.
They are emaciated. Because they do not believe that this sutra is the father and mother of all sentient beings, they have no one to rely upon or take refuge in.
Though they associate closely with others, those people pay them no mind. One might say that this Dharma sleeps and rises together with humans and can be considered a close relative;
yet, they never possess even a single thought of compliance, which is called being ungrateful. Therefore, though they are close...
It attaches to people, yet people do not take it to heart. Those who gain something only to lose it again fail to see the fundamental root because they have not yet awakened the Buddha-wisdom.
As for those whose illnesses are aggravated by treatment: the Buddha is the King of Physicians, capable of curing the fundamental mental illness of all sentient beings.
Because they do not believe in the Buddha-dharma, they follow medical prescriptions to treat their ailments, only to find that their conditions instead worsen.
He fell ill and died. As for those who do not treat their own illness and instead allow it to worsen, this sutra is like the King of Medicine Tree of Excellent Vision (*Sudarśana*):
those who see it attain purity of sight, and those who hear it attain purity of hearing, and so forth. Thus, it uses the medicine of the mind to cure the illnesses of the mind.
Now, if one does not believe in this sutra, there will be no medicine, and it will be difficult to eliminate the afflictions of the mind.
Because of illness, even though one takes medicine, it conversely increases the severity of the ailment. As for those who act with rebellion and opposition:
if they accord with this sutra, then every single thing is the lamp of the luminous wisdom-body, and every head is the practice-gate of Samantabhadra.

If they do not accord with it but instead oppose it, then they will clash with whatever they encounter and struggle daily with their own minds, robbing themselves of their own family treasure. Therefore, there is...
These calamities are visited upon their bodies. They shall never see the Buddha or hear the Dharma;
having been born into the three miserable realms and the eight difficult conditions, they further contract diseases such as madness and deafness, and thus they shall forever neither see nor hear.
Those who are born deaf and mute from birth do so because they did not partake of [the teachings] or offer praise. "Gardens" refers to places of pleasure and recreation; "dwellings" refers to houses.
It is the place where one dwells in peace. "The place of practice" refers to the place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). "Water-swelling" refers to being conceited and self-satisfied.
"Emaciation" refers to not being moistened by the flavor of the Dharma. Because they lack the wealth of the Dharma, they are poor; because they lack the root of virtue, they are ill.
Since poverty and illness follow them wherever they go, it is called "adornment," and it is also called "robes. As for the body being long and foul-smelling, it is because—
Because they have touched the pure and wondrous fragrance of the lotus, those who are deeply attached to the view of self are the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*).
Those who increase their anger are the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*). Those in whom lust is rampant are deficient in the precepts.
From "Tell Śāriputra" onwards, it is concluded that this should not be transmitted to those who are not vessels. "Do not preach this sutra among people without wisdom" means that although this is...
This repeated exhortation also subtly reveals the Tathāgata’s intention to keep [this teaching] secret and unsaid for forty years;
it was also out of fear that those lacking wisdom might hear it and slander it rather than believe it.

If there are those of sharp faculties, whose wisdom is clear and bright, who are widely learned and possess strong memory, and who seek the Buddha-way—for such persons as these, you may indeed preach it.
Or if there are those who have previously seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, who have planted various roots of goodness, and whose profound resolve is firm and steadfast.

To such a person as this, one may preach it. If there is a person who is diligent, constantly cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, and does not begrudge their own body or life, then to them one may preach it.

If there is a person who is respectful, free from divergent thoughts, and has distanced themselves from all the vulgar and foolish, dwelling alone in the mountains and marshes—then to them one may preach it.

To such a person as this, one may preach it. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if you see someone who has abandoned evil associates and draws near to virtuous friends—to such a person as this, one may preach it. If you see a son of the Buddha whose observance of the precepts is pure...
Like a pure, bright pearl, one who seeks the Mahāyāna sūtras—such a person may be taught this.
If a person is free from anger, upright and gentle, always compassionate toward all beings, and reveres the Buddhas—such a person may be taught this.

Furthermore, there may be a son of the Buddha who, amidst the great assembly, with a pure mind, employs various causes and conditions, parables, and expressions to preach the Dharma without hindrance.
To such a person as this, you may speak [this teaching]. If there is a bhikṣu who seeks omniscience, [you may also speak it to him].

One who seeks the Dharma in the four directions, receives it with palms joined at the crown of the head, and takes pleasure solely in upholding Mahāyāna sūtras—even to the point of not accepting a single verse from any other scripture—such a person may be taught this. They are like one who, with a sincere heart, seeks the relics of the Buddha.

One who seeks the sutra in this manner and, having obtained it, receives it upon the crown of their head, no longer sets their mind on seeking other sutras, nor has they ever thought of the texts of external paths—it is for such a person that one may preach. Śāriputra, I speak of these characteristics.

Those who seek the Buddha-way will not reach their end even throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; such persons as these are able to believe and understand. You should preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them.
This statement refers to those of great capacity who are then granted [the teaching]. Those with sharp faculties and clear wisdom are like those who act upon seeing the shadow of a whip;
they are not people of dull faculties and meager intelligence. Those who are widely learned and possess strong memories are those who revere [the Dharma] and delight in study.
This is not for those who are attached to appearances or possessed by pride. One who seeks the Buddha-way must directly take responsibility;
this is not for those of inferior capacity or weak practice. Since these individuals are all vessels for carrying the Way, they may be spoken of:
those who provide offerings to the Buddhas, plant manifold roots of goodness, possess a profound and firm resolve, and never regress—such as Changqing, who broke seven cushions of hemp. Incense...
Those such as Lin, who for forty years have attained a state of unified integration, may be described as vessels for the Mahāyāna.

Those such as the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Snow Mountain Youth, who cultivate loving-kindness with such diligence that they do not spare even their own bodies or lives, may be described as heroic men.
As for those who are respectful and free from dualistic thoughts, they are what is called "Heaven."
Even when honored by dragons, he did not take pleasure in it. He departed from the foolish and common folk to walk alone and stride solitary.
Dwelling among mountains and marshes, he harbored no longing and sought nothing—like Hengchao, Lanzan, and Daowu.

Because his mind was free from distracting conditions and external things could not entice him, it can be said that he abandoned evil and drew near to the good; this is one who can distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox.
Therefore, it may be said that one who maintains pure precepts is like a bright, clean pearl;
such a person upholds the pearl of the Buddha-nature precepts and is fully endowed with the pure and white Brahma-conduct.

Thus, it may be said that one who is free from anger, upright, and gentle, who pities all beings and reveres the Buddhas, dwells in the power of patience, and is fully endowed with both the field of compassion and the field of reverence.

Therefore, it may be said: those who preach the Dharma with a pure mind and without obstruction have attained the wisdom of the Buddha, inherited the family legacy of the Buddha, and propagated the Buddha-way to repay the Buddha’s kindness; thus, it may be said.

As for those who delight in the Mahāyāna yet refuse to accept even a single verse from other scriptures—this is like the case of the Dharma Master Sengchou who would not accept the books of the immortals. This is so.
One who eats only pure nectar and tastes nothing but the *amṛta* can thus be described as follows: "Just as a person [descends...
This metaphor illustrates the single-mindedness with which one seeks the Dharma; it should be like Kang Senghui’s quest for the *śarīra*.

One who does not accept even a single verse from other scriptures and does not contemplate the texts of non-Buddhists is one whose mental path does not branch and whose various views remain unshaken; therefore, they can be so described.
As the ancient masters have said: "It is like being in a land infected by *gū* poison; one must not let even a single drop of water touch it.
Inform the household below that the great root must first be bound before it may be transmitted.
The fourth verse of the *Adhimukty-adhikāra* (The Chapter on Resolute Belief), "The Parable of the Poor Son," says:
"Unaware of the treasures of his own house, He has utterly forgotten the affection between father and son; Therefore, he was given a vessel for removing dung."
He has become a beggar for pity, wearing sores and scabs as his constant raiment; this fragmented body is his retribution.
Yet, in a sudden flash of insight, he directly mounted the Dharma King’s wheel.
Having previously heard the Dharma being preached, he was moved by delusion and gave rise to doubt; now, hearing this parable, he gives rise to faith and understanding. Therefore—
This is titled the "Chapter on Resolute Belief. Both chapters employ the metaphor of father and son. In the preceding chapter, the Great Wealthy Elder is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata;
because his wealth and resources are inexhaustible, it is said that he bestows upon them equally the great white ox-carts.

In this chapter, the young, impoverished children are used as a metaphor for the disciples; because they had no aspiration or seeking, it is said that they suddenly obtained the Tathāgata’s treasure-store.

[Section] One. In the preceding chapter, the Tathāgata’s compassionate heart, which regards [sentient beings] as his own children, was depicted as most urgent; therefore, it is said that he "startled them into entering the burning house.
In this chapter, the foolishness of the disciples and their frequent acts of turning their backs on their father are depicted; therefore, it is said that they "ran away quickly.

In the preceding chapter, the Tathāgata’s act of inducing and leading them out through the gate of the triple world was depicted; therefore, it is said that [the father] is "now outside the gate. This...
This chapter describes how the impoverished son was unwilling to enter the gate of the Tathāgata; thus it says he "stood by the side of the gate.
Father and son each revealed their innermost hearts, recounting the many hardships and twists of the forty years that had passed, reaching the ultimate depth of their respective experiences.
Only today have they finally found a mutual resonance as father and son, and the teacher and disciple have attained harmony with the Way. Question: Regarding the four great elements...
"Son, you are a leader among this assembly and stand at the head of the *saṃgha*. Why did you not first realize and enter [the truth], but instead become agitated, confused, and give rise to doubt?
Śāriputra, how was it that you were the first to attain realization? The answer is: simply look at the accounts of realization in both places, and you will know the essential point.
It was because Śāriputra, while usually staying in mountain forests or beneath trees, had been harboring doubts within himself.

He repented, reproaching and blaming himself for being unwilling to willingly accept the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Upon hearing a single praise of the Buddha’s wisdom, he immediately gave rise to doubt;

upon hearing that an Arhat could become a Buddha, he felt a sense of responsibility at that moment and said, "Today I finally know that I am truly a son of the Buddha and have obtained a share of the Buddha-dharma.
Although the four great disciples were habitually weary and indolent, they did not harbor such doubts.
It was only after being exhorted by the Tathāgata’s urgent words and hearing of Śāriputra’s prediction that they began to harbor doubts.
It was only when Śāriputra requested the Tathāgata on their behalf to provide an analogy that they finally attained faith and understanding. Therefore, it is first stated:
"We ourselves believed we had already attained nirvāṇa; we did not know that we were truly the sons of the Buddha, nor did we further seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Now that we have heard this parable, we truly know ourselves to be śrāvakas; we truly know ourselves to be arhats.
As for those who sleep lightly, they respond at the first call; as for those who sleep soundly, they must be shaken before they are startled.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
having heard from the Buddha this unprecedented teaching— the World-Honored One’s bestowing of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon Śāriputra—
conceived a sense of rare wonder. Overjoyed and leaping for joy, they immediately rose from their seats and adjusted their robes.

Exposing his right shoulder, placing his right knee upon the ground, joining his palms with single-minded devotion, and bowing respectfully while gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We occupy the foremost rank among the Saṅgha; our years are advanced and we are decrepit. We have long considered ourselves to have already attained Nirvāṇa."
I was incapable of anything further and no longer sought *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

World-Honored One, in the past when you had been preaching the Dharma for a long time, I was seated among the assembly; my body grew weary and exhausted, and I thought only of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Regarding the Bodhisattva-dharma—sporting with supernatural powers, purifying Buddha-fields, and maturing sentient beings—we find no joy in our hearts. Why is this?
World-Honored One, you have caused us to emerge from the triple world and attain the realization of nirvana. Furthermore, we are now advanced in years;
regarding the Buddha’s teaching and transformation toward the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the bodhisattvas, [we lack the capacity].

We did not give rise to even a single thought of longing [for such a thing]. Now, before the Buddha, we have heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the śrāvakas; our hearts are filled with great joy, having attained what we never had before.
We did not expect that today we would suddenly hear this rare Dharma, and we deeply congratulate ourselves for obtaining such great and virtuous benefit—an immeasurable treasure.
They attained it spontaneously without seeking.
At the outset, the narrator described the realization of a "never-before-heard dharma," which refers precisely to the principle of the equality of all dharmas.
Having already heard the Great Dharma and now hearing their own prediction of enlightenment, they likewise give rise to a mind of unprecedented wonder; this is why they leap for joy.
[He] leaped up, just like Śāriputra. "Immediately from below" refers to the ritual of paying respect with the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind] raised in utmost sincerity.
"We, from below," is a retrospective account of past exhaustion and indolence; it means that for over forty years, we no longer aspired to seek the Buddha-way because there was a reason:
since our Dharma-ordination years were all advanced, we occupied the foremost positions among the monks and considered ourselves [superior].

Having already attained the bliss of ultimate *nirvāṇa* and extinction, and having already transcended the suffering of birth and death within the triple world (*traidhātuka*), he considered his great task finished and felt there was nothing further to be done. He beheld the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
though he himself had not attained them, he no longer aspired to seek them. He was just like a man whose roots were destroyed, regarding the five [aggregates]...

Because [my] desire was no longer capable of benefiting [others]. Below, in the passage beginning with "The World-Honored One," it is further stated that there is a reason why for more than forty years I did not delight in the Bodhisattva Dharma.

Having observed that the World-Honored One had been teaching the Dharma for a long time, and having also constantly seen the Tathāgata praise the Bodhisattvas and bestow upon them the prediction of their attainment of Buddhahood, at those times, although I was present among the assembly, my body was weary and exhausted.

Regarding the bridge across the ford, they sit in the state of rightness; they simply contemplate the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and thus take no pleasure even in the Bodhisattva’s playful exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) or the task of purifying Buddha-lands.
As for the "playful exercise of supernatural powers," examples include Vimalakīrti’s invitation to the meal at Gandhavyūha and his borrowing of a seat from King Dīpaṃkara.
Regarding "purifying the Buddha-land": sentient beings are the Buddha-land of the Bodhisattva.
This refers to how a Bodhisattva takes on a Buddha-land according to the beings he transforms, and takes on a Buddha-land according to the beings he disciplines.
Below this, there is further inquiry and explanation regarding the reasons for not seeking bodhi and not delighting in saving sentient beings. This is because...
"In the past, we dwelt in false views and were greedily attached to this burning house, suffering under the oppression of various pains.

World-Honored One, you have caused us to emerge from the suffering of the triple world and realize the bliss of nirvana; because our hearts are thus fulfilled, [we shall abide] within the precious treasury of the Buddha-dharma."
We ourselves have had no aspirations. Furthermore, we are now advanced in years; we consider our own parinirvāṇa sufficient and think that with this alone our purpose is fulfilled.
We have nothing further to do beyond this, and therefore we have no desire to teach and transform sentient beings in pure Buddha-lands.
There is no joy or delight whatsoever. We shall now describe our present state of jubilation.
Having heard the voice of the prediction for the śrāvakas, we are filled with joy and celebration; though we had no intention for bodhi, bodhi has arrived of its own accord.
It is just like immeasurable treasures that are obtained without seeking. The two characters "without seeking" reveal that this is not like the ordinary case of Śāriputra.
He reproached himself and blamed himself. When Master Shuilao of Hongzhou first visited Mazu, he asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Mazu said, "Prostrate yourself. As soon as the Master prostrated, Mazu stepped on him right at the chest.
The Master attained great enlightenment; rising up, he clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "How extraordinary! How extraordinary! A hundred..."
The thousand samādhis and immeasurable wondrous gates are all to be recognized at their very source upon the tip of a single hair.
After his realization, he would often tell people: "Ever since that one time I was kicked by Mazu, I have been laughing without ceasing until now.
This is what is meant by "joyful celebration."
World-Honored One, we now wish to provide an analogy to clarify this meaning.
Suppose there were a man who, while still young, abandoned his father and fled. He lived in another country for a long time—perhaps ten, twenty, or even fifty years.
As he grew older and became increasingly impoverished, he wandered in all directions in search of food and clothing. After traveling by degrees, he eventually encountered [his father].
In our own country, those who delight in employing parables to clarify this meaning say:

"Since the World-Honored One has already expressed his heart of compassion through parables, we too shall express our state of folly through parables; that is to say, 'throwing a peach in return for a plum.'"
Among these, first is the account of father and son turning away from each other; second, the account of father and son meeting; third, the account of father and son gaining mutual trust.
Only then does he inherit the family legacy of the Tathāgata. As for "being of tender age," it means having no discernment yet.
"Leaving his father and fleeing" means turning one's back on awakening and uniting with the sensory dust. "Dwelling long in another land" means abandoning one's home and dispersing.
They flee. When they reach fifty years of age, a single movement of the mind causes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to arise together.

As their years decline—meaning that though they claim to be grown old, they become increasingly impoverished and distressed—they have no garment of shame upon their bodies and no flavor of dhyāna-joy in their mouths.
Having no choice, they willingly become beggars, wandering in all directions to solicit clothing from others.

It is food. This is analogous to one who, having already suffered intensely within the three realms, suddenly gives rise to a single thought of revulsion toward the world and flees outward in search of the Dharma that brings peace.
As he gradually wanders about, he encounters his way back to his own country.
This is a true analogy for the Buddha-land of no-mind. Because he gradually sought out teachers and searched for the Way, he eventually encountered the direction toward the Buddha-land.
His father had previously come there seeking his son but could not find him, so he stayed in a certain city; that family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable riches and treasures.
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, crystal, pearls, and the like; all his granaries and treasuries were completely overflowing.
He had many servants, ministers, officials, and subjects, as well as countless elephants, horses, carriages, cattle, and sheep, from which he derived great profit through their trade and investment.
He then traveled throughout other lands, where merchants, traders, and guests were also very numerous.

[The son] said above: "I abandoned my father and wandered abroad; thus I have encountered him upon returning to my native country. [The father] said: "I sought my son but could not find him; therefore, I stayed in this city.
One moved and one stayed, their words corresponding perfectly as if they had been written down together. The father had arrived before [the son].
The phrase "seeking his children but not finding them" is the summary. At that time, the householder was standing outside the gate and heard someone say:
"Your sons, because they were previously playing, have entered this house; being young children without understanding, they take delight in it with joyful attachment.
Having heard this, the elder was startled and entered the burning house, thinking, "It is now appropriate to rescue and provide for them," as described in the text. This is precisely what is meant.
"In the past and the future, he has previously manifested his body within the three realms for our sake; therefore, he is called 'one who came before.

Regarding the phrase 'staying in a single city,' it means that although the Tathāgata previously provided guidance and transformation, it was because our karmic conditions were not yet mature and the time had not yet arrived."
Because he could not find a son, he did not remain long in the human realm; he subsequently concealed his form and dwelt in the Land of Reward (saṃbhogakāya) to await the ripening of conditions.
At the bottom of that [painting], the boundaries of the Land of Reward are depicted to demonstrate that the Tathāgata is indeed a great wealthy elder.
Regarding the term "great wealth": it is called "great" because it is vast and all-encompassing, and it is called "wealth" because there is nothing that does not exist within it.
Regarding "immeasurable wealth and treasures": merit constitutes the wealth, and prajñā is called the treasure; this signifies that merit and wisdom are inexhaustible.
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and so forth, refer to the ten powers, the four immeasurables, the four analytical knowledges, and the like.
That which stores grain is a granary; that which stores utensils is a treasury. To be "full" means to be replete within; to be "overflowing" means to flow outward. This—
All these are metaphors for the Tathāgata’s own objects of enjoyment. The servants and laborers represent the assembly of ministers and assistants who provide support;
the officials and commoners represent those who first listen to and obey his instructions. The elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep represent the means by which vehicles are transported.
The "profits from income and expenditure" that extend to other countries refers to the interest generated from what is produced, which is still capable of being distributed widely as charity.
He benefits the multitude not only within a single country, but extends his reach to other lands as well, seeing that his root is vast and his manifestations are manifold.
This refers to the statement: "If I were to distribute these goods throughout an entire country, they would still not be exhausted.
The fact that merchants and traders exist everywhere serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata bestowing his supernatural power upon bodhisattvas to preach the Dharma.
Saving sentient beings is like a merchant taking his capital and earning interest. These are all metaphors for the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya*) for benefiting sentient beings.
Being fully endowed with both self-benefit and benefit for others, as well as the two wisdoms (*jñāna*), he is therefore called "Greatly Wealthy."
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and cities, eventually arriving at the city where his father resided.
Previously, it was explained that the impoverished son had come from another country to his own; here, however, he is shown traveling from his own country to wander among the villages.
Traveling from village to state, from state to town, and from town to city, though one may wander through them all, one truly does not recognize one’s own biological father.
It is just as when every place appears to be one’s native landscape, yet one simply fails to see one’s own original face.
This is what is meant by "not recognizing the true face of Mount Lu," which is due solely to...
The phrase "one's body is within this mountain" refers to this very point. Previously, it was said that the father sought his son but could not find him and stayed in a certain city;
here, it is said that the son traveled through villages and arrived at the city where his father resided. Thus, both father and son were in the same city, yet they simply did not see one another.
The father constantly thought of his son; though they had been separated for over fifty years, he never spoke of this matter to anyone.

He merely pondered it within himself, harboring regret and remorse. Thinking to himself that he was old and infirm, yet possessed of abundant wealth—gold, silver, and precious gems—with storehouses overflowing—and that he had no offspring, he feared that once he passed away, his property would be dissipated and left with no one to whom it could be entrusted.

Thus, out of earnestness, he constantly remembers his son and further reflects: "If I were to find my son and entrust my wealth and possessions to him, I would be at ease and happy, free from all anxiety."
This refers to a father’s anxious concern for his son. Regarding the phrase "separated for more than fifty years," the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states:
"It is like a lost son who holds a gold coin in his hand but does not know it exists.
He wanders through the ten directions for fifty years, suffering from poverty and hardship, devoting himself solely to seeking and begging to sustain his life, yet never finding sufficiency. Its...
The father saw his son in such a state and said to him, "Why do you not take and use this gold coin?
Whatever you require shall be fully provided according to your wishes. Once the son had awakened and obtained the gold coin, his heart was filled with great joy.
The father said, "Do not be so exultant; this gold coin is your original property. It was not something you acquired through your own effort."
"How is it that this is so pleasing? The Bodhisattva Non-Abiding said: "That father, knowing his son was deluded, waited fifty years before speaking.
During those fifty years of wandering through the ten directions in poverty and suffering, he finally spoke these words. The Buddha said:

"'Wandering through the ten directions for fifty years' refers to a single movement of the mind, wandering through the ten directions, traveling afar, and engaging in pervasive conceptualization. The Bodhisattva Non-Abiding said: [This is so.]
"How is it that a single movement of thought lasts for fifty years? The Buddha said: "When a single thought moves, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) arise together.

Within the arising of these five aggregates, the fifty evils are fully present. To speak precisely, when the father constantly thinks of his son, 'May we originally be in one place,' it is because of that single movement of thought in the past that the five aggregates arose together, fully possessing the fifty evils."
Thus we parted, and for over fifty years I traveled far to other regions, never seeing him again.
The reason I have never disclosed this matter to others is that I feared their karmic conditions were not yet ripe and they would be unwilling to take up the responsibility.
My heart harbors regret and resentment: I regret that I did not remain [with him] in the past, and I resent that we do not meet today.

"Reflecting on oneself," and so forth. Next, one reflects on being decrepit and that the time of death is approaching; having no son to inherit the enterprise, there would be wealth and property with no one to whom they could be entrusted.
For this reason, one earnestly and constantly remembers the son—this is what is meant by "old age awakens many feelings, and one thinks of one's descendants.
Furthermore, "making [the vow]," and so forth. Third, one reflects: "If I were to obtain a son, I could entrust the family business to him, and only then would my original purpose be fulfilled."
"Be at ease; there is no longer any cause for anxiety. Whenever the father thought of his son, he would reflect upon this himself, repeatedly forming these three phrases of thought.
This summarizes the meaning of the seven days and nights of contemplation.
“World-Honored One, at that time the impoverished son, wandering about in search of employment, happened upon his father’s house. Standing by the side of the gate,
he saw from afar his father seated upon a lion throne with a precious footstool supporting his feet, surrounded with respectful homage by Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and householders,
his body adorned with pearl necklaces worth ten million pieces of gold, and attended by officials, citizens, and servants.”
Holding white whisks, they stood in attendance to his left and right. A precious canopy covered him above, with various flowered banners hanging down.

Fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground, and many kinds of famous flowers were scattered. Precious objects were arrayed, being brought forth, taken away, or presented. Such were the various kinds of magnificent adornments.
His majestic virtue was exceptionally sublime. When the impoverished son saw his father possessed of such great power and influence, he immediately felt terrified and regretted having come here.
He thought to himself in secret: "This must be a king, or perhaps someone equal to a king; this is no place for me to obtain wealth through hired labor."
"It would be better to go to a poor neighborhood where there is ample scope for labor and food and clothing are easily obtained.
If I remain here long, I may be coerced and forced to work against my will. Having thought this, he ran away quickly.
This clarifies that while the father constantly thinks of his son, the son does not think of his father.
"Hired laborer" means one who is employed by others to take their wealth (kārṣāpaṇas). "Wandering about" means moving from place to place without fixed destination.

"Arriving at his father's house and standing by the side of the gate" means that from the city to the house, he did not dare enter the gate; therefore, he stood by the side of the gate. He saw him from afar...
Not recognizing his own father, he mistakenly took him for the king; at first sight he was terrified, and upon seeing him again, doubt arose.

Failing to realize that the Dharma King was his father and that he himself was the son of the Dharma King, he willingly remained in the poor quarters and fled in haste—what is called "missing the mark right before one's face. This is precisely what is meant by "a single leaf obscuring the eyes."
From afar he saw his father descend, depicting the manner of a wealthy and noble elder. The lion throne is a metaphor for the seat of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*).
Supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) serve as its legs, and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) serve as its footstool; these assist the supernatural powers.
The *brāhmaṇa* represents those of pure conduct; the *kṣatriya*, the royal lineage; and the *gṛhapati*, the gentleman who dwells at home yet possesses the Way. These are metaphors for the Bodhi...
The retinue surrounding him represents the fact that the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) is adorned with immeasurable colors;
these colors possess immeasurable marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and these marks possess immeasurable secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), which serve as its adornments.

The officials and commoners standing in attendance to his left and right represent the application of immeasurable skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) in accordance with sentient beings. This is covered by compassion.
The precious canopy of compassion covers and protects all living beings; the flowered banners of the four means of integration guide all things.
The water of the Dharma irrigates the ground of the human heart, while the flowers of awakening drive away the emotional dust beyond the realm.

As for the array of precious objects, they are displayed for people to admire and enjoy; as for their being brought forth or put away, taken or given, it is done with effortless mastery. His majestic virtue is exceptional...
"Venerable Sir, the majestic Vairocana is not one who can be equaled by an emanation Buddha. From 'the impoverished son' downward, [the text] describes the state of the impoverished son’s fear.
Because the Dharma is vast while his faculties are small, he is not only terrified, but moreover regrets having come. This was composed in private."
This refers to harboring private thoughts such as, "Perhaps this is for the King or others. Here, "King" refers to the sovereign;

"others" refers to the King’s brothers, relatives, or kinsmen. Upon seeing the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya), they give rise to fear, thinking, "This is not a place where I can obtain [the fruits of] things," just as it is said:
"The Buddha-way is long and distant; only after enduring diligent suffering for a long time can it be accomplished."
Therefore, I do not desire it. It would be better to go to a poor neighborhood and exert my strength where there is a field for such labor;
this is the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), which is within my reach. This is what is meant by "willingly accepting inferiority" and "enduring poverty.
If I remain here for long—meaning if I do not leave early now and stay here—he will surely use his power and influence to force me [to do as he wishes].
He worked without being paid his wages. Thinking thus, he departed in haste, fearing that others might pursue him.
At that time, the wealthy elder, sitting upon the lion throne, recognized his son at once and was filled with great joy; he then thought to himself:
"My wealth and storehouses now have one to whom they may be entrusted. I have constantly thought of this son, yet had no means to see him;
that he should suddenly come of his own accord is most agreeable to my wishes. Although I am old in years, I still cherish [him] with greed.

He immediately dispatched attendants to pursue and bring him back in haste. At that time, the messengers ran swiftly to seize him, and the impoverished son was struck with alarm and distress, crying out in grievance and lamentation."
"I have committed no offense. Why am I being seized? The messenger held him even more tightly and forcibly dragged him away.
At that time, the impoverished son thought to himself, "I am innocent yet I am imprisoned; this means certain death. He became increasingly terrified, fainted, and fell prostrate upon the ground.
The son sees his father but does not recognize him; therefore, fear and doubt arise. The father sees his son and recognizes him immediately;
therefore, joy and delight arise. Thus, even though the son flees swiftly, he causes one to pursue him urgently.

As for the phrase "greedily cherishing," it means that although the son does not recognize me as his father, he nevertheless turns his back on me and flees because I am old and infirm and have no other son. Even though he... [is so].
"He has turned his back on me, yet I still cherish this child no differently than I did in the past. This is truly the point where the "old woman's heart" is most earnest.
The bystander who pursues him urgently is like the Buddha bestowing his supernatural power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) upon the Bodhisattva, commanding him to preach the Dharma and deliver the being.
At that time, the messenger descends; this is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva preaching the Mahāyāna Dharma of the stages of abiding, inclination, and practice.
[The phrase] "The impoverished son" [indicates that he] fears the Great [Vehicle]. Because he has arrived without cause, he is struck with alarm and astonishment.
Regarding the phrase "crying out in resentment": in the Hīnayāna, afflictions (*kleśa*) are regarded as enemies and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as thieves.
If it is taught that afflictions are the very seed of the Buddha and birth-and-death is itself Nirvāṇa, then these "enemies" confront him; thus, crying out in resentment, he calls out loudly. I...
"Why am I being seized when I have committed no offense? he asked. "I originally did not intend to make a livelihood out of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and afflictions (*kleśa*).
Why do you force me? When the messenger descended, although he would not listen, the messenger nevertheless forced him to listen by means of this Dharma.
At that time [he said]: "My aspiration and delight were originally not for the study of the Bodhisattva Dharma."
Furthermore, I do not wish to dwell within the afflictions of birth and death, yet you force me into these afflictions;
this is to be imprisoned and seized without having committed any crime. If this were to continue, my life of wisdom would surely be extinguished. Thus he reflected.
He became even more terrified, until he fainted and fell to the ground.
His father saw him from afar and said to the messenger, "There is no need for this man; do not force him to come here.
He sprinkled cold water on his face to restore his consciousness and told him, "Do not speak with him again. Why was this? Because the father knew that his son’s disposition was not [yet fit].

Being of low status himself, he knew that his own noble and wealthy lineage would be challenged by his son. Having ascertained with certainty that it was indeed his son, he employed skillful means and did not tell others, saying, "This is my son."
As for the father seeing him from afar: because he saw his son was terrified, distressed, and fainting, he entrusted the Bodhisattva to guide him through skillful means.
There is no need to go down; that is to say, it is not necessary to forcefully preach the Mahāyāna Dharma to him, nor is it necessary to force him into the realm of the Buddha.
It is appropriate to use the cool water of the Four Noble Truths to remove his burning afflictions and cause him—
He awoke and further instructed him, saying: "From now on, you must by no means reveal to him that I am his father and he is my son.
Why? Because I know his faculties are inferior, and I also know my own noble status;
even if I were to tell him, he would find it difficult to believe at once and would be unwilling to accept it. Although [the truth] was perfectly clear...
He knew with certainty that this was his own biological son, yet through skillful means, he never revealed these words in the presence of others.
Although father and son are close, they remain two distinct individuals; therefore, he was unwilling to believe it to be so.
A monk asked Dawsui, "Father and son are most intimate; why then do their paths diverge? Sui said, "It is precisely because there is father and son.
The messenger said to him, "I now release you; go wherever you please. The impoverished son rejoiced, having attained what he had never experienced before.
Rising from the ground, he went to a poor neighborhood to seek food and clothing.
This Bodhisattva addressed them with skillful words, saying: "I shall no longer constrain you with the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
You may simply act according to whatever you desire in your hearts; I shall comply with all of it."
"You, impoverished son, were not coerced by the Bodhisattva; rather, you have now attained what you desired. Your confusion has finally cleared, and you no longer fall to the ground.

Rising immediately from the earth, because your faculties are inferior, yet having been thoroughly cultivated and not forgotten, you turn toward the gateway of the Four Noble Truths to seek the Dharma that accords with the poor for your own sustenance—namely, casting aside the bright pearl."
It is like seeking the eyes of a fish.
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, devised a skillful means. He secretly dispatched two men who were haggard in appearance and lacked majesty, saying:
"You should go to that place and speak slowly to the impoverished son, saying: 'There is work here; we shall pay you double wages.'"
"You are welcome. Poor son, if you consent, we shall bring you here to work for us. If he asks, 'What is it that you would have me do?', you may simply say to him, 'I am hired to remove the refuse;
we two shall also work together with you. Then the two messengers immediately sought out the poor son.
Having already attained this, he fully recounted the aforementioned matters;

this was the Bodhisattva’s entrustment of the hidden reality and the manifestation of expedient means. As for his secretly dispatching two persons, it was to cause the Bodhisattva to conceal his sovereign power of majestic spiritual authority (*vīrya*), and to manifest the appearance of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha externally in order to transform them. Therefore, it is said:

This refers to being secretly dispatched. As for those whose appearance and form are haggard and who lack majestic virtue, their bodies are like withered wood and their minds are like extinguished ashes.
As the subsequent text states: "Knowing that the multitude delights in inferior teachings and fears great wisdom, for this reason the Bodhisattvas..."

"This refers to those who become Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. You may go to them and tell them that for the sake of the impoverished sons, you should entrust them with the Lesser Teaching and gradually guide them;
you must not again pursue or forcibly drag them away with the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
As for the statement, 'If there is work to be done here, I will give you double wages,' it means that if you wish to go to the poor neighborhoods to hire yourself out as a laborer..."
If he seeks food and clothing, there is a place where work can be done, and its wages are twice those of other places.
To say "twice" is a metaphor for practicing the Four Noble Truths: being able to transcend birth and death while also attaining nirvana.
If the impoverished son agrees to come and perform labor—meaning, if one asks him and he consents—one should immediately lead him away to take up service; do not...
This is to encourage him. If he should ask, "What do you wish for me to do? one must not further inform him that it is to purify Buddha-lands or to bring sentient beings to maturity.
One should say instead, "It is nothing more than having you sweep away filth and excrement;
there is no difficult task. Furthermore, the two of us shall also perform this work together with you. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva—
It is through "sameness of purpose" (*samānārthatā*) that one guides others. Because the two delusions of views and thought defile the field of the mind, they are called "filth.

"At that time, the two [disciples] below" refers to their following the teaching and practicing accordingly. "To fully recount the aforementioned matters" means to inform them with the words of the Tathāgata’s earnest exhortation.
At that time, the impoverished son first took his wages and immediately began clearing away the filth. When the father saw his son, he felt both pity and wonder.
On another day, he saw the son from afar through a window; his body was emaciated and haggard, covered in dust and soil.
Filthy and impure, he immediately cast off his necklaces, fine soft garments, and ornaments of adornment; instead, he put on coarse, tattered, and greasy clothes.
Dust covered his body, and in his right hand he held a refuse-removing tool, appearing as though filled with dread.
He says to the laborers, "Work diligently; do not be weary. By means of this expedient, he is able to draw near to his son.

These words represent the Tathāgata’s concealment of the ultimate truth and manifestation of provisional skillful means. "First taking the price and afterwards removing the filth" refers to first receiving the price of the Path to Cessation (*nirodha-mārga*) and afterwards removing the filth of Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*). "Seeing his son and feeling pity and wonder" refers to pitying him...
Though he possesses vast majesty and spiritual power, he does not employ it; one wonders why he delights in such inferior deeds.
Peering at his son through the window, he fears that the child might again be struck with terror;
therefore, rather than manifesting himself before him in his body of extraordinary majesty and honor, he gazes from afar through the window. Thus, the flavor of the Dharma does not satisfy him.

Therefore, he is emaciated; because his merit and virtue are incomplete, he is haggard. "Earth" is a metaphor for the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); "dust" is a metaphor for the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).
Because the delusions of view are coarse while the delusions of thought are subtle, they are divided into two. "Removing precious and elegant garments" refers to concealing the *śānta* body.
"Wearing tattered and filthy clothes" refers to manifesting the form of sixteen feet. "Dust and dirt covering the body" [is likewise a metaphor].

"Carrying a vessel of excrement" means that he condescends from his noble status to the lowly, manifesting his form among human beings; it also signifies his revulsion toward birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and his praise of *nirvāṇa*.
"Commanding them to work diligently" means to encourage the cultivation of right effort (*samyak-vīrya*). This refers to what was said previously:
"You should simply cultivate diligence with vigor. "Because of skillful means (*upāya*), he is able to draw near to his son" means that by means of various kinds of wholesome [dharmas]...
Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), the father and son were finally able to meet one another, and the son gave rise to neither doubt nor fear.
This clarifies the occasion when the Four Noble Truths were first turned at the Deer Park. The above constitutes a general summary of how difficult it was for the father and son to meet.
Later, he spoke to him again, saying: "Ho! Man, you shall always do this work here; do not go elsewhere again. I shall increase your wages.
Whatever you may require—such as basins, vessels, rice, flour, salt, or vinegar—do not hesitate or feel any doubt. I also have old and worn-out servants who will provide what you need.
Set your mind at ease; I am like a father to you, so do not worry or be anxious. This was why...
"Why? I am old and aged, while you are young and vigorous. When you work, you never show deceit, laziness, anger, resentment, or complaints;
I do not see these evils in you at all, as I do in other laborers. From this day forward, you shall be like a son born of my own body.
Thereupon, the elder gave him another name, calling him "Son."
Below this, he again consoles him with gentle words. "Ho, man! is a term used to awaken his attention.
It means: "You should always work diligently here; do not harbor the thought of going elsewhere.
I shall double your wages beyond the standard labor fee. Furthermore, I shall provide all the tools you require, as well as the daily necessities for sustaining your life."

These items are for your use; do not harbor any doubts or difficulties regarding them. Furthermore, whatever aged or infirm servants you may require for your service, they shall also be provided to you.
Thus, both the articles for your enjoyment and the persons to be employed at your command are granted.
Everything is fully provided. Rest your mind in peace; there is no need for further thought. I am indeed like your own father;
whatever you desire, I shall provide it all. Do not give rise to anxiety over any perceived deficiency.
At this point, he has just slightly revealed himself as a great wealthy elder who possesses everything, yet he does not speak of it to them.
To reveal the truth is to speak of one’s own biological father; therefore, it is said that they are "like" [the father]. As for why I am like your father:
it is because my years are advanced and my time for passing away is near, and furthermore, I have no offspring. Since you are already young and vigorous, [you shall take my place].
Furthermore, you are willing to exert yourself with diligence. I shall constantly observe your daily activities and movements;
internally, I see no heart of self-deception; externally, I see no signs of indolence; and in speech, I see no words of anger or resentment.
Because you are free from these three evils, you surpass all other laborers. From this day forward, as for your affairs...
We are of one family; I am like your biological father, and you are like my biological son.

Thereupon, he bestowed upon him two characters and named him "Er" (Son). This passage describes the period within the twelve years of the *Āgama* when he exhorted [the disciples] to practice the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, he still considered himself a lowly hired laborer.

For this reason, for twenty years he was constantly made to remove filth. After this period had passed, their hearts accorded with one another and they trusted each other; he entered and left without hindrance.
Nevertheless, the place where he resided remained his original location.
Although the father earnestly exhorted and entreated him to become his son, the impoverished son was nonetheless delighted by this encounter;
he merely rejoiced at having found a virtuous master, yet he did not realize that the man was his biological father, nor that he himself was truly the father’s own son.
Consequently, he continued to regard himself as a lowly hired laborer. Because of this...
Because he was unwilling to believe that he was his own biological son, for twelve years of the Āgamas and eight years of the Vaipulya sūtras,
he was constantly made to perform the tasks of a lowly hired servant and was not entrusted with the family business.
This describes how, once father and son were finally able to meet, their mutual trust was so difficult to establish that it took twenty years.
Only after seeing the Buddha for such a long time did their habitual tendencies (vāsanā) become deeply transformed, and they were finally able to attain a heartfelt, essential trust.
