They moved freely between the outer hall and the inner sanctum without any interval, showing no sign of hesitation. Yet, the place where he resided remained the same as before. It was as if...

He dwelt in the quarters of lowly laborers; for he firmly maintained the station of non-action (*avivikta-bhūmi*), that is to say, his former place of practice from which he did not move even a single step.

This describes the period after the *Vaipulya* [sutras], when he neither rejoiced in praising the Perfect and extolling the Great, nor was he terrified by disparaging the Partial and denouncing the Small.
World-Honored One, at that time the elder was ill and, knowing that his death would soon come, spoke to the impoverished son, saying:
"I now possess much gold, silver, and rare treasures; my storehouses are overflowing. You must know all that is therein—how much there is, and what should be taken or given.
My mind is thus; you should embody this intent. Why is this? Now, between me and you, we shall become—"
"It is no different. You must apply yourself with diligence and ensure that nothing is lost.

At that time, the impoverished son accepted the instructions and took charge of the various goods, the gold, silver, precious jewels, and all the storehouses; yet he had no intention of seeking even a single meal from them.
Moreover, he continued to reside in his former place, and his lowly disposition remained unabandoned.

"Knowing that my death will not be long hence" is a metaphor for being close to the time of entering *nirvāṇa*. "That which should be taken and given" refers to matters of benefiting oneself and others.
"One should embody this intent" means that one should take my mind as your own mind.
My mind is to transmit the *prajñā* and to continue the life of wisdom; you, too, should act in this same way. Now, I—
"To say that you are not different from me" means: "I am not different from your father, and you are not different from my son.
These two words, "not different," are even more intimate than the previous word "like. Because they are not different, what belongs to me is yours;
you should apply your mind to this and comprehend it point by point, ensuring that nothing is lost.
Although the impoverished son has received the instructions and taken charge of the various goods, he merely follows them out of faith in the Buddha’s words;
he does not yet believe that the items within this treasury are rightfully his own.
He still considers them not to be his property, but rather the property of the King, of whom he is merely a guardian. Consequently, he does not dare to take much.
As for its use, one does not even dare to take or use the small fee for a single meal.
Yet, if one still remains in that very place, one has not yet escaped the trap of the impoverished child. The ancients compared this state to a pit of non-action.
The "Golden Lock" is difficult; it refers to the Pure White Ground, the Night-Bright Curtain, Cold Ashes, and Dead Water.
That one's inferior mind has not yet been relinquished means that they cling to their fixed achievements and are unwilling to take up the family business.
This describes the time during the Prajñāpāramitā assembly when [the Buddha] commanded him to manage the household affairs and transmit the teaching.
After a short time had passed, the father perceived that his son’s mind had gradually become open and at ease, that he had achieved great resolve, and that he now despised his former thoughts.
As he was about to pass away, he summoned his son and assembled his kinsmen, as well as the king, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders.
When they had all assembled, he immediately made this proclamation: "Gentlemen, you should know that this is my son, born of me.
Having abandoned me in such-and-such a city, he fled and wandered in hardship for more than fifty years. His original name was so-and-so."
"My name is [Name]. Formerly, while in my own city, I was filled with anxiety and searched for him everywhere. Suddenly, in this very place, I have encountered and found him.
He is truly my son, and I am truly his father. Now, all the wealth and property that I possess belongs entirely to my son."
"World-Honored One, what was previously brought out and put away is known only to this son.

At that time, hearing these words from his father, the impoverished son was filled with great joy, having attained what he had never experienced before, and he thought to himself: 'Originally I had no mind to seek anything;
now this treasure trove has come to me spontaneously.'"
"Again, after a short time" means that having passed beyond the *Prajñāpāramitā* period, the time for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* has arrived.

"No one knows the son like the father"—thus it is said that the father knows the son's intent. "Gradually becoming open and expansive" refers to not being obstructed by the Lesser Vehicle; this is what is meant by "open."

To find peace of mind within the Great is called "serenity" (tai). One who has accomplished their great aspiration and comes to despise their former mindset realizes that the Dharma King is now known as their own biological father, that they themselves are the son of the Dharma King, and that the treasure store is an inherent possession.
Furthermore, they awaken to the fact that for forty years they have needlessly lived as a poor child. At the moment of impending death, one then proclaims:
This is the time of his passing away. His summoning of his son is a metaphor for the bestowal of the prediction of Buddhahood (*vyākaraṇa*).

Although he had previously designated him as his son, there was as yet no formal verification; thus, he assembled the multitude to serve as witnesses. The buddhas who have manifested their bodies are like his kinsmen.
Prabhūtaratna Buddha was a king; the bodhisattvas were great ministers; and the kṣatriyas and householders were the fourfold assembly.
These are the four subsequent lines, which bestow the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. Under the phrase "In such-and-such a place," it reveals the reason why he received this prediction today:
he states, "I have constantly taught the Buddha-dharma under twenty trillion Buddhas."
"O you, I am indeed his father. Because he abandoned me and fled, we have not recognized one another for more than fifty years while traveling through cities and towns.

As for his original name being so-and-so and my name being such-and-such—just as his former name was Śāriputra and his current name is Puṣpārāma, and so forth—I was formerly in the lower station; that is to say, I was formerly in this city searching [for him]."
“I did not see you, and so I stayed in a certain city; it is only now that I have finally encountered you.

That ‘all that I possess is yours’ refers to the entrustment of the matter of attaining Buddhahood. That ‘what was previously brought in and sent out is known by you’ refers to the entrustment of the matter of saving sentient beings.
Below this, the World-Honored One bestows the prophecy, and [the recipient] rejoices just as a poor man who has obtained a treasure.
When a layman is appointed as a high minister, how could he not rejoice? Yet, [the Buddha] speaks of him as being inferior, saying:

"I originally had no intention or aspiration to seek the path of the Buddha, yet now I have suddenly heard that I am granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood. This treasure-store has arrived of its own accord without being sought.
This is why his joy exceeds all expectations.
“World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder is the Tathāgata. We are all like the sons of the Buddha; the Tathāgata has always spoken of us as his sons.
World-Honored One, because of the three kinds of suffering, we undergo various torments within birth and death.”

Deluded and ignorant, we delighted in and were attached to the lesser teachings. Today, the World-Honored One has caused us to reflect and sweep away the dung of conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena.
Within this, we have applied ourselves with diligent effort and obtained the price of a single day’s worth of nirvana.
Having obtained this, our hearts were filled with great joy; we considered ourselves sufficient and said to ourselves: "Regarding the Buddha-dharma..."

Because you have applied yourselves with diligent vigor, what you have attained is vast and abundant. Yet, the World-Honored One previously knew that our minds were attached to base desires and we delighted in inferior teachings;
he therefore overlooked us and did not provide individual instruction, [saying]: "You all shall have a share in the treasure-house of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision."
This is the application of the dharma to the analogy. The Tathāgata corresponds to the father; "resembling a son" corresponds to the son.
To say "resembling" means to be a mere semblance rather than the reality. It means that while the Tathāgata constantly regards us as his sons, we do not believe that the Tathāgata is our father;
therefore, it is called "resembling. Once one has faith, one is then a true son. As for the three sufferings:
These are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
Within the cycle of birth and death, those who undergo various fevers and afflictions are scorched and boiled by birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and despair.

Those who are deluded and ignorant likewise do not know what constitutes the fire or what constitutes the house. Those who delight in and cling to minor dharmas take pleasure in the lesser realms of humans and devas.
As for the result: they did not understand that the Tathāgata’s treasure-store belongs entirely to them.

When the World-Honored One said, "I cause us," this means that the World-Honored One, as if fashioning a cap upon our heads, caused us to know suffering and abandon its origin over the course of twenty years.
It is the clearing away of the dung of the six consciousnesses, the three poisons, and conceptual proliferation.
Our diligent application of effort therein consists of cultivating the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment. To obtain even a single day’s wage [of merit] leading to nirvana—
Having attained the realization of the bliss of nirvāṇa, their hearts were filled with great joy, and they thought to themselves that what they had gained was vast and abundant;
yet they had only received the wages for a single day’s labor. Their benefit was extremely slight, yet they felt self-satisfied, considering it a great acquisition of precious treasure.
If one possesses the vision of the River Lord or the well-frog, believing that all the beauty in the world resides within oneself, one does not know the vastness of the ocean.

The World-Honored One, descending [to our level], spoke thus: "The World-Honored One previously knew that our minds were attached to coarse and inferior forms and sounds, delighting in minor dharmas and taking no pleasure in the Mahāyāna; therefore, the World-Honored One likewise set us aside and did not grant [the teaching]."
I have said that we have a share in the Tathāgata’s precious treasury.
Just as [the father] knew clearly that this was his son, yet by means of skillful means did not tell others, "This is my son," so too are we called "pseudo-sons.
This accords with the account found in the Āgamas.
The World-Honored One, through the power of skillful means, has preached the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
We have obtained from the Buddha the price of a single day’s wages—nirvāṇa—and considering this a great gain, we have had no aspiration to seek this Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, by the power of skillful means, the World-Honored One, within the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras, praised the Perfect and extolled the Great.
When he spoke of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, it was likewise to urge us forward toward the Buddha-way;
yet we remained sitting, guarding our own nirvāṇa, considering a single day’s wages to be a great gain, and neglecting the Bodhisattva dharmas such as the playful exercise of supernatural powers.
We are unwilling to aspire toward it; this is why we are called "pseudo-sons. This accords with what occurs within the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras.
Furthermore, by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, we have revealed and expounded it for the sake of the bodhisattvas, yet as for ourselves, regarding this—
We had no aspiration [for the Great Vehicle]. Why was this? The Buddha knew that our hearts delighted in the Lesser Dharma;
thus, by the power of skillful means, he taught us according to our capacities. Yet we did not realize that we were truly the sons of the Buddha.

Furthermore, when the World-Honored One, in the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, commanded us to transmit the Tathāgata’s wisdom to the bodhisattvas, he intended for us to take charge of all the various goods and treasuries, entrusting the family estate to us. We did not understand this;
we merely acted as messengers, conveying words from one person to another to ensure their smooth circulation and communication. And yet—
Not for a single thought did he harbor a mind of delight; how is this different from encountering a royal banquet yet not eating?

This accords with the events within the *Prajñāpāramitā* assemblies. Below, [the text] investigates and explains the meaning behind the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma at three distinct times.
The reason the World-Honored One’s teachings at these three times differ is that he knew our inclinations and preferences were set upon the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), and not...
Being able to shoulder the family business of the Tathāgata, he employs various skillful means to lead and entice us so that we may enter the Buddha-wisdom.
Yet, we did not know that we were truly the sons of the Buddha; this is why we are called "pseudo-sons."
Now we have finally come to know that the World-Honored One has no begrudging or parsimony regarding the Buddha’s wisdom. Why is this?
Because although we have from the past been true sons of the Buddha, we have merely delighted in the lesser Dharma. Had we possessed a mind that delights in the Great [Dharma],...
The Buddha then taught the Mahāyāna Dharma for my sake. Within this sutra, he speaks only of the One Vehicle;
yet previously, in the presence of bodhisattvas, he disparaged those śrāvakas who delight in inferior teachings. Nevertheless, the Buddha truly uses the Mahāyāna to transform and guide beings.
Through these three periods, he has guided and encouraged me in many ways until this very day. The World-Honored One’s declaration was:
"I am truly your father; you are truly my son. All this wealth is indeed yours.
Only then did I realize that the Tathāgata had never been stingy with the Buddha-wisdom and failed to reveal it to me, nor had he ever begrudged the treasure-store and refused to grant it.
"Give it to me! Even I have never failed to be a true son of the Tathāgata.
However, because we delighted in the inferior dharmas favored by the poor and were unwilling to accept our responsibility, the Tathāgata did not entrust the treasure-store to us.
Had we possessed the aspiration for the Great [Vehicle] in the past, he would have long since entrusted the Tathāgata’s treasure-store to us; why wait until now?"
It is so today; thus, we have already long been failing the World-Honored One. Only today do we realize this.

Reflecting upon it, I see that not only does the World-Honored One preach only the Single Vehicle (ekayāna) within this sutra today, but even in the past, during the assemblies of the Vaipulya [sūtras], when he extolled the bodhisattvas and disparaged the śrāvakas, he was in fact teaching the Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas.

"You have taught and transformed us; yet because we were attached to and delighted in the lesser teachings, we were deluded and unaware, having no aspiration to seek this Mahāyāna. This is why we are called 'pseudo-sons.'"
Therefore, we say that originally our minds had no aspirations; yet now this great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously.
All that a son of the Buddha ought to obtain has already been obtained.

He said, "In the past, during the time of the *Āgamas*, I delighted in and were attached to the Lesser Dharma; therefore, I had no aspiration to seek it. During the time of the Vaipulya [sutras], I was despondent and thus did not seek it.
During the time of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, I considered it merely partial and thus did not seek it. I sought nothing at all, yet today I have suddenly received this prediction.
This is because, though I had no heart for seeking, the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived of its own accord. Thus it continues until now.
It was only upon this that he knew he was truly a son of the Buddha. When Master Dazhu first visited Mazu, Mazu asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "From Dayun Temple in Yuezhou. Mazu asked, "What do you intend to seek by coming here? He replied:
He came seeking the Buddha-dharma. The Patriarch said, "I have not a single thing here. What Buddha-dharma do you seek? You fail to look after your own precious treasury;
why do you abandon your home and wander about? He asked, "Which one is the precious treasury of Huihai?
The Patriarch said, "That which is asking me right now is your precious treasury. It is fully complete; there is nothing lacking."
It is few. When one attains mastery over its use, why rely on external seeking? The Master, upon hearing these words, recognized his own original mind;
this is precisely the model for obtaining the great treasure of the Dharma King.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Today we have heard the Buddha’s teaching; with joy and exultation, we have attained what we never had before. Thus has the Buddha spoken of the śrāvakas."
One shall attain Buddhahood; this unsurpassed mass of jewels is obtained spontaneously without seeking.

It is like a young boy who, being immature and ignorant, abandoned his father and fled, traveling far to another land and wandering through various countries for more than fifty years, while his father grieved and longed for him.
He searched in all four directions. Having grown weary from his search, he halted at a certain city and built a house. There he indulged himself in the five desires;
his family was immensely wealthy, possessing much gold and silver, mother-of-pearl and agate, pearls and lapis lazuli, as well as elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep.

With palanquins, carriages, and vehicles; with fields, estates, and servants; and with a vast multitude of people whose income and profit extended throughout other lands—there was no place where merchants and traders did not exist.
Surrounded and revered by thousands of millions of followers, he was always a king.
He was beloved and cherished by his ministers and noble clansmen, who all held him in high esteem and honored him. Because of these various circumstances, many people came and went to see him.
Thus wealthy and possessing great power, yet advanced in years, he grew increasingly anxious for his son, contemplating him day and night.
"The time of my death is approaching; my foolish son has abandoned me for over fifty years. As for the treasures and goods in the storehouse, what shall become of them?
We now provide a verse below to describe those who have attained awakening upon hearing the Buddha’s teachings; this refers to hearing an Arhat performing the work of a Buddha.
For example: A son turns his back on his father and flees; one person constantly forgets [his kin].
Abandoning his own biological father, he willingly becomes a beggar; discarding his native home and country, he wanders far away as a vagabond.

This refers to one who lacks faith and, despite being noble and honorable, willingly degrades himself to the status of a lowly person. His father—this refers to the Tathāgata—constantly remembers his son. One person constantly recalls [him].

As for "searching in all four directions," this refers to beating the drum to seek the man of Tang. As for "stopping in one city," it is precisely because he feared that the more he sought, the further away [the goal] would become;
therefore, he halted in one city to wait for him to come of his own accord. "Many various things" below refers to objects for his own use.
"Elephants, horses," and so forth, refer to objects for the benefit of others. "Beneficial for inhalation and exhalation" is a metaphor for what is... [beneficial].
The multitude of those he transforms is exceedingly great; that merchants and traders are found everywhere is a metaphor for the many people who are capable of transformation.
The "multitude of thousands of myriads of koṭis" refers to being surrounded by the eight classes of beings, including the nāgas and devas.

"Night and day thinking only that the time of death is approaching" means reflecting upon one's own appearance becoming withered and emaciated, with hair turning white and the face wrinkled, as *nirvāṇa* draws near.
He has arrived. As for how you should deal with the various goods stored in the treasury, I have been thinking of handing over my family estate, but I have not found the right person.
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing, traveling from town to town and from country to country; sometimes he obtained something.
Having obtained nothing, he became emaciated by hunger and malnutrition; sores and scabs broke out upon his body. Traveling by stages, he arrived at the city where his father resided.
Seeking employment through various means, he eventually reached his father’s house.
The son suddenly arrives at the gate. The preceding several lines provide a descriptive portrayal. The four lines beginning with "a poor child" describe the journeying of the impoverished son;
the two lines beginning with "hunger" describe his physical condition and demeanor.
As for the phrase "he eventually arrived," it means that he originally had no intention of reaching his father’s residence, but arrived there by chance while begging for food.
At that time, the elder had set up a great jeweled canopy within his gate.

Seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by his retinue and attended by his servants, some were calculating gold, silver, and precious objects, while others were recording the income and expenditure of his property in written ledgers.
The impoverished son saw his father, who was noble, wealthy, and majestic; he thought him to be a king or someone like a king.
Terrified and wondering at himself, he thought, "Why have I come here? If I remain for long, I may be coerced or forced into labor."
Having reflected thus, he ran off and inquired after a poor neighborhood, intending to go there to seek work as a hired laborer.
At that time, the elder was seated upon his lion throne; seeing his son from afar, he recognized him silently and immediately commanded his attendants to pursue and bring him back.

The impoverished son cried out in alarm; bewildered and distressed, he fell prostrate upon the ground, thinking, "This man has seized me; I shall certainly be put to death. Of what use are food and clothing that have brought me to this state?"
"At that time" and below describe the wealthy elder’s state of opulence. "The impoverished son" and below describe the poor son’s astonishment upon seeing his father.
"This king" and so forth means that the impoverished son did not recognize him as his father;
having missed him face-to-face, he mistakenly took his own father to be the king and the king’s kinsmen and retinue, and did not dare to approach or grasp him. On the contrary...
He was struck with terror. Those who are forced to labor against their will do not receive wages for their work.
As for those who hire themselves out in impoverished neighborhoods, it is said they abandon the delicacies of their own homes to seek the dregs of others' tables.
When the elder pursued him urgently, the son saw his father but did not recognize him, and so he was startled and marveled at himself; the father saw his son and recognized him silently. Thus...
"He is being pursued and brought here. This person, fearing that he will certainly be killed, is like one who, when a "night-light" is thrown at him, instinctively draws his sword.
"The impoverished son cried out in alarm," meaning he was filled with dread and remorse, saying: "Why did you provide me with food and clothing to bring me to this state?
He meant that he originally sought food and clothing to sustain his life, yet now he has instead come to this.
"To have clothing and food and yet be killed; to die despite having clothing and food—it would be better to live in hunger and cold.
Of what use are clothing and food, that they cause me to meet with such execution? These are the words of the impoverished son, expressing his self-reproach.
The elder, knowing that his son was foolish, narrow-minded, and inferior, did not believe his words nor recognize him as his father.

He therefore employed a skillful means and sent other men—those with squinting eyes, short stature, and unsightly appearance, lacking in majesty and virtue—saying to them: "You may tell him that he shall be hired by us."

"I shall remove all filth and excrement for you and pay you double the wage. When the impoverished son heard this, he was filled with joy and followed along. He cleared away the filth and excrement and cleaned the various rooms and dwellings.
This elder dispatched a person to employ skillful means to entice him. "The foolish" refers to those whose minds are not clear;

"the narrow-minded" refers to those whose capacity and measure are petty and shallow. He further sent another person who was one-eyed and short and ugly, meaning that he used one-eyed people to convert the one-eyed, and those who were short and ugly to convert the short and ugly—just like the intention of Queque when the State of Qi welcomed the State of Jin.
It is said: "I shall hire you and pay you double the wage; this is not like others who force one to labor.
Because he came following his own joyful wish, his initial alarm was transformed into joy.

From the window, the elder constantly saw his son; mindful that his son was foolish and inferior, delighting in base tasks, the elder thereupon put on tattered, soiled clothes, took up a dung-removal tool, went to where his son was, and by means of skillful means drew near him, speaking to him to urge him to work diligently.
Having increased your wages and provided you with oil for your feet, sufficient food and drink, and thick, warm bedding, he spoke these harsh words:
"You must work diligently. Yet, using gentle words as well, he said, "If you were like my own son," for the elder was wise and gradually allowed him to come and go.

After twenty years had passed, he was made to manage the household affairs; he was shown the gold, silver, pearls, crystal, and all other goods, and was ordered to know everything regarding their income and expenditure.
Yet he still remained outside the gate, lodging in a grass hut, thinking to himself of his poverty: "I possess none of these things."
"O Elder, he employs skillful means to draw near to him. One who delights in menial tasks does not delight in wealth and honor, but finds sweetness in being lowly and inferior.
Regarding the wearing of tattered and filthy garments and so forth: first, he causes those of similar status to lead him by the hook, and only then does the elder stoop down to approach him;
likewise, he takes up a vessel for filth and draws near to him. 'To draw near' means to attach oneself to his location."
One should draw near to his person so that others, upon seeing him, will not give rise to doubt. Applying oil to the feet is like the joy of preventing the hands from cracking;
it is for the purpose of moisturizing the feet. Having food and drink in abundance is for filling the belly.
Having thick and warm mats and bedding is for the ease of the body. "You should work diligently" means that all matters are fully prepared; you should [attend to them] as one.
The mind applies itself with diligent effort; this is a metaphor for the *Āgama* period.
Furthermore, using gentle words such as "if you are like my son" or "you are indeed my child," he further raises them and gives them the name "son"; this is a metaphor for the *Vaipulya* period.
Those who have managed household affairs for twenty years act as great stewards; this is precisely the time of transmitting the teachings within the assembly of Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who still remain outside the gate, dwelling in thatched huts, may indeed have encountered [the teaching], yet they are unwilling to take responsibility for it;
in the end, they remain separated by a single door, acting as outsiders. Question: Since those of the Hīnayāna have already transcended the three realms...
Why does he stay overnight in a grass hut? The answer is: although his afflictions (*kleśa*) are empty, his objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) have not yet been exhausted;
thus, though he has exited the gate of the burning house, he still stays overnight in a grass hut and has not yet entered the gate of the Tathāgata.
When he thinks to himself, "I am poor and lack this thing," it shows that his inferior mind has not yet been abandoned.

The father, knowing his son’s mind had gradually become broad and expansive, desired to bestow wealth upon him. He immediately assembled his kinsmen, the king, ministers, *kṣatriyas*, and householders;
before this great multitude, he declared: "This is my son. He abandoned me and went abroad, and fifty years have passed."
"It has been twenty years since I last saw my son. Long ago, in a certain city, I lost this son; I have traveled everywhere searching for him and have finally arrived here.
Whatever I possess—my house, my lands, and my people—I entrust entirely to him, to be used as he sees fit."
"He hands over the family estate" means that as [the son's] capacity gradually becomes vast, he grows weary of his former base activities.
"Saying 'this is my son'" means to declare that he is truly his son, rather than being merely like a son as was said previously.
"Since seeing this son come back twenty years ago" refers to the long narrative of clearing away filth for twenty years; this refers to the previous twenty years.
Years. These twenty years are the twenty years within the *Prajñāpāramitā* assembly. During the first twenty years, his mind was still fearful and timid;

because there were instances of concealment and evasion, he was unable to see [the Buddha]. During the latter twenty years, their minds accorded with one another through mutual trust and understanding.
"Coming and going was without hindrance; thus I have been able to see you. All that I possess, including my household affairs, I now entrust to you.
You recall your former poverty and your lowly aspirations; today, in the presence of your father, you have obtained great treasures as well as this house and estate."
Regarding all these riches and goods, he was filled with immense joy, having attained what he had never experienced before;
he attained the joy of his karma. He said, "In the past, I was a poor child who willingly dwelt in impoverished villages and alleys, seeking clothing and food.
Originally, I had no such thought as to attaining great treasures. Now, being in my father’s presence, I have obtained this great [wealth]."
"Rare treasures! All those things which I never possessed in the past are now all present. How could I not leap for joy and rejoice?
The Buddha is likewise; knowing that we delighted in the lesser [vehicle], he never previously said, 'You shall become Buddhas,' yet now he speaks to us."

Having attained the various outflows-free states and accomplished the Lesser Vehicle, the śrāvaka disciples are like the metaphor used for the Dharma. "The Buddha is also like this" means that the Buddha is like the elder;

As for being a son: because you knew that we delighted in inferior teachings, upon hearing it said that we would become Buddhas, you were immediately struck with fear.
For this reason, the World-Honored One likewise set us aside and did not distinguish that we possessed a share in the Tathāgata’s precious treasury;
instead, he caused me to clear away the dung of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), so that I might attain the untainted Dharma (*anāsrava-dharma*) and achieve liberation.
It is merely for human beings. This is the time for the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* [sūtras].
The Buddha has commanded us to expound the supreme path; those who practice this shall attain Buddhahood. Thus, I follow the Buddha’s teaching.

He was able to approach his father; although he knew all manner of things, his mind had no desire to take them. Although we preach the precious treasury of the Buddha-dharma, we ourselves likewise lack such aspiration.
This section corresponds to the assembly on Prajñāpāramitā, wherein he manages the affairs of the Dharma and acts as the Buddha’s representative to propagate the teaching.

Furthermore, we have attained internal cessation and considered ourselves sufficient; having understood only this matter, we believe there is nothing further.

All are entirely empty and quiescent; without birth and without cessation, without large and without small, without outflows and without conditioned action.

Abiding in our final bodies, there is now nirvana; the Buddha’s teaching has not been in vain, as we have attained the Way.

Thus we have already repaid the Buddha’s kindness. Within the three realms, I am a man who has brought his affairs to completion, a man of no-mind (*amati*).

I no longer know anything of the "great matter" (*mahā-kāraṇa*), nor of the Dharma for transforming bodhisattvas. Therefore, although I hear of purifying buddha-lands, it is like the wind passing over trees;
I feel no joy or delight whatsoever. The reason I do not feel such joy is precisely because I have thoroughly realized all things, both defiled and pure.
All phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent; therefore, they lack the characteristics of arising and ceasing, or of being great or small.
Because they are untainted and unconditioned, one purifies buddha-lands and transforms sentient beings;

yet because these involve non-emptiness, the presence of characteristics, and volitional activity, I have reflected upon them and find no cause for delight. That is to say, while knowing true emptiness, one does not know—
This is the "wondrous existence" (miao you). It accords with what the ancient masters said: "Do not say that 'no-mind' (wuxin) is the Way;
even no-mind is still separated by one further barrier. One day, while Yaoshan was sitting beside Shitou, Shitou asked him, "What are you doing here?
He replied, "I am doing nothing at all. Shitou said, "If that is so, then you are just sitting idly. The Master said, "If it were idle sitting..."
[The Master] said, "It is precisely 'acting'. [The monk] asked, "You say it is not acting; what is it that you do not act? [The Master] replied, "Not recognized by the thousand sages.

[The monk] then asked, "Tell me, is this non-action the same as or different from that [non-acting]? [The Master] said, "Although we have attained internal extinction (nirvāṇa), we still dwell in the long night."

They could not be enlightened regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, nor did they possess any aspiration for it. Furthermore, they considered themselves to have attained arhatship, believing it to be the ultimate dharma;
they also considered themselves to be in their final existence, believing they had fulfilled their duty of repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Because I reflected in this way, although I preached the Dharma to these bodhisattvas, I myself truly lacked any aspiration or delight [in that teaching].
Furthermore, the World-Honored One, knowing that my resolve was inferior, simply let me be and did not initially encourage me to advance.
Nor did He explain to me that He Himself truly possessed such benefits; He merely remained silent, intending for others to willingly take up the responsibility themselves.

Therefore, I was unaware of it and had no aspiration or joy [in it]. As in the verse beginning with "Like a wealthy man," this praises the prior application of skillful means and the subsequent entrustment of the household.
This is the karmic result. The Buddha also provides a downward analogy:
"We have today attained what we have never before experienced; it was not what we previously hoped for, yet now we have obtained it ourselves, just like that impoverished son."
We have obtained immeasurable treasures. World-Honored One, we have now attained the Way and its fruits; regarding the untainted Dharma, we have attained the pure eye.
Throughout the long night, we have upheld the Buddha’s pure precepts, and only today do we finally receive their retribution within the Dharma of the Dharma King.
Having long cultivated the pure conduct, we have now attained the untainted, supreme, and great fruit.
We are now truly śrāvakas, who cause all to hear by means of the sound of the Buddha-way. We are now truly arhats within all the worlds.

Among gods, humans, Māras, and Brahmās, you alone are universally worthy of receiving offerings. World-Honored One, by your great kindness and through this rare occurrence, you have compassionately taught and transformed us for our benefit.
Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, who could ever repay such a debt? Even by providing for you with hands and feet, we cannot do so.
Prostrating with one's head, making all manner of offerings—none of these can repay [the debt].

Even if one were to carry [the teacher] upon the crown of the head or bear him on both shoulders for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, honoring them with all one’s heart, and furthermore provide exquisite food, immeasurable precious garments, and various bedding;

Even if one were to offer various medicinal decoctions, ox-head sandalwood, and all manner of rare treasures to construct stūpas and temples, and spread precious robes upon the ground—performing such acts of worship for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—one could never repay [the debt] to the Buddhas, who possess rare, immeasurable, and boundless, inconceivable, great supernormal powers;
who are untainted and unconditioned; and who are the Kings of all dharmas.
Being able to act for those who are inferior, they endure these matters; for the sake of ordinary people who grasp at signs, they teach according to what is appropriate.

All Buddhas have attained supreme mastery over the Dharma; knowing the various inclinations and pleasures of all sentient beings, as well as their mental capacities and strengths, they teach according to what each can bear.
Using immeasurable metaphors, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, according to their roots of goodness from past lives.
Furthermore, having discerned through various considerations who has reached maturity and who has not, he teaches the three vehicles as appropriate within the single vehicle path.
"Congratulations on having attained it today. Regarding "attaining the Way," it means: "We previously attained the Eightfold Noble Path; now we have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
Previously we attained the fruit of a Śrāvaka; now we have attained the fruit of Bodhi. Previously we attained the outflow-free dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*);
now, within those outflow-free dharmas, we have further attained the Treasury of the Pure and Right Dharma-Eye. As for "previously... [the text continues].
"By upholding the Buddha’s pure and complete precepts, today we have obtained this great fruit of retribution.

Having long cultivated the pure and white Brahma-conduct, only today do we finally attain the unsurpassed, supreme fruit. Only today do we realize that those who were previously called Śrāvakas [were merely so in name]."
By hearing the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, one first attains self-benefit; yet such a person is not a true śrāvaka.
Now, by using the voice of the Buddha-way to cause all to hear, one is finally named a true śrāvaka. The arhats of former times severed the delusions of views and thought.

Having emerged from the suffering of the triple world, they considered this a great attainment; yet they did not believe in the Buddha-vehicle, were not true Arhats, nor disciples of the Buddha, and were not called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).

Today, having heard the Buddha-vehicle and realized the Tathāgatagarbha, they are worthy of receiving offerings from devas and humans, and only now can they be called true Arhats and true Worthy Ones of Offerings. Previously, they had considered themselves to abide in...
In this final body, with the attainment of *nirvāṇa* with remainder, I have already repaid the Buddha’s grace.

Only now do I realize that the Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One is something that cannot be fully requited. From time immemorial, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I had fallen into the fires of affliction.
Day and night they are scorched and boiled, dwelling within the cycle of birth and death. The World-Honored One, throughout immeasurable kalpas, has given rise to a heart of compassion;
furthermore, by means of various skillful expedients and gentle words, he guides, assists, and exhorts them, causing them to emerge from the burning house of afflictions.
I abide in the cool and quiescent state of nirvāṇa. For immeasurable kalpas, this Blessed One has truly performed great deeds for me.
Yet, although the Blessed One sees that I abide in nirvāṇa, I have not obtained the treasure-trove of the Tathāgata.
He revived various forms of compassionate concern for me. He entered immeasurable meditative absorptions to manifest them to me, and emitted immeasurable light to manifest it to me.
After emerging from concentration, he further instructed and transformed me with gentle words; yet I was unable to believe or understand.
He then used parables to lead me. Seeing my poverty, he further benefited me with the precious treasury of the Dharma King.
Such profound kindness is as vast as the great heavens and has no limit. Who can repay it?

Providing for one’s hands and feet—such as preparing soup and serving meals, performing manual labor and attending to one’s needs—or bearing them upon one’s head or shoulders: this means carrying them on the crown of the head or slinging them upon the back.
Even if one were to do so with the utmost devotion and respect throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one still could not repay their compassion.
This compassionate heart is but one ten-thousandth part [of what is required].

Even if one were to offer him stūpas and temples made of sandalwood and precious gems, spread jeweled robes upon the ground as a cushion for his feet, and provide the four requisites of life to sustain his daily needs; yet—
Even if one were to spend as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River, one could not repay even a ten-thousandth part of this.
[The passage] from "All Buddhas" below extensively praises the Buddha's kindness: All Buddhas possess inconceivable great supernormal powers and are Great Dharma Kings;
yet they are able to endure this without revealing themselves, casting off their precious robes to don tattered rags, and taking up a vessel of filth to associate with us. We—
He causes even those who are base and lowly to believe him with their whole hearts, entrusting them with his family estate.

Furthermore, he is able to take the signs of ordinary worldlings and, according to their individual capacities, bestow upon them the Dharma so that each may be cured of their deep-seated maladies and attain happiness.
Why is this? Because the Buddhas have realized all dharmas and know the faculties of sentient beings; thus they are able to bestow the Dharma according to those faculties as is appropriate.
Regarding the illness and the medicine, there is nothing that does not prove effective. The six subsequent lines explain the "knowing faculty" (*jñendriya*).
The first line and the second line explain the "bestowing of the Dharma. This indicates that the Tathāgata’s profound kindness is such that it can ultimately never be repaid.

Commentary by the Jinting Bhikṣu Tongrun on the Fifth Chapter, "The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs," Verse: The verse states: "The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world; He has manifested the Dharma of the Great Vehicle. The various kinds of medicinal herbs, Each obtain their nourishment according to their nature. The commentary says: "Various kinds of medicinal herbs" refers to the various types of sentient beings. "Obtain their nourishment according to their nature" means that although the water of the Dharma is one, the capacities of sentient beings are diverse; therefore, they receive its benefits according to their respective dispositions. This is because the Tathāgata’s great compassionate wisdom is impartial and equal toward all, yet it manifests according to the differences in the faculties of those to be transformed. Just as the sun and moon shine equally upon all things, yet the colors of the flowers they illuminate appear differently, so too does the Tathāgata’s Dharma-light shine universally, yet the capacities of sentient beings perceive it differently. Furthermore, just as the rain falls equally upon the earth, yet the roots of the various plants absorb it according to their own natures, so too does the Tathāgata’s Dharma-rain fall equally upon all, yet sentient beings receive its benefits according to their own capacities. Thus, although the Tathāgata’s Dharma is one, it appears as many according to the differences in the faculties of those to be transformed. This is why it is said that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world and manifested the Dharma of the Great Vehicle. Because the Tathāgata’s great compassionate wisdom is impartial and equal toward all, he manifests the Dharma of the Great Vehicle for all sentient beings. Therefore, it is known that the Tathāgata’s Dharma is truly the Great Vehicle. It is not that there is a separate vehicle apart from this; rather, it is precisely this Great Vehicle that is called the "Buddha-vehicle. Two trees and three types of grass, their roots and stems vastly unequal, All receive the rain at once, yet each sprouts its own shoots according to its lot.
Dense trees form a circular canopy; tender blossoms scatter like a brook.
Most pitiable are the duckweed and the water-rafts, Year after year submerged in the deep mud.

The Chapter on Parables (Upamāna-parivarta): For the sake of the four great disciples, this chapter uses parables to clarify that what was taught during the forty years prior—the three vehicles—was provisional, whereas what is taught today—the supreme One Vehicle—is the reality. The Chapter on Faith and Understanding (Adhimukti-parivarta):

In this chapter, the four great disciples receive and realize the intent behind the teachings of the three and the one. Although this chapter is composed as a dialogue with the four great disciples, [it serves to establish the truth].
He then shifts his previous intention, saying: "The Dharma I have taught during the forty years prior was all of the One Vehicle; fundamentally there were not three.
It is only because sentient beings possess three types of capacities that they perceive the Dharma as being threefold. Thus, the title of this chapter inherently contains two meanings:

namely, in terms of the capacities [of sentient beings] and in terms of the Dharma itself. Regarding the capacities, it refers to the three kinds of grasses and two kinds of trees, which represent the various spiritual lineages (*gotra*).
They are different; yet that which they produce and that which they moisten have never been anything other than one.
This is like the different seeds of the five vehicles, while the Dharma of the single characteristic and single flavor is fundamentally equal.

Now, although the chapter does not mention two types of trees but speaks only of medicinal herbs, this precisely reveals that during the forty years [of his teaching], the Tathāgata truly and equally rained down the Dharma-rain of the Mahāyāna.
[The rain] falls and sprinkles. However, because the nature of those medicinal herbs is inferior, they receive moisture only according to their own capacity; they are self-centered and narrow-minded.
It is not that the Dharma-rain has partiality; therefore, the subsequent passage says: "Though grown from the same earth and moistened by the same rain, each of the grasses and trees differs.
Regarding the Dharma, this refers to all that was taught during the forty years [of his ministry].

The Dharma is entirely composed of sublime medicinal verses (*gāthā*) capable of healing all chronic and terminal illnesses. Merely by touching it with the mouth or moistening the lips, one gains benefit.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "The Tathāgata observes that sentient beings are infinite in number, their faculties being either sharp or dull, and their diligence either vigorous or lax;
according to what each can endure, he preaches the Dharma for them, causing them all to rejoice and find joy."
This is what is meant by "attaining a wholesome benefit. Because it possesses these two meanings, it is given this name.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa and the other great disciples: "Excellent, excellent, Kāśyapa!"

"You have well expounded the true merits of the Tathāgata; it is exactly as you have said. Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits, which you could not exhaustively describe even in immeasurable billions of kalpas.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all Dharmas; whatever he speaks is never false."
"Your excellent exposition of the Tathāgata’s true merits is indeed as you have said. That is to say, the true merits of the Tathāgata cannot be fully proclaimed by words;

yet, what you have cited—of the elder who began [his search] but stopped midway at a city to wait for his son, who constantly felt regret and longing for his son, who dispatched others to pursue his son, and who sprinkled cold water to revive his son—is precisely it."
He employed skillful means to entice his son; he wore soiled garments to draw near to him; he held a refuse vessel to stay close to him;
he urged him to work diligently to encourage him; he treated him like rice or flour to settle him; he never deceived or showed negligence to praise him; he worked alongside him to honor him;

and he brought out various treasures to show them to him, until finally their hearts were in accord and they trusted one another, while [the father] himself looked back upon his former ways with self-reproach.
[The Buddha said: "Excellent! You have first established the foundation of the mind, and then exhausted your family estate to entrust it to your son. Such a description truly captures my own mind;
it is indeed a well-spoken discourse. However, this too is merely called a 'well-spoken discourse' because it accords with the scope of your own mental capacity—what can be known and reached by you."
"You do not know that the Tathāgata still possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits, which you could not exhaustively describe even in immeasurable billions of kalpas.
It is not the case that the true merits of the Tathāgata are merely as you have described."

This sentence serves as the foundation for this chapter and is also the thematic outline for the "Chapter on the City of Transformation. From the passage beginning with "Kāśyapa," there is an exhortation to believe:
it states that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas, and that every single word and syllable is true speech;
therefore, one must not fail to give rise to deep reverence and faith.
Regarding all phenomena, he expounds them through wisdom and skillful means. All that he teaches reaches the ground of omniscience.
The Tathāgata perceives the ultimate destination of all phenomena and knows the deep mental activities of all sentient beings with unimpeded penetration.
Furthermore, having thoroughly investigated and clearly understood all phenomena, he reveals them to others.
Regarding the "all-encompassing wisdom of sentient beings" and why it is said that the Tathāgata’s merits cannot be fully described:

this is because all the mundane and supramundane dharmas taught by the Tathāgata during the forty years prior [to his final teaching] were none other than the application of wisdom and skillful means according to the capacities [of beings].

He expounds the teaching according to their dispositions; yet all that he teaches is of a single characteristic and a single flavor, being nothing other than the desire to cause all sentient beings to reach the stage of the Tathāgata’s omniscience.
In truth, there are no so-called three vehicles. "The Tathāgata" (below) refers to the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the Dharma; that is to say, the Tathāgata knows the ten wholesome paths of action.

To teach the Dharma to humans and devas and to cause them to know the Four Noble Truths is the teaching of the Hīnayāna. To know the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination is the teaching of the Mahāyāna.
To know the Six Perfections is the teaching of the Bodhisattva. Even down to teaching all various other dharmas, he fully understands them all;
each has its ultimate point of resolution. Furthermore, "knowing the lower" refers to the Tathāgata’s knowledge of capacities (*indriya*). Moreover, he knows...
The ten wholesome paths are the practice of the profound resolve of humans and devas. The Four Noble Truths are the practice of the profound resolve of those of the Small Vehicle.
The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are the practice of the profound resolve of Pratyekabuddhas. The Six Perfections are the practice of the profound resolve of Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, he knows all that is practiced by beings of various classes through their profound resolve, without any obstruction. Moreover—
"One who has thoroughly investigated and clearly understood all phenomena" means one who has reached the ultimate reality of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"One who reveals all wisdom to sentient beings" means revealing the equal wisdom of the Buddha. This indicates that the Tathāgata knows both the capacities [of beings] (*nairmāṇika*) and the Dharma;
therefore, he is able to reveal the equal wisdom of the Buddha amidst diverse capacities. Question: Regarding the capacities of sentient beings...
Since there are differences [among sentient beings], why does the Tathāgata employ the Buddha-wisdom of equality? Answer:
Although their capacities (*indriya*) differ, the wisdom they possess is equal and without distinction.

If one were to claim that because capacities differ, wisdom also differs, then every phenomenon would be distinct; in that case, the Tathāgata could not be called "ultimately and clearly enlightened. Furthermore...
One must not say that he "reveals all-encompassing wisdom. This wisdom is possessed by all sentient beings; it is equal in every thing. Only the Buddha has exhausted it;
only the Buddha understands it clearly. Therefore, whenever he opens his mouth or moves his tongue, there is nothing that does not reveal this Dharma to others.
Because you have not yet exhausted it and have not yet understood it clearly, you claim that the Tathāgata’s Dharma exists [as something separate].

How could a crow ever fully know the merits of the Tathāgata? Therefore, although you may be called "skilled speakers" regarding the true merits of the Tathāgata, you have not yet reached the end of describing them.

Kāśyapa, it is like this: suppose there were mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands within a trichiliocosm, producing various kinds of plants, trees, thickets, forests, and medicinal herbs, each with different species and distinct names and forms.

Then, dense clouds spread out, completely covering the trichiliocosm, raining down equally all at once, so that their moisture universally saturates the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, and all [other things].
Medicinal herbs—those with small branches and small stalks, small branches and small leaves; those with medium roots and medium stalks, medium branches and medium leaves;

and those with large roots and large stalks, large roots and large leaves—all trees, great and small, according to their superior, middling, or inferior natures, each receives its share. Though rained upon by a single cloud, they grow in accordance with their respective seed-natures, blossoming with flowers and bearing fruit.

Although they are produced from the same ground, [they differ]... one... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a larger passage, likely from a Mahāyāna sūtra such as the *Lotus Sūtra*. The translation reflects the available portion.)
Moistened by the rain, yet each of the grasses, trees, and shrubs has its own distinctions.
This metaphor is established to clarify that within the diverse capacities of sentient beings, the Buddha’s wisdom is shown to be equal.

The mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands represent the innate nature (*prakṛti*) upon which the five vehicles are based; the various flowers, trees, thickets, forests, and medicinal herbs represent the five vehicles themselves.

The nature of the stage of cultivation (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*) arises from the first ground. The three types of grass and two types of trees serve as a metaphor for the fact that the nature-ground (*prakṛti-bhūmi*) is one, yet it is divided into the five vehicles (*pañca-yāna*) due to the seeds of cultivation.
"The dense clouds descend" serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata manifesting his body to universally shelter sentient beings, just as a great cloud covers the entire world.
"At one time" serves as a metaphor for the Tathāgata preaching with the wisdom of equality.
The Dharma of equality universally benefits all sentient beings, just as seasonal rain equally nourishes all grasses and trees.

The phrase "grasses and trees" below serves as a metaphor for the root-natures of the five vehicles; according to their superior, middling, or inferior capacities, each receives the equal rain of the Dharma.
The phrase "a single cloud" below serves as a metaphor for the persons of the five vehicles who, receiving the equal rain of the Dharma, produce sprouts according to their habitual seeds.

The sprouts emerge, the flowers bloom, and the fruits form, each being distinct. Although they are "one" [in their origin], this serves as a metaphor for how the five vehicles all abide together within the ground of equality and equally receive the rain of the single flavor of the Dharma;
yet, according to their respective habitual seeds (*vāsanā-bīja*), there are differences, which do not arise from any difference in their fundamental nature.
As the Sixth Patriarch said: "The mind-ground contains all seeds; when the rain falls universally, they all grow."
This is precisely what is meant by "germination. This single metaphor captures with extreme clarity the World-Honored One’s intention in preaching the Dharma with impartiality.

Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is likewise so: appearing in the world like the rising of a great cloud, he uses a great voice to pervade the world of devas, humans, and asuras, just as that great cloud completely covers the three thousandfold world system.

In a great assembly across a thousand lands, he proclaimed these words: "I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

I shall cause those who have not crossed over to cross; I shall cause those who have not been liberated to be liberated; I shall cause those who have not found peace to find peace; I shall cause those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain it."
"May they attain nirvāṇa. Know this as it truly is: in this world and in future worlds, I am the all-knowing one, the all-seeing one;
I am the knower of the path, the opener of the path, and the proclaimer of the path. You, the assembly of devas, humans, and *ārhat*s, should all come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
At that time, countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings came to the Buddha.

They come to hear the Dharma. At that time, the Tathāgata observes the sharpness or dullness of these sentient beings' faculties, their diligence or indolence, and according to what they are capable of, he preaches the Dharma for them in various and immeasurable ways, causing them all to rejoice and swiftly obtain excellent benefit.
When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma, they will enjoy peace and security in the present life and be reborn in favorable realms in the future, experiencing happiness through the Path.
They shall also hear the Dharma; having heard it, they will be freed from all obstacles and, within the various teachings, act according to their own capacity.
Gradually they enter the Path, just as that great cloud rains upon all the grasses, shrubs, forests, and medicinal herbs, which,
according to their respective natures, fully receive its moisture and each attains growth.
This applies the Dharma to the analogy. "Just as a great cloud arises" corresponds to the dense clouds spreading everywhere.
"With great [rain]" and so forth corresponds to the simultaneous and equal pouring down, whereby the moisture universally permeates all. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* also says:
"For example, when the Dragon King Manasvin intends to send down rain, he does not do so immediately; first he raises a great cloud that completely covers the void."
It remained suspended for seven days, waiting for all sentient beings to complete their labors. After the seven days had passed, it sent down a fine rain that universally moistened the great earth.
The Tathāgata is also like this: when he is about to let fall the rain of the Dharma, he does not do so immediately.
First, he raises the Cloud of Dharma to bring sentient beings to maturity; once they have matured, he then universally showers the nectar-like rain of the Dharma.
"Singing below" refers to the so-called Great Sound. This means that those who have not yet attained the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata—
I cause those who have not yet crossed over to cross; I cause those who do not yet understand the impartial Dharma of all Buddhas to understand it;
I cause those who harbor doubts and regrets and have not yet attained peace of mind to find peace; and I cause those who remain within affliction and have not yet attained nirvana to attain it.
I cause them to attain these four dharmas, which may be attained in this life or in future lives;

I know them all truly, namely, knowing the opportune moment (*kāla*) and knowing the dharma. As for my being "inferior" [to others], I further explain the reason why I am known as one who knows the opportune moment and knows the dharma:
one who possesses all-knowledge is endowed with the four wisdoms (*jñāna*), and one who possesses all-seeing is endowed with the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*). By virtue of possessing...
Possessing the four wisdoms and five faculties, he is thus able to know this path for himself and further to reveal and explain it to others.
He can cause those who have not crossed over to cross over; those who have not been liberated to be liberated; those who have not attained peace to find peace;

and those who have not attained [realization] to attain it. "You all, come down" refers to summoning them to approach. "For the sake of hearing" refers to summoning and addressing them with a single voice; therefore, it is called "Great."

"Multitudes of clouds" refers to the gathering of rain. "The Tathāgata descends" refers to observing the faculties [of sentient beings]. "Accordingly" refers to providing instruction. For those who are diligent, he teaches the Six Perfections;
for those who are indolent, he teaches the Four Noble Truths; for those with sharp faculties, he teaches the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;

and for those with dull faculties, he teaches the Dharma of humans and devas, and so forth. Although this is the observation of capacities and the provision of instruction, it is none other than [the manifestation of the Buddha's power].
All these are the equal rain of the Dharma; thus, they cause immeasurable sentient beings to give rise to joy and obtain wholesome benefit.
This corresponds to how [plants] each receive the rain according to the size of their roots and stems. These various [beings] below correspond to receiving the rain and thereby growing.
For example, when people hear of the ten wholesome actions, they are immediately able to accept and uphold them, attaining peace in the present life.
[The practitioner] vanishes. In future lives, by relying on the power of the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma*), they are reborn in the heavens.

Through this cultivation and growth of the seeds of the ten wholesome actions, they again experience the fruits of happiness. While in the heavens, they further hear the Dharma of the ten wholesome actions;

through the power of this cultivation of the wholesome Dharma within the celestial realms, it grows even more in subsequent lives, becoming free from all obstacles. Such is the nature of the ten wholesome actions.
The same applies to other phenomena. It is thus for humans and devas, and likewise for the three vehicles.
Within all dharmas, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma according to the capacity and capability of each being, causing their seeds to be perfumed and to grow.
Entering the Way gradually is like this. As stated below, the analogy may be understood by applying it to the Dharma.

When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, it has a single characteristic and a single flavor; that is to say, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, and the characteristic of cessation, ultimately reaching all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
If there are sentient beings who, hearing the Tathāgata’s Dharma, uphold, read, recite, and practice it according to the teaching—
They practice, yet they do not themselves perceive or know the merit they have attained. Why is this?

Only the Tathāgata knows these sentient beings—their seeds, characteristics, and essential natures; what they contemplate, what they reflect upon, and what they cultivate; and how they contemplate and how they reflect.
How does one cultivate? By means of what dharma does one maintain mindfulness? By means of what dharma does one contemplate? By means of what dharma does one cultivate?
By means of what dharma does one attain what dharma? Sentient beings abide in various stages; only the Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are, with clarity and without obstruction.
It is like the various plants, groves, forests, and medicinal herbs, which do not themselves know their own superior, middling, or inferior natures. As it is said:

They have come to know this Dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor—namely, the characteristic of liberation, the characteristic of detachment, the characteristic of cessation, ultimate nirvana, the characteristic of eternal quiescence, which ultimately returns to emptiness. Having known this, the Buddha observes the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings and protects them;
for this reason, he does not immediately teach them the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). "O Kāśyapa, this is truly rare."
There are those who can understand the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate; they can believe it and accept it. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate, and this is difficult to comprehend and difficult to know.

The following section clarifies that the Tathāgata knows the Dharma and knows the capacities [of sentient beings], and is thus able to apply the Dharma to those capacities. First, it clarifies his knowledge of the Dharma:
the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata is such that every phenomenon is as-it-is (tathatā), sharing one and the same characteristic; every single thing is thoroughly moistened.
It is of one and the same flavor. Because sentient beings are moistened by the rain of the Dharma and thereby transcend their fetters, this very Dharma is called the "characteristic of liberation.
Because they are moistened by the rain of the Dharma and depart from the twelve links of dependent origination, this very Dharma is called the "characteristic of detachment.

Because they are moistened by the rain of the Dharma and attain quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), this very Dharma is called the "characteristic of quiescent extinction. Although there are three names, its [essential nature]—
In the end, all reach the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes; this is what is meant by the "one-flavor Chan" that is the ultimate source.
Therefore, the Great Sūtra says: "For example, all waters are of one flavor; it is only because they follow the differences of their containers that the water appears to have distinctions."
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is of but a single flavor; yet, because the mental capacities of sentient beings differ, it appears with immeasurable distinctions.
This is how the Tathāgata perceives and knows the ultimate destination of all phenomena. As for those who are inferior...
Next, I shall clarify the knowledge of capacities. It is said that when sentient beings hear the Dharma and achieve the Way with all virtues complete, they do not perceive this themselves;

it is known only by the Tathāgata. Regarding "species, characteristics, essence, and nature": "species" refers to the seeds of perfuming; "characteristics" refers to the beauty or ugliness of the retribution received;
"essence" refers to the distinctness of individual physical forms; and "nature" refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral natures. This is the knowledge of sentient beings.
This concerns past matters. What matters are they recollected? For example, recollecting the enjoyment of bliss received in the heavens, or the desire to be born in the heavens, and so forth.

How are they recollected? It means knowing the reason for what is being recollected; for instance, because one feels weary of the suffering experienced among humans, one recollects the bliss of the heavens, and so forth.
By means of what dharma are they recollected? It means by means of which dharma one is subsequently able to be born in the heavens.
When mindfulness is thus, so too are reflection and cultivation. As it is among the devas, so it is for the three vehicles.
This is knowing the present affairs of sentient beings. Regarding "by what dharma one obtains what dharma":
as one cultivates such causes in the present, one will necessarily receive such fruits in the future. This is knowing the future affairs of sentient beings. By means of sentient beings...
The various stages at each location, I truly do not know; only the Tathāgata knows them.

That is to say, the Tathāgata also knows all that is practiced within the profound mind, penetrating it without obstruction in this manner. As indicated below, the analogy may be understood by applying it to the Dharma.
From "The Tathāgata" onwards, the three sections clarify how the Dharma is applied according to the capacity of the recipient. The Tathāgata fully understands the three...
These characteristics are, in fact, a single characteristic; they ultimately converge upon the primary truth that, from the beginning, there is no thing—this is the great emptiness of noble wisdom.
Because the Tathāgata knows this one dharma, he observes that the spiritual dispositions (*gotra*) of sentient beings are not the same and their inclinations differ.

Fearing that they might be unable to bear the burden, he protected and guarded them; therefore, although he secretly expounded [the truth] with a single voice, he did not immediately reveal it to them.

He waited until their faculties were mature before speaking. This is what is meant by "having thoroughly investigated and fully understood all dharmas, he reveals them to all sentient beings" regarding universal wisdom.
From the words "You all... onwards, the text concludes with praise for those who are suited to receive the teaching.
The true merits of the Tathāgata are such that they could not be fully exhausted even by speaking for immeasurable kalpas.
Yet, you have been able to believe and accept them upon hearing this single parable. Because the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, know that this is most rare.
Why is this? The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand and difficult to know; that you are now able to believe it is truly marvelous.
To be able to receive [this teaching]—is this not most rare?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Dharma King who destroys existence has appeared in the world; according to the desires of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma in various ways. The Tathāgata is worthy of honor."

This wisdom is profound and far-reaching. For a long time, I have kept this essential teaching in silence, not seeking to proclaim it hastily. Those with wisdom who hear it will be able to believe and understand;
those without wisdom will harbor doubt and regret, thereby suffering eternal loss. Therefore, Kāśyapa, I teach according to circumstances, employing various skillful means.
This causes them to attain right view.

The first four lines of the verse praise expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). "Destroying existence" (*bhava-bhaṅga*) has two meanings: first, it refers to destroying the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*) and thereby emerging from the triple world;
second, it refers to manifesting within the mundane world while destroying the sentient beings' grasping at existence. Thus it is said:
The Tathāgata shatters the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) and manifests within the world to preach various dharmas;

this is nothing more than following the inclinations of beings to free them from attachment, remove their fetters, and destroy their sense of existence. From the very beginning, he has never bestowed any real dharma upon others.
For the Tathāgata is the teacher of the triple world and the father of the four modes of birth; as venerable as Mount Sumeru and as weighty as the nine [mountains].
The Tripod: The wisdom he has attained is profound, firm, deep, and far-reaching, like the great ocean that is difficult to fathom, or like space that is difficult to measure.
Therefore, in every word and every movement, there must be the proper time for its manifestation; he is unwilling to leak it lightly.

For this reason, during the forty years [of his ministry], he remained silent for a long time and did not strive to speak hastily. Why was this? Because only when the faculties were mature and the vessels were pure [could he teach].
Once it enters the faculty of hearing, one is able to believe and enter [the path] immediately, never again to regress. If those of shallow faculties and small wisdom hear it, they will surely doubt;
having doubted, they will surely regret; having regretted, they will surely slander; and having slandered, they will surely fall into the evil realms.
For such people, not only do they fail to attain [it], but they suffer eternal loss. This is because the Tathāgata does not employ his impartial Buddha-wisdom [for them].

He swiftly bestows [the Dharma] upon others; thus, through gradual refinement and permeation, day by day and month by month, he causes them to abandon partiality and deviance and attain the right eye.
This is why the Tathāgata is called the Dharma King who shatters existence.
Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like a great cloud arising in the world, covering everything. This cloud of wisdom contains moisture;
its lightning flashes with brilliant radiance, and its thunder resounds afar, bringing joy to all beings. It eclipses the sunlight, making the earth cool and refreshing.
It hangs down in dense, pervasive clouds as if one could grasp it; the rain falls equally everywhere, streaming down in immeasurable torrents from all four directions.

The entire realm is thoroughly saturated. In mountains, rivers, precipitous valleys, and remote recesses, all that grows—herbs, trees, medicinal plants, and various species of flora, both large and small;
the hundred grains, sprouts, and crops, including sugarcane and grapes—all are made abundant and sufficient by the moisture of the rain. Even the parched lands are everywhere moistened.
The medicinal herbs grow lush and abundant. From that cloud issues water of a single flavor, which the grasses, trees, and forests receive as nourishment according to their respective capacities.
All the trees—whether superior, middling, or inferior—each attain growth and development in accordance with their size, including their roots, stems, branches, and leaves.

Regarding the flowers and fruits and their radiant colors, wherever a single rain falls upon them, they all attain freshness and luster. According to their respective forms and characteristics, and the size of their natures and capacities, though the moisture that nourishes them is one and the same, each flourishes and thrives in its own way.

This verse describes the dense spreading of clouds. "The cloud of wisdom contains moisture" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which fully encompasses the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Its sharp spiritual edge is like lightning; hence it is said that "the flash of lightning dazzles. His Dharma discourse is like thunder.
Therefore it is said that the sound of thunder resounds afar; the sixty-two kinds of heterodox lights do not appear, hence it is said that the sunlight is eclipsed;
the ninety-eight kinds of feverish afflictions are all eliminated, hence it is said that the earth is cool and refreshing; he manifests his body in the world.
Like clouds and vapors hanging and spreading, it is said: "Suspended and diffused. Humans may attain equality with them, yet they cannot be intermingled with them;
thus it is said: "As if one could grasp them. The four lines concerning the rain praise how, at one and the same time, the moisture falls equally and its benefits are universally pervasive.
The fourteen lines beginning with "mountains and rivers" praise how the various plants, trees, and forests each receive their portion according to their nature.

Furthermore, the phrase "the dry land is universally moistened" is a metaphor for the fact that not only do those with faith receive the nourishment of the Dharma, but even those without faith receive its benefit.
The four lines beginning with "All... eulogize how [beings] attain growth, flowers, and fruit in accordance with their nature.
The eight lines beginning with "Roots and stems... eulogize how, despite the same ground and the same rain, there are differences according to each seed-nature.
It is distinct.
The Buddha is also like this. His appearance in the world is like a great cloud that universally covers all things.
