Having appeared in the world, he expounds and explains for the sake of all sentient beings the reality of all dharmas. The Great Sage, the World-Honored One, [acts thus] toward all devas and humans.

In the midst of all the assemblies, he proclaimed these words: "I am the Tathāgata, the Honored One among two-legged beings, who has appeared in the world like a great cloud to moisten and nourish all withered sentient beings, causing them all to leave suffering behind and attain peaceful, secure happiness."
The pleasures of the world and the bliss of nirvana—let all you hosts of devas and humans listen with single-minded devotion!
You should all come here to behold the Unsurpassed Honored One. I am the World-Honored One, whom none can equal; I have appeared in this world to bring peace and security to all sentient beings.
The first four lines correspond to the great clouds covering everywhere. Having produced the following four lines, they correspond to the uttering of a great sound.
The phrase "the Great Sage" refers precisely to this great sound. As for the term "withered sentient beings," it refers to those who have not yet been moistened by the rain of the Dharma.
"Attaining peaceful and secure bliss" means causing those with doubts and regrets to attain peace of mind. "Worldly bliss" refers to...
The four dhyānas and eight samādhis. As for the bliss of nirvāṇa, it is the bliss of quiescent extinction. The eight lines beginning with "all the devas" are a summons to the great assembly.
He speaks for the sake of the great assembly:
the pure Dharma of ambrosia. This Dharma is of a single flavor: liberation and nirvāṇa. With this one wondrous voice—

I expound this meaning to constantly serve as a causal condition for the Mahāyāna. I observe that all things are universally equal, without distinction between self and other, and without a heart of attachment or aversion.
I am free from greedy clinging and likewise without obstruction; I always act for the sake of all beings.
He preaches the Dharma with impartiality; as he does for one person, so it is for many. He constantly expounds the Dharma, never engaging in other affairs.

Whether walking, coming, sitting, or standing, he is never weary or fatigued. He satisfies the world like rain that universally moistens all, regardless of whether they are noble or humble, high or low.
Whether they uphold the precepts or violate them, whether their deportment is complete or incomplete, whether they hold right view or wrong view, and whether they possess sharp or dull faculties—
to all of these he rains down the rain of Dharma equally, without weariness.
This verse describes the Tathāgata’s impartial preaching of the Dharma, which is like a uniform downpour that universally moistens all things.
Regarding the term "ambrosial Dharma" (*amṛta-dharma*): it is so called because it can eliminate the feverish afflictions and thirst of sentient beings.

Below the word "liberation" (*vimukti*), it is stated that the liberation and *nirvāṇa* taught to the three vehicles in the past were all expounded with a single voice; there are not two. It is always thus.
Regarding that which serves as the causal condition for the Mahāyāna, it is said that entering the Mahāyāna is the foundation.
"I observe," and so forth, means that the reason I preach the Dharma with impartiality is that I observe all sentient beings as being fully endowed with the nature of equality;
therefore, I have no mind of attachment or aversion toward this or that, and I constantly preach for the sake of all.
The Dharma of equality does not distinguish between one person and many; rather, it teaches and exhorts with this very matter tirelessly and without weariness.
It causes those who seek the Dharma to be fully satisfied according to their respective capacities, so that they depart empty-handed but return with reality.
This is just like a rain of a single flavor that universally moistens all things. The eight lines beginning with "noble and base" are as follows:
These are the capacities reached by the rain of Dharma.
All sentient beings who hear my Dharma receive it according to their capacity, dwelling in the various stages or abiding among humans and devas.

The universal wheel-turning kings, Śakra, and the various Brahmā kings are like minor medicinal herbs. Those who know the outflow-free dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), are able to attain *nirvāṇa*, give rise to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), and obtain the three insights (*trividyā*);
dwelling alone in mountain forests, constantly practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they attain the realization of a *pratyekabuddha*.
Among these, those medicinal herbs who seek the state of a World-Honored One, thinking "I shall become a Buddha," and who practice the concentration of diligence, are the superior medicinal herbs.

Furthermore, those sons of the Buddhas who single-mindedly focus on the Buddha-way, constantly practicing loving-kindness and compassion, and who know for themselves that they will become Buddhas with certainty and without doubt—[these are the great medicinal herbs].

These are called small trees. Those who dwell securely in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), turn the wheel of non-retrogression, and deliver immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings—such Bodhisattvas are called great trees.
The Buddha teaches with impartiality, like a rain of a single flavor, according to the dispositions of sentient beings.
What they receive differs, just as those grasses and trees each receive their nourishment differently.

This [passage] below explains that the reception of the Dharma differs according to the faculties and natures [of the practitioners]. "Abiding in the lower" refers to hearing the Dharma and remaining in the vehicles of humans or devas;
these are called "small grasses. "Knowing the lower" refers to hearing the Dharma and attaining the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. These are called...
The middle section. Seeking the world below. Practicing the six perfections while looking toward the Buddha to seek the Buddha is the superior section.
Furthermore, "various below" refers to seeking the Buddha beneath one's own heels rather than seeking it elsewhere; this is the small tree.
"Abiding securely below" means attaining the mutual functioning of the six sense organs, partially realizing the emptiness of dharmas, and delivering immeasurable multitudes.

This refers to those of great capacity. The Buddha levels himself down; in conclusion he declares that the Buddha equally teaches the Dharma of a single flavor, yet the reception of it by sentient beings is as diverse as this.

The Buddha uses this analogy as a skillful means to reveal and instruct; through various words and phrases, he expounds upon a single dharma, which, compared to the wisdom of a Buddha, is like a single drop in the ocean.

This concludes the response to Kāśyapa. When he says, "I today [rain down] with the Dharma-rain of equal single flavor, universally moistening all," this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s various causes and conditions, parables, and skillful means used to expound the One Dharma.
They deliver immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to attain the impartial wisdom of a Buddha.
Nevertheless, when compared with the profound Buddha-wisdom realized by the Tathāgata, it is just like using a single drop of water to illustrate the great ocean.
Such is the Buddha’s wisdom; even I cannot express even ten thousandth of a part of it, so how could you possibly do so?
This should be placed below the section on "Attaining the Realization of Each."
I rain down the rain of Dharma, filling the world. This Dharma of a single flavor is practiced according to one's capacity;
just as the medicinal herbs and various trees in that forest grow more lush and beautiful, each according to its size, so too the Dharma of all Buddhas is always of a single flavor.
He causes all the worlds to attain universal sufficiency; through gradual cultivation, they all attain the fruits of the Way.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas dwelling in mountain forests, abiding in their final bodies, hear the Dharma and attain the fruits. These are called medicinal herbs, each attaining growth.
If there are bodhisattvas whose wisdom is firm and stable, who thoroughly understand the three realms, and who seek the Supreme Vehicle, they are called "small trees" that attain growth.
Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna, attain supernatural powers, and upon hearing that all phenomena are empty, experience great joy in their hearts.
It emits countless rays of light, delivering all sentient beings; this is called a great tree that attains growth.
In this way, Kāśyapa, the Dharma taught by the Buddha is like a great cloud: with rain of a single flavor, it moistens the flowers of humanity, each of which attains its fruit.
From this point downward, they shall collectively receive the rain of the Dharma and flourish, blossoming into flowers and forming fruit.
"Practicing according to one's capacity" means to act within the limits of one's own ability. "Gradually increasing in lushness and beauty" means gradually attaining entry into the Path.
"The medicinal herbs grow" refers to the beginning: hearing the Dharma of the Four Truths, severing birth and death, and realizing nirvana, thereby attaining the fruits of the Path.
Having heard the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, they severed all conditions and realized the supreme nature.
To attain the fruit of the Way, they have now attained the unsurpassed great fruit; they are true śrāvakas and true pratyekabuddhas—is this not growth?
As for those who grow like small trees, they initially knew for themselves that they would become Buddhas, resolving it with certainty and without doubt; now their wisdom is firm and eternal.
They are without regression and are further able to realize that the three realms are like flowers in the sky. Seeking the Supreme Vehicle, they do not give rise to fear or退缩 (shrinkback);

is this not growth? As for those who grow through great rain, they first abide in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), dwell in the samādhi of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*), and attain mastery over the mind.
Yet, they are unwilling to deliver sentient beings. The Tathāgata then employs the three bridges and seven exhortations to preach the Dharma for them.
The mind becomes empty and filled with great joy, immediately able to emit light and deliver immeasurable multitudes; is this not growth?
Thus, the following section summarizes both the Dharma and the analogy. Regarding the phrase "moistening humans and flowers so that each attains fruition":
it means that the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma of a single flavor, enabling all sentient beings to receive the flavor of the Dharma and each realize the fruit of the Path, just like a great cloud.
With a rain of a single flavor, it universally moistens all shrubs, trees, and medicinal herbs; this is called attaining the blossoming of flowers and the ripening of fruit.
Kāśyapa, you should know that using various causes and conditions and diverse parables to reveal the Buddha-way is my skillful means.
The Buddhas are likewise. Now, for your sake, I shall declare the most ultimate truth: none of you among the assembly of śrāvakas have attained final nirvāṇa;
the path you have practiced is the bodhisattva path. By gradually training and studying it, you shall all become Buddhas.

This earnest exhortation is intended to strengthen their faith. I declare that throughout forty years, by means of various causes, conditions, and parables, I have taught the Dharma solely to reveal and point toward the path of the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
For forty years, I had not yet fully disclosed it; therefore, today I speak to you of the most ultimate reality. All the [śrāvakas]...
"O assembly, you have hitherto sat waiting for nirvana and accomplished not a single thing; this is not true extinction.

You should know that all activities performed in daily life—bending, turning, bowing, looking up, picking up the spoon, and grasping the chopsticks—are all the magnificent great path of the Bodhisattvas.
You should gradually practice and study from this point on, until your merit is perfected and your conduct fulfilled."
Only upon attaining supreme perfect enlightenment can one truly be said to have attained ultimate nirvana.

Formerly, when Master Shitai saw his attendant carrying the alms bowl toward the hall, he called out to him. The attendant responded, "Yes? The Master asked, "Where are you going? The attendant replied:
As he was leaving for the midday meal after ascending the hall, the Master said, "I am asking you about your fundamental matter.
The monk replied, "If it is my fundamental matter, I am indeed going to the hall for the midday meal. The Master said, "You are not mistaken in serving as my attendant.
Furthermore, while Zhaozhou was on the latrine, he saw Wenyuan passing by. He suddenly called out, "Wenyuan! Wenyuan responded, "Yes? The Master said, "Latrine."
I cannot speak of the Buddha-dharma to you, for that which you practice is the path of the bodhisattva.
As stated in the sixth chapter, "The Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies," in verse:
When the disciple takes up the burden, it is the time of the Tathāgata’s prophecy.
From this point on, one changes one's countenance and no longer clings to the thatched hut. Though the realm has a new ruler, the flowering clusters are all but withered stalks;
even if one arrives today, it would truly be considered too late.
In the Sanskrit language, it is *vyākaraṇa*; here it is translated as "prediction" (*jùjì*). "Bestowing" (*shòu*) refers to the act of earnestly entrusting [the teaching] to another;

"recording" (*jì*) refers to having it clearly present in one's mind. It means that from afar, while at the place of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, and from near, at the places of twenty trillion Buddhas, I have constantly taught and transformed you for the sake of the unsurpassed path. You have now forgotten all of this; therefore, on this day, I once again...
Again, he picked it up and earnestly entrusted it to him, saying: "You must keep this clearly in mind; do not forget it. Question:
Why is it necessary to wait until after awakening before the transmission is bestowed? Answer: It is like the Patriarch, who only transmitted the robe and bowl after his own awakening.

Therefore, when Śāriputra heard the Dharma-exposition once, his doubts were severed and faith was born; he leaped for joy, and the Tathāgata immediately bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
However, the four great disciples heard the parables twice before they realized their previous errors and developed deep faith and understanding, only then receiving their predictions.
Thus, prior to their attainment of faith, the Buddha employed indirect guidance and subtle instruction, leading them from the left and supporting them from the right, waiting for them—
It must be most thoroughgoing; one must realize it with the heart and verify it with the mind before it is bestowed, so that it is never forgotten or lost.
Therefore, it is necessary to receive the prediction only after awakening. Question: All the great disciples have emerged from birth and death and realized nirvana;
yet, at the time of their predictions, it was said for all of them that they would serve immeasurable Buddhas, fulfill the bodhisattva path, and eventually attain Buddhahood.

Why is this? The answer is: although the assembly of śrāvakas has severed the six consciousnesses, destroyed the grasping at a self, realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and attained mastery over the mind, they have not yet exhausted the karmic consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), destroyed the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), or attained mastery over phenomena.
Regarding the Buddha-dharma, their realization is no more than a single grain in the Great Granary or a single hair on a nine-headed ox. Therefore, they must serve various Buddhas extensively.
One studies the Dharma of the Way so that every matter is refined and perfected, and every dharma is clearly penetrated.

Through diligent cultivation of bodhisattva practices for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one transforms the karmic consciousness of ignorance into a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening.

Only then does one attain the status of a Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya-buddha*). Therefore, from this day forward, after receiving this prediction, one who practices the Bodhisattva path is truly called a person who studies the Buddha.
Only then did they first claim the title of "Buddha’s disciples. For this reason, it took them many kalpas to pass. Question:
Kāśyapa attended upon three million *koṭi* Buddhas before attaining *bodhi*. Subhūti made offerings to three million *nayuta* Buddhas before attaining *bodhi*.
Kātyāyana made offerings to twenty-eight thousand *koṭi* Buddhas before attaining [it].
“Bodhi! Maudgalyāyana attained bodhi only after making offerings to twenty trillion eight thousand buddhas.

Since all the great disciples heard the wondrous Dharma together, received their predictions together, and likewise accomplished bodhi, why is it that there are differences in the speed [of their attainment]?
Answer: This also depends upon their respective faculties and natures. This is known only by the Buddha; the great disciples do not know it.”
Furthermore, they do not know for themselves; this refers to what was previously called "not knowing for oneself" the superior, middling, and inferior natures.

Because they do not know for themselves, the Tathāgata has repeatedly entrusted [this teaching] to them, so that it may be clearly present in their minds and they may practice it diligently without ever forgetting it again.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he addressed the great assembly, proclaiming these words:
"This disciple of mine, Mahākāśyapa, shall in a future age behold three hundred million buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
He made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised them, widely proclaiming the immeasurable Great Dharma of all Buddhas.
In his final body, he attained Buddhahood, named the Tathāgata Prabhāsa, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata.
He was the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
His land was named Radiant Virtue; the eon was named Great Adornment. The Buddha’s lifespan was twelve minor kalpas;

the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remained for twenty minor kalpas. The realm was magnificently adorned and free from all impurities, filth, tiles, rubble, and thorns.
It is free from impurities. Its land is level and even, without elevations or depressions, pits, hollows, or mounds.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli, with rows of jewel trees and golden cords marking the boundaries along the roadsides. Various precious flowers are strewn about, making it pure throughout.
The bodhisattvas in that land number in the hundreds of billions, and the assembly of śrāvakas is likewise incalculable. There are no demonic disturbances; although...
There are Māras and the subjects of Māra who all protect the Buddha-dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses, addressing the bhikṣus:
"With my Buddha-eye, I see that this Kāśyapa, in a future age after incalculable kalpas have passed..."
You shall attain Buddhahood. Furthermore, in a future age, you will make offerings to and attend upon three hundred trillion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

For the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom, you will purely cultivate the Brahma-faring life. Having made the highest offerings to the Honored Ones among two-legged beings, you will practice and master everything.
With unsurpassed wisdom, in his final body, he shall attain Buddhahood. His land will be pure, with lapis lazuli for its ground.
There will be many jeweled trees lining both sides of the roads, demarcated by golden cords; those who see them will rejoice, and they will constantly emit exquisite fragrances.
Various kinds of exquisite and wonderful flowers were scattered about as adornments; the ground was level and even, without any mounds or pits.
The assembly of bodhisattvas was beyond measure, their minds disciplined and supple, having attained great supernormal powers, and they upheld the teachings of all Buddhas.
The Mahāyāna sūtras, the assembly of śrāvakas, those in their final bodies free from outflows, and the sons of the Dharma King were likewise incalculable;
even with the divine eye, one could not enumerate them. That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve small kalpas, and the True Dharma shall remain in the world for that duration.
The Semblance Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty intermediate kalpas. Such were the deeds of the World-Honored One Prabhāsa.

Regarding the phrase "planted merit" (at the end of the first section): it refers to the cultivation of merit. Regarding the phrase "widely proclaimed" (at the beginning of the second section): it refers to the cultivation of wisdom.

Only through the twofold adornment of merit and wisdom does one become a "Bipeds Honored One" (Dvipada-sarvasattva-agrya). As for his specific epithet "Prabhāsa," it was because during his causal stage he anointed the forms and images of the Buddha with purple-gold. Life after life...

Life after life, his body was always golden in color; therefore, when he was an Arhat, he was named Kāśyapa (Drinking Light), and when he attained Buddhahood, he was named Prabhūtaratna (Abundant Light).
Furthermore, because he had received the light of the Dharma of equality from all Buddhas within this assembly, when the World-Honored One finally held up a flower, Kāśyapa smiled.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata transmitted to him the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa.
It was entrusted to Kāśyapa. Kāśyapa took this single light and transmitted it to Ānanda. After Ānanda, it was passed down through successive generations until it reached this land.
That a single flower has borne five petals, continuing without interruption—was this not all due to the power of Kāśyapa?
Thus we know that he was one who transmitted the heart-essence of the Buddha. One must pay homage to three hundred million *billion* Buddhas to attain this.
One attains the realization of Bodhi. Who could say that in the School of the Lineage (Zongmen) there is no Buddha to be realized?

As for the land named "Radiant Virtue" (Guangde), it is because this land manifests superior and inferior virtues through its radiance. As for the eon named "Great Adornment" (Dazhuangyan), it is likewise because radiance serves as its adornment.
The passage beginning with "The boundaries of the land" describes the matters of adornment. "The ground is made of lapis lazuli" means it is free from defilement.
It is free from evil. As for the rows of jewel trees, they are without thorns. As for the paths demarcated by golden cords, they are without pits, hollows, mounds, or hills.
As for the pure, pervasive jewel flowers, there is no filth such as excrement or urine. Below that land—
They are his retinue. These Māras are all protectors of the Dharma; they are all inconceivable Bodhisattvas. The meaning of the verse can be understood accordingly.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, and the others were all struck with awe and stood trembling. One.
With palms joined and gazing up at the Honored Countenance without averting their eyes for a moment, they spoke these verses in unison:
"O Great Hero, O Fierce World-Honored One, Dharma King of all the Śākyas! Out of compassion for us, please grant us the Buddha’s voice."
If you know my deep intention and grant me this prediction of enlightenment, it is like being sprinkled with nectar, which dispels heat and brings refreshing coolness.
It is like one who has come from a land of famine and suddenly encounters the meal of a great king; though the heart still harbors doubt and fear, one does not yet dare to eat at once.
If we were further to receive the King's command, only then would we dare to eat. We are just like this; we constantly reflect upon the faults of the Hīnayāna and do not know what should be done.
Only upon attaining the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom will we truly hear the Buddha’s voice saying, "You shall become Buddhas."
Our minds still harbor anxiety and fear, such that we do not yet dare to eat. Only if we receive the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment shall we find true peace and joy.
O Great Hero, O World-Honored One, who ever desires to bring peace to the world, we pray that you grant us this prediction; it is like one who is hungry and must be taught what to eat.
This disciple requests a prediction [of his future enlightenment]. Having seen that he was granted a prediction yet his name was not mentioned, he fears he has lost a great benefit;

thus, he trembles with awe. He has severed what others cannot sever, endured what others cannot endure, practiced what others cannot practice, and realized what others cannot realize; therefore, he is called the Great Hero, the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, it was said that he is the Dharma King among all Śākyas. Moreover, for a long time the World-Honored One has taken pity on us;
yet, failing to obtain the Tathāgata’s treasure-store, we have suffered in vain through poverty. Thus, he granted us the words of a prophecy of Buddhahood.
Now, though the prophecy has been given, the name of a Buddha has not been bestowed, leaving none of us without a heart burning with distress. If only the Tathāgata would bear witness to us...

Regarding the "equal profound mind": to be seen by [the Buddha] and receive a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) upon having one's name called—how is this different from sprinkling nectar (amṛta) upon the heart, suddenly causing the inner organs to feel cool and refreshing?
This is clarified by the following analogy: it is just as if someone were coming from a land of famine and suddenly encountered a time when a great king was bestowing a banquet;
though rare delicacies filled the trays and precious foods were set before them, they could not partake without the king’s command.
This is called "summoning. We do not dare to accept the banquet; only if we receive an imperial decree (a *lun-yin*) shall we venture to accept it.
As for us of the lower rank, it is in accordance with the Dharma that we constantly contemplate the faults of the Hīnayāna and long for the Buddha’s wisdom.
Yet we did not know how we might attain it—just like a hungry person yearning for food. Suddenly, we hear the Tathāgata bestowing upon us this prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

They have become Buddhas; yet, as their names have not yet been proclaimed, they do not know what those Buddha-names shall be. Their hearts are filled with anxiety and fear, and they do not dare to accept the burden.
It is just like encountering a royal banquet, yet because it is neither named nor summoned, one does not dare to eat.
If they were granted the Buddha-names, at that time they would attain joy, refreshment, and peace, and no longer harbor anxiety or fear. Furthermore, such is the compassion of the Tathāgata.
O Compassionate One! You always desire to comfort all the world. Now we are filled with trepidation; could it be that the World-Honored One has no means to comfort us?

We now pray that you would grant us our names, for only then can we advance in practice—just as a hungry person must wait for instruction before they dare to eat. Please take note of these words; this too is the Small Vehicle.
He took up the practice of collecting payment for removing excrement.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of his great disciples, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Subhūti, in a future age, shall behold three hundred trillion nayutas of Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring, and respecting them."
He was praised with repeated hymns of praise. Constantly practicing the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), he perfected the bodhisattva path.

In his final existence, he attained buddhahood, receiving the name of the Tathāgata Nāmanimitta (The One Whose Marks are Renowned), Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The eon was named Ratnavatī, and the land was named Ratnasambhava. His...
The ground is level and even, with crystal for its surface. Adorned with precious trees, it is free from mounds, pits, gravel, thorns, and the filth of excrement and urine.
Precious flowers cover the earth, which is everywhere pure. The people of that land all dwell in precious terraces and exquisite pavilions.
The śrāvaka disciples are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy. All...
The assembly of bodhisattvas numbered countless thousands of millions of billions of nayutas. The Buddha’s lifespan was twelve small kalpas;
the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty small kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remained for twenty small kalpas.

That Buddha constantly dwelt in the void, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes and delivering immeasurable bodhisattvas as well as the assembly of śrāvakas. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to proclaim this again...
Regarding this meaning, he spoke in verse:
"O assembly of bhikṣus, I now address you all: with single-minded attention, listen to what I shall say. My great disciples..."
Subhūti shall attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be Mingxiang (Renowned Aspect).

He shall make offerings to countless billions of Buddhas, following the conduct of those Buddhas and gradually perfecting the Great Way. In his final body, he shall obtain the thirty-two marks, being upright, exquisite, and wondrously beautiful.
It is like a mountain of jewels; that buddha-field is the most sublime in its adornment and purity. Among sentient beings who behold it, there are none who do not feel love and joy.
Within it, the Buddha delivers immeasurable multitudes. In his Dharma, there are many bodhisattvas, all of whom possess sharp faculties.
He turns the wheel of non-retrogression. That land is constantly adorned by bodhisattvas. The assembly of śrāvakas is beyond measure;

they have all attained the three types of clear knowledge, possess the six supernormal powers, and abide in the eight liberations. They possess great majestic virtue. Such is the Dharma taught by that Buddha.

He manifests immeasurable and inconceivable supernormal powers and transformations. Gods and humans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all join their palms in reverence to listen to and receive the Buddha’s words.
That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twelve small kalpas, and the True Dharma shall remain in the world for that duration.
For twenty minor kalpas the Semblance Dharma shall also remain, and for twenty minor kalpas [the True Dharma].
Subhūti, while in his mother’s womb he already knew emptiness and stillness; when he was an arhat, he was named Kūṭadanta (Empty-born);

when he attained Buddhahood, his specific epithet was Lakṣaṇa (Characteristics). This means that he first attained true emptiness and subsequently attained wondrous existence. He is free from names and characteristics.
To speak of emptiness while it is not true emptiness, or to speak of names and forms while departing from true emptiness, is not wondrous existence.
Now, form is identical to emptiness, and emptiness is identical to form; this may be called "true emptiness as wondrous existence" and "wondrous existence as true emptiness.
Therefore, one should know that this is what was taken up prior to the kalpa of emptiness, and what was realized before the Buddha appeared in the world. One must reverently behold it.
After three million billion nayutas of Buddhas, one who has perfected the bodhisattva path finally attains buddhahood.
The kalpa is named "Possessing Jewels" (Youbao) and the land is named "Jewel-Born" (Baosheng), because from true emptiness one obtains the jewel of wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus: "I now tell you:
this Mahākātyāyana shall, in a future age, with various offerings and requisites, serve and attend upon eight thousand koṭis of Buddhas, honoring and respecting them.

After each of those Buddhas has passed into parinirvāṇa, he will erect for them stūpas and temples one thousand yojanas in height, and five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, perfectly equal in all dimensions."
It was composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby—and adorned with various flowers and necklaces.
With powdered incense, ground incense, and burning incense, as well as silken canopies, banners, and streamers, they made offerings to the stupas and temples.
After this was done, they further made offerings to twenty trillion buddhas in the same manner. Having made offerings to these buddhas, they perfected the path of a bodhisattva.
He shall attain Buddhahood, with the title Tathāgata Jambūnadīprabhāsa-golden-light,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
That land is level and even. Its ground is made of crystal and adorned with precious trees. Golden cords demarcate the sides of the roads.
Wondrous flowers cover the earth, which is everywhere pure; those who see it rejoice. There are no four evil realms—the paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras.
It abounds with devas and humans, as well as assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, in immeasurable numbers.
Ten trillion [deities] adorned that land. The Buddha’s lifespan was twelve small kalpas;

the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty small kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remained for twenty small kalpas. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O assembly of bhikṣus, all listen with a single mind. What I have spoken is true and without deviation.
This Kātyāyana shall, with various kinds of exquisite offerings, make offerings to the Buddhas. After the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas, he shall erect stupas made of the seven precious gems."
They also made offerings of flowers and incense to the śarīra. In their final bodies, they attained the wisdom of a Buddha and realized equal and perfect enlightenment.
Their lands were pure, and they delivered immeasurable tens of billions of sentient beings, all of whom became objects of veneration for the worlds of the ten directions.
The Buddha’s radiance is unsurpassed. That Buddha is named Jambūnada-prabhāsa (Jambu Golden Light).
His bodhisattvas and śrāvakas have severed all existence; they are immeasurable and innumerable, adorning his land.
Kātyāyana, because he diligently swept the Buddha’s grounds during his causal stage, when he became an arhat, he was able to adorn the light of the Buddha’s wisdom through his discourses;

thus he was named Maṇḍitaka (The Adorned). When he attained Buddhahood, he was titled Jambūnada-prabhāsa (Golden Light of the Jambu River), because the radiance of his body was like the gold of the jambu tree.
One should know that those whose sharpness of speech is like an arrow and whose eloquence is like a river [are such as this].
Furthermore, one must make offerings to twenty-eight thousand billion Buddhas before attaining bodhi.
As for this absence of the names of kalpas and lands, it may be that they were lost during the translation process.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly: "I now tell you:
this Mahāmaudgalyāyana shall, with various kinds of offerings, make offerings to eight thousand Buddhas, honoring and respecting them.

After those Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, he shall each erect a stūpa, one thousand yojanas in height and five hundred yojanas in both length and breadth, made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and musaragalva."

With agate, pearls, and roses—composed of the seven treasures—as well as various flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers, he shall make offerings. After this, he shall likewise make offerings to two hundred trillion Buddhas in the same manner.
He shall then attain Buddhahood, and his name shall be Tamālapatracandanagandha Tathāgata.
Come, O Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. The eon is named Priyapūrṇa; the land is named Manojña.
That realm is level and even, with crystal for its ground, adorned with jewel trees, strewn with pearls, and everywhere pure, so that all who see it rejoice. It is vast.
The number of devas, humans, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas was immeasurable. The Buddha’s lifespan was twenty-four minor kalpas;
the True Dharma remained in the world for forty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma likewise remained for forty minor kalpas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
This disciple of mine, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, after casting off this body, shall behold eight thousand two hundred trillion Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
For the sake of the Buddha-way, he shall make offerings to and revere them, and in the presence of those Buddhas, he shall constantly practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
For immeasurable kalpas, they upheld the Buddha-dharma. After the parinirvāṇa of various Buddhas, they erected stupas made of the seven treasures, with tall poles and golden *śikharas*.
They made offerings of flowers, incense, and music. Having gradually perfected all the stūpas and temples of the Buddhas, they completed the path of a bodhisattva.
In the land of Intention (Āśaya), he shall attain Buddhahood, named Tamāla-candana-gandha.

That Buddha’s lifespan shall be twenty-four kalpas, during which he will constantly expound the path of the Buddha for devas and humans; his śrāvakas shall be immeasurable, like the sands of the Ganges.
They possess the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and have great majestic virtue. There will be innumerable bodhisattvas whose resolve is firm and who are diligent in their practice;

regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, they shall all be non-retrogressive. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain for forty minor kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise endure for that same duration.
My disciples, endowed with majestic power, numbering five hundred, shall all receive predictions that in a future age they will all attain Buddhahood.
I shall now speak of the karmic causes and conditions from our past lives—my own and yours. Listen well!
When Maudgalyāyana was an arhat, he was foremost in supernatural powers; therefore, when he attained Buddhahood, he was named Candanagandha.
If even one *zhu* of this incense is burned, its fragrance universally permeates a small chiliocosm.

Because it is also swift and miraculous, one must know that he can fly, move with light ease, manifest fire, and manifest dragons. One must make offerings to two hundred trillion and eighty thousand Buddhas.
Only then will one attain Bodhi. The kalpa is named *Pūrṇapriya* (Joy-Filled), and the land is named *Manoratha* (Wish-Fulfilling).

This is because sentient beings rejoice upon seeing the fragrance of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and find delight in hearing the fragrance of supernatural powers. The phrase "I and the four propositions" concludes the preceding section and gives rise to the following one.
The seventh verse of the "Parable of the City of Illusion" states:
"Beyond five hundred yojanas, who would say this is their former dwelling? The scenery is not the original land."
Even if it is good, it is still transient; whatever exists is not ultimately real. There is no city, yet it is a plundering of the void.
Among the sons of the Great Pervader, try asking: what is it truly like?

Originally non-existent, suddenly existing—therefore it is called a "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*). To ward off enemies and prevent wrongdoing, it is called a "city. Although this chapter is similar to the [previous] chapter for the younger brother...
The Master explains the causes and conditions of past lives, truly unfolding the remaining store of parables concerning medicinal herbs.
For while the intent of the "Parable" chapter lies in the burning house and the white ox, the intent of this chapter lies in the conjured city and the treasure site.
To emerge from the burning house and enter the conjured city, and to mount the white ox and reach the treasure site—only when these two are joined does the meaning become complete. This chapter...

Although it was said that when the Tathāgata was under the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he preached the Lotus Sūtra for the sixteen śrāmaṇeras, thereby establishing the causes and conditions for your liberation today; yet, it is precisely in the "Chapter on the Herbs" that this is clearly revealed:
the rain of Dharma falls equally upon all, yet each receives according to its capacity, and among all dharmas, one gradually attains realization according to one's own ability.

Regarding the passage on "entering the Way" and so forth, it refers to that which was stated: "The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits, such that you could not exhaustively describe them even in immeasurable billions of kalpas. However, within the Parable Chapter (*Upamā-parivarta*), it says:

As soon as Śāriputra attained realization, [the Buddha] explained the causes and conditions for him, saying: "In the past, when I was in the presence of twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, I constantly taught and transformed you;
you, too, followed me through the long night to receive instruction. The causal conditions for this are thus proximate.
This chapter explains the causes and conditions for the twelve hundred arhats, which date back to inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Previously, when he was a novice monk, he had already guided and transformed you all; thus, the causal conditions [for this] are remote.
Because these causal conditions have both remote and proximate aspects, each shall speak of their own, so that they may inspire one another and clarify one another's accounts.
At the beginning of the text, the mention of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū is intended to show that he was formerly Śākyamuni’s...
Father, this refers to Vairocana, the Lord of the Dharma-body, who does not fall within spatial dimensions and does not involve numerical quantity.
His acts of attaining Buddhahood and turning the Wheel of Dharma are merely performances suited to the occasion.

As for the sixteen śrāmaṇeras, from the very moment they left the household life, they requested the Great Dharma and turned the wheel on behalf of the Buddha; their air and demeanor were, moreover, beyond compare.

Those who are petty and trivial are thus compared [to such creatures]. Therefore, he was able to immediately succeed to the position of Great Pervasive Penetration (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*), breathing from the same nostril as Great Pervasive Penetrating Wisdom-Victory.
How could this be the same as the inferior Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), which is like a lame donkey or a sluggish horse that refuses to move forward despite being spurred?
That the World-Honored One cites the past to corroborate the present is likewise to stimulate the Small Vehicle, so as to cause them— [The text ends here.]
Exerting themselves, they abandon inferior wisdom and enter into the wisdom of great penetration.

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna."
Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One:
the name of that land is Good City, and the eon is named Great Sign. O Bhikṣus, since that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, an exceedingly long time has elapsed.
Suppose, for example, there were all the earth elements within a trichiliocosm.

If someone were to grind them into ink and, having traveled eastward across a thousand lands, drop a single dot as small as a minute speck of dust, and then travel across another thousand lands [to drop another].
Again, he places another dot. In this manner, proceeding successively until all the ink for the earth-element is exhausted—what do you think?
Could a mathematician or a mathematician’s disciple reach the limit of these lands and know their number? "No, World-Honored One.
"Monks, as for the lands traversed by that person, whether marked with dots or not, if they were all ground into dust, one [particle of dust]..."

A single speck of dust represents one kalpa. Since that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, an immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable number of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas have elapsed.
By means of the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, I observe that distant past as if it were today.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
I recall a past age, immeasurable and boundless kalpas ago, when there was a Buddha, the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
Suppose a person were to grind the entire three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system with all its earth and seeds until they were completely reduced to ink by their own strength.

Passing beyond a thousand lands, one deposits a single mote of dust. Continuing in this manner, depositing mote after mote until all these motes of ink are exhausted, such that the number of lands deposited and not yet deposited are equal;
then, having ground all remaining lands into dust, let one mote of dust represent one kalpa.
The number of these atoms is such that the kalpas exceed it even further. Since that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa until now, there have been immeasurable kalpas.
With his unimpeded wisdom, the Tathāgata knows that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, as well as those of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas; he perceives and sees their present parinirvāṇa.

"O bhikṣus, you should know that the Buddha’s wisdom is pure and subtle, untainted and unimpeded. It penetrates immeasurable kalpas; it is called 'Great' because it is universally pervasive and vast in its capacity.
It is called 'Penetrating' because it opens up in the four directions and reaches through the eight gates. It is called 'Wisdom' because it can respond appropriately to all phenomena.
It is called 'Supreme' because it transcends everything. As for the name of the land, 'Good City,' it is adorned with exquisite beauty, surpassing all other cities."
Regarding the eon named "Great Mark" (*Mahālakṣaṇa*): it is vast, immense, and remote, such that its measure is difficult to exhaust. The passage from "That Buddha...

onwards reveals that this Buddha existed prior to the empty eon (*śūnyakalpa*); he was originally without beginning or end and does not involve measurable quantity, and thus the metaphor of "dust-points" is employed.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "In the empty eon, are there still people who practice cultivation? The Master said, "You call..."
"What constitutes the kalpa of emptiness? [The monk] said, "There is not a single thing that is. The Master said, "This can only be called 'cultivation.

What do you call the kalpa of emptiness? The monk was speechless. Thus one knows that all paths involving cultivation belong entirely to the realm of the *bhava-kalpa* (the kalpa of existence), not the *śūnya-kalpa* (the kalpa of emptiness).
By the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, I observe that even such a vast duration of time...

If it were today, by virtue of my opening up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, I would observe events from kalpas as numerous as motes of dust through that very Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision no differently than if I were observing what is before my eyes. This precisely reveals that the Way of Bodhi has neither going nor coming.

In the verse below, starting with "The Tathāgata," it says that although these events of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust have lasted for such a vast duration, the Tathāgata, by means of his non-...
Unimpeded wisdom observes the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha, as well as the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, with such vivid clarity as if it were today.
This is because the Tathāgata is endowed with the four wisdoms: "Buddha-wisdom" is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; "Pure" is the Wisdom of Equality;
"Subtle and Wondrous" is the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; and "Untainted and Unobstructed" is the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is to be Done.
It is the wisdom of what has been accomplished (*kṛtānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Possessing these four wisdoms, one is able to penetrate immeasurable eons as if they were this very day.

The ancient Buddha was named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū; Śākyamuni penetrates [the past] with the four unhindered wisdoms (*pratisaṃvid*), like space merging with space, or like a mirror reflecting a mirror. One does not know which is the ancient and which is the present.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "The lifespan of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was five hundred and forty million *nayuta* kalpas.

When that Buddha first sat at the site of enlightenment and had defeated the armies of Māra, he was on the verge of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet the dharmas of a Buddha did not manifest before him.
This continued for one intermediate kalpa, and so on, up to ten intermediate kalpas."
He sat cross-legged; his body and mind were unmoving, yet the teachings of all Buddhas still did not appear before him.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven first prepared for that Buddha a lion throne beneath the Bodhi tree, one yojana in height.
The Buddha sat upon it, intending to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. As soon as he sat upon this seat, at that moment...
Brahmādeva rained down various celestial flowers over an area of one hundred *yojanas*. A fragrant breeze blew at intervals, blowing away the withered blossoms and raining down fresh ones.
In this manner, it continued without ceasing for ten minor *kalpas*, making offerings to the Buddha until his parinirvāṇa; he constantly rained down these flowers.
Furthermore, the gods of the Four Great Kings, in order to make offerings to the Buddha, constantly struck celestial drums, while the other devas likewise performed [their offerings].
Celestial music played for ten intermediate kalpas until his parinirvāṇa; it was likewise so for all [the Buddhas].

O bhikṣus, after ten intermediate kalpas had passed, the Dharma of all Buddhas appeared before the Great Penetrating Wisdom-Victorious Buddha (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū), and he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This refers to Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attaining Buddhahood and requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. Regarding the phrase "originally seated at the site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa):
it means that although this ancient Buddha was originally seated at the site of enlightenment and had never moved from there, he nonetheless had to utterly destroy the armies of Māra.
Only then can one be called a newly accomplished ancient Buddha. As for the current statement that although one is about to attain Bodhi, the Buddha-dharma does not manifest:

this is because the ignorance of the "mark of arising" (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) still persists. Consequently, there remains a mind that thinks "I am about to attain," and one has not yet reached the state of perfect Bodhi where one returns to non-attainment.
Therefore, the Buddha-dharma does not manifest. As the ancient masters have said: "A difference of a hair’s breadth leads to a discrepancy as vast as heaven and earth."

This is what is meant by being "separated by a vast distance. Even if one remains with body and mind unmoving for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma still does not manifest, it is because one’s right view clings to and guards its own achievements;
one sits within the realm of sickness. One fails to realize that when one stands alone in peril without a fixed position, the Way is truly high.
Long ago, Nanyue said to Mazu Daoshi: "Do you study sitting meditation, or do you study sitting as a Buddha? If...

One studies seated meditation. Yet, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If one studies by taking the Buddha as the object of meditation, the Buddha has no fixed characteristics; this is precisely the principle.
Because that person’s mind has not yet relinquished [grasping] and the form of "sitting" has not yet been emptied, they fall into the realm of numerical limitations.

Therefore, the immeasurable and profound wisdom of the Buddha cannot manifest before them. From the words "At that time" onwards, it refers to the period before the Buddha sat cross-legged; [the gods of] the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven...
The deva first prepared a seat for the Buddha, while the Lord of Devas stood below. As the Buddha sat down, the Lord of Devas offered this benediction:
"The Greatly Penetrating One has just now sat upon this very seat. At that moment, Brahmā scattered flowers, the Four Heavenly Kings of the Desire Realm beat drums, and the other devas played music.
From the time he attained Buddhahood until his final nirvana, it was always thus; this clearly demonstrates the Tathāgata’s presence.
The world’s nirvana is fundamentally non-dual. As for the manifestation of the Buddha-dharma after ten minor kalpas: "ten" is the end of numerical calculation;
when numbers are extinguished, there is the single severance of all severance and the single realization of all realization.

This section precisely reveals that Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, from the very moment he first conceived a single thought of aspiring toward attainment, allowed this very thought to give rise to its own obstruction.

Separated [from it], one cannot attain great penetration; wisdom likewise will not be supreme. Only when one reaches the point where quantity and number are forgotten does the Buddha-wisdom of equality manifest before one; only then can one be called "Greatly Penetrating and Supremely Wise.

How much less so for those of the Lesser Vehicle who cling to the meditative absorption of cessation without relinquishing it, and who cling to limited wisdom without departing from it—how could they possibly know the profound, immeasurable, and equal [wisdom]?
How wondrous is the Buddha-wisdom!
Before that Buddha had left the household life, he had sixteen sons. The eldest was named Zhijí (Jñānakośa).
Each of the sons possessed various rare and extraordinary playthings. Having heard that their father had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*...

The three who were to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* all renounced their most cherished possessions and went to the place where the Buddha was. Their mothers wept as they followed and escorted them.

Their grandfather, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, together with one hundred ministers and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other people, all surrounded them and followed them to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), desiring to draw near to the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, to make offerings to him, and to pay him homage.

He paid his respects and offered praise. Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet. After circumambulating the Buddha, he joined his palms with single-minded devotion, gazed up at the World-Honored One, and spoke in verse:
O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, you attained Buddhahood only after immeasurable billions of years.
All your vows are now fully fulfilled; how excellent, how auspicious, how unsurpassed! O World-Honored One, you are most rare and extraordinary, remaining seated for ten minor kalpas.
The body, along with the hands and feet, remains tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving; his mind is always serene and detached, never once becoming distracted.
Ultimate and eternal quiescence, abiding in the untainted Dharma—now we behold the World-Honored One, who has peacefully attained the Way of the Buddha.
We have gained a sublime benefit; we celebrate with great joy. Sentient beings are constantly afflicted by suffering, blind and ignorant, with no guide.
Failing to recognize the path that exhausts suffering, and not knowing how to seek liberation, they increase the realms of evil for the long night and diminish the hosts of the devas.
Passing from darkness into further darkness, they shall never again hear the name of the Buddha. Now the Buddha has attained the supreme, peaceful, and untainted path.
We, as well as the devas and humans, have obtained the greatest benefit; therefore, we all bow our heads and take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One.

The fact that the Lamp-Lighter had eight sons who left the household life symbolizes the eight consciousnesses within the bonds of affliction; the underlying intent is that these eight consciousnesses are to be transformed into the four wisdoms.
The fact that the Great Pervasive One had sixteen sons who left the household life symbolizes the sixteen moments of mind; the underlying intent is...

This means turning away from small wisdom and heading toward great wisdom. As for the first being named Jñānakūṭa (Wisdom-Peak), it signifies that although he possessed great wisdom, there was still some stagnation and he had not yet reached universal penetration.

Regarding the phrase "the sons," it means that these sons all cast aside—as if they were spittle—whatever they had cherished, treasured, and protected throughout their lives; they went to the Buddha’s presence to seek the equality of Buddhahood.
It is also the treasure of wisdom. Since the various sons were not born of a single mother, they are called "sons of various mothers.
Those who weep and bid them farewell have not yet been able to sever their affection. Their grandfather, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, was none other than the father of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
That the Wheel-Turning Sage King prostrated at his son’s feet means that as a Dharma King who has transcended the world, he did not treat his son merely as a son. [The Verse:]
Below the section on the Middle World-Honored One, the events of the ten minor kalpas are praised. The two lines concerning the body praise the immovability of the body;

the two lines concerning the mind praise the immovability of the mind. Having applied effort in this manner for these ten kalpas, one reaches the point where both arising and ceasing are extinguished.
Only when quiescence manifests before one can dwell securely in the dharma of untainted great bodhi.
Now that we see the World-Honored One has transcended the three realms and safely attained the Way, we shall surely partake in the bounty of his grace; this is why we celebrate with such great joy.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings constantly dwell within the three miserable realms, undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, and have long remained in darkness.
It is dark. Furthermore, though there is a guide who possesses the eye of wisdom, he employs skillful means only to lead them away;
yet they neither recognize the method for exhausting suffering nor know the path to liberation. In the long night of ignorance, they are shrouded in gloom, without refuge and without rescue.

Consequently, those in the evil realms increase while the gods become ever fewer. Within the three miserable states, they emerge and submerge like heads in water, passing from darkness into darkness. How could this be otherwise?

We were unable to see the Buddha, nor did we ever hear his name. Now that the Buddha has attained the supreme Dharma, both we and the devas have been able to hear his name and behold his form. Hereafter, we shall surely receive the greatest benefit;
therefore, we celebrate with joy and prostrate ourselves in refuge.
At that time, the sixteen princes, having praised the Buddha in verse, entreated the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of Dharma, all saying these words:
"World-Honored One, your preaching of the Dharma brings peace and security to many; out of compassion, you benefit the devas and humans. They spoke again in verse:
"O Hero of the World, peerless and unequaled, adorned by a hundred merits, having attained unsurpassed wisdom, we pray that you will preach it for the sake of the world."
Deliver us and all classes of sentient beings; for our sake, you have analyzed and revealed this so that we may attain such wisdom.
If we are to become Buddhas, so too shall it be for all sentient beings. The World-Honored One knows the deep thoughts within the minds of sentient beings.
He also knows the path they travel, as well as their power of wisdom, their aspirations, their cultivation of merit, and the karmic deeds performed in past lives;
having fully known all this, the World-Honored One shall turn the unsurpassed wheel.

These sixteen śrāmaṇeras requested the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. As soon as these sixteen śrāmaṇeras had left the household life and seen the Buddha, they conceived the resolve to save the world and immediately requested the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. Their spirit was so majestic that it surveyed the entire age;
truly, they were great men indeed! Regarding the statement "bringing peace and security to many": it means they could cause the ignorant to become wise and the unworthy...
The worthy find support; the weak find strength; those hanging upside down find release. Because the benefit is so vast, it is called "much.

Regarding the section of the verse beginning with "the World-Honored One": this means that because the Tathāgata possesses the ten powers (*daśabala*), he knows what matters present sentient beings are contemplating, what paths they are practicing, what wisdom they have attained, what dharmas they delight in, and what merits they are cultivating. Furthermore, he knows [their deeds] of the past.
By what karma is it that he is able to bestow the Dharma according to their capacities? Now we aspire to the Mahāyāna;
the World-Honored One must surely know our minds, and he will certainly turn the unsurpassed wheel for us as well.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "When the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, five million *koṭis* of Buddha-worlds in each of the ten directions shook in six ways.

Those regions situated between them that were dark and obscure—places where even the majestic radiance of the sun and moon could not reach—were all filled with great light. The sentient beings therein..."
They were all able to see one another and spoke thus: "What is this? How is it that sentient beings have suddenly appeared here?
Furthermore, the entire realm, including the palaces of the various devas and even the Brahma-heavens, shook in six ways, and a great light shone everywhere, pervading the entire world.
It surpasses the radiance of all the devas;

this is the proclamation to the great assembly by means of light. Śākyamuni’s emission of light constitutes the final stroke, while Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū’s emission of light constitutes the first phrase. For the first phrase is no different from the final stroke; therefore, its...

The light also penetrates both above and below. Because it penetrates below, the sentient beings dwelling in the ghost caves between the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) are each able to see one another.
Because it penetrates above, the Brahma palaces tremble, surpassing the radiance of all the devas. As for what is meant by "surpassing": it means that [the light] eclipses them.
Because the Buddha’s light shines everywhere, it eclipses the celestial light; therefore, it is called "victorious.
At that time, within five hundred million *koṭis* of lands in the eastern direction, the palaces of the Brahmā heavens were illuminated with brilliant radiance.
The radiance was twice that of usual brightness. Each of the Brahma Kings thought to themselves: "The light of these palaces is such as has never been seen before.
By what cause and condition does this sign appear? At that time, the Brahma Kings each went to meet one another.
They deliberated upon this matter together. At that time, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Savior of All, who spoke these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:
"In all our palaces, there is a radiance such as has never existed before. What is the cause and condition for this? We should each seek it together:
Is it because a Great Virtuous Being has been born, or has a Buddha appeared in the world? For this great radiance shines everywhere throughout the ten directions."
At that time, the Brahma Kings of five million billion lands, together with their palaces,

each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively toward the west to investigate the cause of this omen. There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment,
beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
Gandharvas, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others respectfully surrounded him.

Upon seeing the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, the Brahma kings immediately prostrated themselves before the Buddha, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and scattered celestial flowers over him;
the flowers they scattered were like Mount Sumeru, which they offered as well to the Buddha’s enlightenment.
The Bodhi tree was ten *yojanas* high. Having made offerings of flowers, each [Brahmā] presented his own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words:
"May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us; we pray that you graciously accept the palaces we have offered.
Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahmā kings, with one mind and in a single voice, recited in verse:
The World-Honored One is most rare and difficult to encounter. Endowed with immeasurable merit, he is able to rescue and protect all.
The Great Teacher of gods and humans takes pity upon the world; all sentient beings throughout the ten directions universally receive his benefit.
We have come from five hundred million billion lands, having abandoned the bliss of profound meditative concentration for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha.
By virtue of our merits in previous lives, our palaces were most magnificently adorned; we now offer them to the World-Honored One. We pray only that you will compassionately accept them.
At that time, after the Brahma kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each of them spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the Wheel of Dharma, deliver sentient beings, and open the path to Nirvana. Then the Brahma kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke this verse:
"O Hero of the World, Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings, we only pray that you will expound the Dharma; by the power of your great compassion, deliver all suffering beings.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
"Each had this thought" refers to the gods conceiving doubts. They wondered by what causes and conditions such an auspicious omen had appeared;

because they did not know the cause of the light, they were filled with doubt. "At that time, below" refers to their deliberating and investigating together. Regarding the phrase in the verse, "for the sake of the Great Virtuous Gods":
because the Brahma gods cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) while simultaneously cultivating the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), it is so stated.
"Venerable Deva, at that time, descending and following the light, he saw the Buddha together with his palace; 'together' is said because he possessed a palace that followed his person.
As for 'filling a robe-sack with flowers,' it means he was prepared to make offerings to the Buddha. To investigate these signs..."
He sought and investigated the source from which the radiance emerged. "Immediately thereafter" means that he scattered flowers as an offering to the hall.
That he scattered flowers reaching even to the trees was because he respected the master and extended that respect to the trees.

That he first offered flowers and subsequently presented the hall was because he first advanced with a minor courtesy and subsequently advanced with a grand offering. At that time, [the text] below explains.
They praised the Buddha with verses. "We, the lower [deities]," refers to their self-announcement of their place of origin and the purpose of their arrival.
They said, "In our past lives, we cultivated the merit of *rddhi* (supernatural power); consequently, we have obtained these palaces that accompany us, and thus we offer them to the Buddha.

At that time, "the various Brahmās" and so forth refer to their request for the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. At that time, "Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū" and so forth indicates that the Tathāgata silently consented; this is what is meant by "silent consent."
This means that although one does not speak with the mouth, one assents in the mind. The above has been a sequential narration of various Buddha-activities;

the underlying intent lies in the emphasis on seeking the light to see the Buddha. Since every person possesses the Buddha and each individual possesses the light, it is only because they do not know the source from which the light originates that they are unable to see the Buddha.
If one knows the origin from which the radiance emerges, then one shall see the Buddha.
It was not far away. Thus, Brahmā thought to himself: "By what causes and conditions has this sign appeared?
The Heavenly King of the East looked toward the West; the celestial beings of the South looked toward the North; the celestial beings of the Southeast looked toward the Northwest, and so forth.
All of these were descriptions of the Buddha’s light, which is nowhere and yet nowhere is it not present; it exists, yet there is no place where it does not exist.

Because their positions were fixed, looking east meant facing west, and observing south resulted in facing north. In reality, this light did not depart from the side of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū;
therefore, upon seeing the Buddha, they all rejoiced and offered praise, immediately relinquishing what they held most precious to seek the supreme Great Treasure of the Dharma King.
Furthermore, monks, in five million billion lands to the southeast, the Great Brahma Kings each saw their own palaces illuminated by a radiance such as they had never experienced before.
Overjoyed and leaping with delight, they conceived a sense of wonder and immediately went to one another to discuss this matter.
At that time, among that assembly, there was a Great Brahma King named Mahākaruṇā (Great Compassion).
For the sake of the assembly of Brahmās, he spoke these verses:
"By what cause and condition has such a sign appeared? Within all our palaces, there is a radiance never seen before."
Is it for the sake of a Great Virtuous One being born? Or is it because a Buddha has appeared in the world? Never before have we seen such a sign; let us together seek it with a single mind.

Crossing over thousands of myriads of kotis of lands, let us follow the light and investigate it together. It is most likely that a Buddha has appeared in the world to deliver and liberate sentient beings from suffering.
At that time, five million billion Brahma kings, together with their palaces,

each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively toward the northwest to investigate the cause of these signs. There they beheld the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū at the site of enlightenment,
beneath the Bodhi tree, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.

Mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others respectfully surrounded him. When they saw the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, the Brahma kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha;
the flowers thus scattered were as vast as Mount Sumeru, and they also used them to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having made offerings of flowers, each offered their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words:
"May you look upon us with compassion and benefit us; we pray that you graciously accept the palaces we have offered.
Then, before the Buddha, all the Brahma Kings, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke in verse:
We now pay homage to the Holy Lord, the King among Gods, whose voice is like that of the kalaviṅka bird, who has compassion for all sentient beings.
The World-Honored One is most rare; he appears but once in the vast expanse of time. For one hundred and eighty kalpas, they passed in vain without a Buddha.
The three evil realms are filled, and the hosts of devas are diminishing. Now the Buddha has appeared in the world to act as eyes for sentient beings;
he is the refuge of the world, the protector of all, the father of sentient beings, who brings compassion and benefit.
"By virtue of the auspicious merit of our past lives, we have now been able to encounter the World-Honored One.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with these verses, they each spoke these words:

"We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for all beings, will turn the Wheel of Dharma to deliver and liberate sentient beings. Then, the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, said:
He spoke in verse:
"The Great Sage turns the wheel of Dharma, revealing the characteristics of all phenomena. He delivers sentient beings from suffering and distress, causing them to attain great joy.
When sentient beings hear this Dharma, some attain the Path and others are born in heaven; the various evil realms diminish, while those who practice patience and goodness increase."
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
Previously, they had deliberated and sought out the various Great Brahmās; since there is a Great Brahmā in each and every world-system, they are referred to as "various.
The verse stating that they "traversed thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands" while following the light and seeking him together means that this light was not located [within those lands].

"In this land, one should seek it beyond thousands of millions of billions of lands; yet one must know that although this light passes beyond thousands of millions of billions of lands, it fundamentally does not depart from its original location.
From "At that time" onwards, [the text describes] seeing the Buddha by following the light; from "At that time, all... onwards...
They scattered flowers as an offering to the hall. When the Holy Lord descended, he spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha, saying:
"The Holy Lord is the King among the gods; he is the Sage among sages, and is therefore called 'Lord' (主). He is the God among gods, and is therefore called 'King' (王). Kan Ze said:
"The teachings of Confucius and Laozi are practiced in accordance with Heaven, for they dare not disobey Heaven. The teachings of Śākyamuni are followed by all the heavens, for [they] dare not..."

Because he does not contradict the Buddha, he is called the "King among Gods. Regarding the phrase "passed in vain": it means that because there is no Teacher in the world, there is nothing to guide and transform beings;
thus, those who commit evil are many, while those who perform good deeds are few. He acts as the eye for sentient beings.
For one hundred and eighty kalpas, the world passed in vain without a Buddha; sentient beings remained in the long night of ignorance, shrouded in darkness with nothing to see. Nothing...
To "tend toward" means that now the Buddha has appeared in the world to act as eyes for sentient beings, enabling people to see and to have a direction toward which they may tend.
Regarding the term "rescue and protection": those who have already entered the evil paths are rescued so that they may emerge from them;
those who have not yet entered the evil paths are protected so that they do not enter. Therefore, it is called "compassion," and it is also called "benefit. Now, having encountered...

"The Buddha’s [appearance] is certainly not due to minor causes; it is entirely because we have planted blessings and merits in our past lives that we have now, in this life, just barely encountered the Buddha.
The above are words of self-congratulation. "At that time," and so forth, refers to the request for the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.

"The characteristics of all phenomena" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) refers to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the characteristics of arising and ceasing (*utpādanirodhalakṣaṇa*), the characteristics of non-arising and non-ceasing (*anutpādānirodhalakṣaṇa*), and the characteristics of the dharmas of humans and devas.
The characteristics of the Śrāvaka-dharma, the characteristics of the Bodhisattva-dharma, and the characteristics of the Buddha-dharma are as follows:

it is said that all sentient beings have long dwelt within the three miserable realms (*tṛtīya-mārga*), undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, and have not tasted the flavor of the Dharma. If they should hear these characteristics of the Dharma, they will practice them with diligent application.
They will certainly attain the fruits of the Path, or be reborn in the heavens; thus, they shall turn from evil paths to wholesome paths, and from wholesome paths to the Noble Path.
Because there is such benefit, he requested that the Wheel of Dharma be turned. At that time, [the phrase] "and so forth" indicates that the Tathāgata silently granted his consent.
Furthermore, the great Brahma kings of five million billion lands in the southern direction each saw their own palaces illuminated by a radiance such as they had never experienced before.

Overjoyed and leaping for joy, they conceived a sense of wonder and immediately went to one another to discuss this matter: "By what cause and condition do our palaces possess such radiance? And those multitudes...
In the midst [of this], there was a Great Brahmā King named Subhadharma, who spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of Brahmās:
"The palaces of us all are filled with a most majestic radiance. This cannot be without cause or condition; we should seek out its significance."
For more than hundreds of thousands of kalpas, such a sign had never been seen before. "Is this due to the birth of a Great Virtuous Deva, or has a Buddha appeared in the world?

At that time, five hundred trillion Brahma Kings, together with their palaces, each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and went collectively toward the north to investigate the cause of this sign. There they saw the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū dwelling at the site of enlightenment.
