At the site beneath the Bodhi tree, he sat upon the lion throne, surrounded with reverent devotion by devas,
nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others. Seeing the sixteen princes requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma,
the Brahma kings then prostrated themselves before the Buddha, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and immediately offered celestial flowers.
They scattered flowers over the Buddha until the flowers were as high as Mount Sumeru, and they also used them to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having completed the floral offerings, each offered their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words: "We pray only that you will look upon us with compassion and benefit us;
we beseech you to graciously accept the palaces we have presented. At that time, the Brahma Kings [stood] before the Buddha.
Then, with single-mindedness and in unison, they spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One is most difficult to behold; he who has shattered all afflictions has not been seen for over one hundred and thirty kalpas, yet now we have obtained this single vision."
All sentient beings who were hungry and thirsty have been filled by the rain of Dharma. One such as you, possessed of immeasurable wisdom, has never before been seen;
today we have finally encountered one like the udumbara flower. Our various palaces have become magnificently adorned because they have received your light.
"World-Honored One of great compassion and pity, we pray that you will graciously accept [this offering].
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha with verses, each of them spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will turn the Wheel of Dharma, so that all in the world—gods, Māras, Brahmas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—may all attain peace and security."
And they attained liberation. Then the Brahma Kings, with one mind and in unison, spoke in verse:
"We pray only that the Honored One among Gods and Humans will turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, beat the great drum of the Dharma, and blow the great conch of the Dharma."
"May you universally rain down the great Dharma rain and deliver immeasurable sentient beings. We all turn to you with this request: please manifest your profound and far-reaching voice.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent. It was likewise so for those from the southwest direction down to the nadir.
First, they deliberated together to seek him out. At that time, following the light, they saw the Buddha. Then, [the assembly] scattered flowers as an offering to the Hall.
At that time, they spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha: "The Destroyer of All Afflictions" refers to the complete exhaustion of the five stages of dwelling; thus, it is called "all.

"All hungry and thirsty sentient beings" means that when the Buddha does not appear in the world, sentient beings have long been destitute of the joy of the Dharma and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
They delight in the food of the Dharma and the nectar of liberation; thus they are all hungry and thirsty.

Now that they have been able to behold the Buddha, he will surely provide them with the food of the Dharma to satisfy the world, so that the hungry may be satiated and the thirsty may attain refreshing coolness.
Having not seen him for more than one hundred and thirty kalpas, his appearance today is no different from that of the udumbara flower.
An auspicious omen has appeared; furthermore, because of the radiance reaching my palace, the palace itself has been graced by light and its adornments have been further enhanced.
At that time, [the Buddha] requested the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. Māra and his celestial hosts perform evil, while Brahmā and his celestial hosts cultivate goodness.
Śramaṇas are upright, whereas Brāhmaṇas are heterodox. Whether their words be good or evil, heterodox or upright, the mind remains unsettled.
Those who were not yet at peace all find peace; those who have not yet attained liberation all attain liberation. The Brahmā is named Śakra;
therefore, he is able to entreat the turning of the Great Dharma Wheel. One who beats the drum awakens the indolent;
one who blows the conch unifies the will; rain nourishes the withered and parched. Because the unsurpassed wheel is turned, it thus unfolds [the teaching].
This is a profound and far-reaching sound. At that time [the phrase] "below" refers to the Tathāgata’s silent assent. From "southwest" below, two directions are omitted for brevity.

At that time, in the direction above, the Great Brahma Kings of five million billion lands all beheld their respective palaces, which were brilliantly illuminated with a majestic radiance such as had never been seen before. They leaped for joy, giving rise to a sense of wonder, and each immediately...
They approached one another and deliberated on this matter: "By what cause and condition do our palaces possess such radiance?
At that time, within that assembly, there was a Great Brahmā King named Śikhin, who spoke these verses for the sake of the host of Brahmās:
"By what cause and condition now Do all our palaces Shine with majestic power and light, Adorned in a manner never seen before?"
"Such a wondrous sign as this has never before been heard of or seen. Is it because a Great Virtuous One has been born, or is it because a Buddha has appeared in the world?

At that time, five hundred trillion Brahma Kings, together with their palaces, each took celestial flowers in the folds of their robes and traveled together toward the lower direction to investigate the origin of this sign. There they beheld the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū dwelling at the site of enlightenment.
At the site beneath the Bodhi tree, he sat upon the lion throne, surrounded by and revered by devas, nāga kings, gandharvas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others. Seeing that the sixteen princes had requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma,
the Brahma kings then prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and immediately offered celestial flowers.
They scattered flowers over the Buddha until the flowers were as high as Mount Sumeru, and they also used them to make offerings to the Buddha’s Bodhi tree.
Having completed the flower offerings, each presented their own palace to that Buddha and spoke these words: "We pray only that you will look upon us with compassion and benefit us;
we beseech you to graciously accept and dwell within the palaces we have offered. Then, in the presence of the Buddha, those Brahma kings—
With one mind and one voice, they praised him in verse, saying:
"How excellent it is to behold the Buddhas, the Holy Honored Ones who save the world! They are able to exert themselves to deliver all sentient beings from the prison of the three realms."
The Honored One of Universal Wisdom, Sovereign of Gods and Humans, out of compassion for all classes of living beings, is able to open the gate of ambrosia and extensively deliver all.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, time passed in vain without a Buddha; when the World-Honored One had not yet appeared, the ten directions were perpetually shrouded in darkness.
The three evil realms increase, and the asuras also flourish; the hosts of devas steadily diminish.
Many die and follow the evil paths, for they do not hear the Dharma from the Buddha and constantly perform unwholesome deeds. Their physical strength, vitality, and wisdom—all these decrease.

Due to the causes and conditions of sinful karma, they lose both happiness and the perception of happiness. Dwelling in the teachings of false views, they do not recognize virtuous conduct and fail to receive the Buddha’s transformation;
thus, they constantly fall into the evil realms. The Buddha is the eye of the world, appearing only after a vast expanse of time has passed.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, you have appeared in the world; having transcended [all realms], you have attained perfect enlightenment.
We are filled with great joy, as are all other multitudes, who marvel at this unprecedented event. Our various palaces have been adorned and made magnificent by the light of your presence.
I now offer this to the World-Honored One; I pray that you will compassionately accept it. By the merit of this act, may it extend universally to all beings.
May we and all sentient beings together attain the Way of the Buddha.
At that time, five million billion Brahma kings, having praised the Buddha with verses, each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will turn the Wheel of Dharma, bringing peace and security to many, and delivering and liberating many.
Then the Brahma kings spoke in verse:
The World-Honored One turns the wheel of Dharma, beats the drum of the nectar-like Dharma, delivers sentient beings from suffering and affliction, and reveals the path to nirvana.
We only pray that you will accept our invitation and, out of compassion, expound it with your great and subtle voice—the Dharma practiced throughout immeasurable kalpas.
"First, we shall deliberate together and seek him out. At that time, [the Bodhisattvas] followed the light and beheld the Buddha. Then, [the assembly] scattered flowers and honored the hall.
"Excellent! [they cried], and spoke verses in praise of the Buddha. Regarding the phrase "the prison of the three realms": previously, the three realms were compared to a burning house.
Because they are scorched and boiled by the five desires, this [world] is likened to a prison because it is bound by the captives of afflictions.
"The multitude of sprouts" refers to the multitude of living beings. "Sprout" (*meng*) refers to the initial growth of grass;
it means that all living beings possess the sprouts of goodness budding within them, which simply lack the conditions to bring them forth. Now, the Tathāgata, out of compassion, [bestows them].
It moistens them with the nectar of immortality, enabling each, whether great or small, to fulfill its life. Before the World-Honored One appeared, there was no radiance to illuminate the world;
therefore, sentient beings throughout the ten directions all dwelt in the long night.

They did not cultivate the ten wholesome deeds and all fell into the three miserable realms. All of this was due to their failure to behold the Tathāgata’s dignified and wondrous marks. Furthermore...

Failing to hear the sound of the Tathāgata’s ten wholesome dharmas, they constantly practice the ten unwholesome deeds; thus their ignorance grows ever heavier and the scope of their minds ever more narrow.
Consequently, their physical strength and wisdom also gradually diminish as they undergo the subtle form of the womb, which develops through successive lifetimes.
They commit various evil karmas and receive retribution in the three miserable realms. Having already lost the bliss of humans, devas, and nirvana, they furthermore—

They conceive the notion that [this path] leads to birth in the human or celestial realms and to *nirvāṇa*. Thus, there are those who have begun to sprout a wholesome mind, yet they lack the eye of wisdom;

furthermore, encountering false teachers, they practice the dharmas of wrong views. They do not recognize the three thousand dignified demeanors (*trīṇi sahasrāṇi īryāpathāni*) nor cultivate the eighty thousand subtle practices (*aśīti-sahasra-sūkṣma-caryā*).

Instead, they mistakenly observe the precepts of cattle, dogs, and so forth as the cause for rebirth in heaven, seeking thereby the fruit of liberation from suffering. This is because they have not encountered a [True Teacher].

They have come to be transformed by the True Dharma; though they seek to escape suffering, they instead enter further into it. At that time, [the Buddhas] below requested the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
Then, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū accepted the request of the Brahmā Kings of the ten directions and the sixteen princes.
I requested that he immediately turn the Wheel of Dharma in its three phases and twelve aspects— a wheel which no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā,
or anyone else in the world could turn— namely: this is suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

This refers to Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū’s acceptance of the invitation to turn the wheel of Dharma. To proceed from the Small Vehicle to the Great Vehicle is the constant rule of the Buddhas of antiquity;
therefore, he first taught the Four Noble Truths. Regarding the "three turnings," the first is the turning that demonstrates their characteristics:

"This is the nature of suffering as oppression; this is the nature of accumulation as the cause of attraction; this is the nature of cessation as that which is to be realized; this is the nature of the path as that which is to be cultivated."
As for "showing the characteristics," it means showing them by way of the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths.
"This is the nature of suffering’s oppression" means that this body is the dwelling place of birth, old age, sickness, and death;

because one possesses this body, one is oppressed by manifold sufferings and lacks autonomy. "This is the nature of accumulation that invites [suffering]" means that this body of suffering is entirely...
Because it is gathered through one’s own craving for the five sensory desires, it is precisely the ignorance that initiates karma and moistens rebirth.
This is the "nature that can be realized as cessation," meaning that to emerge from the fruit of suffering, one must realize the bliss of nirvāṇa;
this refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). This is the "nature that can be cultivated as the path," meaning that to realize nirvāṇa, one must...
Because it concerns the factors of the path to cultivation, it consists of the thirty-seven auxiliaries to enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*). Second, the turning toward cultivation:
this further encourages them to advance in practice by means of four dharmas: "This is suffering; you should know it. This is its origin; you should abandon it.
This is its cessation; you should realize it. This is the path; you should cultivate it. Third, the turning toward realization: furthermore...
This is to encourage them by taking oneself as a witness. "This is suffering; I have already known it;
you too should know it. This is the origin; I have already abandoned it; you too should abandon it. This is cessation; I have already realized it; you too should realize it. This is the path;
I have already cultivated it; you too should cultivate it. As for the term "turning," it refers to turning over these teachings [to others].

It enters into the minds of sentient beings. There must be three turnings because there are three faculties (*indriya*). As for the twelve aspects (*ākāra*): "aspect" refers to the aspect of practice (*karmapatha*).
Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are mundane practices; cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are supramundane practices. These three turnings together comprise twelve aspects.
Regarding the "Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*): a wheel has the sense of crushing and grinding; this refers to the four truths turned three times.
This is because they are all capable of crushing and grinding away the afflictions of the three realms.

However, these four dharmas can only be turned by the Tathāgata, who is fully endowed with the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*); others, such as Māras and Brahmās, lack this wisdom of skillful means and therefore cannot turn them.

And he extensively expounded the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging;

clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations...

Consciousness ceases. With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease. With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases.
With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases. With the cessation of existence, birth ceases. With the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.

Regarding the "extensive exposition": this refers to taking the Four Noble Truths and elaborating them for those of middling faculties into the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

This is the extensive explanation of Suffering and its Accumulation as the gate of forward evolution (*pravṛtti-mukha*), and the extensive explanation of Cessation and the Path as the gate of reverse cessation (*nivṛtti-mukha*).

Regarding "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*): the *Mahā-sūtra* states that non-comprehension of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called ignorance; it refers to delusion (*moha*).
This refers to first becoming deluded regarding the objects that should be known, and subsequently initiating wrong conduct and so forth toward those very objects.
This ignorance arises from emptiness in a state of horizontal deviation, based on delusion regarding the principle of the Four Noble Truths; this is precisely the ignorance that initiates karma.

The fruit of the karma that has been performed is "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the term "karma," it refers to meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karma, because these are fruits arising from that ignorance.
As for "formations as the condition for consciousness" (*saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam*), the *Mahānidāna-sūtra* states: "Consciousness is the initial mind upon which formations depend.
This means that with formations as a condition, there is the initial consciousness; through the perfuming of the mind by formations, there exists the seed of future fruit, as well as the present...

Regarding "conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness conditions name-and-form" (*saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānaṃ nāmarūpapratyayam*): the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* states that the four aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) arising simultaneously with consciousness constitute "name-and-form.
As for the term "consciousness," it refers here to the active member (*pravṛtti-aṅga*) of consciousness; in its aspect as a seed, it is exclusively the *ālayavijñāna*.

In its state of active manifestation (*pravṛtti*), it pertains to all six consciousnesses. Now, in order to distinguish this from the seeds, it is said that it arises together with the four aggregates.

Since the aggregate of consciousness already belongs to the supporting consciousness itself, the [remaining] four aggregates constitute "name" (*nāman*), while the *kalala* and so forth constitute "form" (*rūpa*).
Regarding "name-and-form as the condition for the six sense bases," the *Mahānidāna Sūtra* states: "The growth of name-and-form constitutes the six sense bases.

This refers to the period following the fourth and seventh [weeks], when the stage of the sense faculties is complete and the six sense bases become clear and prominent. The increase of "name" (nāma) establishes the mental faculty (*manas*), while the increase of "form" (rūpa) establishes the other five.

When the four aggregates are designated as "name," the characteristics of consciousness have not yet been differentiated; now, because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is clear and distinct, it is called "increase. Because of its solidity...

At the stage of the embryo (kalala), before the five sense organs have differentiated, it is merely called "one form" (rūpa). Now, as the material sense organs gradually become complete, they are further divided into five.

Regarding the statement that the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) condition contact (sparśa), the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "The conjunction of the three factors—the sense organ, the object, and consciousness—constitutes contact."
Although contact (*sparśa*) is a single entity, it is divided into six according to the consciousnesses. Furthermore, these six contacts are subsumed into two:

the first five are called "contact through resistance" (*pratigha-sparśa*), while the mental contact (*manas-sparśa*) is called "contact with designation" (*adhivacana-sparśa*). Although contact itself lacks resistance, its five bases—the sense faculties—are characterized by resistance.
Therefore, the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, take only blue and so forth as their objects, but do not take the names of "blue" and so forth as their objects.

Mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can take both blue and so forth as its objects, as well as the names of "blue" and so forth. Because it is established by name based on its object, it is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*). As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"Regarding the three causes of craving, that which is distinct and not yet understood is called contact. The "three causes of feeling" refers to the objects of the three feelings; these objects are capable of [producing] them.

Because it gives rise to feeling (*vedanā*), it is called the cause. Specifically, from the time of birth until the age of three or two, because one is still unable to fully comprehend, it is not called "feeling" but is termed "contact" (*sparśa*).
Regarding contact as the condition for feeling, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "That which arises simultaneously with contact is called feeling;
the discernment of the three types of feeling and the experiencing of contact is what is meant by 'arising simultaneously with contact. The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* says: "In the realm of desire..."

Craving precedes feeling (*vedanā*). This refers to the period from five or six years of age up to fourteen or fifteen, when one has already discerned the three types of feeling through their distinct characteristics, yet sexual desire has not yet arisen;
at this stage, it is merely termed "feeling. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Attachment to a single craving is called 'feeling,' which refers to the craving for food and clothing.
Regarding "feeling conditions craving," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "To be stained by and attached to feeling is craving."

This refers to being entangled with and longing for pleasant feelings (*sukha-vedanā*) among the three types of feeling; hence it is called "defiled attachment. This is precisely greed of middling and inferior grades.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Greed for requisites and sensual desire. This refers to the craving for exquisite requisites from the age of fifteen or sixteen onwards.

When sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) manifests but has not yet been extensively pursued, it is simply termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). This is precisely the ignorance that moistens rebirth (*upapatti-avidyā*).

Regarding "craving conditions grasping" (*tṛṣṇā-pratyaya-upādāna*), the *Mahā-sūtra* states: "The increase of craving is grasping. This means that although other afflictions are included, craving is predominant in its capacity to moisten [rebirth];
therefore, it is said that craving increases. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Pervasive seeking is called grasping. Grasping refers to greed (*lobha*). That is to say:

As one grows older, one craves the objects of the five desires and rushes in all directions to seek them, undaunted by toil or fatigue; for this reason, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are distinguished.

That which first arises is called "craving," while its continuous progression is termed "grasping" as a distinct category. Regarding "grasping conditions existence" (*upādānapratyayo bhavaḥ*), the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"The outflowing karma (*sāsravakarma*) produced by grasping constitutes existence (*bhava*). This is because the various karmas created by the mind through grasping result in existence.
Therefore, it is called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). Because this karma can directly bring about its future fruit, it is termed "existence" (*bhava*).

As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Existence refers to the karma that is currently capable of drawing forth a future fruit. Because of its restless seeking, one accumulates the karma capable of drawing forth a future fruit;
thus, karma is called "existence. Since it possesses a future fruit, and because the cause is designated by the name of the fruit, karma is termed "existence."

Furthermore, regarding "birth conditioned by existence," the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The arising of the aggregates from karma constitutes birth. This refers to "arising from karma" in terms of its predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Beginning from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) up until the fundamental state (*mūlabhava*), as long as one has not yet undergone decay and transformation, all of this is termed "birth."

Since karma is either wholesome or unwholesome, while birth is its resultant fruit, which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): if we consider them in terms of causes and conditions, birth arises directly from the seeds of the two types of grasping (*upādāna*).
Aging is the maturation of the aggregates (*skandha*), and death is the disintegration of the aggregates. Specifically, the state of various forms of decay is called the maturation of the aggregates;
from the age of forty onwards, as the countenance gradually declines, it belongs to aging. When the body breaks up and life [ends]...
The end is called death. The above sequence of conditions arising from one another is termed the "Gate of Flowing On" (*pravṛtti-mukha*).

Specifically, the three afflictions (*kleśa*)—ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—and the two factors of formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) belong to the path of karma.

From consciousness (*vijñāna*) through sensation (*vedanā*), along with birth and old age/death (*jāti-jarāmaraṇa*), these seven items are collectively termed the single path of suffering; that is, the triad of delusion, karma, and suffering. Below the section on the cessation of ignorance, it returns to...
This is the extinction of the door [of ignorance]. Take the single dharma of ignorance as an example: first, employ the wisdom that investigates causes to investigate its cause;

next, employ the wisdom that examines causes to examine its cause. By investigating and examining in this sequence, one realizes that it has no self-nature whatsoever across the present, past, and future;
only then can it be eliminated. If this is true for a single dharma, it is so for all dharmas. Question: Does ignorance have a realm?
Regarding the internal realm and the external: what does this sever? Answer: This severs the ignorance within the realm, namely the two types of ignorance that give rise to and moisten [existence].
As for the ignorance outside the realm, it is severed partially during the initial stages of dwelling, until it is completely exhausted at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi).

When the Buddha preached this Dharma amidst the great assembly of devas and humans, six hundred *koṭi-nayuta* of people attained liberation of mind from all outflows (*āsrava*) by not grasping at any phenomena.

They all attained profound and wondrous meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), the three knowledges (*vidyā*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and were endowed with the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). When he preached the Dharma for the second, third, and fourth time, ten million...

Sentient beings as numerous as billions of *nayutas* of Ganges sands likewise attained liberation of mind from all outflows (*āsrava*) by not grasping at any phenomena. From that time forward, the assembly of *śrāvakas* became immeasurable, boundless,
and incalculable.
This refers to the benefit gained by the fourfold assembly. "Not receiving any dharmas" means that the mental consciousness has been extinguished.
"Outflows" (*āsrava*) refers specifically to the three outflows. "The mind attains liberation" means that with the exhaustion of all outflows, one attains mastery over the mind.

"Profound and wondrous meditative concentration" refers to the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). "Possessing the eight liberations" is also called the eight renunciations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), which are as follows:
Because one turns one's back on these pure five desires and abandons this mind of attachment, it is called "turning away" (*pratikūla-vimokṣa*).

First, regarding "having internal perception of form while externally perceiving forms": this means that the practitioner first contemplates the appearance of their own physical body as putrid, decaying, impure, and not to be desired.
With a single-minded tranquility, they further imagine the skin and flesh falling away until only white bones are seen. There are eight [aspects].

Because it is the radiance of form, it is called "having the internal appearance of form. Furthermore, because the greed of the desire realm is difficult to sever, although one has already contemplated the impurity of one's own internal form, one further contemplates the form of others as impure to engender revulsion and thereby seek its abandonment;
thus it is also called "contemplating external form. This is the first liberation (*vimokṣa*), situated at the beginning.
The meditative absorption of the dhyāna heavens: second, "internally without perception of form, one perceives forms externally.
This means that when a practitioner has entered the second dhyāna, they have already extinguished the perception of internal bodily form; hence it is said, "internally without form.

Furthermore, because the craving of the desire realm is difficult to sever, they continue to contemplate external signs of impurity to engender revulsion, seeking thereby to eliminate it; hence it is further said, "perceiving externally."

This is form (*rūpa*). This is the second liberation (*vimokṣa*), situated in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the Second Dhyāna Heaven. Regarding the "third pure liberation, realizing with the body":
this refers to taking a pure object as its focal point (*ālambana*). That is to say, after the practitioner has completed the second liberation...
Having set aside the impure signs of external forms, one practices within meditative concentration upon the eightfold radiant light, which is pure, brilliant, and like the color of a wondrous jewel;

therefore, it is called the "pure liberation" (*śubha-vimokṣa*). Once the mind is luminous and pure, bliss gradually increases and pervades the entire body, resulting in total joy; therefore, it is further called "bodily realization. This is the [third]...

The third liberation (*vimokṣa*) is situated within the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the third *dhyāna* heaven. The fourth is the liberation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*).

This means that after the practitioner has already discarded the impure form of their own body in the desire realm following the first liberation, and after discarding the color of the white bones of the internal body following the second liberation, they further discard all impurities of the external body.
Regarding form (*rūpa*): there remain eight kinds of pure form (*śubha-rūpa*) that all abide dependent upon the mind. If the mind relinquishes form, form immediately ceases and perishes.

When the single mind takes emptiness as its object and accords with emptiness, one enters the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*). Therefore, it is called the "rejection of the sphere of space" (*ākāśāyatana-pratipakṣa*).
This is the fourth rejection (*pratipakṣa*), situated within the meditative absorptions of the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven. [The fifth is] the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

The liberation through turning away (*vibhūta-vimokṣa*). This refers to when a practitioner, having abandoned the sphere of infinite space, focuses the mind one-pointedly on consciousness and enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

At that time, they contemplate this absorption as being entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, based upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth; seeing it as deceptive and unreal, the mind gives rise to aversion and turns away from it without attachment.

Therefore, it is called the "liberation through turning away from the sphere of consciousness" (*vijñānānantyāyatana-vibhūta-vimokṣa*). Sixth is the liberation through turning away from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vibhūta-vimokṣa*).

Equanimity (*upekṣā*). This means that when a practitioner relinquishes the sphere of consciousness and enters meditative absorption by focusing the mind one-pointedly on the sphere of nothingness, they then contemplate this concentration as being entirely impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, as well as deceptive and unreal, based upon the five aggregates and so forth.
Because the mind gives rise to aversion and detachment rather than craving and attachment, it is called the "rejection of the sphere of nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vairāgya*).
Seventh is the "rejection of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-vairāgya*).

This refers to when a practitioner, having relinquished the sphere of nothingness, enters meditative absorption by single-mindedly taking the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their object; at that time, they contemplate this very concentration as being entirely composed of the five aggregates and so forth.
All are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; they are deceptive and unreal. One gives rise to revulsion toward them and does not cling to them;

therefore, this is called the "liberation by way of equanimity that is neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Eighth is the "liberation by way of equanimity through the cessation of sensation and perception. Sensation (*vedanā*) refers to the sensation of desire;

perception (*saṃjñā*) refers to conceptualization—namely, the two mental factors of sensation and perception among the five aggregates. This means that the practitioner feels weary of and afflicted by them.
This mind is distracted; wishing to enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for rest, one turns away from and extinguishes all mental states of feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*).

This is called the "rejection and liberation of feeling and perception" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*). By cultivating this contemplation, one gives rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), severs the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of the three realms, and realizes the fruit of Arhatship.
It is then renamed the "eight liberations" (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*). The above constitutes the Great Pervasive [Contemplation] as the middle and lower grades.
He taught the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
At that time, the sixteen princes all left the household life as youths and became śrāmaṇeras; their faculties were keen and sharp.

Their wisdom was clear and penetrating. Having already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas and having purely cultivated the Brahma-faring, they sought Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Together they addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great virtuous Śrāvakas have all already achieved [their goals]. World-Honored One, you should likewise preach to us the Anuttara..."
"the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Having heard it, we shall all together practice and study it.
World-Honored One, our aspirations, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and what is contemplated in our deep hearts—may the Buddha himself bear witness to this.

At that time, among the multitude led by the Wheel-Turning Holy King, eighty trillion people, seeing the sixteen princes leave the household life, also sought to leave the household life. The King then...
“Grant your permission.
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras request that you turn the Great Wheel of Dharma. Since these youths left the household life, they have delighted in the Great Dharma;
thus, at the very moment of their first birth in this Sahā world, they declared: ‘In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am supreme.’”

"Venerable One," refers to those whose faculties are inferior. "Praising virtues" means: "Penetrating, sharp, clear, and lucid" indicates that being penetrating, one does not become mired in minor paths;
being sharp, one does not delight in gradual vehicles; being clear, one does not dwell within the realms of the aggregates; and being lucid, one does not stagnate midway.

"Having already made offerings to Buddhas" means the planting of merit has already been extensive. "Purely cultivating the Brahma-faring life" means the sowing of virtue has already been accomplished.
"Profound. [The phrase] "both petitioned below" means they requested the Great Dharma. They said, "The followers of the Small Vehicle delight in the Small Dharma;

the Tathāgata has accordingly bestowed the Small Dharma upon them, and they have thereby attained the fruits of the Path. We, however, aspire to and delight in the Great Dharma; the Tathāgata should bestow the Great Dharma upon us.
If we practice and study it, we shall certainly realize the Great Fruit. Furthermore, they said, "This is what our profound minds contemplate."
This alone was sufficient: the Tathāgata, possessing all-encompassing wisdom, must have known our minds without waiting for us to make three earnest requests.
That eighty billion people sought to leave the household life was simply because those above acted and those below followed.

At that time, that Buddha accepted the śrāmaṇeras’ invitation; after twenty thousand kalpas had passed, he then preached this Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma*, the teaching for bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas, amidst the fourfold assembly.
Having spoken this sūtra, the sixteen śrāmaṇeras, for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all together received and upheld it.
They recited it with complete mastery. When this sutra was being preached, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras all believed and accepted it;

among the assembly of śrāvakas, there were also those who believed and understood; yet the rest of the sentient beings, numbering in the thousands of myriads of koṭis, all gave rise to doubt and confusion.
The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or resting. Having finished preaching this sutra, he immediately entered a quiet chamber and dwelt therein.
He entered meditative concentration for eighty-four thousand kalpas;
this was because the Great Penetrating One preached the Great Dharma for those of great capacity.

As for why he accepted the invitation and only after another twenty thousand kalpas did he preach—it was likewise because he long remained silent regarding this essential point, not being in a hurry to speak, but waiting until they were truly frustrated and eager to learn.
It is only after one has reached the height of delight that one may be inspired to begin. This explains the following: regarding the *śrāmaṇera* who upholds the sūtra.
"Receiving" means internalizing it within the mind without omitting a single word. "Upholding" means respectfully wearing it upon one's breast, guarding it so as not to lose it.
"Reciting" means reading aloud and practicing the recitation. "Believing and accepting" means receiving with deep faith.

As for "the others all giving rise to doubt," it is as the saying goes: "A loud voice does not enter the ears of those within a village. The Buddhas Sun-Moon-Lamp Brightness preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The sixty minor kalpas are said to be like the duration of a single meal. This refers to those who have not ceased or desisted for eight thousand kalpas;

that is to say, they preach in the dust, they preach in the lands, and they preach with blazing intensity without interruption. As for "entering meditative concentration at the conclusion of the sutra," this means he further silently reveals [the truth] through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras, knowing that the Buddha had entered his chamber and was in silent meditative concentration, each ascended a Dharma seat.
For eighty-four thousand kalpas, they extensively expounded and analyzed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly.
One by one, they delivered six million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
He caused them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After eighty-four thousand *kalpas* had passed, the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū arose from his samādhi, proceeded to the Dharma-seat, sat down with composure, and addressed the great assembly.
These sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras are truly rare; their faculties are keen and sharp, and their wisdom is clear and lucid.
They have already made offerings to immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of buddhas, and in the presence of those buddhas, they have constantly cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya).
They have received and upheld the Buddha-wisdom, revealing and teaching it to sentient beings so that they may enter therein. You all should repeatedly draw near to them and—

One should make offerings to them. Why is this? If śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas can believe in the Dharma of the sutras spoken by these sixteen bodhisattvas, and receive, uphold, and do not disparage it, such persons shall all attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

This śrāmaṇera is one who turns the wheel of the Dharma on their behalf. As for the term "bodhisattva-śrāmaṇera," it means that even while at the stage of a śrāmaṇera, one is already capable of shouldering the great task; thus they are called a "śrāmaṇera" and yet also a "bodhisattva.
Long ago, the senior śrāmaṇera Gao visited Yaoshan. Yaoshan asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Nanyue. Yaoshan asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "To the Yangtze River."
Ling received the precepts and departed. Mount [Shan] asked, "What do you hope to achieve by receiving the precepts? Ling replied, "I hope to escape birth and death.
The Mountain said, "There is a person who does not receive the precepts, yet for whom there is likewise no birth and death to escape.

Do you know this? Ling said, "If that is so, then the Buddha's precepts are useless. The Mountain said, "This śrāmaṇera still has his teeth hanging on his lips. Ling then prostrated himself and withdrew.
One day, Shanshan said, "Chang'an is very noisy. [Wuzu] said, "In my country, all is peaceful.

Shanshan asked, "Did you obtain this from reading the sutras? Did you obtain it by requesting instruction? He replied, "I did not obtain it from reading the sutras, nor did I obtain it by requesting instruction.

Shanshan said, "There are many people who do not read the sutras and do not request instruction; why is it that they do not obtain it? He replied, "I do not say they do not obtain it; it is simply that..."
He was unwilling to accept the responsibility. One day, Shanshan said to him, "Why do you not go to receive the precepts? He replied, "Knowing this kind of matter, I simply let it be.
What else could one call 'precepts'? If one speaks of the novice Gao, he may truly be called a Bodhisattva novice.

Regarding "each ascending the Dharma seat": because the Buddha had entered meditative absorption, the assembly heard nothing; therefore, each [disciple] took the Buddha's place to turn the wheel of Dharma.
"One by one descending" refers to the multitudes being delivered. "Showing" (*śāsana*) means pointing out, such as saying, "This is good," or "This is evil.
"Teaching" (*anuśāsana*) means instructing, such as saying, "Good should be practiced," or "Evil should be abandoned. "Benefiting" (*anugraha*) means...
Benefit (*anuśaṃsa*) means causing those who practice evil to abandon evil and practice good, thereby enabling them to obtain benefit and the like. Joy (*muditā*) refers to sympathetic joy;
it means praising their minor virtues according to their merit, causing them to give rise to gladness, and inspiring them to practice diligently without regression.
By adorning the Buddha-dharma with these four matters, one causes them to resolve upon *bodhicitta*. [In the passage] "The Great Penetration" and below, the novice monk attained...
"Bestowing predictions and revealing [the truth] to sentient beings so that they may enter therein" means to deliver all sentient beings and cause them all to enter the Buddha-wisdom.
Since it is said that one delivers sentient beings into the Buddha-wisdom, it can be understood that one has personally realized the Buddha-wisdom oneself;
therefore, although the word "bestowal of prediction" is not explicitly mentioned, this is precisely the matter of bestowing a prediction.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "These sixteen bodhisattvas always delight in preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Each of these bodhisattvas has converted six million *koṭi-nayuta* of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;

in every lifetime they have been born, they have been together with these bodhisattvas, and having heard the Dharma from them, they have all attained faith and understanding. By virtue of these causes and conditions, they have attained..."
They encountered forty trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and even now that number is not exhausted. O Bhikṣus, I tell you now:
those sixteen śrāmaṇeras who were disciples of those Buddhas have all attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
they currently reside in lands throughout the ten directions, preaching the Dharma, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
They shall become his retinue. Those two śrāmaṇeras will become buddhas in the eastern direction: the first named Akṣobhya, who resides in the Land of Joy;
the second named Sumerukūṭa. In the southeastern direction there are two buddhas: the first named Siṃhanāda and the second named Siṃhavikrāmin. In the southern direction there are two buddhas:
the first named Gaganasthita and the second named Nityoparata. In the southwestern direction there are two buddhas: the first named Śakra... [and so forth].
[The Buddha] with the marks. Second is the Buddha named Brahma-mark. In the western direction are two Buddhas: first, Amitābha;
second, Sarvalokadhātūpadravodvegapratyuttīrṇa. In the northwestern direction are two Buddhas: first, Tamālapatracandanagandhābhijña; second, Merudhvaja.
In the northern direction are two Buddhas: first, Meghasvara; second, Meghasvararāja. In the eastern [direction...]
The Buddha of the north is named Destroyer of All Worldly Fears.
I, the sixteenth, Śākyamuni Buddha, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the Sahā world-system.
This refers to the period following the bestowal of predictions upon the sixteen śrāmaṇeras, during which they performed the work of Dharma masters to deliver sentient beings.
Each entry below states that those transformed were all of great capacity (mahāmūla).

By virtue of the causes and conditions of hearing the wondrous Dharma, six million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand-like numbers of sentient beings of great capacity, in life after life and birth after birth, were constantly [endowed] with the ten...
Six bodhisattvas were born together in the same place; hearing the Dharma from him, they all attained faith and understanding.
Furthermore, by virtue of this causal condition of hearing the sutra and attaining liberation, they encountered forty trillion buddhas without interruption until the present day.
The phrase "various [others]" below refers to the sixteen śrāmaṇeras who, following the Dharma Master, became Dharma Kings. The East is the direction of the *zhèn* (thunder); *zhèn* represents...
Thunder is a moving entity. Among those that move all things, none is swifter than thunder. The name of the Buddha, Akṣobhya, translates as "Immovable.
The summit of Mount Sumeru translates as "Wondrously High"; its towering protrusion is likewise a symbol of immovability.
This clearly reveals the locus where ignorance moves, thereby realizing the Wisdom of Immovability. The southeast is the direction of *Xun*. *Xun* represents wind;
among those that stir all things, none is more swift than wind. The Buddha’s name is Lion Sound (*Siṃhanāda*). Regarding the lion-like aspect:
when a lion roars once, the hundred beasts are distressed and torn asunder. When the *Xun* wind blows once, the myriad apertures roar in fury. Thus, the *I Ching* says: "By means of *Xun*..."
"Practicing Expedient Means" (*xingquan*) means that by means of the two wisdoms of expedient means (*upāya*) and reality (*bhūta-artha*), one subdues Māras and overcomes enemies;

thus it corresponds to the southern direction of Li. Li represents fire, which dries things. Among all things that dry the myriad objects, none is as drying as fire. The Buddha is named "Dweller in Space" (*ākāśa-sthita*);
like the sun in the sky, there is nowhere he does not illuminate. He is also named "Ever-Extinct" (*nitya-nirvṛta*); because he possesses the sun of wisdom, [there is no darkness].

It is because it clarifies the constant cessation [of phenomena]. When the sage faces south to listen to the world, and when a youth travels south to seek out wise teachers, they both take their inspiration from this.

To the west lies the region of the various directions (where *kun* represents earth, which accords with all things). Among those that support the myriad things, none is more substantial than the earth.

The Buddha is named Dìxiàng (Emperor Aspect) and Fànxiàng (Brahmā Aspect). He is the "Emperor Aspect" because his profound virtue sustains all things; he is the "Brahmā Aspect" because he presides over the great trichiliocosm.
He resides in the western direction, the trigram *Dui*. *Dui* represents the marsh; nothing brings joy to the myriad things more than the marsh.
The Buddha is named Amitābha, which here means "Immeasurable Life," for his wisdom and grace are inexhaustible. He is also called "Deliverer of All Worlds."
Regarding "intermediate suffering": it refers to using the moisture of wisdom to reach others, causing them to eliminate their feverish afflictions and attain cool serenity;
therefore, it is the northwest, the direction of *qian*. *Qian* represents heaven (*tian*), the vigorous entity. Among those that initiate the myriad things, none is more divine than heaven.
The Buddha is named Candanagandha-ṛddhimat (Sandalwood Fragrance with Supernatural Powers). He is called so because he arrives swiftly without hurrying and reaches his destination without traveling.

He is also named Sumeru-lakṣaṇa (Having the Mark of Mount Sumeru), for he rises high above all things. This corresponds to the northern direction, Kan. Kan represents water; that which moistens all things.
Nothing moistens more than water. The Buddha is named Cloud-Sovereign (*Abhramati*), also known as King Cloud-Sovereign (*Abhramatirāja*).
Because he moistens the myriad things with a mindless heart, like the movement of clouds and the falling of rain, he belongs to the northeast, the direction of Gen. Gen is the mountain;
among those that bring all things to completion and initiate all things anew, none is more flourishing than Gen. The Buddha is named Destroyer of All Worlds (*Sarvalokavidhvamsaka*). One.

Because *śamatha* (calm abiding) can destroy and eliminate all worldly phenomena, he is also named Śākyamuni, which translates as "The Benevolent Sage" (*Śākya-muni*). Furthermore, because *śamatha* can accomplish all worldly phenomena:

when the fires of calamity were about to destroy [the world], they were extinguished at once with a single breath; when the world was about to be formed, it was entirely gathered in with a single thought. These ten...
This is how all things begin and end. The *Yī Jīng* says: "The Lord emerges at Zhèn; He becomes equalized at Xùn; they see one another at Lǐ;
He dispatches His service at Kūn; He expresses joy at Duì; there is battle at Qián; He rests from labor at Kǎn; and He completes His expression at Gèn.
This corresponds exactly with what has been said here; therefore, it is cited to demonstrate the fundamental nature of both mundane and supramundane phenomena.
There is no duality. The Buddha has no fixed direction, yet he establishes fixed directions because he reigns as a sovereign in each direction for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, one sees that the Buddha’s body is nowhere, yet there is nowhere it is not. That each direction has two [aspects] is a combined exposition of patience (*kṣānti*) and wisdom (*jñāna*).

"O bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras, each of us individually taught and transformed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, who heard the Dharma from us and [set their minds] upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Among these sentient beings, there are some who now abide on the stage of the śrāvaka; I have constantly taught them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
[They shall attain] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. These people should enter the Buddha-way gradually by means of this Dharma.
Why is this? Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
Those immeasurable beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time—namely, you bhikṣus and my śrāvaka disciples in future ages after my parinirvāṇa—are they.

At this point, he finally reveals his true intention, saying: "In the past, when we were śrāmaṇeras preaching the Lotus Sūtra, we each taught and transformed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. These sentient beings followed us..."

Upon hearing the Dharma, they all originally aspired to achieve unsurpassed bodhi. However, midway through their journey, they completely forgot their original vows and considered themselves sufficient.
To this day, there are still some who abide in the stage of a śrāvaka. Yet, I have never failed to bestow the Dharma of bodhi upon them;
it is only because their capacity is narrow and small that they are unable to receive it in its entirety. Therefore, by me—
The rain of the Dharma of a single flavor nourishes all equally and universally, causing them to gradually enter the Buddha-way.
That is to say, among all dharmas, those who gradually attain entry into the Way according to their respective capacities are like this.

From "At that time" onwards, the text clarifies that the immeasurable sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whom I transformed when I was a śrāmaṇera in the past, were none other than [these very beings].
These are none other than the twelve hundred arhats present here and now, as well as the śrāvaka disciples of the future.
Speaking from this perspective, it is not only today that I have preached the Dharma of the One Vehicle for you;
rather, since immeasurable kalpas past, I have already preached the Dharma of the One Vehicle for you, and until this very day, there has never been any variation.
Why is it that you are still unable to bear this burden?
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be further disciples who have not heard this sutra, and who neither know nor realize the conduct of bodhisattvas.
Regarding the merit they have attained, they conceive the thought of extinction and enter into nirvana;
yet I shall become a Buddha in another land under a different name. Although these people conceive the thought of extinction and enter into nirvana, in that land—
They seek the wisdom of the Buddha and, having heard this sutra, attain extinction solely through the Buddha-vehicle;
there is no other vehicle, except for the skillful means employed by the Tathāgatas in their preaching of the Dharma.
This refers to future disciples who shall likewise enter the Buddha-way gradually by means of this Dharma.

The intention is that while the Buddha was in the world, his present disciples personally beheld the Buddha and heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and thus it is certain they entered the Buddha-way.
However, in future ages, once the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and there is no one to preach the Dharma, they will not hear this sutra, nor...
They perceive that the conduct of their daily lives is the bodhisattva path, yet they claim for themselves that they have already attained ultimate nirvana.
Toward such disciples, I do not abandon them; I manifest as a Buddha in other lands under different names and titles.
There, they again encounter me through the causal conditions of their past lives, where they are born together in one place and seek the wisdom of the Buddha. It is then that I preach this to them.
The Sūtra causes them to enter the equal wisdom of the Buddha; thus we know that what has been taught from beginning to end is entirely the One Buddha Vehicle.
Apart from the Buddha Vehicle, all other teachings are merely the expedient words of the Tathāgata.
This reveals that the Tathāgata’s compassion extends through the three periods of time; such is the manner in which he brings to completion both the beginning and the end. As it is said:
"Thus, monks, immeasurable and incalculable merits cannot be fully exhausted even if explained for immeasurable eons.
When the Tathāgata himself knows that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and the assembly is pure, with firm faith and understanding—"
Having fully realized the dharma of emptiness and entered deeply into meditative concentration, he then assembled the bodhisattvas and the community of śrāvakas and preached this sutra for them.
"In the world, there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction; it is only through the single Buddha-vehicle that one attains extinction.

Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata, through his skillful means, has entered deeply into the nature of sentient beings and knows that their aspirations and inclinations lie in the lesser dharmas."
Attached to the five desires, for the sake of such people as these, he speaks of *nirvāṇa*. If these people hear it, they will immediately believe and accept it; this is the primary metaphor.
"The time for *nirvāṇa* has arrived" means that the time has already come. "The assembly is also pure" means that their faculties have matured.
With firm faith and understanding, they cannot be confused by the various teachings; having thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness, they [are unshakable]. The ten thousand...
No dharma can enter [his mind]. Having entered deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), he cannot be moved by praise or blame.

Then, [the text] says "assembling the inferior," meaning that when the faculties (*indriya*) of the assembly have matured and their resolve is pure, he finally assembles the multitude and preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The passage beginning with "bhikṣu" (monk) means that when the faculties have not yet matured, he preaches the Dharma according to those faculties. As for "entering deeply into the nature of sentient beings," it is because they do not know the superior or the middling.
Regarding those of inferior disposition, I thoroughly understand their nature; therefore, I expound the Dharma according to their capacities and preach nirvana for them.
That is to say, I also know all that they practice with their profound intentions, penetrating it all without obstruction in this manner.
For example, there is a perilous and difficult evil path five hundred *yojanas* long, desolate, uninhabited, and a place of terror.

Suppose there is a great multitude who wishes to traverse this path to reach a place of precious jewels. There is a guide, wise, intelligent, and discerning, who thoroughly knows the characteristics of the dangers and the open passages of the treacherous road.
He leads the multitude, intending to get them across this difficulty. However, while the people he leads are on the way...
They grew weary and despondent, saying to the guide: "We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear; we can no longer proceed.
The road ahead is still long, and we now wish to turn back. The guide, possessing many skillful means, thought to himself: "These people are truly pitiable."

"How can you abandon such great treasures and wish to turn back? Having thought this, by the power of skillful means, he created an illusory city within the perilous path after three hundred yojanas had been traversed. He addressed the multitude, saying:
"Do not be afraid; do not turn back. You may now rest here in this great city and do as you please. If you enter this city, it will be a source of joy."
"You shall attain peace and security. If you can proceed further to the place of treasure, you may go there.
At that time, the exhausted multitude felt great joy and marveled at this unprecedented occurrence, saying, "We have now escaped this evil path; we have swiftly attained peace and security.
Thereupon, the people entered the conjured city, conceiving the thought that they had already crossed over and the thought that they were secure. At that moment, the guide knew...
Once this multitude had attained rest and was no longer weary, he immediately extinguished the conjured city and spoke to the people, saying:
"Come, you all! The place of jewels is near. That great city you saw earlier was created by me merely as a place of rest."
This parable is established to clarify the intention behind first teaching the three vehicles and subsequently teaching the one vehicle.
The five hundred yojanas symbolize the triple world and the two types of nirvāṇa. The perilous and difficult evil path symbolizes the evil path of saṃsāra.
"Desolate and devoid of people" refers to a vast and remote wilderness cut off from all sides, where there is no human habitation to provide rest or support;
this is a metaphor for the absence of Nirvana as a refuge within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). It is like a great multitude wishing to traverse a perilous path.

"Reaching the place of rare treasures" is a metaphor for those who have not yet attained *nirvāṇa*, desiring to transcend the perilous path of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and enter the wisdom of the Buddha.
"The guide" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, who is the one who points out the way.

"Skillfully knowing the passable and the obstructed" means knowing what constitutes the main thoroughfare for escaping birth and death, and what constitutes the evil paths for entering into birth and death.
"Road" (*lu*) means that one intends to lead the multitude across this difficulty; "will" (*jiang*) means to guide.
This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s direct intention to lead [beings] out of the evil paths of birth and death and straight into the Buddha-wisdom.

"The multitude of people being led who become weary and retreat midway" refers to those who, due to their indolence, wish to withdraw halfway through the journey. "They address the Guide," and so forth, is a metaphor for hearing the Great [Vehicle].
"Because of this Dharma, we have become weary and fallen back. Our strength is exhausted, and we have encountered a desolate and terrifying place where no people dwell.
Although we wish to reach the place of treasure, the road ahead remains far distant; therefore, we all desire to turn back.
The Teacher, having reflected on this, employs a skillful means as a parable: he transforms [the distance] beyond three hundred yojanas.
"The construction of a city" is a metaphor for wandering through birth and death within the triple world (*triloka*), a vast and desolate place where no one dwells.
"To provisionally establish two nirvāṇas" refers to creating small sites for temporary rest. "The passage beginning with 'He addressed the assembly'" is a metaphor for preaching about nirvāṇa.
"'One may stay therein' means that this place can serve as a temporary lodging. "'Acting according to one's own will' means either..."
Whether sleeping or sitting, there is no lack of comfort; this is a metaphor for the unimpeded exercise of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
"If one enters this city, one quickly attains peace and security" is a metaphor for realizing *nirvāṇa*, by which one may be free from fear.

"If you can proceed to the place of treasure, you may also go there" refers to yourselves; it means that you do not betray your original resolve and have not abandoned what you have previously cultivated.

"It is three hundred *yojana*s away; exert yourselves and press forward. If you are willing to reach the place of treasure, then this conjured city shall serve as a convenient path, and from here you may also proceed. At that time, the multitude enters the conjured city.

Those who conceive the thought that they have already crossed over and the thought of having attained peace and security are likened to those who take *nirvāṇa* to be the ultimate goal and no longer advance in their quest.
Little do they realize that a traveler’s lodging is merely for one night; it is not a place for long-term residence.
That having found rest, one no longer feels fatigue is a metaphor for the exhaustion of the afflictions of views and thought, and the full restoration of the spirit and vital energy.

The immediate dissolution of the conjured city is because its attachment was perceived, and thus it was extinguished. That the place of jewels is near means that proceeding directly forward is precisely the way.
This was to urge them to enter. As for what was previously called a "great city" that I manifested as a place of rest—it refers to the manifested city seen earlier.
Because you were weary and refused to proceed further, I manifested it for you to take a rest and briefly relieve your fatigue;
it was not the actual place where the treasure is found. Question: Why did he speak only of the "treasure"?
As for its location being described as "nearby" without specifying a distance, the answer is: if there were a specific distance, it would still be a conjured city and not the true treasure site.
To know the treasure site, one must realize that it fundamentally has no direction and does not involve a journey; it is not apart from what is before one's eyes, yet no one is able to reach it.
Therefore, it is said to be "nearby. One should know that those who enter through language and text all remain within [the realm of the conjured].
Regarding the "transformed city," an ancient master said: "The pleasures of the journey do not ultimately lead one home.
Only that which flows forth from within one's own breast is truly the "Jewel Place."
"O bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is likewise so. Now, for your sake, he acts as a great guide.
He knows that the cycle of birth and death, the afflictions, and the evil paths are perilous, difficult, and far-reaching; those who should depart and those who should be delivered.

If sentient beings were to hear only of the Single Buddha Vehicle, they would not wish to see the Buddha, nor wish to draw near to him, and would instead think: 'The path of the Buddha is long and distant; it will take a long time...'"

One must undergo diligent hardship before it can be accomplished. The Buddha, knowing that such a mind is timid, weak, and inferior, employs the power of skillful means to bring about a cessation midway;
for this purpose, he speaks of two nirvāṇas. If sentient beings abide in these two stages, the Tathāgata—
At that time, he immediately spoke for them: "What you have accomplished is not yet complete. The stage upon which you abide is close to the wisdom of the Buddha;
you should observe and deliberate that the nirvāṇa you have attained is not the ultimate reality.

It is merely through the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means that, within the single Buddha-vehicle, three are distinguished and taught—just as that guide, for the sake of providing rest, conjured a great [city]."
Once he knew they had rested, he told them: "The place of treasure is near. This city is not real; it was created by me as an illusion.
This is the corresponding teaching: the evil paths of birth and death correspond to the perilous and difficult evil paths of five hundred yojanas and so forth.
"Knowing those who should be sent away and those who should be delivered" means one should properly understand the signs of what is passable and what is obstructed.

"If the assembly is inferior" refers to those who previously grew weary and retreated midway. If the Tathāgata were not to guide sentient beings by means of the teachings of the Two Vehicles, but instead directly reveal the immeasurable path-dharmas of all Buddhas, they would not wish to see the Buddha, nor would they wish to draw near to him.

The Buddha [left], and before the Dharma Hall, the grass grew a fathom deep. This was because he reflected that the path of the Buddha is long and distant, difficult to accomplish, and that they would be unable to swiftly escape the birth and death of the triple world. From "The Buddha knew" downwards, it indicates that he should employ skillful means.
"The timid and weak" refers to those who are fearful, cowardly, and frail, lacking the equipment of valor and diligent effort. "The inferior" refers to those of low capacity.
This refers to those who are base, lowly, and inferior, lacking the magnanimity and far-reaching vision of the sublime.
For the sake of such people, by means of skillful power, one speaks of two nirvāṇas along the way; these are like the conjured cities established beyond three hundred yojanas.
Yet they do not realize that although these two nirvāṇas lie beyond three hundred yojanas, they still remain [within the realm of delusion].
This refers to within five hundred *yojanas*. As for sentient beings dwelling on the two stages, they have already formed the notion that they have transcended birth in their previous lives;

thus, they conceive a sense of security and, being attached to it, do not relinquish it. The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata" below punctures [this view] by revealing that *nirvāṇa* is not real.
I say that you must still practice and study many vast Buddha-activities before it can truly be called nirvana; you must not yet claim it to be the ultimate.
Furthermore, the stage in which you currently abide is close to the wisdom of a Buddha, but it is not yet the attainment of the Buddha-wisdom itself.
What is meant is that merely being free from delusion is called attaining liberation. As stated below, he again employs a metaphor to illustrate the principle:
it is just as a guide, in order to rest a group of people exhausted by travel, conjures a great city along the way.
He causes them to cease for a moment; seeing their attachment, he again destroys the phantom city to hasten them toward the treasure place.
This is what is meant by "departing is immediately sealed as abiding, and abiding is immediately sealed as breaking"—the functional capacity of the Iron Ox.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood."
The various devas, nāga kings, and hosts of asuras constantly rained down celestial flowers to make offerings to that Buddha.
The devas beat celestial drums and performed various kinds of music; fragrant winds blew away the withered flowers and rained down fresh and beautiful ones in their stead.
After ten intermediate kalpas had passed, he finally attained the path of Buddhahood; all the devas and people of the world felt their hearts leap with joy.
The sixteen sons of that Buddha, each surrounded by hundreds of thousands of millions of followers, together proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
Bowing my head at the Buddha’s feet, I entreat him to turn the wheel of Dharma. May the rain of the Holy Lion’s Dharma fill me and all beings.
A World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter; appearing but once in the course of vast eons, he causes all things to tremble in order to awaken the multitudes of living beings.
In the worlds of the eastern quarter, across five hundred million kotis of lands, the palaces of the Brahmās shone with a brilliance such as had never been seen before.
When the Brahmās perceived these signs, they immediately came to where the Buddha was, scattering flowers as an offering and presenting their palaces to him.
They requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma, praising him with verses. Knowing that the time had not yet come, the Buddha accepted the request by remaining silent.
In the three directions, the four intermediate points, and likewise above and below, they scattered flowers and offered palaces, requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
The World-Honored One is most difficult to encounter. We pray that, out of your original compassion, you will widely open the gate of ambrosia and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
The World-Honored One of immeasurable wisdom accepted the request of those people and proclaimed for them various teachings: the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
From ignorance to old age and death, all arise with birth as their condition. You should understand these manifold afflictions.
When this Dharma was proclaimed, six hundred trillion *nayutas* reached the end of all suffering and all became Arhats.
During the second preaching of the Dharma, ten million *koṭis* of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained arhatship by not grasping at any dharmas.
From that time onward, those who attained the Way were beyond measure; even with the calculations of ten trillion *kalpas*, one could not reach their limit.
At that time, the sixteen princes left the household life as śrāmaṇeras and together entreated that Buddha to expound the Mahāyāna Dharma, saying:
"We, along with our retinues, shall all attain the Way of the Buddha; we pray to become like the World-Honored One, whose eye of wisdom is foremost and pure."

The Buddha, knowing the mind of the youth and his practices in past lives, through immeasurable causes and conditions and various parables, expounded the six pāramitās and the matters of the supernormal powers; he analyzed the true Dharma and the path traversed by bodhisattvas.

He preached this Lotus Sūtra in verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. After that Buddha had finished preaching the sūtra, he entered meditative concentration in a quiet chamber and sat with single-minded focus in one place for eighty-four thousand kalpas. These śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha was still in meditation and had not yet emerged.
For immeasurable billions of beings, they expounded the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom; each sat upon a Dharma-seat and preached this Mahāyāna sūtra.
After the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, they proclaimed and assisted in the transformation through the Dharma; every one of these śrāmaṇeras saved all sentient beings.

There were six hundred trillion beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all those who had heard the Dharma were born together with their teacher in every buddha-field. These sixteen śrāmaṇeras fully practiced the path of the Buddha.
Now, throughout the ten directions, each has attained perfect enlightenment. Those who heard the Dharma at that time are now each in the presence of various Buddhas;
those among them who dwell as śrāvakas are being gradually taught the Buddha-way. I was included among the sixteen [disciples], and I have also preached it for you in the past.

Therefore, by means of skillful expedients, I have led you toward the Buddha-wisdom. For this fundamental cause and condition, I now preach the Lotus Sutra to enable you to enter the Buddha-way; be careful not to harbor fear or alarm.
Regarding the statement that one may sit at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas without attaining the Buddha-way:
it is as Yunmen said—that reaching the Dharma-body yet failing to forget attachment to dharmas, such that one's own views still persist and one falls into the side of the Dharma-body, is a sickness.
Foyan also said: "One who rides a donkey and refuses to dismount is likewise sick. Only after passing through ten small kalpas does one finally attain realization.
As for the Way: it refers to the Tathāgata’s attainment of Bodhi, which is truly not bound by days. "That Buddha descended" [refers to] the śrāmaṇera requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
"In the eastern direction" [refers to] the various Brahmās requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma. "The Buddha knew" [refers to] the Tathāgata’s silent assent.
"In the three directions" [refers to] the nine directions requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma. "Immeasurable" [refers to] the Great Penetration explaining the Two Vehicles.

The Dharma. From "proclaiming and expounding" below, the great assembly received benefit. At that time, from "the ten [novices]" below, the śrāmaṇeras requested the Great Dharma. From "the Buddha knowing" below, he preached the Great Dharma for the śrāmaṇeras.
From "that Buddha" below, at the conclusion of the sutra, he entered samādhi. From "these various" below, the śrāmaṇeras succeeded to the throne of the Dharma King.
At that time, from "then" below, this correctly reveals the fundamental cause of the Dharma being preached today. It says: "That which you all..."
Because you have been able to hear the Lotus Sūtra, it is precisely because in the past, during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he once expounded this sūtra for you all.
Due to those past causes and conditions, I now speak it for you once again.
You should directly accept and take it upon yourselves; do not harbor further fear or apprehension within your hearts.
It is like a perilous and evil road, remote and desolate, abounding in venomous beasts, and furthermore lacking water and grass—a place feared by all people.
Countless tens of millions of people wish to cross this dangerous path, yet the way is exceedingly vast and distant, spanning five hundred yojanas.
At that time, there was a guide who possessed strong memory and wisdom; his mind was clear and resolute, and he rescued the multitude from their peril.
When the people were all exhausted, they said to the guide: "We are now utterly weary; we wish to turn back from here."
The Guide thought to himself: "These people are truly pitiable; how can they wish to turn back and lose such a great treasure?
