He immediately contemplated an expedient means and, employing his supernatural powers, manifested a great city with its walls and gates, adorned with magnificent mansions and dwellings.
Surrounded by gardens and groves, with flowing canals and bathing ponds, and featuring multi-storied towers and high gateways, it was filled with both men and women.
Having created this transformation, he comforted the multitude, saying, "Do not fear. You may enter this city; each may follow what brings you joy."
Once the people had entered the city, their hearts were filled with great joy; they all conceived the thought of security and each considered themselves already delivered.
Knowing that they had rested, the Guide assembled the multitude and addressed them, saying: "You should proceed further; this was merely a conjured city."
I saw that you were utterly exhausted and wished to turn back midway; therefore, by the power of skillful means, I have provisionally conjured this city.
Now, through diligent application of effort, you shall together reach the place of treasure.
"Remote and isolated" means that no people travel there. "Lacking water and grass" means that provisions for the journey are exhausted.
This is unlike the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness, who possess the necessary provisions to advance directly. At times, the guide descends to rescue those in distress;
at other times, the multitude descends because they have become weary. Since they lack provisions and the road is vast and far-reaching, they consequently become prostrate with exhaustion.
And they wish to turn back. The Guide descends and, by means of skillful means, establishes an illusory city. "Dwelling" refers to the place where one rests the body;

it is a metaphor for emptiness and stillness. "Gardens and groves" refer to the place of recreation; they are metaphors for the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). "Bathing pools" refer to the place for washing the body;

they are metaphors for the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). "Heavy gates" refer to the place of entry and exit; they are metaphors for the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. "Pavilions" refer to the place for gazing out.
The dwelling-place is a metaphor for the divine eye. As for "men and women," taking pleasure in their dwelling-place is a metaphor for the bliss of nirvana.
I am likewise thus: as the Teacher of all, I see those who seek the Way faltering and falling into despondency along the path.
Unable to cross over birth and death, nor the perilous paths of the various afflictions, he therefore uses the power of skillful means to preach nirvāṇa for their relief, saying:
"Your suffering is extinguished; all that was to be done has been accomplished. Once they know they have reached nirvāṇa, they all attain the state of an arhat.
Thereupon, he assembled the great multitude and preached the Dharma of ultimate reality. By the power of the skillful means of all Buddhas, he distinguished and taught the three vehicles.
There is only the Single Buddha Vehicle; the two were taught as resting places. Now I shall speak the truth for you: that which you have attained is not final extinction.
To become a Buddha with all-encompassing wisdom, you must arouse great diligence. You shall realize all-encompassing wisdom, the ten powers, and other Buddha-qualities;
endowed with the thirty-two marks, this is indeed true cessation. The Guide of all Buddhas speaks of nirvana for the sake of bringing rest.
Once they have thus rested, they are led into the Buddha-wisdom.

"I also descend" corresponds to [the Buddha] descending. "Seeing all [beings]" corresponds to [the Buddha seeing] the multitude. "Announcing weariness" corresponds to the manifestation of the *nirmita-nagara* (the conjured city).
As for saying "Nirvana is taught for the sake of rest," it means that Nirvana is taught so that you may rest from the afflictions (*kleśa*). Once...
"Knowing this" refers to the destruction of the conjured city and the hastening toward the place of the true treasure. "The Buddhas" indicates the location of ultimate reality.
*The Great Outline of the Lotus Sutra*, Volume Three.
The Great Sections of the Lotus Sutra, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Annotated by the Bhikṣu Tōngrùn of Jintíng.
The eighth verse of the *Śrāvakavyākaraṇa-parivarta* (The Parable of the Sewn-in Jewel) says:
"The entire world is intoxicated; Deep in intoxication, poverty grows ever deeper. How could they know that within their tattered robes"
A close friend secretly hides treasures; though possessing jewels, he cannot use them. Whatever he requires does not satisfy his heart;
he seeks food and clothing from others, suffering cold and hardship unto this day. As for the term "disciple" (dizi):

one's learning follows that of the teacher, hence they are called "younger brothers" (di); their understanding arises from the teacher, hence they are called "sons" (zi). This is the chapter [on disciples].
Regarding the bestowal of predictions upon one thousand two hundred arhats, yet the names of only five hundred are specifically recorded:

it is because these five hundred received their predictions under identical names and personally declared their realization. Through the preceding chapter, one sees the beginning and end of the Tathāgata; through this present chapter, one sees the beginning and end of the disciples.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra heard from the Buddha this wisdom and skillful means of preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
he further heard the bestowal of the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the great disciples;
he further heard the matters concerning causes and conditions from past lives; and he further heard that all Buddhas possess the power of great sovereign supernormal abilities. He attained...

"Unprecedented! My heart is pure and leaps with joy. He immediately rose from his seat, went before the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance, he did not for a moment turn his eyes away, and thought to himself: "The World-Honored One is most extraordinary!"

What you have done is truly rare. You accord with the world and, through various dispositions, employ skillful means and insight to preach the Dharma for them, drawing sentient beings out from their attachments to all things. We are unable to fully proclaim the Buddha’s merits in words;
only the World-Honored Buddha can know our deep-seated hearts and original vows.
First, the narrator describes the realization. From "following the Buddha" downward, he takes up the meaning of the two preceding chapters on Expedients and Parables.

Furthermore, from "hearing again" downward, he takes up the meaning of the Chapter on Prediction. Finally, the two phrases beginning with "hearing again" take up the meaning of the Chapter on the Phantom City.
The phrase "All Buddhas possess great sovereign supernormal powers" refers specifically to the sixteen princes who, having become śrāmaṇeras themselves, proceeded until they attained [Buddhahood].
The Buddha has individually taught and transformed immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and even as many beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.

He does so without abruptness or violence, guiding them gradually and steadily until the present day, never ceasing or abandoning his efforts, as if it were but a single day. Is this not great sovereignty?
Furthermore, with a single mind, he penetrates immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and even as many [realms] as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
He adapts the Dharma to the capacities of sentient beings, such as those like sand, causing each of them to gradually enter the Buddha-way;
is this not great supernormal power? "The mind being pure and leaping with joy" is also like the disciples who attained awakening and rejoiced.

"And then [he] acts below" refers to silently requesting the bestowal of a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). "In accordance with below" refers to receiving the aforementioned teaching of the Dharma according to their capacities. It says:
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the two pāramitās of skillful means (*upāya*) and knowledge-and-vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

Furthermore, he is able to penetrate deeply into the nature of sentient beings; therefore, he can prescribe medicine according to their ailments. For instance, he leads ordinary worldlings who are attached to existence (*bhava*) into emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

he leads those of the Two Vehicles who are attached to emptiness into the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*); and he leads Bodhisattvas who are attached to the Middle Way into the Buddha-wisdom (*buddha-jñāna*), and so forth. The Tathāgata possesses such [qualities].
The immeasurable and incalculable merits cannot be fully known; therefore, even throughout immeasurable kalpas, we are unable to describe them exhaustively.

Although we, being of inferior capacity, cannot fully comprehend the Tathāgata’s true merits, may we, in birth after birth and kalpa after kalpa, never be separated from the Tathāgata and always remain in his presence.
"Have you not realized that the original vows of our body and mind were originally for the sake of attaining Buddhahood and delivering sentient beings?
These words are intended precisely to borrow the Tathāgata’s own voice to explain his own original intent for appearing in the world.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra?
I have always declared him to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma. I have also constantly praised his various merits:

his diligent protection and upholding [of the teachings], his assistance in proclaiming my Dharma, his ability to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly, and his complete understanding."
He has expounded the True Dharma of the Buddha and brought great benefit to his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life.
Since the Tathāgata’s passing, no one has been able to exhaust the eloquence of his discourse. You should not think that Pūrṇa is merely able to protect and assist in proclaiming my Dharma.
Furthermore, in the presence of ninety billion Buddhas of the past, he upheld and assisted in proclaiming the Buddha’s true Dharma;
among those who expounded the Dharma, he was also the foremost. Moreover, regarding the teaching of emptiness spoken by those Buddhas, he clearly understood and thoroughly mastered it.
He attained the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom and was always able to preach the Dharma with profound discernment and purity, free from all doubt.
He was fully endowed with the supernatural powers of a bodhisattva and constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) throughout his entire life.
To the people of that Buddha’s world, he was universally regarded as a true śrāvaka. Yet, through these skillful means, Pūrṇa benefited immeasurable hundreds of thousands of beings.
He was born. Furthermore, he transformed immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* beings, causing them to establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For the sake of purifying Buddha-fields, he constantly performs the work of a Buddha, teaching and transforming sentient beings.
O monks, Pūrṇa was also foremost among the Dharma-preachers under the seven Buddhas; now, among the Dharma-preachers in my own teaching, he is likewise [foremost].

They shall be the foremost; among the Buddhas yet to come in this Bhadrakalpa, they shall likewise be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma, all of whom will protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, in the future, they will protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming the teachings of immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, teaching and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, and establishing them in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"For the sake of purifying the Buddha-land, he constantly exerts himself with diligence to transform sentient beings.
From this point downward, the text correctly explains the supramundane original vows of the disciple. "Do you all see this Pūrṇa?
This is a question to the great assembly intended to alert them; it means that you all [have been] with Pūrṇa day after day.
When they met, they saw only his physical form and did not know his mind. Now, for your sakes, I shall explain its beginning and end;

therefore, I first warn you: "Do you see this Pūrṇa? We [the Buddhas] below first praised his skill in preaching the Dharma as being unsurpassed—purity in being unmixed, diligence in being untiring, and protection in being non-injurious.
"Not losing" is called "upholding. "Assisting" means providing support. "Proclaiming" means expounding extensively. "Possessing in full" refers to having it within oneself.
"Explaining" refers to bestowing it upon others. "The True Dharma of the Buddha" refers to the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma.
"Benefiting fellow practitioners" means benefiting one's companions who cultivate the pure Brahma-faring together by means of the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma.
They are companions. This means that they mingle among the masses and preach the Dharma according to the occasion, assisting the Buddha in propagating his transformation.
As for the phrase "I always praise and extol," it shows that they do not belong to the class of those who revile or disparage. From "Having personally abandoned...

onwards, he praises their eloquence to the utmost, noting that it transcends all others and is peerless. From "You all... onwards, he reveals their profound intention, stating that it is not only within me [that this exists].

Within this assembly, he is the foremost in assisting in the proclamation of the Buddha-dharma; likewise, in the assemblies of all past Buddhas, he was also the foremost in assisting in the proclamation of the Buddha-dharma.
From this, one knows that when the Tathāgata preached the sutras while he was a śrāmaṇera, [he was the foremost].
He was already present within the assembly, assisting in the proclamation and transformation of the Dharma. Not only today, but as stated below, he manifested his original vow.

As for the "Dharma of emptiness" that he preached, it is the single characteristic, the single flavor, the dharma of quiescent extinction. Regarding "clearly understanding and thoroughly penetrating":
"clarity" refers to refined vision; "understanding" refers to complete penetration; "penetration" refers to being unimpeded; and "thoroughly attaining" refers to reaching the profound depths.
This is called "penetration. It means that his vision of the Dharma is precise and thorough, and his realization of the Way is profound.

Regarding the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), these are the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*), language (*nirukti*), meaning (*artha*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*). This indicates that he has attained the great wisdom of a bodhisattva, rather than the limited wisdom of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
"Always able to put [himself] below" means that if one attains the Dharma but does not attain wisdom, there is substance without function; one cannot...

He preaches the Dharma. Now, having personally realized the Dharma with intimacy and attained the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*), he is able to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
his eloquence flows like a cascading river, free from any doubt or obstruction. If one lacked the roots of virtue within, how could one possibly discourse thus without?
The phrase "fully endowed" below reveals that this Bodhisattva’s playful mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*) and his purification of Buddha-lands are all completely perfected.

This is sufficient. "According to their lifespan" reveals that he manifests transformation bodies according to the various classes of beings, sharing the same conditions as the multitude, just like a bodhisattva.
"Constantly practicing the pure conduct" reveals that he is fully endowed with the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s pure and white *brahmacarya*.
That people of the world all claim he is truly a *śrāvaka* is because they see only his coarse appearance and do not know his subtle essence.
Seeing his traces, yet not knowing their source; "and enriching the lowly" means seeing him preach the minor Dharma to deliver sentient beings of lesser faculties.
Furthermore, "transforming the lowly" means seeing him preach the Great Dharma to deliver sentient beings of superior faculties.
"For the sake of purification" means seeing him manifest outwardly while keeping the secret within; it is not that he does not truly give rise to even a single thought of joy and delight.

It is the mind. From the passage "The bhikṣus below" onward, it is seen that the Buddhas of the three periods of time preach the Dharma, and Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra assists in propagating the Buddha’s transformation;
both are foremost in this regard. The "Seven Buddhas" are the Buddhas of the past. "I" refers to the present Buddha. The "Worthy Kalpa" (Bhadrakalpa) refers to the future Buddhas.
"Causing him to stand" refers to the "standing at thirty" mentioned in the Analects, meaning to cause him to stand out prominently and firmly on his own.
It stands upright, neither leaning nor falling, like a mountain of silver or an iron wall.
Gradually fulfilling the path of a bodhisattva, after the passing of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
you shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in this land, and be named Dharmaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
He is the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
That Buddha’s buddha-field consists of a single great trichiliocosm as vast as the sands of the Ganges River.

Its ground is composed of the seven treasures and is as level as the palm of a hand, without mountains, hills, valleys, gullies, or ravines; it is filled with towers and pavilions made of the seven treasures.
Within it, the palaces of the various devas are situated close to the void; humans and devas interact, being able to see one another.
There are no evil realms, nor are there women. All sentient beings are born by transformation; they are free from lustful desire, possess great supernormal powers, and their bodies emit radiance.
They travel through the air with ease, their resolve and mindfulness are firm, and they are endowed with diligence and wisdom. Universally...
He is golden in color and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man. The sentient beings of that land constantly subsist on two kinds of food:

first, the food of the joy of Dharma; second, the food of the bliss of dhyāna. There are immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas who have attained great supernormal powers and the four kinds of unhindered wisdom, and who are skillfully able to transform and guide all classes of sentient beings.
The assembly of his śrāvakas is beyond the reach of calculation or reckoning; they have all fully attained the six supernormal powers, the three insights, and the eight liberations.
That buddha-field possesses such immeasurable merits and is adorned with these accomplishments.

The eon is named Jewel Radiance (Ratnaprabhāsa), and the land is named Pure Excellence (Suvimala). The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and the Dharma shall endure for that long.
After a very long time, following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven precious jewels shall arise and fill his entire country;
this is his prediction of enlightenment. As for the Buddha named Dharmaprabhāsa (Light of Dharma), it is because he clearly understands the dharma of emptiness taught by all Buddhas.
Thus, one should know that his swift eloquence is like thunder and his sharpness of discourse is like a flying arrow. One must fully perfect the practices of a bodhisattva.
Only then does one attain Bodhi. When that Buddha descends, he sees that his teaching and transformation are vast and great;
it does not stop at a single trichiliocosm as a single land. The Flower Treasury World (Huazang Shijie) is its capital. Regarding the statement that "the ground is as level as the palm of a hand":
beneath the ocean there is a stone named "Palm," which is not uneven by even the measure of a single mote of dust. It should be understood as being like the ocean.
"Palms. The *Bhadrapāla-vaipulya-sūtra* says: "It is like the palm of a Buddha, not the palm of a human being.
Because human palms are uneven, whereas this is taught as the Dharma of the level ground of the mind; therefore, the ground is likewise so.

That various seven-jeweled towers and pavilions fill its midst is because it is adorned with the various treasures of the Dharma. When the devas descend and see humans, they have never before seen such a thing."
Heaven. Heaven was originally not non-human, for the human and the celestial are one body.

Because the human and the celestial are one body, it is called a "near place," and it is further said that the two are able to see one another. The phrase "without the lower [defilements]" reveals that this land is a pure land.
