His land will be pure, named Constantly Erected Exalted Banner.
He transforms and guides bodhisattvas, their number like the sands of the Ganges. The Buddha possesses great majestic power, and his fame fills the ten directions.
His lifespan is immeasurable; out of compassion for sentient beings, the True Dharma shall last twice as long as his life, and the Semblance Dharma shall last twice that duration.
Countless sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, have planted the causes and conditions for the Buddha-way within this Dharma of the Buddha.
Previously, there were those who requested a prediction [of their future enlightenment]; Ānanda was the younger brother of the Tathāgata, and Rāhula was his son.
I do not bestow the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) privately; I must wait for them to form the aspiration before granting it.

This is what is meant by "willingly coming so that both hands may hand it over. When we say, "We too should have a share in this," we refer to those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Although their stages differ, if one relies upon my original vow, then we too should have a share in this Dharma.
Furthermore, among the disciples, there are those who first relied upon non-Buddhist paths and later left the household life; even they have now all received their predictions.

How much more so for us, who have resolved to leave the household life and immediately returned to the Tathāgata, having no other teacher, daily hearing the True Dharma, and being free from any seeds of heterodoxy—how could we not have our share and fail to receive a prediction? Why wait for a formal request? This is the preservation of one's entire person.
Regarding these words of "shouldering the burden": we, however, are the eyes of gods and humans;

we both know and recognize that one is the younger brother of the Tathāgata and the other is the son of the Tathāgata. Therefore, the great assembly has turned their hearts toward you with eager expectation.

If you do not receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), it would cause the assembly to lose heart. Thus, by receiving this prediction, our own wishes are fulfilled, and those of the multitude are likewise fulfilled.
This is the hope [of the assembly]. At that time, the great assembly requested a prophecy. At that time, the Buddha said... [and so forth], the Tathāgata bestowing the prophecy.

As for the name of the Buddha, "King of the Sovereign Supernatural Powers of Mountain-like Ocean-like Wisdom" (Shanhai Zizai Tongwang): "Mountain" represents the immovable wisdom of ultimate reality (*bhūtatajjñāna*);

"Ocean" represents the expedient wisdom that responds to the world. Because it is suddenly unmoving, it is called "sovereign" (*svairin*); because it swallows and spits out all streams, it is called "supernatural power" (*abhijñā*).

"Making offerings" refers to performing the duties of a Dharma Master. One must know how to memorize and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures, just as a vessel receives water without leaving behind a single drop.
One must make offerings to sixty-two billion Buddhas before one can attain Bodhi.
"Teaching and transforming" refers to the assembly of beings to be delivered. As for the land named "Victorious Banner," its inhabitants possess great learning and wisdom.
Because he is victorious over all, the kalpa is named "Exquisite Sound," for the sound of the Dharma pervades the entire land.
Because his life of wisdom is inexhaustible, the Buddha's lifespan is immeasurable.
At that time, eight thousand bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds within the assembly all had this thought:
"We have not even heard of the great bodhisattvas receiving such a prediction; by what cause and condition do these śrāvakas receive such a definitive assurance?
Then the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those bodhisattvas, addressed them, saying: "O sons of good family..."
"Son, Ānanda and I simultaneously resolved our minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of the Buddha Śūnyarāja.
Ānanda always delighted in much learning, while I was always diligent and energetic;
therefore, I have already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whereas Ānanda has protected and upheld my Dharma, and shall continue to do so."
This is the treasury of the Dharma of all Buddhas, which teaches and brings to fulfillment the assembly of bodhisattvas; such was his original vow, and therefore he has received this prediction.
In the presence of the Buddha, Ānanda personally heard his own prediction and the adornments of his buddha-field;

his aspirations being fully realized, his heart was filled with great joy at having attained what he had never experienced before. At that moment, he recollected the past immeasurable thousands of millions of billions [of eons].
He has attained unimpeded mastery over the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, just as he has heard it now, and he also recognizes his original vows.
At that time, Ānanda spoke these verses:
The World-Honored One is most rare and marvelous! He has caused me to recollect the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, just as I have heard them today.
I now have no further doubt; I abide securely in the Buddha-way, acting as an attendant through skillful means to protect and uphold the teachings of all Buddhas.
This Bodhisattva raises a doubt. "Those who have newly resolved their minds" refers to Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Three Worthies (*trividha-ārya*).
"All of them think thus" means: "We, as Bodhisattvas in training (*śaikṣa*), who extensively practice the six perfections, do not yet receive a prediction [of enlightenment].
For what reason, then, do Śrāvakas in training—whose afflictions of thought (*kleśa*) still remain—obtain this decisive assurance? Is it not too remote?"

"To distance those who are distant and to draw near those who are near"—this is to probe the Tathāgata with private, biased intentions. From the passage beginning "At that time" below, he shows the sequence from root to branch:
he states that he and Ānanda both resolved their minds for enlightenment at the same time; therefore, in birth after birth, they have always been brothers.
However, while their initial resolve was the same, their powers of aspiration differed, and thus what they have realized differs. In reality, [he is] equal to me.
We breathe from the same nostrils; therefore, I have now received this prediction [of enlightenment], not out of partiality.
"Ānanda, below..."—having received this prediction, he rejoiced. "Immediately, below..."—he attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).

Furthermore, he saw that Ānanda protects and maintains the Dharma-treasury of the past, and does not merely protect and maintain the Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas of the present and future. This, moreover, is similar to Pūrṇa...
They shared the same quarters and dwelling. In the verse, it says that acting as an attendant through skillful means was precisely Ānanda’s original vow.
At that time, the Buddha told Rāhula: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood;
your name shall be Tāpitasaptaratnapuṣpa (Treading upon the Seven-Jeweled Flower) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi..."

“O Noble One, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, you shall make offerings to as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are atoms in ten worlds, and you shall always be the eldest son of those Buddhas, just as you are now. This is the Buddha who treads upon the seven-jeweled lotuses.”

The adornment of his buddha-field, the number of kalpas for his lifespan, the disciples he transforms, and the duration of his True Dharma and Semblance Dharma shall be no different from those of the Tathāgata Śāgaramati-vikrīḍita-abhijñārāja. He shall also serve as the eldest son of this Buddha.
After this period has passed, he shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this, [spoke in verse:]
He spoke in verse, saying:
"When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son; now that I have attained the Way of the Buddha, he has received the Dharma and become my Dharma-son."
In future ages, he shall see immeasurable billions of Buddhas and serve as their eldest son, seeking the Buddha-way with a single mind.
Rāhula’s secret practices are known only by me; appearing now as my eldest son, he does so to manifest this to all sentient beings.
Immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis—his merits are beyond counting. He dwells securely in the Buddha-dharma to seek the unsurpassed path.
The Buddha’s name is “He Who Treads Upon Seven-Jeweled Flowers”; whether lifting his foot or setting it down, he always treads upon jeweled flowers.
This is the fruit of secret practice. As for "should offer" below, this refers to the secret mechanism and secret practice that even spirits and deities cannot fathom.
One shall attain Bodhi after making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten worlds.
One will constantly be a son of the Buddhas, no different from being my own son today. The adornments of the lands and kalpas are all identical to those of Sāgarabuddhivikrīḍita;
this is because he knows that practice is not different from wisdom, and wisdom is not different from practice, for he proceeds with both wisdom and practice in tandem. This...
Furthermore, he walked into the forest arm-in-arm with Ānanda. In the verse, he manifested as the eldest son to instruct sentient beings.
From these two characters, "manifestation" (示現), it is evident that he was one of their own.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw that these two thousand individuals—both those in training and those beyond training—were gentle in mind, tranquil and pure, and gazing at the Buddha with single-minded devotion.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, “Ānanda, do you see these two thousand individuals, both those in training and those beyond training? “Indeed, I see them,” [Ānanda replied].
“Ānanda, these people shall make offerings to as many Buddhas and Tathāgatas as there are atoms in fifty worlds.”

Come! With reverence and respect, protect and uphold the treasury of the Dharma. At the end of time, you shall simultaneously attain Buddhahood in lands throughout the ten directions, all bearing the same title:
Tathāgata Ratnākṣa (Jewel-Aspect), Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. Your lifespan shall be one...
The eons, the adornments of the lands, the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, and both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma shall all be identical.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
These two thousand śrāvakas now stand before me; I bestow upon them all the prediction that they shall in the future attain Buddhahood.
The number of Buddhas they have made offerings to is as previously described, as numerous as atoms of dust; having upheld their Dharma-treasury, they shall later achieve perfect enlightenment.
In each of the lands throughout the ten directions, they shall all share one and the same name; simultaneously sitting at the site of enlightenment, they shall realize unsurpassed wisdom.
All shall be named Ratnalakṣaṇa (Precious Mark), and their lands, disciples, True Dharma, and Semblance Dharma shall all be equal and without distinction.
All, by means of their various supernormal powers, deliver sentient beings throughout the ten directions; their fame is universally pervasive as they gradually enter nirvana.
At that time, two thousand disciples—both those still training and those beyond training—hearing the Buddha’s bestowal of predictions, leaped for joy and spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One is the lamp of wisdom; hearing the sound of my prediction, my heart is filled with joy, as if drenched by nectar."
This was the bestowal of predictions upon two thousand learners (*śaikṣa*). "Those whose minds are supple" means they lack a mind that is stubborn or difficult to transform.
"Tranquil and pure" means they lack a temperament that is violent or uneven. "Single-mindedly contemplating the Buddha" means...
This is also because he wishes to realize and know his original vow. "The Buddha told [them]" and below, this is the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*).

Those who share the same name, "Precious Appearance" (*Ratnākāra*), are all able to protect and uphold the Dharma-treasury. In the verse, "sitting together at the site of enlightenment" means that they attain the Way simultaneously.

It is not as if these twelve hundred people were receiving their predictions of enlightenment in successive order. From the passage "At that time" onwards, they receive their records and rejoice, praising the Buddha.
Thus, the lamp of his honored wisdom shines brilliantly, illuminating my long night of ignorance and further illuminating my original vows.
Therefore, he bestowed upon me this prediction. Having heard the sound of this prediction, it was like nectar poured into my heart and lungs, instantly bringing me refreshing coolness.
Chapter Ten: The Dharma Master (The Parable of the Well).
The verse says:
A sacred spring originally has a hollow, But it remains blocked and never opens. If one briefly borrows the strength of spade and hoe, The gushing water comes forth of its own accord.
Its color is reflected upon the surface of the bowl; Its flavor returns to the root of the tongue.
I alone regret that the vessel is frail as the days pass; even those nearby look upon him with suspicion.

"Dharma" refers to the Dharma of the Way; "Master" refers to one who serves as a model for others. Because he takes the Dharma of the Way to serve as a model for humanity, leading others to follow his standard, he is called a *dharmācārya* (Dharma Master).
By virtue of the previous prophecy, he was already established as a Dharma King (*dharmarāja*), yet the position of Dharma King had not yet [been fully realized].
There are those who attain realization not through a Dharma Master; therefore, following the Bestowal of Prophecy, the Chapter on the Dharma Master follows immediately.
Now, the Dharma King is the sovereign holder of the lineage of the Way, while the Dharma Master is a branch stream of that lineage of the Way.
The *dhāraṇīs* are like the ocean, and their branches flow like rivers. Without the great ocean, the river currents would have nowhere to return;

without the river currents, the great ocean could be exhausted. Thus, once the position of the Dharma King and Dharma Master is established, the lineage of Śākyamuni’s Way will continue unbroken from generation to generation.
Yet, the previous prophecy specifically refers to the present disciples who lack faith.
Because they will become Buddhas themselves, the Tathāgata, in the "Expedient Means" chapter, exhorted them with urgent words:

"These bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs consider themselves to have already attained arhatship; dwelling in their final body, they believe they have reached ultimate nirvāṇa and no longer aspire to seek unsurpassed bodhi. These are not disciples of the Buddha; they are not arhats. Not...
The Pratyekabuddhas were called people of overweening pride. Therefore, as soon as Śāriputra heard [the teaching], he gave rise to faith and said, "I now know that I am truly a son of the Buddha.
Consequently, the Buddha bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment.
When the four great disciples heard the parables and gave rise to faith, they said, "We previously considered ourselves to have attained ultimate Nirvāṇa and no longer aspired to seek further."
[They have] ascended to Bodhi. They are like impoverished sons; it is only now that I know they are truly Śrāvakas.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata bestowed predictions upon his five hundred disciples after [they heard of] the "transformed city," they said:

"We ourselves thought we had already attained parinirvāṇa, but now we know it is as if we were ignorant men. For this reason, the Tathāgata likewise bestowed predictions upon them, even regarding those who...

There were six thousand who were still in training (*śaikṣa*) and had not yet realized the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); therefore, they did not say that they had attained ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
They merely said, "We too should have a share," and looked toward the Buddha with an expression of concern.

Those disciples who today received their predictions of enlightenment on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa all owe this to the power of the Tathāgata’s single exhortation. As for this chapter, it is precisely for the sake of the Tathāgata...

After my parinirvāṇa, when no Buddha is manifest before the world and the Tathāgata’s true Dharma is as fragile as a single thread, it must rely upon the great bodhisattvas and great disciples to act as the six kinds of Dharma-preachers to circulate this sutra.
This is both to continue the life-force of wisdom of all Buddhas and to enable oneself to become a Dharma-king; therefore, this chapter is [established].
The opening section serves to extol the merits of the Dharma Master to the utmost, so as to cause people to feel admiration and delight in practicing it.
Upon reaching the "Treasure Stupa" chapter, the Buddhas of the past, present, and ten directions each take this entire single-fascicle sutra and clearly display it to the great assembly;
thereafter, with a great voice, they universally proclaim to the fourfold assembly: "Who among you can, in this Sahā..."
Throughout the Sahā world, [the Buddha] widely proclaimed this sutra. The Buddha wished to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to those who would uphold it;
yet, within the world of the five turbidities, those who act as Dharma masters encounter many demonic obstacles. Without great vows, they cannot persevere for long.
Therefore, it is further said that this is a difficult task and that one must give rise to great vows. Thus, in the "Chapter on the Entrustment," there are twenty thousand [bodhisattvas].
The Bodhisattvas vowed to uphold this sutra in this land; the five hundred disciples and the eight thousand learners all vowed to uphold the sutra in foreign lands;
and eighty trillion nayutas of bodhisattvas vowed to travel back and forth throughout the worlds of the ten directions to uphold the sutra.
None of these fulfilled the Tathāgata’s original intention, until the emergence of the thousand worlds from the earth.

The Bodhisattvas of the Realm of Micro-dust made a vow that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they would extensively expound this sutra in whatever lands the World-Honored One’s emanations might reside.
Thereafter, teacher and disciple would reach perfect accord, and the teaching would be entrusted for its circulation.

All of this was the power of the Tathāgata’s great voice proclaiming it universally and his single exhortation. This was concluded just as the "Expedient Means" chapter ended, regarding the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Regarding such sutras as these, those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain their meaning are as rare as one might find such a person;
for this reason, I say that this sutra is the definitive seat of the Dharma King and the Master of Dharma, serving solely as the transmission of Śākyamuni’s spiritual lineage.
There was nothing else [to discuss].
At that time, the World-Honored One, because of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, addressed eighty thousand great beings:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, do you see within this great assembly the immeasurable devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras..."
Naras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—
those seeking the path of the śrāvaka, those seeking the path of the pratyekabuddha, and those seeking the path of the Buddha— all such beings as these who, in the presence of the Buddha,
hear even a single verse or a single phrase of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, or even for a single moment rejoice in it; I [shall protect them].
All were granted the prediction that they would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja:
"Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, if there should be anyone who hears even a single verse or a single line of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*..."
"To those who rejoice even for a single thought, I likewise grant the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

To bestow this extensive prediction, I spoke to the eighty thousand great beings by means of Bhaiṣajyarāja. The conduct of the Dharma-preacher consists simply in compassion, patience, and the emptiness of phenomena;
since Bhaiṣajyarāja possesses these three qualities, it was through him that [the prediction was granted]."
He then addressed the Great Being (Mahāsattva), truly desiring that the Great Being act as a Dharma Master in emulation of Bhaiṣajyarāja.
Below the section on Bhaiṣajyarāja, this is a detailed record of the assembly currently listening to the Dharma.

Whether of the same or different species, mundane or supramundane, anyone who stands before the Buddha and hears even a single phrase or a single verse, or even for a single moment rejoices in it—these are all [included].
"Receiving the prophecy. From "The Buddha told [them]" downwards, this concerns the bestowal of prophecies for the future.

That is to say, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who hear even a single phrase or a single verse from a Dharma-preacher and rejoice in it for even a single moment shall all receive a prophecy. Why is this?
Having already fulfilled the primary cause for attaining Buddhahood, one should enter the Buddha-way gradually by means of this Dharma.

It is like a person who has ingested a small amount of *vajra*; it will ultimately never be destroyed. It is like being asked about a drum smeared with lethal poison, or touching a dagger coated in venom, or drinking wine laced with deadly poison;
contact with any of these results in death. Yet, it is also like obtaining the "returning-soul" incense, or obtaining the medicine of immortality. Like...
He obtained the Nine-Transformation Elixir; because anyone who touched it was restored to life, he knew that this substance could both kill and bring life.
Bestowing the prediction for the present life is like tying a jewel to one who is sober; bestowing the prediction for after death is like tying a jewel to one who is intoxicated.
This occurred precisely when he was preaching the sutra and bestowing predictions upon the sixteen śrāmaṇeras; at that time, a single wooden tablet slipped out [from the collection].
Thus we know that the present-day disciples who have obtained the jewel all do so because of the sandalwood novice who tied the jewel on in the past.
Furthermore, tying the jewel on today serves as the ground for future disciples to obtain the jewel.
Furthermore, Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that if there are people who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, or transcribe even a single verse of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*,
and who regard this scripture with reverence as they would the Buddha, making various offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, burning incense,
silk canopies, banners, streamers, robes, and musical performances, or even merely joining their palms in respectful salutation.

These people have already made offerings to ten trillion buddhas. Having fulfilled their great vows in the presence of those buddhas, they have been born into this human world out of compassion for sentient beings.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if anyone should ask, "What kind of sentient beings will attain buddhahood in future ages?
you should point to these people and say that they will certainly attain buddhahood in future ages.
Why is this? If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, should receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, or copy it;

and should make various offerings to the scripture with flowers, incense, garlands, powdered incense, unguents, burning incense, silk canopies, banners, flags, robes, and musical instruments; and should join their palms in reverent salutation—such a person, throughout all worlds...
They should be revered and honored with the same offerings as those given to a Tathāgata.

You should know that such a person is a great Bodhisattva who has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, out of compassion for sentient beings, has made a vow to be born in this world to extensively expound and analyze the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
How much more so for one who can fully receive, uphold, and provide various kinds of offerings?
Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such a person, having voluntarily relinquished their own pure karmic retribution, will, out of compassion for sentient beings,
be born in an evil age after my parinirvāṇa to widely expound this sutra. If a son or daughter of good family, after my parinirvāṇa,
is able to secretly preach even a single verse of the Lotus Sutra to a single person, you should know that such a person is like...
These messengers were dispatched by the Tathāgata and carry out the work of the Tathāgata; how much more so for those who extensively preach this for others amidst the great assembly.
Furthermore, there are those who hear the sutra from a Dharma Master and become five kinds of Dharma Masters, all of whom receive predictions of enlightenment.
As for those who uphold it, they silently maintain mindfulness, guarding it without loss, such as Prajñātāra and others.
"Reciting" means to chant and practice repeatedly, without ceasing throughout the six periods of the day and night.
If one speaks of works such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "explaining" means to clarify the meaning of what is taught, so that those who uphold it know where their refuge lies.

"Transcribing" means to circulate the text of the Sanskrit manuscript, so that those who recite it know toward what they should aspire. "Making offerings" refers to those who are unable to personally uphold [the teachings].
Whether one upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes [this text], even those who can merely worship it with a sincere and earnest mind will ultimately obtain this great treasure.
Below this, the intention for worship is set forth; below "flowers and incense," the objects of worship are set forth.
Among the nobility of the Western Regions, they use famous incense as a powder and have their attendants (*qingyi*) rub it onto their bodies; this is called "incense for anointing the body."
Necklaces and garments are the adornments of the body; silk canopies, banners, and streamers are the external adornments of the body.
"Artistic performances" refers to the arts of dance and music. "Joining palms in reverence" means that while the former constitutes material offering, this constitutes offering through the mind.
From the passage on "Bhaiṣajyarāja" downward, his great vows are set forth, stating that if there should be these five types of persons in the final age...

All of these have received the Buddha’s instructions and, by the power of their great vows, manifest transformations among human beings out of compassion for sentient beings to assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s transformation.

This is not in vain. Below the section on "Bhaiṣajyarāja" (Yàowáng), it is stated that these five kinds of Dharma-preachers are all practicing the Bodhisattva path and will certainly attain the great fruit in future ages. The following section provides an interrogative analysis to explain this point.
Regarding those who have attained the fruit: because this Dharma is most preeminent, one first uses a single phrase to manifest the excellence of the entire sutra.
It is said that even if one merely upholds, or even makes offerings to, a single phrase of this sutra among the five kinds of Dharma teachers, such a person shall immediately achieve *bodhi*.
All the world should regard them as a Buddha, for they know [this].
Because they possess the equal Buddha-nature, they are called Bodhisattvas. Since they have already been able to fulfill the ten thousand practices,
these individuals— who, by the power of their great vows, manifest among human beings to extensively expound and analyze this sutra,
or even those who merely uphold, recite, or make offerings to a single verse of this sutra— should already be revered as Buddhas and regarded as such.
O Bodhisattvas, how much more so for those who uphold, let alone merely offer worship to, even a single verse of this sutra, as well as the sutra in its entirety?
Below the section on Bhaiṣajyarāja, it further reveals the merit of upholding, let alone offering worship to, the sutra in its entirety. You should know that such persons—

These are all bodhisattvas who go against the stream. Out of compassion for sentient beings, they relinquish their pure lands of retribution and are born into this turbid world to extensively expound this sutra.
Even if one is of inferior capacity, by expounding even a single verse, one manifests the excellence of the entire sutra.
As for the statement that it is not only those who extensively expound this sutra who are Bodhisattvas manifesting in person:
after my parinirvāṇa, even one who takes but a single phrase of this sutra and privately explains it to a single person has once personally received the instructions and edicts of the Dharma King;
they too act on behalf of the Dharma King. How much more so for those who ascend the lion throne to teach the great assembly!
[This is] explained at length. Furthermore, it is not merely a matter of comparison with [the sin of] stealing for one person alone.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there were an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind, stood before a Buddha throughout an entire kalpa and constantly reviled and abused him, his transgression would still be light.
However, if a person, with even a single evil word, disparages those—whether lay or ordained—who recite and study [the Dharma], [his transgression is far greater].
The Lotus Sūtra is of such great weight that its transgressions are very grave, O Bhaiṣajyarāja.
You should know that anyone who reads and recites the Lotus Sūtra is adorned with the adornments of the Buddha; they are carried upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata.
Whichever direction they go, you should turn toward them, pay homage, join your palms with single-minded devotion, and respectfully offer them flowers and incense, honoring and praising them.
With necklaces, powdered incense, unguents, and burning incense; with silk canopies, banners, and streamers; with robes and choice delicacies;

and by performing various musical performances—offering these supreme human offerings to him. One should hold celestial jewels and scatter them, and present the gathered treasures of the heavens as an offering.
Why is this? Because this person joyfully preaches the Dharma, and upon hearing it for even a brief moment, one immediately attains [realization].
Because they have ultimately attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The preceding section reveals the merits of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers; the following section reveals the retribution for slandering and reviling these Dharma-preachers.
Why is it that the sin of slandering the Buddha for an entire kalpa is still light, whereas the sin of slandering these five kinds of Dharma-preachers with even a single word is even more grave?

Therefore, because the Buddha is endowed with great compassion, even if one were to revile him—as a son might revile his father—it would still constitute a light offense as it serves to establish a karmic connection.

However, if one slanders a Dharma Master, it severs the lineage of the Buddhas; because the five types of Dharma Masters are all those who continue the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom, this is a grave offense.
This has already been explained in detail at the end of the second fascicle. Below, under the section on Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is clarified:

These five kinds of Dharma masters should be venerated. Those who adorn themselves with the adornments of the Buddha mean that the essence of the three bodies and four wisdoms is perfectly complete within them.

As for those "borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata," because they carry the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata likewise bears them. These five types of persons—regardless of whether they are near or...
Far indeed! In whatever place one’s footsteps may turn, one should make offerings to it with the highest human offerings;

one should hold celestial jewels and scatter them there, and furthermore, one should present a "heap of jewels" (*ratnarāśi*). As for what is called a "heap of jewels," it means that the jewels do not consist of only one kind;
therefore, they are called a "heap. Below this, [the text] explains why one ought to show reverence: for what reason? If...

I am able to make offerings with a sincere heart to such a person. Perhaps they will accept my sincerity and, their hearts filled with joy, preach this sutra, hoping that my faculty of hearing may briefly hear the Dharma.
If even a single phrase should permeate my spirit, I shall immediately obtain the unsurpassed great treasure of the Dharma King;
how could worldly treasures ever compare to it? Therefore, I constantly relinquish what I hold dear in order to exchange it for this.
This is why it is considered a treasure. Therefore, Bodhidharma said: "This is a worldly treasure; it is not yet sufficient to be supreme.
Among all treasures, the Dharma-treasure is supreme. Alas, O Dharma Master! How could you thus disparage yourself and fail to live up to the praise from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one desires to abide in the Buddha-way and achieve spontaneous wisdom, one should always diligently make offerings to those who receive and uphold the Lotus Sutra."
Those who wish to swiftly attain the wisdom of all modes should receive and uphold this sutra, as well as make offerings to those who uphold it.
If there are those capable of receiving and upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, know that they are sent by the Buddha out of compassion for all sentient beings.
Those who are able to receive and uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* abandon the pure lands and are born here out of compassion for sentient beings.
You should know that such persons can be born wherever they wish; they are able to extensively proclaim the unsurpassed Dharma in this degenerate age.
One should offer celestial flowers and incense, as well as divine robes and heaps of exquisite heavenly jewels, to those who preach this Dharma.
In the evil age after my parinirvāṇa, one should join one’s palms in reverent salutation to those who can uphold this sutra, just as one would worship the World-Honored One.
With the finest delicacies and various garments, I shall provide offerings to these sons of the Buddha, hoping that they may hear [this teaching] for even a brief moment.
If there are those who, in future ages, can receive and uphold this sutra, I shall dispatch them among human beings to perform the work of the Tathāgata.
If one were to constantly harbor an unwholesome mind throughout an entire kalpa, frowning and reviling the Buddha, they would incur immeasurable and grave offenses.
Yet, if someone who reads, recites, and upholds this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* should be subjected to harsh words for even a moment, their offense would exceed that of the former.
Suppose there were someone seeking the Buddha-way who, for the duration of an eon, stood before me with palms joined and praised me with countless verses.
Because of this praise of the Buddha, they would obtain immeasurable merit; yet the merit of one who extols and praises those who uphold this sutra exceeds even that.
For eight billion eons, one may offer the most exquisite forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile objects to those who uphold this sutra.
Having made such offerings, if one should hear it for even a moment, one ought to rejoice within oneself: "I have now attained a great benefit."
Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have preached, this Lotus Sūtra is the foremost.

The first eight lines of verse praise the Dharma-preachers who are worthy of offerings. If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way and achieve the equal wisdom that is neither cultivated nor realized, neither deficient nor incomplete, one must first draw near to and make offerings to these five kinds of Dharma-preachers.
"Quickly attaining the Buddha-wisdom" refers to those such as the youth Sudhana, the butcher Wide-Forehead, and the nāga-girl Sagara;
all of them attained the fruit of kalpas of cultivation in a single lifetime. Therefore, it is said they "quickly attain" it. "If there are... and so forth praises the virtues of the Dharma-preacher.
One should know that "the one sent by the Buddha" refers to the aforementioned "those dispatched by the Tathāgata. "Leaving the pure land" [refers to his departure from Sukhāvatī].
This means that one voluntarily relinquishes the karmic retribution of one's own pure deeds.

Regarding "being born according to one's own will," this refers to being born not through carnal desire, but by virtue of the power of the vow of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). "As follows" refers to such acts as taking celestial jewels and scattering them, and so forth.
Just as with making offerings to the World-Honored One, one should make offerings using the manner of offering to a Tathāgata.

Furthermore, the superior offerings of various delicacies and sweets constitute the "provisions for humans. Regarding the eight lines below, it is said that the sin of slandering a Dharma Master is even greater than that of slandering the Buddha;
and regarding the eight lines below those, it is said that the merit of praising a Dharma Master is superior to that of praising the Buddha.
Following these eight lines, it is stated that although the offerings are extremely abundant, the Dharma obtained is very little; this too should be a cause for rejoicing.
One shall obtain benefit; do not regard this as ordinary. The four lines beginning with "O Bhaiṣajyarāja" conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one:
"At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:

'Of the immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of sūtras I have spoken—those already spoken, those now being spoken, and those yet to be spoken—among them all, this Lotus Sūtra is the most difficult to believe.'"
It is difficult to understand, O Bhaiṣajyarāja. This sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas; it must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others.
It is protected by the World-Honored Buddhas and has never been openly proclaimed since ancient times.

Even while the Tathāgata is currently present, this sutra still encounters much resentment and jealousy; how much more so after his parinirvāṇa? Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that when the Tathāgata has passed away...

Furthermore, those who are able to write it down, uphold it, read and recite it, make offerings to it, and explain it to others—the Tathāgata will cover them with his robe, and they will be protected and remembered by the Buddhas currently residing in other directions. Such persons possess great power of faith.
And by the power of their vows and the power of their various roots of goodness, you should know that such persons dwell together with the Tathāgata;

it is as if the Tathāgata were to stroke their heads with his own hand. Bhaiṣajyarāja, wherever this may be—whether it be spoken, read, recited, written, or wherever a volume of this sūtra may reside—one should erect a stūpa made of the seven precious substances, making it exceedingly high, wide, and magnificently adorned. There is no need for further [elaboration].
Rest the śarīra. Why is this? Because within it already resides the entire body of the Tathāgata.
This stūpa should be honored, revered, respected, and praised with all kinds of flowers, incense, necklaces, silk canopies, banners and streamers, musical performances, songs, and hymns.
If there are those who see this stūpa, pay homage to it, and make offerings, you should know that they are all drawing near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. This reveals the excellence of the sūtra.
"Has already been taught" refers to the time of the sixteen śrāmaṇeras; "is now being taught" refers to [the present occasion].
At the Dharma assembly on Vulture Peak, those who were to preach [this sutra] and those who would become Buddhas in other lands found it most difficult to believe and understand;
because they were unwilling to shoulder this heavy burden, [the Buddha] entrusted its circulation to Bhaiṣajyarāja and others below.
Since Bhaiṣajyarāja was the foremost among the Dharma-preachers, he was thus entrusted with it. This is the same intent as the entrustment to Śāriputra. It is a secret essential.
"Treasury" means that there are many essential and practical things within it that people do not know; all such things are stored therein.
"They must not be distributed or recklessly bestowed upon others" means that one should select the recipient according to their capacity before bestowing them.
If the right person is found, they will become a great sage of their time; if the right person is lost, it will lead to lawlessness and lack of restraint.

For those who are deluded, it is therefore necessary to select and bestow [this teaching]. That which the Buddhas have guarded and never openly proclaimed is this Sūtra, the Seal of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā).
The Tathāgata has always worn it and never parted from his person; yet he did not openly proclaim it to others by saying it was located in a specific place.
Rather, he explained it indirectly and through various approaches, merely causing people to know that such a thing exists. It is just like the imperial court...
The seal that transmits the state is like a sharp weapon of the nation; it is not shown to people indiscriminately. This is because, as stated below, this [teaching] is not yet openly proclaimed.

Even while the Tathāgata is currently present and preaching this sutra, there are still those who harbor resentment, hatred, jealousy, and envy—such as those who have left their seats. How much more so after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata? How could there not be...?
How pitiable are those who harbor resentment and jealousy! [The passage] from "O Bhaiṣajyarāja" downward praises the five kinds of Dharma-preachers.
"Those covered by robes" are beneath the sheltering protection of the Tathāgata. "Those protected by the Buddha's mindfulness" are within the sphere of the Tathāgata’s thoughts.
"Those who sleep with the Tathāgata" are never parted from his bedding and pillow. "Those whose heads he strokes with his hand" are never far from his left or right side. (Comparison)
The one previously sent shall become even more intimate. Below the section on "Medicine King," it says: "One should show reverence. One must honor the Dharma and, simultaneously, honor the person.
Therefore, one should erect a stūpa and make offerings; there is no need to enshrine śarīra relics, for this sūtra is already present."
Therein lies the entire body of the Tathāgata; furthermore, because it is superior even to the *śarīra* relics, one honors both the person and the stūpa beneath this monument.
If there are those who make offerings to the stūpa, they too shall draw near to Bodhi.

This means that since the original purpose of constructing the stūpa was to make offerings to the Dharma Master, those who now offer to the stūpa all draw near to Bodhi—how much more so for those who practice the fivefold Dharma!
"O Master! Previously it was said that seeking the sutras should be like seeking śarīra; now it is said that places where the sutras exist are even more superior to śarīra.
In both cases, the intent is to cause people to give rise to a sense of rarity and a thought of reverence. Why is this?
It is not because a fisherman fails to see the waves."
Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many people, both householders and renunciants, who practice the bodhisattva path;
yet if they are unable to see, hear, read, recite, copy, uphold, or make offerings to this Lotus Sūtra, you should know that these persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path.
If there are those who hear this sutra, they will be able to practice the bodhisattva path well.

Any sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way, whether they see or hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and who, upon hearing it, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it—know that such persons have drawn near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. O Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is as if, for example, there were a person...
Thirsty and in need of water, one digs into that high plateau to seek it; yet seeing only dry earth, one knows the water is still far off.
Without ceasing one's efforts, one gradually encounters moist soil and eventually reaches mud; with a resolute mind, one knows the water must be near.

It is the same for a bodhisattva. If they have not heard, not understood, and not yet practiced this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, one should know that such a person is still far from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If, however, they hear and understand it, contemplate it, and practice it, they will certainly know that they are close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
The Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Bodhisattvas is entirely contained within this sutra.
This sutra opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the true reality. This Dharma Flower Sūtra-treasury is profound, firm, remote, and unfathomable; no one can reach it.
Now, as the Buddha teaches and transforms beings, he reveals this for the sake of accomplishing bodhisattvas.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, are startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that these are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds.
If śrāvakas hear this sūtra and are startled, doubtful, or terrified, you should know that these are those possessed of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This is the fundamental analogy. One who practices the bodhisattva path but does not hear this sutra is not called a bodhisattva, for this sutra is the teaching for bodhisattvas.
One who seeks the Buddha-way but does not hear this sutra is running outward in pursuit;
they are not called one who seeks the Buddha, for this sutra is that which the Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Therefore, those who seek the Buddha-way must...

One must hear this sutra; it is by means of this that one enters. Why is this? Although sentient beings and Buddhas are separated by a vast distance, as soon as a person hears this Dharma, they should know that they have drawn near to Bodhi, because there is no difference between the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings.
It is like the great ocean, whose hidden currents flow through the four continents; for anyone who digs and excavates, there is none who does not [find water].
One obtains water. If one seeks water on high ground, even if one exerts effort in digging and boring, seeing only dry earth indicates that the water is still far off;

if one abandons the task midway, one will ultimately not obtain the water. However, if one continues to apply effort without ceasing, eventually seeing moist soil and soft mud, one knows that the water must be near.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the illumination of the lives of all beings.
Every day we engage in a single great matter, yet people regard it as ordinary and refuse to seek or investigate within this very realm of daily life.
Instead, they seek it in lofty, remote, and inaccessible heights; though they expend much effort, they remain only halfway there.
It is just like digging for water on a high plateau and encountering only dry earth.

If, through this, one exerts effort without ceasing and turns toward hearing [the Dharma] within the ordinary course of daily life, reflecting upon it in daily life, and practicing it in daily life, one should know that such a person will certainly draw near to Bodhi—just as when seeking water, one finds moist soil and mire. This is like the saying:
"To be loyal and sympathetic is not far from the Way; to be resolute, firm, and unassuming is close to benevolence."

The meaning is the same. The following provides the evidence and explanation: the reason one must desire to hear this sutra is that all *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is entirely contained within the single volume of the Great Sutra of everyday life.
It is for this reason that the Tathāgata opens various gates of skillful means, and it is also for this reason that the Tathāgata reveals the various marks of reality.
This is because, apart from this sutra, no other expedient means can be found, nor can any ultimate reality be attained.
Therefore, one should know that this sutra is the secret treasury of the Tathāgata; it is profound, firm, remote, and deep, such that no one is able to reach it.
Because those without nature cannot fathom its bottom, it is called "profound. Because śrāvakas cannot enter its gate, it is called "firm.
Because pratyekabuddhas cannot behold its radiance, it is called "mysterious. Because those at the stage of equal enlightenment cannot exhaust its limits, it is called "distant.
Knowing in total that it cannot be understood through conceptualization or discrimination, it is said that no person can reach it.
The Tathāgata reveals this sutra solely for those whose power of faith has been perfected and made firm;
therefore, it is called "the teaching for bodhisattvas. The passage beginning with "If there are" serves to spur on their firm faith.
If there are bodhisattvas or śrāvakas who, upon hearing this sutra, become startled, doubtful, or terrified, they are all like those who seek water on a high plateau and encounter only dry earth.
One has not yet been a person who sees wet earth and mire. If one were to see wet earth and mire, one would know that water is certainly near;
one would certainly not be startled, doubtful, or give rise to fear.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are sons or daughters of good family who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, wish to expound this Lotus Sūtra for the fourfold assembly, how should they speak?
Those sons or daughters of good family must enter the chamber of the Tathāgata, don the robe of the Tathāgata, and sit upon the seat of the Tathāgata;
only then should they extensively expound this sūtra for the fourfold assembly. The chamber of the Tathāgata...
"Great compassion toward all sentient beings is the Tathāgata’s garment. A mind of gentleness and forbearance is the Tathāgata’s robe.

The emptiness of all phenomena is the Tathāgata’s seat. Abiding therein, you should then, with a mind free from indolence, extensively expound this Lotus Sūtra for the sake of the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly. Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands..."
I shall dispatch emanated persons to assemble the listeners of the Dharma; I shall also dispatch emanated bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to listen to their preaching of the Dharma.
These emanated persons, having heard the Dharma, will believe and accept it, following it in accordance and not opposing it.
If the preacher of the Dharma is in a secluded place, I will at that time extensively dispatch devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras.
...and so forth. Listen to their preaching of the Dharma. Although I am in another land, I shall from time to time cause the preacher to behold my own body.
If they should forget or lose any phrases or clauses in this sutra, I will preach them again for them, so that they may attain completeness.
This is the method for a Dharma-preacher to bestow the teaching of the Dharma. To address King Bhaiṣajyarāja is to address the great assembly;

this is termed "universal penetration. Because those of the Hīnayāna take emptiness and quiescence as their dwelling and are unwilling to deliver sentient beings due to a lack of compassion, they are taught to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber.
A "chamber" is where one constantly dwells and rests. Those of the Hīnayāna wear the robes of detachment from defilement.
Having transcended the three realms, because they are unable to endure suffering, they are taught to don the robe of patience; for "robe" refers to that which is constantly worn.

Because they occupy the empty seat of a person of small capacity, and have not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), they are taught to sit upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena.
Because those who sit [in meditation] find constant rest, these three are all realized by Bhaiṣajyarāja. Therefore, he informs the great assembly of the method for upholding this sutra:
one should emulate Bhaiṣajyarāja. Although one dwells securely in these three dharmas, one must further exert oneself with diligence.
Exert yourselves as pioneers and expound this widely for the sake of all beings; only then will the model for saving sentient beings reach its completion at the end of the age.

This is the section on "Bhaiṣajyarāja," wherein all Buddhas provide protection and support. If one can indeed preach the sutra in this manner, then even though I am not present in this Sahā world, I shall be acting as a Buddha in other lands, and I will likewise dispatch transformed bodhisattvas to assemble the audience listening to the Dharma, and dispatch transformed members of the fourfold assembly to join them.

Come to listen to the Dharma. If the preaching of the Dharma does not take place in the marketplace, but rather in mountain valleys, beneath forest trees, or by the shores of empty and secluded stillness where no one is listening to the Dharma, I shall extensively dispatch the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others to serve as the assembly of listeners.
I will also manifest my own body to show myself to the preacher of the Dharma, so that they may obtain benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Those who wish to abandon all indolence should listen to this sutra. This sutra is difficult to hear; those who believe and accept it are likewise rare."
It is like a person who, thirsty and needing water, digs into a high plateau; seeing only dry soil, they know the water is still far off.
Gradually seeing moist earth and mud, they know for certain that the water is near. O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that it is the same with all such people.

Those who have not heard the Lotus Sūtra remain very far from the Buddha’s wisdom. If they hear this profound sūtra—which definitively clarifies the Dharma of the śrāvakas and is the king of all sūtras—and having heard it, contemplate it with earnest attention, you should know that such persons are close to the Buddha’s wisdom.

If a person speaks this sutra, they should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat, remaining fearless among the assembly and explaining it in detail. Great compassion is the chamber; gentleness and patience are the robe.

Taking the emptiness of all phenomena as my seat, I dwell here and preach the Dharma. When this sutra is being preached, if someone should revile me with foul language or strike me with swords, staves, tiles, or stones, I shall endure it by recollecting the Buddha.
Throughout thousands of millions of billions of lands, I manifest a pure and steadfast body.
For immeasurable billions of kalpas, I have preached the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be those who can preach this sutra, I shall dispatch transformed members of the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and pure laymen and women—to make offerings to that Dharma-preacher.

They guide all sentient beings, gathering them together to listen to the Dharma. If anyone should wish to inflict harm with swords, staves, tiles, or stones, they shall dispatch emanated beings to provide protection for them.
Even if the one who preaches the Dharma is alone in a secluded place, [they will protect them].
In a secluded place where there is no sound of human voices, one should read and recite this sutra. At that time, I shall manifest for them a body of pure radiance.

If they should forget or lose any passages, I will explain them so that they may master them thoroughly. If a person possesses such virtues, whether they preach it to the fourfold assembly, I will appear before them.
Those who read and recite the sutras in empty places shall all behold my body.

If there is a person in a secluded, quiet place, I shall dispatch devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, ghosts, spirits, and others to serve as the assembly for hearing the Dharma. Such a person will delight in preaching the Dharma, distinguishing its meanings without any hindrance or attachment.
Because they are protected and remembered by all Buddhas, they can bring joy to the great assembly. If one draws near to the Dharma Master, one will swiftly attain the Bodhisattva path.
By following and training under this teacher, one shall behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

The intention is to set aside the first four lines, which serve as the original analogy. "As a person" and so forth introduces the analogy; "Medicine King" and so forth provides the doctrinal application (*dharmasaṃkhyāna*).
"If a person" and so forth explains the method for expounding the sutra. Because one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha, one ought to exercise patience. There are three meanings:

first, one should reflect on for whom the Tathāgata ultimately preaches the Dharma when manifesting his body in thousands of millions of lands throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas. Ultimately...
What is it that he teaches? It is nothing other than appearing in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition;
it is nothing other than his desire to deliver sentient beings by means of this Dharma. Since the Tathāgata has endured these matters for the sake of sentient beings, how could we not emulate him?
Second, one might think: "He is a Buddha, and I must practice patience. As it is said: "I dare not treat others with contempt..."

"You all—each and every one of you shall become a Buddha. This means that because you have contemplated within yourselves that you are Buddhas, you should practice patience and gentleness, have compassion for all beings, and must not cause them distress.
If I were to send forth transformed beings to listen [to your words], [they would report this].

Regarding the Dharma: if there are those who are inferior, he dispatches emanated beings to protect the Dharma; if there are those who preach [inferiorly], he manifests his own body to cause them to obtain benefit.

If there are those who are inferior, he dispatches the eight classes of supernatural beings to listen to the Dharma. The four phrases beginning with "if one is intimate" summarize the benefits for the Dharma Master.
"Intimate" means not being separated from one's side, like a shadow following a form. If one is intimate yet does not receive [the teaching], the instruction will be of no benefit. Since...
If one draws near to them and is willing to receive their teachings, that person will swiftly attain the path of a bodhisattva and shall also behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This is because the path of all Buddhas and bodhisattvas does not depart from this single dharma.
The eleventh chapter, "The Precious Stūpa," states in verse:
A single stūpa, towering and majestic, Surges from the earth into the void; The master of this stūpa is named Prabhūtaratna.
The entire body dwells within this, from which wind and smoke issue forth from the eight directions; the stars and moon pass through the six windows.
They gaze at one another from afar with upturned faces, reaching high toward the sun’s palace.
In the Sanskrit language, it is called *stūpa*; here it is translated as "Numinous Temple" (*lingmiao*). This refers to how this *stūpa* emerges from the earth, such that every person [perceives it].
Because they were able to behold it with their own eyes, this is titled the "Chapter on Beholding the Jeweled Stupa.

From the beginning up to this point, three gates—the expedient means, the parables, and the causal conditions—have been opened to enable those of the three capacities to all attain realization, each receiving a prediction that they shall become a Dharma Prince and succeed to the noble rank of the Dragon King.
By thus completing the two characters for "perfect awakening," one also completes the section on the Gate of Wisdom, which is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
Section. After they have attained awakening, [the Buddha] desires that they shall make vows to uphold this sutra and perform the duties of a Dharma Master;
therefore, he first preaches the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," extensively praising the merits of a Dharma Master.

Furthermore, fearing they might be unwilling to accept and uphold it, he causes Prabhūtaratna to personally present the model of the stupa, and the Buddhas of the ten directions each take a single scroll of the Great Sutra as witness, presenting them face-to-face.
Only after causing them to see [the truth] directly once will they be willing to make a vow and undertake its practice; only then can they enter.

By means of the two characters "completely revealing" (*liǎoshì*) and "entering" (*rù*), this also completes the section concerning the Buddhas' wisdom being profound and immeasurable. Therefore, this chapter [is concluded].
The first half demonstrates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; the second half causes one to make vows and uphold [the teaching].
This is what is meant by the saying: "A single drop of ink forms two dragons. Formerly, when National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang was about to manifest his passing, he took leave of Emperor Daizong.
The Emperor asked, "After you have entered nirvana, what shall I, your disciple, offer? The Master replied, "Inform the donors to construct..."

[Zhao] Zong took a seamless stūpa. The Emperor said, "I request a model of the stūpa from you, Master. After a long silence, the Master asked, "Do you understand? Zong said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "After I have departed, my disciple Yingzhen will know this matter. Later, Zong asked Yingzhen about it. Yingzhen remained silent for a long while and then asked, "Does Your Majesty understand? Zong said, "I do not understand. Yingzhen then recited a verse: The Great Sage has gone to the West; The seamless stūpa remains here. If you wish to see the Buddha’s form, Look at the seams of the stūpa. The Emperor then understood. He had the stūpa built in the capital and sent a messenger to invite the Master to see it. The Master said, "The Emperor has already seen it. Why must you bring me to see it? It is called a "Tower of Longevity. At the assembly on Vulture Peak, it was called a "Tower of Vows. The *Cien* (Compassion) and *Ba'en* (Requital of Kindness) [temples] do not fall within this category.
At that time, before the Buddha, there appeared a tower made of the seven precious substances, five hundred yojanas in height and two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
It emerged from the earth and remained suspended in mid-air, adorned with various kinds of precious objects and five thousand railings.
There were shields and ten million grottoes, adorned with countless banners and streamers. Precious necklaces hung down, and billions of precious bells were suspended above them.
From all four sides issued the fragrance of *tamarapa* sandalwood, pervading the entire world.
Those various banners and canopies were made of the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearl, and ruby.
It was joined together, reaching as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
There, the devas rained down *mandārava* flowers as an offering to the jeweled stūpa. All other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and kiṃnaras likewise did so.

Mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and assemblies of many hundreds of thousands of millions, with all manner of flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, canopies, and musical performances, made offerings to the precious stupa, honoring, respecting, and praising it. At that time, from within the precious stupa, a great voice issued forth, exclaiming:
"Excellent, excellent! Śākyamuni, World-Honored One, you are able to employ the great wisdom of equality."
The Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—was preached for the great assembly.
"It is so, it is so," [said the assembly], "O World-Honored One Śākyamuni, that which you have spoken is entirely true.

At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the Great Jewel Stūpa abiding in mid-air, and hearing the sounds issuing from within the stūpa, they all attained the joy of the Dharma, marveling at what they had not seen before.
There was one who rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and withdrew to stand to one side.
As for "surging forth from the earth," "earth" refers to the mind-ground; this is because the stupa does not exist within the human realm, but rather flows forth from within one's own breast.
As for "dwelling in the void," it has no original location, for it dwells in non-dwelling.
"Various adornments" refers to the majestic array of the ten thousand virtues. "Five thousand railings" manifests the abundance of *dhāraṇīs*.
"Innumerable grottoes and chambers" reveals the vastness of compassion. "Hanging jeweled necklaces" signifies the fulfillment of the ten thousand practices.
"Jeweled bells suspended above" represents the grand proclamation of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). "Fragrance emanating from all sides" [signifies] the entire body...
This is the fragrance of the Dharma-body. As for the banners and canopies composed of the seven treasures, this refers to using various Dharma-treasures to guide and lead sentient beings.
"Reaching as high as the four heavens" means rising above all things. "Devas and nāgas presenting offerings" means that their minds are filled with aspiration and admiration.
From the phrase "At that time" onwards, the great sound of praise—exclaiming "Excellent!"—emanates from within the stupa. This is because...

it is precisely this. It is precisely this that constitutes the bodhisattva’s playful exercise of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). It is precisely this.
The *Buddhānusmṛti-sūtra* is likewise nothing other than this very thing. This means that, in total, it does not transcend this single seamless stupa.
As for what has been said—that all is truly real—what Śākyamuni taught is precisely this substance;
it is not any other thing. It is entirely real and devoid of any falsehood. All of the above serves as proof.
Regarding the words of Ming: Śākyamuni preached this fascicle of the sutra from both left and right, yet it was not as intimate or flavorful as that which was spoken by Prabhūtaratna.

This presents a doubt regarding eloquence (*pratibhāna*). Eloquence is one of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); because its reality exists, it possesses that name.

Below, the causes and conditions of the stūpa are explained. The land is named Ratnaviśuddha because it is pure with various jewels.
The Buddha is named Prabhūtaratna because he is fully endowed with the Dharma-jewel. That Buddha possessed a great power of aspiration during his causal stage:

"If, after I have attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa, wherever the Lotus Sūtra is preached, may my stūpa emerge and appear before them. Thus, one should know that [the stūpa belongs to] Prabhūtaratna.
The Buddha-stūpa is not fashioned from the seven treasures of the human realm; it emerges from the heart of great vows. To serve as a witness, he says:
"That which I manifest is equal to and no different from that which you have described. As for his exclamation of "Excellent!
(Sādhu), it means that their divine principles are in perfect accord; thus, he utters words of praise from a state beyond speech.

Since it serves as a witness, is it the precious stupa itself, or is it the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, or is it the emergence of the great sound?
Is it the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? Examine this carefully. When that Buddha descended, he exhorted people to construct stupas. By...
Where there is a vow, there is a stūpa; where there is a stūpa, there is the entire body of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, those who wish to make offerings to the entire body of the Tathāgata should first resolve to construct this stūpa.

Because the Tathāgata constructed this stūpa of vows during his causal stage, it manifests before him wherever he preaches the Dharma after his parinirvāṇa. [The section] "Great Bliss" below answers [the question].

The second question: Regarding the statement that when the *Prabhūtaratna* heard the preaching of the wondrous Dharma, he immediately surged forth from his stupa to bear witness and offer praise—this is what is meant by "the mountains resound and the valleys echo.
From this point downward, [the text describes] Mahāratnaketu’s desire to behold the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
The rumors from the neighboring room were not for the sake of meeting face-to-face. From "The Buddha told [them]" below, he reveals his great vow:

that his own body shall only appear after all his emanations have gathered in one place. Because of Prabhūtaratna...
