since one desires to see both the entire body and the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), this is intended to manifest the unimpeded relationship between the one and the many—the universally pervasive and perfectly interfused realm.
At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from the tuft of white hair between his brows.

Immediately, one saw the Buddhas of five hundred *koṭi-nayuta* worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction. In those lands, the ground was made entirely of crystal, adorned with jeweled trees and precious garments.
Countless thousands of millions of *koṭis* of bodhisattvas filled them, and precious canopies were spread everywhere.
Above the jeweled nets, the Buddhas of those lands speak all dharmas with great and wondrous voices.
Furthermore, one sees immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas filling all those lands, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.

It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—everywhere reached by the light of the white tuft between the eyebrows. At that time, each of the Buddhas of the ten directions...

He addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "Sons of good family, I shall now go to the Sahā world to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha, and also to make offerings to the precious stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna. At that moment, the Sahā world was immediately transformed into purity.
The ground is made of lapis lazuli, adorned with precious trees. Golden cords demarcate the eightfold paths.
There are no villages, hamlets, camps, or cities; no great oceans, rivers, mountains, streams, forests, or marshes. Great precious incense is burned, and *mandārava* flowers abound.
It was spread across the ground and covered above with canopies of jeweled nets, from which various jeweled bells hung. Only the assembly of this gathering was left;

all other devas and humans were moved and placed in other lands. At that time, each of the Buddhas took a great bodhisattva as an attendant and arrived at the Sahā world, each reaching beneath a jeweled tree. Each of these jeweled trees was five hundred [yojanas] high.
The branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits were adorned in succession. Beneath each of these jewel trees was a lion throne five yojanas high, likewise embellished with great jewels.
At that time, the Buddhas each sat cross-legged upon these thrones. In this manner, they spread throughout the entire trichiliocosm, filling it completely. And as for Śākyamuni...
The emanated bodies of Śākyamuni Buddha were still not yet exhausted.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, wishing to provide space for all those emanated Buddhas, further transformed two million *koṭi-nayuta* lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure and free from the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras. He then moved [the beings]...
The various devas and humans were placed in other lands. The realms where they were transformed likewise had ground made of lapis lazuli and were adorned with jewel trees.
These trees were five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arranged in successive layers of adornment.
Beneath each tree was a precious lion throne five yojanas high, decorated with all kinds of jewels. Furthermore, there were no great oceans or rivers.

The rivers, as well as Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, Sumeru and other kings of mountains, all together constitute a single Buddha-field. The ground of jewels is level and even;
canopies of interlaced jewels cover it everywhere, with various banners and parasols suspended from them. Great precious incense is burned, and celestial jewel-flowers are strewn everywhere.

As for that land, because Śākyamuni Buddha intended for all Buddhas to sit there in the future, he further transformed two million billion nayutas of lands in each of the eight directions, making them all pure. There were no longer any hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras.
Furthermore, he moved the devas and humans to other lands. The lands thus transformed were likewise...
The ground is made of lapis lazuli and adorned with precious trees. The trees are five hundred yojanas high, their branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arranged in successive layers of adornment.
Beneath each tree is a precious lion throne five yojanas high, likewise embellished with great jewels.
Furthermore, there are no great oceans or rivers, nor Mount Mucilinda or Mahāmucilinda.
Mountains such as the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, and Sumeru—the kings of all mountains—constitute together a single Buddha-land.

The ground is made of jewels, level and even, covered everywhere by jeweled latticed canopies. Banners and parasols are suspended from above, great precious incense is burned, and celestial jewel-flowers are strewn across the entire earth.

This refers to the light illuminating the manifested bodies. One light illuminates the Buddhas in worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of five hundred million *nayuta* Ganges Rivers;
this is vastly different from the previous light, which illuminated and perceived eighteen thousand lands.
At that time [the passage] below describes the manifested bodies responding to the call. At that time, Śākyamuni transforms the land, meaning that he is about to...
The defiled and turbid Sahā world was transformed into purity; its uneven elevations and depressions were transformed into a ground of lapis lazuli jewels.
Thorns and thickets were transformed into jeweled trees; villages, hamlets, and camps were transformed into boundary paths marked by golden cords.
Furthermore, precious incense perfumed the heavens and exquisite flowers covered the earth; it was draped with jeweled nets and adorned with jeweled bells. [He] remained there with a pure assembly.
In this place, the devas and humans were placed in other lands. At that time, the emanated bodies descended from below and gathered together.
As for the jewel trees, all of which were five hundred yojanas high, they were equal in height to the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.

Regarding the fact that the emanated bodies in one direction were still not yet exhausted, it refers to those in the eastern direction numbering as many as five million billion nayutas of Ganges-sands.
The lands of the various Buddhas—even this trichiliocosm—cannot contain them all, because one sees the vast number of Śākyamuni’s emanations.
At that time, Śākyamuni transforms the pure land once more; as for the statement that the eight directions are further transformed:
This refers to the eight directions outside the Sahā world-system. Mount Mucilinda is a mountain of stone.
"Taken together as one Buddha-land" means that sixteen million *koṭi-nayuta* lands are collectively regarded as a single land.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Śākyamuni," he transformed the pure land three times; this was as previously asked concerning the Tathāgata’s land, which had never [been so described].
It is impure, yet one must necessarily transform it; once transformed, why must it necessarily be threefold? Answer:
If spoken of in terms of worldly dharmas, when Qi undergoes one transformation it reaches Lu, and Lu undergoes one transformation it reaches the Dao.

If spoken of in terms of supramundane dharmas, one enters the City of Transformation from the Burning House, and proceeds from the City of Transformation to the Treasure Place. If spoken of in terms of spiritual capacity, there are capacities... [text ends]
Three. Therefore, the transformations are also three. Question: The World-Honored One possesses all-encompassing wisdom;
even regarding the straightness of pines and the curvature of thorns, or the whiteness of cranes and the blackness of crows, he thoroughly understands their fundamental origins.

Why does he not transform once and fully accommodate [all beings], rather than transforming a second time because he cannot fully accommodate them? Is it that the Tathāgata’s wisdom also has something it does not know?
Answer: Every transformation and every movement of the Tathāgata is entirely for the sake of sentient beings. If he were to manifest his full capacity all at once, their number could not be known;
therefore, he first transformed the Sahā world, which could not contain them all. Thus, the Buddhas who are emanations from the eastern direction have a knowable quantity.
This is precisely because those who cannot accommodate the infinite number are shown a finite number. If this were...
When a person exceeds their capacity, one transformation already becomes much; how much more so when it occurs twice or thrice?

Therefore, the entire body of Prabhūtaratna does not leave its original place, revealing the extreme profundity of the Buddha’s wisdom. The emanations of Śākyamuni pervade the worlds of the ten directions, revealing the immeasurability of the Buddha’s wisdom.
One must know that the one is immeasurable yet not many, and the immeasurable is one yet not few—this is the perfection.
The bodies of sentient beings are fundamentally without distinction; this realm and other directions have originally no duality.
Without departing from their current location, they pervade the ten directions; and while pervading the ten directions, they do not depart from their current location.

Therefore, within the assembly of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*, the Sahā world was placed within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*); and at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Flower Treasury World was moved and placed within the Sahā world.
Within the Sahā world, we thus know that the Buddha-flower and the Dharma-flower are a single, continuous whole from beginning to end.
That which is called the "thusness" of essence, characteristics, and fruition—the ultimate equality of the Buddha-wisdom—is precisely this.

For this reason, for over forty years, the World-Honored One cast off his precious robes to don coarse garments; he condescended to the lowly and endured these matters until the assembly at Vulture Peak.
It appears for the first time now, just like the udumbara flower; how could it be easily seen?

At that time, the various Buddhas who are emanations of Śākyamuni from the east—residing in lands as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Ganges Rivers—each preaching the Dharma, have gathered here one after another in this manner.
The Buddhas of the ten directions all gathered together and sat in the eight directions.
At that time, in each direction, there were Buddhas, Tathāgatas, filling four million *koṭi-nayuta* lands.
Each of these Buddhas was seated upon a lion throne beneath a precious tree and dispatched their attendants to inquire after the health of Śākyamuni Buddha, each bringing [a lute].
Filling his cupped hands with precious flowers, he addressed him, saying: "Good son, go to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha resides.
Speak these words on my behalf: 'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you physically strong and at ease?

The Buddhas of the ten directions likewise desired to open this jeweled stūpa, and the Buddhas dispatched their messengers in the same manner.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha saw that all the emanated Buddhas had already assembled and were each seated upon lion thrones.
All heard the various Buddhas saying, "We wish to open the precious stūpa together with you. They immediately rose from their seats and stayed suspended in mid-air.
The entire fourfold assembly stood up and joined their palms, single-mindedly gazing upon the Buddha.

Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha opened the door of the seven-jeweled stūpa with his right finger, producing a great sound like the removal of a bolt and the opening of a great city gate. At that moment, one—

The entire assembly all beheld the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna within the jeweled stupa, seated upon a lion throne, his entire body intact and undispersed as if he had entered into meditative concentration.
Furthermore, they heard him say: "Excellent, excellent, Śākyamuni Buddha! You have well expounded this Lotus Sūtra.
It is for the sake of hearing this sūtra that I have come here. At that time, the fourfold assembly saw...
Buddhas who entered parinirvāṇa countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas ago spoke these words, praising this as something unprecedented,
and scattered clusters of celestial jewel-flowers over the Buddha Prabhūtaratna and upon Śākyamuni Buddha.

The Buddhas of the eastern direction all gather in the Sahā world; the Buddhas of the nine directions each sit upon the eight sides, forming a solemn picture of the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha*).
As the Great Sūtra says: "All dharma-gates, an inexhaustible ocean, are gathered together within the site of enlightenment of a single dharma.
This is precisely that meaning. At this time, the emanated bodies dispatch attendants to inquire after their well-being; this is the true manifestation of the profound.
The Buddha’s wisdom is fundamentally not separate from the ordinary activities of daily life. [Regarding the passage] "At that time," etc.:
the manifested Buddhas and Śākyamuni together opened the precious stūpa. Question: Why must the manifested Buddhas wait for Śākyamuni when they wish to open the precious stūpa?
"Is it that the supernatural power of the manifested bodies is not equal to that of Śākyamuni? Answer: "Śākyamuni is the fundamental Buddha of the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

All the manifested bodies from the ten directions are transformations within the transformation of Śākyamuni. In contrast, Prabhūtaratna is the fundamental Buddha of the complete body (*sambhogakāya*)."
Śākyamuni is the manifested body (nirmāṇakāya) of the fundamental Buddha (mūlabuddha). Only the fundamental Buddha can see the fundamental Buddha; only the complete body can see the complete body.
Therefore, in wishing to open the stupa, one must wait for Śākyamuni so that the body may become whole. This is not due to a lack of supernatural power (ṛddhi).
Thus, when Śākyamuni dwells in the void from below, it is because the past Buddhas dwell in the void while the present Buddha [dwells] above.
They likewise abide in empty space; for by seeing all Buddhas, one realizes ultimate nirvana, which ultimately returns to emptiness.
Thereupon, below, he snapped his fingers to open the stupa. At the assembly of the Buddha-flower Sūtra, Samantabhadra snapped his fingers and the gate of Maitreya’s pavilion opened;
at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, Śākyamuni pressed his finger and the Many-Treasures Stupa was revealed. Immediately, the multitude—
All those in the assembly who behold the Many-Treasures Buddha have, from immeasurable kalpas past, each possessed their own stupa containing a single Many-Treasures Buddha.
However, because the present Buddhas lacked spiritual efficacy, they were unable to press their fingers;
thus the stupa doors would not open, and the Many-Treasures Buddha would not manifest. Now, all those in this assembly are able to see the past Many-Treasures Buddha.
The Buddha is the power of a single finger-snap of the present Śākyamuni. That which was previously unseen has now been seen;
furthermore, as for "having heard," that which was previously unheard has now been heard.
At that time, the fourfold assembly scattered flowers because they were resolved to seek the great fruit.
At that time, within the jeweled stupa, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna offered half of his seat to Śākyamuni Buddha and spoke these words:
"Śākyamuni Buddha, please take this seat. Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha entered the stupa and sat upon that half-seat, assuming the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
At that time, the great assembly beheld the two Tathāgatas seated upon the seven... [jewels].
Within the jeweled stupa, upon lion thrones, they sat cross-legged and each thought to themselves: "The Buddha sits high and far away;
we pray only that the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, may cause us all to dwell together in the void.
Immediately, Śākyamuni Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, received the great assembly and placed them all in the void. Then, with a great voice, he proclaimed universally:

Śākyamuni transforms his land, assembles the emanated Buddhas, and the Stūpa of Many Treasures surges forth, manifesting the whole body of the Buddha.

Since all do not depart from this single stūpa, Many Treasures shares half his seat with Śākyamuni.
Kāśyapa, Śākyamuni then sat upon half of that seat, thereby clarifying that the Way of Buddha to Buddha is identical and remains unchanged throughout antiquity and the present.

At that time, the great assembly thought to themselves: "The Buddha’s seat is so high and remote" was intended precisely to show that those who have not yet attained the *paramārtha-śūnyatā* (ultimate emptiness) cannot approach the Stupa of Prabhūtaratna;
therefore, he used his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to bring them near. By means of this...

"Below. This refers to seeking out those who will circulate [the text]. When the Buddha wishes to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to those who shall preserve it, one must regard these two characters with gravity.
Is it merely black ink on white paper that is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
Or is it merely yellow silk and red rollers that are called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? It is precisely for this reason that—
This great sūtra of the school is vast and profound, majestic and transcendent; it is without seams or cracks, beyond words and beyond thought, suddenly present before everyone.

Therefore, the Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions, giving rise to compassion and manifesting in the world, do nothing more than wish to take up this single scroll of the Great [Sūtra].
The sutra has been entrusted to others so that it may be transmitted from one to another, ensuring that the flame is never extinguished and the light never fades.

They did not diligently practice the Dharma. Since the parinirvāṇa of that Buddha, for countless kalpas, they have sought the Dharma everywhere because it is so difficult to encounter.
By the original vow of that Buddha, after my parinirvāṇa, wherever they go, they shall always listen to the Dharma; furthermore, I shall manifest my emanations there.

furthermore, they behold the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who has entered parinirvāṇa, and each of whom has relinquished their wondrous lands, along with their assemblies of disciples, devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, and all matters of offering, so that the Dharma may endure for a long time.
Therefore, I have come here for the sake of the seated Buddhas. By means of supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), I have moved immeasurable multitudes and purified the lands.
Each of the Buddhas proceeds beneath their respective jewel-trees, which are adorned with lotuses like pure ponds. Beneath those jewel-trees...

From their bodies issued a sublime fragrance that pervaded the lands of the ten directions; sentient beings who were perfumed by it experienced a joy they could not contain, like being struck by a great wind.
He blew his small tree-staff. By this expedient means, he caused the Dharma to endure for a long time. He addressed the great assembly:
"After my parinirvāṇa, who will be able to protect and uphold this sutra, and read and recite it? Now, before the Buddha, I shall personally utter a vow. Then, that Buddha Prabhūtaratna—

that both the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and my own person, along with all the manifested Buddhas who have gathered here, shall address you, sons of the Buddha: "Who among you is able to protect the Dharma? You should now make a great vow."
To enable it to endure for a long time, whoever is able to protect this Dharma of the sutra thereby makes offerings to me and to Prabhūtaratna.
This Buddha Prabhūtaratna, who dwells within the jeweled stupa, constantly travels throughout the ten directions for the sake of this sutra; such a person likewise makes offerings to him.
The emanated Buddhas who have come from all worlds, adorned with magnificent radiance— if one preaches this sutra, it is as if one sees me,
the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, and all those emanated Buddhas.
Desiring to entrust this Dharma to those who shall uphold it, he first versifies the purpose for the arrival of Prabhūtaratna in order to exhort the great assembly.
"Even for the sake of the Dharma," he says, "the ancient Buddhas, having already realized this Dharma and entered parinirvāṇa, do not forget their original vows;
they still come to hear the Dharma. Yet you all have not yet attained realization, and you are unwilling to make such a vow."
As for those who uphold this sutra: why is this? Because throughout incalculable kalpas, wherever they hear the Dharma, they do so because this sutra is rare and difficult to encounter;
thus, there is no time or place where they do not go to listen. Yunmen said:
"The flames preach the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and the Buddhas of the three periods stand upon the ground and listen. This is the preaching of one who has no tongue.
Regarding the Dharma: those who are deaf lack the intention to listen to the Dharma. Furthermore, from "I" onwards, the purpose for which the emanations come forth is revealed.
As for the statement that they have come here so that the Dharma may endure for a long time, it refers to the Buddhas of the ten directions gathering at this place; this is not without cause.

Desiring that the lineage of the Buddhas not be severed in the final age and remain long in the world, each [Buddha] brings a single scroll of the Great Sūtra and shows it directly to people, causing their hearts to give rise to joy and diligence in practicing this Dharma.

If they were not shown directly, those who have never personally seen it would harbor doubts and be unwilling to advance in their practice; for this reason, the emanated bodies all come together in assembly.
[This is] the ear[-root]. For the sake of those sitting below, [the text] provides a verse on the threefold transformation of the pure land.

Regarding the phrase "adorned with lotus flowers like a pure pool," it means that when the Buddha approaches the jeweled tree, he is exactly like a lotus flower in a pure pool. The Buddha is beneath the tree.
It is adorned with radiance, like a torch lit in the darkness. When sentient beings encounter this fragrance, they rejoice so intensely that they fall prostrate.
It is like a great wind blowing through the branches of small trees; there are none that do not bend and sway.
By these skillful means, he causes the Dharma to endure for a long time—meaning that by employing such various expedients, he truly desires to inspire people’s admiration and longing.
"To shoulder this Dharma" means to cause the Dharma to abide for a long time without allowing it to be severed. "Announcing to all below" refers to summoning and informing those who uphold the sutra.
"Speaking one's own vow" is an exhortation for others to make vows. It is said that ancient Buddhas possessed the power of vows, which is called a "vow-stūpa.
Because of this vow-stūpa, they were able to attain Bodhi; therefore, although they have entered parinirvāṇa, the vow-stūpa still remains.
Now, within this assembly, he has uttered a great sound and let out a lion’s roar.
You have also, by virtue of the power of past vows, been able to hear this sutra and have now received your predictions of enlightenment.

Therefore, if you wish in the future for the circulation of this sutra to remain uninterrupted, you should make great vows to bring this stupa to completion. Thus spoke the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna of the past.
The Buddha. The "I. The present Buddha. The transformation Buddhas. The Buddhas of the ten directions. This means that all the Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions have assembled here;

there is nothing else. You should know that the purpose for which all these Buddhas have come is none other than for the sake of this single great sutra before each person. Because this sutra is protected and sustained by all the Buddhas, it is so named.

It is that which the Buddha protects and keeps in mind. If you wish to protect and uphold what the Buddha protects and keeps in mind, you must make great vows to provide special protection and guardianship;
only then will it be able to circulate in the world and abide forever in this age. Without the power of vows, it cannot be so.
[Otherwise, it] would immediately be lost and dispersed. Below, there is praise for the merit of upholding this sutra:
if anyone protects and upholds this sutra, they are identical to making offerings to all Buddhas;

for it is for the sake of this sutra that I have appeared, for the sake of this sutra that the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna has emerged, and for the sake of this sutra that the manifested Buddhas have gathered together. Therefore, whoever protects and upholds this sutra [attains such merit].
Furthermore, those who preach this sutra shall be as if they personally behold the single assembly on Vulture Peak, no different from being there.
O sons of good family, each of you should reflect deeply: this is a difficult task; you ought to make great vows. This is not so with other sutras.
Even if there were as many [beings] as the sands of the Ganges, though one were to speak of such things, it would not yet be considered difficult.

Nor would it be considered difficult to take Mount Sumeru and hurl it to other world-systems, across countless Buddha-fields. Furthermore, to move the great trichiliocosm with a single toe and cast it far away to another land—this too would not be considered difficult.
This is not yet difficult. Nor is it difficult to establish oneself at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and expound countless other sūtras for the sake of the multitude.
However, if one is able to preach this sūtra in the evil age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, that indeed is difficult. Suppose there were a person who...

To walk about while grasping empty space with one’s hand is not yet difficult; but after my parinirvāṇa, for one to either write it down oneself or cause another to write it down—this indeed is difficult.
Or, to place the great earth upon the tip of one’s toenail and ascend to the Brahma-heaven.
This is not yet difficult. To read this sutra even for a moment within the evil world after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—this is truly difficult.
Even if one were to carry dry grass on one's back and enter into the conflagration at the end of an eon without being burned, that would not yet be difficult. But after my parinirvāṇa, [to do so]...

If one upholds this sutra and explains it for the sake of a single person, that is difficult. Even if one upholds the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, expounding them for others so that all listeners attain the six supernormal powers—even though one could do such a thing—[this is not as difficult].
This is not yet difficult. But after my parinirvāṇa, to hear and receive this sutra and inquire into its meaning and intent—this is truly difficult.
Suppose a person were to preach the Dharma and cause thousands of millions of billions, immeasurable, incalculable, Ganges-sand-like sentient beings to attain arhatship.

To possess the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), though it brings such benefit, is not yet difficult. But after my parinirvāṇa, if one can receive, uphold, and recite a sūtra such as this, that indeed would be difficult.
For the sake of the Buddha-way, throughout immeasurable lands, from the beginning until now, I have [striven].
I have extensively expounded various sutras, and among them, this sutra is the foremost. If there are those who can uphold it, they shall be upholding the body of the Buddha.
O sons of good family, after my parinirvāṇa, who will be able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra? [Speak] now before the Buddha.
He spoke this vow of his own accord: "This sutra is difficult to uphold. If one upholds it even for a moment, I shall rejoice, and so too shall all the Buddhas.
Such a person is praised by all the Buddhas; such a person is courageous and such a person is diligent. This is what is called upholding the precepts."
Those who practice the dhūtas will swiftly attain the unsurpassed path of the Buddha. Those who are able to read and uphold this sutra in future ages are true sons of the Buddha;
they dwell in the ground of pure goodness. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who can explain its meaning are the true gods and humans.
The Eye of the World, who is able to speak for even a moment within this world of fear, should be venerated by all devas and humans;
this is an exhortation for the multitude to make vows. "Each should contemplate with careful attention" means to cause them to reflect deeply and examine thoroughly.
It is said that to shoulder this task is exceedingly difficult; were it not for those who possess great power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), they would be unwilling to undertake it.
Thus we know that wherever the aspiration is, there the Sūtra is; wherever the Sūtra is, there the Buddha is. As the Great Sūtra says:
"The power of Vairocana Buddha’s aspiration pervades the entire realm of sand-grains; throughout all Buddha-lands..."
"Constantly turning the unsurpassed wheel," Śākyamuni said: "I originally established a vow, desiring to cause all sentient beings to be no different from myself.
Now, for the sake of this very sutra, the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna has appeared before us.
If you wish to obtain this sutra, you should likewise resolve to make great vows. The subsequent sections extensively reveal the practice of upholding this sutra during the final age.

This is difficult because it encourages one to make such a vow. However, to catch Mount Sumeru with one's palm and hurl it beyond the four quarters, and to move the great trichiliocosm with a toe and cast it into another land—this is truly difficult.
Even to ascend to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and preach other sutras, though these are difficult tasks, is not yet the most difficult;

for worldly people are all capable of placing their trust and faith in them. However, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if one were to preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* within a defiled and evil world, that would be the most difficult task of all.
This is because people would not believe it, would give rise to resentment and jealousy, and would subject the preacher to abuse.
Because of reviling [the Dharma], because of inflicting blows with a staff, and because of succumbing to despondency if one lacks a great vow.
As for "grasping at empty space": empty space is fundamentally ungraspable; that it might somehow be grasped is not difficult.

However, to be able to take up a brush and write out a sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa is even more difficult than grasping at empty space. To speak of "reading for a moment" means reading it for a brief duration.
"Not reading constantly" means that one who explains it to a single person does so out of personal interest, privately for that one individual rather than for many.
"Listening to the sutra and inquiring about its meaning" refers to desiring to understand the meaning after having heard the sutra.
"Upholding" means holding it in one's hands and fixing it within the heart and mind, so as not to forget it. The above constitutes a general description of the final age.
The passage beginning with "Creating five kinds of difficulties for the Dharma-preachers" [is intended] to show that I am inferior, thereby manifesting the supreme excellence of this sutra.

Those who uphold this sutra are likewise gladdened by all Buddhas. Such individuals are those of courageous and diligent exertion, for they have fully practiced the immeasurable Dharma of all Buddhas.

Regarding "the one who receives offerings from devas and humans": this refers to the Teacher of Devas and Humans.
As stated in the twelfth verse of the *Devadatta-parivarta*:
Aoxiang plotted against Yu Shun; Devadatta harmed Śākyamuni. Though their domestic circumstances differed slightly, their fates were not at all different.

Therefore, in this chapter, its cause is revealed and the prophecy is bestowed. The general purport of this chapter is twofold:
first, to inspire the fourfold assembly to make vows and uphold the sutra, [the Buddha] cites his own person as a witness, saying:

By showing that one can attain Buddhahood immediately upon hearing this sutra, he caused them to give rise to joy and devotion, so that they would not fall into regression or hesitation. Thus, in the *Laṅkāvatāra*...

Second, the prediction of enlightenment for enemies as beings of different species clearly reveals the profound Buddha-wisdom:
ultimate equality, wherein there are no signs of enemy or kin, and no signs of male or female. If one simply resolves to be willing, one will certainly not be deceived.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly of devas and humans:
"Throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* without ever becoming weary or indolent.
During many kalpas, I constantly served as a king, making vows to seek unexcelled bodhi with a mind that never regressed. Desiring to fulfill the six *pāramitās*, I diligently practiced giving."

His mind was free from stinginess. For the sake of the Dharma, he did not spare elephants, horses, the seven treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, male and female slaves, attendants, nor even his own head, eyes, marrow, brain, flesh, body, hands, or feet;
he did not cherish his own life. At that time, the people of the world had immeasurable lifespans. For the sake of the Dharma, [he gave all these things].
He renounced his royal throne and entrusted the administration to his crown prince. He beat the drum to proclaim a decree, seeking the Dharma throughout the four quarters:
"Whoever can explain the Mahāyāna to me, I shall serve as their attendant for the rest of my life. At that time, there was a rishi who came and addressed the king, saying:
"I possess a Mahāyāna teaching called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. If you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim it for you.

Upon hearing the words of the seer, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately followed the seer, providing whatever was required: gathering fruits, drawing water, collecting firewood, and preparing food;
even using his own body as a seat, he remained free from physical or mental weariness. Thus he served him for a thousand years.
For the sake of the Dharma, he served him with diligent effort, ensuring that nothing was lacking. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
I recall my past lives. For the sake of seeking the Great Dharma, although I was a king of the world, I did not crave the pleasures of the five desires.
I struck the bell to proclaim to the four quarters: "Who possesses the Great Dharma? If you shall expound it for me, I will become your servant."
At that time, there was the Rishi Asita, who came and addressed the Great King: "I possess a subtle and wondrous Dharma, rare in this world.
If you are able to practice it, I shall explain it for you. When the King heard the words of the Rishi, his heart was filled with great joy.
Even as he followed the rishi, providing whatever was required—gathering firewood and fruits—he offered them with respect at all times.
Because his mind was set upon the sublime Dharma, his body and mind were free from weariness; for the sake of all sentient beings, he diligently sought the Great Dharma.
Nor was it for my own sake, nor for the pleasures of the five desires, that I became a great king and diligently sought to obtain this Dharma;
thus I eventually attained Buddhahood, and for that reason, I now speak it for you.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, he sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* without ever succumbing to weariness or indolence.
This clearly demonstrates that this sutra cannot be attained by those who are lazy; only through diligent and courageous effort can one truly shoulder its burden.
During many kalpas, he constantly served as a king, such as when he was Prince Mahātejas in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, making vows in life after life and birth after birth.
"Seeking the fruit of bodhi" refers to this. "Desiring to" and so forth refers to seeking its cause. "Elephants, horses," and so on, are external gifts; "head, eyes," and so on, are internal gifts.
"For the sake of" and so forth refers to seeking the Dharma. One who abandons their royal throne to seek the Dharma is as described.
He knew that the rank of Heaven (*deva-pada*) is more noble than the rank of men (*manuṣya-pada*). Who could fail to lower himself? He issued an edict seeking the Dharma.
At that time, there was one who lowered himself; a *ṛṣi* came upon hearing the wind of his reputation. When the King heard this, he did not disregard his word, providing for him throughout his life.
[The Ṛṣi] gathered fruits [for him]; it is said that a single person constantly attends to many tasks, even using his own body as a seat and couch. And so it was.
"Without weariness. This refers to the long duration of serving one's teacher. This is Śākyamuni’s own account of how, in the past, he diligently sought the sublime Dharma and attained Bodhi;
it is for this reason that he is specifically praised as "valiant. Regarding the verse beginning with "I recall," etc.:

He relinquished his position for the sake of the Great Dharma. "Beating the bell" below refers to proclaiming an edict to seek the Dharma. "At that time" below refers to the arrival of the Dharma-preacher.
The long passage says: "If you do not oppose me, I shall preach it for you. This is rendered here as: "If you can practice accordingly, I shall preach it for you.
"Not opposing me" means practicing in accordance with the teaching. It is precisely because he fears [the listener] might know [the truth]...
It was not permitted. To speak of it would have been of no benefit; therefore, he first used these words to rouse him. At that time, the King complied with the command and provided for his needs.

His heart was set upon the wondrous Dharma, and his body and mind were without indolence. This is precisely what is meant by "moment after moment without interval," desiring only to clarify this matter and having no other aspiration.
Thus, although his efforts were arduous, he felt no weariness. [The section] ending with "universally for" concludes [the passage].
This demonstrates that the Tathāgata sought the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings and not for his own person;
therefore, he was able to renounce the pleasures of the five desires and undergo arduous toil and hardship to realize Bodhi.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The king at that time was none other than myself. The rishi at that time was Devadatta.
It was because of the spiritual friend Devadatta that I was enabled to fulfill the six pāramitās."
The [Buddha’s] qualities of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; the purple-golden hue;
the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four means of attraction, and the eighteen unique attributes; his supernatural powers and spiritual strength; his attainment of perfect enlightenment;
and his vast deliverance of sentient beings—all these were due to the good friend Devadatta. He addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta, in the past..."

After the passing of immeasurable kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood, named Tathāgata Devendra, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. His world shall be named Devamārga.
At that time, the Buddha Devendra shall remain in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, extensively benefiting sentient beings.

He preached the sublime Dharma, whereby sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the fruit of Arhatship; immeasurable sentient beings resolved upon the mind of a Pratyekabuddha;

and sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges resolved upon the unsurpassed path, attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
After the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Devendra, the True Dharma remained in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas.
A stupa made of the seven precious jewels was erected over his entire body relics; it was sixty yojanas in height and forty yojanas in length and breadth.
All the devas and human beings offered various flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, unguents, robes, necklaces, banners, flags, jeweled canopies, and performed music and song.
Verse: Through prostrating and making offerings to the wondrous stupa of the seven jewels, immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruit of Arhatship;
immeasurable sentient beings awakened to the state of Pratyekabuddha; and inconceivable numbers of sentient beings resolved upon Bodhicitta and reached the stage of non-retrogression.

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In future ages, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the 'Devadatta Chapter' of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, believe and revere it with a pure heart and do not give rise to doubt, they shall not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
They shall be born before the Buddhas of the ten directions, and in every place where they are born, they shall constantly hear this sūtra. If they are born among humans..."
In the heavens, he experienced supreme and wondrous bliss. If he were before the Buddha, he would be born by transformation within a lotus flower.
First, he points to his past realization to demonstrate the present; from "Byeti" downwards, he reveals the causes for becoming a deva, thereby attributing the merit to his teacher.

He addressed the assembly below and bestowed upon Deva the prophecy: "The Buddha whose name shall be Heavenly King possesses great majestic power, for he has accomplished the great causes and great fruits of a Tathāgata.
The world shall be named Heavenly Path, for on the Heavenly Path there is no partiality; it is always associated with virtuous people.
One must understand that Deva’s current heart of hatred is no different from his former practice of the wondrous Dharma.
"Śākyamuni’s enemy today is no different from his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of the past. Only by not harboring two minds can one be called 'equanimous.

Extensively preaching the Dharma for those below to deliver sentient beings, they may receive benefit during his lifetime or after his parinirvāṇa. The Buddha told [the assembly] below to exhort sentient beings to have faith.
Question: Devadatta committed the five heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma), yet while still in his living body, he sank into the earth.
Question: When the Buddha was preaching the Dharma, Devadatta had not yet emerged from hell; for what reason did he nevertheless receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*)? Answer:
While Devadatta was in hell, the Buddha commanded Ānanda to ask him, "Are you at peace in hell? He replied, "I am in hell."
It was like the bliss of the third dhyāna heaven. The Buddha again had him ask whether he would still seek to leave. He replied, "I shall wait for the World-Honored One to come and then I will leave.
Ānanda said, "The Buddha is the teacher of the three realms; how could he have any portion [of karma] that leads to entering hell?
He replied, "Since the Buddha has no portion that leads to entering hell, how could I have any portion that leads to leaving hell? These few words alone constitute...
"O Tathāgata Heavenly King, why wait for a prediction of enlightenment?
At that time, from below, a bodhisattva named Zhijī (Jñānakośa), who had followed the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna, addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna.
As they were about to return to their own land, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Zhijī (Jñānakośa), saying: "Good son, wait but a moment.
Here is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī with whom you may meet and discuss the sublime Dharma; only then may you return to your own land.
At that time, Mañjuśrī was seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel, together with the accompanying bodhisattvas.
He too sat upon a precious lotus flower. Emerging spontaneously from the palace of the Sāgara Dragon King in the great ocean, he remained suspended in mid-air and proceeded to Vulture Peak Mountain.
Descending from the lotus, he arrived at the place where the Buddha was and paid homage with his head at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones.
Having completed his respectful salutations, he went to the place of Prajñākūṭa, exchanged greetings with him, and withdrew to sit to one side. Prajñākūṭa...
The Bodhisattva asked Mañjuśrī, "Virtuous One, how many sentient beings did you transform while in the Dragon Palace?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Their number is immeasurable; it cannot be calculated, it is beyond what can be proclaimed by speech, and it cannot be fathomed by the mind."

"Wait but a moment; you shall know for yourself. Before he had finished speaking, countless bodhisattvas emerged from the ocean, seated upon precious lotus flowers, and proceeded to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, where they remained suspended in the air. All these bodhisattvas had been converted and guided by Mañjuśrī;
they were fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva and were all together discussing the six *pāramitās*. Their original voices—
He heard people in the midst of the void expounding the practices of the śrāvakas; now they all practice the Mahāyāna meaning of emptiness.
Mañjuśrī said to Jñatikauṇḍinya: "The manner of his teaching and transformation in the ocean was such as this. At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñatikauṇḍinya...
He praised him with these verses:
"O one of great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor, who brings immeasurable multitudes to transformation and liberation—now this entire great assembly, as well as I, have all witnessed it.

You have expounded the meaning of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and revealed the Dharma of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*), widely guiding all sentient beings so that they may swiftly attain Bodhi."
Mañjuśrī said: "In the midst of the ocean, I have constantly preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

As for the previous request by Jñānākara to return—it was because he still possessed cognitive obstructions; though he had no [notion of] wisdom and no [notion of] attainment, he still had the hindrance of wisdom.

His request that the Buddha return to his land means that the Buddha's work was complete, and he was exhorted to return to his own country. [The text continues: "Wait a moment below; let us speak in detail."

He left him behind. Although this pertains to the distinction between host and guest, it was also intended for Zhizhi and Mañjuśrī to meet and discuss the wondrous Dharma, thereby manifesting the internal style of the bodhisattvas in this land and also [serving as an example] for the bodhisattvas of other lands.
They gave rise to a heart of yearning and thirst, obtaining the flavor of the revealed Dharma, so that their purpose in coming was not in vain. Regarding the passage "At that time," etc.:

Mañjuśrī’s emergence from the ocean symbolizes his flowing forth from the ocean of nature (*dharmatā*). His first prostration at the Buddha’s feet and his subsequent consolation of the Bodhisattva constitute the ritual of homage.
Regarding the passage "Zhijizhang" (Zhiji), he inquires about those he has converted; his intention is that the nature of dragons is prone to anger and they are incapable of [enduring]...
Regarding the "Dharma of Receiving": the question asks how many beings are to be transformed. The passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī" answers that those to be transformed are exceedingly numerous.
The phrase "the assembly of those being transformed surges forth and dwells in the void" means they have equally realized the emptiness of the Mahāyāna.

The section beginning with "At that time" is a verse of praise for Mañjuśrī: "Wisdom" refers to establishing transformations according to the capacities of beings; "Virtue" refers to the state of undifferentiated unity where no traces remain.
To be fearless in the face of the powerful and the obstructive is called "courage. To never cease teaching and transforming others is called "vigor.

One who possesses these four qualities is capable of delivering sentient beings; therefore, he is praised with these terms. The phrase "expounding and clarifying" (演暢) and what follows are words of inquiry:
it asks whether the assembly you transform is transformed by expounding and clarifying the meaning of the true reality (*tathatā*), or [by means of] the meaning of the true reality itself?
[The Buddha] opens various gates to guide [beings]. Below the passage concerning Mañjuśrī, it says: "I do not open separate gateways;
I reveal only the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) to people.
Jñatikauṭilya asked Mañjuśrī: "This sutra is extremely profound and subtle; it is a jewel among all sutras, [unknown] by the world..."
"How rare! Is there perhaps any sentient being who, through diligent and zealous application, practices this sutra and quickly attains Buddhahood?
Mañjuśrī replied, "There is the daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara; she is only eight years of age, yet her wisdom is sharp and her faculties keen.

She well understands the faculties, karma, and activities of all sentient beings. Having attained dhāraṇīs, she is fully capable of [understanding] the profound and secret treasury spoken by all Buddhas."
He upholds [the teachings] and enters deeply into meditative concentration. Having thoroughly realized all dharmas, he gives rise to the bodhicitta in a single kṣaṇa and attains non-retrogression.

His eloquence is unimpeded; he regards all sentient beings with compassion as if they were his own infant children. Endowed with all merit, what his mind contemplates and his mouth articulates is subtle, wondrous, vast, and great.
Compassionate, benevolent, and yielding, his will is harmonious and refined; he is able to reach Bodhi. Thus was Zhijī (Jñānakuṭi).

The Bodhisattva said: "I have seen that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable kalpas, performed difficult practices and ascetic austerities, accumulating merit and virtue while seeking the path to Bodhi without ever ceasing.

He surveyed the trichiliocosm and found not even a space the size of a mustard seed where he had not sacrificed his body and life for the sake of sentient beings; only after this did he finally attain it."
"Having accomplished the path to Bodhi, this woman did not believe it would take her even a moment to attain perfect enlightenment.

Before their conversation had concluded, the Dragon King’s daughter suddenly appeared before them. She prostrated herself with her head at his feet in reverent salutation, then withdrew to stand to one side and praised him in verse:
"You profoundly penetrate the nature of sin and merit, Shining universally throughout the ten directions. Your subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body Is endowed with the thirty-two marks."

Adorned with the eighty secondary marks, the Dharma-body is thus embellished; revered and looked up to by devas and humans, and respected by all dragon spirits, there are no classes of sentient beings who do not pay homage to it.
Furthermore, I have heard that the attainment of Bodhi is something that only a Buddha can personally witness and know.
"I propagate the Mahāyāna teachings to deliver sentient beings from suffering.

This was a formal inquiry by those of sharp faculties. He stated that this sutra is profoundly deep and subtle, a great wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) among the treasures of the Dharma, rare in the world.
Since it possesses such extraordinary qualities, there are surely those who, upon hearing of it, will apply themselves with diligence.
"By applying further diligence, can one suddenly attain unsurpassed bodhi in a single lifetime? Below the passage concerning Mañjuśrī, the answer brings forth the dragon girl (*nāgakanyā*).
Referring to her as a "dragon girl" reveals that she is of a different species; this clarifies that she has not been practicing for a long time in the past.

Stating that she is "only eight years old" shows that she is extremely young, which clarifies that she has not been training in this present life. The four characters "wisdom, sharp faculties" constitute the general [description].

The praise of the dragon girl begins with "well-knowing the [faculties]" (*indriya*), which specifically praises her wisdom. The "faculties" (*indriya*) refer to the five faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

"Karmic activities" (*karma-patha*) refers to the good and evil deeds one performs; this constitutes her knowledge of the capacities of beings (*jñāna-indriya*). The section beginning with "attaining the *dhāraṇīs*" and so forth concerns her knowledge of the Dharma.
It states that because the dragon girl possesses the ten powers (*daśabala*), she is able to know both the capacities of beings and the Dharma. Regarding benefit...
Below, there is a separate praise for those of sharp faculties: at the very moment they first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], they immediately attain non-retrogression.

"Possessing unimpeded eloquence" means attaining the four kinds of unhindered knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). "Compassionately mindful of sentient beings" means cultivating the body through loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

"Fully endowed with merit" means the perfection of the myriad practices (*sādhana*). "Mentally contemplating and verbally expounding" refers to benefiting both oneself and others. Subtle and wondrous...
"Vast" means attaining vastness while exhausting the subtle and minute. "Benevolent" means not possessing one's own virtue as one's own.
"Humble" means not boasting of one's own achievements. "Harmonious" means being free from abruptness, and thus able to accord with things.
"Elegant" means being free from sharp edges, and thus able to complete things. Because this woman is fully endowed with these many virtues, she shall most swiftly attain Bodhi."
Mañjuśrī is the teacher of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; he is also the teacher of all bodhisattvas; furthermore, he serves as the teacher for the hosts of nāgas and nāga maidens.
Whether among those of similar or different species, whether acting in opposition or in accordance with the norm—all are without exception places where wondrous light is revealed.
Therefore, in seeking the Dharma, one should emulate Śākyamuni; yet in preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, one must also emulate Mañjuśrī.
"Below 'Jñānakūṭa,' the Bodhisattva raises a doubt; that is to say, even non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas cannot know it either.
Below 'discourse,' the Dragon Girl reveals her body. Below 'profoundly attaining,' she praises Mañjuśrī in verse. 'Sin' refers to the Dragon Girl."

"Merit" refers to the Tathāgata. To realize that these two characteristics are fundamentally empty and quiescent is what the Buddhas of antiquity meant when they said that both sin and merit are empty and have no place of abiding.
It is by means of this praise of Mañjuśrī that Chih-chih (Jñānakūṭa) is humbled;
for Chih-chih still possesses these two characteristics. "Illuminating the ten directions" refers to the light of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom, which pervades and harmonizes everywhere.
"Penetrating" means it is not like the wisdom of Zhiji, which is obstructed and lacks penetration. "Subtle and wondrous" below praises Mañjuśrī; he is also an ancient Buddha manifesting in this body.
Furthermore, "And I have heard" below states: that I shall attain Buddhahood is known only by the Buddha’s witness;
that I preach the Dharma to save sentient beings is likewise known only by the Buddha’s witness. This serves as a contrast to show that Zhiji was unable to know these things.
Then Śāriputra said to the dragon girl, "Your claim that you will soon attain the unsurpassed path is difficult to believe. Why is this?
A woman's body is defiled and impure; she is not a vessel for the Dharma. How could she possibly attain unsurpassed bodhi?"

The path of the Buddha is vast and remote; it is only after passing through immeasurable kalpas, accumulating practices through diligent toil, and fully cultivating all the pāramitās that one finally achieves it.
Furthermore, the female body still possesses five obstructions: first, one cannot become a Brahmā King; second, [one cannot become] Śakra.
Third, the Māra King; fourth, a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning Sage King; fifth, the body of a Buddha. How can a woman’s body quickly attain Buddhahood?
At that time, the Dragon Girl had a precious jewel worth a trichiliocosm. She held it up and offered it to the Buddha, who immediately accepted it.
The Dragon Girl then addressed the Bodhisattva Zhijie and the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "I..."
She presented a precious jewel. The World-Honored One accepted it. "Is this matter not swift? she asked. He replied, "It is very swift.
The girl said, "By your supernatural power, observe my attainment of Buddhahood; it shall be even swifter than this.

At that moment, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl suddenly transform into a man, fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva, and immediately depart for the stainless world in the south, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower.

He attained perfect enlightenment, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and extensively expounded the wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.

At that time, the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings—humans and non-humans alike—in the Sahā world, all saw from afar that the dragon girl had become a Buddha and was preaching the Dharma to the assembly of gods and humans; their hearts...
Greatly rejoicing, they all paid homage from afar. Immeasurable sentient beings, upon hearing the Dharma, attained realization and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
Immeasurable sentient beings received the prediction of their future enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). The World of Stainless (*Vimalā*) shook in six ways.
In the Sahā world, three thousand sentient beings dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression; three thousand sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and received their predictions. Wisdom...
Jizhi Bodhisattva, as well as Śāriputra and the entire assembly, accepted this in silence with faith.
This presentation of doubt by Śāriputra implies that even he could not know it;
for those who are defiled and unfit vessels, it is said that their bodies are foul-smelling and carnal, and moreover, they are neither dragons nor human beings.
Therefore, they are not vessels for receiving the Dharma. The Buddha’s path descends; [the text] matches with Zhiji (Zhiji) character for character.
The Brahma King is the Lord of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); he is called "Brahma" because of his purity, whereas the female body is impure.
Furthermore, he is a manifestation of a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Śakra is the Lord of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); he is a manifestation of a Bodhisattva of the second stage.
The Māra King is Maheśvara, for he is a manifestation of a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).

The Wheel-Turning King is the most honored among humans, for he is the place where all Buddhas descend to be born; he is also a manifestation shown by a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
Because the Buddha is the most honored among all sages, it is said that even a female body cannot attain the status of a worldly sovereign;
how much less could one swiftly become the supreme Dharma King who transcends the world? Śāriputra of Accumulated Wisdom—these are all merely non-empty physical forms;
his cognitive obscurations have not been shattered, and he remains fallen within the views of a Buddha and the views of sentient beings. [The Master] then took the dragon...
The woman was weighing and measuring with petty precision; one should know that this Bodhisattva from another land is fit to stand in equal rank with the Śrāvakas of this land.
At that time, the Dragon Girl presented the pearl. The Dragon Girl indeed possessed the magnanimity of a great man;
she did not engage in debating right and wrong with him, but directly produced and presented a single, perfectly luminous, priceless, ocean-taming bright pearl.
It was as if the World-Honored One himself; yet he required the World-Honored One to act as a witness. The World-Honored One immediately accepted it for him, providing a formal attestation.
The dragon girl then used a red cotton cord to loop back around the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and asked:
"I offered this precious jewel and the World-Honored One accepted it—was this matter not swift? This is like finding a thorn in soft mud. Zhi Ji.
The two Venerable Ones had mouths and beaks identical to his own; they could not help but answer, "What is so urgent?

However, their nostrils were already in the hands of the Dragon Girl. The Dragon Girl then gently twisted the nostrils of the two Venerable Ones and said, "You all observe my attainment of Buddhahood with your supernatural powers.
The swiftness of your visual power is even swifter than my attainment of Buddhahood."
"Buddha, you yourself do not yet know; how then can you claim to know that my attainment of Buddhahood was so swift?
Even the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas from other lands and this world were utterly deceived face-to-face by an eight-year-old dragon girl and did not realize it. Therefore it is said:"
If a person lives for a hundred years without comprehending the pivotal mechanism (*ki*) of the Buddhas, it would not be as good as living for a single day and being able to decisively realize it.
At that moment, the Dragon Girl wagered her body rather than her voice; suddenly transforming before she had even become a man, she attained Buddhahood on the spot.
Thus one can see that the Way of Bodhi has neither long nor short, neither sudden nor gradual, and neither slow nor fast—it is only...
It lies solely in diligent effort; it lies solely in wondrous awakening. Formerly, Guankui visited the nun Moshan.
Moshan asked, "Where have you come from today, Venerable One? He replied, "From the crossroads. Moshan said, "Why do you not cover it over?
He then prostrated himself. She asked, "What is Moshan? Moshan said, "The crown is not revealed. He asked, "Who is the master of Moshan? Moshan said—
"It is neither male nor female. The Master then shouted, "Why do you not transform? Shanshan said, "I am neither a god nor a ghost; what would I transform into?
The Master was deeply impressed and served as the head gardener for three years. Moshan said, "It is not that there is no transformation; it is that the Dragon Girl transformed.
Now tell me, is it transformation or is it non-transformation? Puhui descended to preach the Dharma and save sentient beings. Now tell me— [is this transformation or non-transformation?]
What kind of Dharma was preached to transform the dragons? As stated previously in the sutra, he attained *bodhi*, expounded the Great Teaching, and delivered sentient beings;
this is witnessed and known only by the Buddha. Such is the view [of the author]. "At that time" and below refers to the great assembly rejoicing and paying homage.

This is merely following the heterodox and pursuing the strange. "Immeasurable" and below refers to hearing the Dharma and gaining benefit. "The vexing spring wind never ceases"—[the author] remains silent.
As for those who believe and accept [this teaching], they immediately find their sharpness gone and their tongues tied, remaining silent and speechless.
The thirteenth verse of the "Chapter on Upholding" (Dhāraṇī-parivarta) says:
In this degenerate age, human sentiments are full of guile, and rumors spread as swiftly as spirits. To prove a tortoise, one can claim it is a soft-shelled turtle;
by pointing at a table, one makes it appear as a person. When the medicine rots, it is called the tooth of Dharmaruci;
when a blade cuts into the body of a lion, one remains utterly unmoved. Only then does one see the true essence of upholding the Dharma.
The preceding *Ratnakoṭi-parivarta* states: "I wish to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to those who shall uphold it," and further says:

"This is a difficult task; you should resolve to make great vows. Having thus stirred the aspirations of the great assembly, [the Buddha], fearing that their resolve might not be sufficiently intense or fervent, again cites his own past quest for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, leading up to...

Taking oneself as the seat, one should never grow weary but instead exert oneself. Furthermore, by enabling others to personally witness the dragon girl hearing the Lotus Sūtra and immediately realizing bodhi, one encourages them to advance.
It was from this that those first began to make vows to uphold the sūtra; hence it is called the "Chapter on Upholding" (Dhāraṇī-parivarta).
The single character "uphold" (dhāraṇī) is the essential key to the five kinds of Dharma-preachers; therefore, this chapter is specifically designated.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna,
together with a retinue of twenty thousand bodhisattvas, all made this vow before the Buddha: "May the World-Honored One not..."
We resolve that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we shall uphold, recite, and expound this sutra.

In the future evil age, sentient beings will have diminished roots of goodness and will largely increase in overweening pride; they will covet profit and offerings, further increasing their unwholesome roots and distancing themselves from liberation.
Although they are difficult to transform and teach, we shall exert the power of great patience to read, recite, uphold, and expound this sutra.
They shall transcribe it and offer various kinds of worship, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.

At that time, five hundred Arhats within the assembly who had received predictions of enlightenment addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we too vow that in other lands we shall extensively expound this sutra.
Furthermore, eight thousand persons, both those still in training and those beyond training, who had received predictions of enlightenment rose from their seats and joined their palms.
Facing the Buddha, they made this vow: "World-Honored One, we too shall extensively expound this sutra in other lands. Why is this?
Because in this Sahā world, people are for the most part corrupt and evil; they harbor overweening pride, their merit is meager, and because their minds are impure with anger, turbidity, and deceit."
Previously, among the assembly of bodhisattvas who made vows to uphold this sutra, there were eighty thousand;

yet when Bhaiṣajyarāja Mahāratnakūṭa was accompanied by only twenty thousand bodhisattvas, this was a word of consolation for those who perceived the remaining ones as fearful or reluctant and did not consider it a concern.
The phrase "we, the lowly" is a statement of taking responsibility, corresponding to the previous question: "Who among us is able to [uphold this]?"

The phrase "widely proclaiming the sublime Dharma in the Sahā world" and so forth constitutes the words of making a vow; these should be connected with the preceding words, "Who can protect the Dharma?
which refer to the extensive making of great vows. When it says "in the later evil age," this specifically refers to the period of the final five hundred years when strife is firmly entrenched.
When it says "roots of goodness," this refers to the three [wholesome roots]: non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
These are the roots of goodness. As for the roots of unwholesomeness, they are the three unwholesome roots of greed, hatred, and delusion.
This means that in the final age, roots of goodness are few while roots of unwholesomeness are many; good people are few while unwholesome people are many.
To give rise to the power of great patience is precisely to make the vow to become one of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers. The intention is that for sentient beings in the final age...
Although they may be stubborn and difficult to transform, one should perform these five kinds of Buddha-works through the power of great patience.
By gradually soaking and permeating them, one slowly leads them in. Even if they revile one with foul language or strike one, even unto the dismemberment of every limb, one must endure it all.
In the past, the bhikṣu Kālakarṇī complained to the Buddha, saying: "Śāriputra reviled me and spoke ill of me. The Buddha [replied]...
He called for Śāriputra and asked him, "Did you truly speak in such a way as to revile me? Śāriputra replied, "One whose mind is unsettled might be said to revile;
my mind is already settled—how could I revile? I am like an ox with its horns broken, who does not provoke or disturb others;
I am like a castrated youth, who feels shame and does not trouble them. My mind is like the earth, indifferent to whether it receives pure or impure things, great or small."
"It is convenient; it accepts everything. The mind is like a broom; it sweeps away both the pure and the impure. Why, then, would one revile others?
The Buddha asked, "Regarding such an evil person, how do you view them? He replied, "There are five types of people.
There are those whose bodies are virtuous but whose speech and minds are not. One should simply attend to their bodies and not attend to their speech or minds."
Just as a *pāṃśukūlika* bhikṣu, seeing rags among a heap of refuse, cuts away the impure parts and takes what is pure, so too do I:
I contemplate the purity of that body to regulate my own body, and I contemplate his speech and mind to guard my own speech and mind.
There are those whose speech is pure while their body and mind are impure; they should likewise use that speech to cast aside their body and mind.
There are those whose mind is pure while their body and speech are impure; they should likewise use that mind to cast aside their body and speech. There is a type where all three are impure;
although there is nothing that can be used, one should feel deep regret for them. If all three are pure, one should always maintain this in the mind.

Using this to regulate and instruct oneself is also a gradual step toward great patience (*mahākṣānti*). "At that time" and below refers to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who make a vow to uphold the sūtra in another land.
Furthermore, "there are others" and below refers to those still in training (*śaikṣa*) who make a vow to uphold the sūtra in another land.

This is the initial aspiration of a śrāvaka who receives a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), learning the bodhisattva practices and cultivating the duties of a Dharma master. Regarding the term "depraved and evil": it means...
In this Sahā world, those who ruin others and those who do evil are many. "The wrathful" refers to those who are rigid and violent, lacking a gentle countenance.

"The turbid" refers to those who are defiled and impure, lacking conduct of purity and clarity. "The sycophantic" refers to those skilled at flattery and pleasing others, yet devoid of the spirit of a true man.
"The crooked" refers to those habituated to fawning and welcoming, yet lacking a heart of integrity and straightforwardness. Because such are these people, therefore—
Because the true Dharma cannot be transmitted to them, he does not wish to enter the Sahā world.
Thus we know that the sentient beings of the Sahā world are all regarded as abandoned by the śrāvaka disciples.

If there were no bodhisattvas with the power of great patience to act as Dharma masters, providing them with thorough and comprehensive explanations, would they not for the most part become members of other species?
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs—both those in training and those beyond training—rose from their seats.
With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, their eyes never wavering for a moment.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Gautamī: “For what reason do you look upon the Tathāgata with such a sorrowful expression? Is it because your heart...”
"Do not think that I have not spoken your name when bestowing the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Gautamī, I have previously given a general prediction for all the śrāvakas. Now, if you wish to know your own prediction,"
In a future age, you shall become a great Dharma teacher among sixty-eight thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas,
and together with six thousand *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* bhikṣuṇīs, you shall all serve as Dharma teachers. In this way,
gradually perfecting the Bodhisattva path, you shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Tathāgata Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna.
One who is perfect in conduct; a Sugata; one who understands the world; an unsurpassed being; a charioteer of men; a teacher of gods and humans; a Buddha; a World-Honored One;
Gautamī—these, including the Buddha Liked by All Beings to Behold and six thousand bodhisattvas, were each given a successive prediction of enlightenment.
He attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, Rāhula’s mother, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, had this thought:
"The World-Honored One has not mentioned my name alone among those who have received their predictions. The Buddha said to Yaśodharā:
"In future ages, within the teachings of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, you shall practice the bodhisattva path."
Great Dharma Master, you shall gradually perfect the Buddha-way and attain Buddhahood in the land of *Sukhāvatī*.

You shall be known as the Tathāgata Endowed with Myriads of Radiant Marks, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One.
The Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One— whose lifespan lasts for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—
at that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā, together with their retinues, were all filled with great joy,
having attained what they had never experienced before. They then spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“O World-Honored One, Guide, who brings peace and security to devas and humans! Having heard this prophecy, our minds are fully at ease.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses, they addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, we too shall widely proclaim this sutra in other lands.”
Because he had not been granted a prediction by name, he did not dare to make a vow to uphold the sutra;

thus, he fixed his gaze upon the Tathāgata without momentarily looking away, desiring that the Tathāgata would know his intention. From the words "At that time" onwards, [the text] first clarifies the meaning of his gazing with eyes transfixed.
From the words "Kauṇḍinya" onwards, the Tathāgata grants him a prediction, designating him as a Great Dharma Master, desiring that he shall widely proclaim the Great Dharma.
This is the gradual fulfillment of the bodhisattva path. The Buddha is named *Sarvasattvapriyadarśana* (He Whom All Sentient Beings Delight to Behold).
Because he was able to practice the Great Path of Love (*mahāmaitrī*) as a great Dharma-master during his causal stage, all beings delight in beholding him upon the fruition.

The Buddha is also named *Samantaprabhālakṣaṇasampanna* (Endowed with the Mark of Universal Radiance). Because he acted as a great Dharma-master during his causal stage, elucidating and clarifying the great Dharma-light of the Tathāgata, he is so named.
This refers to the mark of radiance being fully perfected upon the fruit. Regarding the phrase "the mind is peaceful and fully perfected" in the verse:

when one has not yet received the prediction (vyākaraṇa), the mind cannot find peace and one's aspirations cannot be fulfilled. Now that one has received the prediction, the mind is at peace and the aspiration is likewise fulfilled.

Therefore it is said: "The mind is fully satisfied. From the passage beginning with "All these... onwards, they receive their predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) and likewise make vows to uphold this sutra.

Question: Since the assembly of śrāvakas has already received their predictions and made vows to uphold the sutra, why is it that they all wish to go to other lands and do not wish to enter the Sahā world, which differs from the bodhisattvas? Answer: It is because the śrāvakas uphold...
When maintaining pure precepts, one should not give rise to even a single thought of receiving further bodies within the three realms.
When a Bodhisattva maintains pure precepts, they are able to endure receiving further bodies for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas without giving rise to weariness or indolence.
Because their habitual mental applications differ, the vows they now make also differ; all of these accord with their original intentions.

This follows their respective seeds of habituation; it is not a matter of forced contrivance. If one speaks in terms of "concealing within and manifesting without," then because the śrāvaka disciples have long practiced the bodhisattva path in this Sahā world, they should be reborn in a pure land.
At that time, the World-Honored One looked upon eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
These bodhisattvas were all *avaivartika*, turning the wheel of non-retrogression and having attained various *dhāraṇīs*.
They immediately rose from their seats, went before the Buddha, joined their palms with single-minded devotion, and thought to themselves: "If the World-Honored One would command us..."
...and so forth. Those who uphold and preach this sutra should propagate this Dharma extensively in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings.
Furthermore, they should reflect: "The Buddha is now silent; we see no formal injunction. What should we do?

At that time, the bodhisattvas, out of reverence for the Buddha’s intention and desiring to fulfill their own original vows, made a lion’s roar before the Buddha and uttered this vow: "World-Honored One, we..."
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, we shall travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions,

enabling sentient beings to copy this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, explain its meaning, practice according to the Dharma, and maintain right mindfulness— all through the majestic power of the Buddha.
We pray only that the World-Honored One, while remaining in another realm, will behold us from afar and provide protection.
The World-Honored One saw that those who had made vows to uphold this sutra were all in other lands; fearing they would enter the Sahā world, he found them all unsatisfactory.
Therefore, he beckoned the Bodhisattvas with his eyes. They immediately descended. The Bodhisattvas thought to themselves:
