"Because of his gaze, we have arisen and joined our palms; because of his silence, we have again reflected. At that time, as the others descended, they followed the Buddha’s intention and set forth [their resolve].
Aspiration: Because he has received the intent of the World-Honored One’s gaze, it is said that he "reverently accords with the Buddha’s will.
Since his original vow was likewise to be thus, it is said that he "fulfills his own original vow. Regarding "making the roar of a teacher": this is not like the timidness found among śrāvakas.
Regarding "traversing the ten directions": going and returning, he is not restricted to a single realm. "Able to cause... and so forth.
"I myself am able to write down, receive, uphold, recite, explain, and practice with right mindfulness;
furthermore, I can cause sentient beings to receive, uphold, and write [these teachings], performing various Buddha-deeds—all of which are due to the Buddha's majestic power."

They attributed the merit to their teacher, not claiming the achievement for themselves. Seeing the Protectors from afar, they further requested that the Tathāgata’s spiritual power provide secret assistance.
Immediately, all the Bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison and spoke these verses:
We only pray that you do not worry. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the midst of this terrifying and evil age, we shall extensively proclaim [the Dharma].
Should there be those who are ignorant, who revile us with foul language, or who even inflict blows with knives and staves, we shall endure it all.

In this degenerate age, there will be bhikṣus whose intellects are perverted and whose minds are crooked with flattery; those who have not attained realization yet claim to have attained it, their hearts filled with pride.
Some may dwell as forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka), wearing robes of rags in secluded places, claiming to practice the true path while looking down upon those who live among people.
Because of their greed for gain and offerings, they preach the Dharma to laypeople and are venerated by the world as if they were arhats with the six supernormal powers.
Yet these people harbor evil intentions and constantly dwell on worldly affairs; they falsely claim to be forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*) and take pleasure in exposing our faults.
And they spoke these words: "These bhikṣus, for the sake of craving gain and offerings, preach the doctrines of external paths;
they have composed these sūtras themselves to delude the people of the world, and for the sake of seeking fame and renown, they have analyzed this scripture."
They constantly stand amidst the great assembly with the intent to disparage us.

Toward kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and other groups of monks, they slander us by speaking of our evils, claiming we are people of false views who propound the doctrines of external paths.

Out of reverence for the Buddha, we shall endure all these evils. Regarding those who speak with such contempt, saying, "You are all Buddhas," we must accept and endure all such insults. In this defiled age of evil, there will be many terrors.
Evil spirits shall enter their bodies and revile, abuse, and humiliate me. We, who revere and trust in the Buddha, shall don the armor of patience;
for the sake of expounding this sutra, we shall endure these various hardships. We do not cherish our own bodies or lives, but only regret that we might fail to attain the unsurpassed Way.
In future ages, we shall uphold what the Buddha has entrusted to us; may the World-Honored One himself know this.

Those evil bhikṣus of the turbid age will not understand the Buddha’s skillful means regarding the teachings spoken according to what is appropriate. They will speak with foul mouths and knit their brows in frowns;
they will repeatedly see us expelled and driven away from the stūpas and monasteries. Because we keep in mind the Buddha’s admonitions, we shall endure all such evils.
In all villages and cities, wherever there are those who seek the Dharma, I shall go to each of their places and preach the teachings entrusted by the Buddha.
I am the messenger of the World-Honored One; dwelling among the assembly, I am fearless. I shall skillfully expound the Dharma; may the Buddha dwell in peace and security.
In the presence of the World-Honored One and all the Buddhas who have come from the ten directions, I have made this vow.

The Buddha himself knows my heart; this is a single chapter of the Bodhisattva’s aspiration text. The first four lines constitute the general statement, while "There are those... and following are the specific details.
"We shall all practice patience"—the character *ren* (patience) is the antithesis of the character *chen* (anger). As the *Decisive Vinaya Sūtra* (*Niyatadharmaparyāya-sūtra*) states:

If a bodhisattva practicing the Mahāyāna were to violate the precepts while associated with a mind of greed for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, that offense would still be relatively light.
However, if one violates the precepts with even a single thought of anger, that offense is extremely grave. Why is this?
One violates the precepts due to greed, yet through this one gathers in sentient beings; one violates the precepts due to anger, yet through this one abandons sentient beings.
Therefore, regarding all dharmas that are capable of gathering in sentient beings, a bodhisattva should not give rise to fear. Regarding all dharmas...

Because Bodhisattvas should feel dread toward abandoning sentient beings; whereas severing craving is what the followers of the Lesser Vehicle prioritize first, severing anger is the urgent duty of a Bodhisattva.
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva upholds this sutra in a turbid age, they must practice patience.
Below the phrase "in an evil age," the text speaks extensively on the matters one must endure. The mention of "bhikṣus" specifically reveals those who destroy the Dharma.
Such a person does not dwell in white robes but in patched saffron garments; they are what is called "a worm within the lion’s body devouring the lion’s own flesh.
Those with false wisdom lack right knowledge and vision, uttering words like a rudder tossed by the wind.
Those who are sycophantic and crooked display the fawning and servile manner of a slave seeking favor through fox-like seduction. Those with pride do so because of their false wisdom.

Deceitful and crooked, he was able to form alliances with those in power and high station. Like a fox borrowing the tiger’s majesty, his eyes looked down upon the four seas with contempt, treating all things with utter disdain.
He claimed for himself that throughout heaven and earth, he alone was the most honored. Such a person harbors swords and halberds within his heart.
The halberds and spears lie at their tongues. Therefore, wherever they go, they bring calamity and create evil karma. They praise themselves and disparage others;
this is what is meant by "claiming to have attained what one has not attained. Or there are those who, from below, produce the causes for slander.
*Aranya* in Sanskrit means a "place of tranquility. Those who wear patched robes in seclusion refer to those who, wrapped in patched robes, dwell in deep mountains and remote valleys.
Dwelling on the shores of empty desolation and solitude, they claim for themselves that they practice the true and correct path of the Tathāgata.
They regard those in the human world who preach the Dharma, deliver sentient beings, and perform the Buddha-work as followers of heterodox paths, intentionally treating them with contempt.
They say that although such people may feign the outward appearance of decorum and put on a mask of piety to pretend they have no worldly desires, [they are nonetheless...]
To claim purity while one’s conduct is turbid is not true cultivation. Greedily attached to gain and offerings, they secretly preach the Dharma to laypeople (*avadātavasana*), deceiving the ignorant.
Those who are ignorant are deluded by them and revere them as if they were Arhats.
Having gained the respect of laypeople, they further fear that those with clear vision and mastery will see through them in their hearts; thus, their minds are not at ease.
An was harboring malicious intent; thus, in the presence of others, he suppressed them to exalt himself, claiming that he alone practiced the Way while disparaging those of the human world.
Although he did not dwell among men but remained deeply hidden in mountain valleys, the thoughts he focused upon were entirely mundane and vulgar matters.
He was plagued by anxiety over gain and loss, with his mind like a cross between ice and fire; how could there ever have been even a single [moment of purity]?
"Contemplating tranquility—is this not what is called 'aranyaka' by way of conventional designation?

For such people as these, would they not be taking the non-existent to be existent, delighting in creating faults and offenses, and thus producing inferior, slanderous words? Or it may be said: 'This is a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma among men.'"
All of these are for the sake of greedily clinging to gain and offerings; they are the doctrines of non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) and are not the correct teaching of the Tathāgata.
Some say that these were spoken by bhikṣus who themselves fabricated them to delude and mislead the people of the world.
"It is not that they are propagating the Buddha’s transformation on his behalf. Some say: "These bhikṣus seek fame and reputation;
therefore they preach this sutra, not for the sake of delivering sentient beings. They constantly remain in inferior positions and in places of slander and defamation.
Such words of slander may be uttered before those of great power, or before those who practice pure conduct, or before those who follow the Way.
To disparage. Or to disparage in the presence of one's fellow practitioners, saying: "That person who preaches the Dharma is a person of false views;
what he teaches is the dharma of non-Buddhists. Even though they thus slander and revile us, we shall respect the Buddha’s instructions and be able to endure all their wickedness.
For these reasons, the following three phrases are also words of slander and disparagement. There is...
There are two meanings. First, it refers to a wicked bhikṣu who, upon seeing a bhikṣu preaching the Dharma, deliberately utters words of contempt, saying:
"When you all preach the Dharma, you claim these are the living Buddhas appearing in the world; how could this be taken lightly?
Second, it may refer to a wicked bhikṣu who, pointing to the words of a prophecy, says to the assembly: "This was not spoken by the Buddha; rather, it was spoken by a bhikṣu preaching the Dharma."
The Venerable Kāśyapa invited others to revere him, yet intentionally uttered these轻薄 (trifling) words:
"You claim to be Buddhas, but you cannot be fully trusted. Although such wicked bhikṣus may speak thus, I shall set them aside and not dispute with them.
This is because in this turbid age, there are those who slander and defame; it is said that such bhikṣus merely intimidate others, and only in this land [is this so].
There are. These things do not exist in other lands. All these bhikṣus have malevolent spirits entering their hearts and entrails;
therefore, although they revile me with foul language, disparage me, and insult me, we, out of reverence and faith in the Buddha’s words, don the armor of patience.
I practice the path of patience. Because I have received the Buddha’s command to preach this sutra, even when they inflict upon me matters that are difficult to endure, I endure them all.
As for those who revile and insult me, it is not because I cherish my own body that I dare not contend with them;
rather, it is because I personally value the Way of the Dharma King within my own person, and thus I treasure myself [in this way].

This is a matter of great weight. Just as a city of ten thousand cities does not compete in price with mere rubble, and the *yuanchu* and *yunchu* do not cry out in the same manner as the owl and the vulture, I simply cannot help but remain silent.
Nevertheless, all of this is solely because I have received the Tathāgata’s entrustment, which rests upon a single word;
there is no other reason. The World-Honored One himself shall surely know my heart. Below, in this turbid age, there arise those who slander and revile.

The meaning [of this] is as follows: Monks in this defiled age lack wisdom and do not understand that the Tathāgata’s bestowal of the prophecy of Buddhahood is also a skillful means for guiding people.
Therefore, upon hearing these words but once, they immediately respond with foul language and abuse;
they knit their brows and furrow their foreheads, regarding it as the dharma of non-Buddhists. They repeatedly expel such persons and will not allow them entry into the monastery. Thus it is.

"Though various evils may be inflicted upon me, I am able to endure them all. Although I remain far from monasteries and temples, if there are those who seek the Dharma within villages or cities, I shall certainly not fall back or retreat; by the power of my vows, I will go to their places and preach the Dharma for them.
Because I have received the Buddha’s entrustment, I am a messenger sent by the Tathāgata, adorned with the Buddha’s..."
I am solemn and adorn myself; therefore, I dwell among the multitude without fear and do not disgrace my mission.

I always employ virtuous words to guide and discuss with others, leading them to awakening and entry [into the Dharma], so as to continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom and prevent it from being extinguished. My wish is thus:
I only pray that the Tathāgata will dwell peacefully in this world and need not trouble yourself with anxiety. I shall now conclude with a vow below.
The Great Outline of the Lotus Sutra, Volume Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Annotated by the Bhikṣu Tōngrùn of Jintíng.
In the fourteenth verse of the "Chapter on Peace and Bliss" (The Simile of the Topknot Jewel), it says:
"The power of the Dharma generals and their divine armies is now truly strong; the demonic hosts have cast off their armor and are utterly destroyed."
Having personally obtained this single jewel from the topknot, all places of suffering have become fields of joy;
this is due to the previous eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattvas who made vows to uphold this sutra, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.
To endure various hardships—being able to endure the application of blades, staves, and verbal abuse—is not necessarily peace.
To endure seeing what is terrifying and fearful is not necessarily joy. Now, let it be that blades, staves, and verbal abuse cannot be inflicted [upon you].

There are those who, due to fear and dread, are unable to enter; they would thus spend their entire days walking upon mountains of knives and trees of swords, or dwelling amidst masses of ice and clusters of fire.
All of these are the *dharma-maṇḍala* of peace and bliss, yet none can attain them without deeply penetrating the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.
Therefore, one advances by means of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. Yongjia said: "Contemplate..."

Harsh words are themselves a source of merit; they constitute my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Since no enmity or intimacy arises from slander, this demonstrates the power of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these bodhisattvas are truly rare.
Out of reverent compliance with the Buddha, they have made great vows to protect, uphold, read, and recite this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in the future evil age.
World-Honored One, how will these bodhisattva mahāsattvas [proceed] in the future evil age?"

Regarding those who are able to preach this sutra, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to preach this sutra in the evil age to come, they should abide securely in four dharmas.
First, they should abide securely in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice and the sphere of association."
One is able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings. Mañjuśrī, what is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
It is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the stage of patience, being gentle, mild, and compliant, and not impetuous or violent.
The mind is likewise not startled. Furthermore, while not engaging with any phenomena, one contemplates all dharmas as they truly are;
neither acting nor discriminating—this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

First, Mañjuśrī asks: "Respectfully following," and so forth. This means that by looking with his eyes, the Tathāgata enables one to respectfully follow the Buddha’s intention, to give rise to great vows, and to enter the evil age to uphold this sutra; thus, one knows this is truly rare.
However, the sentient beings of the evil age are stubborn, fierce, and coarse; there is much cause for fear. Even if one possesses the power of firm endurance, one might still fear [failing].
[The Bodhisattvas] were able to persevere for a long time; however, they did not know how to apply their minds or what practices to perform before they would be capable of expounding this sutra.
The Buddha told them [the following], which explains the four gates of peaceful dwelling (*catur-āśvāsa-dharma*).

First, "abiding securely in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice (*caryā-vihāra*) and sphere of association (*sevā-vihāra*)" refers to abiding entirely in equanimity regarding the spheres of daily activity and those with whom one associates.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal; it makes no distinction between high and low. Only after [realizing this] does one preach the Dharma, whereby one attains peace and happiness.

What is meant by "low"? First, one should understand that there are two types of bodhisattva practice: first, the practice of phenomena (*vastu-caryā*); second, the practice of principle (*tattva-caryā*). First, the practice of phenomena is explained.

As for the practice of phenomena, it consists in enduring external conditions. To endure external conditions means not to give rise to the hindrances of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*). This is what is meant by "abiding in the ground of patience" (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).
It is said that when a Bodhisattva appears in the world, they must first endure the insults of others. They should not allow their minds to be disturbed by the thought, "A person has insulted me.
To be gentle, kind, and compliant means: if another comes with harshness, one responds with gentleness;
if another comes with anger, one responds with harmony; if another comes with evil, one responds with goodness; if another comes with hostility, one responds with...

In accordance with this principle, not only can weapons and verbal abuse not be inflicted [upon him], but even if a yakṣa harbors the intent to kill, it will instead be transformed into the compassionate countenance of a bodhisattva. This is what is meant by the saying:
"Beholding the countenance of a virtuous person causes one's [malicious] thoughts to dissolve. As for the phrase "neither violent nor startled," "violent" refers to—
The state of urgency refers to a state of alarm; the state of being startled refers to a state of terror. Because one is gentle and supple, one does not act with sudden violence;
because one is virtuous and compliant, one is not startled. This is what Yongjia meant when he said: "Even if you encounter a sharp blade, you remain ever composed;
even if you are given lethal poison, you remain at ease. If one is suddenly violent or once startled, one will be moved by that external stimulus and fall into its entanglement.
Once it is painted over, blades and staves may be applied, and insults and abuse may enter.

This is the excellent prescription for a practitioner of the Way living in the world, and it is also the secret key to upholding the sutras. This is what was meant previously by "donning the robe of patience.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there is an account where someone who heard the Buddha praised as possessing the marks of great merit and virtue became angry and said: "Seven days after he was born..."

The mother then passed away. How could one not say she possessed the marks of great merit? The praiser said: "Though both her years and her will were at their peak, she was neither impulsive nor violent;

when struck, she did not become angry, and when reviled, she did not retaliate. For this reason, I say she possesses the marks of great merit. Upon hearing this, the enraged man submitted with his heart.
Furthermore, below this, [the text] explains the practice of *li-xing* (principle-conduct). As for *li-xing*, it means patience within. Patience...
Regarding "within," one does not give rise to the obstruction of principle (*dṛṣṭi-āvaraṇa*). Regarding "having no practice toward phenomena," "practice" refers to conceptual discrimination;

because one does not perceive any phenomenon as being in accordance with one's own mind, the mind is free from discrimination. Thus, one contemplates all phenomena according to their true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*).
If one perceives that the world truly possesses the two characteristics of good and evil, one will inevitably be turned by them;
thus, there will arise a mind that loves the good and hates the evil, and one will be unable to abide in the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
Therefore, one observes that all dharmas, whether good or evil, have no high or low; they are all equal and of a single characteristic. Consequently, the mind has nowhere to operate. Nor does it...
One who practices non-discrimination does not perceive the absence of phenomena as being contrary to their own experience; thus, being without discrimination, they do not discriminate either.
They do not form views of existence nor views of non-existence. Defilement and purity are both forgotten; the mind and its objects are as one.
When worldly and world-transcending dharmas are forged into a single whole, it is only then called the method of the "Equalizing Contemplation.
The *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā* states: "To have no discrimination regarding dharmas, yet not to practice what is non-dharma—this is called taking refuge in the Dharma.

This is precisely the Bodhisattva practicing world-transcending dharmas while within the world; this is what is meant by the "sphere of activity of a Bodhisattva," which refers to constant observation.
Such is the nature of dharmas; this is precisely what constitutes practicing the bodhisattva path.
What is meant by the "places of association" for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not associate with kings, princes, ministers, or high officials, nor does he associate with various non-Buddhist practitioners, such as brahmins or Nirgranthas (Jains), and so forth. And...
One should not compose secular writings, nor praise non-Buddhist texts, nor the Lokāyata or the Prati-lokāyata.
Furthermore, one should not associate with those who engage in violent games, such as boxing, wrestling, or various performances involving human acrobats (*nara*).
Nor should one associate with *caṇḍālas*, nor with those who raise pigs, sheep, chickens, or dogs, nor with hunters, trappers, or fishermen. All such persons [should be avoided].
Regarding those of evil discipline: if such persons should ever come, one should preach the Dharma to them without any expectation of reward.
Furthermore, one should not associate with or seek out śrāvaka bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, nor should one exchange greetings with them.
One should not dwell together with them, whether in a cell, on a walking path, or within a lecture hall. Or at times...
When others come, one should preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate, without harboring any expectations.

Mañjuśrī, furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not take up the signs of a woman’s body that give rise to thoughts of desire while preaching the Dharma to her, nor should they take pleasure in seeing her.
If one enters the home of another, one should not converse with young girls, virgins, widows, and the like, nor should one cultivate intimacy with the five kinds of impotent persons.
One should not enter the home of another alone; however, if there is a necessary reason to enter alone, one should simply maintain single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha.
If one preaches the Dharma to women, one should not smile showing one's teeth, nor expose one's chest.
Even regarding the Dharma, he was not intimate or close; how much less so for other matters. He took no pleasure in keeping young disciples.
Śrāmaṇeras and young novices do not delight in having the same teacher as him; he always prefers to practice dhyāna in secluded places, cultivating and restraining his mind.

Mañjuśrī, this is called the first stage of close association. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as empty according to their true nature—uninverted, immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-revolving, like empty space. It is without...
All natures have all paths of language cut off; they are unarisen, unproduced, and unoriginated; they are nameless and signless; in reality, nothing exists;
they are immeasurable and boundless, unobstructed and unimpeded, existing only through causes and conditions, and are spoken of as arising from inversion.
One should always joyfully contemplate such characteristics of dharmas; this is called the second intimacy of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
This explains the "places of intimacy. There are both matters (*vastu*) and principles (*dharma*). First, the explanation of intimacy regarding matters:
first, not associating with the powerful and noble. The Sūtra says: "If a bhikṣu associates with a king, there are ten unrighteous things; first, secret plotting."
1. The king issues a command. 2. Two kings execute their great ministers. 3. The treasures of the three treasuries are lost. 4. A palace woman becomes pregnant. 5. The king’s person is poisoned. 6.
Great ministers contend with one another. 7. Two nations engage in war. 8. The king is stingy and does not practice charity. 9. He collects taxes and requisitions from the people’s goods.
10. Many pestilential diseases prevail. All the people say that these are the deeds of the bhikṣu.
To slander a bhikṣu by acting in this manner is to slander the Buddha and the Dharma; therefore, the Buddha does not permit one to associate with kings and the like.
Second, do not associate with false teachers. Those called "non-Buddhists" (tīrthikas) do not take the mind itself as the Way.
Because their minds wander outside the Way. As for the *brahmins*, their ancestors aspired to the Brahma Heaven and practiced the conduct of Brahma.
As for the *Nirgranthas*, they are the eternalist non-Buddhist outsiders; these people claim that sin and merit are fixed and must be experienced, and that there is no path of practice.

Regarding the phrase "those who can sever" (*prahāṇa*), etc., this includes the other five teachers. First is Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who gave rise to false views, asserting that all phenomena are subject to annihilation.
Second is Maskarin Gośālīputra, who reckoned that the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings are not obtained through formative actions (*saṃskāra*), but are entirely spontaneous.
Third is Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, who reckoned that [the world] endures for a long time...
Transmigrating through birth and death, they have passed through many kalpas until the limits of suffering are exhausted. Fourth is Kambala:

this man falsely regards what is not a cause as a cause, taking the fumigation of the nose and the plucking out of hair to be the Way; now he suffers together with others, yet he claims there will be eternal bliss in future lives.
Fifth is Kātyāyana: this man says that all dharmas possess both marks and lack marks. Including the previous teacher, these constitute the six masters. No [further].

Those permitted to associate with are [restricted] for fear they might enter into heterodox lineages. As for secular literary compositions that praise and extol external texts—namely the *Ba-so* (Eight Searches), the *Jiu-qiu* (Nine Mounds), the *San-fen* (Three Tombs), the *Wu-dian* (Five Canons), and the various masters and hundred schools—they are not permitted to be associated with, for "many paths cause one to lose the sheep.
The Sanskrit term *Lokāyata* translates here as "evil discourse"; this refers to the Lokāyata heretics.

As for "reckoning," because it accords with worldly sentiments, the Sanskrit term is *vilokāyata*, which here means "evil questioning. This is because what is reckoned therein does not accord with the world.
As for "not associating [with such people]," it is because one fears falling into an evil lineage. Third, "not approaching those who engage in violent games."
"Nārāyaṇa" refers here to "superior acrobatics," meaning to paint one's body and perform various transformations and plays, such as the Shaolin "divine fist" or "divine staff" arts.
Those who are forbidden from associating with such people do so for fear that it might give rise to a combative mind.
Fourth, one does not associate with those of evil discipline (*pāpa-śīla*), because practicing evil leads to evil. Thus, below, it says: "Regarding such people as these, although I..."

One should not go near them. Should they feel a nascent sense of remorse and be willing to come and associate with me, one should preach the Dharma according to their capacity to guide their innate goodness, causing them to abandon the old for the new; one must not harbor expectations for offerings.

Fifth, do not associate with those of the Hīnayāna. Those of the Hīnayāna do not understand the preaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate; one fears that they might give rise to contentious debate.

For these reasons, one does not exchange greetings with them, nor does one dwell together with them. Sixth, regarding "not associating with women": this is to prevent small evils from developing into great ones.

One does not associate with young girls who do not understand propriety and righteousness, nor with virgins, nor with unmarried women, nor with widows, nor with those who, though married, still refer to themselves as "the widow" (wei-mang-ren).

Seventh, regarding "not associating with those who are not male" (*pandaka*): this refers to those born with intense jealousy or who have become *ardha-pandaka* (half-males). One [should not associate with them].
Entering alone is to guard against the mouths of those who harbor suspicion. Reciting the Buddha’s name with single-mindedness is to cultivate a sense of reverence.
Not smiling with bared teeth and not exposing one's chest is to avoid the manner of intimacy and familiarity.
Even if someone has come for the sake of the Dharma, one should not treat them as a close friend; how much less so should one draw near on account of other matters? (8)
One should not associate with young novices, as described above; for all such things can obstruct meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) by disturbing the mind and its thoughts.
Therefore, one should keep them at a distance. Regarding those who dwell in secluded places to cultivate and restrain their minds:

this refers to staying by the water’s edge, beneath trees, or in empty, quiet locations, restraining the mind with right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). That is to say, above, they do not practice the conduct of benevolence and righteousness, nor—below—[do they engage in worldly affairs].
He does not engage in licentious or deviant conduct, but merely remains silent while regulating his mind. This is not like the practice of those who wear patched robes in secluded places;
this is called the "first stage of intimacy. It means that one first ceases intimacy with the secular world, and thereafter becomes intimate with the Way.
Hong Juefan asked Chan Master Zhi of Jinhua: "What kind of flavor do you find in dwelling in the mountains?"
The answer was: "I dwell in the mountains. Alone, I shut the wattle gate with no other pursuit. Three pieces of firewood are roasted in the shape of the character 'pin' (品);
there is no need to wield the brush for literary brilliance to be revealed. He further said: "When all myriad functions have ceased, one entrusts oneself to simple-mindedness.

One's traces are always open to the company of wild deer. Without removing the hempen robe, one uses the fist as a pillow; for how many lifetimes has my dream remained within the green vine hermitage? This.
Regarding what is called "restraining the mind in a secluded place": previously, one dwelt on the ground of patience and the mind remained undisturbed.
This was because external objects interfered with me, yet I responded to them with a state of equanimity.

As for the statement that one should not associate with the world and so forth, this teaches people not to seek out what is disagreeable within the world; to dwell therein is like being encased in ice.
Pure and jade-like. When dealing with things, one is like a bright breeze and a clear moon. If this is so, then body and mind will naturally be at peace and happy. Question:
Since worldly and world-transcending dharmas are fundamentally not two, why must one demarcate boundaries and establish distinctions between them? Answer:

For those beginning their path, that which is familiar is too familiar, while that which is unfamiliar is too unfamiliar. Therefore, one does not draw near to worldly dharmas; only then can one [attain the world-transcending].
In harmony with the supramundane Dharma, worldly flavors become insipid, and the aspiration for the Path naturally becomes profound.
This is precisely where the mechanism of "transforming birth into maturity" and "transforming maturity into birth" resides.

If, however, one conforms to a defiled world and accords with vulgar customs—running to the gates of noble families to offer flattery, and treating wine shops and brothels as places for recreation alike—then one remains lost in the mundane.

This is the ruinous ordinary person, not a disciple of the Buddha. If one exhaustively discriminates between good and evil without integrating them through principle, such a person belongs to the Lesser Vehicle and is not a vessel for Bodhisattvas.

Therefore, when observing phenomena, things appear distinct and clear, without the slightest confusion; yet once one enters the observation of principle, all dharmas merge and harmonize, and good and evil are equal.
That which is called neither the conduct of ordinary beings nor the conduct of śrāvakas is named the conduct of bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, below this, the principle of "approaching through contemplation" is explained. Regarding the phrase "contemplating that all dharmas are empty": "contemplation" refers to observation.

"All dharmas" refers to the three categories (triskandha), the seven major elements (mahābhūta), and the various phenomena of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. By contemplating these various dharmas, one realizes that they are all [ungraspable].

It is attained; therefore, it is called "emptiness. As for the "true mark" (yathābhūtalakṣaṇa): because all phenomena are the true mark of suchness (tathatā), being devoid of dualistic characteristics.
As for "non-inversion": because all phenomena are far removed from inverted dreams and delusions.
"Immovable" means that all dharmas are fundamentally immovable from the beginning. "Non-retrogressive" means that within the realm of sentient beings, it has never regressed.
"Non-turning" means that within the realm of the sages, it has never shifted.
"Analogous to space" means it is perfectly identical to the great void, being neither deficient nor redundant. "The nature of non-existence" means it lacks self-...
The nature of self and other, the nature of the wise and the foolish, and the nature of the noble and the ordinary—these are called Buddha-nature because they are the nature of no-nature.
That all paths of language are severed means that it does not fall within the range of speech. It was not produced in the past; it does not emerge in the present.

It does not arise in the future, because it does not fall within the categories of enumeration. It is without name and without mark, because the four analytical eloquences cannot describe it and the five eyes cannot behold it.
It truly possesses nothing, because from the beginning there has never been a single thing.
It is immeasurable, because it has no form or measure. It is boundless, because it has no spatial location. It is unobstructed, because it has no walls or barriers.
"Unobstructed" means that because there is no thick undergrowth or obscuration, it is called "empty. One should formulate the syllogism as follows:
All phenomena exist; the thesis is that phenomena are empty. The reason is "because they are as they truly are," or "because they are non-erroneous.
The concordant example is like space. Space is used as the example because it is without confinement and without form or segments.
The mind-eye is non-existent. Thus one observes that all dharmas are fundamentally without a single thing;
they all arise from a single thought of non-awakening, which transforms into ignorance. Through the causal conditions of ignorance, they arise in succession and mutual dependence.
Thus, all dharmas are produced from a single thought of inverted delusive conceptualization. Since there is delusive conceptualization, speech subsequently arises.

It is said: "One should know that all phenomena are merely verbal designations and possess no real meaning at all. One should constantly and joyfully contemplate that the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are thus;
this is called 'approaching the Dharma. This refers to dwelling in the seat of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-āsana*)."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If there are bodhisattvas who, in the evil world of the future, desire to preach this sutra with a heart free from fear, they should enter the proper sphere of conduct."
Regarding those with whom one associates: one should always distance oneself from kings, princes, ministers, and high officials; from those who engage in violent games;
from *caṇḍālas* and non-Buddhist brahmins; and likewise, one should not associate with those of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) or those who are greedily attached to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

One must not associate with those who are scholars of the Tripiṭaka, precept-breaking bhikṣus, those who are merely bhikṣus in name, bhikṣuṇīs who delight in frivolous laughter, those who are deeply attached to the five desires, those who seek a nirvana in this present life, or any upāsikās of such kinds. If these are the people [with whom one associates], [one will fall into hell].

If someone comes with a sincere heart to the place where the Bodhisattva dwells in order to hear the Buddha-way, the Bodhisattva shall, with a mind free from fear and without harboring expectations, preach the Dharma for them.
However, one must not associate with widows, virgins, or those who are neuter.
One should not associate with those whom one considers close and dear, nor with butchers, executioners, hunters, or fishermen who kill for profit.
Those who sell meat for their livelihood, those who traffic in women and children—such persons as these, one must not associate with.
One must not associate with those who engage in violent wrestling matches, various forms of frivolous entertainment, or with courtesans. Do not preach the Dharma to women in a secluded place alone.
When preaching the Dharma, one must not engage in frivolous laughter. When entering a village for alms, one should be accompanied by another bhikṣu;

if there is no other bhikṣu, one should single-mindedly recollect the Buddha. These are called the "proper sphere of activity" and the "nearby sphere. By means of these two spheres, one is able to preach with ease and joy.
Furthermore, they do not practice with regard to superior, middling, or inferior dharmas; conditioned or unconditioned dharmas; real or unreal dharmas.
They also do not discriminate between male and female. Not attaining any dharmas, neither knowing nor seeing them—this is called the sphere of practice of a bodhisattva.
All dharmas are empty and non-existent; they neither abide permanently, nor do they arise or cease. This is what is called the sphere of intimacy for the wise.
To engage in inverted discrimination regarding the existence or non-existence of all dharmas, or whether they are real or unreal, or born or unborn—[is the domain of the ignorant].
Dwelling in a secluded place, he cultivates and restrains his mind, abiding immovably like Mount Sumeru.
He contemplates all phenomena as being utterly non-existent, like empty space, lacking any solidity; they neither arise nor emerge, neither move nor recede.
It is eternally abiding in a single mark; this is called the "place of proximity.

If there is a bhikṣu who, after my parinirvāṇa, enters this sphere of practice and this place of proximity when preaching this sutra, he will possess no weakness. At times, the bodhisattva enters into tranquil emptiness.

With right mindfulness, he contemplates the Dharma according to its meaning. Rising from meditative concentration, he expounds and elucidates this sutra for kings, princes, ministers, subjects, brahmins, and others, his mind remaining peaceful and free from any timidity.
Mañjuśrī, this is called the bodhisattva who dwells securely in the first dharma and is able to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in future ages.

The six lines beginning with "If there be... provide a general verse for two locations. The lines beginning with "Always remaining far from... specifically praise the location of attending upon [the teacher].
Regarding the scholars of the Tripiṭaka: when the Buddha was at Vārāṇasī, he first preached the Sūtra Piṭaka to the five [bhikṣus]. The Buddha...
In Rājagṛha, the Buddha first taught the Vinaya Piṭaka to Sunakṣatra. While the Buddha was at the Markaṭahrada Lake in Vaiśālī, he first taught the Abhidharma Piṭaka to the son of the Vṛji clan.
Therefore, the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras are collectively termed the "Piṭaka Teachings.
One who studies these three piṭakas is called a "Tripiṭaka Master. As for a bhikṣu who violates the precepts, this refers to the aforementioned [Sunakṣatra].
This refers to one who has deficiencies and leaks in their precepts. As for the "Arhat in name only," this is one who previously bore the title of "liberated" but in reality had not attained it.
One who "delights in jesting" is not a person who has abandoned all frivolity and draws near to the wise.
To "seek extinction while clinging to the five desires" is like seeking fish by climbing a tree or searching for sesame oil by washing ashes.

"Gold-like person. This refers to those who are inferior. Even if one does not intentionally seek to associate with such people, if they approach with a heart of devotion desiring to hear the Great Dharma, one should receive them with a joyful mind and preach the Dharma for their sake;
one must not reject them out of fear. Furthermore, the following verse explains the practice in accordance with the principle.
"Non-practice" means that one should not engage in mental discrimination regarding the existence of distinct dharmas, because all dharmas are in fact one and the same dharma.
"Superior, middling, and inferior dharmas" refers to the dharmas of the Three Vehicles. "Conditioned dharmas" refers to...
The phenomena of arising and ceasing are conditioned dharmas. Unconditioned dharmas are those that neither arise nor cease. Real dharmas are the dharmas of true reality.
Unreal dharmas are the dharmas of the false and illusory five aggregates. It is said that one should not merely fail to differentiate these dharmas.
Furthermore, one should not discriminate as to whether this person is male or female. This person does not attain the Dharma nor perceive the Dharma;
for through wisdom, both the foolish and the wise, the noble and the base, can all know it, all see it, and all attain it. Question:
Previously it was said that one should not associate with women; here it is said that one should not even discriminate between male and female.
Is there not a contradiction between these two statements? Answer: The former refers to their *lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics), while this refers to their *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature).

Although phenomena appear as distinct and sequential, the principle is in fact perfectly integrated (*pariniṣpanna*). Therefore, the verse below [states] that one should associate [with them] according to this principle. There is no permanence, nor is there...
Regarding arising and ceasing: to call it "permanently abiding" is the view of eternalism; to call it "arising and ceasing" is the view of nihilism.
Because it follows conditions, it is not eternal; because it does not undergo change, it is not annihilated. It is neither annihilated nor eternal.

As the fruit arises and the cause ceases—observing the Dharma in this way, one remains constantly in a single place, never for a moment departing from it. This is what the ancient masters meant by "night."
At night they embrace the Buddha as he sleeps; at dawn they arise together with him. Whether rising or sitting, they are ever in his company; whether speaking or silent, they dwell together.

For the wise person, intimacy consists simply in this. Why is this? Because all phenomena are fundamentally neither annihilated nor eternal, and possess no such characteristics as existence or non-existence;
it is only through inverted, deluded conceptualization that one discriminates and calculates them as being "existent" or "non-existent," or as being "real."
It is not real; it is both arising and non-arising. Ultimately, one does not know it as existing or non-existing, nor as real or unreal.
It is without birth and without cessation, fundamentally equal, and originally cannot be sought through discursive thought.

Therefore, in a secluded place, one should cultivate and restrain the mind, placing it in a single point so that it does not fall onto the path or into the weeds, remaining settled and unmoving. Just as...
Like Mount Sumeru, one contemplates all phenomena as being utterly non-existent, like empty space, eternally abiding in a single mark.
This is called the place where the beginner first draws near to the Buddha-dharma.

"If there are those of inferior [capacity]" and so forth means that if Bodhisattvas in the末法 (mofa) age can occupy the seat of the emptiness of phenomena, then the timid shall stand firm, the weak shall become strong, their courage shall fill them like a divine king, and they may speak freely.
Thus it is said. One will not give rise to fear or timidity. "The Bodhisattva" refers to the second section: the method for preaching the Dharma.

If one wishes to preach the Dharma, one must first enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to contemplate the dharmas and observe the capacities of sentient beings. "By means of right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*): "by means of" indicates the instrument.
As for "right mindfulness," it is called right mindfulness when not a single thought arises; one employs this right mindfulness and does not employ a second thought.

Furthermore, as for "contemplating the Dharma according to its meaning," this means following only the meaning and not clinging to words and phrases; it is what is called "relying on the meaning, not relying on the letter.
From "descending from dhyāna": having arisen from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one speaks; because the speech is necessarily true and appropriate, there is also no timidity.
From "Mañjuśrī" downward: this concludes the section clarifying the location. As for the "seat of the emptiness of dharmas": only after [occupying] this can one preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the period of the final dharma, those who wish to preach this sutra should abide in the practice of peaceful conduct.

Whether they proclaim it orally or read it from the text, they should not take pleasure in speaking of the faults of people or of other scriptures, nor should they treat other Dharma-preachers with contempt.
They should not speak of the good or evil, the long or the short, regarding others, and even toward those of the śrāvaka vehicle, they should not...
One does not mention their names to speak of their faults, nor does one mention their names to praise their virtues; furthermore, one does not give rise to thoughts of resentment or aversion.
Because one has well-cultivated such a mind of peace and happiness, those who hear [the teaching] do not oppose one’s intent.
When there are difficult questions or inquiries, one does not answer with the teachings of the Hīnayāna, but explains them solely through the Mahāyāna, so that they may attain everything.
The Knowledge of All Modes. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva always delights in preaching the Dharma with peace and security; upon a pure ground, he provides seats and couches; he anoints his body with oil."

Having bathed to cleanse away dust and impurities, and having donned fresh, clean robes so that both the interior and exterior are pure, he takes his place upon the Dharma-seat and speaks according to the questions asked.
Whether there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, or kings and princes...

The ministers, officials, and common people were addressed with a serene countenance through subtle and profound meanings. Whenever there were questions or challenges, he answered them in accordance with the principles, elaborating and analyzing them through causes, conditions, and parables.
By these skillful means, he caused them all to resolve their minds toward enlightenment, gradually increasing their merit.
They enter the path of the Buddha. They eliminate slothful intent and thoughts of indolence, and remain free from all grief and affliction.

With a mind of loving-kindness, they preach the Dharma, constantly expounding the unsurpassed teachings of the Way day and night. Through various causes and conditions and immeasurable parables, they reveal and instruct sentient beings.
They cause all to rejoice. Regarding clothing, bedding, food and drink, and medical requisites, they harbor no expectations therein;

rather, with single-minded devotion, they contemplate the causes and conditions for preaching the Dharma, vowing to attain the Buddha-way and causing all beings to do likewise—this is the great benefit.

They shall provide peaceful and joyful offerings. After my parinirvāṇa, if there be any bhikṣu who can expound this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, being free from envy and malice, from all afflictions and obstacles, as well as from sorrow, lamentation, and verbal abuse, and furthermore, being without fear—

Even when subjected to weapons, staves, and the like, they are never expelled because they abide in patience. Thus, the wise person who skillfully cultivates the mind can dwell in peace and happiness.
As I have described above, the merit of such a person cannot be calculated or illustrated by analogy for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
It cannot be fully described.
This second "Peaceful Practice" (anurakṣaṇā-pratipatti) is that one should not commit transgressions; it is the purity of verbal action.

If one proclaims this sutra or reads this sutra, one must not take pleasure in speaking of others who do not proclaim or read this sutra, nor should one praise the proclamation or reading of other sutras.
Furthermore, one does not treat other Dharma masters with contempt— such as those who rely on the Perfect and Sudden teachings to disparage gradual cultivation,

or who depend on the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) to belittle provisional explanations— and one does not speak of the likes or dislikes, the strengths or weaknesses of others— whether by clinging to the Small Vehicle to challenge the Great,
or using the Great to subvert the Small, or having Chan and Vinaya contradict one another, or various schools and sects mutually revile each other. Each...
Opening doors and windows, they each established their own schools; all were but hollow echoes of the ladle and spoon. Which was right and which was wrong?

Therefore, there is no need to pass judgment on them. One does not disparage or praise the Śrāvakas, nor does one harbor resentment toward them. For if one disparages them, it increases their arrogance and leads to a lack of faith;
if one praises them, they become complacent in their inferiority and fail to progress; and if one harbors resentment, it ultimately...
This is because they have abandoned [the Mahāyāna] out of aversion and are not yet delivered. Regarding "not opposing their intentions":
when those of the Hīnayāna pose difficult questions, one should guide them by following the clarity and transparency of their own minds, leading them into the Mahāyāna;
one must no longer lead them with the teachings of the Hīnayāna. This is what is meant by "penetrating them so that they enter into the faultless. If there is [a verse] within the gāthā:

Regarding the section on "Difficult Questions": When there are difficult questions to be posed, one should not oppose their intent, but rather guide them through skillful means so that they all resolve to attain the Mahāyāna mind.
This will cause them to progress day by day and month by month until they enter the Buddha-way.

If, however, they harbor resentment or aversion toward the Hīnayāna, they will give rise to a state of anxiety, distress, indolence, and laziness; therefore, it is appropriate to address both [attitudes] simultaneously.
Set them aside. You should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to transform small virtues into great ones and all to experience joy.
Furthermore, you must not harbor expectations for the four kinds of offerings from others; rather, with single-minded focus, you should think to yourself:
"By means of this causal condition of preaching the Dharma, may I vow to attain Buddhahood, and may those who hear my Dharma likewise attain Buddhahood."
This is what is called receiving great benefit, receiving great peace and happiness, and receiving great offerings.
Regarding "dwelling securely through patience": this refers to patience toward speech. Because one is able to exercise patience within the mind, one is able to endure speech;
because one endures speech, things such as fear do not arise. That is to say, externally there are no foul odors, and flies do not come of their own accord.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when the Dharma is about to perish during the final age at the end of time, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra must not harbor thoughts of jealousy, flattery, or deception.

Nor should they disparage or revile those who study the Buddha-way, nor seek out their faults. This applies whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās seeking the voice [of the Buddha].
Those who hear this—whether they seek the path of a pratyekabuddha or seek the bodhisattva path—must not be troubled or led to doubt and regret.
One should not say to them, "You are far removed from the Way; you will never be able to attain all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā). Why is this?
Because you are people of negligence and are indolent regarding the Way. Furthermore, one should not engage in frivolous speculation regarding these matters.
Regarding the Dharma, when there is dispute or contention, one should conceive thoughts of great compassion toward all sentient beings; conceive thoughts of a loving father toward all Tathāgatas;
conceive thoughts of a great teacher toward all Bodhisattvas; and with a profound mind, one should constantly pay respect and prostrate to the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
One should preach the Dharma equally to all sentient beings, for the sake of conforming to the Dharma. Do not...
Neither too much nor too little; even for those who deeply love the Dharma, he does not speak excessively.

Mañjuśrī, when this Dharma is being taught by a bodhisattva mahāsattva in that final age when the Dharma is about to perish, if they have accomplished this third practice of peace and happiness, no one will be able to disturb or trouble them.
They will obtain good companions in study who will together read and recite this sutra. Furthermore—

They will come to hear and receive it from the great assembly; having heard it, they will be able to uphold it; having upheld it, they will be able to recite it; having recited it, they will be able to explain it;
having explained it, they will be able to write it down, or cause others to write it, and will offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise to the sutra scrolls.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
If you wish to preach this sutra, you should abandon jealousy, anger, and pride; the mind of flattery, deception, and hypocrisy; and always cultivate straightforward conduct.
Do not look down upon others, nor engage in frivolous speculation regarding the Dharma. Do not cause others to doubt or regret by saying, "You shall not attain Buddhahood."
These children of the Buddha preach the Dharma; they are always gentle and capable of forbearance. They are compassionate toward all and do not give rise to a mind of indolence.
The great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions practice the Path out of pity for sentient beings; one should give rise to a heart of reverence toward them, for they are my great teachers.
Toward all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, one should conceive the thought of them as one’s unsurpassed father; shattering the mind of pride, one preaches the Dharma without obstruction.
This third dharma is thus: the wise should guard it, practicing with single-minded tranquility and joy, and will be revered by immeasurable multitudes.
The third is the practice of peaceful conduct (*anurakṣita-śānta-vihāra*). Not giving rise to evil thoughts is the purity of mental action (*manas-karman*).

The three characters "without" (*wu*), "not" (*wú*), and "not to" (*wù*) are all terms of prohibition. "Envy" (*īrṣyā*) consists of pursuing one's own fame and profit while being unable to endure the prosperity of others;
its nature is that of jealousy. "Deceit" (*māyā*) consists of falsely assuming a particular appearance and demeanor for the sake of deluding others; it is treacherous and crooked.
Deceit (*māyā*) has the nature of hypocrisy; for the sake of gain and sustenance, one falsely manifests the possession of virtues. Guile (*śāṭhya*) has the nature of craftiness and deception.

This is the third of the minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*). In the past, Chan Master Shangu said: "To observe whether a person will live long or die young, one must examine their mental application.
How can one whose every movement enters into deception be a person who endures for a long time? Hanshan said: "Straightforward speech has no front or back."
The mind itself is truly without sin or merit. Great Master Midao Zhen taught his disciples throughout his life that all actions must be grounded in reality.
Whenever Master Yungai Zhi gave instruction, he invariably said: "Only do not deceive the mind; the mind is itself numinous and sagely.

Therefore, those who study the Way must first begin with the absence of flattery and deception. Even a slight instance of such behavior gives rise to a state of negligence and contempt, leading to self-reproach.
"To add evil words to one's mouth" means to speak ill of others. "To seek out their long and short" means to pick at faults as if blowing on a hair.

Speaking of the lower [level], it refers to uttering words that cause distress and confusion. You say that you are unwilling to seek the Buddha within your own person, yet instead seek him at the corners of others' mouths;
is this not exceedingly remote? Even if you pass through a thousand kalpas, in the end you will still be nothing more than eating mud.
"Eating earth. This is because you all run outward in pursuit, refusing to restrain the mind to a single point;

it is because you pluck leaves and seek branches, failing to exert effort upon your own person. Although these words are direct and straightforward, they are like a square base and a round lid for those of lesser capacity;
yet when addressed to those of superior capacity, they serve as an excellent medicine. Formerly, Chan Master Huilang, at first...
He visited Shitou and asked, "What is the Buddha? Shitou said, "You have no Buddha-nature. The Master said, "How about all the wriggling and breathing creatures?
Shitou said, "They all possess Buddha-nature. The Master said, "Why then does Huirang have none? Shitou said: [The text ends here.]

Because you were unwilling to accept this, the Master attained awakening upon these words; this is what is called the "superior capacity. One should not engage in frivolous speculation regarding the dharmas or engage in contentious disputes.

It must be said that one should not cling to language or written characters, nor should one judge the various Great and Small Vehicles as being right or wrong, for all are merely the skillful means taught by the Tathāgata. As for the "notion of great compassion," it is because...

All sentient beings rely upon me; therefore, I cherish them as my own children. Regarding them with the thought of a compassionate father means that because all Buddhas can give birth to me, I honor them as my father.
Regarding them with the thought of a great teacher means that because Bodhisattvas can bring me to fulfillment, I serve them as my teacher.
Regarding the teaching of the Dharma with equanimity means that since all sentient beings are my children, I must regard them with an impartial mind.

This is the teaching of the Dharma of equality. To say that it accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) neither more nor less means that the nature of phenomena is originally without deficiency and without excess.
When preaching for others, one should likewise accord with the nature of phenomena;

one should not speak excessively because people love the Dharma, nor should one speak sparingly because people do not love it. This is because all sentient beings are endowed with the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
This is because of the characteristics of wisdom and virtue. From the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī" below, the conclusion of the practice and the attainment of benefits are established.

Regarding the phrase "obtaining good companions," it means that since one is already able to preach the Dharma with equanimity, there will naturally be those of like mind and like virtue who flock to the steps of meditation like spokes converging on a hub, rushing toward the cave of principle like the wind.
They incline their hearts and lend an ear, receiving and practicing with faith; they will furthermore respect and praise them.
At leisure, how could there be any who cause disturbance? In the verse, it first praises those who harbor no heart of jealousy, flattery, or deception.

"Arrogance" (*māna*) refers to relying on oneself in relation to others, characterized by loftiness; as the saying goes: "I shall be reborn in heaven before Lingyun, and attain Buddhahood after Lingyun.
"Devious" (*śathya*) means partiality and crookedness. "Falsity" (*māyā*) means hypocrisy. "Sincerity" (*dhṛti*) means reality.

It is also as follows: "The medicine for treating flattery and deception" refers to straightforwardness as the medicine for treating deviance and falsehood. "Not disparaging others" is the medicine for treating pride.
Furthermore, the line "nor engage in frivolous discourse regarding the Dharma" is a verse stating that one should not engage in frivolous discourse concerning any phenomena.
The two lines beginning with "If there is contention and dispute" are a verse stating, "You are very far from the Path," and so forth. The section beginning with "Compassion" is a verse.
One should give rise to thoughts of compassion toward all sentient beings, saying, "I shall have compassion for sentient beings.

One should preach the Dharma with equality to those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities, guiding, supporting, and encouraging them; whether walking, coming, going, sitting, or standing, one must never grow weary or tired.

[The section] from "In the ten directions" below is a verse on giving rise to the thought of the Great Teacher toward all bodhisattvas. [The section] from "Toward all" below is a verse on generating loving-kindness toward all Tathāgatas.
The notion of a father. As for those with a mind of arrogance, they exalt themselves while disparaging others; they are self-satisfied and treat others with contempt.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, in the future final age when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Among both householders and renunciants, they shall give rise to a heart of great compassion, even toward those who are not bodhisattvas.

Among human beings, one should give rise to a heart of great compassion and reflect thus: "Such people have suffered a great loss regarding the Tathāgata’s skillful means and his preaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate;
they have neither heard nor known it, neither awakened to it nor inquired about it, and they neither believe nor understand it.
Although these people do not inquire about, believe in, or understand this sutra, may I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, wherever they may be, by means of their power of supernatural faculties and their power of wisdom, he shall lead them so that they may abide in this Dharma.

Mañjuśrī, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, accomplish this fourth dharma, will be without fault when preaching this Dharma; they will always [be honored] by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and...
The upāsikā Sāḷha will be honored, revered, respected, and praised by kings, princes, ministers, commoners, brahmins, householders, and others.
Furthermore, the devas of the void shall attend upon her in order to hear the Dharma.
Whether she is in a village, a city, or a secluded forest, if anyone comes to challenge her with difficult questions, the devas will constantly [protect her] day and night.
For the sake of the Dharma, they shall protect it and enable all who hear it to attain joy. Why is this?
Because this sutra is protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

The fourth peaceful practice is the generation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). To generate great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) means to pity those in the three realms who mistakenly take suffering to be happiness, and thus desires to uproot their suffering.

To generate great loving-kindness also means to have pity for those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) who aspire to and delight in inferior pleasures, and thus desires to bestow upon them the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). To be a "great failure" means to fail to understand the equality of the Tathāgata.
Because of the Buddha’s wisdom, there is the Tathāgata’s precious treasury which they cannot obtain; there is vast majestic power which they cannot employ.
[The text] should read "should act below" [as a transition]. It is out of pity for those who do not understand the Tathāgata’s skillful means in preaching the Dharma.
Because they have not heard it, they do not know; because they do not know, they do not realize; because they do not realize, they do not inquire; and because they do not inquire...
They lack faith; because they lack faith, they do not understand. Such persons are inferior. One should truly give rise to a mind of compassion and say:

"Although they have no intention to seek the Dharma, wherever those sentient beings may dwell in any land, I shall, by means of the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual power and the power of profound, immeasurable wisdom, lead them so that they may abide within this Dharma. That is to say:

Great compassion is the chamber. (The section) beginning with "Mañjuśrī" concludes the practice and its resulting benefits. If one possesses the first three practices, they can cause the practitioner’s three karmas to be pure.
If one possesses the fourth practice, it can cause the practitioner to be diligent and untiring.

(The section) beginning with "Always" [means] being respected by the fourfold assembly. (The section) beginning with "Empty space" [means] being attended by the various devas through the spiritual power of all Buddhas.

Because it is protected [by the Buddha], it is called "protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha. As for that which is protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha, how could there be any among humans or devas who would not provide protection?
Mañjuśrī, in immeasurable lands, even the name of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* cannot be found.
How much more so for those who are able to see, receive, uphold, read, and recite it! Mañjuśrī, it is like this:
suppose a powerful Wheel-Turning King, wishing to subdue various kingdoms by his majestic authority, finds that the minor kings do not obey his commands.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King raises various armies to go and wage war. When the King sees his troops and observes those who have performed meritorious service in battle, he immediately feels great joy.
He was delighted and bestowed rewards according to his merit. He gave him fields and houses, villages and cities; or he gave him clothing and ornaments for the body;
or he gave him various kinds of rare treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, elephants, horses, carriages, and male and female servants.
Yet, he alone did not give him the bright pearl from within his topknot. Why was this?
"Only upon the crown of the king's head is there this single jewel. If he were to give it away, the king’s entire retinue would surely be greatly astonished and amazed.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is likewise so: by the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he has attained the kingdom of the Dharma."
The King rules over the three realms, yet the various Māra kings refuse to submit in obedience. The Tathāgata’s noble and holy generals engage them in battle;

those who achieve merit therein also rejoice in their hearts. Among the fourfold assembly, he preaches various sūtras for them, causing their minds to find delight, and bestows upon them the wealth of the dharmas of dhyāna, samādhi, liberation, the untainted faculties (indriya), powers (bala), and other such qualities. Furthermore, he grants them—
He speaks of the city of Nirvana and attaining extinction, guiding their minds and causing them all to rejoice, yet he does not preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them.
Mañjuśrī, it is like a wheel-turning king who, seeing among his troops those who have performed great deeds, [bestows rewards].

His heart was filled with great joy. This jewel, so difficult to believe in, had long remained within his topknot; he did not give it to others recklessly, yet now he gives it. The Tathāgata is likewise thus:
within the triple world, he is the Great Dharma King, teaching and transforming all sentient beings through the Dharma.
He beholds the army of the worthy and holy ones as they battle against the Māra of the five aggregates, the Māra of afflictions, and the Māra of death. Therein...
Having achieved great merit and virtue, extinguished the three poisons, transcended the triple world, and shattered the net of Māra—at that time, the Tathāgata also felt great joy.
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* can cause sentient beings to reach all-knowledge; yet throughout all worlds, it is met with much enmity and is difficult to believe.
That which was not previously spoken, I shall now speak. Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the foremost teaching of all Tathāgatas;

among all teachings, it is the most profound. It is bestowed at the very end, just as a powerful king, having long guarded a bright jewel, finally grants it. Mañjuśrī, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is [the teaching] of all Buddhas.
This treasury of the Tathāgata’s secrets is the most supreme among all sutras;
I have guarded it through the long night and have not proclaimed it recklessly. Only today do I expound it for you all.
The name [of this scripture] cannot be heard; this clearly demonstrates that all Buddhas protect this sutra and do not proclaim it recklessly.
The Wheel-Turning King is a metaphor for the Tathāgata. The minor kings of various small states who do not obey his commands are a metaphor for the various Māras who cause disturbance.

Their raising of various armies is a metaphor for those of the Three Vehicles. The soldiers achieving merit in battle is a metaphor for those of the Three Vehicles severing the afflictions of views and thought.
Each emerged from the triple world. As for the distribution of rewards according to merit: those of minor merit were granted fields, houses, and villages;
those of intermediate merit were granted articles for adorning the body; and those of great merit were granted the seven treasures, elephants, horses, and subjects.
The three vehicles of the Dharma are likened to [the other jewels]. The bright pearl within the topknot is likened to the supreme Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Following the passage concerning the King alone, it says that this bright pearl exists only upon the crown of a Wheel-Turning King; it is because of this pearl that he is a Wheel-Turning King.

If one were now to give this pearl to an ordinary person, that person would surely be struck with wonder. The following section on the Tathāgata applies the analogy to the Dharma: having attained the Dharma...
The land takes the Dharma-realm as its territory, corresponding to the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin). When the Demon King is disobedient, it corresponds to various kingdoms being rebellious.
The Tathāgata’s noble and holy generals assemble various troops and preach the various sūtras, which are precisely the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
This corresponds to rewarding according to merit; they bestow the great Dharma-treasures of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), corresponding to various kinds of rare jewels, and bestow *nirvāṇa*.
The city of Bandhumatī, together with its fields, houses, villages, and towns, corresponds to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*’s parable of the topknot jewel.
In the passage where Mañjuśrī descends, it is said that the topknot jewel is bestowed only upon those who have achieved great merit. This is analogous to the following:

when Bodhisattvas, as generals of the Dharma, wage war against the Māra of the five aggregates, and when those of the Two Vehicles, as generals of the Dharma, wage war against the Māras of afflictions and death, they all achieve great merit; therefore [the jewel is bestowed].
The Tathāgata joyfully preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Master Zhilin of Hunan, however, would regularly revile Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra as mere malevolent spirits.
Holding a wooden sword in his hand, he claimed to be subduing demons; as soon as he saw a monk coming to pay his respects, he would say, "A demon has come!
and, brandishing his sword wildly, retreat to his quarters. In this manner, for twelve years, he kept his sword set aside.
A monk asked, "Why did you subdue the demons twelve years ago? The Master said, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor.
The monk asked, "Why did you not subdue the demons after twelve years? The Master said, "Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor.
If Master Zhishen were one who had achieved great merit in subduing demons, it would be like being granted a reward at the very end. This is Zen.
The fundamental principle is called the "final word"; therefore, it is bestowed at the very end. As in the passage beginning with "Just as that below," the analogy is applied to the Dharma;
in the passage beginning with "Mañjuśrī below," the Dharma is applied to the analogy.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Always practicing patience and compassion for all beings, one is then able to expound the sutras praised by the Buddha. In the future, at the end of the age..."
Those who uphold this sutra—whether they be householders or renunciants, and whether they be bodhisattvas or not—should generate compassion for them.

If such people do not hear or do not believe in this sutra, it will be a great loss for them. Once I have attained the path of Buddhahood, I shall use various skillful means to preach this Dharma for their sake.
He causes them to dwell therein. It is like a powerful Wheel-Turning King who, when his soldiers have performed meritorious service in battle, bestows various rewards:
elephants, horses, and chariots; ornaments for the body; as well as fields, houses, villages, towns, and cities; or he grants them clothing.
Various kinds of rare treasures, male and female servants, and wealth and goods were bestowed with joy.

Just as when one is brave and capable of performing difficult tasks, the king unties the bright pearl from within his topknot and grants it to them; so too is the Tathāgata, who, as the King of all Dharmas, possesses the great power of patience.
Possessing a treasury of wisdom and great compassion, he transforms the world in accordance with the Dharma.

Seeing all people undergoing various sufferings and afflictions, desiring liberation, and battling against the various māras, he preaches diverse teachings for the sake of these sentient beings through great skillful means.

Having preached these various sutras and knowing that sentient beings had already gained their strength, he finally preached this Lotus Sutra for them, like a king untying his topknot to give away the bright pearl. This sutra is the most honored, the supreme among all sutras; I have always guarded it.

I have not taught this in vain. Now is the very time; I shall speak it for you. After my parinirvāṇa, those who seek the Buddha-way and desire to attain peace and security should, when expounding this sutra, draw near to these four dharmas. Those who read this sutra [should likewise do so].

They shall always be free from sorrow and affliction, and likewise free from illness and pain. Their complexions shall be bright and pure white; they shall not be born into poverty, nor into lowly, base, or ugly circumstances.
Sentient beings will delight in seeing them, as if yearning for sages and saints. Divine youths shall serve as their attendants, and weapons or staves shall never be used against them.
Poisons cannot harm them. If someone reviles them with evil words, their mouth shall be sealed shut. They wander about without fear, like a lion king;
the radiance of their wisdom shines like the sun. Even in their dreams, they see only auspicious things and behold all the Tathāgatas.
He saw himself seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by a multitude of bhikṣus, preaching the Dharma.
