He also saw nāgas, devas, asuras, and others, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with palms joined in reverence; he saw himself preaching the Dharma to them. Furthermore, he saw various buddhas.
His physical form was golden in color, emitting immeasurable light that illuminated all things. With a Brahma-like voice, he expounded all dharmas.

As the Buddha preached the unsurpassed Dharma for the fourfold assembly, [the bodhisattva] saw his own body situated therein; with palms joined, he praised the Buddha and rejoiced upon hearing the Dharma.

He made offerings and attained dhāraṇī, realizing the wisdom of non-retrogression. The Buddha, knowing his mind and that he had deeply entered the path of the Buddhas, immediately bestowed upon him a prediction:
"You shall become a Most Perfectly Awakened One. O son of good family, in a future age, you shall attain immeasurable wisdom."
The Great Way of the Buddha’s land is majestic and pure, vast beyond compare. There are also the fourfold assembly, with palms joined, listening to the Dharma.
Furthermore, one sees oneself in mountain forests, practicing wholesome dharmas, realizing all true marks, and entering deeply into meditative concentration.
One sees the Buddhas of the ten directions; their bodies are golden in color, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits. Hearing the Dharma, they explain it for others;

such are the auspicious dreams one constantly has. Furthermore, one dreams of being a king who abandons his palace, retinue, and the five exquisite sensual pleasures to proceed to the site of enlightenment.
Seated beneath the Bodhi tree upon a lion throne, he seeks the Way for seven days and attains it.
The wisdom of all Buddhas, having accomplished the Unsurpassed Way, arises to turn the wheel of Dharma and preach the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
For thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, they preach the subtle Dharma free from outflows, delivering immeasurable sentient beings.

Thereafter, they shall enter nirvana, like a lamp extinguished when the oil is spent. If, in future evil ages, one should preach this foremost Dharma, that person will obtain great benefit, as [if they had served]...

The supreme merit [of the Buddha] consists of patience and compassion. The first four verses of the hymn describe the two modes of peaceful conduct (*anulomika-pratipatti*). As for the analogy below, it is like a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) bestowing rewards according to merit.

For instance, as in the case of one who is brave and strong, he is granted the crest-jewel. Likewise, the Tathāgata below obstructs the faculties [of those not yet ready] while preaching the Dharma; this corresponds to bestowing rewards according to merit.
Bestowal. Having already understood the preceding section, he now preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. "Should bestow the crest-jewel" (as in the passage beginning with "As the king...

uses the parable to correspond to the Dharma; "This sutra... (as in the passage beginning with "This sutra... uses the Dharma to correspond to the parable. "When I have passed away... (as in the passage beginning with "When I have passed away... concludes by exhorting the four practices. "Those who read this...

(as in the passage beginning with "Those who read this... reveals the karmic fruit of reading the sutra. "Always free from sorrow and affliction" means that in the present life, weapons and staves will not be used against them, and verbal abuse will not reach them.
Therefore, their body and mind are peaceful and happy, free from sorrow and affliction. Furthermore, they are without illness or pain because they heal the maladies of many.
Their complexions are bright and pure because they harbor the roots of virtue within. They do not fall into poverty because they are fully endowed with the wealth of the Dharma.
Because they provide for all, they are not lowly; because they are born into the family of the Tathāgata and are honored everywhere, they are not ugly;
because they are fully endowed with compassion and adorned with the primary and secondary marks, sentient beings delight in seeing them as if yearning for sages and saints;
because they perform the deeds of the Tathāgata, the youths of the devas serve as their attendants, and the devas guard them.
Because they are protected, blades and staves cannot be applied, and poison cannot cause harm; for the rhinoceros has nowhere to thrust its horn, and weapons have no place to set their edges.
If someone reviles them with evil words, their mouth is shut; there is no place for such words to lodge, as they instead return to the person who uttered them.
They wander without fear like lion kings because they are fully endowed with majestic virtue (*tejas*). Wisdom...
"The radiance of wisdom is like the sun's illumination" means that the four wisdoms are perfectly luminous.
Regarding the phrases "attaining peace by day" and "attaining peace at night": the former refers to daytime, while the latter refers to nighttime.

"Seeing only wondrous things in dreams" means that one’s spirit and essence resonate with and receive the transmission of the Tathāgata’s vital energy; thus, all that is seen within the dream consists solely of wondrous events.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "He saw": first he saw the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, surrounded by a great assembly; next, he saw himself preaching the Dharma to the assembly.
This is like Yangshan’s dream of entering Maitreya’s Inner Courtyard, where all the seats in the hall were occupied except for the second one.
The Master took his seat, and a venerable elder struck the gavel, saying: "The second seat is now duly filled."
He preached the Dharma. The Master rose and struck the gavel, saying: "The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
Listen closely, listen closely! The assembly all dispersed. Upon waking, he recounted this to Guishan, who said: "You have already entered the rank of the sages."
Furthermore, see "the lower. This refers to seeing the Buddha preaching the Dharma in a dream; the Buddha acts for the sake of the lower.

Furthermore, see oneself praising the Buddha, making offerings to the Buddha, realizing wisdom, and receiving a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). This is the language of the prediction received within the dream; it says, "You are good at the lower. Furthermore, see "the lower.

This refers to entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in a dream, seeing various Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and explaining a single phrase to others. This highlights what was seen within the dream.
These wondrous matters all arise from preaching the sutras for others. Whether eyes are open or closed, whether in sleep or in dreams, there is nothing that is not the realm of the Buddha.
Furthermore, as for "dreaming of descending": one abandons the position of a king to become a Dharma King; one leaves the pleasure grounds to enter the site of enlightenment;
one relinquishes the imperial throne to occupy the seat of the Buddha; and one casts off the golden wheel to turn the Wheel of Dharma. If...
The subsequent section concludes with a summary of the excellence: "If one preaches this sutra while possessing these four practices, one will consequently possess all the merits mentioned above;
what cause for alarm or fear could there be?
This concludes the fifteenth chapter, "The Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth."
The verse says:
In cold ravines, with backs turned to the sun, spring comes late; Ten thousand upon ten thousand branches of plum flowers frozen by snow.
Once touched by the eastern wind, they all burst forth in white; There is no one who does not give rise to thoughts of their old garden.
Emerging from the earth from beneath the jeweled stupa, the Tathāgatas gathered like clouds, their emanations pervading the worlds of the ten directions.
Having already witnessed the profound depth of what the Tathāgata has realized, they summoned the bodhisattvas and exhorted them to make vows to uphold this sutra.
Among them, some made vows to uphold the sutra in this very land; some made vows to uphold it in other lands; and some made vows to—
Among those in the lands of the ten directions who uphold this sutra, there are still sixty thousand bodhisattvas within this assembly who do not make vows to uphold it;
these are all those who fear difficulty and settle for complacency, which does not accord with the Tathāgata’s original intent.
Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims the four practices of peaceful bliss and transmits the methods for upholding the sutra. Thus, beyond the eight directions of this Sahā world...
There were bodhisattvas from other lands, numbering as many as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers, who made vows to uphold this sutra; however, the Tathāgata did not grant his permission.
The Tathāgata then summoned sixty thousand Ganges Rivers’ worth of great bodhisattvas from the lower regions, who surged forth from the earth.
They made vows to uphold the sutra, seeing the vastness of the Tathāgata’s deliverance. It was for this single great matter that the Tathāgata acted.
The appearance [of the Buddha] in the world through causes and conditions is now clearly elucidated. Previously, that which the Tathāgata realized was shown;
hence the jeweled stupa emerged from the earth. Now, that which the Tathāgata delivers is shown; hence the bodhisattvas also emerge from the earth.
This correctly reveals that such causes and such conditions are all inseparable from their original ground.
At that time, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from other lands, numbering more than the sands of eight Ganges Rivers, rose from within the great assembly,
joined their palms in prostration, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if you would permit us, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha,
to remain diligently and with fervent application in this Sahā world to protect, uphold, recite, copy, and make offerings [to the teachings]."
"This sutra shall be widely expounded in this land. At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:
"Cease, sons of good family! There is no need for you to protect and uphold this sutra. Why is this?
In my Sahā world, there are already bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers; each and every one of these bodhisattvas..."
Each had a retinue as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers. These individuals will, after my parinirvāṇa, be able to protect, uphold, recite, and extensively expound this sutra.
When the Buddha spoke these words, throughout the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system of the Sahā universe, [all beings were moved].
The earth quaked and split asunder, and from within it, immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas simultaneously surged forth.
These Bodhisattvas were all golden in color, possessed the thirty-two marks, and emitted immeasurable radiance.
Previously, they had all been dwelling beneath this Sahā world, suspended in the void of space within this realm. When these Bodhisattvas heard...

The sounds spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha issued forth from below. Each and every bodhisattva was a leader who exhorted the great assembly, each bringing with them a retinue of sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [Ganges-sand] beings;

how much more so those who brought retinues of fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or ten thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* beings? How much more so, even down to a single *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*?
A single grain of sand. Half of the sands of the Ganges. One-quarter. Even down to a ten-millionth part of a hundred-thousand-billion-nayuta.
How much less, then, a retinue of a hundred-thousand-billion-nayuta? How much less, a retinue of a hundred-million?
How much less, a retinue of ten-million, a million, or even ten-thousand? How much less, a thousand, a hundred, or even ten? How much less, five?
Those who have four, three, two, or one disciple—how much more so those who dwell alone—and those who delight in the practice of seclusion;
such as these are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.

When these bodhisattvas had emerged from the earth, each proceeded through the air to the seven-jeweled, wondrous stupa where the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni Buddha were located. Having arrived, they turned toward [the Buddhas].
The two World-Honored Ones were bowed to with their heads at their feet. Then, proceeding to the various jeweled trees, they likewise paid homage before the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones.
Circumambulating them three times to the right, they joined their palms in reverent respect and praised them with the various modes of praise used by bodhisattvas.
Standing to one side, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gazed up at the two World-Honored Ones with joyful devotion. These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, from the moment he first emerged, he praised the Buddha with various kinds of bodhisattva praises.
During this time, fifty intermediate kalpas passed. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha sat in silence, and the fourfold assembly likewise remained silent for those fifty intermediate kalpas.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he caused the great multitude to perceive it as if...

Half a day passed. At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the fourfold assembly also saw all the bodhisattvas filling the voids of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands. Within this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four leaders:

the first was named Superior Conduct (Urdhvaga), the second Boundless Conduct (Anantagati), the third Pure Conduct (Śuddhacaryā), and the fourth Established Conduct (Pratiṣṭhitagati). These four bodhisattvas, at...
Among that assembly, the foremost leader and guiding teacher stood before the great multitude;
with palms joined together, he gazed upon Śākyamuni Buddha and inquired after his well-being, saying: "World-Honored One, are you free from illness and affliction?
Are you dwelling in peace and happiness? Are those who are to be delivered easy to instruct? Do they not cause the World-Honored One any fatigue? At that time, the four great bodhisattvas...
He spoke these verses: "Is the World-Honored One at ease? Are you free from illness and affliction? In teaching and transforming sentient beings, do you experience no weariness?
Furthermore, are the sentient beings easy to transform? Do they not cause the World-Honored One to become fatigued?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas: "So it is, so it is, noble sons.
The Tathāgata is at ease, with little illness and little affliction. These sentient beings are easy to transform and deliver, and I am without weariness.
Why is this? Because throughout successive lifetimes, these sentient beings have constantly received my transformation, and likewise..."
These sentient beings have, in the past, honored and respected the Buddhas of the past and planted various roots of goodness;

thus, upon first seeing my body and hearing what I say, they all immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata—except for those who previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna.
For such persons as these, I shall now also cause them to hear this sutra and enter into the Buddha’s wisdom.
At that time, the great bodhisattvas spoke in verse: "Excellent, excellent! Great Hero, World-Honored One! All sentient beings..."
Those who are easily transformed and able to inquire of the Buddhas regarding profound wisdom, having heard it, shall believe and practice;
we rejoice in this.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the leading great Bodhisattvas, saying: "Excellent, excellent! O sons of good family, you..."
They were able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata.
Bodhisattvas from other directions made vows to uphold this sutra here. "Other lands" refers to those outside the Sahā world-system;
their number is as great as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers. From the words "At that time" onwards, the Tathāgata did not...
"Permits" means that it is intended to reveal the Tathāgata’s original and manifested traces. "The Buddha spoke" refers to the Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth.

"Shaking" means to cause to tremble; "tearing" means to split open. When the World-Honored One had just spoken these words, the Bodhisattvas from the lower direction immediately emerged from the earth;
this is the dynamic of the "beak and the egg" (the simultaneous response). "First exhausted" and so forth clarifies their dwelling place. "These various" and so forth reveals their [names].

Regarding the intention for their coming: they have either heard the voice proclaiming who is able to extensively expound this sutra in this Sahā world, or they have heard the words that within the Sahā world itself there are as many beings as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers;
therefore, they surge forth from below. Although they appear to be from above or below, they seem as if they were face-to-face.
[Each] face. [The phrase] "one by one" clarifies their retinues. Regarding the term "chanting leaders" (*changdao*): it means that this one chants while that one harmonizes;

this one leads while that one follows. [The phrase] "each leading" and so forth indicates that each chanting leader Bodhisattva likewise has sixty thousand *Ganges-sand* Bodhisattvas as their retinue.
How much more so for the retinues led by those [other] Bodhisattvas! Their...
The numbers range from fifty thousand, forty thousand, down to ten thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges], gradually decreasing until there are those who are solitary and without retinue;
their number is likewise immeasurable and boundless. The passage beginning with "These various... describes the ritual for meeting them at one time:
first one pays homage to the whole body, then one pays homage to the emanated bodies (*vibhakta-kāya*). This is the ritual of prostration. The passage beginning with "These various... [continues].
Regarding the ritual for praising the Buddha: A question arises concerning Śākyamuni in the Sahā world. From his beginning until his end, he lived for only some seventy-odd years;

yet at the single assembly on Vulture Peak, the bodhisattvas praised the Buddha for fifty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), and the Tathāgata remained silent for another fifty intermediate kalpas, causing the great multitude to perceive it as being like an ordinary day. Is this not excessive?

Is this absurd? Answer: This is the inconceivable realm of the Buddha. A single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) is immeasurable eons (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*), and immeasurable eons are a single thought-moment.
This is what is called mastery over extension and contraction; thought-moments and eons are perfectly interfused, such that their length or brevity cannot be measured by the mind.
As the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "Immeasurable past eons are placed within the future and the present."
"Immeasurable kalpas of the future are placed within the past. Furthermore, it is said that what is experienced as lasting years while dreaming is but a mere moment upon awakening;
thus, although time is immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa.
Regarding the passage "At that time," when the fourfold assembly saw the bodhisattvas filling the void, they first beheld the emanation-buddhas filling the land.
The earth. Now we see Bodhisattvas again pervading the void, principal and retinue in perfect harmony. What kind of phenomenon is this?
Furthermore, these Buddhas of divided bodies are those realized by Śākyamuni, while these Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth are likewise those transformed by Śākyamuni.
The causes and conditions of their origin and conclusion are infinite and boundless. As it is with one Buddha, so it is with all Buddhas. All...

As it is with the Buddha, so it is with all sentient beings. Because sentient beings possess such great matters and conditions, yet remain unaware and without vision, it is for this reason that the Tathāgata appears in the world. Below this passage concerning the Bodhisattva, the Guide inquires after their well-being;
these four Guides are all called "Practitioners" (yōgyō), as they have all attained the four practices of peaceful bliss (shianraku-gyō) and thus abide in the patience of the Dharma (hōnin).
Abiding on the stage of non-retrogression is called "Superior Conduct. Not opposing sentient beings and having many who are transformed by one’s teaching is called "Boundless Conduct.
Preaching the Dharma with equanimity and having a mind free from love or hatred is called "Pure Conduct.
Establishing all beings through a heart of compassion is called "Establishing Conduct. Possessing these four conducts, he further acted as a guide for sixty thousand Ganges-sands of worlds.
He is the foremost among them; thus he is called the preeminent teacher who leads and guides. The following inquiry consists of words of greeting.
While the World-Honored One dwells in the Sahā world, saving beings and sharing the same activities as the multitude, if the beings are ill, the Tathāgata is also ill;
if the beings are afflicted, the Tathāgata is also afflicted. Therefore, he inquires whether the Tathāgata’s manifestation within the three realms is slight.
"Are you free from illness and affliction, and are you dwelling in peace and happiness? Are the sentient beings you seek to deliver easy to transform?

Do you not weary the World-Honored One with your work as a bridge and ferry? These Bodhisattvas, being about to make vows and uphold this sutra, first secretly probed the Tathāgata’s tone of voice to test whether the task of delivering sentient beings would be difficult or easy. From "At that time" below, the Tathāgata provides his reply. Thus it is said.
"This" refers to what you have asked; it accords with my own mind. "The Tathāgata" and below is the answer that sentient beings are easy to deliver.

"Therefore" and below explains the meaning of being easy to deliver. It says that those of sharp faculties, when they were śrāmaṇeras in the past, have already received my instruction and transformation.
Now, upon seeing my body once and hearing my Dharma once, they immediately enter the Buddha-wisdom. If...
In past lives, those who did not believe in the Buddha’s wisdom and studied the Hīnayāna were gradually guided and transformed over the course of forty years;
now, having heard the wondrous Dharma, they have likewise entered the Buddha-wisdom.

This is because the Tathāgata secretly knew that these bodhisattvas had made vows to uphold this sutra, and thus he secretly bestowed upon them the method for saving sentient beings. From "At that time" onwards, a verse is spoken in praise of the Buddha, saying:
The Tathāgata saves sentient beings in this manner; he is truly a great hero of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
The sentient beings of this world are fierce, stubborn, and rigid; they are difficult to discipline, difficult to subdue, difficult to transform, and difficult to deliver.

Today, the World-Honored One has been able to transform those who are difficult to transform and deliver those who are difficult to deliver—is he not indeed the Great Hero? The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable.
There are none who dare to ask questions; yet were there those who asked, people would not wish to hear them. Were there those who heard, they would be unable to believe them.

Were there those who believed, they would again be unable to practice them. That now there are those who are willing to ask, willing to hear, and willing to believe—and having believed, willing to practice—is truly rare. Not only do all the Buddhas give rise to hearts of joy, but even...
We who delight in tranquility and do not delight in being amidst the multitude also give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).

This shows that upon seeing the Bodhisattva, they have conceived the aspiration to uphold this sutra and thus experience great joy. From the phrase "At that time" onwards, the text praises those who give sympathetic joy;
it is for the purpose of perfecting their intention to conceive the aspiration to uphold this sutra.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers, all had this thought:

"Since the distant past, we have neither seen nor heard of such a multitude of great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas emerging from the earth, standing before the World-Honored One, joining their palms in worship, and inquiring after the Tathāgata’s well-being. Then, Maitreya Bodhisattva...
The Mahāsattva, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers,
and desiring to resolve his own doubts, joined his palms toward the Buddha and questioned him in verse:
Immeasurable thousands of millions of billions—this great assembly of bodhisattvas has never been seen before. We pray that the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings will explain:
from where have they come, and by what causes and conditions have they gathered? They possess massive bodies and great supernormal powers; their wisdom is inconceivable.
Their resolve is firm and steadfast, and they possess the power of great patience; they are a joy for all sentient beings to behold. From where have they come?
Each of these bodhisattvas brings with them a retinue of immeasurable number, as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
There may be great bodhisattvas who, together with a great assembly as numerous as sixty thousand Ganges sands, single-mindedly seek the path of the Buddha.
These great masters, numbering sixty thousand Ganges sands, will all come together to make offerings to the Buddha and to protect and uphold this sutra.
Fifty thousand Ganges-sands, with numbers exceeding even that; forty thousand and thirty thousand; twenty thousand down to ten thousand;
one thousand, one hundred, and so forth, even down to a single Ganges-sand; half, or a third or fourth part; or even a ten-millionth part of one.
Ten million nayutas, ten trillion disciples, down to fifty million, with numbers exceeding even that;
from one million down to ten thousand, one thousand, and one hundred; fifty, ten, and down to three, two, and one.
Those who were alone without retinues and who delighted in dwelling in solitude all came to where the Buddha was; their number exceeded even that mentioned above.
If one were to count these great assemblies by casting tally-sticks, one could not know them all completely even in more than *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
These hosts of bodhisattvas of great majesty and vigor—who taught them the Dharma? By whom were they taught and brought to maturity?
From whom did they first resolve their minds [on awakening]? Which Buddha-dharma did they extol? Whose sutras did they receive, uphold, and practice? And which path of the Buddhas did they cultivate?
Such are these bodhisattvas, with their supernormal powers and great wisdom-force; the earth in the four directions has split asunder, and from within it they have all surged forth.
World-Honored One, since my past, I have never before seen such a thing. I pray you tell us from where they come and the names of their lands.
I have constantly traveled through various lands, yet I have never before seen such an assembly. Among this multitude, I do not recognize even a single person.
How is it that they have suddenly emerged from the earth? I pray you, explain the causes and conditions for this great gathering of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions.
All these bodhisattvas wish to know this matter—the causes and conditions regarding the origins and endings of these assemblies of bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One of immeasurable virtue, we pray that you will resolve the doubts of the multitude.
This is Maitreya expressing his doubt. If one wishes to know where [the Buddha] has come from, even the Bodhisattva who has just emerged cannot know from where he himself has come;
how then could Maitreya know? Furthermore, how could the bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of eight thousand Ganges Rivers know?
It is therefore appropriate that there be a question seeking a definitive resolution. In the verse, it says: "Never before seen."
The phrase "I have always been at the Buddha’s side and have never seen such [beings]" clearly reveals the Tathāgata’s secret power of supernatural penetration (*ṛddhi*).
"From where have they come? asks the place from which they have arrived. "By what causes and conditions have they gathered? asks the reason for their arrival.
The section beginning with "These beings of massive bodies" praises their virtues. The section beginning with "Each one by one" praises their retinues.
Among these many, those below asked about the masters from whom they derived their teachings: "Whose song does the master sing?
Whose ancestral style does he succeed? To "proclaim" refers to what issues from the mouth; to "uphold" refers to what resides within the mind.
"Practitioner" refers to the manifestation of the matter. "World-Honored One," and so forth, is a repeated inquiry as to the place from which [the practitioner] has come.

"I have always," and so forth, is a repeated inquiry as to the reason for coming. "Now this," and so forth, is the formal request to resolve doubts regarding the causal conditions of the beginning and the end.
"Please resolve for us this entire sequence of causes and conditions from beginning to end.

At that time, the various emanations of Śākyamuni Buddha who had come from immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands in other directions were seated cross-legged upon lion thrones beneath the various jeweled trees in the eight directions. Those Buddhas—
The attendants each saw this great assembly of bodhisattvas emerging from the earth in the four directions of the trichiliocosm and remaining in the air.

Each addressed their respective Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, from where have these immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) assemblies of bodhisattvas come? At that time, the Buddhas each told their attendants: "All..."
"Good son, wait but a moment. There is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Maitreya, who has been prophesied by Śākyamuni Buddha to become a buddha immediately after him.
He has already asked about this matter, and the Buddha is now answering it;
you shall hear it for yourselves through him. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the bodhisattva Maitreya: "Excellent!"
Excellent, Ajita! That you are able to ask the Buddha about such a great matter as this. You all should now be of one mind, don the armor of diligence, and resolve with firm intent.

The Tathāgata now wishes to reveal and proclaim the wisdom of all Buddhas, the sovereign power of the supernatural faculties of all Buddhas, the lion-like prowess of all Buddhas, and the majestic might of all Buddhas.
The power of momentum. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"One should practice with diligence and single-mindedness; I wish to explain this matter. Do not harbor any doubt or regret, for the Buddha's wisdom is inconceivable."
Now you must exert the power of faith and abide in the goodness of patience. The Dharma never heard before shall now all be heard by you.
I now comfort you: do not harbor doubt or fear. The Buddha’s words are never untrue; his wisdom is immeasurable.
The supreme Dharma that has been attained is profound and difficult to discern; this I shall now explain, so listen with a single mind.
Regarding the phrase "the attendants of the emanated bodies": those who harbor doubts are the great Bodhisattvas each led by the Buddhas of the eight directions who have manifested their bodies.

From the words "At that time" onwards, after the emanated bodies have offered consolation and encouragement, the phrase "asked about these matters" refers to the fact that Maitreya had already inquired.
The causal conditions regarding the beginning and end of this matter, the Buddha is now about to answer. You shall hear them through the Tathāgata’s response to Maitreya’s questions.

From the passage "At that time" onwards, he exhorts those who have faith to don the armor of diligence and encourages them to exert themselves in delivering sentient beings, lest they become indolent.
He urges them to resolve with firm intent and encourages them to strive in seeking the Dharma, lest they fall back or regress.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable; people are unable to know it.

Now, wishing to manifest the Tathāgata’s profound wisdom by means of these Bodhisattvas who have emerged from the earth, the Tathāgata dwells on Vulture Peak Mountain, extensively performing Buddha-works that are fully known to people.
Yet, the Tathāgata’s immobility within the site of enlightenment pervades all places—a fact unknown to people.
The bodhisattvas who have now emerged from the earth are all transformations of the Buddha; thus one knows the sovereign spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
For forty years, the Tathāgata has preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, which all people fully know.
The Tathāgata uses the rain of the single-flavored Dharma to moisten all equally and universally; as he does for one person, so it is for many. It is just like a lion leaping forth.
[The Buddha’s] rapid movements all employ his full power, yet people cannot perceive it.

Now, that the Bodhisattvas who have emerged from the earth and their retinues are all transformations produced by the Tathāgata’s full power allows one to know the Tathāgata’s force of vigorous exertion (*vikrīḍita*).

That the Tathāgata wears tattered, soiled garments, holds a refuse-removing vessel, and appears without majesty or authority in order to transform impoverished sons is something known to all people. Just as...
When they come wearing precious and majestic robes to transform the various bodhisattvas, people do not know [their true nature].
Now, when one emerges from the earth, one knows the power of the Tathāgata’s fierce and great majesty. This is like seeing the intensity of the rain and knowing that the dragon is great.
One knows the depth of a pond by seeing its abundant flowers. Regarding the verse that speaks of "emerging with the power of faith and abiding in the goodness of patience," it means:
"I now wish to speak of this matter; all of these are the secret, skillful, and expedient deeds of the Buddhas for delivering sentient beings through their preaching of the Dharma.
You should all emerge with the power of faith and endure this within your hearts; do not forget it."
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "I now announce to you all within this great assembly, Ajita:
these great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable, who have surged forth from the earth—whom you have never seen before—I have attained [this] in this Sahā world."
Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he teaches, instructs, and guides these bodhisattvas, subduing their minds and causing them to resolve upon the path.
These bodhisattvas all dwell beneath this Sahā world, suspended in the space of this realm;
they read, recite, and master the various sūtras, contemplating, analyzing, and correctly recollecting them.
Ajita, these sons of good family do not delight in being among the crowds nor in speaking much;
they always delight in solitary places, practicing with diligence and vigor without ever resting.

They do not rely upon or dwell among humans or devas, but always delight in profound wisdom that is free from obstruction, and they also always delight in the Dharma of all Buddhas, seeking the Unsurpassed with single-minded diligence.
“Wisdom. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
‘Ajita, you should know that these great bodhisattvas have, since incalculable kalpas past, cultivated the wisdom of the Buddha.’”
All these have been transformed by me, causing them to resolve upon the Great Vehicle. They are my children, dwelling in this world;
they constantly practice the dhūta austerities and take delight in secluded places. Having abandoned the clamor and bustle of the great assembly, they do not delight in much speaking.
In this way, these sons of mine study my Way and Dharma, always diligent day and night for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way.
They dwell in the space below the Sahā world, their resolve and power firm and steadfast, constantly and diligently seeking wisdom.

He preached various sublime Dharmas with a mind free from fear. In the city of Gayā, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, I attained supreme perfect enlightenment and turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma;
only then did I transform and guide them, causing them to first resolve their minds upon the Way.
Now they all abide in non-retrogression; they shall all attain Buddhahood. I now speak these true words: you should believe them with one mind.
From long ago, I have been teaching and transforming this assembly.
The phrase "These [beings] below" answers the first question. Since the preceding question asked, "By whom were they taught? From whom did they resolve their minds?

Regarding these immeasurable bodhisattvas, how could they have been taught and inspired to resolve their minds for enlightenment, thereby abiding on the stage of non-retrogression, in such a short time?
Those who give rise to doubt in their hearts are adding suspicion upon suspicion.

The purpose for the introduction of this chapter is twofold. Thus, in the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya*) and "Parables" (*Dṛṣṭānta*) chapters, the immeasurable skillful means of the Tathāgata were revealed; and in the "Herbs" (*Oṣadhi*) chapter, the immeasurable rain of the Tathāgata’s Dharma was seen.

In the "Chapter on the Earth-Sprung," one sees that the bodhisattvas transformed by the Tathāgata are immeasurable. Nevertheless, all of these are merely gateways for the Tathāgata’s responsive manifestations.
However, this has not yet fully revealed that the life-force of wisdom of the Dharma-body is equal and immeasurable.

Therefore, this chapter specifically speaks of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable lifespan in order to reveal that the essence of the Tathāgata existed prior to the kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, having already completed his attainment of enlightenment long ago;
it could not possibly be attained on this very day. Hence, it is named the "Chapter on the Lifespan. It is through this single chapter that one subsequently comes to know [this truth].

The Buddha appears in the world; without cause, the Buddha enters nirvana. He transforms sentient beings everywhere, like the moon reflected in water.
It is neither permanent nor annihilated; it is neither arising nor ceasing. Arising has never truly arisen, and ceasing has never truly ceased.
"Seeing clearly the state where there is no mind, naturally there is no dharma to be spoken. The Emperor was greatly pleased and came to hold the Chan school in even higher esteem.

"As for their number, even we who dwell on the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) do not comprehend them in this matter.
World-Honored One, such worlds are immeasurable and boundless. At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of great bodhisattvas:

With the Buddha-eye, he observes that among all sentient beings, the five faculties—faith and the others—are each either sharp or dull; they are incapable of being taught the ultimate truth.

Furthermore, he preaches the Dharma according to their individual capacities; the teachings he delivers include both the provisional and the real, as well as the sudden and the gradual.
There is nothing that does not inspire joy in people and lead them into the Buddha’s wisdom. To speak in terms of ultimate reality: there is not a single thing that is not the body of the Tathāgata;

It is so. It is so in every thought-moment; it is so in every thing. How could it be limited by a single body, a single name, a single time, or a single place?
This reveals that in the past, by the power of secret spiritual penetrations, he manifested birth from within non-arising.

there is no birth-and-death, neither passing away nor emerging; nor is there remaining in the world or entering extinction.
That which is liberated is neither real nor unreal, neither identical to suchness nor different from it. It does not conform to the three realms, yet it perceives the three realms.

Enduring these matters, by the power of skillful means, you manifested birth in this world; at nineteen you left the home life, practiced austerities for six years, and attained the realization of Bodhi.
Yet, in truth, since I truly attained Buddhahood, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have already passed.
It is only to entice and lead inferior beings to enter the Buddha-wisdom that I speak thus. This is what is seen.

The Tathāgata’s renunciation and attainment of enlightenment are skillful means. The passage beginning with "All the various good [deeds]" below reveals that his turning of the wheel of Dharma during the forty years [thereafter] is likewise a skillful means.
Regarding the phrase "or speaking of one's own person": it is as when he says, "In the past, the sixteenth prince was my own body;
the past king was my own body; the past [Bodhisattva] Sadāparibhūta was my own body."
And so forth. Or, regarding what is called "another's body": for example, the seer Asita of the past was Devadatta;
sentient beings who heard the Dharma in the past are the present śrāvaka disciples; and the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana of the past is Bhaiṣajyarāja and others.
Or, regarding what is shown as both one's own body and another's body: it may show the various Buddhas who are emanations in the present. This is...
Whether it be by manifesting as a Bodhisattva emerging from the earth and saying, "This is my transformation," or by manifesting one's own deeds or the deeds of others—
whether manifesting the event of one's own attainment of Buddhahood, or manifesting the event of a disciple’s attainment of Buddhahood,
or manifesting one's own past lives, or manifesting the past lives of others— and then declaring, "I have spoken thus," all [of these are for the purpose of guiding beings].

These are true words; they are entirely free from falsehood. Because I have attained Buddhahood since immeasurable kalpas ago and have experienced much, I am able to know and see the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are:
fundamentally there is no birth-and-death, nor do I see a single sentient being who falls back into the triple world, nor do I see a single sentient being who transcends the triple world.
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): one does not perceive the Tathāgata appearing within the three realms, nor does one perceive the Tathāgata attaining parinirvāṇa within the three realms.
The One Vehicle has never been real; the Three Vehicles have never been false. The Single Truth has never been suchness;

the three periods of time have never been different. This is not the same as the characteristics of the three realms perceived by sentient beings within the three realms, who truly believe they exist.
Death is real; nirvana is real; the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles are real; true suchness and the three periods of time are real. Why is this?
Because I clearly perceive that birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday; that the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles are nothing other than skillful means;
and that true suchness and the three periods of time are all merely empty names. Therefore, I am able to view that which is remote as if it were today.
He regards sentient beings as his own body and views the three realms as if they were the palm of his hand; there is not the slightest error or deviation.

Therefore, it is said that whether concerning one's own body or the bodies of others, one's own affairs or the affairs of others, these are nothing other than means for leading [beings] into the Buddha-wisdom. Question:

If this is so, why not simply instruct them directly with the Buddha-wisdom, rather than necessarily speaking of one's own body and the bodies of others, or one's own affairs and the affairs of others?

What is the reason for this? Answer: Because the dispositions of sentient beings in the past were diverse, their inclinations in the present are diverse, their various karmic actions are diverse, and their various thoughts are diverse;
in order to cause these diverse sentient beings to give rise to various kinds of goodness, [the Buddha] speaks of numerous causes and conditions, numerous parables, or speaks of himself.
Whether speaking of matters concerning my own person or matters concerning others, I speak from left to right and from horizontal to vertical;
from the past until now, there has never been a single moment’s pause. By this you shall know that it has been a long time since I attained Buddhahood.

It is clear that [the Buddha] is eternally abiding and indestructible; how could there truly be arising and ceasing? This reveals that the various teachings expounded throughout forty years were all skillful means. Question: If it is said that he is eternally abiding and indestructible, for what reason did the Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, say, "I shall now enter nirvana before long"? The answer begins with "All you good [people]" and continues as follows: ...namely, [he spoke thus] because sentient beings have deep-seated attachments to the body and life, and their minds are weary of suffering. Therefore, the Tathāgata, out of compassion, manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to feel sorrow and distress, thereby inducing them to practice the Way. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the world and do not seek liberation, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to fear death and dread the cycle of birth and death, thereby inducing them to cultivate wholesome roots. Moreover, because sentient beings are attached to worldly pleasures and do not seek the Dharma, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that such pleasures are impermanent and subject to change, thereby inducing them to renounce the world and seek the Path. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the Lesser Vehicle and do not seek the Great Vehicle, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the Lesser Vehicle is inferior and the Great Vehicle is supreme, thereby inducing them to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and aspire to the Great Vehicle. Moreover, because sentient beings are attached to the provisional and do not seek the ultimate, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the provisional is empty and the ultimate is real, thereby inducing them to abandon the provisional and seek the ultimate. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the mundane and do not seek the supramundane, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the mundane is suffering and the supramundane is bliss, thereby inducing them to abandon the mundane and seek the supramundane. Additionally, because sentient beings are attached to the conditioned and do not seek the unconditioned, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the conditioned is impermanent and the unconditioned is eternal, thereby inducing them to abandon the conditioned and seek the unconditioned. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the impure and do not seek the pure, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the impure is defiled and the pure is stainless, thereby inducing them to abandon the impure and seek the pure. Moreover, because sentient beings are attached to the false and do not seek the true, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the false is deceptive and the true is authentic, thereby inducing them to abandon the false and seek the true. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the shallow and do not seek the profound, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the shallow is superficial and the profound is deep, thereby inducing them to abandon the shallow and seek the profound. Additionally, because sentient beings are attached to the narrow and do not seek the vast, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the narrow is limited and the vast is expansive, thereby inducing them to abandon the narrow and seek the vast. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the inferior and do not seek the superior, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the inferior is lowly and the superior is sublime, thereby inducing them to abandon the inferior and seek the superior. Moreover, because sentient beings are attached to the finite and do not seek the infinite, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the finite is partial and the infinite is universal, thereby inducing them to abandon the finite and seek the infinite. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the transient and do not seek the permanent, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the transient is fleeting and the permanent is enduring, thereby inducing them to abandon the transient and seek the permanent. Additionally, because sentient beings are attached to the illusory and do not seek the real, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the illusory is deceptive and the real is genuine, thereby inducing them to abandon the illusory and seek the real. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the non-Buddhist and do not seek the Buddhist, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the non-Buddhist is heterodox and the Buddhist is orthodox, thereby inducing them to abandon the non-Buddhist and seek the Buddhist. Moreover, because sentient beings are attached to the external and do not seek the internal, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the external is distracted and the internal is focused, thereby inducing them to abandon the external and seek the internal. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the distracted and do not seek the concentrated, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the distracted is scattered and the concentrated is unified, thereby inducing them to abandon the distracted and seek the concentrated. Additionally, because sentient beings are attached to the coarse and do not seek the subtle, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the coarse is gross and the subtle is refined, thereby inducing them to abandon the coarse and seek the subtle. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the inferior and do not seek the superior, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the inferior is base and the superior is noble, thereby inducing them to abandon the inferior and seek the superior. Moreover, because sentient beings are attached to the dark and do not seek the bright, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the dark is obscured and the bright is luminous, thereby inducing them to abandon the dark and seek the bright. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the deluded and do not seek the awakened, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the deluded is ignorant and the awakened is enlightened, thereby inducing them to abandon the deluded and seek the awakened. Additionally, because sentient beings are attached to the unwholesome and do not seek the wholesome, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the unwholesome leads to suffering and the wholesome leads to happiness, thereby inducing them to abandon the unwholesome and seek the wholesome. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the evil and do not seek the good, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the evil is calamitous and the good is auspicious, thereby inducing them to abandon the evil and seek the good. Moreover, because sentient beings are attached to the afflictions and do not seek the cessation of afflictions, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that afflictions are the root of suffering and the cessation of afflictions is the path to liberation, thereby inducing them to abandon the afflictions and seek the cessation of afflictions. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the cycle of birth and death and do not seek the Great Nirvana, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that birth and death are suffering and Great Nirvana is bliss, thereby inducing them to abandon birth and death and seek Great Nirvana. Additionally, because sentient beings are attached to the provisional teachings and do not seek the ultimate meaning, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the provisional is expedient and the ultimate is definitive, thereby inducing them to abandon the provisional and seek the ultimate. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the traces and do not seek the essence, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that traces are manifestations and the essence is the reality, thereby inducing them to abandon the traces and seek the essence. Moreover, because sentient beings are attached to the secondary and do not seek the primary, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the secondary is derivative and the primary is fundamental, thereby inducing them to abandon the secondary and seek the primary. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the derivative and do not seek the fundamental, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the derivative is dependent and the fundamental is independent, thereby inducing them to abandon the derivative and seek the fundamental. Additionally, because sentient beings are attached to the superficial and do not seek the profound, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the superficial is shallow and the profound is deep, thereby inducing them to abandon the superficial and seek the profound. Furthermore, because sentient beings are attached to the partial and do not seek the universal, the Tathāgata manifested the appearance of entering nirvana to cause them to realize that the partial is limited and the universal is all-encompassing
Proclaiming extinction is also a skillful means. He says: "The life of wisdom I have accomplished through practicing the bodhisattva path in the past exceeds even countless eons and is without end;
how much more so for one who has already realized the indestructible diamond body—how could it have an end?
Yet, though there is fundamentally no extinction, proclaiming extinction is likewise a skillful means to deliver sentient beings. By proclaiming...
Because its cessation brings benefit.
Why is this? If the Buddha were to remain long in the world, those of meager virtue would not plant roots of goodness;
being poor, lowly, and base, they would be greedily attached to the five desires and enter the net of conceptualization and false views. If they were to see that the Tathāgata remains forever...

They do not cease [from their delusions], and thus they give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, harboring weariness and indolence; they are unable to conceive the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find, nor do they develop a heart of reverence.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks through skillful means: "Bhikṣus, you should know that the appearance of Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter.
Why is this? Because those of meager merit may pass through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas before they might perhaps see one."
“Buddha. Or, if they do not see him, it is for this reason that I say: “O monks, the Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.
When these sentient beings hear such words, they will certainly conceive the thought that he is hard to meet;
with hearts full of longing and yearning for the Buddha, they will plant roots of merit. For this reason, although the Tathāgata does not truly pass into extinction, I speak thus.
...enter parinirvāṇa. Furthermore, good son, for all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, the Dharma is thus: in order to deliver sentient beings, it is entirely real and not false.
For the following reason, the proclamation of extinction is beneficial; it serves as the basis for the analogy. If one were not to proclaim extinction, then...
If the Tathāgata were to remain in the world for a long time, beings of meager merit would rely upon the Buddha’s compassion and affection, failing to plant roots of goodness.
Having already experienced the fruits of poverty and low status, they would not turn back to contemplate virtuous deeds;
even in their sleep and dreams, they would think only of the five desires and enter the net of false views, refusing to seek escape from the three realms. Thus, the Tathāgata...
If he did not proclaim his parinirvāṇa and remained forever in the world, people would come to regard the Tathāgata as something ordinary, treating this person of vital importance with indifference.

Not only would they fail to conceive the thought of reverence for one so difficult to encounter, but they would further give rise to arrogance and license, harboring feelings of aversion and indolence. For this reason, the Tathāgata again employed skillful means and spoke thus.
The appearance of one who has come forth into the world is difficult to encounter, just like the udumbara flower, which appears only once after the passage of a vast period of time.
Why is this? Because those of meager virtue and shallow merit may, over the course of immeasurable kalpas, obtain a single sight of such a person;
yet others, even after passing through immeasurable kalpas, may not obtain a single sight of them. For this reason:
I say that Buddhas are difficult to encounter, yet before long they will enter parinirvāṇa.
When these sentient beings hear these words, not only do they fail to give rise to thoughts of arrogance, indulgence, or indolence, but they further conceive feelings of longing and yearning.
They cease to crave the five desires and immediately plant roots of goodness; such is the benefit. Therefore, although the Tathāgata—
He does not enter parinirvāṇa, but rather proclaims through skillful means that he has entered parinirvāṇa. The conclusion below states:
"As previously described—from leaving home, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, up to proclaiming his passing—such skillful means are not employed by this Buddha alone;
all Buddhas of the three periods of time speak in this same way. There is nothing that is not for the purpose of delivering sentient beings. Thus it is said.
To speak of birth where there is no birth, and to proclaim extinction where there is no extinction—these are all the true and sincere words of the Buddhas;
they are not false teachings.
It is like a skilled physician, wise and discerning, who is well-versed in prescriptions and medicines and excels at treating various ailments; such a person possesses many...
"O son, suppose there are ten, twenty, or even a hundred of you, who for some reason travel far away to another country.
Later, while you are there, you drink a poisonous drug; when the poison takes effect, you become dazed and confused, rolling about on the ground. At that time, your father returns home.
Whether those who drank the poison have lost their original minds or have not, they all see their father from afar and are filled with great [joy]."
They were filled with joy. Prostrating themselves and kneeling, they inquired after his well-being: "May you return in safety and peace. We were foolish and mistakenly took poison;

we pray that you will save and heal us, granting us our lives once more. Seeing his sons suffering in such a manner, the father followed various medical treatises to seek out excellent medicinal herbs, which were fully endowed with perfect color, fragrance, and flavor. He pounded, sifted, and blended them together, gave them to his sons to drink, and spoke thus:
He said, "This is a great and excellent medicine, fully endowed with color, fragrance, and delicious flavor. You all may take it;

it will quickly eliminate your suffering and distress, so that you will no longer have any ailments. Among his sons, those who had not lost their minds saw that this excellent medicine was both fine in color and fragrance, and they immediately took it;
thus their illnesses were entirely cured. As for the others who had lost their minds, although they saw their father arrive, even though...
He joyfully inquired after his health and sought to treat his illness; yet, although he was given what was pleasant, he refused to take it. Why was this?
Because the poisonous vapor had penetrated deeply and his original mind was lost, he regarded these fine colors and fragrant medicines as unpleasant.
The father thought to himself: "This son is pitiable; struck by poison, his mind has become completely inverted. Though he sees my joy, he seeks [only what is harmful]."
"Though this is such excellent medicine for healing, you are unwilling to take it. I shall now employ skillful means to cause you to take this medicine," he said, adding:
"You should know that I am now old and decrepit; the time of my death has arrived. This is excellent, wholesome medicine."

"I remain here now; you may take this medicine and drink it. Do not worry that you will not recover. Having given these instructions, he departed for another country and sent a messenger back to announce:
"Your father has already died. At that time, when the sons heard that their father had passed away, their hearts were filled with great sorrow and distress.
He then thought to himself: "If my father were still alive, he would have compassion for us and been able to protect and save us.

Now that he has abandoned us and passed away far away in another land, I find myself orphaned and exposed, with no one left to rely upon. Constantly harboring such grief and emotion, his mind finally awakened.
He then realized that this medicine possessed color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor; he immediately took it and his toxic illness was completely cured.
When his father heard that his son had fully recovered, he returned at once to see him. "Good sons, what do you think? [the Buddha asked].
"Could anyone say that this skilled physician has committed the offense of falsehood? "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "I am also like this.

Since I attained Buddhahood, for immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas, for the sake of sentient beings, I have used the power of skillful means to say that I shall enter parinirvāṇa; yet there is no one who can rightfully say that [this is a falsehood]."
Regarding "my fault of falsehood":

this is established as a metaphor to clarify the benefit of proclaiming extinction. The "skillful physician" who is "wise and discerning" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata, who possesses both provisional and ultimate wisdom (*upāya-jñāna* and *jñāna*).
Because he knows the Dharma and knows the capacities [of sentient beings], he is able to extensively transform sentient beings. He is "well-versed in prescriptions and medicines."

This is like the Tathāgata’s ability to know the medicinal remedies for the Dharma. "That man has many sons" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata regarding the ten classes of sentient beings as his children.

"Because of certain affairs, he travels far to another land" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata responding to and transforming beings in other directions, rather than remaining in this Sahā world. "The sons mistakenly ingest poison" is due to [their lack of...]
The Buddha transforms sentient beings who have mistakenly fallen under the influence of the three poisons and further succumbed to false views, thus transmigrating through the three realms.
The passage beginning with "At that time" serves as an analogy for the Tathāgata manifesting the eight phases of attaining enlightenment within the three realms.

The passage beginning with "The sons" serves as an analogy for the humans and devas of the three realms requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. Those who have lost their original mind are an analogy for those whose poison has run deep; those who have not lost it...
"The original mind" is a metaphor for the poison being shallow. "Seeing his father and rejoicing" refers to the joy, respect, reverence, and praise felt upon first seeing the Buddha.
"We are foolish and ignorant," and so forth, is a metaphor for requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
"Seeing his sons in distress" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s compassion for sentient beings who are being scorched and boiled by the fires of the karma of the three poisons.
Furthermore, "seeking excellent medicinal herbs according to the methods of various sutras" means expounding the Dharma of the Three Vehicles in accordance with the rituals of the Buddhas.

"Fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor" refers to the color adorned by manifold virtues, the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body, and the flavor of unsurpassed *amṛta* (clarified butter); there is nothing that is not fully present. [The herbs are] pounded, sifted, and blended.

Regarding the harmonizing and administering of these to the sons: it is like blending various colors into a single color, blending various flavors into a single flavor, and grinding various fragrances into a single fragrance;
this is a metaphor for taking the ten wholesome deeds and the conditions of the Truths and harmonizing them into the Dharma of a single characteristic and a single flavor.
This causes people to practice. The passage beginning with "and then" encourages them to take medicine, saying that even if one merely dares to wet one’s lips, all will recover from their illness.
This is a direct metaphor for the medicinal Dharma of the Mahāyāna, which is complete with the ten thousand practices; if one simply prepares a willing mind, all shall be liberated from suffering.
As for those sons who, without losing their composure, took the medicine and were cured of their disease, this directly metaphorizes the Three [Vehicles].

Among those who ride this vehicle, there are those of sharp faculties whose afflictions are shallow and thin. Having previously undergone transformation and guidance in past lives, they possess a glimmer of insight;
with a single point of realization, they apply themselves with diligence to cultivation and thus transcend the three realms.
Others, who have lost their minds and refuse to take medicine, serve as a metaphor for those of dull faculties; though they likewise see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, they do not...

Believing that they themselves can become Buddhas, they are unwilling to advance in their practice. Why is this? Because their afflictions (*kleśa*) are deep and heavy, their cravings are manifold, and they have lost their original mind.
The phrase "the father acts below" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s contemplation and establishment of skillful means (*upāya*).
Since the minds of all sentient beings are inverted, they take suffering to be pleasure; thus, although there are the paths of the Three Vehicles for escaping suffering, [they do not enter them].
"Willingly proceeding with cultivation" refers to the period after preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when he immediately announces his parinirvāṇa.

"This is good" refers to leaving behind the scriptural teachings so that people may receive, uphold, read, and recite them, thereby all gaining benefit. "Acting thus" refers to the completion of his work of transforming beings in this land;
having finished his mission here, he passes away from this realm and proceeds to other lands. He dispatches messengers.
"Below. This is a metaphor for what the Dharma-preacher who propagates the sutra tells [the people] after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa.
If, after the Buddha’s extinction, there were no Dharma-preachers to propagate the sutra, then this Dharma would be utterly extinguished without remainder. "At that time," and so forth.
This is a metaphor for hearing of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and then diligently practicing according to the Dharma, thereby attaining the fruits of the Path. The meaning is this:
if one’s father were still alive, out of compassion for me, he could protect me whenever I suffered from illness;
now that my father has passed away, I reflect upon being alone and exposed, with no one left to rely upon. Overcome by grief and lamentation, I have therefore taken medicine to treat myself.

It is an illness. His father’s descent below is a metaphor for attaining the vision of the Buddha. When one’s knowledge and vision have not yet been awakened, even though the Buddha is present, he is as if a thousand li away.
Once knowledge and vision are opened, one realizes that the Buddha has never perished. Therefore, know that proclaiming his extinction was for the sake of sentient beings;
entering extinction was for the sake of sentient beings; and leaving behind medicinal teachings was also for the sake of sentient beings. This is the method for oneself... [text ends]

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the Buddha-dharma spread throughout the world; this was entirely due to the merit of the medicines left behind by the Tathāgata, as well as the power of the dharma-preachers who propagated the sūtras.
Question: For what reason is it that there are also those who take medicine yet their illness does not heal?
Answer: It is because there are underlying causes. As the former Master Lingyuan said: "The practitioner's cultivation of self-preservation is like a person who is ill."
One must take medicine. The efficacy of medicine is easily seen; however, it is essential to observe dietary restrictions (*jìkǒu*) for it to be effective.

Otherwise, what benefit is there in taking the medicine? Birth and death are a grave illness. The teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are the excellent medicine; a defiled mind is a mixture of poisons.
If one cannot refrain from these [defilements], the disease of birth and death will never be diminished. [End of] "The Various Good [Deeds]," Part Two: Discernment and Verification.
Regarding the distinction between the real and the unreal: if one says a good physician will not die when they say he will die, does this not constitute the transgression of false speech?
"No, World-Honored One," [he replied]. "It is not false speech, because by this skillful means, he entices sentient beings to take the medicine."
The Buddha said: "This is in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
'Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed is immeasurable—hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and asaṃkhyeya kalpas.'"
Constantly preaching the Dharma to teach and transform countless billions of sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way.

Having come forth for immeasurable kalpas for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests nirvana through skillful means, yet in reality he does not pass into extinction; he dwells eternally here, preaching the Dharma.
I always abide here; by means of various supernormal powers, I cause deluded sentient beings not to see me even though I am near.
When people perceive my parinirvāṇa and extensively make offerings to my relics, they all harbor longing and affection, giving rise to a heart of yearning and devotion.

Once sentient beings have gained faith and submission, becoming upright in character and gentle in mind, desiring with single-minded devotion to see the Buddha and not begrudging their own bodies or lives, then I and the assembly of monks shall together emerge from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. At that time, I will say to the sentient beings: "I am always here; I do not perish."
By the power of skillful means, there is both cessation and non-cessation. In other lands, there are sentient beings who revere, believe in, and delight in [the Dharma];
to them, I further preach the unsurpassed Dharma. You have not heard this, thinking only that I have entered parinirvāṇa.
I see all sentient beings submerged in suffering and affliction; therefore, I do not manifest my body before them to cause them to give rise to longing and reverence.
Because their hearts are filled with such devotion, I then appear to preach the Dharma for them. Such is the power of my supernormal faculties throughout incalculable eons.

I am always present on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and in all other dwelling places. When sentient beings see the kalpa coming to an end and being consumed by a great conflagration, my land remains peaceful and secure, filled with devas and humans, its gardens and various halls adorned with diverse jewels.
The jewel trees abound with flowers and fruits, where sentient beings roam and delight. The devas beat celestial drums and constantly perform various musical entertainments.
They rain down *māndārava* flowers, scattering them over the Buddha and the great assembly. My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitude perceives it as being consumed by fire.

Filled entirely with grief, fear, and all manner of suffering—these sinful beings, due to the causes and conditions of their evil karma, shall not hear the names of the Triple Gem for incalculable kalpas. Yet those who cultivate merit, who are gentle, supple, and upright...
Then all shall see my body here preaching the Dharma; at times for this assembly, I shall speak of the Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan;
for those who have seen the Buddha only after a long time, I shall speak of the difficulty of encountering a Buddha. Such is the power of my wisdom; the light of my insight shines immeasurably.
This lifespan of incalculable kalpas was obtained through long-cultivated practice. You who possess wisdom, do not harbor doubts regarding this birth;
you should sever them so they are forever exhausted. The Buddha’s words are true and not false, like a physician skilled in expedient means who acts for the sake of curing his mad son.
In truth, I am dead; no one can say this is false. I am also the Father of the World, the savior of all who suffer.
Yet, for the sake of ordinary people who are deluded by inversion, I speak of my extinction in truth. Because they constantly perceive me, they give rise to a mind of arrogance and self-indulgence.
Those who are heedless and attached to the five desires fall into the evil realms. I always know whether sentient beings are practicing the Path or not;
according to what is appropriate for their deliverance, I preach various teachings for them. I constantly reflect within myself: "By what means may I cause sentient beings..."
One attains entry into unsurpassed wisdom and swiftly accomplishes the Buddha-body.
The first seven lines are a verse on the attainment of the Way and the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; this is an expedient means for the sake of saving [beings].
The following four lines are a verse on *nirvāṇa*, which is likewise an expedient means. In reality, he has never departed from this Sahā world. "I always... and so forth—this is the question.
If the Tathāgata constantly dwells in this world, preaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings, why is it that sentient beings do not see the Buddha?

Answer: Although I constantly dwell in this realm, by means of the power of secret spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*), I cause all those sentient beings who are subject to delusion (*viparyāsa*) to be as if separated by a thousand li, even though they face me all day long; thus they do not see me, and instead claim that I have entered extinction.
Dù asked: "Since you do not see the Buddha, what benefit is there? He replied: "When the multitude sees his parinirvāṇa, they build stupas and temples and make offerings to his relics.

Like children longing for a compassionate father, or as one thirsting for nectar, they focus their minds with the utmost resolve and harbor deep affection and yearning, desiring nothing less than to see the Buddha—even to the point of not sparing their own bodies or lives—just as it was during the time of Bhaiṣajyarāja. Thus, I [have caused this to be so]."
He personally beholds that single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as remaining solemnly without dispersing. If he has indeed seen my body, you should tell him with words of truth:
"I am always here in this Sahā world preaching the Dharma and saving sentient beings; I have truly never entered extinction."
Furthermore, when I perceive their inverted views, I manifest the appearance of extinction; when they have faith and submission, I manifest my physical presence.
All of this is done through the power of skillful means to lead them into the Buddha-wisdom. Regarding the phrase "in other lands" and below:

it is said that not only do I manifest birth and extinction in this single land of Sahā, but the various Buddhas who are emanations throughout the lands of the ten directions do likewise. Thus one sees.
Their faith and aspiration manifest as my birth; seeing their suffering at death manifests my passing away; and because of their longing and devotion, I preach the Dharma.

Regarding the four lines on supernatural powers: this concludes the statement that the power of my secret supernatural abilities is such that, although I manifest birth and passing away across immeasurable kalpas within this world and other worlds, they do not realize that the Tathāgata is without [birth or death].
At that time, there was nowhere it did not pervade. Thus, sentient beings perceive the exhaustion of an eon and see the great fire destroying the world;

yet how could they know that while the kalpa-fire blazes intensely and the trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, this world remains peaceful as before, with its devas and humans still full, even down to their places of recreation and all their objects of enjoyment? It is no different.
Not even a single hair’s breadth [of the Tathāgata] was ever moved. All this is due to the karmic power of sentient beings; thus, they see everything consumed by fire and fail to see the Tathāgata.
