Regarding the passage "sorrow and fear" below: this correctly clarifies the causes and conditions for not seeing him. Because sentient beings commit various evil deeds, they are submerged in sorrow and affliction;
they see only the matters of sorrow and affliction within the three miserable realms, and do not see the peace and bliss of the Tathāgata.
In such places, one hears only the sounds of suffering in the three miserable realms, but does not hear the names of the Three Jewels, who are most sublime and victorious.
It is like the waters of the Ganges: ghosts see them as fire, fish see them as their home, humans see them as water, and the devas see them as lapis lazuli.
Each perceives differently according to the power of their own karma. This is what is meant by "if the mind is defiled, the land is defiled; if the mind is pure, the land is pure."

Purify your ears. Regarding those below, this clarifies the causes and conditions for seeing [me]. If there are those who are willing to cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action, the Four Noble Truths, and other such dharmas;
whose resolve is gentle and supple rather than impetuous; and whose mental conduct is straightforward and free from hypocrisy, then they will see my body constantly preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, because the faculties and capacities of those beings differ, what they perceive is not the same. Therefore...
My teaching of the Dharma also accords with the capacities of sentient beings. At times I say that the Buddha’s lifespan is eternally abiding in the world;
at other times I say that the Buddha appears only once after a vast interval of time, like the udumbara flower. Such is the power of my skillful means and wisdom.
However, their wisdom-light is immeasurable and their lifespan is incalculable; it is not attained in a single morning or evening, nor in a single lifetime or a single kalpa.
It is all obtained through the long cultivation of pure karma throughout immeasurable kalpas. This is no empty talk.
"You all, descend and encourage them to give rise to faith. This is like the physician’s downward illustration; "I also" [descends] to apply the analogy to the Dharma.
It is said that because a skilled physician treats the illness of a mad son, he says he is dead even though he is actually alive.

This precisely corresponds to the Tathāgata treating the disease of deluded ordinary beings; thus, although he is actually present, he proclaims his extinction. As for why he proclaims extinction while actually being present:

Because those beings constantly see the Tathāgata, their minds become arrogant and self-indulgent; they become greedily attached to the five desires and commit various evil deeds, falling into the three evil realms.

Since I know that among these beings there are some who, upon seeing the Buddha, immediately practice the Path, while others, upon seeing the Buddha, conversely give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence and do not practice the Path, I also preach various dharmas according to their individual capacities.
Therefore, although he constantly dwells in the world, he speaks of birth and speaks of extinction through skillful means.

His reason for dwelling in the world and manifesting birth and extinction is not for any other purpose; it is nothing other than his desire to cause all sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s wisdom of equality and to achieve the Buddha-body.
The seventeenth verse of the "Chapter on Discerning Merit" says:
Amidst endless waves of smoke and mist stretching toward distant sands, A light boat with short oars rests among the reeds and white flowers.
At dawn, taking advantage of the eastern wind, he hoisted his reed sail and went straight home.

Although the *Ayuṣparyanta-parivarta* (Chapter on the Duration of Life) speaks of the proclamation of extinction, it actually encompasses all matters from leaving home and attaining enlightenment, to turning the wheel of Dharma and saving sentient beings—the beginning and end, the root and the branches. Therefore, the great assembly each received benefits according to their individual capacities.
Because each aspect, from shallow to deep, has been analyzed, the chapter is titled "Analysis of Merit.

At that time, when the great assembly heard the Buddha speak of the lifespan being so long, spanning such immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, countless sentient beings attained great benefit. Then the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya.

Ajita, when I spoke of the long duration of the Tathāgata’s lifespan, six hundred and eighty million billion nayutas of sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Furthermore, there were a thousand times more bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attained the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining. Additionally, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms within a world-system...
Sā. [They] attained the unhindered eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, there were Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a world-system, who attained immeasurable hundred-thousand-ten-million *dhāraṇīs* of revolving cycles.

Furthermore, there were Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm, who were able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma (*avaivartika-dharmacakra*). Furthermore, there were [Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas] as numerous as the atoms in two thousand middle-sized worlds...
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms of earth will be able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms of a small thousand-fold world system shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* after eight births.
Moreover, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms of four sets of four-continent worlds shall attain it after four births.

[They shall attain] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Furthermore, there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in three sets of four-continent worlds who shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after three more births.
Furthermore, there are Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in two sets of four-continent worlds who shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi after two more births.

[They attained] the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*). Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in one four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*), who in their next life shall attain the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, there were sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight world-systems, all of whom gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The Buddha spoke of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attained this great benefit of the Dharma, mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers rained down from the void,
scattering over the Buddhas seated upon lion thrones beneath immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of jewel trees,
as well as scattering over Śākyamuni Buddha seated upon a lion throne within the stupa of the seven treasures, and the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna who had long since entered parinirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata also scattered [offerings] over all the great bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
Furthermore, he rained down fine powders of sandalwood, aloeswood, and other incenses from the midst of the sky. Celestial drums resounded spontaneously with profound and wondrous sounds.
Moreover, he rained down a thousand kinds of celestial garments, hanging down various necklaces: necklaces of pearls, necklaces of maṇi jewels, and necklaces of wish-fulfilling jewels.
Pervading the nine directions, various precious incense burners burned priceless incense, which spontaneously reached everywhere to make offerings to the great assembly.
Above each Buddha, there were bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies, ascending one after another until they reached the Brahma Heaven.
These bodhisattvas, with wondrous voices, sang immeasurable verses in praise of the Buddhas.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
The Buddha has preached a rare and marvelous Dharma, the likes of which have never been heard before. The World-Honored One possesses great power, and his lifespan is immeasurable.
When the countless sons of the Buddha hear the World-Honored One’s detailed exposition, those who attain the benefit of the Dharma experience a joy that pervades their entire bodies.
Some abide on the stage of non-retrogression; some have attained *dhāraṇīs*; some possess unimpeded eloquence and the *koṭi-nayuta-parivarta-dhāraṇī*.
Or there may be Bodhisattvas in a great trichiliocosm, as numerous as motes of dust, each of whom is able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, there are Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a medium chiliocosm, each of whom is able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.
Moreover, there are Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm, who have eight births remaining before they shall attain the path of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, there are those with four, three, or two [lifetimes remaining]. Just as there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in these four continents who attain buddhahood according to their respective numbers of births, so too there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a single four-continent world-system who have but one birth remaining before they shall attain all-knowledge.
Sentient beings such as these, hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, attain immeasurable, outflow-free, and pure karmic fruits.
Furthermore, sentient beings numbering as many as the atoms in eight worlds, hearing the Buddha speak of his life span, all resolve their minds upon the Unsurpassed Way.
The World-Honored One has preached immeasurable and inconceivable dharmas that bring great benefit, as boundless as space.
Heavenly *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers rain down, while Śakras, Brahmās, and others, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, come from countless Buddha-lands.
Sandalwood and aloeswood rain down in profusion, scattering and falling like birds flying from the sky to descend and make offerings to the Buddhas.
In the void of space, celestial drums spontaneously produce wondrous sounds, and tens of millions of kinds of heavenly robes swirl as they descend.
With exquisite incense burners made of various jewels, they burned priceless incense, which spontaneously pervaded everywhere as an offering to all the World-Honored Ones.
The assembly of great bodhisattvas held banners and canopies made of the seven treasures, in ten trillion varieties of sublime height, reaching successively up to the Brahma Heaven.
Before each and every Buddha, jeweled banners hung with exquisite pennants; they also sang praises of all the Tathāgatas with ten million verses.
Such various matters as these had never occurred before. Hearing that the Buddha’s lifespan was immeasurable, everyone rejoiced.
The Buddha’s name is heard throughout the ten directions; he extensively benefits sentient beings, causing all to be endowed with roots of goodness, thereby assisting their unsurpassed resolve.
The preceding section generally clarifies that benefit derived from hearing the sutra; this benefit is known only by the Tathāgata, which is why it is taught here.

From the passage beginning "At that time," the text specifically clarifies that there are both sudden and gradual [attainments]. First, it clarifies sudden enlightenment: within one's own mind, there is a sudden attainment of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
The "Dharma-patience" (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti) is what the Great Sūtra refers to as knowing that the self-nature of all phenomena is precisely the mind itself;

it is the accomplishment of the body of wisdom, realized not through the awakening of another. Regarding the "dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining": *dhāraṇī* is a Sanskrit term, which here means "total retention" (*saṃgraha*).
It signifies that upon hearing this Dharma once, one is immediately able to retain it without loss; hence it is called "hearing and retaining. Furthermore—
It is called "dhāraṇī. That which is said to "enter from conditions" refers to that which is forever without decline or loss.
"Unimpeded eloquence" is one of the four types of unimpeded knowledge; it is the stage of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). As for the "infinite revolving dhāraṇī":
"Revolution" (*xuan*) means "to turn. This refers to what is called the "turning of the Lotus Sūtra through the awakening of the mind. Regarding "turning the non-retrogressive wheel":

because one transcends directly and enters [the path] at once, it is called "non-retrogressive"; this is precisely the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). Regarding "turning the pure wheel":
cultivation and realization are not absent, yet one remains unstained by defilement; therefore, it is called "pure. All of the above clarify the sudden entry into the ranks of the sages.

Furthermore, there is the "lower" [category], which clarifies the gradual attainment of bodhi. Regarding the phrase "to be attained within eight births," it means that one does not attain it in this present life, but shall attain the fruit of bodhi after passing through eight births; this extends down to those who attain bodhi in four, three, two, or even one birth.
Furthermore, there are those who, upon hearing this, give rise to the bodhicitta; these are Bodhisattvas at the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the realization attained upon hearing the Dharma differs for each individual: this refers to what is called "the preaching of the Dharma in a single voice, yet each according to their kind attains realization.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The Buddha spoke," as for the deities making offerings by first raining down flowers:

it is because they wish to obtain the great cause of the Tathāgata. Next, as for raining down incense: it is because they wish to obtain the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body. As for beating the celestial drums: it is because they wish...
To strike the great Dharma-drum of the Tathāgata; to offer rain-garments is to desire to be covered by the robes of the Tathāgata;
to hang jeweled necklaces throughout the nine directions is to desire that all sentient beings within the nine realms may attain the adornment of the Tathāgata’s ten thousand virtues;
and to burn incense in precious censers is to desire that the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body may pervade the great...
This is the assembly. As for the Bodhisattvas holding banners and ascending to the Brahma Heaven, this symbolizes hearing the Dharma and progressing therein.

Furthermore, as for praising the Buddha with wondrous sounds, this signifies being moved by the Buddha’s virtues and giving voice to them. “The Buddha spoke” and below, first the verse praises the benefits gained from hearing the Dharma.
“Or they abide” and below, specifically clarifies sudden attainment. “Furthermore, there are those of a small thousand-world system” and below, clarifies gradual [attainment].
"It is attained. Furthermore, "there are eight worlds below" praises the generation of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

"The rain falls from heaven" praises the various devas raining down flowers, incense, and so forth. "Its greatness... praises the bodhisattvas holding banners and extolling virtues. "In this way... refers to the great assembly rejoicing.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Ajita, if there are sentient beings who, upon hearing that the lifespan of the Buddha is thus long and far-reaching, are able to give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding, the merit and virtue they shall acquire will be without limit or measure.
If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
Therefore, for eighty quadrillion *nayuta* eons, they practiced the five *pāramitās*— the *dāna-pāramitā*, the *śīla-pāramitā*,
the *kṣānti-pāramitā*, the *vīrya-pāramitā*, and the *dhyāna-pāramitā*— excluding the *prajñā-pāramitā*.
If these merits are compared with the former merits, they do not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part.
Not even one part in a hundred million would equal it; indeed, it is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family possesses such merit as this, yet should fall back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, [it would be impossible].
This is impossible. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom, And for eighty quadrillion *nayuta* kalpas Practices the five *pāramitās*..."

Throughout these kalpas, they made offerings of food and drink of rare excellence, superior garments, and bedding, as well as sandalwood monasteries adorned with gardens and groves, to the Buddhas, the pratyekabuddhas and their disciples, and the assemblies of bodhisattvas.
Such acts of giving as these, all of them subtle and wondrous, throughout the entirety of these kalpas, are dedicated toward the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, if one upholds the prohibitive precepts, pure and without flaw, seeking the unsurpassed path, they are praised by all Buddhas.
If one further practices patience and dwells in the stage of gentleness, even when various evils are inflicted upon them, their mind does not waver.
Even if those who have attained some dharma harbor overweening pride and thus slight or harass them, they are likewise able to endure it.
If one further exerts diligent effort, with a will and mindfulness always firm and steadfast, throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, remaining single-mindedly without slackening;
and furthermore, throughout countless kalpas, dwelling in secluded places, whether sitting or walking, constantly restraining the mind and removing drowsiness.
By these causes and conditions, one is able to give rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*). For eighty billion *koṭi* of eons, one dwells peacefully with an undisturbed mind.
Taking this merit of single-mindedness, one vows to seek the unsurpassed path. May I attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and reach the ultimate limit of all meditative concentrations.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who, throughout hundreds of thousands, ten millions, and billions of kalpas, practice all these meritorious virtues as described above,
yet another son or daughter of good family hears me speak of this lifespan and believes it for even a single thought-moment, their merit shall exceed that of the former.
If a person is entirely free from all doubts and regrets, and with a deep mind believes for even a moment, their merit shall be such as this.
As for those bodhisattvas who have practiced the Way for immeasurable kalpas, upon hearing me speak of the lifespan, they will be able to believe and accept it.
May all such people as these receive this sutra upon the crowns of their heads;

may I, in the future, possess long life to deliver sentient beings, just as the World-Honored One, the King among the Śākyas, now roars the lion’s roar at the site of enlightenment, preaching the Dharma without fear.
In future ages, when we sit at the site of enlightenment as objects of universal reverence, our lifespan shall be proclaimed in this same way.
Should there be those with profound resolve, pure and upright, who are learned, capable of total retention, and who understand the Buddha’s words according to their meaning—
For such persons as these, there is no doubt regarding this.
As for the phrase "the merit of believing and understanding in a single thought is immeasurable": "believing" means being without doubt; "understanding" means clarity.

This refers to attaining sudden, expansive enlightenment according to what has been heard, entering directly and straightforwardly like a single blade, with no further uncertainty. This is called "a single thought."
Faith and Understanding. An ancient worthy said: "To see is to see directly and immediately; to conceive a thought is already to deviate.

If one were to compare the merit of practicing the five *pāramitās* for eighty trillion *nayuta* kalpas against the merit of a single moment of faith and understanding, the former would not equal the latter. Only those who have attained *prajñā* possess merit that is equal [to this].

Because through a single thought of faith and understanding, one is determined not to regress from bodhi. The four lines beginning with "If a person" constitute a general verse. The section beginning with "In this regard" provides a specific verse on giving (*dāna*).
The section beginning with "If again" provides a verse on ethical discipline (*śīla*). The section beginning with "If again one practices" provides a verse on patience (*kṣānti*).
"Various evils" refers to the forest of blades, tiles, stones, as well as insults and abuse. "Those who have attained the Dharma" refers to those who have realized the teachings.
He merely assumes the name of an araṇya-dweller and claims to be practicing the true path. One who harbors overweening pride has not attained what he claims to have attained.
Furthermore, "diligently below" praises diligence (*vīrya*). Again, "below" praises meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Regarding "removing sleep and gathering the mind," this means that while walking in the forest, he never sleeps, but gathers his mind into a single point. [This concludes] all...

The limit of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) refers to that which is profoundly entered into the boundless. There is a section [beginning with] "There is one who is skillful in humility" which compares and measures merit.

Although one may thus practice the five *pāramitās* for immeasurable eons, if upon hearing the teaching of the lifespan, one gives rise to faith for even a single thought-moment and does not harbor doubt or confusion, their merit exceeds that of the former. The section beginning with "There is one who... correctly reveals the single...

Regarding "the immeasurable merit of mindfulness, faith, and resolve": because this person has previously practiced the bodhisattva path for immeasurable kalpas, upon hearing this Dharma even once, they are immediately able to believe and accept it, uphold it with the highest reverence, and put it into practice.
Furthermore, they are able to make vows to deliver sentient beings; therefore, the merit they obtain is immeasurable. The following eight lines now specifically set forth this point.

"May I decline. The following six lines clarify that only those whose deep resolve is pure, who possess extensive learning and dhāraṇī, and who have attained thorough understanding according to the meaning, can achieve doubtless one-moment faith and comprehension.
Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, and understand the meaning of these words, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable;
they will be able to give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata. How much more so for those who hear this sutra extensively!
Whether one causes others to hear it, or upholds it oneself, or causes others to uphold it; whether one writes it oneself, or causes others to write it;
or whether one makes offerings to the scripture with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, flags, silk canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps—the merit of such a person is [immeasurable].
It is immeasurable and boundless, capable of giving rise to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Ajita, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, upon hearing me speak of the longevity of my life, should believe and understand it with a profound mind, they shall see the Buddha as always dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain, surrounded by great bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, preaching the Dharma. Furthermore, they shall see this Sahā world.
The ground is of lapis lazuli, level and even. The eight paths are demarcated by Jāmbūnada gold, with rows of jewel trees.
All the terraces and towers are composed entirely of jewels. The assembly of bodhisattvas all dwell therein.
If there is anyone capable of contemplating it in this way, one should know that this is the sign of the realization of the profound mind.

Regarding "the merit of explaining the meaning and intent of these words is immeasurable": this refers to the ability, after hearing the sutra, to explain the meaning and intent of what is taught in this chapter using even single words or phrases.
For example, to say: "These lifespans are all equal to those of sentient beings, without distinction;
this is the true word of the Buddha. If one understands this, one is able to give rise to the Buddha-nature of equality.
Because of wisdom, one's merit is immeasurable; how much more so for those who practice below it? Furthermore, let us compare the merit of hearing, retaining, transcribing, and making offerings.
"Hearing" means entering [the teaching] through the ears; "retaining" means storing it within the mind; and "transcribing" means putting it into practice with the hands.

What was previously called "arousing" refers to the sprouting of its buds; what is here called "giving birth" refers to the presence of its roots. Regarding the phrase "profound mind of faith and understanding":
having understood, to extensively cultivate wholesome dharmas is called a "profound mind"; furthermore, it does not consist of a single moment of faith and understanding.
As for the phrase "then one shall see the Buddha and so forth": such a person is able to personally behold the assembly on Vulture Peak.
It remains solemnly as it was, never having been extinguished. Furthermore, one personally perceives that this Sahā world is itself the Pure Land, never having been defiled.
If one can cultivate such contemplation, it is the mark of profound mental faith and understanding (*adhimukti*).
All of the above constitutes a comparative evaluation of the merit of generating faith and understanding upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching in the present.

Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, if one hears this sutra and does not disparage it, but gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, you should know that they already possess the signs of deep-seated understanding;
how much more so for those who read, recite, receive, and uphold it! Such persons shall be as if they were bearing the Tathāgata upon their heads.
Ajita, these sons and daughters of good family need not build stupas or monasteries for my sake again.
Furthermore, they shall construct monasteries and provide the four requisites for the Sangha. Why is this?
Because those sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra have already erected stupas, established monasteries, and made offerings to the Sangha;
they have thereby used the relics of the Buddha to erect stupas of the seven treasures, vast and high, gradually tapering until reaching the Brahma Heaven.
Hanging up various banners and canopies, as well as many jeweled bells, incense, flowers, necklaces, powdered incense, ointments, and burning incense;
with various drums, music, flutes, pipes, lutes, and all kinds of dances and performances;

and with exquisite sounds, singing and chanting praises—for an immeasurable number of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, having performed such offerings as these, Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa one hears...
If anyone is able to receive and uphold this sutra, whether by writing it themselves or instructing others to write it, they will have established monasteries,
constructing thirty-two halls made of red sandalwood, eight *tāla* trees in height, magnificent and well-adorned in both height and breadth,
wherein hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus shall dwell. There will also be gardens, groves, bathing ponds, walking paths, and meditation caves, as well as clothing and drink.
Food, bedding, seats, medicinal decoctions, and all manner of articles of comfort fill them.

Such monastic dwellings—halls and pavilions numbering in the hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions—are immeasurable in their quantity. By means of these, they make offerings before my very eyes to me and the community of bhikṣus.
For this reason, I say that after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, or explain [this teaching] to others...

Whether writing it oneself or instructing others to write it, one should make offerings to this scripture; there is no need to further erect stupas and temples, or to build monasteries to provide for the Sangha.

How much more so for one who can uphold this sutra while simultaneously practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom—their merit is supreme, immeasurable, and boundless, like space extending to the east, west, south, and north.
To the north, and in the four intermediate directions, above, and below—limitless and boundless—is the merit of this person;
it is likewise limitless and boundless, leading swiftly to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). If a person reads and recites, upholds, and explains this sutra to others;
or if they write it themselves, or teach others to write it; and furthermore, if they can erect stupas, construct monasteries, and offer worship and praise to the śrāvakas.
The assembly of monks likewise praised the bodhisattva’s merits with hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of eulogistic dharmas.
Furthermore, for the sake of others, they explained this Lotus Sūtra through various causes and conditions according to its meaning, and were moreover able to maintain the precepts with purity.
He dwells together with those who are gentle; he is patient and free from anger. His resolve and mindfulness are firm; he always values seated meditation and attains profound concentrations.
He is diligent and courageous, gathering all wholesome dharmas. Possessing sharp faculties and wisdom, he is skilled in answering difficult questions.

Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and who further possess such virtuous merits as these, you should know that these persons have already set out for the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and are close to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
they are sitting beneath the tree of enlightenment. Ajita, these sons of good family...
O women, wherever she sits, stands, or walks—right there a stūpa should be erected. All devas and humans should make offerings to it as they would to a stūpa of the Buddha.
Below this, there is again a comparative evaluation of the merit of five kinds of Dharma-preachers, which is the same as that in the preceding "Chapter on the Dharma-preacher.
It was previously stated that in the final age, if there are those who act as these five kinds of Dharma-preachers, they should be regarded with reverence as if they were the Buddha;
one should honor them with the same offerings made to the Tathāgata, and one should scatter celestial jewels over them. Herein, the five [kinds of Dharma-preachers] are compared...
Because one plants the merit of the Dharma Master, it is said that there is no need to construct stupas, build monasteries, or make offerings to the assembly of monks;
for by doing so, one has already constructed stupas, built monasteries, and made offerings to the assembly of monks—the merit is no different. Question:

This was already explained in the preceding chapter; why is it explained again here? The answer is: the preceding chapter was spoken for the sake of the bodhisattvas within the assembly, whereas this section is spoken for the sake of the bodhisattvas who have emerged from the earth.

It says that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if one hears this sutra from a Dharma teacher and does not disparage it, but merely gives rise to a single thought of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), this is equivalent to having deep faith and understanding while the Buddha was still in the world.
As for their characteristics, their merit is no different; how much more so after their parinirvāṇa.

Those who are able to receive and uphold [this teaching] while also reading and reciting it—such persons are performing a Dharma-offering to the Buddha. The Tathāgata will also always reside upon the crown of their heads.
It is unnecessary for them to further erect stupas, temples, or monasteries, nor to provide the fourfold requisites as offerings to the Saṃgha.

Because the place where one upholds [the teaching] is itself a stūpa and temple, and the place where one reads and recites it is itself the establishment of a monastic dwelling for the purpose of making offerings to the Saṃgha; this is the first calculation of merit. As for the second calculation:

if there is one who upholds [the teaching] while also transcribing it, that constitutes the construction of a monastic dwelling and the making of offerings to the Saṃgha. Therefore, the conclusion follows below.
The merits of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers. Furthermore, the third section provides a comparative evaluation:

the merit of one who upholds this sutra while simultaneously practicing the six perfections is immeasurable and equal to space; moreover, it surpasses that of one who also engages in reading, reciting, and copying the text.
The fourth section provides another comparative evaluation: regarding a person who performs all five activities and cultivates all six perfections.
This person has already set out for the site of enlightenment and is close to attaining bodhi. Furthermore, they surpass those who merely uphold the precepts while practicing the six perfections.
Their resolve and mindfulness are firm and steadfast; even if called upon a thousand times or enticed in ten thousand ways, their will cannot be diverted.
They encompass all wholesome dharmas, meaning they practice all manner of goodness. They are skilled in answering difficult questions, meaning they are adept at responding to inquiries.

Ajita, for those who have correctly undertaken the five practices and cultivated the six perfections together, whether they are sitting, standing, or walking, one should always erect stupas to make offerings to them; these shall not differ from the stupas of the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, one is able to receive and uphold this sutra, the merit of such a person shall be immeasurable, as has been described above."

This constitutes the fulfillment of all offerings: by erecting stupas for the śarīra, adorned with the seven treasures, their spires exceedingly high and broad, tapering gradually to reach the Brahma-heaven, with billions of precious bells that emit wondrous sounds when stirred by the wind.
Furthermore, throughout immeasurable eons, they shall make offerings to this stupa with flowers, incense, various necklaces, celestial robes, and manifold music;
they shall burn fragrant oils and ghee lamps, which constantly illuminate it on all sides. In the evil age of the Dharma’s final period, those who are able to uphold this sutra—
This shall be as described above, fully complete with all offerings. If one can uphold this sutra, it is as if the Buddha were present.
One should construct monasteries for the Sangha using gośīrṣa-candana, with thirty-two halls, each eight tāla trees in height.
Exquisite food and fine garments, couches and bedding—all are fully provided. There are dwellings for hundreds of thousands of beings, gardens, groves, and various bathing pools;

walking paths and meditation caves are all adorned with every kind of excellence. If one possesses a heart of faith and understanding, and receives, upholds, reads, recites, or transcribes [this teaching], [one shall obtain such rewards].

Furthermore, if one teaches others to write [the scriptures], or makes offerings to the scriptural scrolls by scattering flowers, incense, and powdered incense—such as *sumana*, *campaka*, and *atimuktaka*—and constantly burns them with scented oil; those who make such offerings shall attain immeasurable merit.

As space is boundless, so too is their merit; how much more so for those who uphold this sutra, while also practicing giving, observing the precepts, enduring patience, delighting in meditative concentration, refraining from anger and harsh speech, showing reverence to stupas and temples, and humbling themselves before the bhikṣus.
One should remain far removed from pride and constantly contemplate wisdom. When questioned or challenged, one should not become angry, but explain the teachings in accordance with the truth.
If one can practice such conduct, their merit will be immeasurable. If one sees such a Dharma teacher who has accomplished these virtues, [one should honor them].
One should scatter celestial flowers and cover his body with celestial robes; bowing one’s head to touch his feet, one should give rise to the thought of regarding him as a Buddha.
Furthermore, one should reflect: "Before long he will go to the Tree of Enlightenment and attain the untainted and unconditioned state, bringing vast benefit to all humans and devas."
Wherever they dwell—whether walking, sitting, or lying down—even if they speak but a single verse, a stūpa should be erected there and adorned with exquisite beauty, making various offerings to it.
When a Son of the Buddha dwells in this stage, that place becomes the very enjoyment of the Buddhas.
"Always remaining therein, whether walking, sitting, or lying down. In the verse, "If I...
and below, this verse praises the merit of both upholding and reciting. "The power to bind... and below, this verse praises the merit of both upholding and transcribing.
"If there be... and below, this verse praises the performance of the five practices together with the six perfections.
All of these cultivate merit. *Sumanā* is translated here as "well-pleasing. *Campaka* is translated as "yellow flower"; it is small but fragrant.
*Atimuktaka* is translated as "good contemplation. If one sees [the following], at the end of the verse, one should pay homage to the Dharma Master as if to a Buddha.
The Great Outline of the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Five;
The Great Outline of the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Commentary by the Bhikṣu Tōjun of Jinting.
The eighteenth verse of the *Anumodanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Rejoicing) states:
Before the eyes have opened, consciousness has not yet dried; the entire world is but a dream of Handan.
When the brow is slightly raised, the mechanism is penetrated.
[The text] first compares those who uphold and recite [the scripture]; second, it compares those who uphold and transcribe it; third...

This is a comparative evaluation of those who uphold [the teaching] while concurrently practicing the six perfections. Fourth, it is a comparative evaluation of those who perform all five types [of practice] while equally cultivating the six perfections.
This chapter is about evaluating the merit of one who rejoices for even a single moment of thought, as mentioned previously.
Regarding "rejoicing" (anumodana): it refers to when, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, someone happens upon a Dharma assembly and sees people preaching the Dharma. First...

Entering the faculty of hearing, it encounters no resistance and gives rise to no disparagement; it accords with the mind and can produce joy, and for this reason it is called "rejoicing" (anumodana).
When the members of the previous eight assemblies saw Śāriputra receive his prediction, they gave rise to a heart of rejoicing and immediately received their own predictions.
When the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth heard of the Tathāgata’s work of delivering sentient beings, they also gave rise to a heart of rejoicing and immediately received the entrustment.
This is because while the Tathāgata was in the world, there were those capable of preaching who possessed perfect excellence of both form and mind;

thus, upon hearing the sutras, it was easy to give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). However, five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, when the Way and the Dharma decline and strife becomes entrenched, although there may be those who preach the Dharma, it is easy to give rise to disparagement and difficult to give rise to sympathetic joy. This [is the nature of] sympathetic joy.
Regarding these merits, it is for this reason that one must certainly perform a comparative calculation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if there are sons or daughters of good family who hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain? And he spoke in verse:
"After the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, if there are those who hear this sutra and are able to rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:
"Ajita, after the Tathāgata’s extinction, whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, or other wise ones—whether old or young—who hear this..."
Having rejoiced in the sutra, they depart from the assembly and go elsewhere— whether to a monastery,
a secluded place, a city, a street, a village, or a field— and according to what they have heard, they expound it to their parents, kinsmen, good friends,
and spiritual teachers to the best of their ability. These people, having heard it, rejoice and in turn teach it to others.
Having heard it, they likewise rejoice and teach it to others. Thus it is passed on in succession until it reaches the fiftieth person.
Ajita, I shall now describe the merit of that fiftieth son or daughter of good family who rejoices; you should listen well.
If there were beings in four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds—beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth:
those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those with form or without form; those with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception;
those without feet, with two feet, four feet, or many feet—all such as these who are reckoned among the number of sentient beings—and if someone seeking merit were to follow [them]...

Whatever articles for entertainment they desired, he provided them all. To each and every sentient being, he gave as much gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, and various exquisite precious jewels as would fill the entire Jambudvīpa, as well as elephants, horses, carriages, and palaces and towers made of the seven treasures.
This great donor bestowed such gifts in this manner for a full eight [years].
After ten years had passed, he had this thought: "I have already provided sentient beings with objects of entertainment according to their every desire;
yet these sentient beings are all aged and decrepit, over eighty years of age, with white hair and wrinkled faces, and death will soon come."

"I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma. He immediately gathered these sentient beings, proclaimed the transformative teachings of the Dharma, and instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them.
At that moment, they all attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat;
they exhausted all outflows (āsrava) and attained mastery over profound meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi), being endowed with the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa). As for you...

"What do you think? Would the merit obtained by this great donor be much? Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the merit of this person would be exceedingly great—immeasurable and boundless.
If this donor were merely to bestow all instruments of happiness upon sentient beings, his merit would already be immeasurable;
how much more so when he causes them to attain the fruit of Arhatship? The Buddha told Maitreya:

I now speak to you clearly: if a person were to bestow all manner of articles of pleasure upon the sentient beings of the six realms throughout four million *koṭi-nayuta-asamkhyeya* worlds, and further cause them to attain the fruit of Arhatship,

the merit thereby acquired would not equal even a hundredth part or a thousandth part of the merit gained by the fiftieth person who hears a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and rejoices in it.
A hundred thousand million billion parts would not equal even one part of it; it is beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
Ajita, such is the merit of the fiftieth person who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* by way of successive transmission and rejoices in it;
it is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*). How much more so for those who hear it at the very beginning of the assembly and rejoice in it—their merit is [incomparable].
Furthermore, it is infinitely and boundlessly superior, beyond measure and incomparable. Moreover, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra,
goes to a monastery and listens to or receives its teachings for even a brief moment— whether sitting or standing— by virtue of this merit,
in their subsequent rebirth they will obtain excellent and sublime elephants, horses, and carriages, precious jeweled litters, and shall ride upon celestial palaces.

Furthermore, there may be someone sitting at a place where the Dharma is being preached. If another person comes and encourages them to sit and listen, or offers them half of their seat to sit upon, the merit of that person will be such that in their next rebirth they shall obtain the seat of Śakra, or the seat of Brahmā, or the seat of a Cakravartin King.
Ānanda, if furthermore there is someone who says to another person: "There is a sutra named..."

“Let us go together to listen to the Lotus Sutra. He immediately accepted his instruction. By hearing it for even a brief moment, the merit of this person will be such that, upon changing bodies, he will be born in the same place as a *dhāraṇī*-possessing bodhisattva.
With keen faculties and wisdom, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, he shall never be mute or dumb;
his breath shall not be foul; his tongue shall always be free from disease, as shall his mouth; and his teeth shall not be stained.
It is black, not yellow, and not sparse; nor is it missing any parts. It is neither uneven nor crooked.

The lips do not hang down, nor are they shriveled or retracted; they are neither coarse nor rough. They are free from sores or eruptions, nor are they defective or damaged; nor are they harelipped or slanted. They are neither thick nor large, nor are they tawny-black.
There is nothing about them that is loathsome. The nose is not flat or flattened, nor is it curved or twisted. The facial complexion is not dark. Nor...
Neither too long nor too short, neither sunken nor crooked; there was not a single unpleasing feature. His lips, tongue, and teeth were all perfectly adorned. His nose was long, high, and straight;
his face was full and round; his eyebrows were high and long; and his bridge was broad and level. He was endowed with every mark of a superior person.
In every lifetime into which he was born, he saw the Buddhas and heard the Dharma, receiving and accepting their teachings. Ajita, you should know this.
If one observes that encouraging a single person to go and listen to the Dharma brings such merit as this, how much more so for those who, with a single mind, explain, listen to, read,
and recite it, and for those who, within the great assembly, analyze it for others and practice according to what they have taught? At that time, the World-Honored One,
wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
If a person, at a Dharma assembly, should hear this sutra— even but a single verse— and with sympathetic joy explain it to others,
and if it is thus transmitted in succession until reaching the fiftieth person, the merit obtained by that final person shall now be analyzed.
Suppose there were a great benefactor who provided for immeasurable multitudes for a full eighty years, granting them whatever they desired;
yet, seeing their signs of aging—hair white, faces wrinkled, teeth sparse, and bodies withered—he reflects that their death will not be long in coming.
"I must now instruct you so that you may attain the fruits of the Path. He then spoke for their sake through skillful means regarding the true Dharma of Nirvana:
"The world is entirely unstable, like foam, bubbles, or a flame. You all should swiftly give rise to a mind of weary detachment."
When those people heard this Dharma, they all attained arhatship, becoming fully endowed with the six supernormal powers, the three knowledges, and the eight liberations.
Yet, the merit of the last person, the fiftieth, who heard a single verse and rejoiced in it, surpasses theirs; no analogy can express it.

If one hears [of this teaching] by successive transmission in this manner, their merit is already immeasurable; how much more so for those who hear it for the first time at a Dharma assembly and rejoice with sympathetic joy!

If there is someone who encourages even a single person to go and listen to the Lotus Sūtra, saying, "This sūtra is profound and subtle, difficult to encounter in ten million kalpas," [the merit is even greater].
He immediately accepted the instruction and went to listen. Having heard it for even a brief moment, he said: "I shall now explain in detail the karmic reward of this person:

in every lifetime they will have no afflictions of the mouth; their teeth will not be spaced, nor yellow or black; their lips will not be thick, curled, or cleft; and they will possess no loathsome features."
His tongue was not dry, black, or short; his nose was high, long, and straight; his bridge was broad, level, and symmetrical;

and his face and features were entirely dignified and handsome, such that he was pleasing to behold by all people. His breath was free from foul odors, and the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus constantly issued from his mouth.
If one intentionally goes to a monastic dwelling desiring to hear the Lotus Sūtra and hears it for even a brief moment with joy, I shall now describe their merit:
in future lives among gods and humans, they will obtain exquisite elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as precious palanquins and celestial palaces upon which to ride.

If, at a place where the Dharma is being preached, one encourages others to sit and listen to the sutras, by this causal condition of merit one shall obtain the seats of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin king;
how much more so for one who listens with a single-minded focus, explains its meaning and intent, and practices according to what has been taught—their merit shall be beyond measure.
First, Maitreya asks a question; at that time, the following provides the formal answer.

By citing the fiftieth person who rejoices as a point of comparison, it conversely reveals that the merit of the very first act of rejoicing is even greater. Those born from eggs include fish, birds, tortoises, and snakes;
those born from wombs include humans, domestic animals, nāgas, and seers; those born from moisture include crawling insects and wriggling creatures.

As for the categories: those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) are the class of those that metamorphose and fly; those with form are the class of spirits presiding over portents of good and ill fortune;

those without form are the class of those that disperse into emptiness or sink away; those with thought are the class of gods, ghosts, and spiritual essences; those without thought are the class of earth, wood, metal, and stone;
and those who are neither with nor without thought are the class such as the *pulu* (parasitic wasps). As for those who are not without thought...
As for "beings," they include those such as the earth-owl which have no feet; those such as the eel and leech which have two feet;
those such as the chicken and duck which have four feet; and those such as the millipede which have many feet.
"Those who seek merit" refers to people who perform meritorious deeds. "Giving them whatever they desire" means providing everything according to their wishes.
Whatever sentient beings desire in their hearts, he bestows all of it upon them. [The phrase] "one by one" refers to the items bestowed.

[The phrase] "greatly" refers to the time when he practices the giving of material goods. [The phrase] "and then" indicates that after having given material gifts, he further gives the gift of the Dharma.
[The phrase] "at once" refers to hearing the Dharma and attaining the fruit of *srotāpanna*—which is translated as "Stream-enterer"—the first fruit.
*Sakṛdāgāmin* (Sītuohán): translated here as "Once-returner"; this is the second fruit. *Anāgāmin* (Ānahan): translated here as "Non-returner"; this is the third fruit. *Arhat* (Āluohan):
translated here as "Slayer of the Foe"; this is the fourth fruit. *Deep dhyāna-concentration*: refers to the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
"Regarding 'In you... below: this interrogates the extent of his merit. "Maitreya... below: this answers by revealing that his merit is immeasurable.

"The Buddha said... below: this compares the merit; it states that although his merit is great, it still does not equal the even greater merit of the fiftieth person who rejoices in a single verse of this sutra. [This concerns] the fiftieth person rejoicing in a single verse.
The merit is already immeasurable; how much more so for those who first hear it and rejoice in it—how could their merit ever be measured?
Question: If rejoicing in a single verse of the *Lotus Sūtra* can enable one to transcend such vast amounts of merit, is the Tathāgata’s word not too extreme?
Answer: It is like asking a blind person to discuss the patterns of the *fu-fu* (embroidered) designs on ceremonial robes.
Contemplation: The deaf have no means to participate in the subtlety of silk, bamboo, pipes, and strings. These are all the ultimate words of the Tathāgata;
it is only that the deaf and blind are unwilling to believe them. This sutra is like a maṇi jewel, while other sutras are likened to the "illuminating carriage" pearl.
To obtain a hundred bushels of illuminating carriage pearls is not as good as obtaining a single maṇi jewel.
Furthermore, "Again, below" reveals the merit of going alone to listen to the Dharma; because one goes alone to listen to the Dharma, one obtains things for one's own enjoyment.
"If, moreover, below" further reveals the merit of exhorting others to listen to the Dharma;

that is to say, when sitting in a place where the Dharma is being preached, if someone happens to arrive, one exhorts them to sit and listen. Because of exhorting them to sit and sharing one's seat, one is moved to become Śakra or Brahmā.
"The King’s Seat. (Āgata). Furthermore, this reveals the merit of listening to the Dharma in the company of companions.
"Dhāraṇī Bodhisattvas" refers to Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage and above; because they listen together in the company of others, they attain birth in the same place as the Dhāraṇī Bodhisattvas.
"Never being mute" means that their voices are clear and resonant, and their breath is not foul.
One who [possesses these marks] constantly emits the fragrance of the blue lotus. One whose tongue is free from ailment is neither parched nor short, and their speech is fluent and nimble.
One whose mouth is free from ailment is not crooked or askew. "Hanging down" refers to thick lips. "Contracted and shriveled" refers to short lips.
"Lacking or damaged" refers to cleft lips. "Flat and protruding" refers to a flat nose. "Curved and distorted" refers to a crooked nose.
"Concave and curved" refers to a sunken surface. "All are adorned and beautiful" means, for example: the lips are red and straight; the tongue is thin and long;
the teeth are white and closely set; the nose is long, prominent, and straight; the face is round and full; the eyebrows are high and long;
the bridge of the nose is broad and level, and so forth. Below this, [the text] calculates and compares merits, stating that the merit of exhorting a single person to listen to the Dharma—

If such is the virtue [of this teaching], how much more so for those who listen to the Dharma with a single-minded focus, those who recite it with a single-minded focus, those who analyze and explain it for others with a single-minded focus, and those who practice according to the teachings with a single-minded focus—their corresponding merits can be known by analogy.
In the verse: "The world is entirely unstable, like foam on water, bubbles, and flames"—this was spoken for their sake.
The dharma of impermanence causes them to abandon birth and death. As it is said: "This body is impermanent, lacking solidity, and subject to rapid decay.
This body is like a mass of foam that cannot be grasped; this body is like a bubble that cannot endure for long."
"This body is like a flame, born from the category of craving"—this and what follows below are verses exhorting others to listen to the Dharma.

"If intentionally," and so forth, refers to listening to the Dharma oneself. "If at," and so forth, refers to occasionally exhorting others to listen to the Dharma while at a place where the Dharma is being preached.
"How much more so," and so forth, is a comparison of superiority.
The nineteenth verse of the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" says:
Sand in the eyes and dust in the ears, Calling from the east and responding from the west— most clearly distinct.
"The orangutan desires to meet again in grand splendor; he calls out once at the crossroads.
The preceding two sections compared merits, all of which proclaimed the merit obtained from receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, explaining, copying, and making offerings to this sutra.
These were all cases of comparing the superior with the inferior, yet [the merit of this] has never been proclaimed.
This refers to the merit obtained through the six sense faculties when a Dharma teacher is present; therefore, this chapter addresses it.

If these five kinds of Dharma teachers apply themselves with diligent vigor and rely on the power of the Buddha-dharma’s permeation, they will at that time realize the wisdom of a single thought-moment of correspondence and behold the equal Dharma-body, thereby entering the stage of the purity of the six sense faculties.

Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When such pure persons cultivate *samādhi*, their physical bodies—born of father and mother—need not rely on the divine eye to naturally perceive the worlds of the ten directions.
They behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, personally receive the sacred instructions, and attain great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to travel through the realms of the ten directions.
This arises because they have opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thus, every sense organ and every object of perception is the pure fundamental nature."
Nevertheless, because it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, its merits are extensively revealed.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Constant Diligence:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this Lotus Sūtra, such a person shall obtain eight [qualities]..."
The merit of a hundred eyes; the merit of twelve hundred ears; the merit of eight hundred noses; the merit of twelve hundred tongues;
the merit of eight hundred bodies; and the merit of twelve hundred minds. By means of these merits, he adorns the six sense faculties.

They shall all be made pure. These sons and daughters of good family, with the pure physical eyes born of their parents, will see all the mountains, forests, rivers, and oceans within and without the trichiliocosm;
from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above, they will also see all sentient beings therein, as well as their karmic causes and conditions and the arising of their retributive fruits.
He perceives and knows them all. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If, amidst the great assembly, with a mind free from fear, one preaches this Lotus Sutra—listen now to its merits."
This person attains eight hundred merits and a preeminent eye; because it is thus adorned, those eyes are exceedingly pure.
With the eyes born of their parents, they see the entirety of the trichiliocosm: the inner and outer Mount Merus, Sumeru, and the Iron Ring Mountains.

Together with all other mountain forests, the great oceans, and the rivers and streams—down as far as the Avīci Hell and up as far as the Peak of Existence—all the sentient beings therein are seen by him entirely.
Although he has not yet attained the divine eye, such is the power of his physical eye.
First, the merits of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers are explained in general.

It is told to "Ever-Exerting" (Sadāparibhūta) because this title refers specifically to one who is diligent and untiring, and thus it is addressed to him as such a person will attain [these merits] in a single lifetime. "This person shall obtain" refers to this Dharma-preacher.

If one is willing to directly accept and take responsibility for this, constantly practicing with diligence, never departing from it for even a moment even in times of haste or adversity, such a person shall immediately enter the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
In a single lifetime, they will attain the merit of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*).

As clarified in the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi-sūtra*, regarding the eight hundred merits of the eye faculty: because the front is entirely bright while the back is entirely dark, [the eye faculty attains] twelve hundred...
Regarding the merit of the ear: because when drums are struck in the ten directions, they are heard simultaneously in all ten places. Regarding the eight hundred merits of the nose:
because there is inhalation and exhalation, and they intersect within the nasal cavity. Regarding the twelve hundred merits of the tongue:

because speech has spatial divisions, yet its principle is inexhaustible. Regarding the eight hundred merits of the body: because it can perceive when in contact, but does not know when separated. [The thousand...]

Regarding the two hundred merits of the mind: because there is nothing that is not encompassed by them, whether one is a sage or an ordinary person, the six sense faculties are adorned with such merits.
Therefore, when the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are revealed, they immediately attain purity. This refers to what was stated previously:
"In order to cause the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to become pure, he appears in the world. This is it.
This refers to the following. First, it clarifies the merit of the faculty of the eye. "The world" refers to the insentient realm of the physical vessel;
"sentient beings" refers to the realm of conscious life. Although this is but the ordinary fleshly eye, its efficacy is equal to that of the celestial eye;
thus, it can see both the distant and the near, leaving nothing minute or detailed unperceived. An ancient master said: "The entire great earth is but a single [eye] of the śramaṇa."
The eye: throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they all reside within the eyes of the śramaṇa.
In the verse, the single phrase "with a mind free from fear" precisely reveals the reason why the purification of the six sense organs is so great.

Fear arises from a sense of insufficiency because the power of the Way has not yet been fully realized. Now, as for being "fearless," it is because that cultivation and nourishment have already [reached fulfillment].
Long ago, when the power of the Way was fully realized and the spirit was complete, even weapons and insults were insufficient to disturb one’s concerns.
Formerly, when Chan Master Xuansha Bei was gathering firewood in the mountains, a nearby monk called out, "Master, look at the tiger!
Xuansha saw the tiger and looked back at the monk, saying, "It is you. When Dharma Master Lingrun was traveling through the mountains, a wild fire raged swiftly.
It flew toward him, and his companions fled from it. Yun’an walked as usual with a steady pace and said, "There is no fire outside the mind;

fire is truly from within the mind. If one thinks fire can be escaped, how could one possibly avoid it? As soon as the fire arrives, it is extinguished. Furthermore, regarding Master Yuande of Mount Lu:
at that time, Hu Ze occupied Jiujiang, and the general Cao Han led his troops across the river to enter [the area].
At the temple, the practitioners fled in alarm. The Master sat calmly as if it were an ordinary day. When Zhang Han arrived, he neither rose nor bowed.
Zhang Han rebuked him, saying, "Elder, have you not heard of the General who kills without blinking?
The Master stared at him intently and said, "How do you know there is no monk here who does not fear death? Such was his fearless nature; he was able to act in this way.
When one recites this sutra with the mind, the faculty of the eye naturally becomes pure. Otherwise, if there is even slight agitation, the eyes will grow dizzy and the mind will wander;
how then could purity be attained? Regarding the "inner and outer Mount Meru":
*Meru* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "Radiance," referring to the seven golden mountains. They are called "inner and outer" because these seven golden mountains consist of seven tiers.
Therefore, regarding the statement that "everything is manifested therein": as the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says, "All that is secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous is manifested within it.
This means that it does not merely manifest Mount Meru and other such forms internally and externally.
Furthermore, Constant Diligence, if a son or daughter of good family receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra,
they will obtain twelve hundred merits of the ear. With these purified ears, they will hear everything within and without the three-thousandfold world system,
from the Avīci Hell below up to the Peak of Existence above, including all the various seeds therein.
Various kinds of vocal sounds: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of oxen, the sound of chariots, the sound of weeping,

the sound of lamentation, the sound of conchs, the sound of drums, the sound of bells, the sound of gongs, the sound of laughter, the sound of speech, the voices of men, the voices of women, the voices of boys,

the voices of girls, the sound of the Dharma, the sound of what is not the Dharma, the sound of suffering, the sound of pleasure, the voices of ordinary beings, the voices of noble ones, the sound of joy, and the sound of lack of joy.
The sound of gods; the sound of nāgas; the sound of yakṣas; the sound of gandharvas; the sound of asuras; the sound of garuḍas; the sound of kiṃnaras; the sound of mahoragas;
the sound of fire; the sound of water; the sound of wind; the sound of hell-beings; the sound of animals; the sound of hungry ghosts;
the sound of bhikṣus; the sound of bhikṣuṇīs; the sound of śrāvakas; the sound of pratyekabuddhas; the sound of bodhisattvas.

Sounds. As for the voice of the Buddha—to speak briefly—within this trichiliocosm, all sounds, whether internal or external, he hears and knows them all with the pure, natural ears born of his parents, even though he has not yet attained the divine ear.
Thus he distinguished various sounds without impairing his faculty of hearing. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The ears born of one's parents are pure and free from turbidity or defilement; with these constant ears, one hears the sounds of the three thousandfold world-system:
the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and oxen; the sounds of bells, gongs, conchs, and drums; and the sounds of zithers, lutes, harps, flutes, and pipes.
Pure and beautiful vocal melodies, hearing them without attachment; the voices of countless kinds of people, all of which they hear and fully comprehend.
Furthermore, they hear the sounds of the various devas and their subtle, wondrous songs; as well as the voices of men and women, and the voices of boys and girls.
In the midst of mountains, rivers, and precipitous valleys, the cries of the kalaviṅka and other birds such as the jīvañjīvaka are heard;
likewise, the various sounds of agonizing suffering in the hells, and the voices of hungry ghosts, oppressed by hunger and thirst, crying out for food and drink.
When the various asuras dwelling on the shores of the great ocean speak among themselves, they produce a great sound;
yet the Dharma-preacher, abiding here in this place, hears these various sounds from afar without his faculty of hearing being impaired.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the cries of birds and beasts calling to one another—all these the person who preaches the Dharma hears therein.
Furthermore, the sounds of speech from the Brahma heavens—the Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven—hears them all.
The Dharma Master dwells here and hears them all. Whether the entire assembly of bhikṣus or the bhikṣuṇīs recite the sūtras or explain them to others, the Dharma Master dwelling here hears them all.
Furthermore, there are various bodhisattvas who read and recite the sūtras and dharmas, or explain them to others, or compile and interpret their meanings;
all such sounds they hear in their entirety. They also hear the great, holy, and venerable Buddhas as they teach and transform sentient beings.
Within all great assemblies, they expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma; those who uphold this Lotus Sūtra shall hear them all.
From the sounds within and without the trichiliocosm, down to the Avīci Hell and up to the Peak of Existence, [they shall hear them all].
They all hear their voices, yet their faculty of hearing is not impaired; because their ears are keen and sharp, they are able to distinguish and know them all.
Those who uphold this Lotus Sutra, though they have not yet attained the divine ear, achieve such merit with their ordinary, physical ears alone.

Next, the merits of the faculty of hearing are explained. These include the sounds of elephants, horses, and other vehicles; sounds of weeping, lamentation, and sighing that are disagreeable to the mind;
the sounds of conchs, drums, bells, and gongs, as well as the sounds of Dharma music; the sound of the Dharma; gentle, compliant, and soft sounds; sounds of non-Dharma;

sounds of greed, hatred, and strife; the sounds of the gods and those of the eight classes of beings below them; the sounds of the three calamities of fire, water, and wind; and the sounds from the hells below.
The sounds of the three miserable realms. Below "bhikṣu," [the sounds of] the two assemblies and the four noble ones. Those whose faculty of hearing is unimpaired hear them without attachment;
they are distinct and clearly discernible. In the verse, from "parents" downward, the sounds of the desire realm are praised.

"Countless kinds of human voices are all understood and comprehended" refers to mastery of local dialects. The kalaviṅka is the bird of beautiful song; the jīvañjīvaka... [is the bird that lives together].

The "Commanding Bird" [verse] follows; its various subsequent lines eulogize the sounds of the Form Realm. All subsequent lines eulogize the sounds of the two assemblies. Furthermore, there are subsequent lines that eulogize the voices of Bodhisattvas.
The lines following "All Buddhas" eulogize the sound of the Buddhas preaching the Dharma. The section beginning with "The Three Thousand" provides a general conclusion.

If the faculty of hearing has already attained such perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) upon merely entering the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), how much more so when entering the stages of the sages? Formerly, [this was taught by] Dongshan Qing...
Master Bing always remained in seated meditation. One day, he called his attendant and told him to go down to the Dharma Hall to see if there were any ants dragging wood that might damage the steps.
The attendant went out to look but found nothing; returning, he reported that there was no sign of anyone’s presence. Master Bing sent him back to search again.
As the attendant leaned over the eaves and looked down, he saw a swarm of ants dragging the wings of a dragonfly as they crawled up the steps. It turned out to be this.
When stillness reaches its ultimate limit, the spirit becomes aware.

Furthermore, those good men or good women who constantly exert themselves in diligence—whether they receive and uphold this sutra, read it, recite it, explain it, or copy it—will achieve eight hundred meritorious qualities of the nose. By means of this purified faculty of the nose, they shall hear...
Within the trichiliocosm, throughout its upper, lower, inner, and outer regions, there were various kinds of fragrances:

the fragrance of *sumanā* flowers, *jāti* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, *campaka* flowers, *pāṭala* flowers, red lotuses, blue lotuses, white lotuses; the fragrance of flowering trees, fruit trees, sandalwood, and aloeswood.

Incense: *tāmālapatra* incense, *tagara* incense, and ten million kinds of blended perfumes—whether in powder, pill, or ointment form—the one who upholds this sutra, while dwelling here, is able to distinguish them all. Furthermore, they specifically know the scents of sentient beings:
the scent of elephants, the scent of horses, the scent of oxen, sheep, and so forth; the scent of men, the scent of women, the scent of boys, and the scent of girls.
Fragrances of incense, as well as the fragrances of grasses, trees, and forests—whether near or far—all such fragrances can be smelled by one who upholds this sutra;

they perceive them all without error. Although such a person dwells here on earth, they also smell the fragrances of the various devas in the heavens, including the fragrance of the Pārijātaka and Kovidāra trees, as well as the fragrance of the Māndārava and Mahāmāndārava flowers.
He perceives the fragrance of *roha* flowers, the fragrance of *mañjūṣaka* flowers, the fragrance of great *mañjūṣaka* flowers,
sandalwood, aloeswood, various powdered incenses, and the fragrances of diverse blossoms— indeed, there is no fragrance produced by the blending of such celestial perfumes that he does not perceive.
Furthermore, he perceives the bodily fragrance of the devas, including Śakra Devānām Indra as he enjoys the five desires within his magnificent palace.
The fragrance when they sport; the fragrance when they preach the Dharma to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven atop the Hall of Wonderful Dharma;
the fragrance when they play in the various gardens; and the bodily fragrances of the male and female deities of other heavens—all these can be smelled from afar.

In this manner, proceeding successively even as far as the Brahma world, and ascending up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), the bodily fragrances of all those deities are likewise perceived. And...
They smell the incense burned by the devas, as well as the fragrance of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the bodily fragrance of the Buddhas;
they smell them all from afar and know their locations. Although they smell these fragrances, their faculty of the nose is neither impaired nor deluded.
If they wish to distinguish them and explain them to others, they remember them without error. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate...
Proclaiming this meaning, he spoke in verse:
"The nose of this person is purified; within this world, whether it be fragrant or foul substances, all varieties he perceives and knows."

Sumanā, Jāti, Tamāla, sandalwood, aloeswood, and cinnamon; the fragrances of various flowers and fruits, as well as the scents of sentient beings—men and women—the teacher of the Dharma, though dwelling afar, perceives their presence by smelling their fragrance.
The great powerful universal monarch, the minor wheel-turning kings and their sons, the ministers, and all the palace ladies—their locations are known by the scent.
The precious jewels worn upon their bodies, as well as the treasures hidden within the earth, and the precious women of the universal monarch—all are known by the scent.
The various articles for adorning the body—garments, necklaces, and the manifold perfumes applied to them—one knows their persons by smelling their fragrance.
Whether the devas are walking or sitting, playing or performing miraculous transformations, those who uphold this Lotus Sūtra can know it all by smelling their fragrance.
The flowers, fruits, and seeds of all trees, as well as the fragrance of ghee and oil—all these are known by the holder of this sutra while dwelling here.
In the deep and perilous places among the mountains where sandalwood trees are in full bloom, the sentient beings dwelling therein can all be discerned by their scent.
Regarding the Iron Ring Mountains, the great oceans, and all sentient beings within the earth, those who uphold this sutra will perceive their fragrance and know exactly where they are;
even when the asuras, both male and female, along with their retinues, are engaged in combat or sporting, these practitioners can know it all by means of their sense of smell.
In vast wildernesses and perilous narrow passes, whether there be lions, elephants, tigers, wolves, wild oxen, or water buffaloes, by smelling their scent one knows their location.
If there be those who are pregnant, before the sex of the child has been distinguished—whether they be rootless beings or non-humans—one can know them all by smelling their scent.
By the power of smelling fragrances, he knows when a woman has first conceived, whether the pregnancy will be successful or unsuccessful, and whether she will give birth in safety to a blessed son.
By the power of smelling fragrances, he knows the thoughts of men and women—whether their minds are stained by desire, delusion, or hatred—and he also knows those who practice virtue.
The various hidden treasures within the earth, gold, silver, and all manner of precious gems contained in copper vessels—he can know them all by their scent.
Regarding the various kinds of necklaces whose value no one can recognize, he knows their worth, high or low, as well as their origin and location, simply by smelling their fragrance.
The various celestial flowers, such as the māndārava and mañjūṣaka, and the pārijātaka tree—all these he can fully know by their fragrance.
The celestial palaces, distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior, and adorned with various precious flowers—all these he can fully know by their fragrance.

In the celestial gardens, the sublime palaces, and the various halls for contemplating the wondrous Dharma, he dwells in their midst and enjoys himself; by smelling their fragrance, he knows them all.
