Whether the devas are listening to the Dharma or indulging in the five desires, whether they are coming or going, walking, sitting, or lying down—he smells their fragrance and knows them all.
When celestial maidens are adorned with fine garments and fragrant flowers, as they move about and play, one can know them all by their scent.
In this manner, proceeding further upward even unto the Brahma world, one can know by scent those who enter and emerge from meditative absorption.
From the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens up to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra), he can perceive through the scent of their initial birth and their passing away.
As for the assembly of bhikṣus who are ever diligent in the Dharma—whether sitting, walking in meditation, or reciting the sūtras—he likewise knows them all.
Or perhaps beneath forest trees, they sit in meditation with single-minded concentration; those who uphold the sutras perceive their fragrance and know exactly where they are.
Whether the Bodhisattvas' resolve is firm as they sit in meditation, recite the scriptures, or preach the Dharma to others, those who perceive their fragrance are able to know it all.
Wherever the World-Honored One resides, he is revered by all; out of compassion for the multitudes, he preaches the Dharma, and by smelling their fragrance, he knows them all.
Sentient beings stand before the Buddha, and upon hearing the sutras, they all rejoice; practicing in accordance with the Dharma, he knows them all by smelling their fragrance.
Although they have not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted (anāsrava) dharma that arises in the nose, these upholders of the sūtra first obtain this mark of the nose.

Regarding the merits of the three types of olfactory faculties: *Jāti* is translated here as "gold coin flower" (*jina-puṣpa*); *Mallikā* is translated as "garland," so called because it can be made into a garland;
*Campaka* is translated as "yellow flower"; *Pāṭala* is translated as "scented flower"; and *Tamāla*... [is translated as] "dark-colored flower."

*Vada*: translated here as "nature" (*prakṛti*) and "stainless" (*vimala*). *Tagara*: translated here as "root-fragrance. "Blended fragrance" refers to the hundred-fold blended incense (*śatapākya-gandha*).

"Nine fragrances" refers to incense made from cakes. These are all the fragrances of flowers and trees found in the human realm. Furthermore, those listed below are all the fragrances of sentient beings.
"Holding these," etc., refers to the inanimate fragrances of the various devas. *Pārijātaka* is the [tree] of Śakra.
Before the palace stands the Pārijāta tree; its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves emit fragrance even against the wind.
The Kovidāra—here translated as the "Tree of Great Play"—is likewise mentioned below. There is the fragrance of the sentient beings of the various heavens;

the fragrance of pleasure and sport; the fragrance of lustful indulgence; the fragrance of preaching the Dharma; the fragrance of purity; and the fragrance of the Brahma-world, which is the fragrance of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
"And sound" below refers to the fragrance of the Dharma-body of the four noble ones. In the verse, "Sumanas" below praises the fragrance of insentient things;
"and knowing" below praises the fragrance of sentient beings. "Great power wheel-turners" refers to the Golden Wheel-turning Kings who rule over the four continents;
hence they are called the great and small wheel-turning kings, namely the Silver, Copper, and Iron Wheel-turning Kings who rule over three, two, and one continent respectively.
Therefore, it is said to be "small. The "treasure store within the earth" refers to a subterranean hoard (*nidhi*). The "jewel-woman" refers to the *strī-ratna* (the jewel of a woman).

"Knowing their location by smelling their fragrance" means knowing their whereabouts by perceiving their scent. "The various people" refers to the attendants of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
"Knowing their persons by smelling their fragrance" means knowing those individuals by perceiving their scent. "The various devas," or...
Whether walking, sitting, or sporting, one knows their movement or stillness by smelling their scent.
Whether asuras are fighting or sporting, one knows their anger or joy by smelling their scent. If there is a woman who is pregnant, one knows it all by smelling her fragrance;
by smelling her scent, one determines the form [of the child] and knows what the male or female child is contemplating. By smelling...
By smelling their scent, one knows their minds. Regarding those who know all hidden treasures among humans by smelling their fragrance:
by smelling their scent, one knows the objects. Regarding those who know various kinds of necklaces by smelling their fragrance: by smelling their scent, one knows their value.
From the heavens above, by smelling their scent, one knows the affairs of the desire realm. Likewise, from below, by smelling...

By smelling the scent, one knows the matters of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). As for "all those below," it means that by hearing their scent, one knows the matters concerning their progress and cultivation.

Furthermore, Constant Diligence: if a son or daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall obtain twelve hundred merits of the tongue. Whether things are good or ugly, beautiful or not...

Whether it be delicious things or various bitter and astringent substances that come into contact with his tongue-root, they all transform into the supreme flavor, like celestial nectar (*amṛta*), such that there is nothing that is not delicious.
If he uses his tongue-root to preach the Dharma within a great assembly, he produces a profound and wondrous voice that penetrates their hearts, causing them all to rejoice and experience happiness.
Furthermore, when the sons of gods, daughters of gods, Śakra, Brahmā, and the other devas hear him...
This profound and wondrous sound, whatever discourse or speech it may proclaim, is heard in succession by all who come to listen—
including nāgas and nāga maidens, yakṣas and yakṣa maidens, gandharvas and gandharva maidens,
asuras and asura maidens, garuḍas and garuḍa maidens, kiṃnaras and kiṃnara maidens, and mahoragas...
The *kumbhāṇḍa* women all came to attend upon him out of a desire to hear the Dharma, approaching him with reverence and making offerings. Likewise, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās;

kings, princes, ministers, and their retinues; minor wheel-turning kings (*cakra-vartin*) and great wheel-turning kings, together with their seven treasures, their thousand sons, and their inner and outer attendants—all mounted their palaces and came together to hear the Dharma. For this reason...
Because this bodhisattva skillfully expounds the Dharma, brahmins, householders, and all the people within the kingdom will attend upon and make offerings to him for as long as they live.
Furthermore, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas always delight in seeing him.
In whichever direction this person resides, all the buddhas will turn toward that place to preach the Dharma. He is fully able to receive and uphold all the Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, they are able to produce the sounds of the profound and wondrous Dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The tongue-faculty of such a person is pure; They shall never experience unpleasant flavors. Whatever they eat or consume, It all becomes nectar."
With a profound, pure, and wondrous voice, he preached the Dharma to the great assembly. Using various causes, conditions, and parables, he guided the minds of sentient beings;
all who heard him rejoiced and offered supreme offerings. So too did the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others.
All come together with a mind of reverence to listen to the Dharma. If this teacher of the Dharma wishes to fill the trichiliocosm with a sublime voice, he can achieve it at will.
Great and small wheel-turning kings, along with their retinues of a thousand sons, [all gather].
With palms joined in a heart of reverence, they constantly come to hear and receive the Dharma.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas likewise, with joyful hearts, always delight in coming to make offerings. So too do Brahmā, the King of Māras, Īśvara, and Maheśvara.

In this way, the hosts of devas constantly come to where they are; the Buddhas and their disciples, hearing the sound of their preaching the Dharma, always keep them in mind and protect them, sometimes even manifesting their own forms before them.
The fourth clarifies the merit of the tongue faculty. "If superior" reveals the merit of perceiving flavors; "if inferior" reveals the merit of preaching the Dharma.
It means that by means of the Dharma of a single flavor, it flows into the minds of sentient beings, causing them to give rise to joy.
Therefore, they all come to listen to the Dharma. Guizong said: "In other quarters there are five flavors of Chan; here, I have only one flavor of Chan.

This "profound and wondrous sound" refers precisely to this one-flavor Chan. Furthermore, from "Moreover, the various [beings]" below refers to the eight classes of beings listening to and making offerings to the Dharma;

from "and here" below refers to the fourfold assembly listening to and making offerings to the Dharma; and from "moreover, the various" below refers to the four types of sages who delight in seeing [the Buddha].
In the verse, "this person" is below; the hymn attains the flavor of the nectar of immortality. Because it is profound, it is below; the hymn expounds the Dharma of a single flavor.
A monk asked Chan Master Lingguan of Mount Wushi, "What is the Buddha? The Master extended his tongue and showed it to him.
The monk bowed. The Master said, "What did you see that you bow? He replied, "I thank the Master for showing me the mark of the extended tongue."
The Master said, "Recently, sores have grown upon this old monk’s tongue. This refers to the uttering of profound, pure, and wondrous sounds while preaching the Dharma to the great assembly.
Furthermore, as for 'constant vigor': if good sons or good daughters receive and uphold this sutra, whether reading it or reciting it..."

If one explains or transcribes it, one will obtain eight hundred merits of the body and attain a pure body like clear lapis lazuli, which all sentient beings will joyfully behold because of its purity.
When sentient beings in the trichiliocosm are born or die, [they shall see this body].
The superior and inferior, the beautiful and the ugly, those born in good realms and those born in evil realms—all appear therein.
Furthermore, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Mount Meru, Mount Mahāmeru, and all other mountains, as well as the sentient beings within them, all appear therein.
From the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra) above, everything and all sentient beings therein appear within it.
When the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas preach the Dharma, the forms and images [of those beings] all appear within one's own body.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
If one upholds the Lotus Sutra, their body will be exceedingly pure, like that clear lapis lazuli; all sentient beings will joyfully behold it.
Furthermore, like a pure, bright mirror, they see all forms and images within it; upon the Bodhisattva’s pure body, they see everything that exists in the world.
Only he alone understands it clearly; others do not see it. Within his body appear all the various forms within the three-thousandfold world system:
all living beings—gods, humans, asuras, those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—all such images manifest therein.

The palaces of the various devas, up to the Summit of Existence (bhavāgra), the Iron Ring Mountains (cakravāḍa), Mount Meru, Mahāmeru, and all the waters of the great oceans—all appear within his body.
So too do the Buddhas, the Śrāvakas, and the Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Buddha.

Whether alone or in the midst of a multitude, the teaching of the Dharma is manifested in all cases. Although they have not yet attained the subtle body of the dharma-nature that is free from outflows, because their essential nature is pure and eternal, everything is manifested therein.
Fifth, the merit of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). Regarding "attaining a pure body like clear lapis lazuli," an ancient master said:
"The entire great earth is, in its totality, a single body. It is transparent from within and without, like lapis lazuli.

All sentient and insentient beings—the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones—manifest within this body, just as images appear in a mirror. This is what is meant by the verse.
Within this, only one understands it for oneself alone while others do not see it; it is what is meant by "a fish drinking water knows its coldness or warmth for itself.
This pure and eternal essence is the dwelling place of the True Person of No Rank upon the mass of red flesh.
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
receives, upholds, reads, recites, explains, or transcribes this sutra, they shall attain twelve hundred merits of the mental faculty.
By means of this purified mental faculty, even upon hearing a single verse or a single phrase, they will penetrate immeasurable and boundless meanings and understand them.
Having mastered the meaning, he is able to expound upon a single phrase or a single verse for a month, four months, or even a year.
All the teachings he proclaims accord with their underlying significance and do not contradict the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Even when he speaks of secular scriptures, worldly discourse, or the arts of livelihood, all such things conform to the True Dharma. Within this trichiliocosm... [six]...
He fully knows the destinies of sentient beings, the movements of their minds, the activities of their minds, and the conceptual proliferations of their minds.
Although he has not yet attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), his faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) is thus purified. Whatever this person contemplates, [he knows it all].
All deliberated discourse is the Buddha-dharma; there is nothing therein that is not true. This is also what was taught in the sutras of former Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
This person’s mind is pure, clear, sharp, and free from turbidity or defilement. With this wondrous faculty of the mind, they discern dharmas as superior, middling, or inferior;
even upon hearing a single verse, they penetrate immeasurable meanings and explain them in successive order according to the Dharma, whether for a month, four months, or a year.
Within and without this world, all sentient beings— whether devas, nāgas, humans, yakṣas, ghosts, spirits, or others—
who dwell within the six realms of existence and harbor various kinds of thoughts, [the Buddha] knows them all at once through the retribution of upholding the Lotus Sūtra.

The countless Buddhas of the ten directions, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits, preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; [the practitioner] hears them all and is able to receive and uphold them.
Contemplating immeasurable meanings, they preach the Dharma in immeasurable ways, never forgetting or erring from beginning to end, because they uphold the Lotus Sutra.
They fully know the characteristics of all phenomena; they recognize their sequence according to their meaning; they penetrate names and language, and expound them exactly as they have been known.
Whatever this person speaks is entirely the teaching of the former Buddhas. Because they expound this Dharma, they possess no fear among the assembly.
The faculty of mind of one who upholds the Lotus Sūtra is purified to such an extent that, although they have not yet attained the outflows-free state (*anāsrava*), they already manifest such signs.
This person, upholding this sūtra, dwells securely in a rare stage; for the sake of all sentient beings, they are joyful and are loved and revered.
One is able to expound the Dharma through thousands of millions of skillful modes of speech by virtue of upholding the Lotus Sūtra.
Sixth, regarding the merit of the faculty of mind: eloquence resides in the mouth and mastery of meaning dwells in the heart;
thus, upon hearing a single phrase, one understands inexhaustible meanings, and having grasped a single principle, one can expound inexhaustible words. This is just as when a dragon king attains...
A single drop of water can give rise to clouds and bring forth rain. As the Great Sūtra says: "Within a single word or phrase, one expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras.
The section beginning with "All that which... clarifies his knowledge of the Dharma and his speech for governing the world.

Works such as the Five Classics and the Nineteen Histories, as well as livelihoods such as those of physicians, diviners, and various other miscellaneous professions—all these are said to accord with the True Dharma;
that is, they are in harmony with the Tathāgata’s True Dharma and do not contradict it.
Formerly, when Chan Master Panshan Baoji was walking through a marketplace, he saw a customer buying pork and said to the butcher: "Pure..."
Dige brought one *jin* of meat. The butcher set down his cleaver, joined his palms, and said, "Longshi, who among us is not refined?
At this, the Master attained realization. As with Panshan, it is said that even the language of worldly conventions accords with the Way.
"Three thousand [people]" below clarifies his discernment of the opportune moment (*jī*). That which the mind puts into practice is "action" (*xingye*). Mind...

That which is moved and acted upon refers to the formation of thoughts (*manasikāra*). That which the mind conceptualizes (*prapañca*) refers to the thought of what kind of speech one will utter from the mouth.
The passage beginning with "This person" explains that the raising of the mind and the movement of the tongue both accord with the Way of the Tathāgata.
In the verse, "knowing above and below" praises the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*); "this world" and so forth praise the knowledge of capacities (*nairmalya-jñāna*). Ten.
As he descended, he heard the Buddha preach the Dharma; he received, upheld, and contemplated it, and even when expounding it for the sake of the assembly, he was never mistaken.
To explain why his delivery was unerring: because he had received and upheld this sutra, he was able to know the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*);

because he knew the characteristics of dharmas, he was able to comprehend their meaning and intent; and because he comprehended their meaning and intent, he was able to recognize their sequential order.

Because of the sequential nature of consciousness, one is able to comprehend conventional designations (*nāma-pada*). Because of comprehending conventional designations, one is able to teach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.
Because one can teach the Dharma according to those capacities, even worldly speech accords with the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Because it accords with the True Dharma, one dwells among the assembly without fear. "Abiding in the marvelous stage" means that this [wisdom] is able to uphold the True Dharma.

As for the Dharma: its station is such that one walks hand-in-hand with all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, rising far above gods and humans, and being joyfully cherished and revered by all sentient beings.
The twentieth chapter, "Never Disparaging," states in verse:
A golden body was cast, ten fathoms tall; The heart is stable and firm, the feet are steadfast.
Fierce winds and torrential rains cannot blow it away or wash it off; how could knives or staves damage even a single hair?

Previously, wishing for the great Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and disciples gathered in the assembly to make vows and uphold this sutra, the Tathāgata cited his own past life as a king who endured suffering to seek the Dharma in order to encourage them. This was intended for the Bodhisattvas emerging from the earth...
Because Śāriputra made a vow to uphold this sutra, [the Buddha] further cites his own initial practice as a Dharma teacher—his patient endurance and upholding of the sutra—to encourage him;
thus, this chapter exists. Now, regarding the discussion of patience (*kṣānti*) in this chapter, it encompasses the practices of the three patiences and four joys.
Regarding the discussion of upholding the sutra, it reveals the benefit of even a single phrase of the entire scripture. Regarding the discussion of merit, it begins with the attainment of the six...
With the purification of the faculties, one ultimately attains unsurpassed bodhi. This single chapter subsumes the meaning of the preceding chapters.

Furthermore, while the preceding chapter clarifies that which is realized, this chapter clarifies the means by which it is realized. The person who realizes it is named "Ever-Venerable" (Sadāparibhūta);
because he honors the Dharma and respects persons, he does not give rise to contempt or arrogance. Because he is free from contempt and arrogance, he is able to practice.
"By practicing patience, one accomplishes bodhi.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta: "You should now know this:
if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who uphold the Lotus Sūtra, and if someone should revile, abuse, or slander them..."
If one slanders [this], one will incur a great retribution for sin as previously described.
As for the merit obtained, it is as previously stated regarding the purification of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, whereby one attains great power.

In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (*Vaiśvānara-rāja*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and Vidyācaraṇa-saṃpanna.
One who is perfected in conduct; a Sugata; one who understands the world; an unsurpassed being; a charioteer of men; a teacher of gods and humans; a Buddha; a World-Honored One.
The eon was named Free from Decline, and the land was named Great Achievement. In that world, the Buddha King of Majestic Sound preached the Dharma for devas, humans, and asuras.
For those seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths, delivering them from birth, old age, sickness, and death.

For those seeking ultimate nirvāṇa, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination. For those seeking to become pratyekabuddhas, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the twelve links of dependent origination.
For the bodhisattvas, based on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he taught the Dharma corresponding to the six *pāramitās*.

Having attained ultimate buddha-wisdom and great power, this was the Buddha King of Awesome Sound (*Vaiśravaṇarāja*), whose lifespan lasted for four hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sands of eons.
The kalpas of the *saddharma* (True Dharma) remaining in the world shall be as numerous as the atoms of one Jambudvīpa;

the kalpas of the *pratirūpakadharma* (Semblance Dharma) remaining in the world shall be as numerous as the atoms of the four continents. After that Buddha has brought great benefit to sentient beings, he will then enter parinirvāṇa.
Following the total extinction of both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, another Buddha will appear in this land, also named King of Majestic Sound (*Vaiśravaṇarāja*).
Come, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
In this sequence, there were twenty trillion Buddhas, all bearing the same name.

After the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound had first entered parinirvāṇa, and following the extinction of the True Dharma during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there were bhikṣus of overweening pride who possessed great power. At that time, there was a bodhisattva bhikṣu named Never-Disparaging.
He attained Great Power. For what reason was he named "Never Disparaging"?
This bhikṣu, whenever he saw anyone—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—would always prostrate to them and praise them, saying these words:
I deeply respect you all and do not dare to treat you with contempt. Why is this? You are all practicing the bodhisattva path and shall surely attain Buddhahood.
Yet this bhikṣu does not specialize in reading or reciting the sutras, but practices only prostrations;
even when he sees the fourfold assembly from afar, he still goes to them to prostrate and offer praise, saying: "I do not dare to treat you with contempt."
"Regarding you all: you shall all become Buddhas.
At that time, Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty was a śrāmaṇera and asked: "Do not seek by clinging to the Buddha; do not seek by clinging to the Dharma."
"Do not seek the Sangha. Elder, when you prostrate, what is it that you seek? The Master said, "Do not seek the Buddha. Do not seek the Dharma. Do not seek the Sangha.
Always perform your prostrations in this manner. Miyun asked, "What is the purpose of performing prostrations?
The Master then struck him with his palm. Miyun said, "That was too crude. The Master said, "What kind of place is this, where one speaks of 'crude' and 'refined'?"
[The Master] sighed. Thereafter, he folded his hands in greeting. Furthermore, when the Prefect Li Ao visited Yaoshan, the Master held a scroll and did not look at him.
An attendant said, "The Governor is here. The Governor was by nature impatient and narrow-minded, so he remarked, "Seeing the person is not as good as hearing of their reputation."
He brushed out his sleeves and departed. Shanshan said, "How can you, Prefect, value my ears while despising my eyes?
The Prefect asked, "What is the Way? Shanshan pointed up and down and said, "Do you understand? The Prefect replied, "I do not understand. Shanshan said, "Clouds in the blue sky; water in the jar.
Thereupon, the Prefect prostrated himself. These were all instances where they possessed the power of the Great Dharma before doing so.
He is one who is able to transform and bring forth those of great power. From the phrase "At that time" onwards, the name of the Bodhisattva is revealed.

Because he is a bhikṣu who practices the conduct of a bodhisattva, he is called a "Bodhisattva-bhikṣu. From the phrase "Attaining greatness" onwards, it refers to the fulfillment of his vow regarding his name;
for when the fourfold assembly of ordinary beings sees him, they all prostrate, praise, and regard him with reverence as if he were a Buddha—thus he attains this [name].
"Light" refers to the name. "Prostration" is the action of the body (*kāyakarman*). "Praise" is the action of speech (*vākkarman*). "Deep respect" is the action of the mind (*manaskarman*).
"Respect" means being focused on one thing alone without distraction. To say that respect is "deep" indicates the ultimate degree of respect. It means:
"My heart holds deep respect for you all," and thus it is manifested through the body and expressed through the mouth by performing prostrations.
This praise is not mere lip service while harboring inner malice, nor is it outward respect masking inward arrogance.
The reason I revere and honor you is that, in your daily activities—whether moving about, bowing, or rising, or in the manner of welcoming guests and seeing them off—you act with such integrity.
In every respect, there is not the slightest difference between his daily practice and that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
therefore, he will certainly attain Buddhahood in a future life. For this reason, I regard him with the same reverence as a Buddha, prostrating before him and offering praise.
Below this, the intent of the prostration and praise is further clarified: it is said that this bhikṣu does not focus exclusively on reciting the scriptures, but only...
Silently upholding a single verse and cultivating a single verse, he saw from afar the fourfold assembly prostrating and offering praise;
he then used that very same single verse to guide them. An ancient worthy said:
"It is easy to ascend higher step by step, but difficult to let go heart and mind with every thought. The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging was one who truly let go of body and mind.
Among the fourfold assembly, there were those who gave rise to anger and whose minds were impure; they reviled him with harsh words, saying, "This is an ignorant bhikṣu!
From where has he come? He says of himself, 'I do not slight you,' yet he bestows upon us the prediction that we shall become Buddhas.
We have no need for such false predictions. Thus it continued for many years, and they were constantly...
Even when reviled, he did not give rise to anger, but always spoke these words: "You shall become Buddhas.
While he was speaking these words, some among the crowd struck or threw him with sticks, wood, tiles, or stones; yet he would retreat to a distance and still cry out in a loud voice:
"I do not dare to slight you; you shall all become Buddhas. Because he constantly spoke these words, [his merit] increased.
Arrogant bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās addressed him as "Never-Disparaging.
This fourfold assembly reviled and abused him, saying: "He bestows upon us the Buddha-wisdom of equality, yet we consider him ignorant;
he tells us things that are true, yet we consider them false; he pays homage and offers praise..."
He praised it and offered it to him, yet the other instead gave rise to anger and added insults.
It is said that when a "night-light" gem is thrown at people, few do not draw their swords; how could this be limited to merely hearing it and disbelieving, or crying out in resentment?
That one does not give rise to anger despite being reviled for many years is because the Bodhisattva’s practice has reached maturity; even though he reviles me, I—
Respect them. Even if they insult me, I shall respect them myself. Never depart from this single verse, and always teach others by means of this single verse.
In the past, whenever Chan Master Puhua saw anyone, regardless of their status, he would ring his bell once;
sometimes he would bring the bell to the person's ear and ring it, or he would pat [them].
On his back, there was one who looked back and, stretching out his hand, said, "Give me a single coin.
This, too, was a way of guiding people with a single verse of *gāthā*. When the crowd heard this, their anger increased all the more;

they struck him even harder with sticks, wood, tiles, and stones—just as Bian He suffered three times for his jade offering and could not avoid meeting with punishment. Even though he fled and lived far away, he remained highly esteemed.
Regarding the one who utters sounds: when he approaches with anger, I respond with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
This cannot be accomplished by anyone who has not practiced the three kinds of patience (*kṣānti*), possessed the four joys (*sukha*), and attained the great power of the Dharma.

Furthermore, at Hanshan, while the assembly of monks was roasting eggplants, Hanshan took an eggplant skewer and struck one monk on the back. As the monk turned his head, Hanshan held up the eggplant and said, "This is it."
"What? the monk asked. "This madman," the monk replied. Shanshan said to a bystander, "Tell me, how much salt and sauce has this monk wasted?
Furthermore, when the assembly gathered at Guoqing Temple for the fortnightly recitation of the precepts, Shide clapped his hands and said:
They gathered together and formed a plan. [The other] asked, "How shall we proceed with that matter? The *karmadāna* rebuked them.

He replied, "For a virtuous one (*bhadanta*), the absence of anger is itself the precept; a pure mind is itself the renunciant life. My nature accords with yours; all phenomena are without difference.
This is what is meant by 'when anger arises, respond with compassion. Below this, he provides the reason for his name, saying: "We bhikṣus..."
He was constantly insulted and treated with contempt by others, yet he never once looked down upon them. For this reason, the fourfold assembly named him "Never-Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta).
This also serves as a depiction of the state of arrogance held by a monk of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) who has attained great power.
That Never-Disparaging was able to practice patience rested entirely upon the two characters for "profound respect. Had his respect not been profound, [he could not have endured].
If one cannot regard others as Buddhas, how can one endure their insults, blows from sticks, or pelted stones?

A saying goes: "When you step out the door, be as if seeing a great guest; when you employ the people, be as if presiding over a great sacrifice. The *Qulǐ* states: "There is nothing that is not revered.
This single word, "reverence" (*jing*), is the foundation for entering the path through the practice of Never-Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*). Nevertheless, if the fourfold assembly...
Among them were those of the highest faculties, such as Deshan, Linji, Yunmen, Danxia, and their like.
Even they did not always receive trivial prophecies of enlightenment, nor were they spared from being personally subjected to scathing rebukes and venomous insults.

When this bhikṣu was about to pass away, he heard in the midst of the void all twenty thousand koṭis of verses of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* previously preached by the Buddha Prabhūtaratna (Vaiśvānaranirghoṣa).

He was able to receive and uphold them all, and immediately attained the aforementioned purity of the faculty of the eye, as well as the purity of the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Having attained this purity of the six faculties, his lifespan increased further.
For two hundred trillion nayutas of years, he extensively preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for the sake of others.
At that time, the fourfold assembly of arrogant individuals—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—despised this man who had been given the name "He Who Is Not Disdained" (*Adhimāna*).
However, they saw that he had attained the power of great supernormal faculties, the power of eloquence in joyful exposition, and the power of great, sublime tranquility upon hearing [the teaching].

All who heard what he taught believed, submitted, and followed him. This Bodhisattva further transformed and guided thousands of millions of billions of beings, causing them to dwell in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
After his life ended, he encountered two thousand million Buddhas, all named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp).
Within their Dharma, he preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. By these causes and conditions, he again encountered two...
There were a thousand billion Buddhas, all bearing the same name, Cloud Sovereign Lamp King (*Meghasvaradīparāja*).

Because he had received, upheld, read, and recited this sutra within the teachings of these Buddhas, and had preached it for the fourfold assembly, he attained this constant purity of the eye, as well as the purity of the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
He preached the Dharma among the fourfold assembly with a mind free from fear, attaining great power; thus he was named Constantly Unafraid (*Sadāparibhūta*).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Light made offerings to as many Buddhas as these, honoring, respecting, and praising them, thereby planting various roots of goodness.
Later, he again encountered ten million billion Buddhas, and under the teachings of those Buddhas as well, he preached this sutra.
Having accomplished such merit, he shall attain Buddhahood and obtain great power. What do you think? At that time, Constant...
Was the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging anyone else? He was none other than myself.
Had I not, in previous lives, upheld, recited, and expounded this sutra for others, I would not have so swiftly attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because I upheld, recited, and expounded this sutra for others in the presence of former Buddhas, I swiftly attained it.

[They will attain] Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and great power. At that time, because the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—insulted me with thoughts of malice, they shall for two hundred billion kalpas never encounter a Buddha, never hear the Dharma, and never see the Saṅgha;
for a thousand kalpas, they shall undergo great suffering and affliction in the Avīci Hell until it is finished.
After these offenses were committed, he again encountered the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging, who taught him toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He subsequently attained great power. What do you think? Were those four assemblies who formerly habitually disparaged this bodhisattva anyone other than the five hundred bodhisattvas in this assembly, such as Bhadrapāla and Siṃhacandra? They are none other than these.
The five hundred bhikṣuṇīs and the five hundred upāsakas, including Mañjuśrī, are all those who are non-retrogressive from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* brings great benefit to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and is able to lead them to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should constantly receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and copy this sutra.
This statement—that he was not held in light esteem—shows that he obtained benefits in the present life. It says that this bhikṣu ordinarily performed nothing but prostrations.
Because he did not exclusively recite the sutras he had previously heard, they eventually fell into decline and were forgotten.

Therefore, at the time of his death, he was able to hear this sutra in its entirety and fully receive and uphold it. By virtue of receiving and upholding it, he immediately attained the purification of the six sense faculties and further increased his lifespan.
As for "extensively explaining it for others": whereas previously he had bestowed upon others a single verse (gāthā), here he bestows the entire [sutra].

Therefore, he extensively expounds and analyzes [the Dharma]. "At that time" and below refers to the fourfold assembly turning their minds [toward the path] and attaining great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), such as the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

"Eloquent skill in discourse" refers precisely to the extensive exposition and analysis of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. "The power of great, sublime tranquility" refers to [the fact that even when] reviled and insulted, [one remains unmoved].

This is precisely what is meant by being entirely unmoving. Thus, when first hearing [the teaching], he was subjected to humiliation; now, however, he has come to believe, comply with, and be tamed by it.
When first hearing it, he departed immediately; now, however, he follows it like a shadow follows a form. Having thus transformed the fourfold assembly, [he is] the Bodhisattva... below.
Furthermore, he transformed the remainder [of beings], so that they might see the vastness of transformation through the Dharma. After his life ended, they obtained benefit in future lives.
As stated in the "City of Transformation" chapter: when the Tathāgata was under the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he acted as a bodhisattva śrāmaṇera and preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This statement refers to his time as a bodhisattva bhikṣu preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* under the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa. This is sufficient.

Seeing the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestow the prediction of his own future Buddhahood was entirely a skillful means (*upāya*). A mind free from fear is the very root of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*);
therefore, this is brought forth to provide illumination and correspondence. "Attaining greatness" [refers to] attaining the fruit from the cause.

Regarding those who, having accomplished their merit, shall become Buddhas—this refers to the matter of upholding this sutra and acting as a Dharma-preacher. As for the completion of one's practice...

"Only when [the merit] is full will he realize the status of a Dharma King. From "He attains the Great... onwards, the text concludes by manifesting that his own attainment of Buddhahood was entirely due to the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* upheld while acting as a Dharma teacher at the outset.

The section beginning with "Thus ends the proof of the benefits obtained by Not-Light (Adhimātra-prasāda) for upholding the sutra" is followed by the section beginning with "At that time," which further proves the transgressions incurred by slandering the sutra. The phrase "With anger... indicates that the fourfold assembly, out of a mind of hatred...

Because they despised me, they constantly failed to encounter the Triple Gem. After suffering through the miseries of the three evil realms until their karmic retribution was exhausted, they again encountered the One Who Is Not Despised (Adhimātra).
Due to the causal conditions of their slander of the Dharma, they were reborn together with the Bodhisattva, who led them into Bodhi.
Question: It is certainly true that by having faith in the Buddha, one is reborn together with Bodhisattvas and receives the benefits of the Dharma; why is this so?
Therefore, even those who slander the Buddha may be born together with him and receive the benefits of the Dharma. Answer:

Just as taking bitter medicine cures an illness, or burning incense-resin produces fragrance, so it was that Bhadrapāla and others, though they reviled Never-Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta) for a thousand kalpas and suffered in the Avīci hell, encountered Never-Disparaging again once their retribution was exhausted; this was all due to the compassionate mind of the Bodhisattva reaching them.
Therefore, the name "Not-Disparaging" originated from the very day of his verbal abuse. If even through such abuse he obtained benefit, how much more so through respectful faith?
"Obtaining great [benefit]" is the summary concluding that both praise and slander yield benefit. To say "great benefit" means that disparagement and non-disparagement are equal and non-dual.
Those who have already obtained the great fruit through praise—those same individuals who were previously slandered shall likewise obtain it in the future.

The Buddha said: "Therefore, it is said that though one hears [this teaching], one does not believe it; yet by still planting the causes for the fruit of Buddhahood, one’s learning will eventually surpass the blessings of humans and devas.
Thus, if a bhikṣu does not single-mindedly receive and uphold this sutra, his days will pass in vain—what can be said of such a person?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past there was a Buddha named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja). His spiritual wisdom was immeasurable, and he guided all—devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits."
They were all offered joint worship. After that Buddha had passed into extinction, at a time when the Dharma was about to perish, there was a bodhisattva named Sadāparibhūta.
At that time, the fourfold assembly was attached to the Dharma; the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta went to where they were and spoke to them, saying:
"I do not slight you; all of you who practice the Way shall become Buddhas. When the people heard this, they reviled and abused him with insults.
The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging was able to endure them all. Once his transgressions were exhausted, at the time of his death, he was able to hear this sutra.
The six sense organs were purified. By the power of his supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), he increased his lifespan and further expounded this sutra extensively for all people.

All those who were attached to dharmas received the Bodhisattva’s teaching and transformation, achieving fulfillment and being established in the Buddha-way. Thus did Aśvaghoṣa (Not-Disparaging) pass away.
He encountered countless Buddhas; because he preached this sutra, he obtained immeasurable merit, gradually perfected his virtues, and swiftly attained the Buddha-way.

The phrase "and then acts" refers to the words of entrustment, intended to cause him to expand the family enterprise.
