From the stages of the śrāvakas up to the bodhisattvas on the level of equal enlightenment, none can attain it; only the Buddha alone attains it.
Therefore, it is called the "Dharma difficult to obtain. I now entrust this Dharma to you all; it is yours to possess.

You should, with a single mind, cause it to circulate, distribute it from one to another, and transmit it to others, so that it may increase and flourish widely and never be severed. This is the Tathāgata’s...
He has come to hand over this burden of a thousand *qīnjìn* to the great Bodhisattvas. Thus, he repeatedly exhorted them below.
Furthermore, he encouraged them not to be stingy and not to be afraid. "Not to be stingy" means that whatever one possesses should all be given;
one must not harbor any parsimony. "Not to be afraid" means that whatever is given should be given completely; one must not...
It is because they fear being impoverished. The wisdom of the Buddha consists of preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings to awaken them;

this is the wisdom of the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Buddha). The wisdom of the Tathāgata is that which has come from the path of suchness to achieve perfect enlightenment; this is the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* (Reward Buddha).
Natural wisdom is that which is inherently possessed from the beginning, not requiring cultivation to be perfected; this is the wisdom of the *dharmakāya* (Dharma Buddha).
Since the Tathāgata has acted as a great benefactor for all sentient beings, he now bestows this Dharma upon them.
You, too, should receive the Dharma from the Tathāgata and likewise bestow this Dharma equally upon others;
do not give rise to stinginess. Do not harbor thoughts of parsimony regarding what has been given. Whether they have faith or lack faith, you should simply speak the truth.
It is bestowed. Those who have faith possess sharp faculties and superior wisdom; for those who enter upon hearing it but once, it should certainly be bestowed directly.

Those who lack faith possess dull faculties and limited wisdom; for those who are unwilling to accept it, although it is not bestowed directly, one should nevertheless employ skillful means to lead them into other profound teachings, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them so that they may gradually attain this.
Sūtra: "If you are able to preach the Dharma with such equanimity as this, it shall be called repaying the Buddha’s kindness and virtue.

At that time, the various bodhisattvas below received and practiced [this teaching]. This repetition three times was in response to the meaning of the three times the Buddha had patted their heads in blessing.
"At that time," etc.: The Buddha’s work having been completed, he therefore commanded his emanations to each return to their own lands.
As for his further leaving behind Prabhūtaratna, it was because there were still bodhisattvas who sought to see him. "When this was said," etc.: The entire assembly rejoiced together.
The twenty-third chapter, "The Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja," states in verse:
"A disease in the vital organs (gāngū) is most difficult to cure; Yet it is dissolved while standing amidst the light of a blazing fire."
All dregs and skin have been incinerated, yet that single point within the breast has never been burned.
Previously, when he was a king, his own body served as a seat; when he was the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, he constantly practiced patience.
All of these are the Tathāgata’s own accounts of his past lives (*pūrvayoga*), intended to demonstrate that enlightenment is attained through upholding this sutra.
The following six chapters all describe the past lives of bodhisattvas; they serve as objects of faith for those who firmly uphold the sutra, encouraging them to emulate such examples.
What is called a "past life" refers to the planting of the roots of various virtues and the performance of the duties of a Dharma teacher. [The sutra] says... no further text.
It spans immeasurable kalpas, not merely one or two kalpas. As for why the "Former Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" is explained first:

it is because Bhaiṣajyarāja sacrificed his body for the sake of the Dharma; he is truly able to don the robe of patience, truly able to practice diligence, and truly able to perform the offering of the Dharma.
Therefore, he is mentioned first. To speak of his past events, this Bodhisattva was formerly named...
Starlight. Having heard the Buddha’s wisdom expounded by the Venerable Sūryagarbha, he offered medicinal herbs from the Snowy Mountains to the assembly of monks, vowing:
"May I, in the future, be able to cure the physical and mental illnesses of sentient beings. The entire world rejoiced and called him Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King).
If one speaks according to principle, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is itself the Medicine King; it can empty the two attachments and thereby—
This was for the purpose of healing the sick.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja travel through this Sahā world?
World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja possesses hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas [of attendants].”
“It is rare that he has performed such difficult ascetic practices. Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain this briefly.

May the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, as well as the bodhisattvas who have come from other lands and this assembly of śrāvakas, all hear it and rejoice. At that time, the Buddha told them:
In the past, O Bodhisattva Rājanāmanpuṣpa, immeasurable *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. That Buddha had eight hundred million great bodhisattvas.

Mahāsattva, there will be a great assembly of seventy-two *gaṅgā*-sands of *śrāvakas*. The Buddha’s lifespan shall be forty-two thousand *kalpas*, and the lifespans of the bodhisattvas shall be equal to that.
That land shall have no women, nor hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, or any other such difficulties.
The ground shall be level as the palm of a hand, composed of lapis lazuli, adorned with jewel-trees, and covered by jeweled canopies.
Above, jeweled flower-banners hang down, and jeweled vases and incense burners fill the entire realm. Platforms made of the seven treasures stand beneath each tree;
the distance from each tree to its platform is exactly one *jie* (a measure of distance). Beneath all these precious trees sit bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
Upon each of the precious platforms, there are ten billion devas who perform celestial music and sing praises.

The Buddha [accepted this] as an offering. At that time, that Buddha was preaching the Lotus Sūtra for the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, along with a multitude of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana delighted in practicing asceticism;
within the Dharma of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he practiced walking meditation with diligence, seeking Buddhahood with a single-minded focus.
After twelve thousand years had passed, he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms. Having attained this samādhi, his heart was filled with great joy, and he thought to himself:
"That I have attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms is entirely due to the power of having heard the Lotus Sūtra.
I shall now make offerings to the Buddha Sun Moon Pure Bright Virtue and to the Lotus Sūtra. Then...

At that time, he entered this samādhi. From the midst of the void, there rained down *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, along with fine powder of black *kālānusārin* sandalwood, filling the void and descending like clouds. Furthermore, there rained down the fragrance of *sāgara-cīna* sandalwood;
six *zhu* of this incense was worth as much as the entire Sahā world-system, which he used to make offerings to the Buddha. Having made these offerings, he spoke thus:

Having finished his nourishment, he arose from samādhi and thought to himself: "Although I have made offerings to the Buddha through my supernormal powers, it is not as good as making an offering with my own body.
He immediately consumed various incenses—sandalwood, *kunkuma*, *turuṣka*, *pīlu*, *bhallātaka*, and liquid aloeswood resin—and also drank the fragrant oils of *campaka* flowers.
After twelve hundred years had passed, he anointed himself with these fragrant oils.

Before the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he wrapped his body in celestial precious robes, drenched it in various fragrant oils, and by means of his supernatural powers and vows, caused his own body to emit a radiance that shone throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of eighty billion Ganges Rivers.
All the Buddhas therein simultaneously praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, this is true essence."

"Advance! This is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. It cannot be equaled by offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, powdered incense, unguents, celestial silks, banners, canopies, or even the sandalwood from this side of the sea.
Nor can it be matched by the giving away of kingdoms, cities, wives, or children. Good son..."
"Son, this is called the foremost gift; among all gifts, it is the most honored and supreme, for it consists of making offerings of the Dharma to the Tathāgatas.
Having spoken these words, they each remained silent. Their bodies then burst into flames and burned for twelve hundred years;
after that time had passed, their bodies were finally consumed.

To clarify the past life of the Bodhisattva and his causes from former times, the text employs the figure of Śubhavyūha to pose the questions. From the words "At that time" onwards is the formal response.

First, it clarifies the adornments of the kalpa and the land of the ancient Buddha. From the words "At that time" onwards, it next clarifies how the ancient Buddha preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for the sake of Priyadarśana.
He is named Priyadarśana because sentient beings were delighted to behold him due to hearing the wondrous Dharma.
If one’s heart is not permeated by the sublime Dharma, then one’s speech will lack flavor and one’s countenance will be loathsome; how could there be any joy in seeing such a person?
This is the first point. As for the person whom Sudarśana found beneficial—one who delights in practicing asceticism, enduring what is difficult to endure and performing what is difficult to perform;

one who is diligent in the practice of the path, exerting oneself tirelessly three times during the day and three times at night; and one who is single-mindedly focused—[he found such a person beneficial].

Those who seek Buddhahood concentrate their spirits and fix their wills, so that their minds are free from distracting applications. "Fulfilling twelve thousand years" means that by departing from present karmic activities, the faculties and their objects become pure.
The samādhi named "Manifesting All Physical Bodies" refers to the ability to manifest this very body according to the forms that sentient beings joyfully behold.
From the words "Having attained this... onwards, it describes knowing the Buddha's kindness and reflecting upon how to repay it.
Immediately he descended. First, he rained down flowers and incense as an offering. There are two kinds of sandalwood, white and black.
If one burns white sandalwood, it brings coolness to all who desire it. As for black sandalwood, its price is exceedingly high;

if even a single *zhu* is burned, its fragrance pervades a small thousand-world system (*sāhasra-lokadhātu*). Therefore, six *zhu* would suffice to fill a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*) with precious jewels.
This is simply beyond their reach. Following this, one next makes offerings with the body. One says:

"Although I may use my supernatural powers to rain down flowers and rain down incense as worldly offerings, it is not equal to taking this entire body as a single scroll of the Great Sūtra to perform a ritual offering.
*Kung-lu* (薰陸) is frankincense; *Tu-lou-po* (兜樓婆) is a grass incense; *Pi-li* (畢力) [is *bhallātaka*].
*Ka* (ka-śīra) is also called clove. *Agaru* (aloewood) originates from the banks of Lake Anavatapta;

if one pellet the size of a sesame seed is burned, its fragrance permeates the world of Jambudvīpa. *Guggulu* (resin incense) is pine resin. *Vāsaka* (perfumed incense) refers to drinking the oil of the incense.
Furthermore, for twelve hundred years, he caused the wisdom of the Dharmakāya and other qualities to permeate his flesh and bones and saturate his four limbs;
thereafter, donning the robe of patience, he naturally consumed his body with the fire of the power of supernatural faculties and vows.
Thus, his radiance shone throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of eight billion Ganges Rivers. This is what the ancient masters refer to as the "ten [stages]."
The two places where the traces of worldly distraction are forgotten and the pure radiance is emitted throughout the three thousandfold world-system are these very locations.

The place where one relinquishes body and life is precisely the moment when the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is transformed. Because one is able to relinquish the *ālayavijñāna*, there is no mark of self;
thus, one simply knows that the single mind seeks the Buddha, yet sees no mark of diligence. One simply knows that the entire body is the Dharma, yet sees neither body nor mind.
Because of these characteristics, the Buddha merely praised him, saying: "This is true diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata.
Nevertheless, when Medicine King burned his own body, did he perceive pain or not? If he perceived pain, he would be the same as ordinary beings;
if he did not perceive pain, he would be the same as grass and wood. Tell me, at that very moment, where was Medicine King?
[This concludes] the preceding section. From here on, the text truly manifests the offering of the True Dharma, which transcends all offerings of conventional dharmas.
Though a kingdom and city may be of great value, one who prizes a good reputation can relinquish them; though wife and children may be dear, one who values righteousness can abandon them.
Therefore, that which is most cherished is nothing other than this body; now it is abandoned for the sake of the Dharma.

Is this not the foremost of all gifts? Is this not the true offering to the Dharma? That his body burned for twelve hundred years and was only exhausted thereafter means that, by the fire of his supernormal powers and the force of his vows, [the fire] remained at the gates of the six sense faculties.
Through smelting, casting, and forging, the notion of a self (*ātman*) is finally exhausted. It was previously stated that he sought Buddhahood with single-minded devotion for twelve thousand years;
subsequently, he again consumed fragrant oil for one thousand two hundred years, and his body remained ablaze for one thousand two hundred years, providing illumination.
After the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had performed such a Dharma-offering, at the end of his life,
he was reborn in the land of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī. In the house of King Vimalaśrī, he manifested by sudden transformation, sitting cross-legged,
and immediately spoke these verses to his father:
"Great King, you should now know: while I was walking in meditation at that place, I immediately attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Bodies.
Through the diligent practice of great vigor, I relinquished my beloved body."
Having spoken these verses, he addressed his father, saying: "The Buddha Sun-Moon Pure Brightness Virtue still currently exists.

Having first made offerings to that Buddha, I attained the *dhāraṇī* for understanding the languages of all sentient beings, and I further heard this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, including eight hundred thousand million billion *nayuta*, *viṅkāra*, *bimbara*, and *akṣobhya* verses."

"Great King, I shall now return to make offerings to this Buddha. Having said this, he immediately sat upon a platform of the seven precious gems and ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees.
Arriving at the place where the Buddha was, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his ten fingers and toes in reverence, and praised him with these verses:
“Your countenance is most wondrous; your radiance illuminates the ten directions. I have previously made offerings to you, and now I come once more to behold you in person.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana had spoken this verse, he addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One still remains in the world. At that time, the Buddha Sun-Moon Pure Bright Virtue addressed the Bodhisattva Joyful Vision of All Sentient Beings:
"Good son, the time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived; the moment of my final extinction has come. You should prepare and arrange a seat;
this very night, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. He further commanded the Bodhisattva Joyful Vision of All Sentient Beings: "Good..."
"Good man, I entrust to you the Buddha-dharma, as well as the various bodhisattvas and great disciples, and the dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

I also entrust to you the three-thousandfold great thousand-world system made of the seven treasures, including the jewel-trees, jewel-terraces, and the attendant devas. Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, all my relics..."
"I also entrust this to you. You must cause it to be circulated and widely established with offerings; you should erect several thousand stupas.
Thus, after the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa had instructed the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, during the final watch of the night,
He entered into *nirvāṇa*.
Then, having been born in the land of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, he passed away and was reborn into the family of King Śuddhaguṇa.

This clearly demonstrates that from beginning to end, he never departed from the realm of pure virtue (*śuddhaguṇa*). In the verse, the line "I practiced walking meditation in that place" and so forth [refers to this].
This refers to the place of the sun, moon, purity, and brightness; it signifies the benefits gained through cultivation. Regarding "attaining the *dhāraṇī* that understands all languages":

because one has attained the *samādhi* of manifesting all physical forms (*sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*) and has further attained the *dhāraṇī* that understands all languages, one is able to manifest bodies according to the various types of beings and preach the Dharma according to their capacities. From the words "Great King" onwards, [it concerns] the unfulfilled original vows.

[The text] concludes. [The passage] "Re-considering the offering" and the verse "I have just now made an offering," as well as the long prose stating "The World-Honored One still remains in the world," all serve to manifest the intent of his returning.
From the words "At that time" onwards, the Tathāgata announces his parinirvāṇa; from the words "Furthermore, he commanded" onwards, he entrusts [the matter] to the royal family;
from the words "When I have passed away" onwards, he further entrusts posthumous affairs to them; and from the words "In this way" onwards...
He entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, seeing the Buddha’s passing into extinction, was overcome with grief and distress.
Out of longing and devotion for the Buddha, he immediately used *candana* sandalwood from this side of the ocean to construct a pyre and offered it to the Buddha’s body, cremating him with fire.
After his parinirvāṇa, they collected his relics and fashioned eighty-four thousand precious jars to erect eighty-four thousand stupas.
These were three worlds in height, adorned with ornate spires, draped with banners and canopies, and hung with various jeweled bells.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana thought to himself again: "Although I have made these offerings, my mind is still not yet satisfied."
"Excellent! I shall now further make offerings to the relics. He then addressed the assembly of all bodhisattvas, great disciples, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others:
"You all should be single-minded in mindfulness; I am now making offerings to the relics of the Buddha Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsa.
Having spoken these words, he immediately lit a hundred blessings before each of the eighty-four thousand stūpas.
He adorned his arms for seventy-two thousand years as an act of offering,
causing countless seekers of the śrāvaka vehicle and immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
and enabling them all to abide in the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms. At that time, the bodhisattvas, devas, humans, asuras, and others beheld him...
He was without arms; filled with grief, distress, and sorrow, he spoke these words:
"This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana is our teacher and the one who has instructed us, yet now he has burned his arms and his body is incomplete.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana stood amidst the great assembly and made this vow: "I have sacrificed both my arms; I shall certainly attain [the goal]."
"The Buddha’s golden body is real and not false; may my two arms be restored to their former state.
Having made this vow, his arms were naturally restored by the power of the Bodhisattva’s profound and thick merit and wisdom.
At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, celestial flowers rained down, and all humans and devas attained [realization].
"It is unprecedented. The Buddha told the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Ratnaśrī): "What do you think? Is the Bodhisattva 一切眾生喜見 (Sarvasattvapriyadarśana) anyone else?
He is none other than the present Bodhisattva 藥王 (Bhaiṣajyarāja). This is the one who gave up his own body as an act of giving."
In this way, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas.
If anyone should resolve their mind and desire to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they would be able to burn even a finger, or even a single toe of the foot.
Making offerings to a Buddha stūpa is superior to making offerings with kingdoms, cities, wives, and children, as well as the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system,
its mountains, forests, rivers, and ponds, and all manner of rare treasures.
This is the re-establishment of offerings. Sandalwood was piled up to serve as the requisites for the Brahma-body. This is the *dhyāpana* (cremation) rite transmitted by the Buddhas of antiquity.
After the fire was extinguished, he did not forget the entrustment; he constructed a stūpa with the intent of making offerings.
At that time, he offered his arm to the stūpa. Question: For what reason did he first offer his body to the Buddha and subsequently offer his arm to the stūpa? Answer:

For twelve hundred years he offered his body to the Buddha; this was to empty himself of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). Because the grasping at a self is coarse and manifest, it is abandoned first.
For seventy-two thousand years he offered his arm to the stūpa; this was to empty himself of the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Because the grasping at phenomena is subtle, it is abandoned later. Since the grasping at a self is coarse and manifest, it exists in all seven [previous] cases, and thus he is called "the Body" (*kāya*); whereas the grasping at phenomena is subtle...
Subtle. There are only six or seven [fingers], hence they are called "two arms. To cause no decline, the great assembly obtains benefit. At that time, below, the disciples were filled with sorrow.

At that time, below, *Priyadarśana* (Joyful Sight) made a vow: "If by giving up my arm I may attain Buddhahood," which means that by relinquishing attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), one will certainly attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Regarding the restoration of the arm after making the vow: it was seen that the Bodhisattva’s attachment to dharmas had already...

"Empty. All things revolve according to the power of one's vows. This indicates that what is brought about by the profound accumulation of merit and wisdom can be shifted at will, whereas it conversely reveals that those with shallow or inferior merit and wisdom cannot effect such shifts according to their hearts' desires. "The Buddha said, below," cites the past to corroborate the present. "That which, below,"...

This contrasts with the hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of difficult and painful practices mentioned in the preceding text, thereby highlighting that what is now described is but a single drop from the great ocean.

Because Śākyamuni, in former times when he was Prince Mahātejas, diligently made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas of the past, he swiftly realized Bodhi. Now, Bhaiṣajyarāja is able to sacrifice his body and...
Offering his arm to the Buddha, he may be known as a Bodhisattva who has entered the逆流 (*pratyāgama*, "counter-flow").

One must know that the relinquishing of one's body and arm is something that cannot be accomplished by one who has not truly attained the *dharmanidhyānakṣānti* (patience in the contemplation of dharmas). Therefore, the World-Honored One specifically brought this out.

Below the section on "Dharaṇīśvara," he exhorts people to burn their fingers. If there were indeed those who resolve to seek Bodhi, they would simply be unable to burn their bodies like Bhaiṣajyarāja.
One who would burn their arm is immediately able to offer a single finger to a stūpa; this also surpasses all offerings of precious jewels.
Why is this? Among all things in the world that are desirable, nothing is more precious than one's own body.

Thus, there are those who, even when offered the opportunity to pluck out a single hair for the benefit of the whole world, would still be unwilling to do so—how much less would they be willing to burn a single finger? Yet, such a person must truly perceive the reason why [the body] is so precious.
One must truly know that this body is not worthy of esteem and that desires are but empty; otherwise, what benefit is there in merely increasing one's suffering?
Yet, in these degenerate times, there are those who rely on such sophistry to seek fame—is their perversion not extreme indeed?

Furthermore, if there were someone who filled the three-thousandfold world system with the seven treasures and offered them as a gift to the Buddhas, great bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats, the merit obtained by that person would not equal that of receiving, upholding, and reciting even a single four-line verse of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*;
the latter’s blessings would be far greater. Somarāja, it is like all the rivers...
Among all the waters flowing in rivers and streams, the ocean is the foremost. This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is likewise so;

among all the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgatas, it is the most profound and vast. Furthermore, just as among all mountains—the earthen mountains, the Black Mountains, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, and the Ten Treasure Mountains—Mount Sumeru is the foremost, so too is this Dharma...
The Lotus Sutra is also like this: among all sutras, it is the most supreme. Furthermore, just as the Moon Deity is the foremost among all the stars, so too is this Lotus Sutra:
among the thousands of millions of various sutras and teachings, it is the most illuminating. Moreover, just as the Sun Deity is able to dispel all darkness, this sutra is also like this.

It is able to shatter all the darkness of unwholesome states. Furthermore, just as among all minor kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) is the most supreme, so too is this sutra; among all the scriptures, it is the most honored. It is also like Śakra.
Just as the King is the sovereign among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, so too is this sutra the king among all sutras.

Furthermore, just as the Great Brahmā King is the father of all sentient beings, so too is this sutra the father of all noble ones—those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those who have resolved to attain the mind of a bodhisattva. Moreover, just as among all ordinary persons, the *srotāpanna* is preeminent...
Just as among all beings, the Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, and Pratyekabuddha are the foremost, so too is this sutra.
Among all the sūtras and dharmas spoken by all Tathāgatas, or by Bodhisattvas, or by Śrāvakas, it is the most supreme.
Furthermore, anyone who is able to receive, uphold, and recite this sutra shall likewise be so among all sentient beings.
Among them, it is also the foremost. Among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the bodhisattva is the foremost;
this sutra is likewise so, being the most supreme among all sūtras and dharmas.
Just as the Buddha is the king of all dharmas, this sutra is likewise the king among all sūtras. O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, this sutra can save all beings.
Regarding "sentient beings": this sutra can cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and affliction.
This sutra can greatly benefit all sentient beings and fulfill their aspirations, like a cool pond that satisfies all who are parched with thirst;
like one who is cold finding fire; like a naked person finding clothing; like a merchant finding his master; like a child finding its mother.

Like one who has obtained a boat for crossing over; like one who has found a physician when ill; like one who has found a lamp in the darkness; like a poor person who has found treasure; like a subject who has found a king;
like a traveling merchant who has reached the sea; like a torch that dispels the gloom—so too is this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
It can cause sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and all ailments; it can untie all the bonds of birth and death. If a person obtains it...
If one hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, whether writing it oneself or causing others to write it,
the amount of merit obtained cannot be measured to its limit even by the wisdom of a Buddha when calculating its quantity. If one writes out this scripture, and offers flowers, incense, necklaces,
burning incense, powdered incense, ointment incense, banners, canopies, robes, and various kinds of lamps— such as ghee lamps, oil lamps, and lamps of various fragrant oils— at the eaves...
If one makes offerings of tagara oil lamps, sumana oil lamps, pāṭala oil lamps, vārṣika oil lamps,
and navamālikā oil lamps, the merit obtained will likewise be immeasurable.
The preceding passage spoke of the merit of offering one’s body and arms to the Buddha, which already surpasses all worldly offerings.
Below this, it further states that the gift of jewels filling the world-systems is not equal to the merit of upholding this sutra; thus, it employs analogies to explain this extensively.
First, it uses the ocean, mountains, sun, and moon as metaphors for this sutra, because this Dharma-nature is the most vast and profound ocean. This sutra is the merit...
Mount Deshan is uniquely lofty and towering; this sutra is the full moon, for it clearly teaches that sentient beings are themselves mind and themselves Buddha.
This sutra is the sun of wisdom, for it can shatter the dark gloom of the afflictions of the three poisons.
Furthermore, as follows, next the lords of the three realms are compared to the Wheel-Turning Sage King, who is the most noble among human kings.
Robes and grain are scattered about; this sutra is the crest-jewel of the Wheel-Turning King, for it is honored wherever it is found.
Śakra is the supreme sovereign of the desire realm, presiding over those who dwell upon the earth; this sutra is the secret treasury, for it presides over all scriptures.
Just as Mahābrahmā is the progenitor of humanity, this sutra is the father of all noble sages (*ārya*),
for all noble sages flow forth from this sutra. Furthermore, as below,

just as the *pratyekabuddha* is likened to the foremost of the four fruits of the path among world-transcending noble ones, this sutra is the most supreme Dharma, for it stands at the head of all dharmas.
The Bodhisattva is the foremost among the two vehicles; this sutra is the teaching for Bodhisattvas because it is not shared with the two vehicles.
Just as the Buddha is the Dharma King, so this sutra is the Supreme Vehicle among all vehicles. [End of] "The Former King. Below.
Furthermore, using analogies that are most essential and urgent for the world: because this sutra possesses the power of great wisdom, it can save sentient beings;
because this sutra possesses the bliss of great nirvana, it can free them from suffering and affliction;
because this sutra is an inexhaustible treasury, it can benefit all sentient beings; and this sutra is like a pool of cool water, which enables those who are parched and exhausted...
All shall obtain the supreme flavor of ambrosial *amṛta* and *sarpis*, for their entire bodies will be cooled.
This sutra is like fire, for it can cause the sparks of wisdom to burst forth from cold ashes and withered wood.

This sutra is like clothing, for it enables those who lack the adornment of merit to don the robes of the Tathāgata. This sutra is like a master, for it can cause the blue sky and bright sun to play...

The "Essential Spirit" (Soul) refers to the recognition of the True Lord; thus, this sutra is like a mother, for it enables those who have strayed weakly into foreign lands and do not know their way home to find a compassionate mother.
This sutra is like a ship, for it can carry sentient beings to the other shore.
This sutra is like a physician, for it can cure the diseases of body and mind of sentient beings. This sutra is like a lamp, for it can destroy birth and death.
Because it dispels the darkness of the long night, this sutra is like a treasure; because it enables the impoverished son to obtain whatever he requires as he wishes, this sutra is like a king;
because one may rely upon the King of Great Vows amidst the sufferings of birth and death, this sutra is like the ocean;
because one obtains the jewel of great wisdom within the sea of afflictions, this sutra is like a torch; and when the flame of wisdom flares up once, ignorance is instantly extinguished.
Therefore, "freedom from all suffering" refers to the five signs of decay and the eight types of suffering; "all illnesses and pains" refers to the two types of illness, those of body and mind;
and "all bonds of birth and death" refers to the single cycle of birth and death consisting of both the fragmented and the transformative.
Although various metaphors have been presented above to clarify this Dharma, in the end, no analogy can fully reach it. Thus, the Great Sūtra says: "The Buddha..."
The Tathāgata has used all manner of analogies to explain various matters, yet there is no analogy capable of illustrating this Dharma.
Why is this? Because it transcends the pathways of mind and intellect, being inconceivable. As the ancient masters have said:
"The upward path is not transmitted by the thousand sages; students exhaust their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections. This is precisely the meaning. If a person...

Below: This reveals the merit of transcribing this sutra. If one were to discuss the merit of transcribing this sutra, even employing the wisdom of the Buddha to calculate and deliberate upon it, one could not know its limits; how much less so for others? Furthermore, below:
This also reveals that the merit obtained from transcribing this sutra and making various kinds of offerings thereto is likewise immeasurable. Pali.
*Śirīṣa* means "flower blooming in summer. *Nāga* means "various flowers. *Mallikā* is the same as *malli*. [This is] the Flower of the Constellation King (*Nakṣatrarāja*).
If there are those who hear this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," they shall likewise attain immeasurable and boundless merit.
If there are women who, upon hearing this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," are able to receive and uphold it...
These [beings] shall all exhaust this female body and never again receive one. If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years,
there should be a woman who hears this sutra and practices according to its teaching, at the end of her life here she will immediately go to the world of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*),
the dwelling place surrounded by Amitābha Buddha and the assembly of great bodhisattvas, and be born within a lotus flower upon a jeweled throne.
Above, he is no longer afflicted by desire, nor is he afflicted by hatred or delusion, nor is he afflicted by the defilements of pride, envy, and so forth.
He attains the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained this patience, his faculty of the eye becomes pure. With this purified faculty of the eye, he sees seven million two thousand billion [buddhas].
At that time, as many Buddhas and Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in ten billion Ganges Rivers spoke in unison from afar, praising him:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha."
If one contemplates this sutra and explains it to others, the merit obtained will be immeasurable and boundless. Fire cannot burn it;
water cannot wash it away. Even if a thousand Buddhas were to speak of your merit together, they could not exhaust it.
You have now been able to defeat the thieves of Māra, destroy the army of birth and death, and utterly annihilate all other enemies. Good son, [a hundred...]
A thousand Buddhas, by means of their supernatural powers, shall together protect you. Among all the devas and humans in every world, there is no one like you, except for the Tathāgata.

As for all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even bodhisattvas, none possess wisdom or meditative concentration equal to yours. O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, this bodhisattva has accomplished such merit as this.

By the power of virtue and wisdom, if there is anyone who, upon hearing this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," can rejoice in it and praise it as excellent, that person shall in this present life constantly emit the fragrance of blue lotuses from their mouth, and from the pores of their body shall constantly emit the fragrance of ox-head sandalwood.
The merit they obtain shall be as described above. Therefore, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, [you should know this].
I entrust this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Medicine King Bodhisattva" to you.
After my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, you must cause it to be widely proclaimed and circulated throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted.
Let not evil Māras, their followers, nor gods, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and the like, find any opportunity to prevail. Śrīgarbha, you should employ your supernormal powers—
[Exert] power to protect this sutra. Why is this? This sutra is the excellent medicine for the illnesses of the people of Jambudvīpa.
If a person has an illness and hears this sutra, the illness will immediately be extinguished, and they shall neither grow old nor die. Suvarnaprabhāsa, [this is so].
If you see anyone who upholds this sutra, you should take blue lotuses filled with powdered incense and scatter them upon that person.
Having scattered them, you should form this thought: "This person will, before long, surely take grass and sit at the site of enlightenment."
One shall vanquish the armies of Māra, blow the Dharma conch, and beat the great Dharma drum to deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of old age, sickness, and death.
Therefore, those who seek the Buddha-way, upon seeing anyone who upholds this sutra, should give rise to a heart of such reverence.
When this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva" was being preached, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas...

He has attained the *dhāraṇī* for understanding the languages of all sentient beings. Within the jeweled stupa, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna praised the Bodhisattva Rājādhiśvaraguṇasāgaravairocana, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Rājādhiśvaraguṇasāgaravairocana!
You have accomplished inconceivable merit that you are able to ask Śākyamuni Buddha about such matters, thereby benefiting immeasurable multitudes."
Sentient beings.
The preceding section clarified the merit of receiving, upholding, transcribing, and making offerings to the entire sutra;

here, it is further specifically shown that the merit of hearing and upholding even a single chapter is likewise immeasurable, for this single chapter also encompasses the entirety of the sutra. Not only...
This single chapter encompasses the entire sutra; indeed, even the two characters "Medicine King" (Bhaiṣajyarāja) encompass the entire sutra.

The passage beginning with "If there are... further reveals the merit of women who, in their present life, uphold this chapter. As for the statement that these are all women who will not receive [the teaching] again:
it is because women have many worldly attachments to children and grandchildren, and thus tend toward excessive craving; therefore, upon hearing of the Medicine King—
As for "wind," it means that one immediately attains the transformation from female to male and becomes endowed with the marks of a man. Why is this?
Because it is not possible for one who has not abandoned the body and abandoned the arm—a great man of the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena—to achieve this.
As follows, it further reveals the merit of practicing this sutra in the final age. Regarding "at the end of life, one is born in Sukhāvatī": it means one is able to abandon the Sahā world.

Because it is the most beloved object and the most beloved body, one is not moved by the root or secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*), and thus attains the bodhisattva’s playful supernatural powers (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*).

Furthermore, one attains the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and attains the purification of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya-pariśuddhi*).
From this point downward, it also signifies the severance of the innate dual grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) associated with the seven consciousnesses; thus, one attains vision.
The Buddhas, from afar, offered their praise, saying: "You, within the assembly of Śākyamuni, have upheld this sutra and expounded it for others.
The merit you have thereby obtained is immeasurable; it is ultimate, firm, and indestructible.
It is not like the conditioned merits performed in the past, which can be rotted or destroyed by water or fire. Why is this?
For this reason, you have already been able to destroy the demon of the five aggregates and slay the thieves of affliction. Furthermore, it is said:
"Because you uphold this sutra, not only will all the devas protect you, but all the Buddhas shall likewise protect you together;
for this Dharma is that which all Buddhas guard with their mindful concern, as you have already been able to accomplish the great merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata."
Because all devas and humans cannot equal it; because all worthy and noble ones cannot equal it.
Furthermore, this clarifies the merit of hearing this chapter and rejoicing in its excellence: fragrance issues from the mouth, and fragrance arises from the pores.
Because he has attained the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s fivefold Dharma-body, [the Buddha] first entrusts the text to Śuddhipanthaka;
next, he entrusts the entire sūtra to him; and finally, he entrusts those who uphold the sūtra to him.
Having spoken thus, [he describes] the benefits gained by hearing the sūtra: one attains the *dhāraṇī* that understands all languages.
"Ni" (尼) refers to that which the Medicine King attained. "Many Treasures praises the former king" signifies his appreciation for his excellent questioning and the great benefit it brings.
