The twenty-fourth verse of the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound" states:
"The Brahma-voice is profound and wondrous, its fruit difficult to transmit; It is like a flute or pipe that does not move, yet produces sound without plucking strings."
With a light snap of his fingers behind one's back, ten thousand mountains vied in resonance before the bright moon.

This chapter discusses the past life of Gadgadasvara (妙音). In the past, Gadgadasvara made offerings to the Buddha Meghadundubhisvara (雲雷音佛) with a hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments and eighty-four thousand bowls of the seven precious gems; as a result, he attained this foremost subtle [voice].
The Venerable Miaole attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies; thus, he was able to manifest various bodies from a single body and preach various dharmas with a single voice.
Although this Bodhisattva resided in a pure land, his intention was set upon Sahā World;
therefore, Śākyamuni Buddha summoned him with light, and it was also for the sake of the earth-emerging Bodhisattvas who were previously in the lower regions.
He has long dwelt in the joy of the empty sky and in tranquility, taking no pleasure in the realms of humans or devas. It is only now that he has first made the vow to uphold this sutra;
yet, fearing he might not be able to persist for long, the Tathāgata has summoned him here to meet with the bodhisattvas of this land, thereby strengthening his resolve to uphold the sutra.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the radiance from the *uṣṇīṣa*—the mark of a great man—and emitted the light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
This light shone throughout worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of one hundred and eight million *nayuta* Ganges Rivers.
Beyond that number, there was a world named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhālaṃkāra*). In that land, there was a Buddha named Pure...
The Tathāgata Padmashri-rāja-jñāna— the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct,
the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One—

was surrounded by a respectful assembly of immeasurable and boundless bodhisattvas as he preached the Dharma. The light from the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows of Śākyamuni Buddha shone everywhere.
In that land—at that time, in the realm of Universal Pure Light Adornment—there was a bodhisattva named Gadgadasvara.
Having long ago encountered the roots of all virtues, he had made offerings to, drawn near to, and served immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas;
he had fully accomplished profound wisdom and attained the Samādhi of the Wondrous Banner Sign, the Lotus Samādhi, and the Samādhi of Pure Virtue.
The *Rājanirghoṣa* samādhi; the *Animitta* samādhi; the *Jñānamudrā* samādhi; the *Sarvasattvarutakauśalya* samādhi;
the *Sarvaguṇasaṃcayā* samādhi; the *Vimala* samādhi; the *Abhijñāvikrīḍita* samādhi; the *Prajñāulkā* samādhi; the *Vyūharāja* samādhi;
the *Vimalaprabha* samādhi; the *Vimalagarbha* samādhi; and the *Asādhāraṇa* [samādhi].
The Samādhi of Illumination, the Samādhi of the Revolving Sun, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great samādhis equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River—
Śākyamuni Buddha shone his light upon his body.
He manifested the marks of a Great Man. As for the radiance from his *uṣṇīṣa*, he wished to show people the great fruit realized by the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, as for the emission of light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, he wished to show people the great cause cultivated by the Bodhisattva.
The former light shone universally throughout eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction; this was intended to break the [attachment to] the quiescence maintained by the Śrāvakas.

This refers to the aggregates and elements. Now, these two lights shine universally throughout the Buddha-lands of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of one hundred and eight myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Ganges Rivers.
This signifies that the bodhisattvas who uphold this sutra shall exhaustively destroy the ignorance that is as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Following this, there is a world named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhā-vyūha*), which signifies the exhaustive destruction of the sands of [ignorance].
Only when ignorance is eliminated can the world be attained as a land of tranquil light, purely adorned with pure radiance.

The Buddha’s name is Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (Śubhavyūha-tārā-rāja-jñāna). By purifying the obstacles of the dharmas, one attains conduct that is unstained and wisdom that is unattached, thereby becoming a Dharma-body Buddha.
That Śākyamuni’s light illuminates that land signifies that the ultimate fruition is identical [to his].
This is the realization. From "At that time" onwards, it reveals the root of virtue of Subhūti’s wondrous voice, which is the root of merit from making offerings to all Buddhas;
it is the root of wisdom through the accomplishment of wisdom. Because he realizes immovable wisdom within the cave of ignorance, he is called "Wondrous Banner" (Miaodang).

Because the lotus-flower of his mind has blossomed, encompassing and containing all phenomena, he is called "Dharma-Lotus" (Fahua). Because he enters among all classes of beings without the slightest defilement...

He is called Pure Virtue (*śuddhaguṇa*). Because he wanders through all lands without the slightest attachment or dwelling, he is called King of the Pastimes of the Constellations (*nakṣatrarājavihārin*).

Because he is beyond thought and deliberation, he is called Without Conditions (*anupalaṃbha*). Because he responds according to the stimulus and accords with the occasion, he is called Seal of Wisdom (*jñānamudrā*).

Because he fully understands the languages of both similar and dissimilar classes of beings, he is called Understanding All Languages (*sarvabhāṣāvidhijña*). Because he has accumulated all great and small virtues, he is called... [the name continues].
It gathers all merits; it enters the five turbidities without being defiled, and is therefore called "Pure.

It comprehends all marks without leaving a trace, and is therefore called "Liberation through Play. All darknesses are shattered, and is therefore called "Wisdom Torch. All myriad virtues are complete, and is therefore called "Adorned King.
Mirror-like wisdom is perfectly luminous, and is therefore called "Treasury of Pure Radiance. Consciousness is pure, and is therefore called...

Vimalagarbha has attained the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) of the Tathāgata; therefore, he is called "Incomparable Chariot. Because the Tathāgata possesses the inexhaustible wheel, he is called "Sun-Turning.
By means of this, the Bodhisattva turns the sixteen minds and accomplishes the sixteen great samādhis.
Through these samādhis, he further attains hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of samādhis, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. This is the light of Śākyamuni and...
As for his body, his mind was focused on this.
He then addressed the Buddha Pure White Flower Constellation King Wisdom, saying, "World-Honored One, I shall go to the Sahā world to pay homage,
draw near to, and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, and to see the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince."
[Sā. Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, Bodhisattva Śūradatta, Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, Bodhisattva Viśiṣṭacāritra, Bodhisattva Vyūharāja, and Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
At that time, the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña addressed the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara:
"Do not despise that land, nor conceive thoughts of it as inferior. Son of good family, that Sahā world is uneven—"
"It is uneven; the mountains of earth and stone are filled with filth and impurity.

The Buddha’s body is short and small, and the forms of the assembly of bodhisattvas are likewise small, whereas your body is forty-two thousand yojanas in height, and my body is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas."
Your body is foremost in its perfect symmetry; you possess hundreds of thousands of millions of merits, and your radiance is exceptionally sublime. Therefore, go, and do not disparage that land.
If one conceives thoughts of inferiority toward the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or their buddha-fields, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara addressed his Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, my journey to the Sahā world is entirely through the power of the Tathāgata and the supernatural transformations of the Tathāgata."
He sports in play. Adorned with the merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata, his wondrous voice and fragrance were in perfect harmony;
thus he understood the intention of Guangguang. Consequently, he resolved to make offerings to the Buddha and desired to meet the bodhisattvas of this land;
therefore, he addressed the Buddha and requested to go. From the passage "At that time" down to the instruction to Gadgadasvara.
A Bodhisattva of the Pure Land, wishing to enter a defiled land, fears that their mind might harbor dualistic perceptions; therefore, they are cautioned and exhorted:
"When you go to the Sahā world, do not conceive thoughts of inferiority because the Buddha-land is defiled, nor thoughts of contempt because the Buddha’s body is small.
The body of a Bodhisattva is forty-two thousand *yojanas* in height, whereas the body of the Buddha is six million eight hundred thousand *yojanas*."
These ten [marks] are all what are called the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).

The Tathāgata, wishing to cause the Bodhisattvas who uphold this sutra in this land to give rise to joy and admiration by displaying the marks of a Great Man of the floating world, therefore emitted the light and marks of a Great Man to reach them.
Following the passage on "Wondrous Sound" (*Ghoṣadatta*), he attributes the credit to his teacher, saying: "Today, I have set out from my starting point."
In coming to this Sahā world, we all rely upon the power of the Tathāgata’s playful manifestation of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhivikrīḍita*).
Even that my own body is upright, radiant, and exquisite is due to the adornment of the Tathāgata’s merit; it is not something I possess.
How could I dare to give rise to thoughts of contempt or inferiority?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, without rising from his seat and without moving his body,
entered into samādhi. By the power of this samādhi, not far from the Dharma-seat on Vulture Peak, he manifested eighty-four thousand lotus flowers made of various jewels,
with stems of Jāmbūnada gold, petals of white silver, filaments of diamond, and *cintāmaṇi* gems.
[The lotuses] had pedestals made of it. At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, seeing these lotus flowers, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions has this omen first appeared?
There are many tens of millions of lotus flowers, with stems of Jāmbūnada gold, leaves of white silver, filaments of diamond, and pedestals made of *cintāmaṇi* (true-kinsman) jewels."

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara wishes to come from the land of the Buddha Puṣpadhvajarāja to this Sahā world, surrounded by eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas, in order to make offerings to, draw near to, and pay homage to me; he also wishes to make offerings to and listen to the Dharma."

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness has this bodhisattva planted, and what merits has he cultivated, that he is able to possess such great power of supernatural penetration? What samādhi does he practice?
We pray that you will tell us the name of this samādhi; we also wish to diligently cultivate its practice. By practicing this samādhi, one is then able to see this."

"Bodhisattva, regarding his physical appearance, stature, and deportment—whether moving or standing still—I only pray that the World-Honored One will, by means of his supernatural power, cause that bodhisattva to come so that I may behold him. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"This Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who entered parinirvāṇa long ago, shall manifest his form for you all. Then, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed him:
"Bodhisattva, noble son, come! Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, wishes to see you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land and set out together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas.

As they passed through various lands, the earth shook in six ways, and rains of seven-jeweled lotuses fell everywhere; hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments played without being struck.
He resounded spontaneously. This Bodhisattva’s eyes were like the petals of a vast blue lotus;

even if a hundred thousand million moons were gathered together, his countenance would be more upright and handsome than that. His body was of true golden color, adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits.
His majestic virtue was blazing and his radiance was brilliant; he was fully endowed with all the marks, as firm and solid as Nārāyaṇa.
He entered a tower made of the seven treasures and ascended into the void, remaining at a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground.
Surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas who paid him respectful homage, he came to this Sahā world and arrived at Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*).

Having arrived, he descended from the seven-treasure tower and, taking a necklace worth hundreds of thousands, went to the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet.

Having prostrated at the Buddha's feet and offered him a necklace, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom sends his greetings to the World-Honored One.
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?
Are your four elements in harmony? Can you endure worldly affairs? Are sentient beings easy to deliver? Are they free from excessive greed, anger, ignorance, jealousy, stinginess, and pride?"

"No. There are none who are not filial toward their parents, nor those who do not revere śramaṇas, nor those with wrong views or unwholesome minds, nor those who do not restrain the five sensory faculties.
"World-Honored One, can sentient beings subdue all Māras and enemies? "The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, who entered parinirvāṇa long ago, dwells within a stupa made of the seven treasures;
does he come to listen to the Dharma? [He replied: "Furthermore, I inquire after the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna: Is he at ease, free from affliction, and able to endure [all things]?"
“Do you dwell here long? World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna; I only pray that the World-Honored One will show me so that I may see him.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha said to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, “This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara wishes to meet you.
Then, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed Gadgadasvara, saying, “Excellent, excellent! You are able to make offerings to Śākyamuni.”
Because he has heard from the Muni Buddha and listened to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and because he has seen Mañjuśrī and the others, he has come here.

This is the manifestation of the seat by Gadgadasvara. As for the eighty-four thousand lotus flowers made of various jewels that he manifested before the Dharma-seat, these were also accomplished through eighty-four thousand merits; therefore, they were manifested according to his thought.
"The wondrous lotus flower" refers not to an ordinary worldly lotus. The passage beginning with "At that time" asks about the causes and conditions of the auspicious omen;

the passage beginning with "At that time" answers regarding the causes and conditions of the auspicious omen. The section beginning with "Mañjuśrī" asks for permission to see us on behalf of those who also wish to diligently practice the path;
this is an indirect and subtle way of stirring the hearts of the assembly. Mañjuśrī seeks an audience with Gadgadasvara, yet the World-Honored One does not [grant it].

As for the fact that it was the past Prabhūtaratna who was summoned rather than Śākyamuni himself: once Śākyamuni had summoned him with his light and he had appeared upon his seat, his failure to arrive immediately must have been due to some expectation on his part.
Śākyamuni, anticipating this intention, therefore ordered Prabhūtaratna to summon [the other] again. "Come, son of good family," he said;
thus both Prabhūtaratna and Gadgadasvara were seen, and although separated by many hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of lands, they appeared as if they were right before one's eyes.

Facing [the Buddha], the arrival of Gadgadasvara together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas clearly demonstrates that these eighty-four thousand meritorious qualities are all the retinue of bodhisattvas.
From the passage "As he passed through... onwards, it is shown that the majesty and virtue of this bodhisattva are vast and great;
as he lifts his feet and takes each step, heaven and earth are startled and shaken, and thus flowers rain down and music is played. From the passage "This bodhisattva... onwards, [he] emerges.
These are the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). "Eyes like the petals of a vast blue lotus" describes the form of his eyes.
"Even if one were to combine hundreds of thousands of millions of moons" describes the brilliant radiance of his eyes.

From "his face below," there is a general statement that he is adorned with the myriad virtues and fully endowed with all the marks. From "entering the seven [stations] below," it clarifies that Bodhisattvas all abide in the Dharma.

This is the seat of emptiness. "Seven below, seven below" refers to the practice of paying respect and inquiring after one's well-being. First, one inquires after the Tathāgata’s daily life; second, one inquires whether sentient beings are receiving transformation through the teachings;
third, one inquires whether Prabhūtaratna is listening to the Dharma. All of these pertain to both Buddhist affairs and human sentiments. [The afflictions are:
the four root afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, along with dullness; the two secondary afflictions of envy and stinginess; and the one sharp secondary affliction of wrong view.
"The five emotions" refers to the five consciousnesses. "The various demons" refers to the afflictions and the *skandha*-māra.

From "The World-Honored One" downward, [the text] describes seeking Śākyamuni Buddha as an intermediary to see Prabhūtaratna. From "The Buddha said" downward, he praises Gadgadasvara by stating his own purpose for coming;
this is what is meant by "the streams and mountains differ, yet the clouds and moon are the same."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what roots of goodness has this Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound planted, and what merits has he cultivated, such that he possesses these supernormal powers?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue, "In the past, there was a Buddha named Cloud Thunder Sound King, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. His land was named Manifestation."
In all worlds, during the eon named Priyadarśana, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound, for twelve thousand years,
made offerings to the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Voice King with one hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments and presented him with eighty-four thousand bowls made of the seven precious gems.
By virtue of these causes and conditions and their karmic retribution, he has now been born in the Buddha-land of the Buddha Śuddhāṃśusūryaprabhāsa, and possesses such supernormal powers.

Guṇarati, what do you think? At that time, at the place of the Buddha Meghasvararāja, was the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara—who offered music as an act of worship and presented precious vessels—anyone other than this present Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara? It was none other than him.
It is so, Flower Virtue. This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has already made offerings to and drawn near countless Buddhas, long planting the roots of merit.
Furthermore, he has encountered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Flower Virtue, you see only this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara’s body here; yet this Bodhisattva manifests various bodies everywhere for the sake of others.
To all sentient beings, while preaching this sutra, he may manifest in the body of Brahmā, or manifest in the body of Śakra, or manifest in the body of Īśvara,
or manifest in the body of Maheśvara, or manifest in the body of a celestial general, or manifest in the body of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King,
or manifest in the body of a universal monarch (cakravartin), or manifest in the bodies of various minor kings, or manifest...
He may manifest in the body of an elder; or manifest in the body of a lay householder; or manifest in the body of a government official; or manifest in the body of a brahmin;
or manifest in the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās; or manifest in the bodies of the wives of elders and householders;
or manifest in the bodies of the wives of government officials; or manifest in the bodies of the wives of brahmins; or manifest in the body of a youth.
He may appear as a boy with a female body, or manifest in the forms of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth, to preach this sūtra.
He is able to rescue all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and other places of great hardship; even within the royal harem, he transforms himself into a woman.
"Kusumashri, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara is able to rescue and protect all sentient beings in the Sahā world.
This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara manifests various such transformations of his body here in this Sahā land to preach this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings;
in his supernormal powers, transformations, and wisdom, he suffers no diminution whatsoever."
He diminishes it. By means of such wisdom, this bodhisattva illuminates the Sahā world, enabling all sentient beings to each attain what they need to know.
It is likewise so throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions.

If there are those who should be delivered by appearing in the form of a śrāvaka, he manifests in the form of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them; if there are those who should be delivered by appearing in the form of a pratyekabuddha...
To those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of a *pratyekabuddha*, he appears in the form of a *pratyekabuddha* and preaches the Dharma for them.

To those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of a bodhisattva, he appears in the form of a bodhisattva and preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be delivered by appearing in the form of a Buddha, he immediately appears in the form of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them.
In such various ways, he manifests forms according to what is appropriate for each being to be delivered, even unto [the manifestation of] cessation.
Having already attained liberation, he manifests the attainment of parinirvāṇa for those who are to be liberated.
Flower Virtue, such is the manner in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Wonderful Sound has accomplished the power of great supernormal knowledges and wisdom.
First, he requested that the Virtuous Root be questioned. The Buddha replied, "I shall now relate his past life story.
The Buddha’s name was King Cloud-Thunder-Sound; clouds provide shade for all things, and thunder stirs all beings.
The name of the land was Manifesting All Worlds, meaning that the three worlds all flow forth from this land. The eon was named Joyful to Behold, for all sentient beings...
Out of love and delight, the Medicine King burned his own body as an offering to the Sun-Moon Pure Radiance [Buddha] for twelve hundred years;
furthermore, he burned both his arms as an offering to the stūpa for seventy-two thousand years. This symbolizes the emptiness of the two attachments to self and dharmas;
therefore, the Bodhisattva is named "Joyful Vision," and the samādhi is named "Manifesting All Physical Bodies. Gadgadasvara, with a hundred thousand kinds of musical instruments and...
He offered eighty-four thousand bowls made of the seven precious substances as an offering to King Cloud-Thunder-Sound for twelve thousand years.
"Musical instruments" refers to articles of entertainment; "precious bowls" refers to vessels of appropriate measure. They also symbolize the emptiness of the two attachments to self and dharmas.
Because he has abandoned these two attachments, the Bodhisattva is named "Exquisite Sound," and his samādhi is likewise named "Manifesting the One."
It is the physical body of all [Buddhas]. Thus, that which is relinquished has never been the same, yet that which is attained has never been different.

By such causes, such fruits are evoked; this is what is meant by "different paths leading to the same destination. From the passage beginning with "Huade" (Huade), the distinction between the ancient and the present is clarified.
This is because he has served the Buddha for a long time and his cultivation of virtue is profound. "Flower Virtue" (Huade) refers to manifesting the bodies of the six classes of ordinary beings.

As for the statement that this Bodhisattva of Wondrous Sound can rescue and protect all sentient beings in the Sahā world, it means that although this Bodhisattva resides in the Land of Pure Light Adornment, he has in truth never departed from the Sahā world; he manifests various bodies and preaches the One [Vehicle].

The Dharma of marks causes all sentient beings to understand according to their respective types. "If he should respond to those of lower capacity," refers to manifesting the bodies of the four noble ones.
"Huade (Flower Virtue)," etc., concludes by revealing that the supernatural power of Wonderful Sound is vast and boundless in wisdom.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has deeply planted roots of goodness.
World-Honored One, in what samādhi does this Bodhisattva abide, such that he is able to manifest transformations everywhere in this manner to deliver and liberate sentient beings?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī: "Good son, that samādhi is named 'Manifesting All Physical Bodies' (Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana). It is wondrous.
The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara dwells within this samādhi and is thus able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.

When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached, eighty-four thousand people who had come together with the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara all attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
Furthermore, immeasurable bodhisattvas in this Sahā world also attained this samādhi.
...and dhāraṇīs. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara, having made offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha and the stūpa of Prabhūtaratna Buddha, returned to his own land.

As he passed through the various kingdoms, the earth shook in six ways, precious lotus flowers rained down, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various kinds of music were played. Having arrived in his own country, together with eighty-four thousand...
Surrounded by a thousand bodhisattvas, he went to the presence of the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I have arrived at the Sahā world to benefit sentient beings; I have seen Śākyamuni Buddha and the stupa of the Buddha Many-Jewels."
They paid homage and made offerings. Furthermore, they beheld the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, as well as the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja, Vīryadattabala, and Śūradatta.
They also caused these eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas to attain the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
While this "Chapter on the Coming and Going of the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being spoken, [the assembly attained these realizations].
Forty-two thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). The Bodhisattva Puṣpadatta attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

From "When he first asked the name of the samādhi... to "The Buddha told him... is the answer regarding the name of the samādhi. From "When he spoke this... onwards is the section on those of similar type attaining benefits.
Although eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas were in the same place as Gadgadasvara, it was only today that they have met him;

this is what is meant by "those who have attained realization travel together upon the path of nirvana. The phrase "in this Sahā world" further clarifies that the lineage of Gadgadasvara has been transmitted here in the Sahā world.
From the words "At that time," [the text describes] his return to his own land to pay homage to the Buddha and personally recount the benefits he had received.
This corresponds to the preceding text.
The twenty-fifth verse of the Universal Gate Chapter (Pumen pin) states:
His name is manifest everywhere and his body appears in every place; one does not know who is one's original kin.
Recognizing from the very beginning and recognizing anew, one ultimately seeks this person—the Avalokiteśvara.

"Avalokiteśvara" is the name of the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva who has perfectly realized and perfectly awakened. As for the term "World-Sound" (Śabdalo-ka), it refers to—either... [text fragment ends]
These are the sounds of the three periods of time, or the sounds of the three realms of existence.
Although these sounds have immeasurable and diverse distinctions, there is not one that is not the foremost, pure, and wondrous sound.

It is only because sentient beings do not understand them, but instead listen with their ears and follow along with the shifting of the sounds, that there appear to be various distinctions—namely, what are called the sounds of worldly people.
It is simply that his ears are not lacking in acuity; rather, it is that while his ears are acute, they are specifically "deaf" toward anything other than the sutras.

Now, this Bodhisattva, regardless of whether they are sages, ordinary beings, ghosts, or animals—whether sentient or insentient—does not hear various sounds with the ears, but hears them all with the eyes.
There is nothing that is not the pure, wondrous, and supreme sound. Therefore, he is called Guanyin (Avalokiteśvara). As an ancient master said:
If one attempts to hear with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to comprehend; only when hearing through the faculty of the eye does one truly know it to be so.

As for the "Universal Gate" (Pumen): because this Bodhisattva employs this single sound to respond to all living beings and extensively perform Buddha-work, there is no dust that does not manifest, no land that is not encompassed, no category of being that is not reached, and no gate that is not entered. This is what is called Great Compassion.
Compassion is their dwelling place. Although the names of Medicine King, Wondrous Sound, and Avalokiteśvara differ, the samādhis they have realized are equal and non-dual;
therefore, this chapter follows after the two preceding chapters.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him in this way:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara named 'Avalokiteśvara'? The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati:
"Good son, if there be immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings who undergo various..."

In their suffering and distress, if they hear of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly invoke his name, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva will immediately perceive their voices, and they shall all attain liberation.

If there are those who hold the name of this Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them; this is due to the majestic spiritual power of this Bodhisattva. If they are swept away by a great flood...
Distracted and drifting, they call upon his name and immediately find shallow water.

There may be hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, or millions of sentient beings who, seeking gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, pearls, and other such treasures, have entered the great ocean.
Suppose a black wind should blow their ship and cast them adrift into the land of the rākṣasa demons; if among them there should be even a single person...
Those who invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara—all such persons shall attain liberation from the perils of rākṣasas.

For this reason, he is named Avalokiteśvara. Furthermore, if there should be someone who is about to be harmed, and they invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords and staves held by their assailants will immediately break into pieces, and they shall attain liberation. If [there are] three thousand...
Even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with yakṣas and rākṣasas wishing to come and harass people, upon hearing someone invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
these evil spirits would not even dare to look at them with malevolent eyes, let alone inflict harm.
Furthermore, suppose there is a person—whether guilty or innocent—who has their body bound by cangues, shackles, stocks, or fetters;
if they invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, all these bonds shall be broken and destroyed, and they will immediately attain liberation.

Suppose, moreover, that the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with hostile bandits, and a merchant leader, leading a caravan of merchants and carrying precious treasures, was passing through a perilous region.
On the road, one among them raised his voice and proclaimed: "O virtuous sons, do not be afraid!
You should all with one mind invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. This Bodhisattva is able to bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings;
if you invoke his name, you shall be liberated from these enemies and bandits. When the merchants heard this, they...
They all cried out together: "Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva! By invoking his name, they immediately attained liberation.
Ajita, such is the majestic and sublime power of the Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
If there are sentient beings who are full of lustful desire, yet constantly mindfully recollect and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they shall immediately be freed from desire. If...
If one has much anger, by constantly recollecting and reverently honoring Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one will immediately be freed from anger.
If one has much ignorance, by constantly recollecting and reverently honoring Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one will immediately be freed from ignorance.
Akṣayamati, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva possesses such great majestic spiritual power and brings benefit to many. Therefore, sentient beings should always keep [him] in mind.
"Consider this, Ajita. If there is a woman who seeks to have a son, and she pays homage and makes offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, she shall give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom.

If she seeks to have a daughter, she shall give birth to a daughter of upright appearance and auspicious marks, one who has planted the roots of virtue in past lives and is beloved and respected by all. Ajita, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva possesses such power."
If sentient beings pay respectful homage to Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, their merit shall not be in vain. For this reason, all sentient beings should uphold the name of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

Anantamati, if there were someone who upheld the names of sixty-two billion Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and furthermore provided them with offerings of food, drink, clothing, and bedding for as long as they lived;
"Medicine. What do you think? Would the merit of these sons and daughters of good family be great? Ajita said, "It would be very great, World-Honored One.

The Buddha said, "If there were another person who, for even a single moment, received and upheld the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and paid him homage and made offerings, the merit of these two people would be exactly equal and no different. [In a hundred thousand...]
Even in ten billion kalpas, it could not be exhausted. O Akṣayamati, by upholding the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one obtains such immeasurable and boundless benefits of merit.
First, Ajita (Wujin) poses a question. This is because this Bodhisattva of Great Compassion has hands throughout his entire body and eyes throughout his entire body;
his compassion is inexhaustible and his benefit to others is infinite. Were it not for one who is himself without limit, he would be unable to pose such a question;

therefore, he employs the "Inexhaustible One" (Ajita) to inquire into its causes and conditions. From "The Buddha told him... onwards, [the text] first clarifies that [the Bodhisattva] is identical with all sentient beings.
Out of compassionate longing, one is able to attain liberation by single-mindedly invoking the Name. These two characters, "single-mindedly" (*yixin*), are the very root of escaping calamity;
they mean precisely to collect the mind into a single point. This is precisely the moment when Avalokiteśvara appears.
For since Avalokiteśvara is of the same essence as sentient beings, the body of Avalokiteśvara pervades the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the name of Avalokiteśvara pervades the faculty of hearing within all sentient beings;
yet, because they refuse to focus their minds with single-minded devotion, they follow after sounds and wander about, remaining separated from Avalokiteśvara by a distance of a thousand li.

If they would but invoke the name with single-minded devotion, then Avalokiteśvara would not depart from that very place, appearing at every moment. Even if there were hundreds of thousands of millions of...

If sentient beings suffering from afflictions focus their minds with single-minded devotion, they will simultaneously turn their hearing inward toward their own nature and personally behold Avalokiteśvara;
all their sufferings and anxieties shall likewise be liberated at that same moment. Yet, there are those who uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara but receive no response.
This is not because Avalokiteśvara lacks spiritual efficacy; rather, it is because those who uphold the name lack single-mindedness. If one is single-minded...
With the mind focused and the will directed—like a cat catching a mouse, or a hen brooding over her eggs—there is none who fails to obtain spiritual efficacy.
If there is a lower grade, the Bodhisattva manifests before one in water or fire; this occurs because that Bodhisattva has realized that the nature of fire is true emptiness.
The true fire is the emptiness of nature; the true water is the emptiness of nature; the true water is the emptiness of nature.

Because fire and water are of one and the same substance, they cannot burn or drown [the practitioner]. One must understand that the fire and water presently before us are all the sites where Avalokiteśvara manifests his body and preaches the Dharma.
As an ancient master said: "The flames of fire are where the Buddhas of the three periods turn the wheel of Dharma. Furthermore,

He said, "Do you still hear the sound of the Yanxi stream? Thus, when people encounter the perils of fire or water, if they single-mindedly call upon my name, the great fire will transform into a sea of lotus treasuries, and the vast waters will change into a ground of lapis lazuli jewels."

Regarding those who drift and fall into the realm of rākṣasa demons and immediately attain liberation: this is because when a bodhisattva manifests in the realm of demons, there is likewise an Avalokiteśvara within that very realm.
Therefore, if sentient beings who have drifted and fallen into the realm of demons single-mindedly invoke his name, they shall be saved.
Then Avalokiteśvara will appear before them in response to their thought. Not only will they themselves attain liberation, but even the rākṣasa will be transformed into Avalokiteśvara.
As for those who are about to be harmed and whose swords and staves are suddenly destroyed, it is because Avalokiteśvara is present within the executioner’s own mind;
yet, because the intent to kill has manifested, Avalokiteśvara does not appear. Even if one is at the moment of execution, if they focus the mind with single-mindedness—
If one focuses the mind and recites the name of Avalokiteśvara, the executioner is immediately transformed into a bodhisattva, and the swords and staves all become lotus flowers.
Not only is the body not severed, but there are those who "lay down their butcher’s blade and attain Buddhahood on the spot"—this is precisely the moment when Avalokiteśvara manifests before them.
That evil spirits cannot inflict harm is because the Bodhisattva pervades the hearts of those spirits. This is...
Within the minds of ghosts there are also Bodhisattvas; however, because the ghostly mind is so intense, the Bodhisattva becomes hidden, and thus the ghost seeks to come and harass people.
If they hear someone once invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara, then the Avalokiteśvara within the ghost’s mind also leaps forth, and the ghostly mind immediately subsides.
The ghost becomes peaceful and dares not even look at them, much less inflict harm. [This applies even to those bound by] shackles and fetters.
Regarding "severing and destroying": because the Bodhisattva is without fetters and without shackles, by single-mindedly invoking his name, all chains and locks are completely cast off.
Regarding "liberation from enemies and thieves": within the mind of the bandit of wrong views, there is also Avalokiteśvara.

Those with much lust, much anger, and much delusion can also attain liberation. This precisely means that within the minds of those possessed of the three poisons, this is also where Avalokiteśvara manifests his body and preaches the Dharma.

Even for those who possess much lust, much anger, and much delusion, if they are willing to focus their minds single-mindedly on Avalokiteśvara, then the three poisons will be transformed into the three virtues. Those who seek a son shall obtain a son.

Regarding those who seek a daughter and obtain a daughter: because the physical forms and characteristics of male and female differ, while those of Avalokiteśvara remain the same, he does not oppose the inclinations of people's hearts;

thus, whatever they seek, nothing fails to accord with their wishes. Is this not what is meant by the *I Ching* statement that "the Way of Qian results in the male, and the Way of Kun results in the female"?
To invoke one name and offer worship to one form, yet receive the benefits of upholding and making offerings to all—this is precisely what is meant.

The merits of sixty-two billion Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are no different from his, because these Bodhisattvas have attained true perfect penetration, whereby the one is all and all is one.
Should anyone be unable to receive and uphold the entire scripture, [they may instead recite this].
If one is unable to uphold even a single chapter, one should uphold a single verse;
if one is unable to uphold a single verse, one should uphold even a single name. Even this shall yield the benefit of immeasurable merit.
For example, when a lion seizes an elephant or a rabbit, it employs its full strength in both cases. Thus, every verse and every phrase is none other than the sublime essence. As it is said:
This is indeed the name of Avalokiteśvara; it truly encompasses the entire Great Sūtra. How could its merit be considered small?
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara traverse this Sahā world?
How does he preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings? What are the matters concerning his power of skillful means? The Buddha—

He addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati: "Good son, if there are sentient beings in any land who should be delivered by means of a Buddha’s body, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately manifests in the form of a Buddha and preaches the Dharma for them.

If there are those who should be delivered by means of a Pratyekabuddha’s body, he immediately manifests in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and preaches the Dharma for them. If there are those who should be delivered by means of a Śrāvaka’s body..."
For those to be delivered by means of the body of a śrāvaka, he manifests the body of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them.
For those to be delivered by means of the body of a Brahmā king, he manifests the body of a Brahmā king and preaches the Dharma for them.

For those to be delivered by means of the body of Śakra, he manifests the body of Śakra and preaches the Dharma for them. For those to be delivered by means of the body of Maheśvara, he manifests the body of Maheśvara.
And he preaches the Dharma for them. To those who are to be liberated through the body of Maheśvara, he manifests the body of Maheśvara and preaches the Dharma.
To those who are to be liberated through the body of a Heavenly Great General, he manifests the body of a Heavenly Great General and preaches the Dharma.
To those who are to be liberated through the body of Vaiśravaṇa, he manifests the body of Vaiśravaṇa.
He preaches the Dharma by manifesting in various forms. To those who should be saved by the body of a minor king, he manifests as a minor king and preaches the Dharma.
To those who should be saved by the body of an elder, he manifests as an elder and preaches the Dharma.
To those who should be saved by the body of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*), he manifests as a lay devotee and preaches the Dharma. To those who should be saved by the body of a high official...
To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a civil official, he manifests the body of a civil official and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by means of the body of a Brahmin, he manifests the body of a Brahmin and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by means of the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, he manifests the bodies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

He preaches the Dharma appearing in the body of a Vaiśya. To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the body of a householder, a lay devotee, a government official, or a Brāhmaṇa woman, he manifests in the body of a woman and preaches the Dharma.

To those who are to be liberated by appearing in the body of a boy or a girl, he manifests in the body of a boy or a girl and preaches the Dharma. To those who are to be liberated by [appearing as] devas, nāgas, or yakṣas...
To those who are to be saved through the forms of gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, he manifests all these forms and preaches the Dharma for them.
To those who are to be saved by the form of Vajrapāṇi, he manifests as Vajrapāṇi and preaches the Dharma for them. Anantamati, this is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Having accomplished such merits, he travels through various lands in manifold forms to deliver sentient beings.
Therefore, you all should single-mindedly make offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow fearlessness amidst terrors and urgent calamities; for this reason, in this Sahā world—
All address him as the "Bestower of Fearlessness.
How does he wander here? When asked what kind of body he manifests—is it that of a deva, a human, or a śrāvaka?
"Is he a Pratyekabuddha? Is he a Bodhisattva? [The questioner asks: "What kind of Dharma does this teacher of the Dharma preach?

These are the thirty-two types of response bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). If bodhisattvas enter *samādhi* and advance in the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*), their resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) becoming fully manifest, they then manifest as Buddha-bodies and preach the Buddha-wisdom for them.

If those still in training (*śaikṣa*) possess tranquil, wondrous clarity and their superior nature becomes fully manifest, they then manifest as *pratyekabuddhas* and preach the Dharma of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) for them. If those still in training attain the four...

Realizing emptiness, they enter cessation through the cultivation of the path; their resolute understanding becomes fully manifest, and they immediately appear as śrāvakas, preaching the Dharma of the Four Truths.
This refers to manifesting the bodies of the three vehicles and preaching the teachings of the three vehicles.

With a mind of desire clearly awakened, they do not transgress against the dust of desire and become lords of the great trichiliocosm, known as Brahmā Kings, presiding over the various heavens. As lords of those dwelling on earth, they are known as Śakra.

Wandering through the ten directions, unhindered wherever he goes, he is named Īśvara (The Sovereign). Flying through the void without expending mental or physical effort, he is named Maheśvara (The Great Sovereign).
Lovingly governing the spirits and deities, rescuing and securing the lands, sweeping away the camps of Māra, and providing shelter for all living beings, he is named Mahāsena (The Great General).
Lovingly governing the world and protecting sentient beings, he prevents spirits and deities from [causing harm].
One who invades and disturbs is called Vaiśravaṇa; this manifests as the body of a celestial lord and a divine general.

One who acts as a ruler over ten thousand people and serves as the sovereign of a single state is called a minor king (*kṣudrarāja*), characterized by broad benevolence and profound virtue. One who is esteemed by the world for their integrity is called an elder (*śreṣṭhin*).

One who conducts themselves with propriety within the household and maintains purity through self-restraint is called a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*). One who upholds justice, adheres to the law, and discerns [right from wrong]... [text truncated]
Those who govern states and districts are called officials (*kṣatriya*). Those who cultivate pure conduct with diligence and maintain themselves through self-restraint are called *brāhmaṇas*.

Those who strictly uphold the prohibitions and do not violate the five categories of offenses are called *bhikṣus*. Those whose five hundred rules of discipline are as bright as ice and snow are called *bhikṣuṇīs*.
Those who firmly maintain the five precepts are called *upāsakas* and *upāsikās*. Those who diligently practice the way of a wife...
Those who serve their parents-in-law are called "women. Those who have not damaged their male organs and do not contemplate marriage are called "boys" and "girls.
The aforementioned are those manifesting in the bodies of sovereigns, ministers, and subjects. From the devas and nāgas downward, there are those manifesting in the bodies of various species.
Only those of the highest rank can perform the tasks of the lowest; thus, the Vajrapāṇi deity is the same as the bare-shouldered deity who serves [the Buddha].
Regarding Śakra: if one follows the sequential order, he should be placed below Vaiśravaṇa and below Ananta.
This concludes the response to the questions. As for your question, "By what means does he act? the answer now is: "He accomplishes such merits. As for your question, "How does he travel here?
How does he preach the Dharma? the answer now is: "By means of various bodies, he travels through all lands."

On this land, he preaches various dharmas to deliver and liberate all sentient beings. His manifestation of bodies according to their types and his preaching of the Dharma according to their capacities are entirely identical to those of Bhaiṣajyarāja and Gadgadasvara—sharing the same nostril.
This perfect awakening and perfect realization are attained through the power of upholding the sutra in past lives; you all should single-mindedly make offerings to him.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati asked in verse:
"World-Honored One, endowed with wondrous marks, I now ask you again: For what cause and condition, O Son of the Buddha, is he named Avalokiteśvara?"
The Honored One, endowed with wondrous marks, answered the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati in verse: "Listen to the practices of Avalokiteśvara, who skillfully responds to all places.
His great vows are as deep as the ocean; throughout inconceivable kalpas, he has attended upon many thousands of billions of Buddhas and made vast, pure aspirations."
I shall briefly explain this for you: hearing the name, seeing the form, or keeping them in mind—none of these will pass in vain. They can extinguish all the sufferings of existence.
Even if one should harbor malicious intent and push another into a great pit of fire, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, that fiery pit will transform into a pool.
Or if drifting upon the vast ocean, beset by the perils of dragons, fish, and various spirits, by the power of that Avalokiteśvara, the waves cannot submerge them.
Or if atop the peak of Mount Sumeru, pushed down by others, by the power of that Avalokiteśvara, they remain in the sky like the sun.
Or if pursued by evil men, one falls upon Mount Vajra; yet by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, not even a single hair can be harmed.

Or if encountered by vengeful bandits surrounding one, each brandishing a blade to inflict injury; yet by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they all immediately give rise to a heart of compassion.
Or if one encounters the suffering of royal punishment, facing execution as life draws to a close, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the blade shall immediately shatter into pieces.
Or if one is imprisoned in shackles and fetters, with hands and feet bound by cangues and manacles, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one shall find release and attain liberation.
Regarding curses, various poisons, and those who wish to harm one’s body—if one calls to mind the power of Avalokiteśvara, these shall return to the person who originated them.
Should one encounter evil rākṣasas, venomous dragons, various ghosts, and the like—if one calls to mind the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will at that time not dare to cause harm.
If one is surrounded by fierce beasts with fearsome, sharp teeth and claws, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will flee swiftly in all directions.

If there are vipers, pythons, scorpions, and the like, whose poisonous breath blazes like smoke and fire, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will turn back upon hearing the sound [of his name].
When clouds and thunder roll, lightning flashes, and hail falls with torrential rain, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall be dispersed and vanish in that very moment.
When sentient beings are beset by calamity and their bodies are oppressed by immeasurable suffering, the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can rescue them from the world’s pains.

Fully endowed with the power of spiritual penetrations, he extensively cultivates wisdom and skillful means; throughout the lands of the ten directions, there is no realm where he does not manifest his body.
In all the various evil destinies—the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals—he causes the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death to be gradually and completely extinguished.

The contemplation of reality, the contemplation of purity, the contemplation of vast wisdom, the contemplation of compassion, and the contemplation of loving-kindness—I constantly aspire to and gaze upon them.
With stainless, pure radiance, the sun of wisdom shatters all darkness; it can subdue the winds and fires of calamity, shining universally upon the world.
The thunderous roar of the precepts, whose essence is compassion; the wondrous great cloud of a benevolent mind: it pours down the nectar rain of the Dharma, extinguishing the flames of affliction.
In places of legal disputes before government officials, or amidst the terrors of battle arrays—by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, all enemies shall retreat and disperse.
The wondrous voice, the Avalokiteśvara voice, the Brahma voice, the ocean-tide voice—surpassing all voices in the world. Therefore, one should always keep him in mind;
at every thought, do not give rise to doubt. The pure and holy Avalokiteśvara can act as a refuge in the face of suffering, affliction, and the peril of death.
"Endowed with all merits, gazing upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion, an ocean of immeasurable masses of merit—therefore, you should pay homage.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharaṇīdhara rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings..."
When one hears this chapter on the Sovereign Acts of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the supernatural powers manifested through the Universal Gate,
it should be known that such a person’s merit is not small. When the Buddha preached this Chapter on the Universal Gate,
eighty-four thousand beings within the assembly all gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, peerless, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The first verse reiterates the question regarding how the Bodhisattva attains his name. The section beginning with "Endowed with" provides the initial general answer.
Regarding the phrase "skillfully responding to all directions," it means that his emanated bodies are infinite; his vows are vast and profound, fundamentally inconceivable and beyond deliberation.
I shall briefly outline the essentials for you. There are some who, upon hearing his name, focus their minds single-mindedly.
As for "mindfulness": there are those who, upon seeing his form, focus their minds and fix their thoughts upon him;
none of these efforts go in vain, as they are all capable of extinguishing the suffering of the three realms of existence. "Even if," and so forth, refers to the fourteen fearlessnesses.

Because the dharmic characteristics of a bodhisattva are entirely empty, his mind is devoid of fire and water. Therefore, if one fixes their mindfulness on Avalokiteśvara, even if they were pushed into a pit of fire, that very pit of fire—
It is originally a jeweled pond and cannot be burned. Even if it were to drift into the great ocean, the great ocean itself would be like a jeweled ground and it could not be submerged.
Or, if it were below, it is because the Bodhisattva pervades both the heavens and the hells.

Neither heaven can retain them, nor can hell contain them. Therefore, for one who focuses their mind with single-minded devotion, even if their heavenly retribution has already ended and the five signs of decay appear, they will certainly not fall. Thus it is said:
"Even if one were atop Mount Sumeru and pushed down by humans, one would be like the sun dwelling in the sky. Should one nonetheless fall, one will be driven by the ox-headed jailers into...
The mountains of blades and the trees of swords, the glowing embers and the boiling cauldrons, cannot possibly destroy it. Therefore it is said:
"Though pursued by evil men and falling upon the Diamond [Mount], not even a single hair can be harmed.
This is because Mount Sumeru is the capital of Śakra, and the Diamond [Mount] is the abode of the Kumbhāṇḍas. Thus, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "Furthermore, within the trichiliocosm..."
The Great Vajra Mountains encircle the waters of the great ocean. Beyond these Vajra Mountains, there is a second set of Great Vajra Mountains.
Between these two mountains, it is profoundly dark and obscure; therein lie the eight great hells, which cannot be illuminated by the majestic radiance of the sun and moon.
Or, should one fall into them, it is because that Bodhisattva regards enemies and kin with equality, possessing a heart of compassion without [distinction].

[The suffering] is exhausted. Therefore, for one who focuses their mindfulness [on such a person], even if a vengeful enemy inflicts harm, it causes that person’s malice to dissolve, and instead gives rise to thoughts of loving-kindness.
Or, as it says below: "Because that bodhisattva themselves has no intent to kill, even while manifesting as a butcher. Thus, for one who focuses their mindfulness [on them]:
They stretch their necks toward execution, with no place to lay their blades. Or they are imprisoned below;

because the Bodhisattva has already eliminated self-love and purified attachment to dharmas, he is neither constrained nor bound. Thus, for those who fixate their thoughts [on the self], there are immediately shackles, fetters, and manacles.
One cannot be imprisoned; one will naturally attain release. Regarding "curses and incantations" (*zhòuzǔ*):

because that Bodhisattva constantly cures the diseases of body and mind with the medicine of the Dharma and protects and rescues sentient beings through the power of mantras, those who harbor malicious intent—even if they possess curses, incantations, or toxic drugs intending to harm the person—find no place for them to take effect. Thus, [the harm] returns to the original person themselves. Or...

Regarding "meeting [them] below": because the poisonous malice of those bodhisattvas has been extinguished and their demonic intent eradicated, they manifest within the forms of poisonous dragons and evil spirits;
therefore, even when one directs one's attention toward them, these poisonous dragons and evil spirits do not even dare to look, let alone inflict harm.
Regarding "suffering and evil below": because those bodhisattvas have utterly eliminated the predatory instincts of beasts, they manifest themselves in the bodies of animals; therefore...
As for "focusing the mind": it causes those [demons] who see one's shadow to vanish their tracks, and those who follow the sound to turn back;
thus, even if they possess claws and fangs, they are unable to seize and bite, and even if they possess poisonous breath, they are unable to sting or inflict harm.

When the clouds and thunder descend, because the Bodhisattva’s awakened mind remains unmoving, the terrors depart from afar. Therefore, when one focuses the mind, even if encountering fierce winds, rain, and thunder, they shall arrive at the appointed time.
They will dissipate; one can never be deluded. "When sentient beings" and below summarizes the fourteen fearlessnesses.

It says that when sentient beings are beset by calamities and their bodies are oppressed by manifold sufferings, if they are willing to focus their minds with single-minded devotion, the Bodhisattva will, by the power of his subtle and wondrous wisdom, deliver them from all such suffering and distress. This completes two sets of four lines, totaling thirty verses.

Second, the response: Because those bodhisattvas are fully endowed with the immeasurable supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata and have extensively cultivated the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, they are able to manifest their bodies and preach the Dharma in every single land within the lands of Śākyamuni’s emanations.
Thus, they cause the various sufferings of birth and death within the six destinies and the three miserable realms to gradually diminish and eventually lead [beings] to enter [the path].

Therefore, the single name "Avalokiteśvara" is sufficient to encompass the purport of this entire Mahāyāna sūtra. From the section "True Contemplation" (*zhēnguān*) downward, five contemplations are unified under the theme of a single chapter:
one contemplates the faculties of the *śrāvaka* through True Contemplation; one contemplates the faculties of the *pratyekabuddha* through Pure Contemplation;
one contemplates the faculties of the *bodhisattva* through the Contemplation of Vast Wisdom; and through Compassionate Contemplation, one unites with all sentient beings.
One contemplates the superior beings with loving-kindness, identifying them as equal to all Buddhas.

Because the Bodhisattva possesses these five contemplations and observes these five faculties at every moment without ever departing from them, one should constantly aspire to behold them and never for a single instant give rise to indolence or negligence.
"Stainless" (wúgòu) and below clarify the meaning of the five contemplations (*pañca-vipaśyanā*). Because there is true contemplation, one attains stainless light;
because there is pure contemplation, one attains pure light; because there is wisdom contemplation, one attains the sun of wisdom.
By possessing these three kinds of radiance, one is able to destroy the three kinds of darkness and subdue the three calamities of the world. And...
It is able to universally illumine the three worlds. The two phrases concerning the essence of compassion clarify the two contemplations of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Taking the contemplation of loving-kindness as its essence, it awakens all sentient beings, just as the thunder of the precepts moves all things.
Taking the contemplation of loving-kindness as its essence, it provides shelter for all sentient beings, just as a great cloud universally covers everything. From these two...

Contemplation is like thunder and clouds; thus, it can bring down the Dharma rain of equal, single-flavored nectar, causing all sentient beings to receive its moisture, each extinguishing their afflictions and each realizing the fruits of the Path. Regarding "disputes and litigation" below:

because that Bodhisattva is utterly devoid of a combative mind, those who direct their attention toward him will find that even if they have enemies, all shall retreat and disperse. This is the first.

Verse: This should follow under the section "Attaining Liberation through Relinquishment. It is because the Bodhisattva uses these five contemplations to observe these five faculties that he is then able to preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.

Preaching the Dharma for those with the faculties of *śrāvakas* is called "Wondrous Sound" (*Ghoṣa*), because he desires to cause all *śrāvakas* to attain the subtle, wondrous, secret, and perfect sound.
Preaching the Dharma for those with the faculties of *pratyekabuddhas* is called "Observing the Sounds of the World" (*Avalokitasvara*).

In order to cause those seeking Pratyekabuddhahood to investigate and examine the causes and conditions of the three periods of time, he preaches the Dharma for them according to their faculties; this is called the Brahma-voice.

In order to cause Bodhisattvas to fulfill the pure and white Brahma-conduct, by means of the aforementioned thirty-two manifestations that accord with the Tathāgata’s entry into various lands, it is called the Tide-like Voice, because its responses do not miss the proper time. By the latter [the Tide-like Voice], it accords with the multitude...
He gives rise to fourteen kinds of fearless merits, named "Victorious Over the Sounds of the World," because he transcends all sounds of the world.
By means of a single contemplation, the Bodhisattva divides it into five contemplations; by means of a single voice, he divides it into five voices.
Thus, he manifests his body like clouds and preaches the Dharma like rain, causing both the great and the small to receive its grace, including humans and devas.
This is indeed profitable. Therefore, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the practitioner should maintain a constant mental record without forgetting.
From moment to moment, they should always keep it in mind; within every thought, they must also maintain firm faith and not allow doubt to arise. Why is this?
Because this Bodhisattva dwells within the defiled minds of sentient beings yet remains unstained; thus, they are called a "Pure Sage. Consequently, they are able to...
Entering into the suffering and afflictions of birth and death, he is able to serve as a refuge and a protector for sentient beings who undergo the suffering and afflictions of birth and death.
Therefore, know that the Bodhisattva’s virtues are without exception complete, his compassion is without exception impartial, and his blessings are without exception possessed.

For this reason, you all should at all times prostrate yourselves before him; do not forget this. [The passage] from "At that time" onwards is the praise of virtues by Dharanimdhara, hence it is called "Dharanimdhara."

This is because of maintaining the level ground of the mind. By maintaining the level ground of the mind, one is able to be impartial in compassion, impartial in manifesting the body, and impartial in teaching the Dharma.
As for the activity of mastery, it refers to the thirty-two manifestations of the Bodhisattva.
The fourteen fearlessnesses are all in accord with and responsive to beings; they manifest spontaneously and without ever being bound or attached.
Thus, he sports with sovereign ease and is able to manifest his body and preach the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings. This is why this Bodhisattva is also named Avalokiteśvara.
From the words "The Buddha said" onwards, the great assembly attains benefit.
The twenty-sixth verse of the Dhāraṇī Chapter says:
"The Long River and the Celestial Moat cannot serve as boundaries; Iron ramparts and golden cities are difficult to maintain."
"What is this 'Nili-dohi'?"—a *dhāraṇī* in Sanskrit, which here means "total retention" (*saṃgraha*).
Because it can protect what is wholesome and obstruct what is evil, the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth held the sutra.
The Tathāgata’s entrustment and his affairs were thus completed; yet, fearing that the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth might [forget it] after a long time...

Dwelling in the lower realms, he constantly abides in secluded places. Having first entered the mundane world to benefit sentient beings and engage with all things, he finds it difficult to endure and bear;
therefore, he once again brings forth, one by one, the Dharma-gates realized by the great Bodhisattvas of this realm and other directions.
The patience of Bhaiṣajyarāja, the emptiness of the Dharma of Gadgadasvara, and the compassion of Avalokiteśvara—these are the qualities that Bodhisattvas must constantly emulate.
If one possesses patience but does not realize the emptiness of phenomena, the scope of the mind will not be vast.
If one realizes the emptiness of phenomena but does not practice compassion, the work of transformation and teaching will not be extensive. One must necessarily enter into these three aspects.
Only through this Dharma-gate can this sutra be circulated without interruption. The ritual procedures for upholding the scripture have now reached their ultimate point.
Nevertheless, this chapter exists because there is genuine concern that in the final age, false teachers will flourish and demonic deeds will be numerous;

since those with a beginner's resolve who uphold the sutra may lack firm power of faith, the various Bodhisattvas have spoken these mantras to provide protection and support, so that their spiritual powers may secretly bestow grace.
He shall not allow them to be violated or destroyed; this further demonstrates that the Bodhisattva’s compassion is inexhaustible.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if there are good men or good women who are able to receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, if..."
"If one recites and masters [this sutra], or writes out its scrolls, how much merit will they obtain? The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja:
"If there were good sons or good daughters who made offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in eight hundred million nayutas of Ganges Rivers..."
"What do you think? Is the merit obtained thereby not great? "It is very great, World-Honored One.

The Buddha said, "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family can, regarding this sutra, even receive and uphold a single four-line verse, read and recite it, explain its meaning, and practice according to the teaching, their merit will be exceedingly great. At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One..."
"Venerable One, I shall now bestow upon the speaker of the Dharma a dhāraṇī-mantra to protect them.
Thus he spoke the mantra: Aṇe | Maṇe | Mame | Mamame | Ciḷe | Carite | Sāme | Sāvitave |"
Śāṇḍe | Mukhe | Mukhale | Sale | Ave-sale | Saṃsale | Sale-caye | Acaye | Aghane | Śāṇḍe | Śale | Dhāraṇi | Alukapase | Pañjavi-khaṇi | Niviti | Abhinte | Laneti-viti | Abhinte-parisude | Oṃ.
Kauṣṭhila. Maukṣṭhila. Araḍa. Śukra. Asamasame. Buddhapraticchade. Dharmapratichade. Saṃghanirghoṣaṇi. Vāśa vāśa śodhi. Maṇḍala maṇḍala. Kṣayata. Yauluṭa yauluṭa. Kiao.
Śalaka (pronounced with the *l* as in "law"), Akṣaye akṣayate, aparū, amaraṇe, nāta ya bhagavan.
This dhāraṇī mantra has been spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers.
"If anyone should violate or destroy this Dharma-preacher, they would thereby violate and destroy these Buddhas.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Bhaiṣajyarāja!
Because you have compassionately protected this Dharma-preacher, you have spoken this dhāraṇī, which will bring great benefit to all sentient beings."
Regarding those who read and recite until they have mastered the text, it is said that they cannot maintain it for a long duration;

yet, the merit of such a person who has mastered the text through reading and recitation is equal to that of making offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in eight hundred million *koṭis* of Ganges Rivers.

Furthermore, this does not stop at merely erecting stupas to make offerings to the Buddhas or extensively constructing monasteries to support the Sangha. From the words "At that time" onwards, the text explains the dhāraṇī for protective maintenance.

"Mantra" (zhòu) refers to esoteric speech. Since the Medicine King has already manifested his support through supernatural power and further bestowed his secret empowerment through divine mantras, we know that he who sacrificed his body for the sake of the Dharma is the Medicine King;
likewise, he who speaks the mantra to protect people is also the Medicine King.
If there were no Medicine King who would sacrifice his own life for the sake of the Dharma, then the medicine of the Dharma would not endure.

If there were no Medicine King who would exert all his strength for the sake of sentient beings, then the root of illness would not be removed. Thus we know that both the pursuit of the Dharma and the service of sentient beings rely entirely upon the power of the Medicine King.
From the words "The World-Honored One" onwards, the merits of the mantra are revealed; it is stated that this mantra was spoken by all Buddhas. If there is a practitioner...

The Master says: To those who preach this sutra and uphold this mantra—those who have been dispatched by the Tathāgata to perform the work of the Tathāgata—to insult, assail, or slander them is no different from slandering all the Buddhas.

For there is a principle of extending respect for a master to his messengers, and of loving a person to include their cherished trees; thus, to insult or destroy a Dharma Master is equivalent to insulting and destroying the Buddha himself.
"O Buddhas! At that time, Śakra descended and spoke words of praise, saying:

'Since you, in this evil age, have not begrudged your own body or life to protect and uphold this sutra, and furthermore out of compassion for the Dharma-preachers who hold it, you have spoken this mantra to provide secret empowerment, so that those various māras dare not invade, oppress, or slander them—how would they dare to strike them with clubs, wood, tiles, or stones? This medicine..."
This is why the king is able to suppress all illnesses.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Śūradatta addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I too shall proclaim a dhāraṇī for the protection of those who read, recite, receive, and uphold the Lotus Sūtra. If this Dharma-master obtains this dhāraṇī, whether it be a yakṣa..."

Whether they be rākṣasas, pūtanas, kiṃkaras, kumbhāṇḍas, or pretas, none shall be able to find an opportunity to exploit his weaknesses while seeking them out; and so, before the Buddha, he spoke this incantation:
Coe (pronounced with a level tone), Mahācoe, Ukki, Mukki, Ale, Rāpade, Nalede, Naledavade, Icchini, Vecchini, Jicchini, Naledhini, Naledhipade. World-Honored One,
this dhāraṇī mantra has been spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, all of whom likewise rejoice in it.
If anyone should violate or disparage this Dharma teacher, they would thereby violate and disparage all these Buddhas.
As for the statement that "Vīradatta and others also recite mantras with the support of the dark deities," it means that one person chants while the multitude joins in. Yakṣa.
"Kṣipra-rākṣasa" is translated here as "the swift demon. "Rākṣasa" is translated here as "the spirit that devours vital essence. These are also all those who rejoice.
To say that this mantra was spoken by all the Buddhas means that the Buddhas themselves also accord with this mantra and give rise to joy.
At that time, Vaiśravaṇa, the World-Protecting Heavenly King, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings and in order to protect this Dharma-preacher, I shall also speak this dhāraṇī. He then spoke the mantra, saying:
A-li. Na-li. Lou-na-li. A-na-lu. Na-li. Ku-na-li.
World-Honored One, by means of this divine mantra, may you protect the Dharma-preacher; I, too, shall personally protect those who uphold this sutra.
Within a range of one hundred *yojanas*, may there be no afflictions or calamities.
At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was present in this assembly, surrounded by a respectful retinue of thousands of millions of *nayutas* of gandharvas.
He approached the Buddha, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I too, by means of the *dhāraṇī*..."
The *dhāraṇī* mantra for the protection of those who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It is spoken as follows: Agaṇe | Gaṇe | Kauri | Gandhāri | Caṇḍāli | Mātangi | Śaṅkule | Pūrṇaśani | Āṭi ||
World-Honored One, this dhāraṇī mantra has been spoken by forty-two billion Buddhas.
Should anyone injure or destroy this Dharma-preacher, they would thereby have injured and destroyed these Buddhas.
Vaiśravaṇa is the Heavenly King of the North, known as Dhṛtarāṣṭra (King of Abundant Hearing). Dhṛtarāṣṭra is the Heavenly King of the East.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "One who holds the mantra and mudrā in mind gazes with heroic vigor;

therefore, in this evil age, those whose power in upholding the Way through the sūtras is not yet sufficient must rely on the secret assistance of divine mantras to subdue demons and adversaries, thereby attaining freedom from fear. This deity...
This is why the incantation cannot be dispensed with.
